No matter what happens in our life, we constantly remind ourselves that this is God’s plan, and He is greatest.” Holding a door open for someone is among the examples Mostafa gives when explaining his understanding of jihad. “Any act of service, any sacrifice, whether it’s small or big, is jihad.” Those words are part of the steadfast identity he carries into each audition. A role that reinforces their association with violence has consequences for him beyond the time he would spend playing it. He has to trust that there will be another opportunity after the one he declines. “When you walk with your value system intact, you might be saying no to those things. But I have this faith in God that other things will come that are much bigger.” Waiting for the right part leaves much of that future in other people’s hands. With support from Abu Dhabi’s Creative Media Authority, Mostafa established MFM at Yas Creative Hub, putting his business experience to work in film. “I can’t just be an actor with an agent in London waiting for auditions,” he says. “I have to create my movies. I need to collaborate.” The work he had been dividing his time between could now support his ambitions in film. Mostafa had arranged sponsorships for fighters and concerts; he could bring brands into productions and draw on his finance background in discussions with investors. The difficulties he had faced in finding representation gave him a reason to help other Emirati performers approach the industry. Mostafa takes a sip of coffee, holds it up, and suggests it might be one of the best he has had. “Just a little product placement,” he jokes. Behind the brand partnerships, however, is a struggle familiar to the filmmakers who approach MFM. “The biggest problem I’m seeing is funding,” Mostafa says. He is working to explain the film business to investors who are more familiar with property and technology, taking them through production costs, distribution and incentives. He expects it to take years. When City of Life had its premiere at DIFF in 2009, Mostafa watched the industry gather around his brother’s debut feature. When the festival returns, he will have a company to bring into those conversations, as well as his own ambitions as an actor. Finding the money for a film could give several performers their next job, and the time on set they need to improve. He saw how quickly that possibility could take hold on Dune . Fellow Emirati Rashed Dawood, a mixed martial arts fighter, was working on his first film as a stunt performer. Dawood discovered how much he enjoyed being on set and wanted to do it again. For him to develop that interest into a career, there would have to be another production, and another after that. “We’re not going to have a Dune come every year. We need to work on and scale up independent filmmaking,” Mostafa says. Mostafa needs the next production, too. He wants another chance to get as deeply into a character as he did in Khattaf . He is working to help get those films made, while pursuing the roles he believes he can carry. “I’m confident enough to know I can be in a blockbuster film as one of the main cast,” he says. “I just need to keep pushing, but I know I can do it.” The fearlessness that put him in front of Ali’s camera has stayed with him. Now Mostafa wants to take it into a role where audiences around the world will see an Emirati actor leading the story. He is ready for the scrutiny that will come with it, and for the work it will demand of him. “I would never be given that opportunity and not know the responsibility I’ll carry being there,” he says. “And also the responsibility I’d need to have to make sure I perform at the highest level because of what I represent.” Fashion Director: Sarah Maisey Photographer: Chris Whiteoak Shot on location at Jumeirah Beach Hotel and Mohamed's family home in Dubai

title: Alex Eala has 'put the Philippines on world tennis map'
description: Filipina star decided to represent country at Asian Games despite risk of hefty fine from WTA
content: The Philippine tennis body has lauded young sensation Alex Eala for raising the profile of tennis in the country, highlighting her decision to represent her nation at the 2026 Asian Games despite the risk of penalty. Eala had risked a hefty fine for skipping WTA's mandatory China Open as she represented the Philippines at the Japan Asian Games. While she lost her semi-final in Nagoya to Wang Xiyu, her actions did not go unnoticed. Eala has since suffered early exits in Singapore and Wuhan. But for the Philippine Tennis Association (PHILTA), she has already done a lot. “Alex Eala has already achieved what many once thought impossible. She has single-handedly put the Philippines on the world tennis map,” PHILTA secretary general John Rey Tiangco said. “Her rise to world No 18, her WTA title, and her victories over some of the world's best players are milestones that have changed the landscape of Philippine tennis.” Tiangco said Eala's decision to play for her country, even as other athletes decided to feature in China, was praiseworthy. “We are equally grateful for her decision to represent our country at the Asian Games, putting the Philippine flag ahead of other opportunities. “At this level of competition, victories and defeats are part of the journey. What matters is Alex's determination to keep improving, her discipline, and her commitment to the sport. “Alex has already won something bigger than any single tournament. She has inspired a nation and opened doors for the next generation of Filipino tennis players.” Meanwhile, Indonesia's Janice Tjen saw her Wuhan Open campaign come to an end in China on Thursday. American Ann Li, who upset the top seed Aryna Sabalenka in the second round, moved into the quarter-finals with a 6-1, 7-6 (1) victory over Tjen. Li will take on seventh seed Iga Swiatek of Poland in the last eight. Swiatek had on Thursday completed the 150th WTA 1000 win of ⁠her career.

title: Three children and one teacher killed in Oregon school shooting
description: Teenage attacker entered building by shooting through locked doors, police say
content: Four people, including three children, have been killed in a shooting at a primary school in the US state of Oregon. The attack in the city of Bend was carried out by a 16-year-old boy, police said. An armed bystander pursued the assailant into the school and shot him dead, officials added. The children killed were aged five, eight and 11. A teacher was also killed. Another teacher and a ​seven-year-old pupil were taken to hospital with critical injuries, Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz said at a media conference. The attacker entered the school by shooting through locked doors, police said, without ​offering ⁠any further details. Oregon Governor Tina Kotek hailed the armed bystander who "heroically intervened to stop further loss of life" at Silver Rail Elementary School. "No parent should have to have this kind of day, and no community should have to live through this kind of day," Ms Kotek said. "As we learn more about the children and the adults who have been killed or injured, and their families and their loved ones, we are going to do a lot of crying, and we are going to cry together, and we're probably going to cry privately." Bend, in rural central Oregon, is home to about 100,000 people and is about 280km south-east of Portland. Silver Rail Elementary School offers classes from kindergarten through to fifth ⁠grade – about ages five to 11 – and has about 450 pupils and 40 ⁠staff members, officials said. Police said they received a call at about 1pm that indicated a man had shot into a car at Silver Rail Elementary School. Moments later, emergency dispatchers received calls "reporting that a person had entered the school ​and began shooting", police said in a statement. Officers arrived within three minutes and found that the suspect had been shot dead.

title: World Bank sets fivefold minerals goal as Fed chairman Warsh flags financial stability risks
description: Lender targets $19bn in critical minerals financing, as it identifies 20 countries to join projects
content: The World Bank aims to increase its critical minerals business fivefold over the next five years, while US Federal Reserve chairman Kevin Warsh expressed surprise at the resilience of major economies amid geopolitical shocks and tighter monetary policy. "In critical minerals, we ⁠plan to quintuple our business in five years … this ​week, ⁠we launched our ‌first country compacts with MDB partners, to build local industries and keep ​more jobs and value at home," World Bank president Ajay Banga said at the 2026 IMF -World Bank Annual Meetings in Bangkok on Friday, as the multilateral lender seeks to support mining, processing and local industries. He also outlined plans to expand partnerships with countries developing critical minerals industries. The World Bank's new metals and minerals implementation plan is aimed at securing $19 billion in critical minerals financing over the 2026-2030 fiscal period, up from $3.6 billion in the 2021-2025 fiscal period. The lender has identified 20 countries with which it could partner on critical minerals development projects. It also launched its first country compacts with its partners this week, aiming to build local industries and retain more jobs and economic value in producing countries. Mr Banga also laid out a vision on Friday for how the World Bank should operate, focusing primarily on creating jobs, expanding economic opportunity and connecting private capital to developing nations that need investment. Addressing the plenary session at the annual meetings, Mr Banga said the current economic climate of tightening fiscal space, rising debt and global conflicts had made the work challenging – but not impossible. “Those are the twin challenges we have been working to address: making scarce resources go further, while helping countries create jobs at scale. They must be addressed together,” he said in prepared remarks. “The future of development will depend on bringing public finance , private investment, philanthropy and technology together around what each country needs. The partnership – and mix – should evolve as countries do.” He also spoke of the World Bank’s new initiative to focus on “small AI” – bespoke artificial intelligence-enabled applications that do not rely on the most advanced and expensive version of the technology, but can provide solutions for people in the developing world. “Practical, or ‘small’, AI can help a farmer improve yields, a teacher tailor instruction, a health worker make better-informed decisions, or an entrepreneur reach new customers,” Mr Banga added. Separately, Mr Warsh said the Fed needed to consider financial stability risks as it assesses the outlook for the US economy , while declining to offer indications about its next interest-rate decision. ⁠Speaking at the annual meetings, heh said he did not “prejudge” policy decisions before the Fed’s meetings from October 27 to 28, when markets expect interest rates to remain unchanged. The Fed raised rates in September and made it clear that it intended to deliver price stability and withdraw some monetary policy accommodation, he said. “I don't prejudge meetings. I don't believe in saying now what I might do at the meetings that we have in the balance of this year,” Mr Warsh said. He said ⁠the Fed must ​continually bolster its credibility to get ⁠monetary policy right, adding that that includes the supervision and operations side ⁠of the central bank. He also expressed optimism about AI and its potential to transform the real economy, although he said the technology’s near-term impact on employment remained uncertain. Mr Warsh also said he was surprised by the global resilience and how many G20 member ⁠states are “hanging in there” amid the geopolitical shocks of recent months, ​as ⁠most ‌central banks tightened monetary ​policy to deal with inflation. “We're seeing common things and we're taking action and I view that as a positive development,” Mr Warsh said. “I believe, optimistically, ​you ‌might think ⁠naively, at least ​in the US, we're ​going ‌to come out of ⁠this stronger with a ⁠more durable economy, more capable of leading the world on economic growth.” With reporting from Reuters and AFP

title: Israeli company used online ads to run spy operation against 'hundreds of millions of people'
description: Ads only needed to load on website for spying to occur, research groups warn
content: Israeli digital advertising ⁠agency Discover-Tech spied on internet users through a network of online advertisements that it used to track ⁠targets and hack their devices, research groups said. Reports from Canadian group Citizen Lab and US advertising security company Confiant found that Discover-Tech's services gave Candiru, ​an Israeli spyware company blacklisted by the US government, as well as other Israeli surveillance groups, access to advertising platforms run by companies including Google, Comcast and Russia's Yandex. Discover-Tech's online ads, often ⁠for ordinary products such as phones or earbuds , reached more than 120,000 websites and 75,000 apps through its various partnerships, Citizen Lab said. People who visited sites or used apps with ​the malicious ⁠ads could be identified and tracked by Discover-Tech, which would sometimes try to extract phone numbers from smartphone users, researchers said. Ads only needed to load on a website for the spying to occur. Some ads would be used ​to help plant spyware from Candiru on users' devices, the research groups said. But Confiant said that ads it tied to Candiru were a fraction of Discover-Tech's overall volume. Discover-Tech was issuing at least 10 million ads a day around the world, with data-sharing arrangements called cookie matching allowing it to track people beyond the reach of its ads, Confiant co-founder Jerome Dangu said. "Very likely hundreds of millions of people would have been touched by Discover-Tech," he added. Citizen Lab said a powerful form of Candiru spyware delivered through Discover-Tech's ads had been used to compromise 45 Windows devices at Qatar's Al Jazeera between 2024 and 2025. That was confirmed because the media group shared its network logs with the group, it added. Al Jazeera said in a statement that it "condemns the spyware attacks targeting a number of its staff" and that it was taking steps to protect its employees and its systems. "Those responsible must be held accountable," it said. Mr Dangu said the malicious ads had been shown to users in "hundreds of networks in sensitive ​categories", including the Pentagon, the International Atomic Energy Agency and the International Criminal Court. He also said that some regions, including the Palestinian ‌territories, were saturated by the Israeli company's ads. "You go to almost ⁠any site in Palestine – any site – you find a Discover-Tech ad. It gives them ​a very complete visibility on the digital activities of an entire country," he added. Citizen Lab said it had evidence that the malicious ads were ​shown to people in the ‌UN, Nato, the European Commission and more than a dozen national governments. The ads also appeared in networks including technology companies such as Nvidia and Sandisk, as well as media organisations ⁠in Mexico, Israel and Europe. Discover-Tech is now to be frozen out of parts of the online ad market. Google said in a statement that it had collaborated with Citizen Lab and Confiant's investigation and kicked Discover-Tech off its ad platforms "for systematically violating our policies". IAB Europe, the European-level association for the digital marketing and advertising ecosystem, said in an email ​that Discover-Tech had been suspended from its list of globally approved entities last week after an audit identified policy breaches.

title: Animals (Netflix)
description: Ben Affleck directs and stars in this political thriller as Mark Kimball
content: Ben Affleck plays Mark Kimball, a candidate for Los Angeles mayor whose carefully constructed life begins to unravel when his son is kidnapped. Together with his wife Abigail (Kerry Washington), Mark must scramble to raise the ransom while navigating a web of deception that threatens to tear the family apart. Affleck is joined by an ensemble cast including Gillian Anderson, Steven Yeun, Adriana Paz and Luis Gerardo Méndez. The film marks another directorial outing for Affleck, whose previous work behind the camera includes the Oscar-winning Argo . Air date: October 9

title: Who was Tenzing Norgay? The real story behind Apple TV's Everest film
description: As the new movie revisits the ascent of Mount Everest in 1953, we look at the life of the Sherpa mountaineer who reached the summit alongside Edmund Hillary
content: On May 29, 1953, two men stood at the summit of Mount Everest, becoming the first people confirmed to have reached the top of the world's highest mountain. One was Edmund Hillary , a New Zealand mountaineer whose name would become synonymous with the historic achievement. The other was Tenzing Norgay , an experienced Sherpa climber who had spent years attempting to conquer the mountain. Their extraordinary journey is the subject of Tenzing , a new Apple TV film that shifts the spotlight towards the man whose role in one of mountaineering's greatest achievements has not always received equal attention. Directed by Jennifer Peedom, the film stars Genden Phuntsok as Norgay, Tom Hiddleston as Hillary and Willem Dafoe as John Hunt, the British expedition leader. It was released in select cinemas on October 9 and begins streaming globally on Apple TV on Friday. But Tenzing is more than a recreation of the dangerous climb. It also explores the cultural divisions within the expedition, Norgay's determination to be recognised as a mountaineer rather than simply a guide, and his deeply personal relationship with Everest . Born around 1914, Norgay came from a Sherpa family in the Himalayan region, although details of his birthplace remain disputed. Accounts of his early life differ, with some placing his birth in Nepal and others in Tibet . What is clear is that he grew up close to the mountains that would come to define his life. He eventually moved to Darjeeling in India, which had become an important base for mountaineering expeditions attempting to explore the Himalayas . Norgay began working on Everest expeditions in 1935, initially carrying supplies for foreign climbers. Over the following years, he developed into an exceptionally skilled mountaineer, learning to navigate treacherous terrain and work at altitudes where even breathing became difficult. Despite being unable to read or write, he spoke several languages and became an important figure in organising and leading Sherpa climbing teams. By the time he joined the British expedition in 1953, Norgay had already attempted to reach Everest's summit six times. A year earlier, he had come close during a Swiss expedition alongside Raymond Lambert, reaching approximately 8,600 metres before being forced to turn back. His seventh attempt, alongside Hillary, would finally prove successful. Unlike many accounts of the 1953 expedition, which have traditionally focused on Hillary or the wider British effort, Tenzing approaches the historic climb from Norgay's perspective. The film follows his determination to be recognised as a full member of the expedition, rather than simply someone employed to assist the western climbers. His wife Dawa, played by Thinley Lhamo, is portrayed as an important source of encouragement, while Caitríona Balfe plays expedition secretary Jill Henderson, who supports his efforts to secure a place on the climbing team. Australian filmmaker Peedom, whose previous work includes the 2015 documentary Sherpa , has described the film as an opportunity to place Norgay at the centre of a story in which he has often been overshadowed. To prepare for their roles, Phuntsok and Hiddleston travelled to Nepal and trekked towards Everest Base Camp , meeting Sherpa mountaineers and learning more about the region and its climbing history. Norgay's son Norbu Tenzing is an executive producer of the film, bringing a direct family connection to the production. Tenzing is now streaming on Apple TV

title: Below (Netflix)
description: Josh Hartnett leads this six-part thriller set in a small fishing town in Newfoundland, Canada
content: Josh Hartnett plays fisherman Calvin Penney, who is haunted by the mysterious death of his father decades earlier. When an unidentified sea creature begins terrorising the community, Calvin teams up with a visiting marine researcher Fonda Howander, played by Mackenzie Davis ( Speak No Evil ), to uncover what is lurking beneath the water while trying to protect his family and their way of life. Created by The Umbrella Academy writer Jesse McKeown, the series also stars Charlie Heaton ( Stranger Things ), who plays Calvin’s son Wade. Air date: October 8

title: Carrie (Prime Video)
description: The series marks the first time King’s 1974 debut novel has been adapted as a television series
content: Stephen King’s classic horror story is reimagined for a new generation in this eight-part series from Mike Flanagan, the creator behind The Haunting of Hill House and Midnight Mass . Summer H Howell stars as Carrie White, a sheltered teenager who is thrust into a public high school after the death of her father. She becomes the target of a viral bullying scandal while also discovering she possesses telekinetic powers. Samantha Sloyan plays Carrie’s fiercely protective mother, Margaret, with a cast that also includes Amber Midthunder as gym teacher Rita Desjardin, and Matthew Lillard as principal Henry Grayle. The series arrives 50 years after Brian De Palma’s acclaimed 1976 film starring Sissy Spacek. Air date: October 7

title: Investor confidence in Gulf remains strong despite war, says World Economic Forum's regional chief
description: Diversification has helped region withstand crisis despite IMF downgrading growth forecasts
content: Investor confidence in the region remains strong despite the fall-out from the Iran war , with efforts to diversify economies helping to shield them from the crisis, a senior World Economic Forum official has said. Kelsey Goodman, head of Middle East and North Africa at the World Economic Forum (WEF), told The National that the region’s economic fundamentals remained solid despite geopolitical uncertainty. Her comments come as the International Monetary Fund sharply downgraded its 2026 growth forecasts for Gulf economies amid the effects of the war and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz. “There’s still widespread investor confidence in the region,” Ms Goodman said. “The fundamentals are solid even if the surrounding area is uncertain, but it calls for the need for dialogue and co-operation and hopefully a return to peace and resiliency in the region.” Speaking at the Annual Meeting of Global Future Leaders in Dubai , which concluded on Thursday, Ms Goodman said efforts to diversify Gulf economies had helped them withstand recent shocks and would be crucial to their recovery. “Diversification really is key, and the companies and the economies that have been able to have already built in diversity into their plan are the ones that have been most resilient," she said. "Resiliency is something that you have to prepare for. It's not something that you can build only in times of crisis.” Foresight simulations were carried out at the meeting on Thursday, in which participants rehearsed responses to unfolding geopolitical and technological crises. “This meeting has really emphasised that dialogue and co-operation are not luxuries for easy times. They're essential precisely when the world is at its most complicated,” said Ms Goodman. Even with this in mind, she said the mood at the meeting was positive. “I think it speaks to the resiliency of Dubai, and we hope that the participants are leaving with a message of hope and renewed belief in the power of moving from foresight into action,” she said. In recent years, the UAE has prioritised artificial intelligence investments, with trillions of dollars earmarked for the technology, including building data centres. A newly published WEF report showed the potential of artificial intelligence in unlocking upwards of $1 trillion by 2030 in the region. Ms Goodman believes the investments countries are making in the AI sphere could return, but that regional uncertainty creates more barriers to reaching these goals. “For the economies to realise this value, it's going to take a lot of co-operation across all sectors of society,” she said. “That's going to include long-term planning from governments, but also having the regulation, the energy infrastructure, and the business applications for these new technologies.” While blocked trade routes have affected shipping and petrol prices have risen, Ms Goodman said the war's impact on the travel and tourism sector could also affect labour markets, especially given the high numbers of migrant workers in the country. The UAE workforce is made up of approximately 8.7 million migrant workers. “The Gulf really relies on a very mobile labour market with a lot of connections outside the region,” she said. “These are areas where there could potentially be short a ges.”

title: Preparations for 2027 ​Asian ​Cup ​in Saudi Arabia 'progressing according to schedule'
description: Organising ​committee confident of hosting tournament in kingdom in January
content: The local organising ​committee of the 2027 Asian Cup said preparations for hosting the continental tournament in Saudi Arabia are going ahead as per schedule despite recent attacks in the kingdom. Saudi Arabia saw a number of events called off or postponed as fighting intensified between the kingdom and Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi rebels. Multiple attacks on airports in the country forced the Six Kings men's tennis tournament , scheduled for October 21-24, and the Fifa Esports final, set for October 16-25, to be postponed. Three matches in the Saudi Pro League this weekend were rescheduled to later in the season due to “logistical considerations”. Earlier, the Asian Football Confederation (AFC) said ‌it was open to the idea of ⁠delaying the Asian Cup until ​2028 if needed. The continental tournament is scheduled to ​kick ‌off on January 7 across venues in Riyadh, Jeddah ⁠and Al Khobar. However, ⁠the tournament's local organising committee said preparations are going ahead according to schedule. “Preparations across all organisational and operational areas are progressing according to the approved schedule, including work on venues, facilities and supporting services,” ​the organising committee ‌said, adding ⁠that the tournament ​remains on track to ​be ‌held from January 7 to ⁠February 5, 2027. “The LOC ⁠will continue to monitor ​developments relevant to the tournament and ​ensure ‌the appropriate conditions are in place for its successful ⁠delivery.” Earlier this week, AFC president Salman bin Ibrahim Al Khalifa said the confederation was in “no hurry” to decide ​whether the tournament needed to be postponed. “We ​can wait until the end of November. Things can change very quickly for ‌better or worse in the region and ⁠it is question of seeing what happens,” Al Khalifa told ​reporters in Zurich during the Fifa Council meeting. The Korea Football Association (KFA) said it was in ⁠communication with the AFC. “We are closely monitoring the situation in Saudi Arabia and plan to continue discussions regarding overall developments,” the KFA said in a statement. The previous Asian Cup was ​delayed by a year after China withdrew as hosts because of Covid-19 restrictions, with Qatar stepping in to stage the tournament in early 2024. The Asian Tour postponed its ​season-ending ​Saudi International ​⁠in the aftermath of ⁠attacks in Riyadh. "The decision to postpone was taken following an assessment of the organisational and logistical challenges associated with hosting the tournament and ensuring the event is delivered to a standard befitting its international stature," an Asian Tour statement said. The $5 million ​flagship event, which is ‌sponsored by the ⁠Saudi Public Investment ​Fund (PIF), was scheduled to take ​place ‌at Riyadh Golf Club from November 18 ⁠to 21. "The PIF Saudi International is ⁠one of the most important events on the Asian Tour calendar and we look forward to seeing our players ​compete in Riyadh in the future," Asian Tour Commissioner Cho Minn Thant said.

title: Iraqi parliament approves key cabinet posts, including US-sanctioned deputy PM
description: Politicians vote to name son-in-law of former prime minister Nouri Al Maliki as interior minister
content: Iraq’s parliament voted to fill a series of long‑vacant cabinet posts late on Thursday, completing Prime Minister Ali Al Zaidi’s government and approving a deputy prime minister who is under US sanctions . The government formation process has been completed five months after Mr Al Zaidi took office, with 11 key positions approved at a full parliamentary session in Baghdad. Those included the country's Defence Minister, Nayef Al Shammari, and Interior Minister Yasir Al Maliki. Mr Al Zaidi said in a statement that the completion of his cabinet marked the start of “accelerated, diligent work” and pledged to push ahead with the government’s policies . He said the regional conflict had posed exceptional economic and security challenges to Iraq. Politicians also endorsed Laith Al Khazali as one of three deputy prime ministers. He is the brother of Qais Al Khazali, leader of the Iran‑backed Asaib Ahl Al Haq militia. The US designated the group as a foreign terrorist organisation in 2020 and has accused it of attacks on US and coalition forces. Both brothers were named “specially designated global terrorists” and Laith was arrested by US forces in 2007 over allegations related to a January attack in Karbala that killed five American soldiers. Parliament approved two other deputy prime ministers – Mohammed Ali Tamim of the Sunni Taqadum Party and Asas Coalition leader Muhsin Al Mandalawi. Votes were postponed for the nominee for migration and displacement minister owing to disagreement among parties, politicians said. The nomination of Mr Al Khazali drew sharp criticism from Washington. Republican Representative Joe Wilson condemned the appointment , describing him as an “Iranian puppet whose militia killed Americans and Iraqis". “He is no better than ISIS, maybe even worse. It is outrageous but sadly not shocking that he has been appointed deputy PM of Iraq,” Mr Wilson wrote on X. Another controversial name is Mr Al Maliki, the son-in-law of former prime minister Nouri Al Maliki. When he was in power, Iraq lost nearly a third of its territory to ISIS in 2014, a collapse that ultimately forced him to resign. He is known to have strong connections with Iran and is often described as an influential power-broker in Iraqi politics. The nomination raises questions about how Iraq will manage its ties with the US. Sajad Jiyad, an Iraq expert with the Century Foundation, told The National that Shiite parties within the ruling coalition appear confident the appointments will not trigger a major rupture with Washington. Mr Jiyad said the move to nominate Mr Al Khazali might be to encourage other Iran‑aligned factions to integrate into state structures and dissolve their armed wings, by signalling that participation in formal politics can lead to senior government posts. Asaib Ahl Al Haq has grown into one of Iraq’s most influential Shia parties, now holding both ministerial positions and a deputy premiership. Mr Al Zaidi's government has pledged to introduce economic ⁠reforms and anti-corruption measures, as well as taking steps to strengthen state institutions. But many challenges lie ahead, including rebuilding an economy hit by regional instability, ​tackling endemic corruption and bringing Iran-backed armed groups under greater state control.

title: Drop in Gulf student visa applications shows dwindling appetite for UK universities
description: UAE records 59 per cent decline in applications in four years
content: The number of students from the Gulf choosing to study in the UK has plunged in recent years, most drastically from the UAE, figures show. Student visa application numbers have slumped due to a UK migration clampdown that has restricted visas, as well as concerns over social issues, safety and the quality of education in Britain, experts said. While there was an inevitable drop in numbers caused by the Covid pandemic, these had bounced back by 2022, before the UK began issuing its policies to restrict student visas. The number of student visa applications from the UAE then began to drop, falling 59 per cent in the next four years, from 638 in 2022 to 257 students in 2025, Home Office statistics showed. These covered students who have been offered a place at an institution to study for a bachelor, graduate, PhD or other higher education courses. There was a 36 per cent drop in 2025 alone compared with the previous year. There were 13 per cent fewer applications from students in Saudi Arabia between 2023 and 2025, dropping from 5,814 to 5,049. In Bahrain, a 26 per cent decline has been recorded, from 545 applications in 2023 to 403 in 2025. Qatar recorded a drop of about 14 per cent between 2023 and 2025, from 1,056 to 910 applications. The outliers are Kuwait, which saw an 11 per cent rise in applications, from 4,499 in 2023 to 5,034 in 2025, and Oman, which grew from 996 to 1,018. Figures for spring and summer visa applications will be released by the Home Office next month and are expected to continue the downward trend. The first quarter of this year showed a decline of almost a third (29.2 per cent) of applications from Saudi students. UAE applications for the same period remained steady, moving from 16 in the first three months of 2025 to 15 in the same period of 2026. Professionals in the higher education sector have warned the numbers could keep declining as UK immigration restrictions make studying in the country less appealing. Many students regard a degree in the UK as an investment towards a career in the country. But from next year, students will have only 18 months to find a job in the UK after their graduation, compared to the previous allowance of two years. This follows increases to the Immigration Health Surcharge and student visa fees, and a higher chance of visa refusal. The general salary threshold for skilled workers' visas is also set to rise, with the discount for graduates removed, according the Labour government's White Paper on Immigration. The UK government was criticised this week for removing incentives for overseas students to pursue a degree course at a British university. “Given politicians have found it much easier to control clearly defined legal migration routes, such as coming to the UK to study, than to get a grip on other routes, such as the infamous small boats, the factors pulling international students to come and study in the UK have been trimmed back again,” wrote Nick Hillman, chief executive of the Higher Education Policy Institution in an analysis. This is compounded by financial penalties for universities that award spaces to students whose visa applications are later rejected. This has reportedly led to institutions withdrawing their offers to would-be students, mainly from India, China and Nigeria, to avoid paying any penalty should their visa applications be unsuccessful . For Gulf students, other factors such as safety concerns could also be fuelling the decline. A Saudi student was killed last year in a knife attack in Cambridge while studying an English language course, prompting his uncle to say the UK was “rapidly losing its global reputation”. There are also fears of radicalisation on campuses. The UAE – which has urged western governments to ban the Muslim Brotherhood organisation – was reported by the Financial Times this year to have scrapped its state-funded scholarships to some British universities. The UK government introduced new measures to protect students from extremism on campus this year. This includes supporting universities to carry out appropriate risk checks where free speech crosses into unlawful activity or support for terrorism.

title: Serial champions India continue bewildering struggle in bilateral series
description: Team has won every major title in recent seasons but are losing a lot more outside big tournaments
content: Can you be critical of a side that has won every major competition it has entered since 2024? Possibly. Especially when you put in performances like the Indian team has done in between those fine results. Since the 2024 T20 World Cup win , India have won the 50-over ICC Champions Trophy, Asia Cup, and successfully defended their T20 world title and the Asian Games gold medal this year. But right alongside, the team were also been whitewashed at home in Tests by New Zealand and South Africa – having been undefeated in their backyard for over a decade, lost the Border Gavaskar Trophy to Australia, embarrassed by Ireland (in T20s) and England (T20s and ODIs) right after their World Cup win this year and are now being taken apart by a spirited West Indies at home. The double T20 world champions were outplayed in the fourth match of the five-game T20 series against the Windies, falling to a 24-run loss in Hyderabad. The series is now tied 2-2. In the preceding ODI series, the West Indies easily chased down a target of 350 and also smashed 400 in the second game. That series was won 2-1 by India but they were stretched well past their limits. It's the same story in the T20s. In fact, India have been hammered for the third straight bilateral T20 series – defeats to Ireland and England away and now an uphill battle against the Caribbean side. If the Windies secure the T20 series win on Saturday, it wouldn’t be a surprise. Shouldn’t that worry Indian cricket management? It should, but what can they do when the team ends up winning every major tournament? India won a world and a continental title in 2026. The same set of players have also been thrashed by Ireland, England and the Windies in the same year. How do you reconcile both facts? There are two ways to look at it. One is that India have mastered the art of stumbling their way through low priority bilateral series and somehow finding the perfect formula when the big tournaments come around. The other is India were playing major tournaments in Asian conditions for the last two years and would have been found out if any of the events were held in England or Australia. There is only one way to find out – wait for next two years. The next big assignment for all teams is the ODI World Cup in South Africa, Zimbabwe and Namibia, followed by the 2028 T20 World Cup Down Under and the Los Angeles Olympics in the same year. Indian fans and cricket administrators might prefer to wait until all three assignments are completed, before taking stock of the situation. Around 10 or so years back, India were the undisputed champions of bilateral series, home and away. But they did not win a single major tournament, much to the pain of the then captain Virat Kohli. The script has flipped completely, where the players endure bewildering losses home and away in all formats, only to go back to their homes with another winners' medal in the cabinet. This can’t last long though. Conditions in South Africa and Australia are going to be daunting even for the most in-form Indian team, let alone a group that can barely stand still. It could open some deep wounds. One thing is clear – India do not have ready replacements for their veterans. The fitness concerns of all-rounder Hardik Pandya and workload management of Jasprit Bumrah have ruined the balance of the white-ball teams, while they still have not found a reliable substitute for Mohammad Shami or even Mohammad Siraj. No wonder the ageing Kohli and Rohit Sharma are guaranteed to play the ODI World Cup next year. Fast bowler Bhuvneshwar Kumar is back in the T20 team for the forthcoming New Zealand tour; he last played for India in 2022. Fellow veteran quick Shami is highly likely to be back before the ODI World Cup, especially since the Indian team’s selection panel is undergoing a change with older yet in-form players being given a look-in once again. Maybe, India will win a couple of more titles and fans will forget about pain of the bilaterals. If not, then there will be a feeding frenzy.

title: Premier League predictions: Leeds pile pressure on Michael Carrick and Man United
description: We pick out the winners and losers from the latest round of English top-flight fixtures

title: Prevention becomes predictive: How Abu Dhabi is learning to read health risks before symptoms appear
description: Genomics, health data and AI are helping Abu Dhabi develop more personalised prevention, with earlier intervention and healthier lives as the goal
content: For a family welcoming a newborn, prevention can begin before there is any outward sign of illness. For an adult attending a routine check-up, it could mean understanding a developing health risk early enough to change its course. These are the possibilities behind Abu Dhabi’s move towards predictive health care. Advice on exercise, nutrition and regular screening remains essential. The next step is to make prevention more personal, drawing on an individual’s genetic profile, medical history and measurable changes in their health to determine where earlier action could make a difference. That ambition is reflected in To Sense is to Predict, the theme of the Abu Dhabi Future Health Summit, taking place from October 20 to 22. For patients and families, its meaning is practical: recognising the signals of disease sooner and turning that information into care. Future Health - A Global Initiative by Abu Dhabi’s longevity whitepaper places healthspan, the years a person lives in good health, at the centre of this shift. Its focus is on helping people remain well and independent for longer by connecting scientific advances with prevention and everyday care. For UAE families, that means thinking about health across generations. Earlier recognition of risk could help a parent manage a developing chronic condition, support an older relative’s independence or give a child access to specialist care sooner. Genomics can reveal inherited susceptibility. Biomarkers, measurable indicators such as blood glucose or cholesterol, can help clinicians assess what is happening in the body. Medical records add the history of previous tests, diagnoses and treatment. AI can help analyse these sources of information and identify patterns that warrant clinical attention. The value comes from interpreting those signals together. A genetic finding is one part of a person’s health picture; its significance depends on clinical evidence, family history and other risk factors. Predictive care aims to give clinicians a stronger basis for deciding who needs closer monitoring, which screening is appropriate and when to intervene. Earlier insight must lead to better care. Abu Dhabi’s priority is to translate advances in genomics, data and AI into evidence-based decisions that help people stay well. For patients and families, this means understanding their risks, receiving appropriate screening and having a clear pathway to support or treatment. Abu Dhabi has established infrastructure that supports this approach. Malaffi, the emirate’s health information exchange, connects records across public and private healthcare providers, giving authorised clinicians access to a patient’s medical history. This helps them assess new findings alongside previous results and coordinate care across different settings. At the population level, the Department of Health’s Population Health Intelligence platform, unveiled with Microsoft in 2025, brings together clinical, lifestyle and environmental data. It is designed to help identify emerging risks and inform targeted prevention, with obesity and cancer among its initial focus areas. The longevity white paper also stresses the importance of helping people act on health information. Understanding a risk is useful when it leads to appropriate follow-up, support with healthier habits or a treatment decision. That requires prevention to become part of routine care, with progress assessed over time. Abu Dhabi’s Newborn Genetic Screening Programme offers a concrete example. Launched by the Department of Health in August 2025, its first phase was implemented at Kanad Hospital in Al Ain and Danat Al Emarat Hospital, in partnership with M42. Using cord blood collected at birth with parental consent, the programme applies whole genome sequencing to screen for more than 815 treatable childhood genetic conditions. These include disorders that may not be apparent at birth but could affect a child’s health if treatment is delayed. The announced expansion aims to reach all maternity hospitals in Abu Dhabi, covering UAE nationals and children of Emirati mothers born in the emirate. For families, the opportunity is earlier knowledge and a clearer route to care. Where screening identifies a concern, clinical assessment and genetic counselling help explain what the finding means and whether treatment or monitoring is needed. Future Health’s genomics and rare diseases whitepaper examines the next scientific challenge: understanding how genetic variants disrupt biology and using that knowledge to develop targeted interventions. It also explores how rare diseases can reveal biological mechanisms relevant to more common conditions. For patients, this reinforces the importance of connecting discovery with clinical care. Identifying a variant is a starting point. Its value depends on accurate interpretation, specialist expertise and access to an appropriate intervention. As the summit brings together healthcare leaders, researchers, policymakers and innovators, the test of predictive prevention will be what changes for families: a condition recognised sooner, a better-informed care plan or more years lived in good health.

title: In the new world order, expect fewer alliances and more ‘pop-up partnerships’
description: “America has no permanent friends or enemies, only interests.” The observation, widely attributed to Henry Kissinger but originating with the British statesman Lord Palmerston, has long captured the logic of international relations. Nearly two centuries later, it may offer the clearest explanation o
content: “America has no permanent friends or enemies, only interests.” The observation, widely attributed to Henry Kissinger but originating with the British statesman Lord Palmerston, has long captured the logic of international relations. Nearly two centuries later, it may offer the clearest explanation of the new world order taking shape. For much of the past century, international relations were organised around relatively permanent alliances, geographical blocs and established institutions. Countries joined international organisations, aligned themselves with major powers and accepted long-term commitments that extended beyond their immediate interests. Today, that architecture is being supplemented by something more fluid: temporary, purpose-driven coalitions that I would call “pop-up alliances”. The emerging geopolitical advantage may no longer be choosing the right side, but retaining the ability to work with several sides. India illustrates this new geopolitical a la carte menu. It participates in the Quad alongside the US, Japan and Australia, maintains defence relationships with Russia, belongs to Brics and deepens economic ties with Europe and the Gulf. The UAE similarly combines Brics membership with extensive western security partnerships and growing commercial relationships through more than 30 Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreements across Europe, Asia and Africa. These arrangements are not necessarily contradictory. They reflect a world in which countries increasingly choose their partners according to the issue rather than their permanent geopolitical affiliation. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney gave this thinking a powerful expression at Davos earlier this year, arguing that middle powers must co-operate more deliberately because, as he put it, “if you are not at the table, you are on the menu”. His proposed approach of “variable geometry”, involving different coalitions for different issues, captures an important shift in how international influence is exercised. Traditionally, great powers built alliances while smaller countries joined them. Increasingly, middle powers are becoming coalition entrepreneurs, bringing together countries around shared capabilities and interests. Influence depends not simply on military strength or economic size, but on the ability to mobilise capital, technology, energy, natural resources and market access. For countries such as the UAE, Saudi Arabia, Canada, India and Indonesia, this creates opportunities to shape international co-operation rather than merely participate in structures designed elsewhere. The logic also challenges the geographical foundations of traditional alliances. The EU, GCC and the Association of South-East Asian Nations were largely built around regional proximity , whereas emerging partnerships increasingly reflect strategic interdependence. Semiconductor supply chains connect Taiwan, South Korea, Japan, the Netherlands and the US, while critical minerals, artificial intelligence and cyber security create overlapping interests across continents. The next geopolitical map may therefore be drawn less around borders and more around the supply chains, technologies and resources that countries cannot afford to lose. Britain’s evolving relationship with Europe offers another revealing example. Brexit represented a decisive departure from institutional integration, yet the subsequent rebuilding of economic and security co-operation demonstrates that geography and mutual dependence cannot simply be legislated away . The debate over closer relations, including possible, eventual re-entry, reflects a broader movement towards more selective forms of international co-operation. This is not necessarily the end of globalisation, but rather its rewiring. Countries are reconsidering who they depend on, for what purposes and under which conditions. Strategic resilience increasingly means maintaining options rather than placing every national interest within a single alliance. In the future of international relations, every country will be permanently looking for new and better friends. This is an emerging model that can be described as “pop-up governance”: flexible partnerships formed around specific challenges, designed to achieve defined outcomes, and time-bound and designed to possibly dissolve when their purpose was fulfilled. Traditional institutions such as the UN, EU, GCC and Asean will remain, although some may lose influence as governments seek faster and more targeted arrangements. Alongside them, we are likely to see a growing layer of pop-up alliances, organised around shared interests rather than geography, with clear objectives and sometimes explicit time limits. Some will address defence, geopolitical tensions or economic security . Others will be more forward-looking, bringing together countries to develop water technologies, secure critical raw materials, co-ordinate specialised manufacturing capabilities or accelerate industrial innovation. A coalition formed to develop water desalination technologies, for example, might unite Gulf countries, Singapore, Australia and technology providers without requiring a broader political alliance. Such flexibility carries risks. Temporary coalitions can weaken accountability, exclude smaller economies and undermine established international rules. Their effectiveness will depend on whether they complement permanent institutions rather than simply bypass them. Nevertheless, the direction of change is becoming clearer. The emerging international system may resemble a network of overlapping partnerships, some permanent and others temporary, in which countries co-operate where interests converge while accepting differences elsewhere. Kissinger ’s famous principle remains relevant, but its application is changing. National interests may be enduring, yet the alliances through which countries pursue them need not be. The next measure of diplomatic influence may be less about which alliances a country belongs to, and more about which alliances it has the capacity to create.

title: UAE weather: Speed limits reduced after morning fog alerts in Abu Dhabi and Dubai
description: Police in both emirates urge motorists to drive carefully amid heavy fog
content: Heavy fog led authorities to reduce speed limits in Abu Dhabi on Friday morning, with a safety warning issued in Dubai . Alerts were sent to motorists in parts of Abu Dhabi, warning them that speed limits had been reduced to 80kph, while drivers were urged to exercise caution on the roads in Dubai due to poor visibility. " Abu Dhabi Police call on motorists to exercise caution due to reduced visibility during the fog," the force wrote on X. "They are urged to follow changing speed limits displayed on electronic information boards." A similar message was issued by police in Dubai, where motorists were told to drive carefully in the heavy fog. "With the formation of fog and reduced visibility in some areas of the emirate of Dubai, and in the interest of your safety, we remind you of the importance of reducing speed in accordance with road conditions, and exercising caution and care while driving," Dubai Police said on X. The National Centre of Meteorology predicted the foggy conditions would continue until at least 9am on Friday.

title: Naseer Shamma returns to UAE National Orchestra with bigger ambitions for the oud
description: Iraqi virtuoso brings new orchestral arrangements as the ensemble enters its second season
content: When Naseer Shamma joined the UAE National Orchestra for its inaugural concert in January, the performance was a celebration of what the newly formed ensemble could become. Nine months later, the Iraqi oud virtuoso is returning to an orchestra with a full season and more than two dozen concerts across the emirates behind it, and a more ambitious programme ahead. At Friday's Harmony concert at NYU Abu Dhabi's Arts Centre, Shamma will perform four of his compositions in new orchestral arrangements, including a concerto for oud and orchestra. “The first concert was different. It was a celebration. We were saying, here we are, we are together. But now we have a concrete programme. We have something much deeper, with different pieces,” he tells The National . “I think the orchestra is clearly at another level now compared with the first concert. The first show was very good, and if you notice, each concert since then has been about going deeper and finding new forms of creative expression. I am so glad to be part of that journey.” For Shamma, one of the Arab world's most influential oud players and educators, the collaboration continues nearly four decades of experimentation with the instrument's sound, design and repertoire. He has helped to develop a family of ouds covering different musical registers, composed for film and theatre, and founded Bait Al Oud in Cairo in the late 1990s, later expanding the conservatory to Abu Dhabi, Alexandria and Baghdad. His interest in oud-inspired orchestral music is long-standing, having led a 70-member Eastern Orchestra at Abu Dhabi Festival in 2008. Friday's programme includes Concerto for Oud and Orchestra , which Shamma says has been developed through extensive rehearsals and discussions with musicians. Despite previously performing orchestral works, including an adaptation of Vivaldi's Mandolin Concerto for the oud, he describes it as the ideal concerto for the occasion. “I hope it will be a good work because we have taken time with the composition, with rehearsals and with discussing the ideas with different musicians. Now I think it is ready to be presented on stage with the orchestra,” he says. Shamma acknowledges the contributions of earlier Arab composers, including Iraqi oud musician Jamil Bashir, who wrote for the instrument in orchestral settings. He now hopes to expand the repertoire available to future generations of oud players. “For that reason, I think it is time to compose differently. To compose one concerto every year would be great, because this would create a repertoire for other musicians who come after us,” he adds. “Of course, many Arab composers have written concertos for the oud, qanun, nay and other instruments. But when I compose something for the oud as an oud soloist myself, it will be different from what another composer writes. Because that composer may only be a composer, not an oud player.” Writing for a symphony orchestra also means balancing its instrumental range with the oud's distinctive sound and characteristics. “I think the oud has its own special characteristics. Its sound, its power, its chords, its quarter-tones and many other things,” he says. To keep the instrument from getting lost in the orchestra, “we have to preserve the oud's identity ”, Shamma says. “Not in a traditional way but in a contemporary way. It must remain an oud in the middle of the orchestra.” Shamma's collaboration with the orchestra has also developed through his relationship with its musicians. He recalls their curiosity during January's rehearsals about his oud's clarity of sound and his playing style, and how the experience helped to establish a rapport. “It was a beautiful experience. I felt that we had covered a great distance through a single piece of music. “It is a distance that might take two years to cover in ordinary life, just to create a friendship. But we achieved it through one piece lasting eight minutes.” Some of the orchestra's musicians have an earlier connection to Shamma through Abu Dhabi's Bait Al Oud, which he set up with clear expectations. “When I established it in Cairo in 1998, and then the second in Abu Dhabi in 2007, I had a clear idea that one day the UAE would need professional musicians. So I began preparing these musicians.” Several Emirati musicians who trained at the institution have joined the UAE National Orchestra, according to Shamma. “So this is a collaboration. We complement one another. We complete one another's projects,” he says. “We are working to become bridges that lead to the other side, to professional music.” Harmony by the UAE National Orchestra: Friday, October 16 at The Arts Centre, NYU Abu Dhabi. 8pm. Tickets start from Dh100

title: How Abu Dhabi is revealing the roots of the UAE’s global outlook
description: New museum exhibitions show how the Gulf embraced globalisation before the term existed
content: The Gulf has sometimes been portrayed in the West as, until recently, a remote corner of the world, a place defined largely by its desert environment and the relative isolation of its communities. Two new exhibitions in Abu Dhabi museums suggest a different and more compelling account of the history of the region, namely, that far from being a peripheral place, the Gulf was a crossroads of commerce and culture – much like it is today. At Louvre Abu Dhabi , a major exhibition about how the Indian Ocean connected communities from East Africa and the Arabian Peninsula to India, China and South-East Asia explores a millennium of maritime exchange through more than 200 objects. In December, the Zayed National Museum will explore more than 7,000 years of the camel’s place in the life on the Arabian Peninsula. Together, these exhibitions tell a story of land and sea that helps explain the UAE ’s enduring role in connecting people and places. The Louvre exhibition makes this history tangible. Six detailed ship models evoke the vessels that carried goods across the Indian Ocean. A third-century Buddha sculpture from Gandhara, in present-day Pakistan, offers another reminder that religious and artistic traditions travelled alongside commercial cargoes. The Gulf’s pearl industry was part of this wider network, linking its waters to markets and communities far beyond Arabia. The camel exhibition will turn the focus inland. Bones dating to between 4500 and 4000BC, discovered at Baynunah in Abu Dhabi, provide evidence of an extinct wild camel species. Remains from Dubai ’s Saruq Al Hadid illustrate the later relationship between humans and domesticated camels. Meanwhile, recordings of Taghrooda poetry and Alheda’a, the traditional practice of calling camels, demonstrate how deeply the animal remains embedded in Emirati cultural expression. These exhibitions will present a reminder of how the people of the Gulf participated in networks of exchange and developed traditions suited to their environment. Such connections are still evident today. Ports remain vital to the UAE’s international trade, but are now complemented by aviation and rail links. The camel also endures with the animal featuring in racing, competitions and poetry – its place as part of the Emirates’ national identity is irreplaceable. There is also a wider significance in the way these exhibitions tell their stories. Preserving heritage should mean more than celebrating familiar symbols or indulging in nostalgia. Understanding how the past shaped the present helps us today to recognise the complexity of the societies that preceded our modern times. For anyone seeking to understand the UAE, exhibitions such as these are a good place to start. They represent a vital reminder that the country’s cosmopolitan outlook is not a recent invention, but part of a much longer history of exchange and encounter. In other words, they show how the Gulf embraced globalisation before the term even existed.

title: Why it’s important to deepen our understanding of AI
description: Our readers have their say about the safe use of artificial intelligence, Sheikha Shamma’s appointment, support for Saudi Arabia and Lebanon’s generators
content: Write to us: Share your feedback on the news of the week Promoting AI awareness I write in reference to the article titled Dubai launches literacy platform to help parents guide children on safe use of AI (October 14): this is a commendable initiative. As AI continues to transform various aspects of our lives, it is essential to ensure that children understand both its benefits and its potential risks. Parents play a crucial role in helping their children navigate this rapidly evolving digital world by encouraging responsible usage, protecting their privacy, identifying misinformation and developing critical thinking skills. The UAE has demonstrated a keen interest in embracing and expanding the use of AI across various sectors. This initiative clearly reflects the country’s long-term vision of promoting AI awareness, digital literacy and technological advancement while prioritising the safety and well-being of younger generations. Equipping parents with the necessary knowledge and guidance is an important step towards building a society that can confidently and responsibly embrace emerging technologies. Such initiatives will not only benefit families but also contribute to preparing future generations for an AI-driven world. A commendable step by Dubai towards ensuring that technological progress goes hand in hand with awareness, responsibility and the safety of children. – K Ragavan, Bengaluru, India A little knowledge ... With regard to the article headlined Abu Dhabi launches major training programme to teach AI skills (October 7): raising awareness about AI is a great thing. What is not so great is when people attend a few workshops and emerge believing they have become AI experts. That is where things can become dangerous and counterproductive. AI projects can be costly and complex, requiring technical expertise, sound judgment and a depth of understanding that simply cannot be acquired in a week-long workshop. There is a significant difference between understanding what AI can do and having the expertise to design, implement and manage AI projects successfully. – Muhammad A, Dubai Taking the longview I refer to the video captioned Speaking at the World Economic Forum’s annual meeting in Dubai, Minister of State for Artificial Intelligence said trust in agentic AI systems would be difficult to rebuild if they caused harm (October 14): precisely and certainly, but the UAE leadership is foresighted. They want their people to be happy and prosperous. – Muhammad Naeem Ul Fateh, Pakistan An unsurprising decision Regarding the news that Sheikha Shamma bint Sultan has been appointed as an executive fellow by the World Economic Forum, raising her growing international profile in sustainability and climate action (October 14), I will say “bravo”, for she is a true embodiment of deep knowledge, unsurpassed intellect and pure talent. And God is a granter of success. – Dr Aisha Bilkhair Our second home This is regarding the video clip captioned ‘There is no way that somebody will break our back,’ Saudi Arabia’s energy minister, Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman, said following a series of deadly attacks on Riyadh international airport (October 12): we in the Filipino community stand firmly in solidarity with the kingdom of Saudi Arabia. We are deeply grateful to this nation, which has become our second home, providing us with opportunities, security and a place to build a better future for our families. In times of challenge, we stand united with the kingdom and its people. We are ready to offer our support in any lawful and appropriate way, contributing to the safety, peace, stability and prosperity of the nation we proudly call our second home. May peace, unity and protection always prevail throughout the kingdom. Long live Saudi Arabia. – James Rey Romero, Jizan, Saudi Arabia Citizens suffer I write in reference to Nada Maucourant Atallah’s article Lebanon’s power failure: Diesel generators, $300-a-month bills - and a corrupt system milking the profits (October 14): thank you for this report on the less visible impact of war. title: Gazans prepare to return home from Abu Dhabi's Emirates Humanitarian City
description: Thousands of Gazans remain at the centre receiving medical treatment
content: Dozens of Gazans who have been receiving medical treatment at Emirates Humanitarian City in Abu Dhabi are to return to their home country. The humanitarian centre has been a refuge from the Israel- Gaza conflict for thousands of Palestinians since 2023, but many long to be reunited with their families back home. Among them is 59-year-old Ibtisam Salout. She is preparing to return to Gaza in the coming days, after three years in the UAE. Ms Salout is a mother of nine and has 45 grandchildren. “The first thing I’ll do is gather them all and hold them tight. Yes, all of them," she says. She checks her suitcases before checking them again: the dresses for her daughters, the chocolates for her grandchildren. “The sneakers are for the boys. They sent me a photo and asked for these brands specifically," she says. Ms Salout is from Deir Al Balah. She arrived in the UAE in 2023 for treatment. She had breast cancer and her treatment had been interrupted after October 7. The UAE has provided medical treatment and comprehensive health care for 1,000 cancer patients and 1,000 injured children from the Gaza Strip. “When I arrived, they began treatment immediately and discovered the cancer was also in my lymph nodes. They saved my life,” Ms Salout says. Every patient is allowed an escort, but she does not have one. “I didn’t bring anyone with me. My husband said, ‘You are in the safest country in the world, with the kindest people taking care of you. I would be more worried about you in Gaza. Get better and come back to us. I’ll stay with the children and wait for you.' ” Today, she is cancer-free and ready to go back home to Gaza. “I’ll kiss its ground before running to my family," says Ms Salout. Her house has been partially destroyed, but her husband and children continue to live there. “We fixed it up like we will fix Gaza,” she says. Ms Salout is one of dozens of Palestinians who have completed their treatment and are heading back home. There remain close to 3,000 Gazans at the UAE’s Humanitarian City under treatment. “The plan was always that they would return home once they completed their treatment, but it is hard to part with them after so many years. They have become our family," says Falah Al Qahtani, spokesperson for EHC. A few Gazans have married at EHC, and others have had children. Younger children are enrolled in schools and nurseries, while adult Gazans are enrolled in online universities. Almost every week, there is a celebration at the complex: a birth, a birthday or a graduation. “This is a bittersweet farewell. We are happy that they are heading back home. We are happy that they are happy and can go back, but they have also formed deep connections with us and the country.” For Ms Salout, this is not goodbye. “You have to come to Gaza. I’ll make you fatteh, and I make the best maftool. You can ask anyone,” she says with pride. There are 30 people living with her but, she says; “I’ve told them to keep a clean room always ready for 'the Emirati'. Without them, I wouldn’t have been alive today.” The EHC has served as a sanctuary for many of those affected by the violence of the war. The centre is part of the UAE's continuing humanitarian operations in solidarity with the Palestinians. About medical 150 appointments are carried out each day within the vast complex, not including admissions to hospitals in Abu Dhabi for complex surgery. A building at EHC has a pharmacy, clinics, a ward with hospital beds staffed by doctors, paediatricians, an internal medicine doctor, psychiatrists, dentists and a rehabilitation specialist. The complex has a medical team of more than 50 doctors, nurses, therapists and administrators. There is also a school serving more than 400 children.

title: Russian bots and influence operations 'weren't disrupted by Ukraine strikes'
description: People started to 'see what they wanted to see' in data after Ukraine drone attack, experts say
content: Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's claim that last weekend's attacks on Russia 's Yandex data centres led to a drop in Pro-Russian bot operations is causing debate. The situation highlights the need to differentiate between bots, social media trolls and sophisticated influence operations , experts say. Prof Olga Belogolova , director of the emerging technologies initiative at Johns Hopkins University School of Advanced International Studies in Washington, wrote a long LinkedIn post to try to give context. Prof Belogolova, who previously led policy at Meta against influence operations, said that too many people saw "what they wanted to see" with data from network and cloud infrastructure company Cloudflare. "The story went viral when people started sharing a Cloudflare screenshot as proof of the silenced troll farms, as it showed a severe drop in bot traffic," she said. "Their motivated reasoning made them see that the internet was cleaner, more friendly, less toxic. "As someone who investigated and disrupted numerous malign influence operations and troll networks, I can also tell you that they do not often host their infrastructure on Yandex ." Prof Belogolova also said that far too many people were confusing and misusing tech terminology. "Bots are importantly not trolls ... as many tech researchers have already pointed out, Cloudflare labels any non-browser, automated script as a bot," she said. She said that when a data centre is taken offline, "its automated web-crawling and indexing traffic cuts out too". Cloudflare Radar, a branch of the company, agreed that nuance was needed when looking at internet traffic data. "Bot traffic refers to automated requests to websites on Cloudflare's network, such as crawlers and scripts, not necessarily activity on social media platforms," a post from Cloudflare Radar read, casting doubt on claims that Russia's social media trolls and disinformation campaign had been disrupted. On Thursday, Cloudflare provided more clarity on the Ukrainian attacks on Russian data centres. "Cloudflare data reveals that while search crawling stopped, malicious bots simply migrated to other networks," the company posted. "There was no evidence that the strikes knocked social media manipulation offline or otherwise disrupted malicious activity on the internet." Yet Prof Belogolova said that there were probably still ramifications faced by Russia after the data centre strikes. "Kinetic strikes on Russian tech infrastructure may disrupt Russia's digital economy and cloud services," she said. "They are not exactly a precise tool for stopping foreign influence operations."

title: US extends sanctions waiver on Russia's Lukoil until 2027
description: Treasury also authorises certain transactions for oil giant's entities over same period
content: The US on Thursday extended a sanctions waiver on Russian oil giant Lukoil , allowing its service operations outside the country to continue until April 2027, the Treasury Department announced. Under the new general licence, Lukoil petrol stations will be able to serve customers until April 25, 2027. This includes petrol stations in the US, the department said. The waiver replaces a previous licence that was set to expire this month. The licence prohibits the “transfer of funds to any person or account located in the Russian Federation”, it reads. It also excludes transactions involving Russia 's central bank, its national wealth fund and the Ministry of Finance. In a separate licence, the Treasury Department also authorised certain transactions for Lukoil Bulgaria's firms in the same time period. The decision comes a week after US President Donald Trump said he had reached a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin that would allow Russia to supply diesel to the US and the global markets. The agreement deepened a rift between the US and its European partners, including Ukraine, and within Mr Trump's Republican Party. Mr Trump said Russia would immediately release 300,000 tonnes of diesel to the US and global markets, with another 500,000 tonnes released in November and a million tonnes “immediately thereafter”. He also said Russia would release three million tonnes of fuel “within a short period of time” depending on the condition of the country's diesel refineries. Oil prices remain high during the seven-month Iran war, as tanker traffic through the Strait of Hormuz is significantly well below its prewar levels and as Iranian attacks continue in the waterway. Futures for Brent global benchmark crude fell 0.27 per cent to settle at $105.8 a barrel on Thursday, with West Texas Intermediate futures gaining 2.76 per cent at $97.71 a barrel. Diesel prices also remained elevated at $6.31 a gallon, compared to the average of $3.65 a gallon at the same time last year. The International Energy Agency's governing board on Thursday said it would quicken the release of more than 20 million barrels of diesel and the remaining volumes of the 400 million barrels of emergency stocks of crude and other oil products previously agreed to in March. The IEA said on Wednesday it expects oil market balances to remain in a deficit well into 2027. “As the remaining buffers in the system continue to erode, in the absence of a resolution to the conflicts in the Middle East, oil markets may experience more turmoil in the months ahead before any eventual surplus emerges in 2027,” it said.

title: Rubio speaks to Lebanon’s Aoun about explosives seized from Hezbollah
description: US Secretary of State also criticises Lebanon’s 1955 Boycott Law
content: US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has urged Lebanese President Joseph Aoun to ensure explosives seized from Hezbollah are not returned to the group, while calling for direct military communication between Lebanon and Israel to reduce the risk of clashes. In a call with Mr Aoun on Thursday, Mr Rubio discussed the confiscation of several hundred kilos of explosives from Hezbollah, a State Department official said. He called for accountability for those who ordered, financed and directed the shipment, and said returning the explosives to Hezbollah should be out of the question. Mr Rubio also criticised Lebanon’s 1955 Boycott Law, which the US official said was used for politicised prosecutions that deter efforts towards peace with Israel. He "emphasised that the law is impractical and urged direct military-to-military communication between Lebanese and Israeli forces for deconfliction", the official said. This would help to reduce miscalculation and to advance sequenced implementation of the Trilateral Framework, the official added. Signed in June, the framework sets out a phased process for the Lebanese army to restore state authority and disarm non-state militias including Hezbollah, and for Israel to progressively withdraw from Lebanese territory

title: Trump accuses Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed of Muslim Brotherhood ties
description: Democrat denies the allegation as Trump repeatedly calls him 'Mohammed'
content: US President Donald Trump has accused Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed of being a member of the Muslim Brotherhood, a claim the Democrat denies. Mr Trump also repeatedly referred to Mr El Sayed as “Mohammed” as the race in the key battleground state heats up. “I call him Mohammed Al Fayed. His name is Abdul, but I think I call him Mohammed Abdul El-Sayed, and he's a Muslim Brotherhood guy, 100 per cent,” he said at the White House on Thursday. The Brotherhood accusation comes less than three weeks before the midterm elections, as the race in the swing state intensifies. Michigan is home to about 300,000 Arab Americans, and Mr Trump has won the state twice. Polls show Mr El-Sayed narrowly ahead of his Republican opponent, Mike Rogers, an ally of Mr Trump. Throughout the campaign, Mr Trump has referred to Mr El-Sayed as a radical and a “jihadist lunatic”, among other Islamophobic insults. The November 3 elections will determine control of Congress, and Michigan is among the most closely watched Senate races. If Mr El-Sayed wins, he would become the first Muslim elected to the US Senate. US media reports this week have quoted social media posts by Mr El-Sayed’s half-sister that allegedly refer to his mother as a supporter of the Muslim Brotherhood. Mr El-Sayed, the son of Egyptian immigrants, has denied the accusations and at times dismissed them. His parents were divorced when he was a child, and he was raised by his American stepmother. “I have no ties. We have no ties,” Mr El-Sayed said in an interview with NBC that aired on Thursday. “I have never had these conversations with my mother. I wasn’t raised by my mother. “You’re using hearsay evidence from a tweet. It’s just not serious.” Mr El-Sayed, an epidemiologist and former health official, has also faced questions about his credentials. During a heated debate last week, Mr Rogers called Mr El-Sayed a “con man” and accused him of having ties to armed groups in the Middle East. “He can't condemn Hamas. He can't condemn the Muslim Brotherhood. He says his home is Egypt,” Mr Rogers said.
