He later suggested that concerns about surveillance could be personal for Mr El-Sayed because he or someone in his family might be suspected of terrorism. “Go ahead and say it,” Mr El-Sayed interjected. “You've been tiptoeing around it the whole time.”

title: Marco Rubio accuses Cuba of helping Iran and other 'malign actors' to attack US
description: Washington imposes sanctions on state-owned Cuban bank, claiming it provided financial services to Iranian lender
content: US Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Thursday accused Cuba of helping Iran and other adversaries to attack the US, as he announced sanctions against a Cuban state-owned bank claimed to have provided financial services to an Iranian lender. Banco Internacional de Comercio has provided services to Iran’s Karafarin Bank since at least 2022, Mr Rubio said in a statement. The US Treasury Department imposed sanctions on Karafarin Bank in 2020. “For too long, Communist Cuba has been allowed to operate as an outpost for malign actors and terror groups – including the Islamic Republic of Iran,” he said. The designation was announced alongside Treasury Department measures against Iranian financial networks, as the US administration of President Donald Trump seeks to restrict Tehran’s access to international finance. Mr Rubio said Washington would continue to identify and dismantle Cuba’s financial and security links with Iran and other states, and those it considers hostile.

title: US imposes Iran-related sanctions on Iraq Development Bank
description: Latest 'Economic Outcast' moves also aimed at Iran-linked entities and people
content: The Iraq Development Bank, among dozens of other targets, was hit with sanctions by the US on Thursday for its relations with Iran , the Treasury Department said in a statement. The bank was one of 10 entities and 16 people hit in the latest round of sanctions under Washington's “Economic Outcast” programme. US President Donald Trump's administration has warned countries and companies that continue to do business with Iran would face significant consequences. “Working with partners across the US government, the European Union, the United Kingdom, Gulf partners, and others, Treasury is targeting any source of the regime’s illicit revenue, as well as its sanctions evasion schemes to move funds,” the department said. The Treasury has previously imposed sanctions on banks in Turkey and a Bank Melli branch in the UAE, among others. The UAE Central Bank last month banned Bank Melli Iran from conducting transactions between its branches in the UAE and Iran after an investigation. Mr Trump's administration has hoped its “Economic Outcast” programme would sever Iran's remaining economic lifelines and force the regime to reopen the Strait of Hormuz. “The noose is tightening around Iran’s economy, and not even Iran’s so-called allies can save it,” Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said. Iraq in 2024 banned the IDB and seven other local commercial banks from engaging in US dollar transactions. The Treasury said the IDB has abused the now-dissolved dollar wire auction and maintains ties to Iran government entities and militia groups in Iraq. It is one of dozens of Iraqi banks that have been cut off for years due to concerns over sanctions evasion, money laundering and illicit finance. The US holds significant influence over Baghdad's financial policies because its international oil revenue is held at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York. Iraqi Prime Minister Ali Al Zaidi has sought to work with US authorities on the country's banking sector , which for years has been marred by corruption. Hiba Abdulwahib, an Iraqi researcher and analyst, said Thursday's move should not be viewed as a punishment for Iraq and it does not necessarily indicate that the US believes Mr Al Zaidi's government is unwilling to reform its banking sector. "Authority in Iraq is fragmented," she said. "The government does not have effective control over every institution or economic actor operating inside the country. I believe Washington understands those limitations, especially when it comes to Iran’s networks in Iraq." Ms Abdulwahib also said she expected the pressure of sanctions to lead to more co-ordination on closer oversight, monitoring of suspicious activities and penalties for breaches. "Baghdad has an incentive to address these problems before Washington imposes further sanctions, and the banks themselves have to take that risk seriously," she said. In July, the Treasury's Office of Terrorism and Financial Intelligence outlined a years-long plan that would eventually allow restricted Iraq banks to be reintegrated into the US dollar system. The process would include an initial phase of reforms from the Central Bank of Iraq, with the second phase consisting of a restricted bank completing the entire reform and licensing process. This would involve successfully undertaking a third-party audit of their compliance function, securing a qualified investor and meeting international standards. The department at the time said “no banned banks have regained access to foreign currency transactions”. "The United States will not tolerate the abuse of Iraqi banks by Iran-aligned militia groups and will take independent action, if necessary, to target such activity,” it said. The move coincided with Mr Al Zaidi's visit to the US, where he had pledged to disarm militia groups in the country by September 30. In an interview with The New York Times in September, Mr Al Zaidi pushed that timeline to June 2027. The disarmament is a crucial part of how he is expected to manage Iraq's relations with the US and Iran.

title: Trump abandons plan to stream execution of Fort Hood gunman after backlash
description: Idea drew condemnation from religious leaders and criticism from within US President's own circle
content: US President Donald Trump on Thursday called off plans for a live-stream broadcast of the execution of a former US army psychiatrist who killed 13 people at a military base in Texas in 2009. The plan to broadcast the firing-squad execution of Nidal Hasan was this month proposed by Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth, but was withdrawn after condemnation, including from within Mr Trump's own political circle. In a post on Truth Social, Mr Trump said the execution by firing squad would proceed as planned but would not be broadcast live. “I think streaming the execution for all to see might have been a strong deterrent for the world to witness how America deals with terrorists and scum like Hasan,” he wrote. “But many very good and well-meaning people would rather not watch him die, through streaming or through any other visual device. “He will die, as scheduled, by firing squad, but this event will not be streamed.” Mr Trump said the victims’ immediate families could witness the execution in person if they wished. Hasan, a former major, was convicted of killing 13 people and wounding 32 in a 2009 shooting at Fort Hood, Texas. He later described his shooting spree as retaliation for US wars in the ⁠Muslim world. Now 56, the son of Palestinian immigrants was scheduled to be ​sent to Afghanistan before the shooting. Hasan was left paralysed from the waist down and confined to a wheelchair after being shot ​by police during ‌his arrest. Mr Trump initially said he had not been involved in the decision to broadcast the execution but understood its rationale. “They want to do that because they want to set an example. I wasn't involved in that decision, but I understand the decision,” he said last week. But the proposal drew scepticism and condemnation, including from figures in Mr Trump’s own circle. Vice President JD Vance expressed reservations, saying he doubted the Pentagon would go ahead with the plan and that he would not watch if it did. Archbishop Timothy Broglio, who oversees the Catholic Archdiocese for the Military Services, issued a statement questioning the morality and purpose of broadcasting the execution. He warned that it could cause “moral injury” to the service members carrying it out and called on Catholic soldiers assigned to the firing squad to seek an exemption. “Do we really want to imitate the terrorists of this world and make a public spectacle of barbarically killing our adversaries? The crime committed by Nidal Malik Hasan was heinous, but does exposing the public to his execution serve any purpose?” he wrote. The controversy has raised questions about the administration’s judgment and its approach to capital punishment, legal experts said, as Mr Trump faces increasing political pressure ahead of November’s midterm elections . Mr Trump is dealing with low approval ratings as Americans increasingly blame him for rising costs and express disapproval of his handling of the war in Iran. On November 3, voters will decide which party controls Congress. “It's nonsensical, the way this has developed. The administration is not playing with a full deck,” said Eugene Fidell, a military law expert at Yale Law School. “This is totally tone deaf. It's very revealing of how out of touch this administration is, and seemingly how little supervision there is.” Mr Fidell also said a public execution would have gone against international human rights standards. The proposed use of a firing squad adds to the controversy. The US military has not carried out an execution by firing squad since 1945. The debate comes as capital punishment and execution methods face renewed scrutiny. Last month, Christa Pike, who was convicted of killing a friend in the 1990s, survived a botched execution attempt in Tennessee involving lethal injection. She was left badly injured. Daniel Urman, a constitutional law expert at Northeastern University, said Mr Hegseth and Mr Trump may have regarded the proposal as a way to project American strength but miscalculated the reaction it would provoke. “It does capture the Trump administration in the second term, where it looks like there's been an impulsive plan set out that might get walked back and might end up being embarrassing for them,” he said. “I think it's a headache he doesn't need. I think he's heard from members of his own party that it's a bad idea. And he needs his own party to stand by him.” Hasan's execution is scheduled for December 3, and it is unclear if any legal challenges could delay it.

title: Israel says entry of commercial goods into Gaza halted amid dispute between traders and Hamas
description: Hamas says $3,200 fee it is charging merchants is actually voluntary contribution to fund the needy
content: Lorries carrying commercial goods are no longer entering Gaza amid a dispute between traders and Hamas over taxes, the Israeli military body that oversees humanitarian affairs in the Palestinian territory has said. Cogat said the traders had decided to stop co-ordinating with it on shipments across the Israeli-controlled border in response to a 10,000 shekel ($3,220) fee imposed ​by ⁠Hamas on each lorry entering ‌the territory and a demand that 30 per cent of sales should be conducted in cash. Hamas denied the accusation in a statement released by the Gaza government's media office, which said the 10,000-shekel fee was, in fact, a contribution to a “voluntary community initiative” to support those in need such as widows and orphans. It also said the demand for cash payments was an “absolute necessity to address the severe imbalances in the Palestinian market, most notably the acute shortage of cash liquidity ”. Cogat said the traders' decision would cut the total ⁠number of lorries entering Gaza , bringing both humanitarian and commercial goods, by half, to around 300. The majority of Gazans are dependent on aid following three years of war, repeated displacement and restrictions imposed by Israel on aid deliveries. A global hunger monitor warned in July that more than two-thirds of Gazans could face acute hunger by the end of the year. Most of the territory's two million population live in makeshift shelters following widespread destruction of buildings and forced displacement during the war. Nahed Shhaibar, the head ​of the private transport union in Gaza, said that not ‌a single lorry carrying commercial ⁠products from Israel entered Gaza on Thursday. However, lorries carrying humanitarian aid had entered, as had lorries carrying commercial ​goods from ‌Egypt via an Israeli-controlled crossing, he told Reuters. Diplomats say that far fewer than 600 lorries normally enter Gaza each day. Mr Shhaibar said the figure was closer to 300, with two-thirds carrying commercial goods. Under the US-mediated ceasefire that halted full-scale fighting in October last year, Israel is obliged to allow a minimum of ​600 lorries carrying humanitarian aid to enter Gaza each day. Nickolay Mladenov, high representative of the Board of Peace overseeing Gaza's recovery under US President Donald Trump's peace plan, said the dispute showed the need to move on to the next steps in the process, which has stalled over Israel's insistence that Hamas must first disarm. “These developments demonstrate why the rapid deployment of the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza (NCAG), supported by the International Stabilisation Force, is urgently needed,” Mr Mladenov said in a post on X. “Civilian supplies, humanitarian assistance and commercial activity must be protected from coercion, exploitation and interference.” The NCAG is a committee of Palestinian technocrats that was formed in January but has not been allowed to enter Gaza so far.

title: How is Europe helping Saudi Arabia? France begins deploying military means
description: Britain and Italy also offer military help as kingdom attacked by Houthis
content: France said on Thursday it had begun deploying military means to help Saudi Arabia as the kingdom comes under attack by Houthi rebels. Britain and Italy have also offered modest military help as Yemen's heaviest fighting in years spills over to Saudi Arabia. There is wariness in Europe of becoming too involved in the Middle East conflict, although the effect of the conflict on energy prices is also a consideration. Here is what major military powers in Europe have said about supporting Saudi Arabia: France ​is ​starting ⁠to put ⁠into action operational ​elements of an ⁠agreement to help protect Saudi oil ⁠facilities, Foreign Ministry ​spokesman Pascal ⁠Confavreux ‌said on ​Thursday. He declined to elaborate on what military means were being sent to Saudi Arabia. President Emmanuel Macron said last month France would send troops ​and ‌defence systems ⁠to ​Saudi Arabia ​to ‌help protect the Red ⁠Sea port city ⁠of Yanbu, which is vital for energy transport. Mr Macron is set to visit the UAE , Bahrain, Kuwait and Qatar on a Gulf tour next week. A summit of EU and Gulf leaders in Riyadh has been postponed from its planned date of October 24. Britain has provided an RAF Voyager air-to-air refuelling aircraft to support Saudi operations in Yemen. It has also offered air defence equipment. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said on Monday that the Voyager aircraft had completed 14 “operational missions”. He said the UK would consider any further requests “as and when they come in”. Mr Burnham has made reducing the cost of living a major theme since taking office in July and indicated last month that this was a factor in approving the RAF Voyager deployment. Defence Minister Guido Crosetto told The National last month that Italy had provided equipment such as radars and anti-missile batteries to Saudi Arabia before the regional war broke out in February. Italy also offered the kingdom “technological assistance in defending itself against Iranian attacks … and capable of assisting it also against attacks when they came from the Houthis,” he said. Last month an Italian F-2000 aircraft was hit at the Taif airbase in Saudi Arabia, where some Italian forces had been stationed on a separate mission. No personnel were injured. Germany has not declared any military support. Chancellor Friedrich Merz offered solidarity in a call with Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman on Tuesday, but there were no concrete announcements. The German parliament did vote on Thursday to extend the country's involvement in an EU naval mission to protect shipping in the Red Sea, which is under threat by the Houthis. Past German governments had blocked the sale of Eurofighter jets to Saudi Arabia, but the veto was declared lifted in 2024 due to the kingdom's “stabilising role”. Poland has one of Europe's largest militaries but has not announced any military aid to Saudi Arabia. Many Polish resources have already gone to supporting Ukraine's war effort against Russia. Saudi Defence Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman spoke to his Polish counterpart Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz on Tuesday. He said the two countries had “reviewed their defence co-operation” and discussed ways to support regional security. It is not known if any military aid was discussed.

title: Gianni Infantino apologises to Fifa Council over World Cup sell-off plan
description: Swiss head of world football's governing body grilled during three-and-a-half-hour meeting in Zurich
content: Gianni Infantino has apologised to the Fifa Council about his failed attempt to sell off stakes in its competitions to private investors. But the president of Fifa also faced continuing questions about his role in the $4.2 billion Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) scheme during a three-and-a-half-hour meeting in Zurich. Infantino was also asked to provide more information regarding the suspension of United States attacker Folarin Balogun's ban during this summer's World Cup in North America and the Fifa Peace Prize controversially awarded to US President Donald Trump. English and German football chiefs said they remained unconvinced Infantino was fit to ⁠continue as the head of football's world governing body. The apology from Infantino again came with the caveat that the FFE plan had been only a proposal and “in no way a done deal”. “First of all I apologised for the mistakes that we made in relation to the communication and consultation process related to the Fifa Forward Enterprise project which led to many consequences,” said Infantino. “But what is important to remember is that it was a proposal and in no way a done deal, that actually intended to enable Fifa to invest more in our member associations, as opposed to replacing support from existing resources.” The FFE plan involved creating a company to run the commercial interests of Fifa competitions, including the World Cup, and selling ⁠a minority stake to private investors. Infantino said it was intended to generate additional funding for Fifa’s 211 member associations. While Infantino appeared to retain strong support among ​African officials, ⁠opposition from some of Europe’s most influential football associations remained ‌pronounced. German FA president Bernd Neuendorf called for a “complete restart” at Fifa, saying the governance reforms the organisation needed could not be delivered with Infantino in charge. “The first thing ​is we need reforms. That's true. And everyone knows that,” Neuendorf said. “The old administration has to be reformed, and the whole governance has to be reformed. But I'm pretty clear here in this that this is not possible with Gianni. “So we need a complete restart, I think, a political restart.” English FA chair Debbie Hewitt, a Fifa vice-president, insisted that too many questions remain unanswered after what she called the “most robust, most frank, most open Council meeting” she had experienced. “One of the disappointing things is that we didn't get answers to anything that we had specifically requested – for example getting the papers from FFE,” Hewitt said. “I asked the question 'why not?' – and we were asked to submit those questions in writing. “I think the man has to answer those questions and if he doesn't answer those questions now, he's not fit to be Fifa president – and that was what was shared in the meeting. “I've repeatedly asked for the papers to be shared. I haven't received them and still in spite of the request today, I haven't received them. “It is the rationale for why FFE happened in the way that it did, the Balogun case, the Peace Prize. “The responses to those questions, which I still don't have answers to, will determine from my personal point of view whether or not Gianni is the right candidate. “That will be the point at which or not we can say that any individual that was involved in FFE can or cannot be trusted because until we see what actually happened it's very difficult to say behaviour needs or not to change.”

title: IEA oil supply pledge to exceed target as it boosts release of remaining stocks
description: Agency's members agree to boost the roll-out of the remaining 100 million barrels, including more than 20 million barrels of diesel
content: The International Energy Agency (IEA) has said that its March pledge to release crude oil stocks will exceed its target, and will be accelerating the release of the remaining supplies as global efforts to tame soaring energy prices continue. Members of the Paris-based agency have so far released 330 million barrels of oil, and the remaining 100 million barrels – which includes more than 20 million barrels of diesel – will be released in a “timely manner consistent with national circumstances”, it said in a statement on Thursday. That would make the total releases exceed the initial 400 million barrels the IEA had pledged in March, at the onset of the war between US and Israel and Iran. “Some IEA members have released higher volumes than initially pledged in March while other members intend to do so,” the IEA said after a meeting. Specific plans are already in place ... [to release the stocks] as soon as possible.” Global energy prices remain volatile and elevated as the war in Iran, now in its eighth month, continues to choke energy supplies. Earlier this month, G7 leaders pledged to accelerate the IEA's co-ordinated emergency stock release by rolling out 100 million barrels of diesel and other reserves through the IEA to help to stabilise markets. And in a surprising move last week, US President Donald Trump's administration lifted sanctions on Russia to enable the latter to supply millions of barrels of diesel to global markets. The Opec + group, meanwhile, kept its oil production targets unchanged for November, extending the pause it started in October after six months of gradual increases. Oil prices rose after the IEA's announcement. Brent, the benchmark for two-thirds of the world's oil, added 0.15 per cent to $106.20 a barrel at 8.27pm UAE time. West Texas Intermediate, the gauge that tracks US crude, jumped 3.28 per cent to $98.21 a barrel. Thursday's IEA statement said it has “encouraged those IEA members holding oil production and refining capacities to boost supply of crude and refined products, particularly diesel”. The IEA said it will continue to monitor the progress of the completion of its March pledge, “and will inform G7 leaders as requested and the IEA governing board on further actions needed, based on an updated oil market assessment, focusing on diesel”, it added.

title: Yemen's Houthi rebels hit presidential palace in Aden
description: Attack caused deaths and injuries among security personnel but government members said to be unharmed
content: Yemen ’s Houthi rebels attacked the presidential palace in the southern city of Aden with five missiles on Thursday, the country's Information Minister Moammar Al Eryani said. He added that the Prime Minister and government members were safe, but two security guards were killed. It was the first attack on Aden since the Houthis and government forces resumed fighting last month after a four-year lull in the civil war. The southern port city has been the seat of Yemen’s government since the Iran-backed Houthis took over the capital Sanaa in 2014, prompting a military intervention by a Saudi-led coalition a year later. “We reassure the children of our Yemeni people that the Prime Minister, and all members of the government are safe and well,” Mr Al Eryani said in a statement. He described the attack as a terrorist act. A statement from the Council of Ministers said the attack involved missiles as well as drones and caused deaths and injuries among security personnel. It said the attack "clearly exposes the militia’s inability to confront the Yemeni people’s resolve to restore state authority across the entire national territory and to put an end to its Iranian-backed subversive agenda". The cabinet said the attack would not weaken the government’s resolve or deter it from carrying out its national and constitutional responsibilities. “Aden will remain the hub for the operations of state institutions as they carry out their duties towards citizens,” the statement said. The Houthi-run Saba News Agency reported earlier that the target was a military operations headquarters at the palace, allegedly run by Saudi officers, and associated weapons depots. The agency quoted a military source as saying the headquarters had been hit. Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said that the attack "falls within the framework of the declared policy to strike Saudi troop concentrations wherever they may be, and to treat any military presence of the Saudi enemy as a legitimate target for our forces, wherever it is located".

title: UK charity trustee belonged to sanctioned Iranian morality council
description: Supreme leader representative Ahmad Vaezi appeals Charity Commission ban
content: A member of a sanctioned Iranian morality body is taking legal action in the UK to appeal a ban which would prevent him from being a trustee of a charity for 12 years. Ahmad Vaezi is also the head of an Iranian propaganda body but has sought to cover up his links to the regime, a tribunal heard. Mr Vaezi is the head of the Islamic Propaganda Office (IPO), a member of Iran’s Supreme Council of the Cultural Revolution (SCCR) and the representative of Iran’s supreme leader on European student affairs. The SCCR was sanctioned in 2023 for its role in enforcing morality laws following the death of Mahsa Amini in prison after she was accused of breaking laws on wearing a headscarf. Mr Vaezi is appealing against a decision by the Charity Commission to disqualify him from serving as a trustee of the Al-Tawheed Charitable Trust. In a submission to a tribunal hearing the case in London, the commission’s lawyer, Adrian Francis, said Mr Vaezi’s close links to the Iranian regime “in themselves render him unfit to be a charity trustee”. Mr Vaezi has attended events in support of Hezbollah and Hamas, both of which are proscribed as terrorist organisations by Britain, said Mr Francis. “The commission’s case is that it is self-evident a charity should not associate itself with a regime of such ill-repute and that doing so brings it, and the charity sector generally, into disrepute,” he said. Mr Vaezi sought to obstruct the watchdog’s inquiry “by deliberate suppression of such links”, said Mr Francis. He also sought to “mislead and obstruct the commission” on events that took place at Al-Tawheed’s premises in West London “and has, at the very least, turned a blind eye to the extremist activities that students and others connected to the London property can be shown to have engaged”. Mr Francis said the Iranian “has dishonestly sought to withhold information about his links to the Iranian regime; then, when confronted with his failure to disclose them, lied about the reasons for doing so”. The tribunal was told that a group called the Islamic Student Associations of Britain (IASL), which is part of the Union of Islamic Associations of Students in Europe, reportedly organised a remembrance event for Qassem Suleimani, the head of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps' Quds Force, who was assassinated by the US in Baghdad in 2020. The student group allegedly live-streamed events featuring current and former IRGC officers, including Gen Saeed Ghasemi, in 2020 and 2021. Gen Ghasemi falsely claimed the Holocaust was “a lie and a fake” and said British students could “bring an end to the life of the oppressors and occupiers, Zionists and Jews across the world”. The video was shared at the time with the BBC by the US-based campaign group United Against Nuclear Iran. Mr Francis said this “demonstrates the British student group has engaged in extremist activity” and given Mr Vaezi’s 20-year association with the charity, it is “inconceivable he was not aware of the near-permanent presence and activities of the London student group”. The regulator is investigating the charity itself over the event and says it “is aware that speakers praised Suleimani and could hear anti-Semitic chants being made during the event”. Mr Vaezi, who also uses the surname Vaeijezei, remains a trustee while he appeals against the 12-year disqualification order imposed on him in January. He did not attend the hearing but details of his defence were provided in the commission’s submission to the tribunal. Mr Vaezi claims there is nothing inappropriate in being a member of the SCCR, despite its designation. He dismisses the designation as a political act and says his role is purely academic. He similarly contests that his leadership of the IPO, which he has held since February 2011, is incompatible with his trusteeship, insisting it is a non-political, educational, scientific and cultural institution that does not engage in propaganda. Another trustee, Seyed Moosavi, has appealed against his four-year disqualification for his role with Al-Tawheed and the Islamic Centre for England, one of the UK’s largest religious and cultural centres. A Charity Commission representative said it was “currently overseeing the remaining trustees’ progress on improving the charity’s governance and we put in place a protective order prohibiting a third party from using the charity’s premises”. “Decisions to suspend or disqualify trustees or senior managers of a charity are not taken lightly and are based on clear evidence it is necessary to protect charities,” the representative said.

title: Earliest evidence of human ancestor killed with wooden spear found in Iraqi cave
description: Violent death ended more than year of suffering for Neanderthal known as Shanidar A
content: Remains of a Neanderthal found in an Iraqi-Kurdistan cave reveal he died a violent death after more than a year of being cared for in agonising pain, a study has shown. The killing 75,000 years ago involved a sharpened wooden spear and may be the earliest example of lethal violence using such a weapon, archaeologists believe. A 15mm circular hole in the shoulder blade suggests a “heart shot”, in which the spear was thrust downwards to pass completely through the body, bringing rapid death. Tiny shards of displaced bone were pieced together to reveal how the spear would have penetrated the body. A spear tip or flint would have left a different shaped hole, researchers said in the study, published in the journal Scientific Reports . Other remains, notably damaged teeth, suggest the unfortunate individual – thought to have been around 45 years old when they died – had suffered a brutal facial injury at least a year earlier, and would have needed looking after. “It is fascinating to have evidence for both compassion and violence amongst Neanderthals, our closest evolutionary cousins, embodied in this one individual,” said Prof Graeme Barker, fellow of St John’s College, Cambridge, who led the excavation. The Neanderthal has been named Shanidar A by researchers, after the cave on the Bradost Mountain in Erbil where the remains were found. The scapula bone, or shoulder blade – broad, flat and so thin in places it is almost translucent – was preserved intact under rock and sediment, along with a mostly complete right hand and two ribs. “It’s extraordinary to have a perfectly preserved scapula from 75,000 years ago. These bones are so thin that you often don’t get complete scapulae from modern burials,” said Dr Emma Pomeroy, study lead author from Cambridge’s Department of Archaeology. “We were able to lift it out in one piece from under almost eight metres of rock and sediment.” The earliest known rounded wooden spear, pulled from the sea in Clacton-on-Sea, England, in 1911, is more than 400,000 years old. But very few wooden objects from prehistory survive due to the inevitable decomposition. Some waterlogged examples of spears dated to around 200,000 years ago – when early Neanderthals roamed Europe – were found in Schoningen, Germany, in the 1990s. They were around two metres long and used for throwing, like modern javelins, to hunt large game. The researchers believe a similar weapon caused Shanidar A’s death. “Holes left by recreations of spears from this time are an excellent fit for the one we found in the Neanderthal scapula,” said Dr Pomeroy. “What evidence we have suggests that Neanderthals and their ancestors developed woodworking and weapon-making skills many thousands of years before the death of Shanidar A.” She said it was possible the death might have been in a hunting accident, but the evidence suggests deliberate violence was more likely. “Animals such as mammoths may have been hunted up close with thrusting spears, so it’s easy to imagine lethal injuries,” she said. “The position of the wound and the force required to push it right through the Neanderthal’s body bear the hallmarks of an intended kill shot directed towards the heart.” It is possible that the fatal blow was struck by an early human, as they had evolved by that time, but violence between Neanderthals seems a more straightforward explanation. “All we can ever know about the end of this Neanderthal’s life is that it was violent, and came at the end of a wooden spear,” said Prof Barker. One of the seven teeth that were found had been split lengthways with only half remaining, with the others twisted inward. The half tooth had significant tartar build-up along the exposed root canal, suggesting it stayed in the mouth for some time after a blow to the face. Surviving a trauma that splits a tooth in this fashion, then continuing to live and eat for at least a year would have required care and support from other Neanderthals,” said Dr Pomeroy. Shanidar A may have been fed soft food. Previous research on sediment in Shanidar Cave shows that plants were being soaked before cooking around the same time. “There’s no doubt that Shanidar A would have had difficulty communicating and been in absolute agony for a long period of time,” said Prof Barker. “The remains of Shanidar A reflect the dual nature of so much of what we recognise as human. On the one hand, we have evidence of a terribly violent end. On the other, this was clearly an individual who was cared for during their lifetime.” The vast cave in the foothills of Iraqi Kurdistan known as Shanidar is one of the world’s most famous Neanderthal sites. Excavations in the 1950s led by Ralph Solecki found remains from 10 individuals, including a “cluster” of four in the same spot despite dying at different times, suggesting the Neanderthals had returned to inter their dead. Remains of a Neanderthal from another part of the cave, who lived thousands of years later, showed evidence of a paralysed arm, arthritis, deafness and partial blindness. Yet they had lived a long life, so must have been cared for. Shanidar A is one of five Neanderthals unearthed in 2020 in a part of a cave just 1.5 metres long and one metre deep, directly behind a large vertical boulder, thought to be a “prominent marker”. The body was positioned on its back, head facing east. “These Neanderthals returned to the same place to lay their dead to rest,” said Dr Pomeroy. “Some were deposited before the earlier body had fully decomposed, so this was happening within years or decades.”

title: UK arm of Iran's 'hate' TV channel reported to police under national security law
description: HispanTV has ties to another Iranian broadcaster that was banned from the UK
content: The UK government has come under fire for failing to tackle an Iranian TV company registered in Britain for the past 15 years, despite links to the banned channel Press TV. HispanTV, focused on the Spanish-speaking world, is part of state-owned Islamic Republic of Iran Broadcasting (Irib) and has faced accusations of acting as Iran's “long arm of hate”. Its UK arm was this week reported to police under national security laws by a senior British politician. Alicia Kearns, the UK's shadow Home Office Minister, told The National she had complained to the Met Police that HispanTV was allegedly breaching the Foreign Influence Registration Scheme. Records show the current and former owners of the UK entity had close ties with Press TV , Iran’s English-language state broadcaster, which broadcast from London studios until 2012 when its licence was revoked by the UK’s media regulator, Ofcom. According to Companies House, HispanTV has been registered as a business in the UK since January 2011, with its current address given as a unit on an industrial estate in north-west London. Seyedmehdi Mirtaleb, who is listed as the director and majority shareholder, was an executive producer at Press TV in London from 2009 until 2020, according to his LinkedIn profile. The 48-year-old is listed as a British citizen on Companies House but in a previous entry his nationality was given as Iranian. The records show that HispanTV was originally registered by a Hamid Khairoldin, 68, but he resigned as a director and gave up his ownership of the company in 2014. When PressTV was registered as a company in the UK, Mr Khairoldin was listed as a director from 2007 to 2010. Ofcom told The National that HispanTV has never been licensed to broadcast in the UK and so it had not acted on its presence as a company. Press TV's licence to broadcast was removed by Ofcom in 2012 after it failed to pay a £100,000 fine imposed for broadcasting an interview with imprisoned journalist Maziar Bahari, which the regulator said had been conducted under duress. Ofcom also said it had breached several broadcasting licence rules over editorial control of the channel. Shortly before PressTV was banned, it shared a Companies House-registered address with HispanTV in a west London office block. The umbrella Irib is sanctioned by the US and EU, while some of its directors were listed by the UK for overseeing the programming decisions that led to human rights violations. HispanTV's global remit is broadcasting news, documentaries, movies and Iranian films 24 hours a day. Its activities in the UK are unclear. It does not appear to make programmes or broadcast from the UK, but its footprint is aimed at Latin American nations. The UK is a global media hub where the industry clusters for business and talent, as well as broadcast assets. When The National visited its current registered UK address, the unit was occupied by another business which said it had never heard of HispanTV. Businesses in nearby units said the lock-up had previously been empty for a number of years. Since a change in the law this summer, the UK requires anyone carrying out political influence activities in the UK at the direction of any foreign power to register their arrangements. The law came into effect in 2025 under the National Security Act to increase transparency and protect the UK from covert state-backed interference. “There is no question that it is not conducive to national security to have these types of outlets operating in the UK – they are cut-outs of the Iranian state,” Ms Kearns told The National. The Tory politician, whose brief includes national security, said she has previously raised the presence of media linked to Iran and its allies with both the police and government. Ms Kearns recently raised the issue of the Houthi TV station Al Masirah TV in the House of Commons. The company's presence in the UK was revealed by The National earlier this year and raised concerns over alleged illicit funding, visa facilitation and intelligence gathering on political rivals. “I feel like I'm sitting in this limbo where I'm screaming and shouting and neither the police nor the government are doing anything at all,” she said. “It's preposterous. We’ve got to get them shut down. What I do not understand is how the government doesn't understand these cut-outs are risks to our society.” Mr Mirtaleb and Mr Khairoldin have been approached for comment. HispanTV'S UK arm was founded with £1 in share capital and has filed limited accounts under rules for small businesses that exempt it from providing details of its turnover. It has been listed as dormant since 2012 and its accounts state its assets have remained at £1 throughout its existence. HispanTV's Spanish-language service went on air from Tehran in October 2011 and was officially launched by President Mahmoud Ahmadinejad in January the following year. “The new channel will limit the ground for supremacy of dominance-seekers,” Mr Ahmadinejad said during a ceremony marking the inauguration. “It will be a means for better ties between people and governments of Iran and Spanish-speaking nations.” The channel was launched on the back of Iran’s attempts to establish strong commercial, political and strategic links with South America at a time when it had been hit with tough sanctions for its nuclear programme. For a time it had a base in Madrid, but it was closed down in 2013 by the Spanish government as part of broader EU sanctions against Iran. In a report earlier this year, HispanTV was described by the Anti-Defamation League as the “leading platform peddling anti-Semitic hate and disseminating anti-Israel prejudice and incitement across Latin America and the wider Spanish‑speaking world”. The study found that HispanTV has significantly ramped up its rhetoric over the last two years through its satellite, cable and live-streaming broadcasting, as well as its website. It has more than a quarter of a million followers on social media. An earlier ADL study called HispanTV: “The Iranian Regime’s Long Arm of Hate in Latin America.” United Against Nuclear Iran (Uani) says HispanTV “serves as an arm of Iran’s public diplomacy outreach to Latin America, a region in which Iran has invested significant political capital”. “The UK continues to harbour a permissive environment for these media arms of the Iranian regime,” Jason Brodsky, Uani’s policy director, told The National . “HispanTV is part of the Irib, which is under US sanctions for its ties to the Iranian intelligence services. “PressTV has those ties as well. Former Irib executives are under UK sanctions. At a time when the Islamic Republic is plotting terror on UK soil, the UK government should be cracking down on these networks' freedom of movement on British soil. There must be a reassessment as to how these networks are using UK soil as a platform.” The continued presence of HispanTV in the UK comes amid an escalation of attacks which Iran is believed to be behind. These include arson attacks on Jewish volunteer ambulances, a synagogue and Iran International TV, a broadcaster critical of the regime. Responsibility for the attacks was claimed by a group named Harakat Ashab Al Yamin Al Islamia, or Ashab Al Yamin. It is widely believed to be a creation of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) .

title: Syria sentences two to death over coastal sectarian violence
description: Military court in Aleppo hands prison terms to three other defendants
content: A Syrian military court has sentenced two men to death over sectarian violence along the country's coast in March 2025, state news agency Sana reported on Thursday. Three other defendants received prison terms and two were acquitted at the Military Criminal Court in Aleppo. Al Waddah Ismail and Maher Ali were convicted of seeking to incite civil war and sectarian fighting, and leading armed gangs with the intent of attacking public forces. Both were sentenced to death. Maher Othman was sentenced to 12 years in prison for complicity in the two offences, while Mohammed Bakour received a 20-year sentence for intentional murder and Ammar Abdul Aal was sentenced to three years for torture. The court acquitted Abdul Raouf Bakrjan and Mohammed Zarzouri. Public hearings began at the Palace of Justice in Aleppo on November 18, 2025. The latest verdicts follow rulings on September 17 in cases involving four other defendants accused of violations during the violence, in which pro-government fighters killed hundreds of members of the Alawite minority. At that hearing, one was sentenced to death, another to life imprisonment and a third to 20 years in prison, while the fourth was acquitted. The violence followed attacks on army and security facilities on March 6, 2025. A national investigative committee reported on July 22 last year that remnants of the deposed regime of Bashar Al Assad had carried out widespread attacks that killed 238 military and security personnel. The committee also documented violations against civilians in the days that followed the attacks. It concluded that the abuses were not organised or systematic, but were committed by individuals and small groups for various motives. Separately, Syria’s General Intelligence Service has arrested Ali Kayali, also known as Mihrac Ural, a key suspect in the 2013 Baniyas massacre , as he attempted to flee across the border, Sana reported. Mr Kayali formed an armed militia that fought alongside forces of the deposed Assad regime during the Syrian civil war. The militia was implicated in mass killings in several parts of the country, including Al Bayda and Ras Al Nabaa in Baniyas. According to the Syrian Network for Human Rights, 264 civilians, including 36 children and 28 women, were killed in Al Bayda, while 195 civilians, including 56 children and 43 women, were killed in the Ras Al Nabaa. Reports and testimonies described summary executions using firearms and bladed weapons, as well as the burning of homes and bodies. Militias affiliated with Kayali were also accused of carrying out massacres in the countryside of Latakia, Aleppo and Idlib, leaving hundreds dead or wounded. He is also the main suspect for the twin bombings in Reyhanli in Turkey’s southern Hatay province in 2013, killing 52 people, according to Anadolu Agency. Earlier this month, Turkish intelligence arrested Omar Al Khatib, one of the alleged planners of the Reyhanli bombing, as he attempted to flee by sea to Europe. He had co-ordinated between the attackers and members of the deposed regime’s intelligence services, according to the report. On October 4, Syrian security forces arrested Jamal Tarabulsi, Kayali’s deputy. The Interior Ministry has said it is continuing to pursue those accused of violations against civilians during the Assad regime as part of efforts to advance transitional justice and hold accountable those responsible.

title: UAE 'better prepared' for war than when US conflict with Iran began, says official
description: Hundreds of members of Iranian sleeper cells arrested, says chairman of FNC's Defence, Interior and Foreign Affairs Committee
content: The UAE is "better prepared" for a resumption of full-scale war should it happen, a senior official said on Thursday, amid a US-Iran diplomatic deadlock and growing signs of a potential return to major confrontation between the two countries. Dr Ali Rashid Al Nuaimi, chairman of the Defence, Interior and Foreign Affairs Committee of the Federal National Council, was speaking to journalists in Dubai. Asked by The National about the possibility of war resuming and the country's level of preparedness, Dr Al Nuaimi said the UAE is “better prepared than it was on February 28”, when the US and Israel launched strikes against Iran, which sparked the regional war . “The war can resume, yes,” he said, adding that “the readiness” in the UAE was in “all aspects” and that “whatever is needed to protect the country and the people, we will do it”. A ceasefire began in June when the US and Iran signed a memorandum of understanding intended to pave the way for a final peace settlement. US President Donald Trump declared the truce and MoU “over” in early July after renewed Iranian attacks on ships in the Strait of Hormuz and retaliatory American strikes. Both sides have indicated in recent weeks that they are preparing for a resumption of hostilities. At the peak of the war, Iran attacked the UAE and other Gulf states with ballistic missiles and drones, attempting to strike civilian infrastructure, including energy sites and airports. The UAE was the most heavily attacked country, facing more than 550 ballistic missiles and 2,265 drones, most of which were intercepted or destroyed before reaching their targets. In April, the UAE State Security Department said it had dismantled a terrorist organisation operating inside the Emirates. The department sanctioned the arrests of the group's members over suspected involvement in activities aimed at undermining national unity and carrying out planned sabotage operations inside the country. The organisation was discovered to be holding secret meetings inside and outside the UAE, surveillance reports said. The group was also found to be trying to recruit young Emiratis by spreading “misleading ideas” in the hope of gaining their support for “foreign allegiances”. The UAE also announced the dismantling of a “terrorist network” funded and operated by Lebanon’s Hezbollah and Iran and the arrest of its members. The network was said to have been operating in the UAE using a fake commercial cover and had tried to infiltrate the national economy and conduct “external schemes” against the country’s financial stability. Dr Al Nuaimi said “hundreds” of members of Iranian sleeper cells were arrested, including several Emiratis, after they were “caught guiding Iranian [attacks using] missiles and drones” to hit targets in the UAE. “They wanted to undermine and destroy this model,” he said. Despite this, he said, dialogue remains a priority for the UAE . He added that if Iran took one step towards rebuilding trust, the UAE would take further steps in response, but stressed that, for now, “we don't trust them”.

title: What are Saudi Arabia's options to deter the Yemeni rebels?
description: Senior US official tells The National that Trump administration has no plans to announce new military operations in Yemen
content: Saudi Arabia is facing a familiar problem in Yemen: having the military resources to strike the Iran-backed Houthis hard, but no guarantee that a campaign will stop the heavily armed militant group from threatening the kingdom again. The latest wave of missile and drone attacks has brought that dilemma into sharper focus, with Houthi strikes hitting Saudi airports and threatening critical energy infrastructure, including Saudi Aramco ’s headquarters in Dhahran. While Saudi Arabia ’s challenge is restoring deterrence, analysts say Riyadh’s options are narrow. They include intensifying air strikes, bolstering Yemeni government forces on the ground, strengthening air defences and seeking renewed diplomatic engagement. “Saudi Arabia should apply military pressure on the Houthis inside Yemen to deter further attacks,” Abdulaziz Sager, chairman of the Gulf Research Centre, told The National . “A key priority is to limit their ability to launch cross-border attacks, particularly by degrading their missile capabilities.” Tensions between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis began to escalate in July, when an air strike hit Sanaa International Airport, an attack the Houthis blamed on Saudi Arabia. Yemen’s Saudi-backed, internationally recognised government claimed responsibility, saying it had hit the runway to prevent an unauthorised Iranian aircraft from landing. The strike tested a fragile period of calm that had largely held since a truce took effect in 2022. The Houthis subsequently launched missiles towards Saudi Arabia, while fighting between the group and Yemeni forces intensified. Mr Sager said that the kingdom had accepted the principle of a ceasefire with the Houthis and remained committed to de-escalation. “However, renewed military pressure may be necessary before agreeing to another ceasefire to secure credible commitments that attacks will stop,” he added. The Houthis have been fighting the Yemeni government since seizing Sanaa in 2014. Saudi Arabia intervened in 2015 at the head of a coalition of regional allies to support the government against the rebels. Saudi Arabia has one of the world’s largest military budgets and a sophisticated arsenal, including American warplanes, missile-defence systems and other advanced weapons. However, Aziz Alghashian, a senior non-resident fellow at the Gulf International Forum, said defeating the Houthis militarily would require more than air power. The kingdom has demonstrated its ability to conduct air operations, but he explained that a successful campaign would also require effective ground forces capable of changing the balance of power in Houthi-held territory. Maritime forces would be needed to restrict the movement of supplies reaching the group through the Red Sea and from the Horn of Africa, he added. That combination could be difficult to assemble. Yemeni forces opposed to the Houthis have improved their capabilities, but continue to face problems of competence and political fragmentation. “The reason why the Houthis may hold what they have is not because of their strength, but really the weakness of the other ground operation,” said Mr Alghashian. “A state-building approach would also be needed.” The Houthis, once regarded as a relatively poorly equipped militia, have developed into a formidable fighting force. Their arsenal includes missiles and drones that can strike targets more than 1,000 miles away. Since the war in Gaza erupted in 2023, the group has launched hundreds of drones and missiles towards Israel . Most were intercepted, but some reached their targets, including a drone strike in Tel Aviv that killed a man in 2024 and a missile strike near Ben Gurion Airport last year. The war between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis is a spillover from the wider war with Iran that the US and Israel launched in February. Washington and Tehran have not yet reached a lasting peace agreement . In recent weeks, they have exchanged proposals to end the war and reopen the Strait of Hormuz, a vital artery for global energy shipments, but negotiations have not resumed. Some observers argue that a broader agreement between the US and Iran offers the most viable path to ending Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia. Under such a deal, the US could seek Iranian commitments to rein in the Houthis and secure an end to their attacks as part of a regional settlement. But whether the group would comply with such an arrangement is not known. The US supports Saudi Arabia in countering the Houthis through arms sales, military advisers, intelligence sharing and targeting assistance, though it has avoided direct military combat operations. President Donald Trump has said he is considering joining strikes against the Houthis, as the rebels attack a US ally and threaten global energy supplies. The Houthis have warned that any US strikes could prompt them to attack American personnel and interests across the Middle East, potentially drawing the US deeper into the seven-and-a-half-month war. But a senior US official has told The National that the Trump administration has “no announcements to make regarding US support for new military operations” in Yemen. The official added that the administration remains in continuous dialogue with Saudi Arabia and the Yemeni government. “We will always fulfil our commitments to our partners,” said the official without elaborating. Mr Alghashian believes American firepower could deter the Houthis, at least initially. But he cautioned that the rebels may be prepared to absorb the strikes and wait for US resolve to weaken. “The Houthis feel they will try to weather the storm. Their calculation seems to be that they have withstood many storms before,” he added. “The Saudis still need their allies and still need to focus on alliances for defence.” Mr Trump ordered a bombing campaign against the Houthis last year, but declared a swift victory after the US expended weapons and munitions at a rate of about $1 billion in the first month alone, according to US media reports. “Saudi Arabia should mobilise the international community to respond to this aggression against the kingdom. Strengthening Saudi defensive capabilities and securing support from regional and international partners are essential to protecting its territory and deterring further attacks,” affirmed Mr Sager.

title: The global water conversation is changing – now the UAE and the world must act
description: Our objective at the UN water conference in Abu Dhabi this year should be to build momentum around investment, international co-operation, innovation and implementation
content: One of the defining characteristics of UN conferences is the opportunity to bring together perspectives and stakeholders whose paths might otherwise rarely cross. During the high-level week at the 81st UN General Assembly in New York last month, I engaged to technology leaders on artificial intelligence, investors on infrastructure, policymakers on climate resilience, business leaders on opportunity, and researchers and development institutions on sustainable development. These conversations reflected different priorities, yet increasingly converged around a common question: how can we build a future that is more resilient, more prosperous and better equipped to withstand disruption? Time and again, the conversation came back to water. This was not simply a matter of increased attention to water as a standalone issue. Rather, it reflected a growing recognition of its fundamental role in addressing the interconnected challenges facing communities, countries and economies. Food security depends on water . The energy transformation depends on water. Economic strength depends on water. And thriving communities require reliable access to safe water. For many years, those working to advance the global water agenda have emphasised the importance of integrating water into discussions on climate, food, energy, infrastructure, economic growth and development. Increasingly, however, water is being recognised as an integral part of these discussions in its own right. This shift reflects an important evolution in how the international community understands the relationship between water and sustainable development. We are increasingly recognising water not only as a resource we need to conserve, but also as a strategic asset we need to invest in – one that underpins resilience, enables opportunity and supports long-term prosperity. The scale of the challenge is clear. Agriculture accounts for about 70 per cent of global freshwater withdrawals, while millions of livelihoods depend on water-intensive sectors. When water becomes unreliable, the consequences extend well beyond the water sector, affecting food prices, employment, businesses, communities and investment. Yet the human impact is even more significant. When water is scarce or unsafe, women and girls often carry a disproportionate burden. Globally, women and girls are responsible for fetching water in more than 70 per cent of households. Instead of receiving an education, learning a new skill or joining the workforce, women and girls are collectively spending 200 to 250 million hours every single day collecting and hauling water. Water security is fundamentally about people. It is about peace, stability and human dignity. When water systems are disrupted, livelihoods are disrupted. When scarcity puts pressure on communities, resilience is tested. And when countries share rivers, aquifers and water systems, co-operation becomes essential . Water can be a source of pressure. But it can also be a reason to co-operate and collaborate. That matters even more at a time when faith in international co-operation is under increasing pressure. We are living through a period of profound global change, when trust between countries and confidence in multilateral institutions cannot be taken for granted. Yet there are challenges that no country can solve alone – and water is one of them. Every country depends on water, every economy depends on it, and every family needs it. That gives us an opportunity to demonstrate that international co-operation can still deliver something tangible: solutions that improve lives, strengthen resilience and create opportunity. Here in the UAE, we understand this connection particularly well. We live in one of the world’s most water-scarce regions . For us, water has shaped how we think about our cities, our economy and our future. This understanding also informs our approach to international co-operation. At Cop28, hosted by the UAE in 2023, the adoption of the historic UAE Consensus by 198 Parties demonstrated the importance of collective action in addressing interconnected climate challenges. It reinforced the need to advance climate ambition through practical solutions, international co-operation and implementation. Beyond that event, we have spent years talking about climate, energy, food, technology and water as separate agendas. But now those boundaries are disappearing. Climate change is intensifying droughts, floods and water variability around the world. Extreme weather is placing greater pressure on economies, infrastructure and communities. At the same time, the world is rapidly electrifying, investing in new technologies, expanding digital infrastructure and seeking pathways to sustainable growth. Water systems require energy. Energy systems require water. Food production depends on both. And the rapid growth of AI and digital infrastructure is creating a new set of demands on these interconnected systems. This is why we recently launched the Crosscurrents Report , examining the growing relationship between AI, water and energy. The report highlights a dual challenge. As digital infrastructure expands, its demand for energy and water will grow. But there is another side to the story: AI is also helping us manage water better – from detecting leaks and improving irrigation to forecasting drought, optimising infrastructure and strengthening decision-making. The significance of this extends beyond AI itself. It points to a broader truth: the systems that underpin our economies can no longer be planned in isolation. Decisions about energy affect water. Decisions about water influence food production , industry, communities and economic growth. Climate adaptation affects all of them. The future will not be built by solving one issue at a time. It will depend on how effectively we understand these connections and plan for them together. What gave me optimism during our discussions in New York was the scale of the coalition engaging with these challenges and opportunities. The most encouraging discussions were not confined to governments or traditional water stakeholders – instead, they involved investors, technology companies, financial institutions, entrepreneurs, researchers, young leaders and development organisations. There is growing recognition that resilience is a shared responsibility. But awareness alone will not close the gap. We know many of the solutions. We have better technologies , better data and better tools than we did a decade ago. We know more about reuse, storage, loss reduction and efficient desalination. The challenge is getting those solutions out of the pilot phase – to translate ideas into impact. How do we connect capital to projects? Innovation to deployment? Technology to communities? And international commitments to action on the ground? These are the questions I heard often in New York . And they are the questions that will matter most at the UN Water Conference in Abu Dhabi in December. The conference, co-hosted by the UAE and Senegal, will bring these conversations together. The event will hold special significance as the first UN Water Conference to be co-hosted by two nations from the Global South, reflecting their role as active partners in shaping solutions and driving international action on water. It is also the first UN conference focused on accelerating the implementation of SDG 6, which addresses clean water and sanitation services. Our ambition is to build momentum around investment, international co-operation, innovation and implementation – and to keep that momentum going long after December. That means bringing governments together with investors, development institutions with the private sector, technology companies with communities, researchers with policymakers. And, critically, giving youth a seat at the table – not simply asking them to listen to the decisions of today, but empowering them to help shape the solutions of tomorrow. We understand that the future of water will not be solved by one government, one institution nor one technology – it will be solved by what we do together. The strongest lesson I took away from the General Assembly last month was that for the first time the global conversation is truly changing. Water is moving from the margins to the centre – of economic planning, climate and humanitarian resilience, sustainable development, technology, food and energy transformations, and international co-operation. At a time when global confidence in international co-operation is being tested, water gives us a practical opportunity to prove what it can achieve. If we get water right, the benefits will be boundless – healthier communities, greater opportunity for women and girls, stronger economies, more resilient food and energy systems, stronger digital infrastructure, and greater peace and stability. The conversation has shifted. Now, the water conference will turn that momentum into action. Together, we invite everyone, no matter where they may be in the world, to join us in reimagining water’s role in creating a better future for all, driving co-operation, growth, resilience and opportunity.

title: Robbery, harassment and fraud rise across England and Wales
description: Robberies against businesses had biggest increase after change in the way UK police record theft and violence in shops
content: Robbery, harassment and fraud are among the offences that rose in England and Wales in the year to March 2026, according to the Office for National Statistics. The broader Crime Survey for England and Wales estimated 9.6 million incidents overall, which reveals no major statistical change from the previous year. However, as some crimes fell, others rose. Police recorded 87,362 robberies, up 10 per cent. That rise came from business robberies, which increased 91 per cent to 29,669. The ONS says this was mainly because police were told to record shop thefts involving violence or threats as robbery from April 2025. Robberies of personal property fell by 9 per cent. Recorded rapes rose 4 per cent to 74,727. Violence without injury edged up 2 per cent, while violence with injury fell 3 per cent. The ONS cautions that police figures for these offences are not a reliable guide to trends, as they can be affected by changes in recording and by more victims coming forward. Harassment rose 6 per cent, according to police records, but the ONS says those figures are not a good indicator of trends. Its survey found a statistically significant rise in repeated harassment: from 2.3 per cent to 3.5 per cent of adults aged 16 and over, or about 1.7 million people. The estimates are interim. The survey also found that the number of adult fraud victims rose 10 per cent to 3.8 million. Bank and credit account fraud incidents increased 15 per cent to about 2.8 million. Total fraud incidents reached 4.5 million, with no statistically significant change.

title: President Sheikh Mohamed offers condolences to Saudi King after airport strikes
description: Sheikh Mohammed bin Rashid, Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed and Sheikh Dr Sultan bin Muhammad Al Qasimi also expressed their sympathies
content: UAE leaders have sent condolences to Saudi Arabia's King Salman bin Abdulaziz following attacks by Yemen’s Houthi rebels on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, which left several people dead and hundreds injured. President Sheikh Mohamed expressed his sincere sympathy for the victims of the attacks and wished the injured a speedy recovery. Sheikh Mohammed bin Rashid, Vice President and Ruler of Dubai, and Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed, Vice President, Deputy Prime Minister and Chairman of the Presidential Court, sent similar condolences to King Salman. Sheikh Dr Sultan bin Muhammad Al Qasimi, Ruler of Sharjah, also sent his condolences to the Saudi King. King Khalid International Airport has been shut since an attack on Saturday killed 13 people and injured more than 300, the deadliest on the kingdom in more than ​a decade. On Sunday, another strike killed one person and injured nearly a dozen others. The Houthi rebels have launched attacks other airports in Saudi Arabia in the past week, hitting sites not only in the capital but in Abha, Jazan and Najran, with a projectile also damaging the airport serving Dammam. The strikes have disrupted air travel across the region, including flights from the UAE. Emirates, flydubai and Air Arabia have cancelled a number of flights to Saudi destinations, while Etihad Airways has cancelled services between Abu Dhabi and Riyadh until October 18.

title: Riyadh Fashion Week postponed to next year in latest Saudi event shake-up
description: Other gatherings that have been rescheduled include the Red Sea International Film Festival and Soundstorm
content: Riyadh Fashion Week has been postponed until next year, organisers said late on Wednesday, a day before the event was scheduled to begin in the Saudi capital. The fourth iteration of the annual fashion event was to run from October 15 to 20, bringing together local and international designers for six days of runway shows and industry meetings. The changes come amid heightened regional tension and Saudi security concerns, although organisers of Riyadh Fashion Week have not publicly linked their decision to the situation. The decision is the latest in a series of changes to Saudi Arabia's cultural and entertainment calendar, after the postponement of the Red Sea International Film Festival and the cancellation of this year's Soundstorm music festival. The Red Sea International Film Festival, originally scheduled to take place in Jeddah from December 3 to 12, has been pushed back to the last quarter of 2027. Organisers said the decision followed a review of the event's timing and logistical requirements, but did not give a more specific reason. Meanwhile, the Joy Awards , which are usually held in January and have attracted leading Arab and international stars to Riyadh, are reportedly set to be scrapped in 2027 amid a broader reassessment of spending on major entertainment events. The General Entertainment Authority and MBC Group, organisers of the ceremony, have yet to officially confirm the move. First held in 2023, Riyadh Fashion Week was launched as part of efforts by the Saudi Fashion Commission to promote the kingdom's growing fashion industry and provide a platform for local designers to reach international audiences. The event has since grown in prominence, attracting major international labels alongside established and emerging Saudi talent. Last year's edition featured British fashion house Vivienne Westwood , which opened the event, while Stella McCartney made her Saudi debut with a runway show that brought the week to a close. The programme also highlighted regional designers, reflecting the event's ambition to establish Riyadh as a destination on the international fashion calendar. Organisers have yet to announce the dates or programme for the 2027 edition.

title: DFSA fines immigration firm Hayman-Woodward Dh1.67m for unlicensed services
description: Breaches were committed for more than six years
content: The Dubai Financial Services Authority (DFSA) has fined the Dubai unit of Hayman-Woodward Global Mobility Services (HWW DIFC) $454,367 (Dh1.67 million) for providing unauthorised services for more than six years. HWW DIFC was found to have carried out client services in or from Dubai International Financial Centre without being registered as a designated non-financial business or profession (DNFBP), DFSA said in a statement on Thursday. The company is incorporated in the DIFC, but its business activities are only permitted for management consultancies and document clearing services. The DFSA found that HWW DIFC breached DNFBP regulations, specifically by acting as a formation agent of legal persons, and providing a registered office, business address, correspondence and administrative address for companies and legal persons. The unauthorised services were provided to 71 clients between August 2018 and February 2025. HWW DIFC also signed agreements with three free zones outside the DIFC to assist in company set-ups and other customer service provider transactions. The penalty comprises the fine and a disgorgement, or the surrender of any profits obtained from unlawful acts. The fine, however, was reduced by 30 per cent, from $522,047.05, after Hayman-Woodward agreed to settle the case. “The DNFBP regime is a key component of the DFSA's framework for mitigating money laundering and other financial crime risks within the DIFC,” said Alan Linning, managing director for enforcement at the DFSA. “Businesses that provide company service provider and other DNFBP services can present elevated financial crime risks and are therefore subject to appropriate regulatory oversight and supervision.” Authorities in the UAE have been vigilant in cracking down on entities that breach regulations as part of efforts to maintain the Emirati financial system's integrity and reliability. Earlier this month, the DFSA imposed a Dh401,000 fine on wealth management services firm Vault Wealth for conducting transactions without authorisation. Last week, the Registration Authority of Abu Dhabi's ADGM imposed fines totalling $100,000 against PKF Accountants and Business Advisers over regulatory failings. The UAE Central Bank has also imposed fines on lenders that have violated rules, especially those on anti-money laundering. “The DFSA remains committed to developing, administering and enforcing world-class regulation of financial services within the DIFC,” the authority said. It added it will continue to take “appropriate enforcement action to protect users and prospective users of financial services and to preserve confidence in the DIFC’s regulatory framework”.

title: Sheikha Latifa hosts women leaders' majlis in Dubai to discuss innovation and opportunities
description: Dubai Culture chairwoman leads discussions on women's role in shaping future of leadership
content: Sheikha Latifa bint Mohammed has hosted an international gathering of women leaders in Dubai , bringing together voices from 22 countries to explore the future of leadership and innovation. The Women Leading the Future majlis was organised as part of the Annual Meeting of Global Future Leaders, which was delivered through a partnership between the UAE Government, the World Economic Forum and the Dubai Future Foundation. The majlis, on Wednesday, brought together 29 women leaders from government, entrepreneurship, science , technology, finance and culture. Discussions considered the choices, responsibilities and collaboration required to create opportunities for the next generation, with a focus on women's contributions to public leadership, innovation, investment and social change. Sheikha Latifa, chairwoman of Dubai Culture and Arts Authority, emphasised the UAE's commitment to investing in women's capabilities and equipping them with the knowledge, skills and experience to drive sustainable change. She highlighted the growing importance of diverse perspectives as artificial intelligence and emerging technology reshape industries, working practices and everyday life. She also noted the critical roles women play across sectors in fostering integration, harnessing technology to create opportunities and strengthening social cohesion. Shaping humanity's future, she said, was a shared responsibility requiring broader participation and practical, sustainable solutions to tomorrow's challenges. This first Annual Meeting of Global Future Leaders brought together more than 700 leaders and experts from 100 countries, including ministers, officials, 300 Young Global Leaders and 150 UAE government leaders. It served as a forum for international dialogue on developing responses to future challenges.

title: Hezbollah claims ownership of explosive-laden vehicle seized by Lebanese army
description: MP says weapons were intended to confront Israeli forces and accuses Lebanese PM of 'sowing internal discord'
content: Hezbollah MP Hassan Fadlallah ⁠said ​on Thursday an explosive-laden vehicle ​seized by the Lebanese Armed Forces last week belonged to the Iran-backed group. Mr Fadlallah said Hezbollah had contacted Lebanese authorities to claim ownership of the vehicle as soon as it was intercepted. Its contents were intended “to confront the Israeli occupation” and Hezbollah's weapons were “pointed exclusively at the [Israeli] enemy”, he added. Lebanon's Prime Minister Nawaf Salam said there would be “no leniency” in the investigation and the government “will not tolerate anyone who dares to toy with the country's security, safety and stability”. About 250kg of TNT-type explosives and 250kg of C4 were discovered in a vehicle bound for Beirut when it was stopped at an Internal Security Forces checkpoint at Dahr Al Baidar in the Bekaa Valley. Then on Monday the Lebanese Armed Forces on Monday said it had seized 200kg of explosives, foiling a smuggling attempt from Syria through the Hermel border region. The Dahr Al Baidar seizure – one of three such interceptions in a matter of weeks – comes as pressure is mounting on the Lebanese government to disarm Hezbollah and bring all weapons in the country under state control. The seizure also caused widespread uproar in Lebanon. While the case is being investigated by a military court, some ministers at a cabinet meeting on Thursday are expected to push for it to be heard by Lebanon's Judicial Council, which deals with serious state security threats. Meanwhile, Hezbollah has remained defiant in rejecting disarmament and says any talks on the fate of its weapons can take place only after Israel halts attacks on Lebanon and withdraws from occupied Lebanese territory. Israel and Hezbollah have engaged in several bouts of fighting since the onset of the Gaza war in October 2023. The latest conflict began on March 2, when Hezbollah fired missiles at Israel in support of Iran in the regional conflict. Israel responded with a devastating military campaign, killing more than 4,000 people and flattening dozens of villages in southern Lebanon, where it continues to occupy vast areas of territory . Direct US-brokered talks between Israel and Lebanon have done little to move the needle, with no real progress on Hezbollah's disarmament or Israel's withdrawal. The interception of the explosive-laden vehicle has prompted fears of renewed political assassinations in Lebanon, a country with a grim history of such killings.
