In a second incident, about 250kg of TNT-type explosives and 250kg of the explosive C4 were discovered in a lorry bound for Beirut. “I understand the anxiety gripping the Lebanese people upon the news of this truck's interception and the materials it was transporting, especially since C4 has been used in several of the infamous political assassinations in modern Lebanese history,” Mr Salam said in a post on X on Monday. Mr Fadlallah dismissed the Prime Minister's words as an “inflammatory campaign aimed at sowing internal discord” and said it would not “deter” the group from “continuing its efforts to defend and liberate their land”. He said Hezbollah had demanded the release of the two men “and the return of the vehicle and everything inside it”. He also castigated the government's decision earlier this year to ban Hezbollah's military activities. “For our people, this decision is null and void, has no existence, and has no effects on the ground that we recognise.” In the 2000s and early 2010s, several high-profile opponents of the Assad regime in Syria and its Lebanese ally Hezbollah were killed or had attempts made on their lives using explosives. Former prime minister of Lebanon Rafic Hariri was killed along with 20 others when a one-tonne lorry bomb was detonated as his convoy was driving through Beirut on February 14, 2005. Hezbollah members were convicted of that attack by the UN's Special Tribunal for Lebanon.

title: Pierre Fabre Laboratories’ new Dubai hub highlights bold plans for regional growth
description: Founded in 1961, the group expanded from its initial activities in the field of pharmaceuticals
content: Dermo-cosmetics and pharmaceutical giant Pierre Fabre Laboratories Group has underlined its ambitions for growth in the Middle East and beyond with the opening of a new regional hub in Dubai. The company is a global player with its dermo-cosmetics brands Avène, Ducray, A-Derma, Klorane, and René Furterer, as well as its entire medical division specialising in oncology, dermatology, and rare diseases. Eric Ducournau, chief executive of Pierre Fabre Laboratories, officially inaugurated the new premises in the Landmark Group building near Dubai Marina. It is the headquarters of the French company’s Middle East, Africa, Russia, Turkey (MEART) subsidiary and will play a central role in its strategy to double its sales in six years. Ducournau said the move confirmed Pierre Fabre Laboratories’ bold expansion route, which also involves leveraging local expertise. “This investment clearly illustrates our desire to expand in this region, and Dubai is ideal for recruiting international talent from the UAE,” he told The National. Ducournau also said the country’s political stability, its investment in science, and its strong commitment to health care were the main reasons for choosing Dubai as the regional centre. Pierre Fabre Laboratories aims to continue its research into “the medicines of the future” while potentially adapting existing medical treatments and dermo-cosmetic products to regional needs. “We work closely with healthcare professionals to understand patients’ needs,” Ducournau said. “Here, the country invests in its hospital infrastructure, equipment, and training for doctors to treat patients. Our expertise, combined with that of healthcare professionals, will enable us to provide medicines and dermo-cosmetic care tailored to the needs of the local population.” Ducournau said: “What is important for a pharma company is to develop products, and to develop products you need scientific partnerships. “And in this area, countries are really investing; the level of hospitals is very high … the equipment, the training, the presence of highly experienced doctors. “The country is investing in good facilities to treat the population…that’s very important because you can’t develop the company more in the field of oncology or dermatology or rare diseases without this footprint in science.” A proud history Founded in 1961 by pharmacist Pierre Fabre, the group expanded from its initial activities in the field of pharmaceuticals to include dermo-cosmetics, investing heavily in research and development - as it continues to do today - particularly in the fields of oncology and dermatology. Upon his death in 2013, Pierre Fabre finalised the donation of his majority stake to the Pierre Fabre Foundation, which he had created. The foundation, recognised by the French government, works to improve access to essential medicines and doctors, particularly in Africa and East Asia. In Lebanon, for example, it has helped Syrian refugee populations in camps by providing them with care. Ducournau said the company is fully committed to caring for patients and its employees, as well as for the environment. Also a botanist by training, Fabre had a strong desire to respect nature, minimise his footprint, and support local communities. Pierre Fabre Laboratories invests in CSR (corporate social responsibility) initiatives and sources many of its active ingredients from plants. Today, the company operates directly in 44 countries and markets its products in all geographies. It is the world’s second-largest player in the dermo-cosmetics market and France’s fourth-largest pharmaceutical company, with an already significant presence in the Middle East. “We have grown significantly in Europe in recent years,” explained Ducournau. “Today, we are continuing our development in this region, as well as in China, Asia at large, and the United States. These regions are very important for the medicines of tomorrow.” In the Arabian Peninsula, Pierre Fabre Laboratories is renowned for its Avène brand - in sun protection and anti-ageing care - and for A-Derma in eczema care. The same is true for Ducray and René Furterer in the field of hair and scalp care, dandruff and hair loss, where the brands rank first in sales. Pierre Fabre Laboratories said it wants to forge scientific partnerships with key healthcare professionals and hospitals in the region to understand the needs of patients here and offer dermo-cosmetic care addressing their specific skin issues. It is also committed to supporting research in oncology and dermatology and wants to support clinical programmes in these areas with innovative partners. “To establish our brands, we seek to build long-term relationships with dermatologists and dermatology clinics, in particular by showing them how these formulas are formulated to be highly tolerable and clinically proven through clinical trials,” said Ducournau. He also confirmed digital technology as another priority area for investment. “We need to develop the online presence of our products and brands,” Ducournau continued. “To do this, we need to recruit talent with real digital and international expertise. “Dubai is an international city with a mix of different cultures. This is a real strength when we want to develop our presence across an entire region such as MEART. “You have a lot of people not from this area, but living in Dubai. And that creates a sort of international framework, which is very important, because we have a different culture mix here, and you want to reach very different parts of the population.” The chief executive said Pierre Fabre Laboratories plans to raise its revenue from €3.1 billion (Dh13.37 billion) in 2024 to a minimum of €5 billion (Dh21.8 billion) by 2032, ensuring a balanced split between its dermo-cosmetics and pharmaceutical activities. The company is investing heavily in developing new, increasingly targeted treatments for patients with cancer or rare diseases requiring targeted therapy. The same applies to dermo-cosmetic care. Ducournau said: “Each region has its own specific characteristics, whether in terms of skin types, lifestyle, or climate. “To establish ourselves, we need to understand these specific characteristics so that we can commercialise products locally that are tailored to them. “Patients in Europe or in the Middle East are not the same as those in America or Asia. So we really need to combine global scale and local grasp to do what’s right for patients, consumers and customers everywhere we operate.” While Ducournau has ruled out developing new brands locally for now, the Pierre Fabre Laboratories boss acknowledged need for localised manufacturing in the future. “Today, we are doing 71 per cent of our revenues internationally, but still manufacturing 95 per cent in France,” he said. “Tomorrow, we will have to manufacture closer to the area where the products are sold and consumed.” Ducournau highlighted that Pierre Fabre Laboratories has been present in this region since the 1980s, and its growth trajectory will continue to be deployed on the basis of the strong regional ties it has built. “I want to emphasise that we found good partners to establish our business here…we believe that this chain of distribution will extend in the region,” he said, re-confirming the Dubai hub’s role as part of the broader strategy to dramatically increase global footprint and revenues. Ducournau added: “We took 40 years to establish a certain level of revenue…and we want to double this in only six years. So, that’s the objective of this opening and this presence here.” This page was produced by The National in partnership with Pierre Fabre Laboratories.

title: Adnoc says decade-old contingency plan kept oil flowing throughout Iran war
description: Years of crisis drills built 'muscle memory' for staff when disruption hit
content: State-owned Adnoc began preparing for major disruption to energy supplies 10 to 15 years ago, building contingency plans and backup infrastructure that helped it maintain oil production throughout the Iran war. “We actually prepared for this scenario in our playbooks 10 years ago, 15 years ago,” Abdulmunim Al Kindy, a board director at Adnoc and chairman of Abu Dhabi energy event Adipec, said on Thursday. Mr Al Kindy, who previously served as executive director of Adnoc's upstream directorate, said the company invested heavily in backup facilities and interconnections that allowed it to switch supply sources and delivery destinations. “[We] built projects at great expense, even though at the time they didn’t make any commercial sense,” he said. “When the time came, we actually kept the lights on.” The company's preparedness extended beyond physical infrastructure to years of emergency drills and scenario planning, giving employees “almost muscle memory” when the crisis struck, he said. Adnoc has increased its oil production capacity by almost 75 per cent over the past decade to 4.85 million barrels per day and is targeting five million bpd by 2027. Last November, Adnoc approved a Dh551 billion ($150 billion) spending plan for 2026 to 2030 to maintain operations and expand production capacity to meet rising global energy demand. Mr Al Kindy was speaking at a press conference ahead of Adipec 2026, which Adnoc will host in Abu Dhabi from November 2 to 5, as energy security takes on greater urgency following months of disruption to global oil and gas flows. “2026 has demonstrated a fundamental truth – energy security is economic stability,” he said. The event will draw its largest Asian participation yet, with 353 companies and six national pavilions representing China, India, Japan, Malaysia, Singapore and South Korea. Organisers expect more than 239,000 visitors from at least 170 countries, with international visitors accounting for 56 per cent of the total attendance. Three quarters of the 2,250 exhibiting companies are expected to come from outside the UAE. The conference will feature more than 16,500 delegates and 1,800 speakers across 13 programmes. Rising electricity demand from artificial intelligence and industrial growth is bringing “energy security, economic stability and competitiveness” closer together, said Thomas Loffler, executive vice president at organiser dmg events. Demand for exhibition space has prompted organisers to move the opening ceremony to the Abu Dhabi Energy Centre and expand the exhibition's AI and robotics zone. Confirmed speakers include Suhail Al Mazrouei, Minister of energy and Infrastructure; Katherina Reiche, Germany's Minister for Economic Affairs and Energy; Meg O'Neill, chief executive of BP; Richard Jackson, president and chief executive of Occidental Petroleum; Wael Sawan, chief executive of Shell; and Roland Busch, chief executive of Siemens. Last year's Adipec generated $53 billion in business deals across 49,131 transactions, the first time organisers tracked the value of agreements reached during the event. It also contributed $420 million to Abu Dhabi's hospitality and tourism economy, Mr Loffler said.

title: David Dastmalchian was told to change his surname to succeed in Hollywood
description: Street Fighter actor reflects on his Middle Eastern heritage, early rejections and the opportunity that brought him to the screen
content: Early in David Dastmalchian’s screen career, one Chicago casting director saw two possibilities for him: a cab driver or a terrorist. The American actor, whose father was Iranian, had been playing a much wider range of characters on stage to that point, but the auditions coming his way offered little opportunity to do the same on camera. “I remember in the beginning of my career being told, ‘You’re gonna have to change your last name,’” Dastmalchian tells The National . But despite needing the work, he resisted racial typecasting again and again. “I don’t want to do that. I want to be able to go after every role that I could possibly swing for,” he continues. Nearly two decades after his film debut, Dastmalchian has become one of Hollywood's most versatile performers. In his latest starring role, he plays M Bison in director Kitao Sakurai’s new Street Fighter adaptation . The villain joins a career spanning superhero films, science fiction and horror, all under the surname he was advised to change. Set in 1993, the film follows estranged fighters Ryu (Andrew Koji) and Ken Masters (Noah Centineo), who are recruited by Chun-Li (Callina Liang) for the World Warrior Tournament. Behind the competition is a conspiracy that draws them back into conflict. Dastmalchian's route into that career began with director Christopher Nolan’s The Dark Knight , released in 2008, in which he played one of the Joker’s accomplices. Casting director John Papsidera brought him in to audition for what would become his film debut. “And thank God for John Papsidera, who came into Chicago and he was casting a movie, and he was willing to see everybody,” Dastmalchian says. “And he saw me as something that other people hadn’t given me a chance to do on camera. “On the stage I always felt like I had an opportunity to swing for the fences with all different types of roles.” Even appearing in one of the biggest films of the decade did not guarantee steady work. In an interview with Backstage , Dastmalchian recalled arriving in Los Angeles without an agent or manager. Despite having The Dark Knight on his CV, he was turned down by the small agencies and management companies he approached. “It was devastatingly humbling to continue to be told, ‘No, we don’t want to work with you,’” he said. He continued auditioning for short films and music videos and attending casting workshops. Few of those auditions produced jobs, but they introduced him to people and helped him build the professional relationships on which his career would come to depend. Nolan later cast him again in Oppenheimer , while director Denis Villeneuve championed his work in the meantime, casting him in Prisoners , Blade Runner 2049 and Dune . Dastmalchian also took a leading role in the Abu Dhabi-produced runaway hit Late Night with the Devil , playing Jack Delroy, a television host whose Halloween broadcast spirals out of control. “I swim in such a giant pool of gratitude, honestly, because it was the people who were willing to see me and see the potential for what’s the human underneath, right?” he says. “That’s the story that you’re always trying to tell.” The actor recognises that nationality and ancestry can be central to how a character is written and performed. His objection, however, is to those factors limiting the roles an actor is allowed to pursue. Having found people willing to give him that freedom, he wants others to have the same opportunities. “I want everybody out there who’s an actor that feels like they want a chance to embrace the art, no matter what they look like, where they’re from, where their parents are from, what language they were raised speaking, to know that all the things we’re dealing with in acting are universal.” Street Fighter is in cinemas now across the Middle East

title: Abu Dhabi F1 Grand Prix: 'Unprecedented demand' and preparations on track with 50 days to go
description: Saif Al Noaimi, chief executive of organisers Ethara, tells The National he was always confident F1 season would finish at Yas Marina Circuit
content: Planning for the 2026 Abu Dhabi Grand Prix “never stopped for one day”, according to Saif Al Noaimi, chief executive of organisers Ethara. The F1 season finale is now 50 days away, and preparations for the race have clicked up a gear at Yas Marina Circuit. Eleven artists, including Andrea Bocelli, Lewis Capaldi and The Script, have been booked for the after-race concerts, with the final headline act set to be announced next week. Doubts were raised earlier this year when the Grands Prix in Bahrain and Saudi Arabia were cancelled because of the Iran war. However, F1 president Stefano Domenicali has said they intend to finish the season as planned, with “everything confirmed for [us to stay in] Qatar and Abu Dhabi”. The season finale will take place in the UAE capital from December 3-6, and Al Noaimi spoke to The National at Yas Marina Circuit as the days tick down to the 18th Abu Dhabi Grand Prix. Q: Given some of the speculation we have seen about the race, what assurances can you give about the 2026 event? A: We are delivering the Abu Dhabi Grand Prix at the same high standard we deliver every year. We are delivering a safe event, just like we do every year. We are planning and preparing ourselves just like we do every year. And from a readiness point of view, we are 100 per cent ready to deliver the Grand Prix this year. Everything is on schedule, the date has not changed. We're really excited to be hosting the season finale on December 6. Q: You are used to seeing a rise in demand every year, so how have ticket sales been this year? We are 50 days away from the Grand Prix, and if you compare where we were last year, 50 days away, we're actually ahead in terms of ticket volume and sales. So, demand is unprecedented. We are fortunate our customers know they're going to come because it's such an important event. Every year, early on, as soon as we go on sale, we see a huge spike in sales. And, you know, the last few weeks we've seen a spike in international sales also. So, interest in inbound tourism is growing, and we're starting to see that in the sales numbers. Q: Considering what happened with the Bahrain and Saudi Arabia Grands Prix, was there ever a fear that this wasn't going to go ahead? To be honest, we haven't stopped planning for the 2026 Grand Prix for one day. We've been full speed ahead since the beginning of the year. Since we delivered the Grand Prix last year, we've been completely full speed ahead. Obviously, being the last race of the season, early on in the year, we were in the planning period and the planning phase. September is when we start to see the venue transform and the build start. But this is our schedule every single year. We haven't had to make any changes to the planning and the execution. Q: Can you give a message to fans thinking about buying a ticket? Come and see Abu Dhabi, come and visit Abu Dhabi. We are seeing a huge growth in international visitations over the last few months. As you can see, everything's functioning normally over here. It's an exciting time to be here. And yeah, we're very, very happy to start welcoming the world back. Q: Are you a little bit worried that Kimi Antonelli is going to win the title before we get to Abu Dhabi? It was very fun last year … It was fun last year; we had the three-way fight. I mean, look, we can't have a three-way fight every year. But what I can assure you is these guys are going to fight till the chequered flag in Abu Dhabi, regardless of the championship. It's great to see someone young like Kimi taking that position. But also, like I said earlier, you can't write off the championship yet. You have Max Verstappen winning the last two races out of nowhere. Six different drivers have won races in 2026. So, regardless, it's still going to be an exciting race. Q: Can you talk about the enhancements the venue has undergone this year? So, we are upping the capacity for the event this year. We have unprecedented demand. We are expanding our Paddock Club (hospitality) offering. We already have the biggest Paddock Club, but we're actually increasing it to surpass 12,000 in 2026. There's a completely new Paddock Club offering that we're building on the west side also. And, you know, every year we look at additions and enhancements. We have a few new exciting products that we have launched already for 2026. And, you know, from a hospitality point of view, we have 16/360 (hospitality) expanding. We launched it last year for the first time, and we're making some additions to that product, which has been very, very popular. And then, in terms of other branded hospitality offerings, we announced our partnership with Nammos at Turn 9. And then we have a few other new branded hospitality experiences that we're launching this year. Q: Today we heard that Rashid Al Dhaheri will race in F3 next season. How long until we see him here? It's really exciting having Rashid and Keanu [Al Azhari] now both representing the UAE in the FIA Formula 3 championship. It really shows how strong our grassroots motorsports programme and our academy are. Both of them came through the Yas Heat Academy. They both raced in Formula Four UAE for Yas Heat. They're both Yas Heat ambassadors. And today they're both participating in the FIA Formula 3 World Championship. It's a huge, huge achievement for us. Huge achievement for them and for their families, who have dedicated so much over the years. And look, it's very, very promising, you know, maybe one or hopefully both of them could be in Formula One in as little as two years. So we're excited to see that. Congratulations to them.

title: Abu Dhabi shuts down cafe over repeated food safety violations
description: Business will remain closed until food safety issues resolved
content: An Abu Dhabi cafe has been temporarily shut down for repeated food safety violations that posed a public health risk . Let's Talk Riz Corner Cafe's licence was suspended by the emirate's food regulator after it failed to take effective corrective action over the issues. The Abu Dhabi Agriculture and Food Safety Authority said it had intervened immediately to protect food safety and consumer health. The closure will continue until the outlet addresses the violations and receives approval to resume trading, the authority added. The closure is part of the authority's work to strengthen Abu Dhabi's food safety system. Food regulators regularly inspect cafes , restaurants and products to ensure compliance with safety standards. The authority urged residents to report any violations they notice in cafes, restaurants or grocery stores, including suspected food contamination, by calling the Abu Dhabi Government’s toll-free number 800555.

title: Gulf-EU summit in Riyadh postponed amid Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia
description: Brussels 'remains committed' to relationship with new date to be announced in due course
content: A summit of Gulf and EU leaders planned for next week in Riyadh has been postponed. Jasem Al Budaiwi, Secretary General of the Gulf Co-operation Council, said on Thursday that attacks on Saudi Arabia by the Houthi rebels in Yemen, and the suspension of operations at King Khalid International Airport, meant the meeting would be rescheduled. Mr Al Budaiwi said the decision was taken to ensure the safety of participating delegations amid continued threats to civilians. The meeting "will be rescheduled to a later date to be agreed upon in due course by the GCC and EU sides", he said. In a separate statement, the European Council said it remained committed to "deepening this partnership." Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman , who travelled to Brussels for the first GCC-EU summit in late 2024, was scheduled to co-host the summit with European Council President Antonio Costa, in the presence of the EU's 27 leaders. This would have been the second time that the leaders gathered in this format, designed to boost ties between the two regions. Houthi missile strikes have also damaged the kingdom's energy and maritime infrastructure. Speaking earlier in the day, Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev said he expected the postponement of the summit "maybe for security reasons". "We highly appreciate the dialogue between the EU and the Gulf countries, especially Saudi Arabia," he said. Mr Radev said his country was pushing to develop a railway corridor to export Saudi oil through Syria, Turkey, Bulgaria and onwards to Europe, to avoid the Strait of Hormuz, currently under an Iranian blockade. "I believe that this new route will find a place in our discussions and solutions and decisions within the European Union," he said. Gulf states had hoped that the summit would pave the way for the harmonisation of Schengen visa waivers. There are different rules depending on states, with the UAE benefiting from an exemption, while citizens from Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, Bahrain and Oman are granted five-year multiple entry visas. EU states have strengthened their relationship with the Gulf since the start of the Iran war, portraying themselves as a reliable ally. Countries like France and Italy have sent air defence systems to the UAE and more recently to Saudi Arabia.

title: Three dead in Istanbul as torrential rain floods Turkish city
description: Residents told to stay at home as record rainfall 'turns roads into lakes'
content: Torrential rainfall has killed three people and caused chaos across Istanbul, as the Turkish city recorded its highest rainfall in more than 80 years. Istanbul Governor Davut Gul instructed the city’s 16 million residents to stay at home unless outings were absolutely necessary, closed schools and banned motorbikes as 8,000 emergency service workers were sent out to deal with the effects of days of downpours. “Rainfall in Istanbul will continue for another two to three days. Do not go outside unless absolutely necessary,” Mr Gul told a press conference on Thursday morning. He said it was “the highest level of precipitation recorded in Istanbul since 1942”, when records began. About 3,000 people were rescued from flooded areas, he said. Many areas of the city had received more than 100kg of rain per square metre, equivalent to 100mm, since early on Wednesday, Istanbul Metropolitan Municipality said. Rainfall in the Beykoz area of north-eastern Istanbul had reached 242kg per square metre, the authority said. An investigation has been launched following the death of a 14-year-old boy who died from electrocution after he stepped into a puddle in the Fatih district, the Istanbul governorship said. He was taken to hospital unconscious but could not be saved, the statement added. A 34-year-old died after slipping and hitting their head on a pavement, and authorities are trying to identify the body of a man found near the banks of the Kagithane Creek, according to the governor’s office. Footage published by state media showed cars drifting down streets, flooded homes and mosques, and passengers trapped in a bus with dirty flood water up to their knees. “Roads turned into lakes in many parts of the city,” state broadcaster TRT reported. At Istanbul Airport, 51 flights were diverted to alternative airports and another 19 flights were cancelled, Mr Gul said. The unusually heavy rain began on Tuesday and continued into Wednesday. Streets began to flood as drainage systems were overwhelmed. Istanbul residents received text messages from disaster management services on Wednesday evening warning them to stay away from riverbanks and flooded roads. Residents of basement apartments were told they “should take precautions”, while power cuts halted water supplies to homes and businesses in parts of the city, despite the torrential rain falling outside. Emergency services received more than 1,200 reports of flooding, 15 of landslides, 47 of people trapped and two of roofs blown off, the governorship said. Heavy flooding also made streets impassable in the city of Antalya on Turkey's Mediterranean coast. The state meteorological service issued warnings for more heavy rain and wind across the country on Thursday. Turkey has been experiencing an unusually wet 2026, the service said in a climate report released in September. Rainfall between January and August was 54 per cent higher than the 30-year average between 1991 and 2020. A third of the extreme weather events in the first eight months of the year were heavy rainfall and flooding.

title: Hormuz matters but UAE has more than one gateway, economy minister says
description: Country's tourism also set for a rebound, Abdulla bin Touq tells The National
content: The gateway to the Gulf is more than one port and certainly more than one road. That is the message from Abdulla bin Touq, Minister of Economy and Tourism. “ Hormuz really matters and it will keep on mattering,” he said in an exclusive interview on the sidelines of the Rise Summit in Dubai . “It's really important to really focus on Hormuz as well, to have it as a gate.” It is a direct rebuttal to US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent's remarks last month, who said the strait would be “a worthless piece of water” within two years. Before the Iran war , roughly a fifth of the world’s oil and gas transited the Strait of Hormuz. However, traffic flows through the waterway have dropped sharply since the war began on February 28. But while the strait matters, it is not the only way in, Mr bin Touq said. “The UAE doesn't have only one road. It has many roads to come to it,” he said. The UAE has revealed plans to reduce its reliance on the strait as part of its “Zero Hormuz” strategy to diversify trade routes and supply chains. It has established regional logistics corridors linking the Arabian Gulf to the Red Sea and the Gulf of Oman. Development of east-coast ports at Khor Fakkan and Fujairah , outside the strait, has been accelerated. The UAE is also building a new pipeline to provide additional capacity for exporting Abu Dhabi oil via the Gulf of Oman. If Hormuz is the front gate, the east coast is the side door and business is already walking through it, Mr bin Touq said. Asked where the next boom would be, he pointed to company registrations on the east coast. “Redundancy means dollar signs. It means investments,” he said. Resilience does not mean retreat, though. The UAE is not making the economy safer by “closing and shrinking it”, he added. However, Mr bin Touq resisted the idea of a dramatic pivot from west to east. He said the UAE continues to function as one connected economy. With Etihad Rail now linking Abu Dhabi to Fujairah in under four hours, “we can have breakfast in Khor Fakkan, lunch in Sharjah or Dubai and dinner in Abu Dhabi”, he said. The rail line binds “these seven economies that [are] very knitted together”. In terms of crises like the Iran war, tourism is the first sector to be hit and the last to recover “anywhere in the world”, with its return heavily dependant on airline capacity. The UAE is working with other countries to secure removal from their travel advisory lists, as tourism figures show signs of recovery after months of disruption because of the conflict. With Lufthansa and Air France committed to resuming UAE flights by the end of this month, “this shows you there is confidence”, Mr bin Touq said. That makes November and December a critical final window for tourism this year. The early signs are encouraging. Hotel occupancy reached about 68 per cent at the end of August. September's figures have not yet been published but the minister described the trend as “really, really nice”. The International Monetary Fund expects the UAE economy to shrink 3.9 per cent this year before rebounding 7.7 per cent in 2027. “It is 3.9 per cent, and there is decimal points, so it's not 4 per cent,” Mr bin Touq noted. The UAE's real gross domestic product also grew 0.4 per cent annually to Dh961.9 billion ($262 billion) in the first half of 2026, driven by non-oil business activity, despite the impact of the Iran war . The minister discussed his plan for the economy as a football formation. “In front, I have attackers: my tourism. My midfielder is the businesses … and my defence is when it comes to IP and innovation capacity,” he said. “What happened is I lost my attacker and my midfielders are scoring goals.” For 2027, tourism must lead from the front again. Meanwhile, the midfield needs reform and access to capital. On reform, he meant legislation and “the things that we tolerated through the crisis”. On capital, he pointed to the Dh1 billion Emirates Growth Fund, where he sits on the board. The fund aims to take companies with revenue of Dh1 million to Dh10 million up to Dh50 million to Dh60 million. “We're already investing,” he said. The government also wants more venture capital in the region and artificial intelligence “embedded within the systems of these companies, of these factories”. As for the interviewer's place in his squad, the minister offered a trial. “Play a winger,” he said.

title: Sharjah Police arrest 33 in crackdown on $2.4bn global money-laundering scheme
description: Suspects accused of being part of gang network involved in cyber fraud and violent crime
content: Sharjah Police have arrested 33 people from 12 countries accused of cyber fraud , digital wallet theft, money laundering and violent assault. Police said they were members of an organised criminal network who targeted individuals and companies through cyber attacks, stolen data, cryptocurrency transactions and physical intimidation. The arrests were the result of an international operation and carried out in the UAE and abroad. The suspects are accused of operating as four separate gangs, each specialising in one area. The first group carried out cyber attacks and stole customer information and databases, police said. The second gang specialised in laundering money through virtual assets and other financial channels, and the third used social engineering to manipulate victims and steal digital wallets. Members of the fourth group are accused of violent assaults, allegedly targeting victims to force them to disclose passcodes to their digital wallets. Lt Gen Abdullah Mubarak bin Amer, commander-in-chief of Sharjah Police, told a press conference on Thursday that more than 30 companies and institutions were targeted by the criminal network, with the operation securing the assets of companies worth Dh65 billion. More than Dh200 million in cash was seized, with about 3,000 digital wallets audited and verified. “What distinguished this gang was that it did not rely on a single type of criminal activity,” he said. The Sharjah Police Digital Crime Combat Department “uncovered the highly complex and concealed infrastructure of the organisation, whose members had made the deepest reaches of cyberspace a home for their activities”, he said. The suspects are accused of hiding their activities behind sophisticated layers of encryption, moving through closed networks. In public, they “cultivated an image of wealth, travelling between world capitals and displaying a lavish lifestyle that concealed a framework managed secretly, and they appeared to be legitimate businesspeople and investors, while their illegal activities extended across countries”. Sharjah Police said initial inquiries alerted them to one suspect in particular, a 15-year-old boy. “We traced the networks and their locations until we reached the teenager,” said Brig Dr Khalifa Balhai, director of Sharjah CID. “He had a digital wallet with huge amount of cryptocurrency. We traced all the suspects through the teenager.” It was discovered the gang had set up a group on social media, which was locked by a code that changed every eight hours. “What has been achieved in this case is the result of integrated institutional work, continued security efforts, and close co-operation and co-ordination with federal, local and international authorities,” Lt Gen bin Amer said. “These efforts led to the dismantling of these networks and groups, the arrest of their members and the thwarting of their plans. “This confirms the efficiency of the UAE's national security system and its ability to handle various cases, regardless of their complexity or whether they extend beyond its geographical borders, and to keep pace with security challenges efficiently and competently.” The security operation, called End of Battle, has also served to protect interests and assets, he added. Anwar Al Harmoudi, Attorney General of Sharjah, said the investigation “revealed a cross-border criminal organisation with integrated criminal roles, beginning with seizing victims’ funds through fraud and hacking”. The suspects are accused of converting stolen assets into property and other investments to give the appearance of legitimacy.

title: New Dubai footbridge and Sharjah buses to improve access to Etihad Rail stations
description: A 400-metre bridge connects Jumeirah Golf Estates Metro station and Dubai Al Yalayis rail station
content: New transport links in Dubai and Sharjah are making it easier to reach Etihad Rail stations, with a pedestrian footbridge opening in Dubai on Thursday and three connecting bus routes launching in Sharjah. Passengers can now switch more smoothly between Metro and train services in Dubai using the new footbridge linking Jumeirah Golf Estates station with Etihad Rail’s Al Yalayis Station . Before the elevated 400-metre footbridge opened, a shuttle bus operated between the stations. Passengers can use a Nol One-Day Pass ticket, which offers unlimited travel on the emirate's public transport network and is valid until midnight. Using digital QR codes on phones eliminates the need for a single-use red paper Nol ticket. In the coming years, Dubai Al Yalayis Station will become a transport super-hub with an interchange between the Metro Red and Gold lines planned for 2032. The station opened to passengers on September 30 for the first rail service to Abu Dhabi, Sharjah and Fujairah. Due to increased demand, extra services were added on some weekends. Variable pricing has been introduced on several routes due to demand, with some tickets increasing by up to Dh69. The F38 bus also serves Dubai's rail station, operating a circular route to Dubai Sports City and Dubai Production City. Sharjah 's Road and Transport Authority on Wednesday announced three new bus routes connecting Sharjah's first rail station in Al Dhaid. ER1 connects Al Madam Bus Station to Al Dhaid Station, stopping in Mleiha and Al Dhaid and taking one hour. ER2 connects Al Sajaa Bus Station with Al Dhaid Station, stopping in Al Batayeh and Al Dhaid, and takes about 43 minutes. ER3 links Jubail Bus Station in Sharjah city with the rail station on a non-stop service, taking about one hour and 42 minutes. These services are vital for connecting some of the smaller towns in Sharjah emirate that previously had limited public transport connectivity to other emirates. Bus journeys are timed to train arrivals and departures, and you can buy tickets with cash or a Sayer Card.

title: Nissan Patrol marks 75 years with limited-edition model exclusively for Gulf
description: Model is limited to initial run of 1,951 vehicles
content: Nissan has announced a limited-edition Patrol to mark the SUV’s 75th anniversary, with an initial production run of 1,951 vehicles exclusively for the GCC region. The number marks the nameplate's debut in 1951. Based on the flagship Platinum V6 Twin Turbo grade, the anniversary edition features copper-gold exterior accents, a Bordeaux red interior and special anniversary detailing. AWR Automotive, Nissan’s dealer in Dubai, Sharjah and the Northern Emirates, introduced the model on Thursday. It costs Dh439,900 ($119,780) including VAT. Nissan says its bespoke copper-gold finish is inspired by desert landscapes. The detailing appears across the grille bars, fog lamp surrounds, fender vents, shoulder line and emblems, paired with dark chrome finishes and black alloy wheels. Anniversary signatures feature on the front grille, shoulder-line graphic and rear emblem. An illuminated carpet light projects a “Patrol Since 1951” graphic and a sand-dune motif. Nissan lists five exterior colours for the Gulf edition, while AWR Automotive has confirmed four options for its customers: grey, white, black and two-tone white with a black roof. Inside, the cabin features copper-gold steering wheel detailing and ambient lighting alongside dark chrome trim. Anniversary detailing appears on the passenger-side dashboard, seat headrests and floor and luggage mats. Other additions include illuminated anniversary kick plates and a deep red leather key fob case. Thierry Sabbagh, Nissan and Infiniti’s divisional vice president and president for the Middle East, Saudi Arabia, India and CIS, said: “To mark 75 years of the Patrol, we wanted to deliver something lasting for our customers, a special product that serves as a memorable token of our shared history.” The anniversary edition keeps the Platinum V6 Twin Turbo’s 3.5-litre twin-turbocharged engine, which delivers 425hp and 700Nm of torque. It is paired with a nine-speed automatic transmission and adaptive air suspension with Intelligent Dynamic Damping. The cabin includes a 28.6-inch Monolith display, a Klipsch audio system and quilted leather seats with heating, ventilation and massage functions. The model also features Biometric Cooling, ProPILOT driver assistance and advanced visibility systems. In the UAE and Saudi Arabia, NissanConnect 2.0 with Google built-in provides navigation , voice assistant functions and connected car services. The anniversary edition joins a regional Patrol range that includes the Platinum, PRO-4X and Nismo. AWR Automotive says the model is available through its Nissan showrooms in Dubai, Sharjah and the Northern Emirates, and can also be viewed at its City Walk location in Dubai.

title: Iran may not order every Houthi attack, but backing Yemen's rebels carries consequences
description: The immediate question is how the militia has been able to threaten airports, energy infrastructure and international transport links
content: Attacks by Yemen 's Houthi rebels on Riyadh 's international airport and Saudi Aramco have exposed the strategic threat posed by a militia whose growing missile and drone capabilities have become a key part of Tehran's regional reach. The attacks have brought the war in Yemen directly into Saudi Arabia's capital and its oil-producing heartland, raising the stakes for the world's largest oil exporter and testing its ability to protect critical infrastructure. A weekend attack on Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport killed at least 13 people and wounded more than 300, Saudi authorities said. A further strike on Sunday killed one person and injured 11. On Tuesday, an attack targeted an administrative building belonging to Aramco in Dhahran, causing a fire but no reported casualties. Debris from intercepted missiles injured four people in Riyadh. The Houthis claimed responsibility for attacks on Saudi targets and threatened further strikes after Saudi-led coalition forces bombed an oil facility in the Houthi-held capital, Sanaa . These latest exchanges mark a sharp escalation in a conflict that had increasingly become intertwined with the wider confrontation involving Iran, Israel and the US. The immediate question is how the Houthis have acquired the capability to threaten major airports, energy infrastructure and international transport links across Saudi Arabia. UN investigators and American military assessments have documented extensive links between Iranian military technology and Houthi weapons systems. A February 2024 report by the US Defence Intelligence Agency identified similarities between Iranian and Houthi missiles and drones. UN experts have also investigated foreign weapons supplies, technical assistance, training and procurement networks supporting the organisation. Such evidence does not establish that Tehran ordered every attack. But it makes Iran's role in strengthening the Houthis' military capabilities central to understanding the threat now facing Saudi Arabia. The militia has its own political leadership and domestic objectives. It emerged from Yemen's internal conflicts and seized Sanaa in 2014, before the Saudi-led military intervention began in 2015. Its independence in decision-making, however, does not negate the strategic importance of external assistance. For Iran, the Houthis offer a partner positioned near the Bab Al Mandeb strait, a vital shipping corridor linking the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden. Their ability to threaten Saudi infrastructure and disrupt maritime traffic gives Tehran an additional source of pressure on regional adversaries without requiring publicly demonstrable Iranian command over every operation. The attacks also carry consequences beyond the immediate damage. Disruption to Saudi aviation, heightened risks to oil facilities and uncertainty over regional security threaten not only the kingdom's efforts to establish Riyadh as a centre for international business but also the global economy that relies on Saudi oil flows. It also threatens the millions of Muslim pilgrims who go to Saudi Arabia as a key tenet of Islam. Saudi Arabia has responded with further strikes on Houthi-held targets in Yemen, including fuel infrastructure in Sanaa, increasing the danger of a wider cycle of retaliation. Tehran has repeatedly rejected the characterisation of the Houthis as a proxy force, despite evidence to the contrary, and it repeats rhetoric that Yemen's crisis requires a political settlement. But the latest attacks sharpen the question of whether Iran is prepared to use its influence to restrain an ally whose military operations have direct consequences for Gulf security. The issue is no longer simply whether the Houthis take orders from Tehran. It is how Iranian assistance has helped build a military capability that can threaten Saudi Arabia's most important economic and transport assets – and whether diplomacy can prevent that capability from driving a wider regional conflict.

title: At least 34 children killed in Pakistan school roof collapse
description: Authorities launch investigation after roof collapses on to classrooms, causing both storeys to cave in
content: At least 34 pupils and a teacher were killed in Pakistan when the roof of a school collapsed during classes in the north-western city of Peshawar on Thursday, authorities said. Most of the students killed were under 13 years old, said Arif Khattak, regional director of the Rescue Department. At least ​45 people ⁠suffered major and minor injuries, ‌he added. Rescue workers spent hours pulling children trapped beneath the rubble of the privately run Al Khair Education Centre, while panicked parents and relatives gathered outside the building seeking news of ⁠their loved ones. The incident took place at 8.48am local time, and the rescue operation lasted four to five hours, Mr Khattak said. Victims of the collapse were taken to the city’s Lady Reading Hospital, according to hospital spokesman Mohammad Asim. “The fatalities include 12 girl students and a female teacher,” Mr Asim said. Three children remained in critical condition, with head injuries, he said. Most of the injured brought to that hospital had been treated and sent home. A rescue official said the roof of an upper floor had collapsed on to the classrooms below, causing both storeys to cave in. Peshawar police chief Mian Saeed said excessive weight from construction on the school roof had caused the collapse. “It was a weak building structure,” he ​said. “Its roof was overloaded with construction on a weak structure, ‌which caused the collapse.” Mr Saeed said ⁠the school's owner had been arrested ​and authorities had opened an investigation. A total of 110 students were attending lessons in three classrooms when the roof caved in. Distraught relatives accused the ​school of ‌ignoring safety concerns about the building's condition and demanded accountability. “Make an example of them, a lesson ⁠for all, so that no one dares open a school just to make ⁠money without providing facilities,” said Mohammad Zaman, who lost two nephews in the collapse. Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif promised “a thorough investigation” into the incident. “My heart is with the families grieving the loss of their children and a teacher in the tragic roof collapse at a school in Peshawar. No parent should have to endure such pain,” he wrote in a statement on X. “I extend my deepest condolences and pray for strength for every family affected. I have directed that the injured receive the best possible care. We will ensure a thorough investigation into this tragedy and take every necessary step to protect the safety of children in schools across the country,” he added. Pakistan’s President Asif Ali Zardari said the incident was a “heart-wrenching tragedy” and called for a comprehensive investigation into the cause of the deadly collapse. “In this hour of sorrow, the entire nation shares equally in the grief of the affected families,” the President’s office posted on X.

title: Aldar enters Sharjah with Dh1.1bn residential acquisition
description: Abu Dhabi developer will acquire nine residential buildings in Aljada development as part of deal
content: Aldar , Abu Dhabi ’s biggest listed developer, has agreed to acquire more than 1,100 homes in Sharjah from Arada for Dh1.1 billion ($290 million), its first real estate investment in the emirate as it expand its income-generating property portfolio. The forward-purchase agreement covers nine buildings within three residential blocks at Aljada, Arada’s flagship mixed-use development, with delivery scheduled for the fourth quarter of 2029, Aldar said on Thursday. The transaction will expand Aldar’s develop-to-hold pipeline to Dh21 billion. Aldar said the nine buildings will cater primarily to end users and long-term renters seeking quality housing at accessible price points within an established integrated community. “Sharjah is a large and growing residential market, and Aljada provides an attractive entry point through one of the emirate’s leading master-planned communities,” Aldar group chief executive Talal Al Dhiyebi said. He added that the investment adds scale to Aldar’s residential-for-rent portfolio. The investment builds on a Dh15 billion development partnership announced last month by Aldar and Arada, which covers projects in Abu Dhabi, a further expansion of their relationship. The partnership, which marked Arada’s entry into Abu Dhabi, includes a mixed-use community at Seih Sdeirah, on the Abu Dhabi- Dubai border, and three residential plots on Yas Island. Arada, a joint venture between KBW Investments – a company controlled by Saudi Arabia’s Prince Khaled bin Alwaleed – and Sharjah-based Basma Group, has been rapidly expanding in the UAE as well as in overseas markets such as the UK, Australia and Syria. Aldar, meanwhile, plans to launch a major development of villas and townhouses in Dubai by the end of this year as part of the company’s expansion across the UAE . The new project, with an undisclosed value, will be built near Dubai Silicon Oasis, Aldar Development's chief executive Jonathan Emery told The National in an interview in London this week. The move comes as the UAE property market continues to perform strongly despite uncertainty stemming from the Iran war. The Emirates was ranked as the world’s leading real estate investment destination in a property market league table released in June. Arada’s UAE Property Investment Index – conducted on behalf of the Dubai developer by US-based Penta Group – found that 56 per cent of global investors have serious interest in the UAE’s property market. The latest acquisition will broaden Aldar’s geographic exposure while adding residential rental assets aimed primarily at end users and long-term tenants seeking housing at accessible price points, the company said. Arada group chief executive Ahmed Alkhoshaibi said Aldar’s decision to make its first investment in Sharjah at Aljada reflected confidence in both the development and the emirate’s residential market. “To have a developer of Aldar’s calibre and track record choose Aljada as its first investment in the emirate reflects the quality of what we have built here, and the scale of the opportunity that Sharjah represents,” he said. Aljada spans 2.2 million sq m and is expected to comprise about 25,000 homes at full buildout, with an anticipated gross sales value of Dh35 billion. Residential handovers at the development began in 2021, with more than 8,800 homes delivered across multiple districts, according to the statement. The community also includes schools, hotels, student accommodation, retail space and the Madar family entertainment district. Aldar said the acquisition adds to its strategy of expanding its portfolio of income-generating properties, as the developer seeks to diversify its revenue streams. The Abu Dhabi developer, which recorded strong second-quarter financial results, is expected to hand over more than 3,000 units this year, representing the largest volume since the company’s launch, with the deliveries going up to 4,500 next year, according to Mr Emery.

title: Abu Dhabi revokes doctor's licence for violating controlled medication rules
description: Second doctor's licence suspended after breaches including missing medical records
content: Abu Dhabi health authorities have revoked a doctor's licence and suspended another's over violations of controlled medication rules. The breaches included incomplete clinical assessments, a lack of proper follow-up care and missing medical records, the Department of Health – Abu Dhabi found. In some cases, the two doctors failed to record the medical reasons for prescribing controlled medications. The health department said it took the action to protect patients and ensure doctors followed medical rules and professional standards. The violations were identified through routine inspections, digital monitoring and co-ordination with other authorities. The health department said it would continue monitoring healthcare facilities and carry out inspections to identify violations and ensure compliance with the rules. Controlled medications are subject to strict regulations because they carry a risk of misuse or dependence. They typically include strong painkillers such as morphine and fentanyl, medicines used to treat anxiety and sleep problems, and drugs that affect mood and behaviour. They also include certain medications for attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). Only licensed doctors are allowed to prescribe controlled drugs in the UAE and should provide documentation to prove the need for a patient. The medicines have to be administered by a registered nurse. Healthcare facilities must comply with all regulations, laws and policies related to narcotics, controlled and semi-controlled drugs. Storing, distributing, dispensing, administering or handling narcotics, controlled or semi-controlled drugs without approval from the Ministry of Health and Prevention and Dubai Healthcare City Authority-Regulatory is prohibited.

title: Love Is Blind on Netflix: Every international edition ranked as US season 11 arrives
description: Reality show that made its debut in 2020 has spawned 13 international spin-offs
content: Is love really blind? Since 2020, couples around the world have been trying to prove as much – mostly unsuccessfully – in Netflix's hugely popular reality show Love is Blind . Following its debut, set in the US, the show has spawned 13 international versions, including Love is Blind: Habibi , the Arabic spin-off that premiered in October 2024. A second season is coming later in the year. The format is similar across all. A group of single men and women looking for love are introduced to each other through “pods”, where they can interact but not see the other person. Once participants have chosen their prospective partners, the couple meet for the first time and become engaged. They are then flown to a luxury resort where they spend time and get to know each other better. In the final stage of the experiment, the couples who are still together go back to their respective lives where they meet each other's families and friends, and are given 10 days to prepare for their wedding. From Brazil to the UK and Japan, each edition of Love is Blind has proved to be a hit, turning some of its cast members into overnight celebrities. Love is Blind: Habibi , for instance, was viewed more than 1.3 million times in the first seven days after its debut. It also ranked No 8 globally among Netflix's non-English shows. With Love is Blind: South Africa set to debut later this year, here are all the editions so far ranked by fan ratings on IMDb. Watch out for spoilers from reunion episodes Number of seasons: 1 IMDb rating: 5.4/10 Viewership in first week: 1.3 million Hosts: Khaled Saqer and Elham Ali The Arabic version of Love is Blind became a massive hit, dominating social media chats and debates for weeks after its premiere in October 2024. Featuring 20 singles – 10 women and 10 men – from across the Arab world and North Africa who are all residents of the UAE, the series was filmed in Lebanon, Dubai and Abu Dhabi. Six couples progressed to the next stage and were flown to a luxury resort in Lebanon, where their relationship was further tested. Eventually, out of two couples who made it to the wedding day, only one – Safa and Mohammed – exchanged vows. Speaking to The National a few weeks after its debut, cast members shared how their lives had changed thanks to the popularity of the show. “This experience didn’t just transform me, it shaped me into a person I never imagined I could be,” Mohammed said. “It opened up a whole new world and revealed aspects of myself I hadn’t recognised before. Beyond discovering ‘the one’, I found myself.” Season two will have celebrity couple Wissam Breidy and Rym Saidi taking over hosting roles. title: Emirati racer Rashid Al Dhaheri takes major step towards F1 dream with Formula 3 move
description: UAE will be represented on F3 grid for first time with two drivers landing contracts for 2027
content: Rashid Al Dhaheri will compete in FIA Formula 3 in 2027 after signing with Van Amersfoort Racing. The Dutch team announced a deal with the 18-year-old Emirati on Thursday in a move that will see him step up in class after finishing fourth in this year’s Formula Regional European Championship. “I’m very proud to be taking the next step into FIA Formula 3 with Van Amersfoort Racing,” said Al Dhareri, a member of the Mercedes Junior Driver Programme since March 2025. “It is an important milestone in my journey, but I know the hard work is only beginning. I’m proud to represent the UAE and the wider region at this level, and I’m looking forward to learning, improving and giving everything I have on and off the track. “Every step has to be earned, and my focus now is on preparing as strongly as possible for 2027. I’m grateful to everyone who has supported me and helped make this opportunity possible.” The move means that the UAE will have two drivers on the grid next season after it was also announced that Keanu Al Azhari had signed for Hitech. No Emirati has previously competed in F3. Brad Joyce, team principal for Van Amersfoort Racing, added: “We’re looking forward to welcome Rashid to [the team]. He has had a very strong season in Formula Regional, with three wins and eight podiums, finishing in fourth place in the championship. “He has shown his pace throughout the year and has been able to fight at the front of a very competitive field. That gives us a good starting point as he steps up to Formula 3. We’re looking forward to working with him during the post season tests and preparing for his first F3 season together.” Al Dhaheri's journey in motorsport began at the age of three, and he quickly rose through the ranks, winning the WSK Super Master Series and the South Garda Winter Cup in the 60 Mini category. In 2023, he made his single-seater debut with Prema Racing in the Italian F4 Championship, finishing 10th overall and taking P3 at Macau. He continued to impress in 2024, competing in the Formula 4 UAE Championship and the Euro 4 Championship. In March 2025, it was announced that Al Dhaheri had joined Mercedes as part of their Junior Driver Programme, becoming the first Middle East driver to be selected for their F1 development initiative. He described the move as “a dream come true” as he took the next step towards his ultimate goal of becoming the first driver to represent the UAE in F1. George Russell, who has raced for Mercedes in F1 since 2019, is also a graduate of the programme. Al Dhaheri has just finished the FIA Formula Regional European Championship campaign with a podium finish at Hockenheim, ending the weekend fourth in the overall standings, 38 points behind title winner Emanuele Olivieri of Italy. It caps an impressive season for the teenager who claimed three victories, eight podiums, one pole position and a fastest lap. Driving for French team R-ace GP, Al Dhaheri recorded victories at the Red Bull Ring, Monza and Hungaroring across the eight-round championship. He became the first Emirati to lead the standings and sat 21 points clear at the halfway stage and, despite some challenging weekends later in the season, arrived at the Hockenheim finale as one of four drivers still able to win the title.

title: Saudi coalition hits back at Houthis with strikes on 120 mountain depots in Yemen
description: Alliance responds to Houthi attacks on Riyadh airport that have killed 17 people and injured hundreds
author_name: Amr  Mostafa, Mina Aldroubi, Nada AlTaher
content: A Saudi-led coalition has hit back at the Houthi rebels with strikes on more than 120 mountain depots in Yemen , it revealed on Thursday. The strikes came in response to a wave of Houthi attacks on Riyadh, where King Khalid International Airport has been attacked 20 times with missiles and drones, the coalition said. Inside Yemen, the government's headquarters in Aden came under attack by Houthi missiles on Thursday, with some security personnel killed. Fears were growing for the population of Taiz, with that city encircled by the Houthis. Attacks on Riyadh's airport have killed 17 people and injured 333 others, the coalition said. It said Houthi attacks on Abha airport, in south-western Saudi Arabia near the Yemeni border, had killed three people and wounded 28. UAE leaders, including President Sheikh Mohamed , have sent condolences to Saudi Arabia's King Salman. A summit of Gulf and EU leaders planned for next week in Riyadh has been postponed, as has a $5 million Saudi golf tournament. The airport attacks were part of a wider campaign against Saudi civilian facilities such as airports, ports and oil facilities, said coalition spokesman Maj Gen Turki Al Malki. Maj Gen Al Malki said 127 mountain storage facilities used by the Iran-aligned Houthis, as well as several launch platforms, had been destroyed in recent days. The announcement came as a Yemeni government minister vowed to continue the fight against the Houthis. Mustafa Al Noman, Yemen's Deputy Foreign Minister, told The National that the government had no option but to “go all the way” with the battle. “If the government stops at this point, that'll be a disaster for the population and give the Houthis a much higher hand in the situation. It will be a disaster,” he said. Mr Al Noman said there was no hope of a political process with the Houthis. “The only solution is a military solution because the Houthis have not left an option for the government to adhere to,” he said. Riyadh has come under heavy fire as Yemen's heaviest fighting in years has spilt over into Saudi Arabia. Four attacks have caused fatalities at King Khalid Airport, with the deadliest on Saturday killing 12 people and injuring 309 others, according to the coalition's toll. Maj Gen Al Malki condemned what he called “cowardly terrorist acts” by the Houthis against civilians. The airport attack, which took place during peak hours, threatened the safety of Saudi citizens, visitors and travellers of other nationalities, including pilgrims visiting Makkah and Madinah, he said. He said the Houthis had acquired advanced military technology with assistance from outside, allowing them to use ballistic missiles, attack and suicide drones, and explosives-laden speedboats. The coalition said it would continue operations to deter Houthi attacks. “We reaffirm our support for Yemen’s legitimate government and armed forces on all fronts, and our commitment to providing air support to units on the ground around the clock,” Maj Gen Al Malki said. “As a final message, the terrorist Houthi militia must stop its attacks on civilians in the kingdom of Saudi Arabia. It must read the coalition’s statement carefully and read between the lines,” he added. In response, Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said in a statement that his group had the right to act until Saudi Arabia ended what he described as its aggression and blockade against Yemen. Mr Saree accused Saudi Arabia of carrying out more than 274,000 air strikes over the past 12 years, allegedly including more than 2,350 during the current escalation. “Anyone who attacks our country should not expect us to salute him,” he said. Saudi Arabia intervened in Yemen's civil war in ⁠support of the government in 2015, fearing the rise of Iranian influence and the prospect of chaos on its borders, after the Houthis seized the capital, Sanaa. The UN brokered a 2022 truce between the warring ⁠sides in Yemen that kept a fragile peace in place until this year. Saudi Arabia resumed its military campaign in Yemen in support of the internationally recognised government in a bid to reverse the Houthis' sudden gains last month, when they swept along the Red Sea coast to the critical Bab Al Mandeb strait. The EU has urged the Iran-backed Houthi rebels to lift their siege of Taiz, as the Yemeni government appealed to the UN for urgent action to avert a humanitarian catastrophe. Taiz, in south-western Yemen, is controlled by government troops but has long been attacked by the Houthis and remains the main front line in the civil war. In recent weeks, fighting between the rebels and government forces has intensified and the rebels have encircled the area. The EU called on the Houthis to allow desperately needed food, water, medicine and fuel to enter the city . It stressed that civilians and civilian infrastructure must be protected and humanitarian partners must be permitted to deliver essential aid. On Wednesday, the Yemeni government sent a letter from Foreign Minister Afrah Al Zouba to senior UN and humanitarian officials, outlining a sharp deterioration in conditions in Taiz governorate amid a new Houthi escalation. Ms Al Zouba warned that the tightening of the siege on Taiz and surrounding villages could trigger a humanitarian disaster affecting more than four million people. They include residents trapped inside the city and displaced families in districts such as Al Shamayatayn, Al Mawasit and Jabal Habashi. The government urged the UN to apply direct pressure on the Houthis to lift the blockade immediately, reopen all access routes for civilians and supply chains, and ensure sustained, unhindered delivery of food, fuel and drinking water. It also called for stronger monitoring and documentation of violations to preserve evidence, hold perpetrators accountable and prevent impunity. Humanitarian agencies have voiced concern over low food and medical supplies, as well as hospitals' ability to care for thousands of injured people. Wheat flour stocks in the city are nearly exhausted, ‌the UN World Food Programme said. The WFP said remaining food supplies may not last long if access constraints ​continue. At least 600,000 people in Taiz depend on aid, including more than 200,000 children. The International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) said front-line hospitals in areas such as Marib, Taiz and Yemen's ​Red Sea coast ‌are taking in unprecedented numbers of patients wounded by weapons, with some admitting more than 700 casualties in one week. More ⁠than 200,000 people have been displaced from their homes since fighting began in ⁠recent weeks, the UN's International Organisation for Migration said. “Trauma care staff are under enormous pressure,” said Feras Abusamra, ICRC health co-ordinator. Only a small proportion of Yemen's functioning health centres can provide comprehensive trauma care, he said, while hospitals face large numbers of wounded people and shortages of ​surgical supplies, anaesthesia, oxygen and medicine. The siege of Taiz, Yemen's third-largest city, has been in place since 2015 and has long been a severe humanitarian flashpoint, with aid agencies warning that shortages of basic goods and medical supplies are pushing civilians towards crisis conditions.

title: AI is changing us as humans, says pioneering Arab scientist
description: Fadel Adib, who won UAE's Great Arab Minds award, further sees powers outside the US and China getting in on the AI race
content: AI will help humans operate at a "higher intellectual level", even if that means ditching some of the life skills we once had, a leading Arab scientist has said. Fadel Adib, an MIT professor and successful AI start-up founder, said it was not necessarily bad that people are coming to rely on large language models such as ChatGPT. "We first augment humans and increase their productivity, and then eventually we also augment humans with robots, not just with AI ... increase productivity there as well. AI is changing who we are as humans," he told The National at a World Economic Forum event in Dubai. His company, Cartesian, uses AI technology to help robots navigate hundreds of warehouses and retail stores in 15 countries, tracking and collecting thousands of different products. "Some of us cannot operate without asking ChatGPT the question, and that might not necessarily be bad," he said at the Annual Meeting of Global Future Leaders, which he co-chaired. "I'm a professor. So I remember when people used to say 'oh, students are not memorising anymore in schools, and we're losing the ability to memorise.' "What's the point of memorising if you can Google everything? And maybe AI is going to help us operate at a higher intellectual level. "And as humans, we've repeatedly managed to do that. We don't learn how to make fire anymore, and we don't need to. "As humans, we've managed to repeatedly figure out how we operate at a higher level of abstraction, and I think we're going to do that again." Dr Adib, who grew up in Tripoli, Lebanon and was given a Dh1 million Great Arab Minds award in 2023 by Sheikh Mohammed bin Rashid, Vice President and Ruler of Dubai, also predicted further challenges to US tech firms' dominance of AI. Speaking earlier at the same event in Dubai, Omar Sultan Al Olama, the UAE's AI minister, said that superpower dominance of AI was not appealing, and that middle powers and sovereign governments would want an alternative. "AI is moving at an accelerated pace. It is moving from the digital into the physical world," said Dr Adib. "If you look at the 1990s, where the internet was growing... that was a US-led world. "Today, there is the race between the US and China on AI. What role is Europe and Africa and Latin America and the rest of Asia going to play? The answer is not clear that just the US or China is gonna win this race." He added: "Our first prime adopters were in Europe. And if you look at the United Arab Emirates, there's a lot of investment. There's a lot of AI investments here in Dubai, and they are deploying it. They're seeing real change. And in Abu Dhabi, with the creation of G42, and the investment in data infrastructure. "And as a scientist, I love challenges, and as a technologist, I love the optimism of it. There is an opportunity for real change and impact."

title: Make peace, Iran reformist urges, as hardliners rule out surrender
description: Conflict has weighed heavily on country's 90 million people, former Tehran mayor Gholamhossein Karbaschi says
content: A former Tehran mayor has urged Iran to reach an agreement with the US to end the war, as internal divisions widen over how to respond to Washington amid a deepening economic crisis. Gholamhossein Karbaschi, a reformist politician, made the remarks on Iranian state television last on Wednesday, warning that a prolonged conflict would deepen domestic hardship. “We cannot take on America’s power and diplomacy,” Mr Karbaschi said. “We must make a non-emotional assessment of the situation." Mr Karbaschi said there was no clear end in sight and that officials should consider the consequences of continuing the fighting. “We were never volunteers for war,” he said, adding that families faced uncertainty over whether hostilities would resume. Iran is facing soaring inflation and pressure on household finances, while restrictions on oil exports have contrained a key source of government revenue. Long petrol queues have also been reported. Mr Karbaschi also criticised the Iranian attacks in June on three oil tankers in the Strait of Hormuz, saying they had derailed the peace process and given Washington a pretext to breach the interim accord. “If the Islamabad agreement had been implemented as it should have been, the incident involving the targeting of the three ships would not have happened,” he said. “We must distinguish between the reason for violating the agreement and a pretext for violating it.” The attacks he was referring to appear to have occurred about 10 days after the US and Iran signed the Islamabad memorandum of understanding on June 17. Mr Karbaschi said the interim agreement had been advantageous to Tehran and had surprised observers because Washington accepted its terms while Israel opposed them. He argued that the subsequent attacks on the ships gave the US an opportunity to breach the agreement. He also questioned who had ordered the strikes, adding that nobody had publicly claimed responsibility. “Everyone says, ‘We don’t know who attacked the three ships,’” he said. Referring to President Masoud Pezeshkian, he asked: “Can it be that the president doesn’t know?” Mr Karbaschi's comments were reported by other media outlets on Thursday morning, including the Entekhab newspaper. The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps responded sharply. Its spokesman, Hossein Mohebi, rejected suggestions that the attacks were unauthorised or carried out without the approval of senior officials. Mr Mohebi described the strikes as a “decisive and crushing response” to what he called the third US breach of its commitments. He accused Washington of breaking its commitments twice during negotiations and a third time after signing the memorandum. “In the armed forces, no action is taken without observing the chain of command and co-ordinating with senior officials,” he was quoted as saying by the reformist Shargh newspaper on Thursday. The dispute has also prompted attacks by Hossein Shariatmadari, editor-in-chief of the ultraconservative Kayhan newspaper, on former foreign minister Mohammad Javad Zarif, former president Hassan Rouhani and politician Hossein Marashi. Mr Shariatmadari accused the three of advancing positions on ending the war or preventing renewed fighting, which allegedly serve US and Israeli interests. He described Mr Marashi’s proposal for a "tactical retreat" to avoid another war as a surrender and rejected Mr Rouhani’s suggestion of a referendum on whether military attacks should continue. “Although the US has no embassy in Iran, some political figures effectively act as Washington’s ambassadors through their positions,” Mr Shariatmadari wrote in an editorial. The comments reflect the level of disagreement among Iranian politicians over the terms of a possible settlement, the conduct of the war and the risks of renewed hostilities.

title: Oil transfers off India's west coast surge as Gulf shipping congestion worsens
description: Gulf producers are cutting prices and absorbing transit risks to retain Asian buyers as shipping costs climb
content: Gulf oil producers are pushing tanker transfers as far as India’s coast and slashing prices to keep crude flowing to Asia, as the makeshift export network around Hormuz buckles under congestion and attack . Ship-to-ship transfers in India's Gulf of Kutch reached 82 cargoes in September, equivalent to about 680,000 barrels a day, according to shipping analytics company Vortexa. Refined products accounted for about 65 per cent of the volume, with crude making up the remainder. " Fujairah and Sohar STS zones were handling record volumes with some indications of delays relating to operational limitations, and thus the activity has spilled over to India,” said Varaleka Pant, senior market analyst at energy intelligence firm Vortexa The expansion shows how the workaround sustaining Gulf exports is coming under strain. Producers have shuttled oil through Hormuz before transferring it to supertankers outside the strait, but congestion and longer voyages are tying up vessels and driving up costs. Crude transfers onto very large crude carriers (VLCCs) have held at about 5 million to 7 million barrels a day since September, accounting for 60 to 70 per cent of total Hormuz flows, according to Rystad Energy. The full process, including waiting time, now takes more than a week, compared with five to six days earlier in the conflict. "The overflow has started to move into the Arabian Sea, but it is still small," said Rahul Choudhary, vice president for oil and gas at Rystad. Some supertankers previously used for Saudi transfers are now discharging directly off India's west coast, he said. A recent tanker strike off Fujairah, the first there in six months, has added pressure to disperse operations. Attacks on Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline have further exposed the vulnerability of alternative export routes. The shift towards India is growing, though analysts differ over its scale. South Korea, India, China and Japan took almost 70 per cent of the Kutch volume, according to Vortexa. In one such transfer, a 2 million-barrel cargo of Saudi Arab Medium loaded at Ras Tanura on September 9 was moved onto the Front Forth VLCC tanker off Kutch in late September. It was bound for S-Oil’s Onsan refinery in South Korea, according to Kpler data. Bimco, the shipping industry association, reported a much smaller figure of 12 STS operations in the area in September, based on Signal Ocean data that counts transfers differently from Vortexa’s cargo-based tally.
