The device has a “thumb-sized development board with a detachable camera sensor, digital microphone and micro-SD storage”, the Justice Department said. Mr Alfozan had started working at OpenAI in July last year and worked on its product team. He was fired on the same day as his arrest, the company said. According to a court motion filed by prosecutors on October 8, actions taken by Mr Alfozan indicated he planned to quickly depart the US. "Indeed, the defendant, his wife, and a third family member have booked one-way tickets from San Francisco to Saudi Arabia (via Istanbul) .. and defendant has the means and the incentive to flee the US sooner if he learns about this case before he is arrested," the court filing reads. California lawyer William Pernik said that he is still waiting to see what other evidence the government has against his client, and that he plans on presenting all appropriate defences in court. “Like countless Americans, Mr Alfozan came to this country years ago as a young person with a dream,” Mr Pernik told The National via email. “These allegations appear wholly out of character for him, and we will relentlessly investigate all evidence produced by the government in this case to understand what actually happened, who was responsible, and any possible reasons why.” He emphasised that his client has been charged with breaching a federal recording statute, not stealing trade secrets or working as a foreign agent. “There is no evidence to suggest otherwise at this time that has been shared with us,” he said. Mr Pernik implied that his client is already facing bias because he was not born in the US. “It is regretful that this is the one factor that seems to have caught the most attention,” he wrote. “Where someone was born is not evidence of anything and national origin is – and always should be – a protected status under our system of laws.” According to his LinkedIn profile, Mr Alfozan has lived in California since 2015 and started working at OpenAI as a lead engineer in 2025. Before his years in California, he was an intern at Meta, Microsoft and SAP. Mr Alfozan received his undergraduate degree from MIT in 2016 and then earned his master's degree in 2025 from the University of California-Berkeley. According to the Justice Department, he was arrested on October 9 and charged with using an electronic, mechanical or other device to intercept oral communications. He is scheduled to appear in court on October 19 for a detention hearing. “If convicted, Alfozan faces a maximum sentence of five years in prison and a $250,000 fine, followed by three years of supervised release,” a press release from the Justice Department reads. OpenAI has faced a barrage of criticism from employees amid allegations that it has disregarded the need for regulations when developing AI technology. American AI companies such as OpenAI also face stiff competition from China, as Washington and Beijing vie for dominance in the technology race. Companies have gone to great lengths to protect intellectual property and trade secrets.

title: India's Bank of Baroda to 'defend interests' after BR Shetty's $15bn lawsuit
description: NMC Health founder alleges lender and employees helped facilitate fraud
content: India's Bank of Baroda on Wednesday ​said ​it would protect ​its interests, a day after UAE-based ⁠businessman and founder of NMC Health BR Shetty filed ⁠a $15 billion case against the lender and ​25 other defendants at Bombay High Court. Mr Shetty alleged ⁠the Bank of Baroda and several current and former employees helped facilitate a fraud that contributed to the collapse of the Middle East healthcare group, according to a ⁠court filing reviewed by Reuters. The firm, then the Gulf's largest private healthcare provider, ​was ⁠placed under administration in 2020 ‌after months of financial mismanagement and disclosed debts of $6.6 billion, way above previous estimates ​of $2.1 billion. Representatives for Mr Shetty did not immediately respond to requests for comment. In a stock exchange notification on Wednesday, the country's second-largest state lender said: “The bank has not been served with such a suit and cannot comment on the contents of pleadings, which are untested in court. If and when the bank is served, the bank will defend the suit firmly and take all steps necessary to protect its interests.” The Bank of Baroda added that it was pursuing recovery and enforcement proceedings in India and the UAE against Mr Shetty for outstanding dues of 28 billion rupees ($294.5 million) and had obtained several decrees against him. The lender will ​not bear any immediate liability until any order is ‌passed or until it ⁠is required to make a provision on ​account of potential damages, the lender said. Bank of Baroda ​shares dropped ‌2.6 per cent on Tuesday after the legal action was reported. The lawsuit, which centres on the bank's lending to ⁠NMC Health and affiliated entities in the UAE, comes three months after the lender agreed to pay $600 million to settle claims brought by administrators of NMC. Mr Shetty alleged that bank officials enabled round-tripping transactions, ignored repeated anti-money laundering warnings and ​accepted documents bearing forged signatures. He is seeking $5 billion in direct damages, $5 billion in consequential damages and an additional $5 billion for reputational harm, the filing showed.

title: Trump threatens renewed military action against Iran
description: Tehran has rejected Washington’s latest response to proposal to end conflict
content: US President Donald Trump has warned of further action against Iran, saying Washington will decide its next move “very soon” as Tehran steps up attacks on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz. Mr Trump, speaking outside the White House late on Tuesday, described Iran as a “failed country” and said its economy was collapsing under severe inflation and financial pressure. “They have no economy … they have no money,” Mr Trump said. “We’ll make a decision on Iran very soon.” The US President later struck a more threatening tone at a campaign event in Alaska, warning of further action against Tehran. “Wait till you see what we do to Iran. We’re going to do a number … wait till you see what we do to Iran, because we’ve sort of had it,” he said. “The big thing is, they’re not going to have a nuclear weapon. That’s buried under thousands of tonnes of rock.” The remarks came after Reuters reported two Iranian officials said Tehran was using new ⁠tactics to target ships sailing through the Strait of Hormuz. The officials declined to ​provide ⁠details but one ‌said Iran had started using different offensive tactics about ​10 days ago, leading to an increase in attacks on such ships. At least 12 vessels have been attacked in and around the Strait of Hormuz in the past week, the UK Maritime Trade Operations agency has said. Six were struck on Sunday alone – five tankers and a container ship. Five incidents occurred in the strait and one near Oman’s Sohar anchorage. “The aim is to frustrate efforts by the United States and its allies to bring down global oil prices,” one was quoted as saying. A second official said Tehran would prevent Washington from lowering oil prices ahead of the US midterm elections on November 3. The US military rejected a claim by Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps that it is in control of the Strait of Hormuz, saying it does not possess an actual naval force. “US forces and their regional partners clearly control the Strait of Hormuz . Just yesterday, US forces assisted their Gulf partners in shipping more than 19 million barrels of crude oil through the strait,” said Central Command, which oversees US military operations across the Middle East. Officials in Tehran have rejected Washington’s latest response to its proposal to end the conflict , which began with US and Israeli strikes across Iran on February 28. Mohsen Rezaei, head of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, described the US response as “insufficient” and warned of possible attacks on regional digital infrastructure if hostilities resumed. Washington has maintained a naval blockade of Iranian ports and expanded sanctions, while seeking an agreement. The Pentagon has also directed US Central Command to complete preparations for possible major combat operations, Axios reported, citing sources familiar with the matter. Mr Trump said last week the US would not attack Iran before the midterm elections, citing progress in negotiations. Israel is also considering its options. Mr Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu have discussed the possibility of renewed military operations against Iran, Axios reported, as the Israeli leader prepared for a general election on October 27. Qatari mediators are awaiting Tehran’s response to a US counterproposal.

title: UAE orders recall of face mask batch over possible contamination
description: Local distributor instructed to retrieve all quantities supplied to the market
content: The UAE has ordered a recall of a batch of face masks because of concerns about possible contamination of the material used in its manufacture. The Emirates Drug Establishment issued the recall for Nin 160 FMB-NML Facemask C G blue, batch number 20251015. It is described as blue in colour and three-ply in structure. The Dubai Health Authority also issued a circular on Monday instructing healthcare centres to comply with the recall. Officials said Ningbo ETDZ Holdings Ltd in China manufactured the masks, and Globemed Care LLC distributed them in the UAE. The drug regulator said the recall was ordered after a quality complaint. Inspections identified foreign material or contamination in units from the affected batch. Healthcare professionals, hospitals and clinics and pharmacies must immediately stop selling, supplying, distributing or using the affected batch. They must identify and quarantine all available stock, then arrange for its return to the local supplier or distributor, Globemed Care LLC. They must also maintain records of quantities identified, quarantined, and returned. Residents who purchased the affected product should stop using any packs with batch number 20251015 and return them to the point of purchase or supplier. Healthcare providers must report any product quality complaints or adverse incidents related to the masks through EDE-approved reporting channels. Globemed Care LLC has also been ordered to retrieve all distributed quantities from the UAE market. It must also provide the regulator with details of quantities imported, distributed, returned, and remaining in stock, as well as a complete UAE distribution list. The regulator also urged people to report any quality concerns or adverse incidents involving the product directly to the authority.

title: UAE offers $1 million prize for winners of global AI challenge
description: 10,000 entrants from around the world will take part in competition
content: The UAE announced a prize of $1 million for the winners of a global competition aimed at improving the quality of life through the use of agentic artificial intelligence . Mohammed Al Gergawi, Minister of Cabinet Affairs, announced the award on Wednesday at the Annual Meeting of Global Future Leaders, organised by the UAE Government and the World Economic Forum (WEF). The competition, a collaboration between Dubai Municipality and the WEF, will feature 10,000 entrants working to improve quality of life through artificial intelligence. The winner of the Agentic AI Award will be announced at next year's event, with organisers hoping it will become a "model for hundreds of cities worldwide". "This is an annual $1 million prize involving over 10,000 global changemakers across 150 countries to develop smart solutions that enhance urban services and quality of life," Mr Al Gergawi said. It was also announced that the Centre for Global Future Opportunities will be established between the Dubai Future Foundation and the WEF, which will "turn technological and economic opportunities into policies, legislation and projects that can be implemented". Also unveiled was the Future 20 initiative, which showcases the effective work of 20 emerging leaders under the age of 30 "capable of driving major global transformations". The first cohort, chosen from around the globe, was in attendance at Wednesday's meeting in Dubai

title: Barefoot calm in the Baa Atoll: A family review of The Westin Maldives Miriandhoo
description: Set within a Unesco Biosphere Reserve, this intimate island combines well-being experiences with a relaxed, family-friendly feel
content: The Westin Maldives Miriandhoo Resort sits on a coral island in the heart of the Baa Atoll. Surrounded by a vibrant house reef and the protected waters of a Unesco Biosphere Reserve, this pocket-sized hideaway recently received its first Green Globe certification, a mark of its focus on sustainability and biodiversity protection. Positioning itself as a family-friendly escape with a focus on well-being, the resort uniquely incorporates subtle Japanese design influences, via minimalist architecture, water features and anchored by a distinctive Japanese-style tree at its centre. I visited with my husband and our toddler daughter and found that, while it's not the most ultra-polished property in the Maldives , nor does it try to be, it offers a quietly confident island stay and slower pace that suits its scale. Arrival is direct to the hotel via seaplane or by a domestic flight to the nearby Dharavandhoo Airport, followed by a 20-minute speedboat transfer. We opted for the former, and the welcome begins before we step on to the island, with resort staff lining up to smile and wave as our seaplane taxis to the jetty. A short buggy ride delivers us to an open-air lobby, where a chilled welcome drink awaits and check-in is handled unhurriedly as we drink in the ocean views. We stayed in a Beach Villa, a category that works particularly well when travelling with a young child. Our room opens on to a terrace with steps down to the sand and a narrow path through dense greenery leading straight to the beach, ideal for early-morning walks and sunset strolls. Inside, the design is relaxed rather than glossy, with dark wood finishes and soft neutral tones. It feels natural and lived-in rather than overtly staged, and I wasn’t worried about letting my daughter run around and make herself at home. The spacious bathroom comes with a delightful open-air shower, there is something unmistakably indulgent about rinsing off under warm water with palm leaves blowing overhead. A Westin Heavenly Bed lives up to its sleep-inducing reputation. A small highlight is the Kids Sleep Manual, designed in collaboration with paediatric sleep specialists and packed with dream-promoting activities like beachside bedtime stories and stargazing walks, alongside a sleep-focused children’s room service menu. All 70 accommodation units have private pools, but note that, at least in our room category, these are not temperature controlled and the water is noticeably cold – so much so that I never managed a proper swim, only braving a quick leg dip. More premium options exist, including the two-bedroom Heavenly Beach Residence or Heavenly Overwater Villa with Pool. Dining centres around four venues, so the choice isn’t vast, but each has a clear identity. The standout is The Pearl, a Japanese restaurant set over the water, with sweeping ocean views and a live kitchen. The sushi and sashimi are exceptional, order the sushi boat for a beautifully prepared platter that ranks among the best I’ve had in the Maldives. Service runs firmly on island time, but the setting, particularly at sunset, is divine. Island Kitchen pairs all-day dining with healthy international dishes, overlooking the pool and sea beyond. This is where the resort’s Eat Well concept comes into play, with nutritious options alongside a dedicated children’s menu. For casual evenings, Hawker brings a lively open-air feel, and the seafood barbecue was one of our highlights, with chefs grilling freshly caught tuna and squid under the stars, accompanied by live music. Sunset Bar is the best vantage point for golden hour, with squishy beanbags perfectly positioned for sundowners. Breakfast at Island Kitchen is a highlight. The buffet is kept behind glass, a simple but effective solution to the fly issue common at island resorts, and the spread is generous but not excessive. There are well-being shots and local options like mas huni, a fresh tuna and coconut dish, alongside a strong Asian selection, plus a separate station for made-to-order fruit platters. For a small island, the range of facilities is impressive. Alongside the main swimming pool, there are tennis courts, running tracks and a fitness studio with TRX and functional training equipment, plus a comprehensive programme of free daily fitness classes. The watersports centre offers everything from scuba instruction to snorkelling trips and dolphin-spotting cruises. We partook of the latter and enjoyed views of shoals of spinner dolphins cruising alongside the boat. Trips also tap into the wider Baa Atoll Biosphere, including to nearby Hanifaru Bay, famous for hosting the world’s largest gathering of manta rays. The Heavenly Spa is one of the resort’s most tranquil spaces. Housed in overwater villa-style treatment rooms, the beds are positioned so guests can gaze directly into the ocean below while enjoying a massage. Watching colourful marine life drift past as a therapist worked her magic was particularly soothing. The resort is family-friendly without being overtly family-centric. The Kids Club features an impressive outdoor area with a swimming pool and a large wooden pirate-ship playground, alongside an indoor play space where staff run workshops and craft sessions. It caters only to children aged four and above, and while younger children may be permitted entry if accompanied by a parent, this is subject to daily capacity and staffing, meaning the space may not always be accessible to families travelling with babies and toddlers. Some staff go the extra mile, from a Sunset Bar bartender creating a custom mocktail for my daughter to the excursion team staging an impromptu Baby Shark- themed disco on a boat trip to local island Eydhafushi. Late restaurant hours – with most venues opening for dinner at 7pm – mean evenings may require forward planning for families with young children, including arranging babysitters in advance. That said, for those with children beyond toddler stage seeking calm surroundings rather than constant entertainment, the balance works. However, while the child-focused sleep manual is a good idea, it perhaps needs some tweaking. When we tried to use it to settle a jet-lagged toddler, we were told, after several back-and-forth phone calls, that most of the Kids Sleep Well menu items were unavailable later in the evening. Sustainability is embedded in the resort’s day-to-day operations, with a focus on energy, water and marine conservation. Solar power plays a central role in operations, alongside an on-site desalination and bottled water plant and the resort team leads coral restoration, sea turtle monitoring and reef-safe tourism initiatives. There are no designated accessible rooms, and as with many coral islands, pathways, overwater villas and boat transfers may present challenges for guests with limited mobility. Rates start from $750 per night. Check-in is from 3pm and checkout is at noon; westinmaldives.com. This review was conducted at the invitation of the hotel and reflects standards during this time

title: Ukrainian ex-officer on trial over Nord Stream bombing argues it was not a crime
description: Serhii Kuznetsov accused of leading group in 2022 attack that ruptured crucial gas pipeline
content: A Ukrainian former military officer went on trial ​in Germany on Wednesday, accused of organising the secret operation that blew ⁠up the Nord Stream pipelines in September 2022, severing western Europe from a vast source ⁠of Russian natural gas. The suspect, Serhii Kuznetsov , 50, is accused of leading a group of Ukrainian agents, including divers and an explosives expert, to mount one of the biggest infrastructure sabotage operations of ⁠modern times. He ​has denied ⁠any involvement in the blasts that ruptured the 1,200km-long ‌Baltic Sea pipeline. His lawyers argued on Wednesday that blowing up the pipeline may not have been a crime. Moving to have the case dismissed, Mr Kuznetsov's lawyer Nicola Canestrini said the pipeline – which provided half of Germany's imports of natural gas before Russia's ⁠invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 – was a “Russian weapon” and therefore potentially a legitimate target. “Is it unlawful to destroy an aggressor's infrastructure without harming any human beings?” Mr Canestrini asked. Mr Kuznetsov said he could not mount a proper defence because he was obliged to withhold Ukrainian state secrets. “He has to mount a defence with his hands tied,” said Mr Canestrini. The case provides the first opportunity for a public hearing of evidence gathered during a years-long investigation, which has been diplomatically and politically awkward for a German government that remains staunchly supportive of Ukraine despite the investigative trail linking Kyiv to the crime. Prosecutors have alleged that Mr Kuznetsov, who was arrested under an international warrant ⁠in Italy last year, worked with other members of the military to plan the clandestine operation on behalf of unidentified Ukrainian state entities. The government in Kyiv has also denied any involvement, a sensitive point in its relations with Germany, Ukraine's largest European supplier of military ​aid. The Russian government said it expected a “just verdict” that would reveal the names of the perpetrators and those who ordered the operation. German prosecutors say the actions of which Mr Kuznetsov is accused – attacking civilian targets and causing explosions that destroyed infrastructure and damaged public services – would amount to a war crime. The alleged aim was to disrupt a major source of foreign revenue for Russia after its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, launched earlier that year. Protesters gathered outside the court in Hamburg, Germany in support of the accused, with a sign that read: “What are war crimes?” “Russia is the only war criminal that belongs in the dock,” said one dozens of protesters outside the court. Mr Kuznetsov is the only person on trial but Croatian authorities have arrested another man, identified as Vladimir Z., who prosecutors believe was one of the divers in the team. The explosion of Nord Stream sealed the end of Germany's long-standing dependence on Russian natural gas, although Moscow had already cut supplies over Berlin's support for European sanctions following Russia's invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Germany previously received half its natural gas imports through the Nord Stream 1 pipeline, by far the biggest and most modern Russian conduit serving western Europe, which allowed Russia to bypass Soviet-era pipelines crossing Ukraine. The supply had been due to double with the opening of a twin pipeline, Nord Stream 2, which was already built, although Berlin cancelled approval to start operations shortly before Russia's invasion. The trial, expected ​to continue into February, could also have domestic political implications. Germany's far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD), leading in ‌opinion polls for more than a year, has called for ⁠an end to military aid for Ukraine and a restoration of energy ​ties with Moscow. In the initial months after the pipelines were attacked, western officials mainly pointed fingers at Russia. Moscow has always denied ​any involvement and called ‌the suggestion it would blow up its own pipelines absurd. It also rejects charges that it has more recently targeted western infrastructure with so-called “hybrid” sabotage and drone attacks. The ⁠Nord Stream system, lying at a depth of 80 to 110 metres under the Baltic and built by Russian energy corporation Gazprom ⁠to supply up to 110 billion cubic metres of gas to Germany, was formerly at the core of economic ties between the two countries. On September 26, 2022, several blasts were detected by Swedish seismologists over 17 hours. The explosions sent huge plumes of methane gas into the atmosphere, as three of the four concrete-coated steel pipelines were ruptured. Prosecutors allege Mr Kuznetsov travelled to Germany through Poland about three weeks before the attack, using ​a forged Ukrainian passport. They say he and his group used a sailboat hired in the northern German city of Rostock to reach an area close to the Danish island of Bornholm, where they rigged specialised military-grade explosives fitted with timers to the sea floor. The weekly Der Spiegel magazine and ZDF public television have previously reported that five men and one woman were on the rented yacht Andromeda, which left Rostock on September 6 and returned on September 23, 2022.

title: Houthi attack hits Aramco's historic nerve centre in Saudi Arabia
description: Dhahran complex houses key research facilities, thousands of employees and their families, and the site of the kingdom's first commercial oil discovery
content: A missile attack on an administrative building of Saudi Arabia's state energy company Aramco hit the historic centre of the kingdom's oil industry , sparking a fire that authorities said caused no casualties. The strike by the Yemeni Houthi rebels hit a complex that serves as the nerve centre of the world's largest oil exporter, housing key research and development site, energy operations and thousands of employees and their families. People living near the building described moments of terror as a powerful explosion shook the area. "This was the loudest explosion I have ever heard in my life," one woman told The National . Another resident said relatives living closer to the site had reported seeing smoke and flames rising from the area following the attack. While no further details have been released about the incident, the site is a key one for Aramco, serving as its central hub for oil, gas, and energy operations. Aramco, at the time known as the Arabian American Oil Company, moved its headquarters from New York City to Dhahran in 1952. Dhahran was where the kingdom’s first commercial oil was found in 1938, at Dammam No 7, the “Prosperity Well". The Saudi government gradually acquired the company, completing a full buyout in 1980, before it was renamed the Saudi Arabian Oil Company (Aramco) in 1988. Aramco’s headquarters is situated within a vast complex spread across 58 square kilometres, with a large residential area housing a reported 11,000 people, including employees and their families. The Dhahran district also has a research and development centre and the Expec Advanced Research Centre, which was inaugurated in 2008. Expec has been upgraded with a building to focus on upstream research and development. The Dhahran complex also houses a large-scale cooling plant, operated by Saudi Tabreed, with a 32,000 refrigeration-tonne capacity that includes thermal storage tanks for energy saving. The chilled water piping network stretches 16 kilometres to reach sites, meeting Saudi Aramco's requirements for cooling. The area also includes Ithra, the King Abdulaziz Centre for World Culture, which was built by Aramco as a cultural and creative destination for the public. The centre has attracted more than four million since its opening in 2018. The Dhahran area was attacked on February 25, 1991, during the Gulf War, when an Iraqi Scud missile struck a US Army barracks, killing 28 American soldiers and wounding 110. Aramco’s other sites in the Eastern province have also faced attacks in the past. Several drones and missiles hit Saudi Aramco’s Abqaiq and Khurais oil processing centres on September 14, 2019, knocking out about 50 per cent of the country’s crude oil production. The 17-minute strike by 18 drones and three low-flying missiles, claimed by the Houthis, caused a surge in oil prices and shut down more than 5 per cent of global oil supply. Saudi Arabia said about two weeks later that it had fully restored oil output. In March 2022, an Aramco plant in Jizan was also attacked by the Houthis with a drone laden with explosives, with a gas station in Khamis Mushait and a power station in Dhahran also hit. In early March this year, after the start of the Iran war, a fire broke out at Aramco’s Ras Tanura refinery , the kingdom’s largest, with 550,000 barrels per day of capacity, due to drone attacks. Operations were halted for 16 days. Ras Tanura, on Saudi Arabia's Gulf coast, hosts one of the world’s largest oil export terminals and a major refining facility. The port handles a significant share of Saudi crude exports. Other sites hit this year include Satorp in Jubail, a joint venture between Saudi Aramco and TotalEnergies processing 465,000 bpd and one of the world's largest export refining platforms, as well as Samref in Yanbu, a 400,000 bpd Aramco-ExxonMobil joint venture. Earlier this month, Aramco’s chief executive Amin Nasser said ​the company had ‌the ⁠strategic ​reserves and ​flexibility ‌to ⁠isolate or shift output ⁠as required. Aramco can ⁠make its maximum ⁠sustainable production ​capacity of ⁠12 million bpd available ⁠within days, ​he ​told the Energy Intelligence Forum in London. “Our system is intact,” he added. Aramco, which is listed on the Tadawul exchange, is majority owned by the Saudi government. It is due to release its third quarter financial results on November 3.

title: UK loses 'leverage' to prevent atrocities in global wars
description: Human rights lawyers fear aid cuts and weakness leave Britain unable to play leading international role
content: Cuts to the UK’s foreign aid and diplomatic arms are hampering Britain's ability to prevent atrocities as global conflicts increase, experts have warned. Yasmine Ahmed, senior director at Amnesty International , said the UK government was not acting fast enough to prevent war crimes, such as those allegedly committed in Sudan and Gaza . “Often atrocity prevention is not prioritised sufficiently in terms of a whole of government policy response,” Ms Ahmed told The National. Last year, Britain’s overseas aid budget was slashed from 0.5 per cent of its gross national income to 0.3 per cent, at a time when conflicts are increasing worldwide. These cuts were issued by former prime minister Keir Starmer in January last year and Britain's spending on overseas aid is expected to fall by 42 per cent, or £6.5 billion ($8.6 billion), over four years, according to the Independent Commission for Aid Impact. One of the first Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office units to feel the impact of the cuts was international humanitarian law cell monitoring war crimes in Gaza. The FCDO has insisted these aid cuts would not affect the department’s ability to conduct human rights assessments of a conflict – but Ms Ahmed was sceptical. “If you’ve got a huge percentage – 20 per cent of the Foreign Office being cut – there’s no doubt this is going to have a significant impact across the board,” she said. “The question is how well will the Foreign Office continue to be equipped to conduct these assessments.” In the past few weeks there has been an escalation of conflict between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis in Yemen, and the possibility of all-out war between Eritrea and Ethiopia has developed. Yet the UK's ability to enforce the laws of war and human rights on the world stage was dwindling. “What we’re finding now is that the UK and certainly other European states and other western states don’t have as much leverage as they used to,” Ms Ahmed said. This was leading to a visible decline in the protection of civilians in conflict. “They [the UK and European governments] are operating in an increasingly volatile political world and it’s increasingly transactional,” she said. “There is less space to be values driven.” On Tuesday, a group of British human rights lawyers and experts in global conflict called on the UK to loosen jurisdiction rules, so British courts can prosecute on a wider range of war crimes as well going after as companies accused of involvement. The group warned that the UK was currently “ill-equipped to identify and respond effectively to the warning signs of genocide and other atrocity crimes”, and that this had “serious implications” for “national security, stability and economic prosperity”. The Atrocities Standing Group, which includes Nobel Peace Prize laureate Oleksandra Matviichuk and Baroness Helena Kennedy, published the results of its 18 months of inquiry and parliamentary hearings on Tuesday in a report. It called for a tougher global policing role by using more “Magnitsky-style sanctions”, targeted punitive measures. Frozen sovereign assets from such sanctions could be repurposed to compensate victims of war crimes, by introducing relevant laws to do so, the report suggested. The UK government is seeking to re-establish Britain’s role in the world as conflicts escalate globally. “As the international rules-based order is facing fragmentation and significant challenges, it is key that the UK uses its global position to lead and support efforts to secure justice and accountability for international crimes,” the report said. Former British prime minister Gordon Brown, who has endorsed the report, said the UK needed to take serious foreign policy steps that go well beyond “condemnation” and “sympathy”. “Sympathy is not prevention, condemnation is not policy,” he said ahead of the report's launch. “The question before the United Kingdom and other democratic states is simple and grave. “Will we continue to respond to atrocity crimes only after they have shocked our conscience, or will we build a serious system to predict and prevent them, and respond to them lawfully and in time?” The upholding of human rights risks being further eroded by the US decision to sanction the International Criminal Court in The Hague. While the UK has made “strong statements” of their continued support for the court, their next step could be putting in place a “blocking statute” that would make the sanctions unenforceable in the UK, Ms Ahmed said. The wars in Sudan and in Gaza have featured clear examples of the UK government’s inability to intervene in time, Ms Ahmed said. She questioned why it had taken the UK months to apply a partial suspension of around 30 out of about 350 arms export licences to Israel for military use in Gaza, which the British government eventually announced in September 2024. Export licensing was one area in which the government could act quickly, by referring to its own criteria and the Arms Trade Treaty, she said. “They have the duty to prevent genocide and other crimes, but that’s very hard to enforce. But when you have the export-licensing criteria, that’s where we find there’s a space where the government themselves has processes to evaluate. “I was going in on a weekly basis with either ministers or high-level officials and sometimes middle-ranked officials. We were presenting the evidence. It certainly took longer than it should have,” she said. “It did so on the basis that Israel couldn’t be found to have a commitment to comply with international law because it was restricting aid.” Likewise, the UK’s response to the Sudanese civil war had failed to activate “the full plethora of government machinery”, despite its key resolutions on Sudan at the UN Security Council. With cuts to overseas aid anticipated for the long term, Ms Ahmed – who previously worked as a legal adviser to the FCDO – outlined options that would reinforce the role of human rights in UK foreign policy. The units involved in human rights and atrocity prevention needed to be “supported at the highest-ministerial level, prioritised, given resources and given the power within the bureaucratic system to have a say when policy decisions are being made,” she said. Instead, government advisers on human rights policy were often sidelined. “So often, what I have found, is that the human rights directorate aren't key stakeholders in key political decisions,” Ms Ahmed said. Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband's declaration last month that settler “terrorists” were responsible for “ethnic cleansing” in the West Bank was a major step, Ms Ahmed said. “That was a really huge development and important to note because it's the first time the government has ever made any such determination and it's clear, given the magnitude of the forced displacement of Palestinians from their land in the West Bank,” she said. Questions remain about how the UK will implement its most significant foreign policy shift in months – the move to impose sanctions on the expansion of illegal settlements in the occupied West Bank. Foreign Office officials have suggested a six to nine month time frame for initial measures to be implemented but campaigners including Ms Ahmed say this is too long. “As I understand it, there is a commitment to implementing it in a way that’s effective,” she said. “The devil will be in the detail to ensure that they in fact do that.” Amnesty International and other organisations are calling on the government to make sure the ban extends to banks and financial services that work with companies involved in illegal settlements. “It’s not just about goods and services to settlements. It’s also about the financial enabling of the occupation … which are involved in continuing the financial stability of the settlements,” Ms Ahmed said.

title: UAE weather: Rainy weekend expected in east of country
description: Winds of up to 50kph expected
content: Rain is expected in parts of the UAE across much of the weekend, according to the latest update from the National Centre of Meteorology (NCM). Wet weather is forecast in the south-east of the country on Wednesday, with winds reaching up to 50kph. On Friday and Saturday, clouds in the east are likely to bring rain, while wet weather is forecast in the north-east. The NCM's website says rain is expected on Wednesday in Fujairah and in Al Ain on Thursday. At the weekend, the highest temperature in the country will be 41°C in Sweihan on Saturday. The temperature will reach 39°C in Abu Dhabi on Saturday, with Dubai's temperature cooling slightly from 37°C on Wednesday and Thursday to 35°C on Saturday and Sunday.

title: Zayed National Museum's first temporary exhibition to explore 7,000 years of camel history
description: Opening in December, Tracks Through Time will feature rare archaeological discoveries, ancient rock art and enduring Emirati traditions
content: Zayed National Museum has announced its first temporary exhibition, exploring more than 7,000 years of camel history and the animal's significance in Emirati culture. Tracks Through Time: The Camel in Society, Trade and Art will open in early December, coinciding with the Abu Dhabi museum's first anniversary. The exhibition will trace the camel's role in trade, society and artistic expression, from its presence in the region thousands of years ago to contemporary traditions such as racing and beauty competitions. Among the highlights will be the first public display of archaeological evidence of an extinct wild camel species. These include bones discovered in Baynunah in Abu Dhabi, from between 4500 and 4000BC, and Bronze Age remains from Al Sufouh in Dubai, dating to between 2000 and 1300BC. Domesticated camel bones from Saruq Al Hadid in Dubai will also be displayed, offering some of the world's earliest evidence of the transition from wild camels to domesticated animals. The artefacts are on loan from the Natural History Museum Abu Dhabi, and the Dubai Culture and Arts Authority. “We are excited to present our first temporary exhibition, which celebrates the camel's profound significance in Emirati culture and the broader story of the UAE,” says Peter Magee, director of the Zayed National Museum . He says the exhibition draws on archaeological research to explore the relationship between humans and camels, from early domestication to the prestige of Al Hejin racing and Mazayna beauty competitions. Other objects include camel rock artwork from Fujairah dating back 3,000 years, a rare children's book from the 1840s detailing camel species and their uses and UAE postage stamps featuring the animal. Archival photographs, film footage and oral testimonies from camel herders will offer further insight into the animal's place in daily life. Recordings of Taghrooda, a form of Bedouin poetry, and Alheda'a , the traditional practice of camel calling, will also feature. Both are recognised by Unesco as intangible cultural heritage. The exhibition will be accompanied by workshops, guided tours and activities as part of the museum's first anniversary celebrations, alongside a dedicated retail offering inspired by the exhibition's themes. Tracks Through Time: The Camel in Society, Trade and Art opens at Zayed National Museum in Abu Dhabi in early December

title: Four Syrian troops killed in ambush on Hama motorway
description: Incident happened on edge of desert area that has witnessed attacks by ISIS and other militant groups
content: Four Syrian security personnel were killed when two patrols were ambushed in the countryside of Hama province on Tuesday night. Nour Al Baba, spokesman for Syria's Interior Ministry, condemned the attacks on the Salamiya-Athriya motorway and said authorities would pursue those responsible. “With deep sorrow and grief, we mourn the loss of four of our brothers – road security personnel – who were killed when two of their patrols were targeted in the Hama countryside,” he said. “The crime will not deter us from continuing to pursue the perpetrators and bring them to justice,” Mr Al Baba said, adding that the incident would strengthen the security forces’ resolve to protect civilians and safeguard lives. Internal security forces said they were continuing efforts to track down those involved. The attack took place on the road linking Salamiya, east of Hama city, with Athriya, an area farther east on the route towards the Syrian desert. The motorway forms part of a transport corridor connecting central Syria with the country’s eastern regions. The area is on the edge of the Syrian desert, where armed groups and ISIS militants have carried out attacks. The ministry did not provide further details about the circumstances of the attack, including the weapons used.

title: To the Ramparts: New missile shield 'protects warships from drone swarms'
description: Laser-guided rockets offer lower cost-to-kill ratio than Patriots
content: A cost-effective missile system to defend civilian and military sites from drone swarms has been unveiled in France . Rampart, developed by Naval Group , can create a defensive shield around warships using large numbers of low-cost laser-guided rockets rather than expensive interceptors such as Patriot, that were expended at high rates in the Iran war. It has completed successful sea trials in the Mediterranean, including a French Navy counter-drone exercise off Toulon. “It is designed to build a defensive shield around a warship in drone warfare,” said Stephan Meunier, a former French navy commander involved with the programme. Naval Group expects to produce up to 10,000 Rampart systems by 2028. In tests, the system struck an aerial drone as well as unguided rockets trained on surface targets. The system fires laser-guided 68mm rockets fitted with proximity fuses and has a range of up to 6km. The launcher consists of four modules, each carrying 20 projectiles, giving a maximum load of 80 rockets. It can be loaded with a combination of weapons, including surface-to-air and surface-to-surface missiles, decoys or precision missiles. An experienced crew can reload a single 20-round module in about 10 minutes. The system weighs about four tonnes, allowing it to be fitted to relatively small warships including corvettes. During the recent Iran war, western forces used large numbers of expensive interceptors against relatively cheap drones. Patriot missiles costing more than $4 million each were used to take out Shahed-136 drones costing just $35,000, roughly the same price as a guided 68mm rocket. “The cost-to-kill ratio is very effective and it can tackle a drone swarm attack,” Mr Meunier said. “Rockets are cheaper and more efficient.” There is growing evidence that shipping in the Arabian Gulf and Red Sea could face “saturation attacks” by drones fired from Iran or the rebel Houthis. Naval ships equipped with Rampart would be able to provide significant close-in protection, Mr Meunier said. Rampart can also be deployed as a ground-based system to protect airports, military bases and civilian areas. “This system would provide good defences for fixed installations such as airports and to protect urban centres or military camps in the Gulf as well as on board warships,” Mr Meunier said. Over the weekend, Saudi Arabia’s main airport came under attack from Houthi rebels, with 13 people killed in two incidents. Missiles were also intercepted in Riyadh and Dammam. Naval Group has also developed a single Rampart module for its Sirenha unmanned surface vessel, allowing an autonomous drone boat to provide an additional defensive layer. The French company is also working with Emirates' defence group Edge to conduct trials of the UAE-developed SkyKnight air-defence missile, beginning with land trials before maritime testing next year. SkyKnight can engage aerial threats at ranges of up to 10km, potentially giving Rampart a more capable missile option alongside its 68mm rockets. There is also a possibility that Rampart could be battle-tested in Ukraine where Kyiv is getting desperately short of air defences against daily Russian drone and missile attacks. If successful, then it could well provide a major step in defending key military and civilians sites from the threat of drone saturation attack at low cost.

title: Geeing up for 6G: What the next mobile standard promises and challenges it faces
description: With AI growing more powerful, reliability and security are priorities
content: Over the past weeks, UAE telecom operators etisalat and du have announced further progress in their march towards 6G, the next generation of wireless communication. The industry is accelerating its preparations for the technology that being presented as vital to the world becoming more connected, underpinned by increasingly intelligent devices and services . Du said on Tuesday it has delivered commercial U6GHz connectivity on its 5G+ network, which will serve as a foundation for high-capacity services across homes, businesses and industries . Meanwhile, Abu Dhabi's etisalat – which recently rebranded back from e& – said it has commercially launched a service that increase upload speeds to smartphones threefold. 6G promises faster speeds and efficiency than the current 5G mobile phone technology, which also has more advanced forms under names such as 5G+, 5G Advanced and 5.5G. Historically, new generations of wireless technology have emerged with every new decade, suggesting 6G could become available in the early 2030s. This is a widely shared industry expectation. The US introduced the third generation in 2002, the fourth in 2010 and 5G in 2018. The second and first generations were in the 1980s and early 1990s, respectively, with the “zero G” before that. While a 6G rollout is predicted in the early 2030s, not all of its features are expected to be available at launch, as the industry would continue testing its deployment. 5G's maximum transmission speed is 20 gigabits per second, which is already 20 times faster that 4G's 1Gbps rate under ideal circumstances. However, 6G's theoretical maximum compared to 5G, has varied from anywhere between 50 times faster, or 1 terabit per second, to 1,000 times, or 2.5 terabytes per second. One can only imagine how much that will increase transmission speeds. A multi-gigabyte file that used to take seconds or a few minutes to download could be done in a snap. The consumer proposition of 6G will always be front and centre, especially as digital consumption and reliance on connected devices will only become more widespread. But on an industrial scale, 6G is expected to power advanced iterations of immersive and mass communication, ubiquitous connectivity, integrated sensing and communication, low-latency and hyper-reliable communication and artificial intelligence communication, according to the International Telecommunication Union, which leads the framework and standards-setting of wireless communications. Communications, business and economic gains aside, the power of 6G will also play a critical role in society by enabling affordable, resilient and energy‑efficient networks for health, education, agriculture and disaster response, the Geneva-based UN agency said. “Advanced networks also present a way to close the persistent digital divide that today leaves many people in low-income countries behind,” it added. Transport, home appliances and security, payment networks, financial transactions and a host of other products and services expected to be highly connected in the future will also rely on the speed 6G would offer. There are a number of issues that need to be addressed to ensure the reliability of 6G networks. Arguably the biggest challenge is to build 6G networks resilient to any AI-induced compromises. Networks of the future should be able to detect threats and adaptive enough to respond to them, according to the EC-Council University in New Mexico. Encryption, especially that which can protect against quantum threats, and integration to blockchain would also be important to avoid unauthorised data access and manipulation, the university added.

title: 'We expect more from the top': Lisandro Martinez takes aim at Manchester United hierarchy
description: Defender says club bosses failed to strengthen squad sufficiently after loss at Atletico Madrid extends poor start to season
content: Manchester United defender Lisandro Martinez did not hold back as he criticised the club's hierarchy ​after ​their ​Champions League defeat to ⁠Atletico Madrid on Tuesday. United slipped to a 2-0 defeat, which means Michael Carrick 's team have now gone winless for five consecutive games across competitions. Martinez, however, attempted to highlight issues outside the pitch, stating that he ⁠expected greater investment to help ​the team compete at the highest level. The Argentina international singled ⁠out director of football Jason Wilcox, saying United needed more signings to compete with their rivals. “I expect more from ​our ⁠technical director. I have ‌to be honest. And also, as players, we ​have to do more,” Martinez told Amazon Prime. “Tonight it is easy to [blame] the coach, easy to say the players but also we have to see other areas.” Atletico took the lead through Pablo Barrios inside the opening minute at the Metropolitano, before Ademola Lookman secured victory in the 79th minute, shortly after United defender Leny Yoro was sent off. United are on three points in the Champions League league phase, having opened their campaign with a 4-0 win over ​Sabah FK . United are returning to the ‌Champions League after a ⁠two-season absence, having finished ​bottom of their group in their previous appearance ​in ‌the competition in 2023/24. “We had a fantastic season last season ⁠and now we expect more from the top, from ⁠upstairs, to bring in more players to compete, because many teams have brought in many players as well,” Martinez added. “Atletico have an amazing team and they deserved to win today. “I have to be honest, as players we have to do more but it is also important when you make a strong squad to be ready for this kind of night.” United, who are 13th in the Premier League , ​visit Leeds United on Sunday before travelling to Como for their next Champions League fixture on October 21. Former Manchester United star Wayne Rooney said Martinez's comments were unwarranted and could throw the dressing room into chaos. “It is disrespectful to his teammates,” Rooney was quoted as saying by the BCC. “He is saying his teammates aren't good enough. “Bruno [Fernandes] is the only one with any right to say that. Behind closed doors, it happens – but that interview isn't going to help. “[Martinez] has tried to speak on behalf of the players but done it the wrong way.” Barcelona recovered well to defeat Galatasaray 4-1. Barca overturned a first-half deficit with Lamine Yamal supplying two assists. Galatasaray went ahead as Alexey Batrakov scored in the 28th minute. The hosts thought they had doubled their lead through a Baris Yilmaz header, only for VAR to identify an offside ​in the build-up. Joao Cancelo equalised just before half-time and Yamal then set up Fermin Lopez and Anthony ‌Gordon to score in the 50th and 53rd minutes. ⁠Karim Adeyemi completed the victory. Also, Arsenal scored three times in seven minutes to defeat Lille 3-0. Arsenal had to wait until the 64th minute for Jurrien Timber to break Lille's resistance from Noni Madueke's pass. Substitute Bukayo Saka then set up Eberechi Eze's goal before Kai Havertz supplied Saka for the ​third in the 71st minute.

title: Ollie Watkins on target for Al Hilal while Sardar Azmoun bags double as Shabab Al Ahli win in Jeddah
description: Iranian striker scores twice as UAE club extend perfect start to AFC Champions League
content: Sardar Azmoun struck both goals as Shabab Al Ahli picked up a superb away win at Al Ittihad in the AFC Champions League on Tuesday night. The victory took the UAE club to a perfect six points from six, while Saudi Pro League Al Ittihad have just a single point after opening their campaign with a draw against Al Shamal SC of Qatar last month. Backed by a full house in Jeddah, the home side started positively with Ahmed Al Julaydan forcing Matheus Donelli into a save from a tight angle in the sixth minute. Shabab Al Ahli , however, struck in the next phase of play when Guilherme Bala powered down the left before teeing up the unmarked Azmoun to slot home. Al Ittihad looked for an immediate response, with Steven Bergwijn testing Donelli from distance in the 13th minute, but the visitors doubled their advantage three minutes later. Reza Ghandipour, who had only just replaced the injured Bala, released Azmoun with a through ball and the forward outpaced his markers before converting from a tight angle. “We conceded two goals because of easy mistakes, which made the task difficult afterwards,” said Al Ittihad coach Jens Wissing. “My job as a coach is to work with the players. We were better in the second half and we reached the opponent's goal, but we were not successful.” He added: “We played with three forwards because we had more crosses, and it was possible to make use of one of the crosses. We did not play the game well. We had many chances and we could have been better.” Elsewhere, Al Hilal recorded their second successive victory after defeating Al Sadd 2-0. Ollie Watkins put Saudi Pro League leaders Hilal ahead in the first half before a Ruben Neves spot-kick confirmed the points as Qatar’s Al Sadd suffered a second consecutive defeat. “I am happy with the players' performance,” said Hilal boss Simone Inzaghi. “We produced a big performance and controlled most of the game, and I saw a wonderful display from the team.” The Italian also praised Gabriel Martinelli after the former Arsenal man gave the Al Sadd defence a difficult evening. “He is a big player and we are lucky to have him with us,” added Inzaghi. “He always proves his high quality and his ability to serve the team and benefit it in more than one different position.”

title: Man United ratings vs Atletico Madrid: Yoro off and Baleba promising on another tough night for Carrick
description: Pressure builds on Old Trafford boss after Champions League defeat in Spain
content: Atletico Madrid needed only 50 seconds ​to punish Manchester United's high defensive line on their way to a 2-0 victory in the Spanish capital on Tuesday night. Alex Baena broke clear down the left before squaring for Pablo Barrios ​to finish and it looked like being a long night for the visitors. United threatened through ‌ Bryan Mbeumo , who shot narrowly wide and later forced a close-range save from Jan Oblak, while Marcus Rashford also squandered an opportunity. Atletico had a Johnny Cardoso ⁠effort disallowed for a Marcos Llorente handball before the break and Julian Alvarez volleyed against the post early in the second ⁠half. United's task became harder when Leny Yoro was sent off in the 74th minute for denying Jonathan David a goalscoring opportunity. Five minutes later, Ademola Lookman tapped into an empty net after David's shot was saved. "I don't see it being a red card, I have to say. I really don't agree with the decision," said United boss Michael Carrick. "I don't know whether I'm allowed to say or not, but I just don't agree with the decision. "He wasn't really moving in a quick direction to goal. Whether it was or wasn't a foul, or not a foul, it was very soft and slow and [to get] a red card for that, especially to be taken to VAR. I just don't understand it." Senne Lammens – 6: Awful start, not that he was at fault, as he conceded to the excellent Barrios after 50 seconds. Then beaten by a Cardoso shot which Atleti thought was a goal, but it was handball. Good save from David before the second. One clean sheet in eight games. Ayden Heaven – 6: Nightmare start for the makeshift left-back despite his best efforts as a simple ball over United’s defence split it. Actually unlucky not to block Barrios’ shot. Some nice turns. Grew in confidence. Lovely ball towards the corner as United attacked on 79 minutes. Lisandro Martinez – 6: Left centre-back and drifted a lovely ball towards Rashford on 14 minutes. Clumsy challenge on Barrios conceded a free-kick. His post-match criticisms of Manchester United will be headline news. Leny Yoro – 6: Right centre-back after playing well on Saturday at right-back. Didn’t realise how much time he had on the ball at times as he ballooned it back towards Atletico or gave up possession. Started second-half well but sent off after 74 minutes – he was the last line of defence. But it was harsh, especially as the referee was so close. It was not a clear and obvious error. Diogo Dalot – 5: Right-back and kept very busy by the excellent Baena and Grimaldo on that flank. Poor on goal as Baena caught him out as the ball came over. He was up against better players. Andrey Santos – 6: First start since the opening day of the season and steady in the middle alongside Baleba. Found his feet, played deeper and played the full 90. There might be something there with him and Baleba. Carlos Baleba – 7: Tame header from an unmarked position eight yards out went straight at Oblak. Beaten by Barrios who then crossed for Alvarez in a superb bit of Atletico play. Otherwise good energy and decent passing in his first United start. Youri Tielemans – 6: Played higher – at least in theory – up behind Mbeumo, whom he played a smart one-two with on 24 minutes, but barely featured in first half. More advanced in second and brilliant vision for a ball to Fernandes. Bruno Fernandes – 5: On the right and less of an impact on the game. Stunning turn to beat Grimaldo – three times in total – as United pushed to equalise on 39 minutes but he didn’t cross. He did at the start of the second – and nearly equalised on 57 minutes as his volley bounced just wide of the post. Moved into his usual role after the subs and was better. Hit crossbar on 70 minutes with a right-foot shot. Bryan Mbeumo – 6: Swept a deflected shot wide in United’s first attack on 11 minutes after he took out two defenders and did a number on Romero. Came close again on 23 minutes – well saved by Oblak. Marcus Rashford – 5: Scored against Atletico last season. Good duels against Llorente. Made a run on goal but couldn’t get on the ball enough before he switched right. Didn’t really get in the game. Ineffective. Booked. Joshua Zirkzee (for Tielemans, 65') – 5: Should have scored in stoppage time when he had time. Floats around. Frustrating. Mason Mount (for Baleba, 65') – 5: No impact Amad Diallo (for Rashford, 65') – 5: See above Matheus Cunha (for Fernandes, 80') – N/A: Outrageously pulled back in a yellow card incident. Shot was well-saved by Oblak. Harry Maguire (for Heaven, 80) – N/A: Late sub.

title: Britain must settle its Brexit argument before seeking an EU return
description: The road back to Europe is fraught with political obtacles
content: Confusion reigns where the UK and EU is concerned. Having been dormant for so long, avoided and ducked by successive recent prime ministers, Britain’s future relations with the EU has suddenly become a major political and diplomatic issue. The uncertainty stems from how far Andy Burnham wants to go and at what speed. He gives every impression of wishing the UK to rejoin and quickly. But then he will say in the next breath that the British public must decide. That raises the possibility, make it probability, of a bitter, protracted Brexit battle all over again. He is pinning much on the forthcoming UK-EU Summit, scheduled for November 20, and has set out his wish-list of what he would like that meeting to achieve – including free trade of food and drink products, greater movement of young people – while giving the impression of this only being the first step. That in itself, though, is radical compared with where the UK and EU were. And, as Leader of the Opposition Kemi Badenoch has rightly observed, it’s a curious way to proceed into a negotiation, showing your hand at one go. It is clear to everyone, not least the EU that he sees this as merely the beginning not the end. How though, can he get there, without resurrecting the old battle-lines and splitting the country? He began by being inflammatory, by suggesting the referendum verdict was improperly obtained. No sooner did Mr Burnham signal his desire for the UK to form closer ties with the EU, with a view possibly to rejoining, than the Prime Minister appeared on a podcast saying there was incontrovertible evidence that Russia interfered in the referendum campaign . Bearing in mind the decision to leave was won by just 2 per cent of the vote, the suggestion that it was some way Russian influenced has the ability to invalidate Brexit, to throw the authenticity of the UK’s departure into doubt (Remainers would argue it was already questionable as part of the Brexiteers’ campaign was based on hyperbole and falsehood). So, we actually didn’t choose to exit after all, which could help our efforts to gain readmission. Except Mr Burnham’s was not a new claim. It had been made repeatedly in the past and had always been denied by government ministers and security officials. Nevertheless, here was Mr Burnham maintaining that upon arriving in No 10 he asked about possible Russian interference in the 2016 ballot and stating: “I’ve had the clear answer that, yes, there was.” Fine, if he has the proof. At the time of writing, none is forthcoming. Indeed, well after Mr Burnham made his comment, Stephen Doughty, the Foreign Office minister, was challenged by the BBC to produce it, and replied he wouldn’t “get into specifics”. Instead, Mr Doughty resorted to vague accusations that “Russia clearly has attempted to interfere on a number of our democratic processes. They’re engaged in information warfare, they’re spending £1.5 billion [almost $2 billion] this year alone on disinformation and propaganda”. Cue Nigel Farage, the Brexit architect, denouncing Mr Burnham as “a liar”. Cue too, a feeling of deja vu, that we’ve been here before, many times, that nothing has really changed, that the old wounds have never healed, but still exist, waiting to be reopened. All this row – and it quickly erupted into a war of words, with Mr Farage, who has been accused in the past of enjoying close ties with Russia, sensing his honour and reputation had been impugned sounding most indignant – served to show was that the UK is nowhere near ready to rejoin, not collectively with a consensus, that EU leaders starting to take Mr Burnham at his word might wish to reconsider. The question they should ask themselves is, does Mr Burnham speak for the nation? He may wish to come back but does the electorate, how certain can they be that the same mixture of disregard, often tipping into open contempt, for the EU and its ideals, won’t simply rear its head again? It’s true that a majority of the British people, far greater than the percentage who chose to quit, now believe Brexit was a mistake . The polls put the figure slightly above 70 per cent. In democratic terms, that’s substantial. But it’s an opinion poll, not the real thing, and however the cake is cut, a significant portion of the populace still argue we were right to go. That slice is inspired by committed and noisy agitators. Mr Farage has already said Mr Burnham’s public ambition has regalvanised his Reform UK party’s support base. Until the senior pro-Brexit players in the epic drama of a decade ago come out and admit they were wrong, those of a suspicious nature in the EU are fully entitled to worry the UK would become the renegade member it was before – harrying, obstructing and yes, insulting, at every turn. It would require former prime minister Boris Johnson to recant, and ideally, Mr Farage. Even better still, for the pair of them together to fall on their anti-EU swords. Well, that will never occur . Rather, what will happen is that they will unpick the scars and a whole new anti-EU front will erupt. In the same way that Britain withdrew by the thinnest of margins, this perception matters. Because should we pursue readmittance, we must clear several hurdles, any one of which could block our path. Mr Burnham clearly would like to make it an election issue, to be included in the Labour manifesto. If he wins that popular mandate, in theory, there ought to be no requirement for a re-run of a separate EU vote. That is the view of the mayor of London, Sadiq Khan, among others. But the EU is likely to insist upon a second referendum as a precursor to commencing membership negotiations. Their argument is that they would want to be persuaded the decision is non-party political, and that a vote for a manifesto covers all manner of issues, only one of which is the EU. A re-run could make the case that recommencing membership would last beyond the lifetime of the newly elected government and extend across successive governments. Virtually all countries joining have done so only after holding a public ballot. So, the UK could not realistically seek special dispensation. The European Commission, which would lead the process, would also need to vote its agreement. So too would a majority of the members of European Parliament. Critically, as well, the 27 member countries would have a say and it is by no means guaranteed they would approve the UK resuming. Traditional anti-Britishness could re-surface and they could have agendas of their own – skilful diplomacy by the UK government and Foreign Office would have to be deployed. That said, British diplomats are indicating privately they think simply going back in and taking up where we left off is a tall, if not impossible, order. The EU too would be right to examine Britain’s motives – why now, why the sudden change of heart, why after all this time, 10 years and counting, do we wish to return? The answer, and one Mr Burnham is correct to proclaim, is because Brexit has not delivered . At a stroke, we ditched a free trade bloc of 450 million people. British businesses too found themselves bereft of skilled EU labour. Nothing we’ve done since has come remotely close to replacing what was lost. The Bank of England estimates a loss to our gross domestic product of 6 per cent to 8 per cent – this at a time of increased global competitiveness, rising protectiveness and sovereignty, energy crisis, supply chain difficulties, rising cost of living, threat of AI to jobs, when just adding 1 per cent is a tough bar. Here was the UK saying goodbye to 6 per cent. Just like that. As welcome as they are, trade deals have helped plug the gap, but they only go so far. We had a huge customs-free market on our doorstep, and we blew it. Business investment post-Brexit also fell, down, according to estimates, by 12 per cent to 18 per cent. That’s what we’d like again and if not through full membership, through a much greater rapprochement, possibly through the Customs Union. We’d love also to be able to stem the tide of illegal immigration, which we have failed to do on our own. But the EU is aware of our need and it realises too, that is a prize worth having and is not something to be awarded easily. Not if it comes with the baggage of anti-EU rhetoric and the likelihood that at any moment, a new administration, one led by Mr Farage, say, could again up sticks. That said, there are those in the EU who would like to see Britain’s return in some form. We bring with us 69.5 million people and we could provide an economic as well as political fillip. In a world dominated by two superpowers, a united EU would be a match for them. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney’s speech to Davos earlier this year, in which he called for the “middle powers” to combine, continues to resonate loudly. The fact Mr Carney has followed that up with a suggestion of “associate membership” of the EU has met with a warm response. Mr Carney and Canada, they can do business with. Are they able to say the same with certainty for an unclear, impatient Mr Burnham and his Perfidious Albion? Therein lies the rub.

title: Aramco building attacked after Saudi-led coalition hits Houthi site
description: Videos show huge orange fireball erupting above Yemeni capital Sanaa as troops take on rebels
content: An administrative building of Saudi Arabia's state oil company Aramco was attacked by a missile on Tuesday night, causing a fire but no casualties, as fighting intensifies between the kingdom and Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi rebels. The kingdom's Energy Ministry said the missile strike happened in Dhahran, in the Eastern Province. Authorities responded to the attack, with no deaths or injuries reported, the Saudi Press Agency reported. People living near the Aramco compound described terror as a powerful explosion shook the area. “This was the loudest explosion I have ever heard in my life,” one woman told The National . Another resident said relatives living closer to the site had reported seeing smoke and flames rising from the area. “They couldn't go outside to check what had happened because the smoke was everywhere,” she said. Debris from two cruise missiles intercepted and destroyed over the capital Riyadh injured four people – two women, a man and a child – state television quoted the Saudi Civil Defence as saying. A Civil Defence representative said the falling debris also damaged 15 residential homes in the Saudi capital. Authorities implemented established procedures in response. Bloomberg reported that the site was Aramco’s executive headquarters, while a company source quoted by Reuters identified the target as an Aramco headquarters complex. Neither Aramco nor Saudi authorities had officially confirmed which building was hit. The Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis in Yemen separately said it had intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile launched towards Dhahran, with debris falling in a residential area. It also reported intercepting a missile targeting Haradh and three drones north of the capital, Riyadh. The coalition said late on Tuesday that it had carried out an operation against energy sites in Houthi-held areas of Yemen, including the Al Sabahah station in Yemen's capital, Sanaa, and piers used for loading fuel at the Red Sea port of Hodeidah. Coalition spokesman Maj Gen Turki Al Malki accused the Houthis of using civilian infrastructure to support their military operations and supply their arsenals. “It has been established that the Houthi terrorist militia uses civilian objects and vital resources to sustain its war effort," he said on X. "These include the Al Sabaha central station in Sanaa, underground strategic fuel reserves and storage facilities and fuel and dedicated fuel-loading and unloading berths in Hodeidah, Sanaa and Dhamar.” Video posted on social media appeared to show a huge orange fireball erupting above Sanaa, followed by a towering column of thick black smoke. The strikes came after the coalition had warned civilians near the oil facility to leave “for their safety”. The scale of the damage to the site and the impact on fuel supplies were not immediately clear. The Houthis said fuel reserves had been dispersed before the attack, a claim that has not been independently verified. Saudi energy infrastructure has been been hit before. A refinery in Jazan, in the kingdom's west, was shut after a strike, and a key oil export port on the Red Sea coast was also targeted. A cross-country pipeline used by Aramco to transport crude to export markets was temporarily shut in September following an attack launched from Iraq. The pipeline is strategically important because it offers an alternative route for Saudi oil exports when shipping through the Gulf faces disruption. Oil prices rose on Wednesday after news of the attack on the Aramco building, as traders weighed the risk of further disruption to regional energy supplies. It is unclear how the latest incidents could affect production, refining or exports. Dhahran lies at the centre of Saudi Arabia’s oil industry, close to major oil fields in Eastern Province and the Gulf.

title: Chinese companies seek Gulf partnerships as physical AI takes shape
description: LinkerBot is exploring UAE partnerships as region increases advanced manufacturing
content: Chinese robotics companies are looking to the Gulf as a possible manufacturing centre for the next generation of AI-powered machines, as the region's capital, energy resources and industrial ambitions create opportunities for partnerships. Beijing-based robotics company LinkerBot is among those exploring opportunities in the UAE, where it is in talks with major institutions on potential partnerships, Weber Su, the company's vice president and head of global markets, said during the AIM Summit in Dubai on Tuesday. One model being considered would involve Chinese companies supplying advanced robotics parts, while the UAE provides capital-intensive assembly and automated production. Such an arrangement could allow Gulf countries to take part directly in making advanced robots, rather than mainly buying the technology. “That could be the business model that we are exploring with Middle Eastern countries, particularly in UAE,” Mr Su said. LinkerBot specialises in dexterous robotic hands, enabling machines to grasp and manipulate objects. It has expanded into components including reducers and micromotors that control robotic movement. The potential collaboration reflects a broader trend in which Asian companies seek international manufacturing partners, while Gulf economies use their capital, energy and infrastructure to build higher-value industries. In September, Chinese electric and extended-range vehicle maker ROX Motor began producing vehicles in Abu Dhabi . The UAE, meanwhile, is also boosting manufacturing and under its Operation 300bn strategy aims to increase the industrial sector's contribution to gross domestic product to Dh300 billion by 2031. The country's industrial exports rose 25 per cent last year to a record Dh262 billion, with medium and high-technology exports increasing 42 per cent to Dh92 billion, according to the Ministry of Industry and Advanced Technology. The UAE is also investing in automation to improve manufacturing competitiveness. Mr Su said Chinese companies could increasingly focus on specialised robotics parts, while Gulf partners develop the capital-intensive assembly operations needed to bring those technologies to market. Turning that potential into commercially successful partnerships will require investment agreements, viable production models and sustained demand for AI-powered machines. The potential partnerships come as the technology industry moves towards what investors and developers describe as the next stage of artificial intelligence: physical AI. Chinese AI developers including DeepSeek , Zhipu AI and Moonshot AI are becoming increasingly competitive with their US rivals, offering advanced models at lower costs, according to Joseph Zeng, founder and chief investment officer of Hong Kong-based Arcadia Fund Management Group. While generative AI has focused on chatbots, content creation and software applications, the next phase is expected to bring intelligent systems into the physical world. Physical AI combines advanced AI models with robotics, allowing machines to interpret their surroundings, make decisions and perform tasks traditionally requiring human intervention. Unlike conventional industrial robots, which are generally programmed for repetitive movements, the ambition is to develop machines capable of adapting to different situations. Applications could include robotic hands manipulating unfamiliar objects, autonomous machines working across production lines and robots assisting hospital patients. Mr Su said advances in computing power and AI models were making these capabilities increasingly possible. LinkerBot is developing robotic hands with built-in movement ability that could eventually be combined with sophisticated AI systems to perform a wider range of tasks. “We're going to have skill stores similar to the app stores,” Mr Su said. China's manufacturing scale could give its companies an advantage as the technology shifts towards commercial production. The country installed about 295,000 industrial robots in 2024, accounting for 54 per cent of global installations, according to the International Federation of Robotics . The figures refer to factory robots rather than humanoids, but demonstrate the scale of China's industrial automation industry and supporting supply chains. SK hynix held 50 per cent of the global high-bandwidth memory market by revenue in the second quarter of 2026, while Samsung accounted for 33 per cent, according to Counterpoint Research data reported by the Yonhap news agency. "Physical AI provides a lot of opportunities for investors,” said Mr Zeng, whose investments include ByteDance and Zhipu AI in China, as well as South Korea's SK hynix and Samsung. The next stage of AI would require advances in computing hardware and infrastructure, he added. He identified high-bandwidth memory, optical transceivers and robotics components among the technologies benefitting from rising investment. Health care could also become an important market. During a recent visit to Suzhou, near Shanghai, Mr Zeng said he encountered a company developing a voice-controlled robot designed to assist bedridden patients with repositioning and personal care. Mr Su said humanoid robots could eventually help to care for elderly people and children in smaller communities, where shrinking populations make it difficult to attract doctors and maintain healthcare services.
