While fully autonomous, general-purpose robots are still being developed, their potential to ease labour shortages, reduce care costs and extend essential services to underserved communities illustrates the social and economic impact physical AI could have beyond factories. For the Gulf, opportunities could include using autonomous systems in established industries. Mr Zeng highlighted electric and autonomous heavy-duty trucks for mining and industrial operations, alongside energy storage and cleaner power technologies. Energy is also becoming increasingly important to AI investment. Global data-centre electricity use is expected to more than double to about 945 terawatt-hours by 2030, according to the International Energy Agency . The forecast highlights the importance of electricity generation, storage and cooling infrastructure as AI adoption accelerates. For Gulf countries with substantial energy resources and growing renewable power capacity, this creates another potential area of collaboration with Asian technology developers.

title: Roma v Real Madrid: Mourinho struggles to solve Vinicius Jr conundrum amid Bernabeu chaos
description: Portuguese coach heads back to former club in Champions League days after out-of-form Brazilian attacker was sent off for pulling opponent's hair
content: The idea that Jose Mourinho was the man to restore order to the mayhem that is Real Madrid and prevent a third successive campaign without a major trophy appears to be unravelling fast. Last season was a turbulent one for Los Blancos that saw managers sacked, players jeered by their own fans, teammates fighting each other, all topped off by bitter rivals Barcelona securing a second successive La Liga title. To control a dressing room of rampant egos, Madrid president Florentino Perez turned to the biggest coaching ego of them all, brining Mourinho back for his second stint at a club who sacked him back in 2013. But just nine matches into the new season, all is not well in the Spanish capital. On Saturday at the Bernabeu, Madrid were labouring towards a 1-0 win over Villarreal – courtesy of teenager Yan Diomande's first goal for the club – when Vinicius Junior scored with a clinical first-time finish. It sparked ferocious celebrations from the attacker, with Mourinho sprinting across the pitch to join in. But the joyous scenes were cut short when referee Isidro Diaz de Mera Escuderos was asked to view the pitchside monitor by VAR, where he saw Vinicius clearly pulling the hair of Nathan Saliba in the build-up to the goal. Just 20 minutes after coming off the bench to replace Trent Alexander-Arnold, Vinicius was shown a red card and the scene quickly descended into chaos as furious Madrid players surrounded the referee, while the Brazilian had to be dragged away by teammates. An incandescent Mourinho, who had already spent the entire game berating officials, earned himself a yellow card, then refused to appear for the post-match press conference. The player himself has since issued a brief apology on social media – saying “sorry to the team and the fans” – but could now receive a three-match ban that would see him miss the Clasico on October 25 against a table-topping Barca team that has won eight from eight in La Liga so far. While Mourinho continues to rant and rave about perceived refereeing agendas against his team, the fact remains they are not playing well. They find themselves in fourth place, six points shy of Barca, having lost to Real Betis and the derby against Atletico Madrid, where Mourinho was again left bemoaning refereeing decisions . And the biggest puzzle facing the veteran Portuguese is coaxing Vinicius – who signed a bumper new six-year contract extension over the summer – back into top form. The 26-year-old has managed just one goal in 672 minutes of action this season prompting questions as to why Mourinho has not turned to other attacking options in his squad. “Some players need time to get back to their usual level … and I’m not going to hide from that,” he insisted ahead of the Villarreal game. “I never criticise the Madrid fan base; I only respect it. It breaks my heart to see a boy like him suffer. He wants to become that Vinicius again who wins matches and makes the difference … Vini deserves support.” Mourinho has also found himself defending top-scorer Kylian Mbappe – who has eight goals in nine games, taking his Madrid career tally to 94 in 112 matches – after the French attacker was criticised for making trips to Paris and Switzerland while still recovering from a minor knee injury picked up on international duty. “What I can promise is when a Real Madrid player doesn't behave the way a Real Madrid player is supposed to … They won't have the chance to whistle, because they'll be at home,” said the 63-year-old, who dismissed the criticism as “ridiculous” while also accusing the media of trying to turn Madrid fans against Mbappe. After starting their Uefa Champions League campaign with a 2-1 win over Inter Milan – with Mbappe and Federico Valverde on target – they now face another of Mourinho's former clubs in Roma at the Stadio Olympico on Wednesday. The Italian side are currently third in Serie A after drawing 0-0 at Como on Sunday, when they had top-scorer Donyell Malen shown a straight red card for a reckless tackle on home defender Kaiki. The Giallorossi's opening European game saw them draw with Fenerbahce in Turkey. Mourinho's three-year spell in the Italian capital was a trademark mix of success and controversy that ended in the sack. He guided Roma to their first major European crown when they defeated Feyenoord 1-0 in 2022's inaugural Europa Conference League final, which also meant Mourinho became the first manager to win all four major European trophies, having previously lifted the Uefa Cup, Champions League and Europa League. “I knew the moment I arrived what it meant to the people,” said Mourinho after the match in Tirana. “They had been waiting for something like this. This was not work tonight, this was history. We had to write history. We wrote it.” But 12 months later, Mourinho was once again left ranting at officials after Roma were beaten by Sevilla on penalties in a Europa League final that witnessed a tournament record 13 yellow cards. His infamous foul-mouthed tirade at referee Anthony Taylor in the car park after the game earned him a four-match ban. The following season, Mourinho was sacked after a poor run of results, but the Portuguese insists his love for the club remains intact. “I think the bond between me and the Roma fans was created by the fact … they understood that for me there was only Roma and the Roma fans. I fought for them, I gave everything,” he said last week in an interview with Corriere dello Sport. “What do I expect from the Olimpico? I do not expect banners. I do not expect anything. I expect respect. ”

title: Cody Rhodes calls for WWE return to Abu Dhabi, before Street Fighter release
description: Co-star Andrew Schulz shares his love for the UAE, which he says has 'some of the best comedy audiences in the world'
content: It's been nearly nine years since WWE last staged a show in Abu Dhabi. Three-time WWE champion Cody Rhodes thinks it's time the wrestling company returned. “Love Abu Dhabi,” Rhodes tells The National . “I only get to stop in for a brief moment usually, but I feel like it’s been a minute because WWE has been over in the Middle East, but we haven’t really hit Abu Dhabi. And we should.” WWE last staged shows in the UAE capital in December 2017 , when Roman Reigns was among the stars who performed at Zayed Sports City Tennis Stadium. The company has since increased its presence in Saudi Arabia, where its next major event, Crown Jewel , takes place in Riyadh on November 7, with Reigns set to face Sami Zayn. Rhodes is speaking alongside American comedian Andrew Schulz, his co-star in the new Street Fighter film. Schulz is no stranger to the emirate as he has performed at Etihad Arena twice, first in October 2023 and again in May 2024 during the inaugural Abu Dhabi Comedy Week. “Abu Dhabi’s great. Some of the best comedy audiences in the world,” Schulz says. In director Kitao Sakurai's adaptation of Capcom's fighting-game series, Rhodes plays US Air Force fighter Guile, while Schulz portrays Dan Hibiki. Set in 1993, Street Fighter follows estranged fighters Ryu (Andrew Koji) and Ken Masters (Noah Centineo), who are recruited by Chun-Li (Callina Liang) to enter the World Warrior Tournament. Schulz came to the film with two decades of stand-up comedy experience, although some of the habits he had developed on stage proved less useful when working alongside other actors. “We’re not getting a big pop or a big laugh,” he says. “So I think in some ways it’s like training yourself out of waiting for the reaction. “This character’s not even looking for a laugh. He’s dead serious about what he’s saying. It might be ridiculous and absurd, but to him, it’s the most important thing in the world. It’s kind of unlearning some things that we’ve both been doing for the last 20 years.” Rhodes found more familiar territory during a tournament scene involving hundreds of extras gathered around the fighters. With Guile surrounded by competitors and spectators, there was an opportunity to draw on the showmanship he has developed throughout his wrestling career. “There is an element of peacocking to what Guile was doing,” he says. “I mean, I even challenged Schulz to an arm-wrestling contest.” Director Sakurai and representatives from Capcom were also on set, providing some of the feedback Rhodes was accustomed to receiving from wrestling audiences. Their encouragement helped him judge whether his interpretation of Guile was working and remained faithful to the character. There was also room to experiment, particularly when Schulz and Rhodes began suggesting ways to add humour to the action. During one scene, Schulz was fascinated by the aerial performers suspended above the set, some of whom were hanging by their hair. “They literally just tied a knot to their hair, and they’re just spinning around,” he says. The sight inspired an idea. Schulz and Rhodes suggested that one of the performers could descend upside down during a conversation involving Guile, interrupting the exchange before disappearing back towards the ceiling. The filmmakers liked the gag enough to include it in the finished film. “They were very willing to just hear our absurd ideas,” Schulz says. Beyond those contributions, Schulz was working within a production in which the broader creative decisions were in other people's hands – an unfamiliar position after two decades building his own comedy career. “It was very cool to be in something where you trust the creators and you just go, ‘OK, for the first time in my career, I completely submit to what your creative is, and I’m going to try to execute that to the best of my ability',” he says. Rhodes is joined in the film by fellow professional wrestlers Roman Reigns, who plays Akuma, and Hirooki Goto, who portrays E Honda. WWE has helped promote the adaptation, with Rhodes wearing Guile-inspired ring gear during his SummerSlam entrance in August. The crossover between wrestling and film offers an opportunity to reach an audience already familiar with their work, while showing fans something they haven't seen before from all three. “What I love is that when they see Roman, when they see Goto, when they see me, they won’t be seeing what they’re used to, which is a credit to what we’ve been able to do and the skills that we were able to develop before we got into this, in terms of creating a brand new character, another layer for us,” Rhodes says. Street Fighter releases in UAE cinemas on Thursday

title: Toxic Trump? President makes midterms all about him but some Republicans are inching away
description: President portrays elections as referendum on his agenda, but party colleagues distance themselves on economy, immigration and Iran
content: On November 3, Americans will elect all 435 members of the House and 35 senators. President Donald Trump will not be on the ballot but he has sought to make the midterm elections all about himself . “I'm asking you to pretend that I'm on the ballot. I'm on the ballot. I'm on the ballot. Just one more time,” he said at a recent rally. “Because if we lose, you’re going to lose your border, you’re going to lose your tax cuts, you’re going to lose your safety and security, you’re going to lose your wealth.” At recent rallies, Mr Trump has campaigned on what he says are his administration’s accomplishments and made the election a referendum on his presidency. He said voters turn out in greater numbers when he is running and that Republican control of Congress is necessary to preserve his agenda. He even pledged $5,000 cheques to every American adult if Republicans retain control of Congress, calling it a “Trump dividend”. Previous similar promises related to tariffs and cuts in government spending have come to nothing and he cannot unilaterally authorise such payments. But amid low approval ratings, rising costs of living and an unpopular war with Iran, some Republican candidates have sought to distance themselves from him on major issues, raising the question of whether Mr Trump has become toxic. John Feehery, a Republican strategist, said the war with Iran presents a particular challenge for the President because it conflicts with his central message of non-intervention in conflicts abroad. “The war is very unpopular, even though it’s probably for a good cause. It hasn’t been really well explained. It’s not the Trump brand," Mr Feehery said. "And so, all these people who voted for Trump because they wanted an end to no more endless wars – it’s kind of a betrayal." Mr Trump has said that the war, which he initially claimed would last only a few weeks, would end after the midterms , and that fuel costs would go down shortly after. Control of Congress is likely to hinge on a relatively small number of contested races in Michigan, Maine, North Carolina, Ohio, Iowa, Alaska and Texas. Republicans hold narrow majorities in both chambers. In the Senate, where Republicans hold a 53-47 majority, Democrats need a net gain of four seats to take control. Historically, the party of the sitting president loses seats in the House. “We’re worried about Michigan. We’re worried about Texas. We’re worried about a few states. But it’s all about 35 different contests – not states, contests,” Mr Trump said at a recent rally. Midterm elections also typically draw fewer voters than presidential polls, and experts say Mr Trump's base is less motivated to vote in the midterms than Democratic supporters. “This is not going to be a high-turnout election, so you have to be very careful – you can’t run against Trump," Mr Feehery said. Still, some Republican candidates have been trying to distance themselves from the President's stance on Iran and other issues. Mike Rogers, the Trump-endorsed Republican Senate candidate running against Abdul El Sayed in Michigan, is running an advertisement saying: “The war with Iran needs to end – and end quickly.” Polling also suggests voters are mainly concerned about the economy and the rising cost of living, with a majority blaming Mr Trump for his handling of the issues. In Iowa, Republican Congresswoman Ashley Hinson, who is running for the Senate, focused her message on the economic impact of the war. “Iowans are being squeezed and shouldn’t have to foot the bill at the pump or the checkout line for the war in Iran,” she said in a statement. Heavy-handed immigration enforcement is another possible vulnerability for Republicans, with polling showing that many voters believe the Trump administration has crossed the line. In a campaign advertisement, Maria Elvira Salazar, a three-term Republican congresswoman running for re-election in Florida, said Mr Trump’s immigration enforcement efforts “have gone too far”. “Be careful what your advisers are telling you about immigration policy,” she said. “The same Hispanics who helped you get to the White House in 2024 feel betrayed today.” Mr Trump has also dismissed criticism from lawmakers from both parties over a recent deal with Russia to supply millions of barrels of diesel to global markets after a call with President Vladimir Putin. The move appeared to be an attempt to slow the rising prices of diesel, but Republican senators said the deal may violate US restrictions imposed after Moscow's invasion of Ukraine. A bipartisan group of senators released a statement at the weekend opposing Russian diesel fuel imports. Senator Thom Tillis, one of the signatories to the statement, told NBC's Meet the Press on Sunday that "there’s a legitimate case for saying the President’s not following the law". “Well, I think these are Republicans that can't really be serious,” Mr Trump said on Monday when asked about the criticism from his own party. Recent polls put Mr Trump's approval ratings in the low 30s nationally, a historic low, and his disapproval ratings above 60 per cent. Chris Christie, the former Republican governor of New Jersey who ran against Mr Trump twice for the party's presidential nomination, highlighted the growing unease of politicians in his party. “With his current approval rating, Republicans are going to treat Trump like he has malaria by the time we get to October,” he wrote in a post on X. Mr Trump, however, appears convinced that his stamp of approval is a boost for candidates rather than the proverbial albatross. "I think we're going to do very well. I think that the rallies I'm doing are really changing around," he said on Tuesday. Mr Trump pledged to visit a different state most days until the election, and forgo playing golf on the weekends.

title: Even during wartime, the UAE is budgeting for the future
description: Latest federal budget is best understood as expression of ambition and investment in resilience
content: There is no denying that for many regional economies, these are uncertain times. Strikes on oil tankers and airports highlight the unresolved nature of the conflict between Iran and the US, and its ripple effects. However, a look at how the UAE is planning its future in this environment is illuminating. The country’s latest federal budget is a reminder that long-term economic ambitions cannot be put on hold every time the region faces a crisis. The decision to commit Dh292.5 billion ($79.64 billion) over the next three years is a serious statement of intent. Of particular note is its emphasis on social development, which has been earmarked as the largest area for spending. Economic strength largely depends on the people who sustain it, particularly their education, skills, health and ability to participate in a changing economy. Investing in citizens is an essential part of the UAE’s long-term competitiveness and is recognition that its most valuable asset is its people. “Our priorities remain fixed and unchanged…” Sheikh Mohammed bin Rashid , Vice President and Ruler of Dubai , said on Monday. “Education, health, housing, social services, and the quality of life and stability of the citizen.” Somewhat counterintuitively, despite the months of violent and dangerous conflict in the region, the UAE is confident in its future. This is borne out by some independent projections; a report on Monday by global advisory firm Boston Consulting Group suggested that wealth in the Emirates is set to jump to $6 trillion by the end of this decade. This reflects the Emirates’ enduring appeal to investors and its accumulation of assets. The country’s long policy of diversifying its economy beyond hydrocarbons has been supported by international capital and a reputation for stability. This is not to be complacent. The International Monetary Fund’s recent decision to downgrade its growth forecasts for regional economies highlights the seriousness of continuing challenges. Even countries with substantial financial reserves and diversified sources of income are not wholly immune from regional shocks of the magnitude being experienced right now. The UAE’s budget can be best understood as an expression of ambition and an investment in resilience. The current regional turmoil actually supports the case for more medium and long-term planning. Funding resilience only when a crisis arrives is not the most effective strategy. It is the decisions that governments make today that will count when the chips are down. Long-term planning and strategic foresight are strengths of the UAE, and essential ingredients for its current and future success.

title: 'He irrigated the tree with his blood': West Bank olive farmers set for another deadly harvest
description: Palestinian growers face extreme settler violence even before the season has officially begun
content: Abdul Latif Al Bazzari, 59, moved slowly and deliberately as he battled through pain to recount the last moments of his cousin, Ali Al Bazzari, at an olive grove in the pale green, dusty hills around the city of Nablus. On Monday, the scattering of olive trees among which he stood was serene. Accessible through a rough dirt track, the only sign of a world outside the grove was a light breeze that travelled through the valley. That peace was shattered last week, on October 7, when the family was subjected to the only settler attack they have faced in that area in 60 years. “He irrigated the tree with his blood,” Mr Al Bazzari said, standing near the trunk where his relative bled to death. “It will forever be the real estate of this attack by Jewish terrorist settlers.” His face barely showed emotion as he described the death of his cousin, a 44-year-old father of four. Perhaps it was too painful: his face was still bruised and covered in a fresh white dressing. Mr Al Bazzari said the settlers shot at them, beat them with metal and wooden objects and threw stones. Eight people were injured, two by gunfire. One of his cousins is still in the hospital. “They don’t want us to stay on any land, or take any of our crops. They are telling us to stay in our villages and cities, and not to go down to our trees,” he said. Palestinian olive farmers across the Israeli-occupied West Bank are facing another harvest season marred by settler violence . Unlike last year, when the crop was poor, the weather this year has been good and the trees are full. The settlers, however, are still as violent, if not more so. The harvest season officially begins on Thursday but the farmers have been out in their groves for weeks, fearing thefts from Israeli settlers who are posting social media campaigns encouraging people to steal their olives. Already, two Palestinians have been killed by settlers since farmers started heading to their trees in late September, and many more injured. The entire harvest season is in danger – a major blow to the Palestinian economy , which has been significantly damaged by violence and severe restrictions in the occupied West Bank during the three years since the Hamas-led October 7 attacks on southern Israel. The olive harvest is not only crucial to the economy but also symbolic of Palestinians' deep connection to the land. “The olive groves and the harvest are the soil of the Palestinian people. This is a strategic crop," Mr Al Bazzari said. "It’s not like wheat or barley; it’s the identity of the Palestinian people. Some of the trees are more than 500 years old, hundreds of years before Israel was established.” Farther south, in the village of Usarin, Warda Adeli, 63, was also nursing wounds from a settler attack, with her arm in a sling and stitches stretching across her bruised right cheek. She was beaten as she rushed towards family members who were ambushed by settlers in the tiny grove outside their house 10 days ago. “I was screaming. I was scared for my son. Then they threw me to the ground and I couldn’t feel anything,” she said. Family members said her entire body is blue with bruising. One of her sons is still in the ICU in Nablus with a severe brain injury after being beaten with a metal bar. Another son, Ghassan Ahmed Adeli, seated next to Ms Adeli, has a broken shoulder and a back injury. He spoke on her behalf during most of the interview because she was still too weak and traumatised. The views from their home are spectacular, but also reveal a bleak situation: vast groves in the valley that farmers have not been able to access for years because of Israeli violence. There are also new settler outposts visible, established amid the blitz of settlement construction since the Gaza war broke out . The empty groves are a reminder of the long-term nature of the problem facing Palestinian olive cultivation under Israeli occupation. This year, however, there has been a worrying new development. The attacks on the Al Bazzari and Adeli families took place in Areas A and B, where the Palestinian Authority is supposed to have either full or partial control. In previous harvests, the attacks focused on Area C, where Israel has full security and civil occupation. In Ms Adeli’s case, the attack actually happened inside her village, in the narrow groves and streets between the homes of this close community, which turned out in great numbers to listen to her describe her ordeal. Some in Israel talk of there being a loss of control in the occupied West Bank , which has accelerated during the tenure of the far-right government of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. Palestinian olive farmers who have been attacked, as well as some of the few Israeli-Jewish activists who try to support them during the harvest, disagree. There has never been more Israeli military and civilian power in the territory. Military vehicles are everywhere, rushing about to open and close various checkpoints and gates installed in the past few years, while settlers travel and build at will. With Israel's general election just weeks away , there is also a heavy presence of candidates' campaign posters. Opposition candidates such as Gadi Eisenkot are visible shortly after passing the separation wall that separates East Jerusalem from the rest of the West Bank. That changes deep inside the Palestinian territory, where the only posters visible are of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and far-right members of his government, including National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir and Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich. Many of them and their supporters laud the “revolution” this government has achieved during its tenure. For them, the unpicked Palestinian olive trees are a sign of progress; the violence inflicted on Mr Al Bazzari, Ms Adeli and many others is not something Israel has to apologise for, but to praise.

title: Haaland vs Mbappe: The race to break Cristiano Ronaldo’s historic Champions League goals record
description: Manchester City striker and Real Madrid forward both have realistic hopes of setting a new benchmark but it will be far from easy
content: Erling Haaland’s two goals against Porto on the opening matchday of the 2026/27 Champions League maintained the Manchester City striker’s incredible scoring rate in the competition. Haaland has scored 59 goals from 59 games at the elite level of European club football, giving him the best goals-per-game ratio of any notable player in its history. In fact, he is the only player to have scored a significant number of goals at a rate of at least one per game. It’s also the best scoring rate of the three active players among the Champions League's all-time top scorers: Haaland, Harry Kane and Kylian Mbappe. The benchmark, however, is still some way off for all three. Cristiano Ronaldo is out in front with a staggering 140 goals from 183 appearances in the competition. So, this raises the question: Can one of this generation’s elite goalscorers actually beat Ronaldo’s record? Kane has an impressive haul of 54 goals in 70 games, but at 33, the England captain can almost certainly be ruled out of the race. Sadly for him, he stayed at Tottenham Hotspur for too long. That leaves us with Haaland and Mbappe. Both are in action on Tuesday night, with Manchester City hosting PSG and Real Madrid visiting Roma. Below is an appraisal of each man’s chances of going down as European club football’s greatest-ever goalscorer. Haaland, 26, made his Champions League debut for RB Salzburg against Genk on September 17, 2019, and scored a hat-trick. Of course he did. Since then, as stated above, he has scored at a rate of a goal per game in the competition. His best return came in 2022/23, when he scored 12 times in 11 games and ended up with a winner’s medal . He currently sits seventh on the all-time list. This season will be his eighth in the Champions League. Among those, there is an outlier – 2021/22 – when he played just three games, scoring as many goals, as his then club, Borussia Dortmund, made an early exit. Every other season, he has played at least eight games. If we remove that campaign and the current one, then he has a tally of 54 goals in 55 games across six seasons, at an average of nine goals per season. By that calculation, he will need another 9.1 seasons (including the current one) to get the 82 goals he requires to break Ronaldo’s record – form, fitness and participation willing, of course. That means Haaland needs to continue scoring at the same rate until the 2035/36 season. The Norwegian star, born in July 2000, will be 35 by then. It’s a big ask to be so consistent for so long, but in this era of supreme athleticism, it’s far from inconceivable. There’s also the frightening prospect that he could still get better and increase his goal output. Mbappe, 27, has 71 goals in 99 Champions League games following his strike in Real Madrid’s 2-1 victory over Inter Milan in their opening game of the 2026/27 competition. That took him to joint-fifth with Raul in the all-time list. He made his UCL debut on September 27, 2016, with a 13-minute cameo off the bench in Monaco’s 1-1 draw with Bayer Leverkusen. He is now into his 11th season of Champions League football. Mbappe has managed at least eight games in each of his first 10 seasons, making his average a pleasingly concise seven goals per season, with 70 goals across the 10 completed campaigns. At that rate, he will need exactly 10 more to chalk up the 70 goals he requires to surpass Ronaldo. Mbappe will be 38 heading into the back end of the 2036/37 season. It's clear he needs to speed up, and there's ample evidence to suggest that he has. His goals-per-game rate has spiked sharply since he moved to Real Madrid in 2024. The France striker managed an incredible 15 goals in 11 games last term – his best return – while he has a total of 22 in 25 games in his two completed seasons at the club. At an average of 11 per campaign, he would need another six-and-a-half seasons to potentially put him within striking distance of the record by the 2032/33 season, when he will be 34, turning 35 in December. The numbers suggest that both Haaland and Mbappe stand a reasonable chance of surpassing Ronaldo’s mark if they can stay fit and play in the majority of matches for their respective clubs. Both will be helped by the extra games offered by the competition’s new format, with teams now guaranteed eight league phase games as opposed to the six group games Ronaldo used to get before the knockouts. If anything, this exercise really underlines Ronaldo’s incredible longevity and potency in front of goal. Interestingly, he scored goal number 140 on his 183rd and final Champions League appearance in a 2-0 win for Manchester United over Villarreal on November 23, 2021. He was 36 years, nine months and 18 days old at the time. Should Mbappe manage to stay at Madrid into the twilight of his career, then you would have to give him a shot, given the number of goals he has scored since his move to Los Blancos, and their consistency in reaching the latter stages of the competition year after year. Ronaldo was 33 when he left Madrid, while Mbappe's compatriot, Karim Benzema , stayed there until he was 35. That said, averaging 11 per season to get there by the time he is 35 is a big ask, and he may need to keep playing into the second half of his 30s to eventually top the list. Haaland, 19 months younger than Mbappe, will feel that 141 is an achievable target if he can regularly play 10 or more games per season in the competition. As the younger man, and with the better goals-per-game ratio, you'd have to make the Manchester City striker a firm favourite. The X-factor is, of course, Mbappe's Real Madrid form. His 15 last season was the third most ever behind Ronaldo in 2015/16 (16) and 2013/14 (17). Either way, it seems certain that both men will finish their careers considered among the finest goalscorers in modern football history. If either eventually stands alone as the best, remains to be seen.

title: 'There are no dreams left': Families of two sailors missing after drone attack off Oman speak of their grief
description: Relatives await news days after drone hit and fire ripped through part of ship
content: Two families are “sick with grief” waiting for news of two young sailors missing days after an empty tanker was struck by a drone off Oman. The oil tanker, MT Petro Dolphin, was hit near the Sohar anchorage on Sunday. Relatives in two northern Indian villages are waiting for information on Amit Singh, 20, and Bir Bahadur Yadav, 25, who were on the main deck when the drone struck and fire spread. Of the 12 crew on the Nicaraguan-flagged tanker, nine Indians and one Bangladeshi national were rescued and two seafarers are missing, India’s External Affairs Ministry has said. It was the first sailing job for both men, and their relatives have described the incomprehensible loss they felt on learning of the attack. “Amit’s parents are in and out of consciousness, they cannot cope. It’s all finished, there are no dreams left, it’s all broken,” Amit Singh’s uncle, Ravindar Singh, told The National from Gopala village in Uttar Pradesh. “It’s as if they are dead. As long as they live, they will be in this condition, like death. We are trying to support them but what can we say to comfort them?” Maritime agency reports show that at least 12 tankers have been attacked in the Arabian Gulf and Strait of Hormuz in the past week as Iran steps up its campaign to stop US-backed efforts to move oil. There have been 24 seafarer deaths and 104 incidents in the Strait of Hormuz and the Middle East since the Iran war began on February 28, according to the International Maritime Organisation. An experienced seafarer , Ravindar Singh, 40, spoke to rescued crew members to find out his nephew’s location when the drone struck. He says there is no hope of survival. “The men told me Amit was working on the main deck in the exact same place of the drone attack. We know he is no more,” Mr Singh said. “The crew were evacuated by fishermen. They went around the vessel to search in case the sailors had jumped into the sea, but found nothing.” Video shot by the crew captures the fire and smoke engulfing sections of the tanker, and a sailor can be heard crying out: “My two crew have gone, Allah, my two men have died.” Amit Singh was from a poor farming community and his family were happy when he followed his uncle into the merchant navy. He signed on with the tanker in January as an able seaman, and his work covered navigation, mooring, handling cargo and maintenance of the ship’s deck equipment. His uncle, a sailor for 20 years, spoke of the rising danger as merchant ships are targeted in the Iran-US and Russia-Ukraine wars. Ravindar Singh returned home in May after a projectile landed near his ship in the Black Sea. His nephew was due to complete his contract on October 20, and the men had planned to find a safe voyage together. “Amit was excited about coming home,” Mr Singh said. “After the Iran war, it is the worst condition for sailors. But Amit’s vessel was not in the Strait of Hormuz, it was in anchorage. How can it be that sailors are not safe near the port?” Mr Singh spoke of his nephew’s plans to build a better life for his family. “Amit was starting out in life. He wanted to save money to get his older sister married. His parents live on a small farm and he wanted a better life for them. “This is so wrong. Why should Amit be gone? We are just seamen. We are like drivers, we load and unload cargo, we do as we are told. But they are targeting us. If the ship is the target, at least give sailors a warning. Property damage can be fixed but a sailor’s life is gone.” The family of the second sailor, Bir Bahadur Yadav, also from Uttar Pradesh in northern India, tried to shield his mother from news that he was missing , but she learnt from villagers who heard it on television. “I didn’t want to tell my mother until we were sure but now she knows, her spirit is broken. She is constantly crying,” Mantoo Yadav, Bir’s elder brother, told The National from India. He works in Abu Dhabi and was visiting home when the attack occurred. “In this war, why are sailors being killed? It is someone’s son, someone’s husband, someone’s brother who is dying. What will you get from killing our brothers?” The night before the drone attack, Bir Bahadur spoke to his family about wanting to return home. The youngest of four, he worked as a wiper, cleaning the engine room and machinery. He had four months remaining on a nine-month contract. “We had a long talk. He told us he had seen attacks and saw one ship hit nearby,” Mr Yadav said. “Bir was worried his ship would become a target. But he thought he should stay and finish the contract. We told him to come home but it was too late.” Mr Yadav, 36, said his younger brother was focused on completing seafarer certifications to earn a higher rank. “Bir wanted to work hard, finish exams to get a good position. He was serious when he spoke but could also make people laugh. He was very loving,” said Mr Yadav. The family continues to hold on to hope. “We have been told that we will know about Bir only when the ship is brought to shore and checked,” Mr Yadav said. “The crew saw the attack and know the other sailor is no more. But the crew did not see Bir. “What if he managed to jump off? There is 10 per cent hope that he is still alive. Maybe in the rescue, they will find him unconscious.” Manoj Yadav, general secretary of the Forward Seamen’s Union of India, spoke of the trauma families suffer as they wait for news from search operations. “It's tough. When a vessel is hit by drone or rocket, there is fire and waterlogging,” said Mr Yadav, who is not related to the missing sailor. “It takes time to search the area for missing sailors, and families may not get an answer for days.” Neither Iran nor the US has taken responsibility for the drone strike. Maritime associations have called for more protection for sailors as the war continues. “This tanker was anchored off Sohar, so what was the need to hit this vessel? The only danger is for sailors,” Mr Yadav said. “It’s a very alarming situation and the threat to sailors is growing. Families are suffering. We need strong measures to protect seafarers.” India’s External Affairs Ministry has condemned the attacks. “The recurring attacks on commercial shipping in the region are deeply concerning and risk further aggravating an already volatile situation,” the Indian government said. “Attacks on commercial vessels, seafarers and civilian infrastructure must cease.”

title: AI could be worth $1 trillion to the Mena region, new research suggests
description: Global Future Leaders in Dubai puts AI in the spotlight
content: Artificial intelligence could be the key to unlocking about $1 trillion in the Middle East and North Africa region by 2030, if used efficiently, research by the World Economic Forum has shown. Two reports have been published as the WEF and the Government of Dubai host the inaugural Annual Meeting of Global Future Leaders this week. The three-day event brings together hundreds of leaders and experts from around the world, who will hold intergenerational conversations aimed at tackling the problems of the future. If the region uses AI for growth in the sustainability and economic sectors, the WEF sees great potential for value by 2030. Across sectors, this could mean up to $200 billion in sustainable financing through the financial sector, $370 billion in sustainable investment flows enabled by the public sector, $250 billion in long-term asset losses avoided, $90 billion in increased valuation through improved sustainability performance for the energy sector and $100 billion in sustainable projects launched through cross-sector partnerships. Altogether, this is valued at more than $1 trillion. The region is ripe for this growth, experts say, but it will require cross-sector collaboration. "Mena has the resources, investment capacity and ambition to become a major centre of AI-led growth,” said Maroun Kairouz, managing director of the WEF. “Turning that ambition into reality will require innovation across data-centre infrastructure, energy and water systems, and the application of AI to drive sustainability solutions." Case studies showed how different UAE and regional companies used AI for sustainable initiatives, from First Abu Dhabi Bank in sustainable finance to Adnoc in the energy sector. The UAE has been at the forefront of AI investment, with the US-UAE AI Acceleration Partnership resulting in an AI campus in Abu Dhabi and a $1.4 trillion investment plan over the next 10 years. Abu Dhabi is betting big on AI, with a $3.54 billion investment to integrate the technology into the government's public services by next year. The second report gave a warning about the consumption of resources such as energy and water through data centres, to power AI infrastructure, especially given that the region faces extreme heat and water scarcity. Data-centre cooling, which uses large amounts of water, was flagged as one of the priority areas for innovation and the incorporation of sustainable methods for long-term efficiency and resilience. The opportunities for data centres in the region, however, are plentiful, experts said. Connecting new data centres to the grid can be much quicker in the region, taking between two and five years compared with other mature markets. “Mena is uniquely positioned to lead the next wave of digital infrastructure by bringing together its energy capabilities, investment capacity and technological ambition,” said Nedaa Almubarak, managing director of SRMG Think. “The opportunity lies in aligning intelligent infrastructure with efficient resource use to build resilient, sustainable and competitive digital ecosystems that drive long-term economic growth and innovation.” The Annual Meeting of Global Future Leaders in Dubai continues until Thursday.

title: Emergency order by US to 'prevent blackouts' could affect data centres
description: Move authorises distributor to direct 'large-load customers' to back-up power resources, if needed
content: The US Department of Energy has issued an emergency order to try to prevent power cuts amid increasing demand. Monday's order prompted PJM Interconnection , a corporation that transmits electricity in parts of the US, to " direct data centres and other large-load customers to switch to back-up generation resources, if necessary". Data centres in the US are commonly blamed for a surge in electricity prices and have driven public opinion on AI to sour, according to polls. In issuing its emergency order, the Energy Department also gave "a high rate of planned generator outages during the autumn maintenance season" as a possible cause of blackouts. The order remains in effect until October 16. Energy Secretary Chris Wright was confident in his decision to order utility companies and others to take emergency measures. "This order will help ensure millions of American families and businesses across the mid-Atlantic have access to affordable, reliable and secure electricity by making additional power generation, including back-up power, available to use as needed," Mr Wright said. The Department of Energy said in a statement that the US had 35 GW of unused back-up generation available nationwide. PJM issued a maximum generation alert for October 13 and 14: "Emergency procedures took place as above-normal temperatures are forecast across much of the PJM region. Additional emergency procedures may be necessary pending system conditions." The company said the alert does not "require any action from customers". The warnings come before the US midterm elections, where energy policy, AI and data centres are key issues. Any blackouts or failure to adequately address them could add to friction between residents in the US and utility companies, as well as AI firms. President Donald Trump has repeatedly dismissed critics of AI in recent weeks and accused them of "hoaxes". But in February he tried to ease the strain data centres were putting on the grid by signing a non-binding ratepayer protection pledge in which technology and data centre companies would provide their own electricity to operate. Meanwhile, the Department of Energy has pushed for the construction of more nuclear reactors to address AI energy needs.

title: Pope Leo has lung cancer diagnosed after surgery, Vatican says
description: Medical experts must still assess size of tumour ​and whether disease has spread
content: Pope Leo XIV has had lung cancer diagnosed after surgeons ⁠removed a part of his right lung on Tuesday, the Vatican said. The Pope , 71, has adenocarcinoma, ​a common form of lung cancer , with tissue tests conducted during the operation confirming what doctors had suspected from preparatory examinations, the Vatican said. He was admitted to Rome's ⁠Gemelli Hospital for surgery to remove the growth that doctors had discovered in a recent health check-up. The Vatican said earlier on Tuesday that the operation had been successful, before providing a more detailed update from the Pope's lead surgeon and personal physician. "In order to make the procedure ⁠curative, the lower lobe of the right lung was removed using a video-assisted technique," the medical update said, making it clear that the aim was to eliminate ​all cancerous ⁠tissue. Medical experts said that in order to assess the Pope's case they would need to know the size of the tumour ​removed from him and whether the cancer had spread to his lymph nodes. Pope Leo is due to make an 11-day tour of ⁠Uruguay, Argentina and Peru starting from November 6 to 17, but it was not clear if this trip would still go ahead. The Vatican has cancelled all of his audiences until October 21 to give him time to recuperate. The American-born pontiff revealed during his regular Sunday blessing on October 11 that doctors had discovered the nodule. The late Pope Francis, Pope Leo's predecessor, was admitted to hospital several times as he grew frail in his later years. He ​died aged 88 in April ‌2025. Pope Leo was elected leader of the world’s 1.4 billion Roman Catholics in May 2025. He has left his mark on the papacy by addressing the social and ethical implications of artificial intelligence and has grown increasingly critical of US military actions, challenging the administration of President Donald Trump's argument that God was on the side of the US in its conflict with Iran.

title: Bank of America fined $1.2bn over claimed sanctions breaches
description: US lender also reaches settlement over 'apparent violations' of sanctions against 'Russia, Belarus, Iran, Burma, Somalia, narcotics and global terrorism'
content: Bank of America was ordered to pay more than $1.2 billion in fines after the US Treasury Department said the company breached anti-money laundering and sanctions laws, the agency said on Tuesday. The authority said the fine is the third-largest in its history. Bank of America was also ordered to pay $750 million to the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, the largest ever issued by the OCC. The department's Office of Foreign Assets Control also announced an $11.6 million settlement with Bank of America over 475 “apparent violations” of sanctions against “ Russia , Belarus, Iran , Burma, Somalia, narcotics and global terrorism”. Bank of America is the second-largest bank in the US, with more than 70 million clients, and processes about $4.5 trillion in payments for customers every year. It enables more than $450 trillion of payments in employee payrolls, supplier payments and corporate credit cards. It also processes an average of $1.9 trillion in wire transfers a day globally for clients. “When a bank of this size fails to meet its anti-money-laundering and sanctions obligations, the consequences extend far beyond its own walls, exposing the entire us financial system to significant illicit finance risks,” Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in a statement. “Today’s actions send a clear message that even the biggest financial institutions are not above the law." The Treasury Department said Bank of America admitted it willfully breached the Bank Secrecy Act, which requires banks to assist the Treasury in detecting and preventing money laundering. Bank of America said it has "invested billions of dollars" to tackle financial crime, and that it is "far along" in its remediation efforts with US regulators. "Financial crime compliance is serious, and we are responsible for getting it right", a Bank of America representative said. The department said the US bank failed to report to the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network more than $5 billion in suspicious transactions, with more than $1 billion implicating national security and other risks "indicative of Chinese Money Laundering Networks, fraud, and potential trade-based money laundering with a substantial nexus to the southwest border." The OCC issued a cease-and-desist order against the bank in 2024 over deficiencies related to its Bank Secrecy Act and compliance programmes. “The bank’s poor response to its BSA deficiencies is unacceptable,” said Jonathan Gould, Comptroller of the Currency. Tuesday's fine followed an action from the OCC last week, in which American Express was fined $350 million after its compliance programme allowed about $13 billion in suspected money laundering activity to go undetected for more than a decade. Bank of America is due to report its third-quarter earnings on Wednesday. The bank said its third-quarter results will include a $1.2 billion non-tax deductible charge, reducing income by roughly 17 cents per share. "We have already dedicated substantial personnel and resources to our ongoing remediation efforts, and those costs are in the current expense base," a bank representative said.

title: US envoy says next UN Secretary General should be chosen on merit, not rotation or gender
description: Security Council works to select successor to Antonio Guterres, whose term ends on December 31
content: US President Donald Trump ’s special envoy for global partnerships said on Tuesday that the next UN Secretary General should be chosen on merit rather than regional rotation or gender, as these are “political traditions” rather than “legal rules” under the UN Charter. “The world should choose the best person for the job – based on merit, reform and results,” Paolo Zampolli said on social media. “After 18 years at the United Nations , I believe this is a moment to think bigger about the future of the institution.” The Security Council is to select a successor to Secretary General Antonio Guterres, whose term ends on December 31. The Trump administration has so far kept its preferences private, leaving uncertainty over who it might support in a contest that has drawn seven candidates , including Guyana’s Carolyn Rodrigues-Birkett and Argentina’s Rafael Grossi. Costa Rica’s Rebeca Grynspan has emerged as the front-runner, but her support has shown signs of weakening. In the fifth round of informal straw voting on October 7 , Ms Grynspan received nine “encourage” votes and six “discourage” votes, with no council members expressing “no opinion”. That was a setback from the previous round, on September 29, when she won 10 votes in favour, three against and two with no opinion. To secure the post, a candidate must win at least nine votes in the Security Council without a veto from any of its five permanent members – the US, Britain, France, Russia and China. The selection process has long been shaped by unwritten diplomatic conventions, including the expectation that the post should rotate among the world’s regions. Since 1946, the position has been held by leaders from Europe, Asia, Africa and Latin America, although no formal rotation system exists. The organisation has also never been led by a woman in its 81-year history, despite repeated calls from member states for more women's representation. The final decision rests largely with the Security Council’s five permanent members, each of which can block a candidate regardless of how much support that person has. “The UN Charter only offers limited guidance about the process for selecting a new UN Secretary General. It requires the Security Council to recommend an individual for the General Assembly to appoint to the role,” said Daniel Forti, head of UN affairs at the International Crisis Group. Much of the process, he said, had evolved through changes to council procedures and agreements with the General Assembly. The expectation of regional representation developed through decades of diplomatic practice and non-binding General Assembly resolutions. A 1997 General Assembly resolution called for regional rotation and gender to be taken into account when selecting a secretary general, while a 2015 resolution encouraged member states to nominate women. Neither resolution is legally binding. Another long-standing convention has excluded citizens of the five permanent Security Council member states from the post, reflecting concerns that a major power could exert undue influence over the institution. “Many other factors, whether the demand for regional rotation, the push for the UN to select its first woman secretary general, or commitments about the SG not being a P5 national, are all informal conventions,” Mr Forti said. "They are not binding on the Security Council even if they weigh heavily in the court of public opinion." The veto is a different matter. “The UN Charter is indirect, but unequivocal, about the permanent members’ veto privileges in the Secretary General selection process,” Mr Forti said. “No one questions that the recommendation of a new UN leader is a substantive decision, so the permanent members’ veto authorities are inconvenient but undisputed.”

title: US senators ask Trump to rescind 'disastrous' Russian diesel deal
description: Bipartisan group of a dozen senators suggests Moscow will use diesel money to help Iran's war effort against the US
content: A bipartisan group of US senators on Tuesday called on President Donald Trump to rescind his deal allow Russian diesel exports, saying it will prolong the Ukraine war and put at risk the lives of American troops in the Middle East. Mr Trump last week said that during a call, Russian President Vladimir Putin had agreed to supply millions of barrels of diesel to global markets. The deal comes amid growing domestic political pressure on Mr Trump to lower diesel prices, caused by supply constraints during the Iran war and Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries , before the November 3 midterm elections. A letter signed by 12 senators, including former Republican senate leader Mitch McConnell, said granting Moscow the ability to freely sell diesel damages American security interests. It "is a betrayal of the people of Ukraine, who continue to defend themselves from Putin's murderous, illegal war. This deal is a gift to our adversary and a betrayal of our allies. It should be rescinded", the letter reads. They also claim that Mr Putin will use the money to help Iran's war effort against the US. US intelligence sources, senior European officials, the UK government and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy have accused Russia of helping Iran . US media reports, quoting officials, have said Moscow provided Tehran with information on American military assets in the region. The deal "will have a negligible impact on fuel prices, but the revenues the Kremlin will receive from this agreement will undoubtedly finance its desired war of attrition and advance its security co-operation with China, Iran and North Korea. It will also endanger service members operating overseas in support of Operation Epic Fury". Mr Trump on Monday acknowledged that Russia and China may be helping Iran "at a very low level" but said he does not "believe" they are. Democratic Senator Richard Blumenthal said Mr Putin has failed to respect a purported truce on energy infrastructure attacks. "Zelenskyy has agreed. Putin continues bombing. Once again, he’s playing Trump for a fool and hoping to weaponise a freezing, starving, bloody winter against Ukraine," Mr Blumenthal said on X. The Treasury did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Last month, Congress passed the Lindsey O Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, which allows Mr Trump and future American presidents to impose tariffs of up to 100 per cent on major importers of Russian energy meeting specified criteria. The US Treasury Department has issued a special exemption as part of Mr Trump's deal with Mr Putin, but some elected officials have questioned the legality of that special licence. And a 2022 law prevents the US importing Russian energy unless a president consults with Congress and observes a 90-day waiting period. “Congress was clear: the US should not import oil from Russia until it ends its aggression against Ukraine and ceases threats against our Nato allies," a different group of senators wrote in a statement at the weekend.

title: Saudi-led coalition and Houthis trade threats over oil installations
description: Saudi Arabia announces more missile interceptions, days after deadly strikes on airports
content: The war between the Saudi-led coalition and Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi rebels escalated further on Tuesday, as the two sides traded threats against oil installations. The coalition announced that it had carried out an operation against energy sites in Houthi-held areas of Yemen, including Al Sabahah station in the capital Sanaa and piers used for loading fuel at the port of Hodeidah. Coalition spokesman Maj Gen Turki Al Malki said the Houthis had been using civilian infrastructure to support their military operations and supply their arsenals. He added that the operation had been focused on neutralising the Houthis’ ability to threaten Saudi Arabia, Yemen, the Red Sea and international shipping lanes. Earlier in the day, the coalition had urged civilians to leave Al Sabahah, owned by the Yemen Petroleum Company, before what it described as a “special operation”. The order was published on social media by Maj Gen Al Malki, alongside a map of the area. In response to the strikes, the Houthis announced that oil installations in Saudi Arabia would be considered legitimate targets and that any civilians working at those sites should stay away. The coalition also said it had intercepted three missiles launched towards Saudi Arabia on Monday evening and yesterday. One of the projectiles was aimed at Riyadh, while the others were heading towards the city of Khamis Mushait, Maj Gen Al Malki said. In the past weeks, Saudi Arabia has faced repeated Houthi attacks on civilian infrastructure, including a strike on Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport on Saturday that left 13 people dead and 308 injured. However, although the attacks have disrupted travel and forced schools in Riyadh to switch to remote learning, the city’s roads remained crowded yesterday, offices were open and sporting events took place as planned, residents told The National . “The usual traffic is there. The streets are full of cars,” said Christina, a Lebanese citizen who lives in the Saudi capital. “I’m working from the office and the roads look completely normal on my way to work.” Meanwhile, Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty held a call with Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi yesterday, during which he pushed for an immediate halt to all attacks on Saudi Arabia, his ministry said in a statement. Mr Abdelatty was quoted as saying that there could be no justification for the attacks.

title: 'Yallah!': Whoop chief celebrates debut of app's Arabic option
description: Members can now access health insights in Arabic
content: Whoop 's decision to provide an Arabic option on its platform is part of a broader commitment to the Middle East, its Egyptian-American chief executive Will Ahmed has said. Arabic has joined English, French, German, Latin American Spanish, European Portuguese and Italian as languages available on the wearable fitness tracker company's app. Mr Ahmed said the addition of Arabic was meaningful for him. “My father is Egyptian and immigrated to the United States, and when I was younger I had the fortune of being able to travel with him throughout the Middle East,” he told The National . “I think the first time I visited the UAE was when I was 14 or 15, and I’ve been coming back to the region ever since.” He added that the Gulf was “our fastest-growing market globally” and said the company viewed the expansion of wearable use in the region as “a critical footprint for growth”. “Launching the Whoop experience in Arabic is part of our wider commitment to residents of the GCC, giving native speakers access to personal health insights in the language they use every day,” Mr Ahmed said. Though some technology companies have struggled to implement the nuances and diversity of Arabic , Mr Ahmed said that Whoop spent a lot of time working closely with Arabic-speaking members to ensure that the launch would be seamless. “Their feedback helped us identify where we could improve and get the details right,” he said. The Arabic language option will be rolled out gradually and will be available in the most recent version of the company's app. Whoop's co-founder also said he viewed the region as quick to embrace the idea that technology can empower people to take care of their health. His Boston-based company shares that vision, he added. “Our continued commitment to the GCC comes from a deep respect for the leadership in the region and what they’re trying to accomplish,” he said. On Tuesday, the company announced the launch of the Arabic option with a video posted to its social media accounts showing users throughout the Middle East working out while wearing Whoop devices . “Yallah!” posted Mr Ahmed as he shared the video. He launched Whoop in 2012 into a crowded wearable technology market. The company has grown steadily, amassing a loyal following, particularly among professional athletes. In a recent interview with The National , Dr Ami Bhatt, who joined Whoop as its first chief medical officer in July, said she was encouraged to see that more women across the Middle East were turning to the company's devices as a way to better understand their health. “Across the GCC , female member growth has increased more than 90 per cent year-over-year, with strong growth across every market we track,” she said. Her comments about the Middle East echoed the sentiments of Mr Ahmed, who in August said the fitness-tracker company would open a second office in the UAE, calling the move “critical for growth”. In March, Whoop announced $575 million in funding from a group of international investors led by Abu Dhabi and Qatari sovereign wealth funds. The Series G round was led by three Gulf investors: Mubadala Investment Company, 2PointZero Group and the Qatar Investment Authority. Whoop partners with fitness initiatives such as the Dubai Fitness Challenge and Doha Marathon. It also “serves as the official health and performance wearable” of UAE Team Emirates-XRG and Al Nassr Football Club. The company was at the centre of controversy during this year's Australian Open when officials made tennis players, including Carlos Alcaraz and Jannik Sinner, remove their Whoop devices. “Data is not steroids,” Mr Ahmed posted on his X account in protest. In April, Mr Ahmed hailed announcements that Whoops can be worn in the French Open, Wimbledon and US Open.

title: Sheikh Mohammed bin Rashid announces Dh2.1 trillion of projects under way in Dubai
description: Ruler of Dubai says emirate is building 'city within a city' in next phase of growth
content: Sheikh Mohammed bin Rashid, Vice President and Ruler of Dubai, has announced a Dh2.1 trillion portfolio of active projects in the emirate that cover housing, transport, aviation and infrastructure. Speaking at the Mohammed bin Rashid Leadership Forum at Dubai World Trade Centre, Sheikh Mohammed said the emirate was “building a city within a city” with further projects set to be announced. The annual forum brought together 1,000 government and private sector leaders, alongside experts, decision-makers and academics. “Our momentum is continuous and our achievements are ongoing. This is a remarkable period for growth and development; the ideal time to invest in Dubai and its infrastructure,” Sheikh Mohammed said. He said the emirate was investing heavily in housing, transport and infrastructure to prepare for a new phase of economic growth. “Cities that aspire for progress act before others,” he said, calling for leaders capable of translating ideas into tangible outcomes. The projects include Dh1.1 trillion allocated for real estate development to 2030, with about 350,000 residential units planned. Aviation investment also features prominently, with Dh128 billion for Al Maktoum International Airport – designed to handle up to 260 million passengers annually, alongside Dh328 billion to expand the Emirates and flydubai fleets and Dh18.7 billion for a new Emirates engineering and maintenance complex. Infrastructure spending includes Dh100 billion for road upgrades and the Dubai Metro Blue and Gold lines, Dh151 billion for new power and water grid infrastructure and Dh80 billion for the Dubai Strategic Sewerage Tunnels system. A further Dh100 billion has been set aside to develop Phase 2 of the Dubai International Financial Centre.

title: Home health tests aim to tackle disease before it strikes
description: Dh599 blood test offers comprehensive analysis of personal markers and illness risk
content: At-home blood tests that can identify potential health risks years before symptoms emerge are to become more easily available in the UAE as healthcare providers shift their focus from treatment to prevention. Health assessments starting from about Dh200 can offer patients insights into their future risk of disease and the lifestyle changes they can make to potentially prevent or delay its onset. More comprehensive services analyse hundreds of biomarkers, while DNA testing costing several thousand dirhams can provide a directory of detailed genetic information. The growing market reflects a wider push towards preventive healthcare in the UAE, with new government initiatives in Dubai and Abu Dhabi encouraging residents to take greater control of their long-term health. Dubai recently launched the Dubai Longevity Authority to encourage people to live healthier lives, free of chronic disease and mental decline. Abu Dhabi has also put preventive healthcare and pre-emptive screening at the forefront of multiple initiatives implemented by the Abu Dhabi Public Health Centre and the Department of Health Abu Dhabi. Private operators have also stepped up their focus on wellness rather than on responding to ill health. For Dh599 ($163), Aster promises a home assessment that can help identify health risks based on more than 120 biomarkers extracted from a blood test and a urine sample. The test promises a comprehensive, personalised health assessment that could help people make more informed lifestyle decisions. “Once the system has your genetic code and understands what's happening with your microbiome, along with your blood work, it can give a very comprehensive view on where your predispositions may be or some vulnerabilities,” said Alisha Moopen, managing director and chief executive of Aster DM Healthcare. “It can show how you can address them way earlier to delay or prevent them becoming a problem. But in the wider longevity, 80 per cent of the work needs to be done by the individual. “If you have the sleep, nutrition, movement and stress management under control, you can benefit from all the other exciting things science is offering. “People can't go in and sit in a hyperbaric oxygen chamber or talk about doing stem cells or cleansing the blood if you don't have the basics right. Longevity can get you to an amazing health outcome, but just doing the shiny things is throwing away money.” The service is the latest in a long line aiming to capitalise on the booming demand for longevity medicine. Medcare Hospitals offer a Lab at Home service where qualified technicians visit homes to collect blood and diagnostic samples across Dubai and Sharjah. Elsewhere, Vesta Care and Health 24/7 offer full-body check-ups, vitamin, hormone and thyroid panels, and routine blood tests at your doorstep, delivered by qualified nurses, with results in 24 hours. The tests form part of a wider switch in attitudes towards a more preventive health strategy. Ms Moopen said insurance companies are also beginning to change their approach and support disease prevention. “My father started off the Aster business being reactive to ill people, but today we can't just be a sick care company,” she said. “There are companies that sponsor enhanced insurance plans which think about prevention, we do see employers being a lot more pro-employees' health and managing that much more closely. We're seeing that shift, especially in the UAE.” The recently formed Dubai Longevity Authority is aiming for 31 per cent annual growth in the longevity sector and a Dh35 billion ($9.53 billion) economic boost over the next decade. Experts, however, said it could be difficult for some to buy into the reality of wellness programmes and avoid being blinded by slick marketing campaigns that fail to deliver results. The House of Longevity is a research and community platform hoping to capitalise on demand. The platform translates clinical and scientific research into practical guidance across seven pillars of sleep, movement, nutrition, mental health, preventative care, healthy environments, and purpose. Alex Zagrebelny, founder and CEO of R.Evolution, the company behind the project, said where we live can have a significant impact on how long we live. “Longevity itself is not an industry,” he said. “As prevention, wellbeing and quality of life become greater priorities, existing industries will need to develop new services, products and infrastructure around them. “The sheer volume of claims, often based on different levels of evidence, makes it difficult for consumers to understand what is genuinely supported by science and what is simply good marketing.” Researchers at the non-profit Global Wellness Institute said property focused on health and wellness was on the rise. Global investment has increased from $151 billion in 2017 to $$876 billion in 2025, the report says. While longevity may have become a buzzword in healthcare and real estate, Dr Eli Abirached, an expert in recovery and biohacking at Dubai’s Restore Fitness, said consumers should do their own research into what works for them. “Whenever there is demand, there's always a clever entrepreneur somewhere coming up with the next problem solving and devised path you must take,” he said. “If you do not have it, you are behind everyone else. Fear of missing out is a great selling, anchor. However, when it comes to biohacking (in health), the equation is incredibly simple. “When you get a longevity device or sign up to a programme, if you do not have a reason for getting it, then you’re the sucker.” “If you have a reason, but you're also trying to track the changes that are happening, you've moved from the sucker to adding real value to your life.”

title: UAE universities must change to equip students in AI age, say leaders and students
description: Minister says evolving jobs market must be reflected in courses and teaching methods
content: UAE universities must overhaul their courses and teaching methods to keep pace with artificial intelligence and the rapidly changing demands of the jobs market, the acting Minister of Higher Education and Scientific Research has said. Dr Abdulrahman Al Awar called for closer collaboration between universities and industry. He warned that emerging technologies were transforming the skills employers require and creating an urgent need to rethink how students are taught. He was speaking at the Zayed Education Foundation’s Partnerships for the Future event, in Abu Dhabi, where 12 institutions came together to strengthen collaboration and expand opportunities for home-grown scholars. “Economies and job markets are undergoing a radical and rapid change, and it is happening at a very rapid pace,” Dr Al Awar said. “New technologies, including artificial intelligence, are creating new opportunities and changing the skills that the market needs. “Fundamental changes must happen in engaging higher education institutions and economic sectors and redesigning the curricula and the skills of both faculty and students.” He said the ministry’s Outcome-Based Evaluation Framework was challenging universities to meet those demands and become more competitive in shaping the future of higher education in the UAE. “The UAE vision for higher education is centred on creating a vibrant higher education ecosystem that is future-ready, globally competitive and connected to the needs of our students, our economy, and our society,” he said. An updated guidebook for the framework was released earlier this year following consultations involving 735 representatives from higher education institutions across the country. Change has not just been called for from the top, but also by students. The National spoke to two Ruwwad Zayed Scholars about their hopes for the future of higher education. Noor Odeh, a UAE resident from Jordan, is a member of the first cohort of the masters scholars and is studying computational data science at Khalifa University. She scrapped her plans to study at an Australian university to stay in the UAE. “I want to be a changemaker. So it's not just the degree that I got excited about when I was accepted [for the scholarship]. It was more that will get to do something for my community because I will receive guidance,” she said. She believes the future of higher education will rely on hands-on experiences and skills rather than grades and metrics. “We need to put less focus on numbers like GPA [grade point average], and more about the skills that you're learning. What has helped me the most was not just the knowledge that I got from my degree, but the skills that I gained,” Ms Odeh said. Fellow Ruwwad Zayed Scholar Jassem Alkhoori is studying digital transformation at Zayed University. He agrees that higher education needs to be agile and keep pace with technological development. “I think currently the education system follows guidelines that are very outdated. Now that AI is actually overtaking most simple tasks such as screening papers, I think there should be more education on how to use these tools to help with research,” he told The National . The push for a competitive higher education sector has accelerated in recent years and has taken major steps since the founding of the country's first university, the United Arab Emirates University, 50 years ago. Zayed Education Foundation hopes to create opportunities for 100,000 students by 2035 and recently announced the first cohort of 50 Ruwwad Zayed Scholars – exceptional Emirati and Arab students who will pursue master’s degrees at universities in the UAE. Saeed Al Nazari, secretary general of the Great Arab Minds initiative – which recognises and empowers exceptional Arab scholars, scientists and innovators – told The National that the talented minds from the region must be nurtured. “With whatever happening around us – conflicts, news, social media, AI – sometimes we even forget to look up to our people in this region who are doing brilliant stuff,” he said. “This region has always been part of the momentum to move educational research forward globally. The good thing is that we have so many people who are willing to invest in knowledge economy. We just sometimes need to connect the dots.”

title: Housekeeper cleared of stealing Jordanian princess’s jewels
description: Colombian worker had been accused of theft from Princess Firyal's home in London
content: A long-serving housekeeper has been found not guilty of stealing expensive jewellery from her employer, a Jordanian princess. A jury in London took less than two hours to clear Maria Virgelina Taborda Henao, 71, of theft. She had been accused of stealing several items from the home in Belgravia when Princess Firyal, 81, flew to Jordan at the outbreak of Covid in 2020. Princess Firyal was married to Prince Muhammad bin Talal, the younger brother of King Hussein of Jordan, from 1964 to 1978. She had told Southwark Crown Court that she had been alerted that items from her jewellery collection were missing when a jeweller friend called to tell her they had appeared for auction in Canterbury. The items included a custom-made sapphire and diamond ring. The court heard police found Princess Firyal’s wedding ring, a pair of earrings and a necklace during a search of Ms Taborda Henao’s home in Fulham. The princess thought the wedding ring had been lost years earlier. Ms Taborda Henao, who is from Colombia and had worked for Princess Firyal for 11 years, told the court, through a Spanish interpreter, that the princess had called her a thief and made similar accusations against other people. Ms Taborda Henao’s nephew, Julian Ramirez, was said to have acted as a conduit for the sale of the items. He was also arrested but fled to Colombia in October 2023 while on police bail.

title: Apple HomeView and Apple TV 4K: What to know about smart hub and updated console
description: New HomeView device available from November 13 in English only
content: Apple has introduced HomeView, a device that the company says incorporates artificial intelligence-driven Siri and an easy-to-use interface to help people at home. A video posted to Apple 's website and social media accounts shows a busy family in the kitchen using the device to answer questions, communicate with others and set reminders. “Siri, ping me my keys,” a woman asks HomeView as she tries to leave her home. The HomePod speaker causes her keys to give off a beeping noise, presumably with the help of Apple 's AirTag. In the video and on the HomeView webpage, Apple says the product is only “available in English to start”. The company says HomeView will be available on November 13 with prices starting at $299. Two options will be available: a device that rests on surfaces and a version that mounts on a wall.
