Everyone knew what they were doing and what needed to happen next. Check-in was quick and easy, and the staff were warm and attentive without being overbearing. That became a theme throughout the weekend. Small requests were remembered and staff would ask us later how dinner, the spa or another part of our stay had gone. They paid attention. The room We stayed in the Deluxe Guest Room with views across the marina and towards the sea. Fruit, macarons and refreshments awaited us as we entered the room. The room wasn't enormous, but we didn't need it to be. There was plenty of storage, an extremely comfortable bed, soft towels and a good-sized bathroom. Grosvenor House is an established hotel, and the design reflects that. This isn't the minimalist look of some of Dubai 's newer hotels. There is wooden cabinetry, marble throughout the bathroom and touches of Art Deco. It feels traditional, in a very elevated way. For a weekend when the whole point was to switch off, the most important things were there: a great bed, a good bathroom and plenty of quiet. The food You could easily spend the whole weekend eating your way around Grosvenor House. Our first dinner was at Rhodes W1 . I started with the watermelon salad which was nice, although I couldn't quite get my head around the almond and orange dressing with fresh za'atar and tarragon. For me, it was one herb too many and needed balancing with something more salty. My husband was much happier with his duck rillette fritters. I followed with a rib-eye steak, and he went for the braised lamb shank: great mains that were traditional and well made. Again, the service made a difference. Staff took the time to talk us through dishes and let us sample drinks before deciding what to order. Breakfast at Sloane's the following morning was busy, but incredibly well run. Everything you would expect from a five-star Dubai breakfast was available: eggs, pastries, Arabic dishes, fruit and plenty of Asian and Indian options. Dinner on our second night was at Toro Toro , which was probably my favourite meal of the stay. The interiors of restaurant are beautiful, but also fun. Staff talked us through the Pan-Latin American influences behind the dishes without making the whole thing feel too formal. The standout for me was the cachapas, a Venezuelan sweetcorn pancake with whipped halloumi, sour cream and pico de gallo, assembled at the table. It reminded me a little of cornbread, but creamier, warmer and sweeter. I followed it with the encocado, with black cod, prawns, squid, coconut, aji mirasol and rice. We had already started with the smoked guacamole, so by this point we were completely stuffed. There were still plenty of things we wanted to try, though, which gives us an excuse to go back. Spa and wellness A weekend away without the children was always going to involve a trip to the spa. Our couples massage at the newly renovated Sanara Spa was one of the highlights of the weekend. We had our consultation earlier in the day and came back later for the treatment. Before the massage we were taken to the separate male and female changing areas, each with a sauna, steam room and Jacuzzi, for some time apart to unwind. For a city hotel, the spa is huge. There is also a hammam and plunge pools at different temperatures, including an ice plunge. I loved the interiors too. There are Japanese influences throughout, including the textiles, particularly two beautiful kimonos hanging as wall art, one behind the reception desk and another in the women's changing room. Then came the massage. Both therapists were excellent and knew exactly where more pressure was needed. I nearly fell asleep, although my husband's snoring from the other side of the room hampered that. By the end, I realised just how tense I had been beforehand. The service There is no shortage of luxury hotels in Dubai. Beautiful rooms, restaurants , spas and pools come with the territory, but good service is harder to get right consistently. From reception and housekeeping to the restaurants and spa, the staff were attentive without constantly hovering around us. More importantly, it never felt scripted. There were fresh roses left on our pillows and a welcome letter in the room, but it was the smaller interactions that I noticed more. Someone remembering where we had dinner and asking how it was. A member of staff recalling something we had mentioned earlier. Not having to repeat a request. None of these things is huge on its own. Put together, though, they mean you don't spend your weekend thinking about logistics or chasing things up. Everything just works. The verdict Grosvenor House isn't Dubai's newest hotel, but it doesn't need to be. There will always be a newer hotel, a bigger room or another spectacular opening around the corner. But what is much harder to replicate is a hotel where the service feels this consistent, confident and luxurious. It worked particularly well for a weekend away for us as a couple. We ate far too much, spent a few hours doing very little at the spa and, for a couple of days, had almost nothing that needed organising. The bottom line A weekend at Grosvenor House made it easy to enjoy the Dubai Marina skyline, attentive service and a good mix of dining, with time to unwind at the spa. Rates currently start at about Dh540 a night, including VAT, though they vary by date and room type. Check-in is from 2pm and checkout by noon. This review was conducted at the invitation of the hotel and reflects standards during this time

title: Lupin part four: The story so far ahead of Netflix return
description: Omar Sy returns as gentleman thief Assane Diop, whose plans for a quieter life are disrupted by a mysterious copycat
content: With elaborate heists, convincing disguises and a revenge plot that puts an entire family in danger, Netflix ’s Lupin has taken its gentleman thief from the Louvre to a prison cell over three parts. The French mystery thriller follows Assane Diop (played by Omar Sy ), who draws inspiration from the adventures of Arsene Lupin, the fictional thief created by French author Maurice Leblanc. What begins as a mission to clear his father’s name develops into a struggle to protect Assane’s own family from the consequences of his crimes. Alongside the thefts and escapes, the series is centred on Assane’s relationships with his estranged wife Claire, their teenage son Raoul and his closest friend and accomplice, Benjamin. His schemes repeatedly test their loyalty, even when he believes he is acting in their interests. Part four finds Assane behind bars, apparently ready to leave his criminal life behind. But a new thief operating as 'Lupin' threatens those plans. As the series returns for its latest season, here is a refresher on what happened in the first three parts. What is Lupin about? As a teenager, Assane’s life changes after his father Babakar, a Senegalese immigrant working for wealthy businessman Hubert Pellegrini, is accused of stealing a valuable diamond necklace. Babakar dies in prison, leaving his son to grow up with the consequences of an accusation he believes was false. Years later, Assane sets out to uncover what happened and expose those responsible. Taking inspiration from Leblanc’s stories, he uses disguises, sleight of hand and elaborate deception to outwit his opponents. But his pursuit of Pellegrini also attracts police attention and places Claire and Raoul in danger. The story so far (spoilers ahead): What happened in Lupin part one? The series begins with a robbery at the Louvre , where Assane steals the necklace his father was accused of taking years earlier. The heist is the first step in a wider plan to expose Pellegrini. As Assane investigates, he uncovers the businessman’s insurance fraud and the involvement of corrupt police commissioner Dumont in framing his father Babakar. Assane joins forces with investigative journalist Fabienne Beriot, who has been looking into Pellegrini’s dealings. But their efforts to bring him down take a deadly turn when his henchman Leonard murders her. Meanwhile, detective Youssef Guedira begins to recognise a pattern in Assane’s methods. A fellow fan of Leblanc’s books, he realises the thief is drawing on the adventures of Arsene Lupin. Part one ends during a family trip where Leonard kidnaps Raoul. As Assane discovers his son is missing, Guedira catches up with him. What happened in Lupin part two? The search for Raoul brings Assane and Guedira together, with the detective ultimately rescuing the teenager. Although Raoul returns safely to Claire, the kidnapping makes clear how dangerous Assane’s pursuit of Pellegrini has become. With Benjamin’s help, he uncovers Pellegrini’s diversion of charitable donations into an offshore account. Assane then confronts him and records his confession to framing Babakar and ordering Beriot’s murder. However, Assane continues his efforts to expose the businessman, reconnecting with Pellegrini’s daughter Juliette and devising a plan centred on the family foundation’s charity concert. The evidence leads to the arrests of Pellegrini and Dumont, finally exposing the conspiracy against Assane’s father. But Assane’s identity is now public, leaving him unable to return home without risking arrest. Part two ends with him saying goodbye to Claire and Raoul before disappearing. What happened in Lupin part three? After going into hiding, Assane returns to Paris to steal the Black Pearl and carry out an even more ambitious deception: faking his own death. He hopes his apparent demise will allow Claire and Raoul to escape the attention surrounding him. But the plan unravels when Keller – a dangerous figure from his past – kidnaps his estranged mother, Mariama. Using her captivity as leverage, Keller forces Assane to carry out further thefts, drawing him back into the life he had been trying to escape. Assane eventually saves his mother and defeats Keller, but recognises that his freedom comes at a continuing cost to those around him. To give his loved ones a chance at a quieter life, he makes a deal with Guedira and turns himself in. During the final scenes, Assane receives an envelope from the neighbouring prison cell, revealing that Pellegrini is being held next door. What to expect in Lupin part four? Netflix says the new instalment begins four years later, with Assane still serving his sentence. He intends to fulfil his promise to Raoul and join his family in Senegal after his release. However, a string of simultaneous museum robberies – announced in Lupin’s name – makes him a suspect once again. Footage appears to show him at one of the thefts, during which police captain Belkacem is seriously injured. With someone apparently impersonating him, Assane must escape from prison to identify the copycat and clear his name. Lupin Part Four is now streaming on Netflix.

title: 'I feel like it’s meant to be': Eight-year-old Emirati acrobat finds her feet in the air
description: Jawaher Essa Sharafi followed her mother into aerial arts and is encouraging other children to join her
content: Jawaher Essa Sharafi wears an outfit splashed with pink, turquoise, lime green and yellow in a brushstroke pattern. Suspended from a hoop, she twists, twirls and drops as she practises at Aerial Lab in Arjan, Dubai. The eight-year-old has already taken her skills to the international stage, winning bronze in aerial hoop at the IAAA Grand Open Cup in Belgrade, Serbia, in September. The youngest competitor among more than 100 athletes from 11 countries, she became the first Emirati to compete internationally in aerial athletics – only two years after she began formal training. View this post on Instagram An aerialist is an acrobat who specialises in performing on suspended apparatus, such as hoops, trapezes and silks. The discipline combines acrobatics and artistic performance, drawing on strength, flexibility and co-ordination as athletes move through holds, spins and drops, often set to music. Jawaher trains on hoop and hammock, a suspended fabric sling, but asked which she prefers, there is little hesitation. “Hoop, hoop, hoop. It's the best. First of all, I like hoop because it's hard. I like to challenge myself in aerial,” she tells The National . The hoop shape and texture also set it apart. It's the “only one that's a circle made out of metal … because the rest [of the aerial equipment] are made out of same thing: fabric”, she says. “Hoop is made out of something different. That made me fall in love with it.” Her enthusiasm is equally apparent when she talks about training. “Whenever I do it, I get all my excitement out,” she says. “I feel like it's meant to be.” Following her mother Aerial arts was familiar to Jawaher long before she attended her first class. Her mother, Fatma Almadani, practised and taught the discipline. Almadani says: “She used to watch me train and she would attend all my trainings and be like, ‘I want to try, I want to try,’ So my trainer would put her up there since she was a baby.” Later, Jawaher began accompanying her mother to the children’s classes she taught. Participants had to be at least nine, and Jawaher was only four or five at the time. Watching from the sidelines did little to diminish her interest. She wanted to help, demonstrate and prove that she could keep up with the older children, her mother says. “I’d come home and she'd be like, ‘Mama, can you please come into the gym room? I want to show you that I can do what you were teaching the kids and I'm good enough to join your classes,’” Almadani recalls. The age restriction prompted her to look for somewhere that offered classes for younger children. Jawaher then began training at Aerial Lab when she was six. “Other than simple things we used to teach her at home, proper training was at Aerial Lab,” Almadani says. Watching other students perform gave Jawaher another goal. When Almadani took her to students' aerial showcases, she began asking when it would be her turn on stage. Finding her confidence Enthusiasm does not mean every new aerial skill comes easily. Jawaher describes the uncertainty of learning a trick that requires her to turn upside down, and wondering what might happen if she falls. However, she tries to reassure herself before attempting a move. “I can do this, no need to be worried, my teacher is here. She'll protect me, she knows what's right for me,” she tells herself. One drop proved particularly difficult after she fell while learning it. Returning to the movement took time, beginning slowly and gradually building speed as her confidence returned. Developing that control matters in competition, where judges assess difficulty, execution and artistry. For Jawaher, one detail requires particular attention: pointing her toes. “I've also been doing karate and in karate you don't point your toes,” she says. “It's been a challenge for me to try and remember.” Jawaher attends aerial classes on Wednesdays, Fridays and Sundays, with more training when a competition approaches. But she recognises the importance of taking a break. “Maybe not [training] every day, because I need rest days . It's important to have rest days,” she says. She sometimes practises at home on days when she does not have a class. The family’s gym room was originally Almadani’s space. “I actually set it up for me and now she took over,” she says. There, Jawaher has room to experiment as well as rehearse. Almadani adds: “She loves coming here and just she puts on music and does her own routines. She tries to imagine new moves.” From classes to competition Almadani did not initially see her daughter’s progress. Parents were asked not to sit in on group classes, so she would drop Jawaher off and collect her afterwards. Then the teachers began approaching her about private training. A competition planned in the UAE offered an opportunity, and Jawaher was selected to represent the studio. Almadani says she was the only child chosen from her age group. But that event was cancelled, and the competition in Serbia became Jawaher's international debut. Her mother was struck by her progress as she watched her prepare. “From seeing her in her first showcase on stage, compared to this year, doing a routine for the competition, I was surprised by how much she advanced in just one year,” Almadani says. Jawaher says she feels both nervous and excited before performing, but finishing her routine brings relief. “I'm like: finally I can get all that energy out of me. And I don't need to worry any more about my routine,” she says. Bigger ambitions What most impresses Almadani is her daughter’s willingness to work towards goals she has set herself. “I find her personality very inspiring. Her confidence is very inspiring,” she says. “It gets hard sometimes to train every day. Sometimes she's exhausted. Sometimes she wants to stay up at night and the weekends. But I'm inspired by how she's very committed to the goals she has.” Still, she wants her daughter to have the freedom to explore other interests. Jawaher has mentioned karate competitions, horse riding and parkour, adding to an already busy schedule. “She wants to try everything,” Almadani says. “But we don't have enough days of the week to do after-school [activities] every day.” Whatever Jawaher eventually chooses, her mother hopes the experience will leave her with habits and confidence that extend beyond competition. “It builds personality, it builds character and gives you skills that you need in life,” she says. For now, Jawaher is preparing two routines for her next showcase, one on hammock and another on hoop, and looking ahead to a competition in Italy next year. She would like more young athletes from the UAE to join her. Almadani recalls her daughter hoping that photographs from the competition in Serbia might encourage friends to enter future contests and help to build a bigger team. Jawaher invites friends to try aerial arts at home and has already encouraged one to begin classes. While keen to share her enthusiasm, she knows not everyone will feel ready to give it a go. “If you tried it, you would love it and you would keep going again and again,” she says. “But if you don't want to, I won't force you.”

title: Beirut commuters switch to motorcycle taxis as rising fuel prices push up fares
description: With even ride-sharing cabs becoming unaffordable, more and more people are turning to unregulated 'moto-taxis' to get around the Lebanese capital
content: Adam cannot afford to say no. Unlike most drivers of Beirut’s “servees ” – shared taxis, the most common form of public transport in Lebanon 's capital – he picks up almost anyone looking for a ride, even if it is for less than the set rate. “A lot of customers can’t afford the fare , so they offer 200,000 lira ($2.20) or less,” he told The National as he drove downtown. “People won’t ride if the price is too high.” His need to pick up every commuter is also driven by growing competition from the cheaper motorcycle taxis, commonly called “moto-taxis”, that more people are turning to as they endure a prolonged economic crisis now in its seventh year. Beirut’s servees drivers raised their fares from 200,000 to 300,000 lira after the government imposed a fuel tax in February, only nine days before the Iran war began. Fuel prices have nearly doubled since, according to the Syndicate of Gas Station Owners, as the war disrupted shipments from Gulf producers. The servees drivers now charge “as they see fit”, according to Zainab, who spoke to The National after dismounting a motorcycle taxi that she had booked through a ride-share app. The journey from her neighbourhood in Ras Al Nabaa to Jisr Al Wati cost her 200,000 lira, she said – “cheaper and faster than flagging a taxi in the street and then haggling with a chauffeur”. Ten years ago, it would have been almost unthinkable for a woman to ride on the back of a motorcycle with a strange man. But Lebanon's economic collapse has made financial necessity a priority over social norms. The crisis, which began in 2019 and which the World Bank has described as among the worst in modern history, has left most of the population struggling. Lebanese depositors were locked out of their savings and the national currency lost more than 98 per cent of its value against the US dollar, eroding salaries and severely diminishing purchasing power. That, combined with the higher fuel prices caused by the Iran war, have made traditional taxis increasingly unaffordable in a country where the monthly minimum wage is only $300. Meanwhile, motorcycles have come to dominate the streets of Beirut, with imports surging as commuters seek cheaper alternatives to cars and conventional taxis. Even car owners are choosing to forgo driving and take motorcycle taxis. “I used to fill up my car for $45. Now it costs almost $90 to $100, or sometimes even more. So we've started turning to slightly cheaper options,” said Moussa, a paramedic in his 30s who took a motorcycle taxi to a doctor’s appointment in Clemenceau, a busy Beirut neighbourhood notorious for its traffic gridlock. Moussa said he hails motorcycle rides by sending his pickup location to a “dispatcher” on a WhatsApp group. Motorcycle taxis “are cheaper and more economical considering how much petrol prices have risen recently. Everyone is trying to save money,” he said. More than a dozen servees drivers interviewed by The National voiced frustration over dwindling passenger numbers, as increasing numbers of commuters like Zainab and Moussa turn to motorcycle taxis, or cheaper but slower alternatives such as vans and buses. Adam, who drives a Nissan Sunny – known for its fuel efficiency – shrugged. “It’s why I take everyone. I can’t afford to pick and choose. But at the same time it’s tough, and sometimes after hours of working I barely break even.” And motorcycle taxis are not the only players in Beirut's informal transport market. There are also the “white-plate” taxis – private cars operating as taxis through ride-hailing apps and WhatsApp groups. A red number plate, which serves as the licence to operate a taxi, costs about $16,000 in Lebanon. Along with the cost of the vehicle itself, this represents a significant upfront investment. Some drivers rent a licensed taxi and pay the owner about $20 a day. With petrol prices so high, drivers say they cannot afford to lower their fares. “Someone with a cheap motorcycle comes along, picks up passengers and drives off like he’s a taxi. It’s not safe. It's not legal. If there's an accident, there's no insurance or anything,” said Ibrahim, a taxi driver parked at the Cola intersection as he waited for customers. He accused motorcycle taxi operators of competing without the licensing and insurance requirements imposed on conventional taxi drivers. I’d be making a lot more money as a taxi driver if it weren’t for the motorcycle competition. They’re taking half our business Wael, Beirut taxi driver “Our cars cost money. We have to repair them, we work hard and we still can't make ends meet. Motorcycles are our biggest [competition].” But Ibrahim also recognised the financial pressures driving passengers to cheaper alternatives. While some servees drivers have started charging 400,000 lira or more per journey to compensate for rising fuel prices, he said he has continued to charge 300,000. “We're being considerate of the public,” he said. “We also can't raise fares for passengers because everyone's situation is difficult.” Other taxi drivers, unable to deny the economic reality, have simply decided to join the motorcycle phenomenon. By day, Wael ferries commuters around Beirut on a motorcycle. At night, he switches to his licensed taxi. His motorcycle uses less petrol, is easier to manoeuvre through daytime traffic and allows him to complete more trips in less time – meaning a higher profit. At night, lighter traffic, airport runs and Beirut’s nightlife make driving a taxi more feasible. “Everyone with a motorcycle now thinks it’s a fast and easy way to make money,” Wael told The National . He belongs to two WhatsApp groups that co-ordinate motorcycle taxi rides, each with more than 350 riders. He said the growing competition has taken a major toll on conventional taxis. “I’d be making a lot more money as a taxi driver if it weren’t for the motorcycle competition. They’re taking half our business,” he said. “But I don’t think they’re the problem. It’s the state, which has done nothing to regulate the taxi-motos or fix the economy. People are turning to motorcycles because they have to, not because they want to endanger themselves.” The dangers are clear to see. Motorcycles weave around potholes and through Beirut's notoriously chaotic traffic unpredictably, rarely a helmet in sight, and often pass through red lights. Beyond the occasional crackdown on unregistered motorcycles, Lebanon’s government has done little to regulate the growth of the informal motorcycle taxi industry. Asaad, another motorcycle taxi operator, thinks state regulation would be the best possible outcome for the moto-taxi phenomenon. “Because motorcycle taxis aren’t going away. They're the future,” he said.

title: Wealth expert Becky Fatemi: Tax the rich, but don’t scare them away from UK
description: With decades of deals under her belt, the Iran-born businesswoman has a message for PM Andy Burnham
content: It was an advertisement for a tele-sales job in the mid-1990s that set Becky Fatemi on the path to success. It meant standing on her feet all day, cold-calling hundreds of people, and talking, talking, talking while knowing she was under pressure to seal a deal in minutes. A role at which many people would baulk came naturally to the self-starting whirlwind of energy, who moved to London from Iran as a baby and was mostly brought up in a single-parent family. It forced Ms Fatemi to rely on her natural people skills, honing her ability to read what people wanted. She went on to use those skills for more than a decade as a top operator at estate agent Foxtons, a similar amount of time at her own property firm Rokstone, and now as a partner at Sotheby’s International Realty where she has evolved into a wealth adviser. Along the way she has worked as a hip-hop DJ, at McDonald’s, in Selfridges, sold tables at nightclubs, been a stylist to celebrities, worked for a children’s charity, founded a charity and launched a social media platform. “Any type of work that I felt that could fortify my CV, I did,” said Ms Fatemi, 50. She spoke to The National during lunch near her office in Marylebone, and over Zoom while she spent the summer in Portugal. Having spent the best part of three decades learning how people are willing to spend their money, and where they wish to invest, she is well positioned to know how those with wealth will respond to Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s leadership, as he and Chancellor John Healey head towards their first budget, on October 28. Taxing The Labour government has already made significant changes to the tax regime: scrapping the non-domicile status, raising employer national insurance contributions, increasing capital gains, applying VAT to private school fees and toughening property taxes. More changes are expected, with the middle classes and wealthiest expected to take the brunt. Ms Fatemi has more confidence in Mr Burnham than she had in his predecessor Keir Starmer, but still does not think he is the right person to steer the UK’s economic fortunes. Trying to please everyone, an accusation immediately laid at Mr Burnham’s door as he entered Downing Street seemingly happy to respond positively to requests for funding, simply will not work, she believes. She is in no doubt those with money need to pay their fair share of tax, to “address the disparity in wealth”, but should not be squeezed too hard. “A lot of my clients are working far longer hours than I've ever seen, and working much harder,” Ms Fatemi says, adding: “Politically, we cannot alienate wealth. It helps support the [country’s] infrastructure and, at the moment, our infrastructure is failing.” Exodus She is well aware of the exodus of the ultra-wealthy from London, especially after the decision to scrap non-doms , the status to ensure only money earned in Britain was taxed. The number of non-dom taxpayers in the UK in the final year before it was scrapped dropped by 1,200 , statistics show, as the wealthy geared up for the change. About 16,000 millionaires were predicted to leave the UK last year as the taxman’s grip tightened. The Bloomberg Billionaires Index suggest about half of the UK’s billionaire wealth – £120 billion ($160.7 billion) – has been lost. It is too soon to tell the true impact of such decisions, says Ms Fatemi, but there is no doubting the direction of travel. The government is avoiding addressing the issue of “a mass exodus of our uber-wealthy who are our biggest taxpayers”. Inheritance tax and being taxed on global wealth has “driven a lot of people out”, but she says: “I don't think we have seen the ramifications of exactly how that has affected the economy. "Someone employing over a thousand staff, who has personal staff, chefs, security guards, physiotherapists, tutors, teachers – all of these things have a domino effect to another workforce, like black cab drivers. I don't think we're going to understand these figures for a good five to six years.” Hidden quitters More than a dozen people with multibillion-pound fortunes have left or loosened ties with the country in favour of more favourable tax regimes, the Bloomberg index showed, including steel tycoon Lakshmi Mittal, Aston Villa co-owner Nassef Sawiris and telecoms investor Shravin Bharti Mittal. The UAE has been the preferred destination for many of the billionaires, along with Monaco, Switzerland and Italy. But for the UK, all is not lost. “Is there money still coming into London? Yes. Could we be more tax-smart? Yes. Do they need to be taxed? Yes,” Ms Fatemi says. She says there is a need for transparency on how any wealth coming into the UK is taxed, with anything enveloped in a company structure paying “ridiculous” taxes. “That’s where the government is missing a really big trick,” she says. The people really making money from the current situation are tax advisers, Ms Fatemi says, as there are so many moving parts. She suggests the government gets a grip on the situation by speaking to wealth advisers like her “who are looking at where that tax position is and speaking to the people at every level to understand exactly what is going on”. Immigrant mindset Ms Fatemi puts her irrepressible work ethic down to her immigrant background, which created a determination to succeed. Born in 1976, with a father who was a pilot with Iran Air before the revolution deposed the Shah, she spent time growing up in Kuwait and Bangkok, but mostly London. She was even a "baby boarder" at the Norland Nursery in London for a year, which she recognises was a bizarre start to life in a new country. “Both my parents felt it was imperative that my brother and I were educated,” she says, adding her father in particular fitted the immigrant stereotype of hoping she would study medicine or law, even though her passion was to work in the music industry. “My mother really wanted us to live in the UK. We came at the time of [Margaret] Thatcher, having to work very, very hard. Nothing was for free, you should be grateful to be here and you're going to work very hard in order to stay here. “It took 10 years to get my passport.” Her father was rarely around, and her mother had multiple sclerosis, so she learnt to fend for herself. Her mother returned to Iran as her health deteriorated, meaning Ms Fatemi left home at 15 and surfed sofas until she found somewhere permanent to live, “on one of the roughest council estates in north London”. She dealt with racism, prejudice and inequality but felt determined that she was going to “make a difference” by being a disruptive force. Ms Fatemi had made her way through university when she saw the tele-sales advert. “It said: ‘Are you good at talking? If you're a good salesperson, come and join us. You'll make a lot of money’. I got to number one in that company.” Still in her early 20s, she then had to deal with both her parents, plus her boyfriend and best friend, dying in quick succession. She needed a change, so she threw herself into her career. She badgered estate agent Foxtons for a job as a receptionist but ended up selling homes. “I came from a tele-sales job of cold-calling over 400 people to this job where people would call me to spend millions. “The Park Lane office, which is where I ended up in the late '90s, early 2000s, was where the real money was. International money was pouring into Mayfair.” Speaking several languages and being well-travelled was an advantage as it gave her an understanding of people. “I know culturally how these people live,” Ms Fatemi says. It was still not easy. “You were just in this pit of sales. Each for their own. It was very cut-throat, very male, very chauvinistic. Very hard to navigate. “But I was just born with this inherent female strength, being Iranian, Persian, but just being an immigrant. When you're an immigrant you're fighting just to be included, to survive. You don't know where your next meal's coming from and you're grateful just to be there.” Wrong side of the tracks Her personal situation also made things difficult. “I was leaving Mayfair and going home to the worst estate in Kilburn, or sofa-surfing in the worst parts of north or south London, living in hostels, while still working at Foxtons. “I was living in two worlds, which allowed me to see the other side of the track how people were really trying to survive. That allowed me that street-smart mentality. It led her to set up a charity years later, called Shadow to Shine, to give opportunities for young people from underrepresented, diverse backgrounds to break into tech, fashion, construction, law or creative industries. Perception When Foxtons was sold, she set up her own conglomerate, Rokstone, inspired by Richard Branson’s multi-pronged business empire. “He did Virgin Brides, Virgin Trains, Virgin planes, Virgin Holidays. And I thought, why can't I do that? So I set up this company called Rokstone.” It allowed her to promote her love of music and entertainment with bricks and mortar, plus tech and philanthropy – all from her living room. Ms Fatemi started travelling the world, running parties and events, amalgamating brands and styling for celebrities such as Rihanna and Beyonce. A phone call from a former client asking her to act as a property buying agent returned her to London. “I didn’t even know what a buying agent was,” she says, not entirely convincingly. She found a £500,000, one-bedroom flat after about 100 viewings on a small commission. Through word of mouth, she gained a few more clients before opening an office in Devonshire Street, Marylebone, the neighbourhood where she still operates. It was all about perception, Ms Fatemi says. If she could persuade customers that Rokstone was a luxury real estate firm, it would live up to her exaggerations. “We had one property to start, then got a house in Mayfair for £5 million and then I was selling two flats in Camberwell for £220,000. All referral, referral, referral.” She would go out on viewings with other agents and pretend she was looking for a place for herself while learning their trade secrets. “I was fearless,” Ms Fatemi says. “I was that ‘Persian princess’, because I had been at one stage, and my mother had been. I believed that I had a right to be there and because of that conviction I think people believed that I was one of them.” She ensured she was “in every conversation, in every restaurant, at every opening” and even got a Hummer that was Rokstone-branded, which kept conveniently breaking down on Park Lane, where it could be seen by everyone. At the time Ms Fatemi also became a single mother herself, so knew she had to make it work “because there was no other option”. Networking After 13 years of running her business, achieving a profit every year from £6 billion worth of sales, even through Covid, it was time to look for the next challenge. During a viewing of a £30 million property in Piccadilly, an old colleague suggested she meet George Azar, who was assembling an "Avengers team" after buying the Sotheby’s franchise. They agreed after a 10-minute Zoom call that she should become a partner, with support for her charity and the wriggle room to set up a tech platform called Blackbook part of her conditions. Blackbook is the culmination of 30 years of networking for Ms Fatemi and is intended as a sort of LinkedIn/Instagram for creatives, to allow them to display and monetise their skills in one place by connecting them with other "talent". But her day-to-day is spent speaking with lawyers, tax advisers, compliance and most importantly, clients. She has just been advising a client in New York, a "prominent billionaire", about bricks and mortar investments. “I am a global wealth adviser, which includes real estate, but really it's looking at their life position, how they're living, what's in their best interest for quality of life as well as investment. “The conversations I'm having now are with the most powerful, leading people in the world.” She says she deals with lots of Middle Eastern royal families and has clients in the UAE and across the GCC. “I make sure I'm in Abu Dhabi and Dubai three or four times a year, in Qatar, in Saudi, and supporting them with the investment that they're bringing into London and globally.” London calling Despite its troubles, she is likely to recommend London as a place for long-term investors to place their money due to its “durability” and “tenacity”. “The market is going to stay firm if you invest in best-in-class and super prime," she says. “And really, the people that I told to do that have made a lot of money.” After three decades of deals, she now has a sixth sense for spotting long-term opportunities. “I'm sad that I never pushed myself into investment banking because I think I would have been one of the best investment bankers in the world,” Ms Fatemi says. But at the very least she can appreciate what she has achieved for herself. “I'm going to be a better billionaire at 50 than I would have been at 30,” she says.

title: Erbil’s historic houses find new life as centre for Kurdish art and heritage
description: Kurdistan Centre for Arts and Culture is creating an archive for rare manuscripts while supporting artists and documenting Kurdish contributions to the region’s cultural history
content: In Erbil’s old quarter, Kurdish history is held in family manuscripts, works of art and memories passed down through generations. Now, four historic houses near the city’s ancient citadel are being brought back to life to give those stories a place to endure. The Kurdistan Centre for Arts and Culture (KCAC) is working on turning the homes into spaces for safeguarding manuscripts, supporting contemporary artists and documenting Kurdish contributions to the region’s cultural history. “One of the houses is dedicated to the archive, as a state-of-the-art storage facility … fireproof, waterproof, bulletproof – as you need here: everything-proof,” said Spede Mizuri, director of public impact at KCAC. The houses were evacuated in 2012 during moves by the regional government to improve the area around the historic landmark, but plans were put on hold when ISIS emerged two years later. The properties have remained vacant ever since. Most predate the Iraqi monarchy, while one is an Ottoman-era house with British influences, Ms Mizuri said. The archive building will be home to a partnership with the city's Salahaddin University to make its manuscript collection accessible to researchers and the public. Ms Mizuri said the collection had remained largely inaccessible since being moved to the university in the 1960s, with little cataloguing or academic study. The second house will become a permanent exhibition space, opening next month with the first solo exhibition in Kurdistan by a Kurdish artist living in exile. The remaining two properties will host workshops and longer-term training programmes in the arts, heritage and cultural sectors. The restoration builds on the organisation’s work to preserve vulnerable collections across Iraqi Kurdistan . Launched in 2024, its initial mobile archiving project used scanners inside a Toyota van to travel between villages, religious schools and private libraries, digitising material and making it freely accessible online. The collections range from political documents and religious manuscripts to personal journals, astrological material and modern printed works. Some were hidden underground during periods of conflict to protect them. “We have a major, major issue in Kurdistan for precious materials and artworks that have been purchased. They've been taken into stewardship, so to say, and nobody really knows what happened to these materials,” Ms Mizuri said. “Some of them are under really, really bad conditions as well, so digitisation is the first immediate crisis response to something like that.” Kurds are spread across Iraq, Turkey, Iran and Syria , with a large diaspora beyond those countries. Despite sharing a distinct cultural identity, Kurdish communities have developed under different political systems and national borders, so their language, literature and traditions play an important role in preserving a sense of shared history. For Ms Mizuri, the work addresses a broader problem: the lack of resources for Kurdish history and its contributions to the region to be documented and studied. “We have left our mark … on the world entirely, but there's very little to showcase that.” That effort to make Kurdish history more accessible extends beyond Erbil. In Sulaymaniyah, KCAC is working with the British Library and the University of Exeter on a project involving the library of the Ministry of Religious Endowment, which holds some of the oldest manuscripts in Kurdistan. The initiative, due to be announced next week, aims to make the collection the first Kurdish library represented in the British Library’s cataloguing system, bringing its manuscripts into a wider international research network. Ms Mizuri said the project was significant given Kurdistan’s history under British imperial rule, and the continued absence of a Kurdish library from the institution’s catalogue. From preserving manuscripts to promoting contemporary artists, KCAC is also seeking to ensure Kurdish culture has a stronger presence across the region. For Kurds, whose history has often been preserved through oral traditions and family accounts, making these collections accessible offers a tangible record of their cultural and intellectual contributions. Manuscripts, artworks and personal documents can help establish connections between generations, while giving researchers and communities material evidence to study and share. Ms Mizuri said the archive could also provide a sense of security by ensuring that Kurdish history was not dependent solely on memories or oral accounts, which can be difficult to substantiate or preserve over time. It also offers a way to understand Kurdish identity within the wider history of the region, recognising the contributions of Kurdish artists, writers and scholars that have not always been acknowledged as such. “We are known for being at the midst of war and continuously the spoils of wars that sometimes maybe we were part of, and other times we're really not,” Ms Mizuri said, adding that having tangible history helps to “introduce ourselves beyond conflict”. 'Ambassador for Kurdish artists' Preserving Kurdish heritage is also a way of bringing it into a wider cultural conversation, ensuring that Kurdish artists and their work are represented even beyond the Kurdistan region. The centre has been building relationships with cultural institutions in Iraq and across the Middle East, including through its participation in the first edition of Art Basel Qatar. Later this year, it will take part in the Sharjah Art Foundation’s art book fair , where it plans to host a workshop and talk and present its publications. Artist and resident Walid Siti was also recently presented at Jameel Arts Centre in Dubai. KCAC’s work extends beyond preserving historical material to exploring contemporary social issues through art. Its first exhibition, held in Akre in 2024, transformed the town’s old Qishla, an Ottoman-era fortress, into an exhibition space for digital artist Kaiwan Shaban. The exhibition was extended three times at the request of the local tourism office, Ms Mizuri said. A subsequent exhibition, Being Lost, was held in a public park in Ranya , a town near the Iranian border, associated with people-smuggling networks and young people attempting to reach Europe. The park, where The National has previously reported from, is known to be a location where those attempting to migrate seek out smugglers. The exhibition brought together memorabilia connected to families whose relatives had left or disappeared, exploring the uncertainty and pain experienced by those waiting for news. Visitors could record messages on phones attached to a transparent wall, with the recordings intended for broadcast on the radio in the hope of reaching those who had left. Seminars were held in nearby Raparin University, in the same district as Ranya , which used to be one the highest performing universities in the Kurdish region, which Ms Mizuri described as the “dichotomy” that exists in the city. “Heritage is collective,” she said of Kurdistan's place in the region. She added that the main priority was to “preserve and then to promote”. For Ms Mizuri, the work is ultimately about giving Kurdish communities the means to understand and share their own history, while recognising the connections between them and their neighbours.

title: The US will remain central to Gulf and Arab security, but the terms must change
description: A more secure region will depend on diversifying partnerships, building resilience and doubling down on diplomacy
content: The wars of recent months have exposed a troubling reality: despite a substantial American military presence and decades of close defence co-operation between the US and Arab countries, the security partnerships have neither deterred Iran nor fully shielded the region from its attacks. Two shortcomings stand out. The first is technical: traditional air defences that the US and its partners used have grappled with Iran’s asymmetric use of large numbers of missiles and inexpensive drones. The second is political: Washington embarked on a war that some of the region’s leaders had warned could have devastating consequences for their countries. They raise two questions. Can the US and its partners repair the gaps in the security umbrella? And will another costly Middle Eastern war weaken American public and political support for a sustained regional role? The answers remain uncertain. But enduring US interests make a wholesale withdrawal unlikely. And Arab states are likely to maintain a central strategic partnership with the US while strengthening their own capabilities, adding partners and pursuing diplomacy to reduce the danger of renewed conflict. Military history is marked by moments when new technologies overturn established assumptions. The widespread use of inexpensive drones, alongside large missile inventories, in Ukraine and the latest war with Iran, has highlighted another such shift. The American umbrella did not fall short because it was not equipped. It did so because it had not anticipated or prepared for the nature of these evolving threats. Saturation attacks can exhaust interceptors and overwhelm defences; the cost of shooting down a cheap drone may vastly exceed the cost of launching it. The US retains formidable offensive capabilities, as demonstrated by its and Israel’s ability to strike targets in Iran. But the ability to punish an adversary is different from the ability to shield cities, energy installations, airports and ports from retaliation. American military planners and defence firms are intensifying work on cheaper interceptors, counter-drone systems, directed-energy weapons and AI-assisted detection and targeting. The outcome of that technological race is impossible to predict. In the near term, however, Iran and its partners are likely to retain the capacity to inflict damage, even against sophisticated defences. In the medium term, new technological advances may once again shift the regional balance of power or give regional countries more effective defences. The military vulnerabilities were compounded by political decisions. The region’s leaders understood that a war perceived as existential by Tehran could prompt attacks on their territory and disruptions to the Strait of Hormuz . They warned against that scenario. Yet US President Donald Trump, encouraged by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, chose a military course that exposed America’s partners to precisely those risks. Mr Trump has subsequently appeared more attentive to regional concerns and has explored a negotiated outcome. But diplomacy has yet to produce a durable settlement, and the risk of renewed large-scale fighting is emerging once again. For the regional governments, the lesson might be concerning: close relations with Washington do not necessarily translate into influence over decisions with existential implications for their security. There is also a longer-term question. After Iraq and Afghanistan, could another costly Middle East war turn US voters and future presidents against maintaining a substantial regional presence? Washington is likely to reassess its regional posture, favouring a leaner, technologically advanced and less vulnerable deployment, but retrenchment is not the same as disengagement. The US has enduring interests in keeping Gulf energy flowing to world markets and critical waterways open; preventing Iran from acquiring nuclear weapons or dominating the region; protecting Israel; and sustaining partnerships with Gulf states whose importance now extends beyond hydrocarbons to investment, defence industries, advanced technology and artificial intelligence. Even an energy-producing America remains vulnerable to a global recession caused by a prolonged Gulf supply shock . Many American politicians from both parties disagree sharply about how the war was launched and prosecuted. Yet disagreement over methods does not amount to a consensus for abandoning these interests. Interestingly, the positions of potential presidential candidates from both parties confirm this view. Future administrations may adopt different strategies, but are unlikely to pull out wholesale from the region; indeed, they will grapple with many of the same dilemmas that have shaped US-Gulf policy since 1979. The regional states face a demanding agenda. Politically, they are justified in asking why exceptionally warm relations with Washington did not prevent a war they considered dangerous. They will need stronger mechanisms for consultation and greater input into decisions affecting regional escalation, as well as a serious role in shaping any settlement with Iran. Militarily, there is no other great power currently able to replace the US as most Arab countries’ principal strategic security partner. Hence, they will work with Washington as it rethinks the shape of its future security presence and relationships in the region. But the American partnership, while necessary, is no longer sufficient. The answer is less a matter of hedging against America than of adding layers to what is likely to remain an American-centred system The answer is less a matter of hedging against America than of adding layers to what is likely to remain an American-centred system: stronger national armed forces and industries; more effective intelligence-sharing and integrated air defence; and additional security relationships. Saudi Arabia’s engagement with Turkey and Pakistan points in this direction, as do opportunities to draw on European, Ukrainian, South Korean and other expertise in equipment, training and counter-drone innovation. Some countries will draw closer to Israel. It is not America or other partners, but America and other partners. The Gulf is understandably focused on building further resilience into its economies. Protecting energy, water, power, transport and digital infrastructure will require redundancy, dispersed facilities, rapid-repair capacity and strategic reserves. Alternative pipelines, ports and overland corridors – which are already in the works – can reduce dependence on vulnerable maritime chokepoints , even if geography cannot be wished away. Finally, Arab countries understand that defence needs to be accompanied by energetic diplomacy. Iran is a permanent neighbour, and Gulf states have every reason to pursue de-escalation, crisis-management channels and arrangements that lower the risk of repeated wars. Military deterrence and diplomatic engagement are complementary, not contradictory. The outcome of the current confrontation remains uncertain. Whether it moves towards another round of escalation or arrives at a limited agreement, the region is likely to be facing years of insecurity. The emerging regional order is unlikely to be a clean rupture with the American security architecture. More plausibly, it will be an evolution towards a flexible, multilayered system: the US still central, but reinforced by stronger Gulf and Arab capabilities, better GCC co-ordination , wider regional and international partnerships, economic resilience and sustained regional diplomacy. For the region, the challenge is not to replace the American umbrella. It is to make security less dependent on any single umbrella – and to gain greater control over the decisions that determine whether the region goes to war or moves towards de-escalation and co-operation.

title: From inshallah to ojala: Havana museum explores Cuba's hidden Arab history
description: Community of immigrants from Arab world has left 'indelible print' on island
content: The Casa de los Arabes in Havana is easy to miss, hidden in one of the ubiquitous colonial-era manses that line the winding streets of the Cuban capital. But inside the “Arab House” the stories of the island's Arab immigrant community and the formative role it played in the country's history is revealed. One room displays traditional Arab weaponry such as swords and rifles, some of which were presented as gifts by foreign dignitaries to Fidel Castro , who led the Cuban revolution in the 1950s. Another room recreates a Bedouin tent in the Kuwaiti desert. And another features photos of early immigrant families, along with letters and personal possessions illustrating their stories. Jackeline Diaz Fuentes, director of Casa de los Arabes, told The National that before Cuba was discovered by European explorers, the Arab world had an influence on Spanish-speaking people through Muslim rule in Spain that lasted more than 700 years. “There are many Arabic words that came into Spanish, even our expression 'ojala' – 'hopefully' – comes from the Arabic phrase 'inshallah' ,” she said. Spanish architecture, heavily influenced by Islamic rule in the country, also made its way to Cuba . Cuba has historically been a major hub for international trade, its ports full of ships shuttling sugar, cotton and manufactured goods between the Americas and Europe. People from all over the world – either of their own free will or as slaves or indentured servants – came to Cuba over the centuries, and most people on the island can claim indigenous roots, alongside African, European, or Asian. Arabs came to Cuba in the second half of the 19th century. The first Arab immigrants came to the island, as well as other parts of the Americas, from the Levant, which was undergoing severe upheaval at the time. Economic depression, high taxes and fears of military conscription under the Ottoman Empire, as well as shrinking available farmland and the collapse of the regional silk trade, pushed many in Levantine countries to seek opportunities in other parts of the world. The ultimate destination for many who came to Cuba from Lebanon , Syria and elsewhere was the US, but the island was a key point of entry to the West, Ms Diaz Fuentes explained. “First, young [Arab] men came alone and got into street vending, eventually establishing stable import businesses,” she said, highlighting that while initially the men would bring families and brides from their home countries, members of the community eventually began marrying into the local population. Over time, this community integrated more and more into the culture of the island. Arab Cubans even took up arms during the war of independence from Spain in 1895. “There are memorable examples of Arabs that were incorporated, that identified themselves with the Cuban people and with their fight to achieve improvements in their standard of living,” Ms Diaz Fuentes said. The community has largely assimilated into wider Cuban culture, but descendants of the first immigrants formed the Arab Union of Cuba in the 1970s to preserve and promote Arab culture and contributions to the island. Today, Cuba is still a magnet for people from the Arab and Muslim world, particularly for the hundreds of students that come to study. Casa de los Arabes used to be the site of the only mosque on the island, which was used exclusively by foreign diplomats and their families. But that changed when another mosque, funded by Saudi Arabia, was built across the street from the museum in 2015. Arab influence can be found everywhere – even the island's distinctive guayabera, a lightweight summer men's shirt, was redesigned and popularised by a Lebanese textile merchant. “There is an inextricable link between Cubans and Arabs,” Ms Diaz Fuentes said. “They left an indelible print on Cuba's national history.”

title: How a hero principal who saved hundreds of pupils from the Nepal floods is rebuilding broken lives
description: Rajendra Dawadi has set up makeshift classrooms in tents and under stairs for survivors of the August 26 disaster
content: The principal of a government school in flood-hit Nepal has set up tents to ensure hundreds of children he guided to safety two months ago can continue their education. Rajendra Dawadi, head of Tribhuvan Trishuli Secondary School in Nuwakot, one of the areas hit hardest by the flash floods, was hailed as a hero when his swift actions helped to save the lives of 900 children, before a torrent of water crashed into the school compound on August 26. He has made it his mission to enable classes to continue, using 20 tents and the shaded sections of a local sports academy. His goal is to provide some normality to families who lost their homes and livelihoods in the flooding that killed at least 1,455 people, with 5,285 listed as missing. “People lost everything. But the children are still eager to study,” Mr Dawadi told The National . “There was a big celebration on the first day – I thought most children would not come back to the school, but more than 95 per cent came back, they cheered, they exchanged happiness. "I was very happy. My school family, the teachers, students, their smiling faces made me more happy.” A video from September 21 shows children cheering as classes resume in tents set up on higher ground. Mr Dawadi, 47, said it could take at least two years to rebuild the school. As thousands across Nepal look to pick up the pieces after the disaster – which was caused by glacial ice and rock collapsing into a Himalayan river – the UN has said funding is urgently needed. Fractured lives The raging waters that cut through the school compound have since receded. Only the roof of a three-storey building is still visible, with the rest submerged in thick mud. Other buildings were swept away. The devastation across six districts has left deep scars in the school. One child became an orphan and 12 pupils lost one parent. “Many children need our support. They lost their father, some their mother,” Mr Dawadi said. “The students had counselling sessions, music classes. We try to motivate them, we make it like a family environment in school. I tell them it was a black day but we saved our lives and had a rebirth for me, my colleagues, my students. It was a rebirth from the great disaster.” Attendance is strong, with 1,621 pupils showing up for class. They sit on the floor in tents and share benches and desks under the stairwell of a sports centre. The tents, books and furniture were provided by Unicef and private foundations. School authorities await a decision on new land where they can rebuild. Until then, there are other pressing matters – pupils will need a library and science labs. Two more buses are also required to help children get to lessons at the tent site. Parents whose children had attended private schools are now sending them to free government institutions. “People are in trauma but they are doing their work, they are trying to be normal,” Mr Dawadi said. “Parents are worried about studies so they send children here, even if it’s in tents.” Critical moments It took only 11 minutes from the time Mr Dawadi first raised the alarm to when floodwater crashed into the school. Two school staff were killed in the flood. Mr Dawadi was teaching when he heard two staff members shouting about heavy flooding in the nearby Rasuwa district. He quickly told teachers to take pupils from each class to higher ground, urging them not to panic. Mr Dawadi turned away a bus with young children that was entering the compound and anther bus was also alerted about the danger. Older pupils who had motorbikes and bicycles were asked to help take other children to safety. “People were saying, 'Flood, flood,' but the sun was shining here,” he recalled. “But I decided to close the school. First, I told my staff to ring the bell. Then I told class teachers to go to separate classes to say school is off due to the flood, to go to a safer place … three girls fainted. When we left the school, the water had already entered. It was 11 minutes.” But Mr Dawadi praised his staff. “I am not the real hero,” he said. “My team worked together, this was my duty. For this, I was recognised all over the world.” Heart of community The school is a vital part of the community and parents have welcomed the return of classes. “We had tears in our eyes when school started – all parents felt it,” said Sharmila Shreshtha, 46, whose home and stationery shop were destroyed in the disaster. “We have nothing. Our homes are gone, our shop is gone, we are so tired. But the school makes everyone happy.” Pupils have appealed for books, computers and lab equipment. Aspiring software engineer Saswot Shah, 14, worries about how a lack of equipment will affect his studies. "Earlier we had smartboards, computers, maths and science laboratories. Now we are just surviving. We work together but we need a proper computer and maths lab,” he said. Pradakshina Shreshtha, 16, lost her home and now lives in rented accommodation. She hopes to be a doctor, but worries about exams. “I’m really happy to study in my own school, meet my friends and learn from my own teachers,” she said. “Before the floods, I thought I would pass the exam and join a science college. My dream is the same but it’s more difficult to study now. We need books. Our study materials are all gone.”

title: Arab and international leaders condemn deadly funeral attack at church in Jordan
description: King Abdullah II describes incident as terrorist attack
content: Regional and international leaders have condemned a shooting at a church in Jordan that killed seven people and injured 34, sending shockwaves across the kingdom. Sheikh Abdullah bin Zayed, UAE Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign Affairs, expressed the Emirates' full solidarity with the kingdom during a phone call on Friday with Ayman Safadi, Jordan’s Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign Affairs and Expatriates. He affirmed the UAE’s support for Jordan's measures to safeguard its security and stability and protect the safety of its citizens, residents and visitors. Sheikh Abdullah also extended his condolences to the families of those killed and wished the injured a speedy recovery. In a separate statement, the UAE Ministry of Foreign Affairs reiterated the country's strong condemnation of terrorist and criminal acts, reaffirming its rejection of all forms of violence, extremism and terrorism aimed at undermining security and stability. Egypt's President Abdel Fattah El Sisi expressed his "unequivocal condemnation of these heinous acts, which violate all human values" in a statement on X. He stressed his country's solidarity with Jordan "in confronting this deplorable attack and all forms of violence and terrorism". Saudi Arabia also condemned what it described as a "cowardly terrorist attack" in the strongest terms. It expressed its solidarity with Jordan and rejected all acts of terrorism aimed at undermining the country's security and stability, the kingdom's Ministry of Foreign Affairs said. Iraq condemned "all forms of terrorism and violence, which threaten the security and stability of societies and seek to sow division and incite discord among their communities". It also called for "enhanced regional and international co-operation and solidarity to combat terrorism and strengthen security and stability". Syria stressed its "unwavering support in confronting any threats to Jordan's security, stability and national unity", while rejecting "all forms of terrorism that threaten the safety and security of civilians", the Foreign Ministry said. Lebanon's President Joseph Aoun said the attack on a place of worship "violated the sanctity of death and mourners" and "all religious and humanitarian values". He said “terrorism has neither a religion nor a homeland" and warned that such actions sought to undermine co-existence and sow discord. Qatar said it rejected "violence, terrorism and criminal acts, regardless of their motives or causes", as well as "attacks on places of worship and the terrorisation of innocent people". Bahrain's Foreign Ministry affirmed its support for Jordan's efforts to "safeguard its security, combat terrorism and extremism, and apprehend those responsible for the attack". Oman and Kuwait also condemned attacks on "places of worship and acts that terrorise civilians", expressing solidarity with Jordan and extending condolences to the families of the victims. International reactions The US embassy in Amman said Washington stood with King Abdullah II against those seeking to sow division and harm people practising their faith. Canada's Prime Minister Mark Carney described the attack as a terrorist act and condemned the violence. Germany's Foreign Office expressed shock over the attack and emphasised the importance of protecting peaceful co-existence between religions. The EU condemned the "cruel attack" and offered its "full support to the ongoing security investigation by the Jordanian authorities". UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres also strongly condemned the terrorist attack. "It goes without saying that an attack not only on a place of worship, but during a funeral procession is especially heinous," spokesman Stephane Dujarric said. The shooting took place during a funeral at Hamoud Church in Karak governorate, where gunmen opened fire. Jordan’s Public Security Directorate said 27 of the injured were receiving treatment in hospitals, while security forces continued to search for the attackers. King Abdullah II described the incident as a terrorist attack and said the attack would be met with force. He vowed to crack down on those responsible and said the shooting would not undermine national unity. “Every Jordanian life is precious, and we will strike with an iron fist against those who dare to threaten our nation,” he said. Opened fire on mourners Gunmen arrived in a vehicle and opened fire on mourners before fleeing, a relative of one of the deceased told The National . They continued shooting for about five minutes, according to a witness quoted by Al Mamlaka TV. Between 150 and 200 people were in and around the church at the time, the witness said, adding that most of the victims were aged between 50 and 70. A video broadcast on Al Mamlaka that appeared to be from a security camera mounted on the church showed three people firing at it from a pavement and hiding behind trees and a low wall. The video showed the attackers then running towards the church's entrance. A member of the Halasah family in Karak told The National that three doctors were among those killed. “This was a direct attack on the church. Christians were the target,” the relative said.

title: Iran sent bomb-making manual as it organised plots in the UK
description: Salam Ahmadyan and Rahman ⁠Salehi to face trial for alleged plot to attack synagogue
content: An Iranian plotter transferred bomb-making instructions to the UK as it sought agents to carry out an atrocity in a major city. A court heard on Friday that investigators uncovered steps for making a “powder chlorine and rake oil fluid bomb” in a document prepared in Iran. Prosecutors alleged that a terrorism suspect was found to have instructions on his phone for making a home-made bomb to attack Jews in the UK. Salam Ahmadyan, 36, and Rahman ⁠Salehi, 34, are accused of plotting acts of terrorism at the behest of a regime agent believed to be in Iran . The targets included the Manchester Jewish Museum and Heaton Park synagogue, the scene of a deadly attack a year ago in which two Jewish worshippers were killed. Mr Ahmadyan, who had a Kurdish Sorani interpreter, and Mr ⁠Salehi, were told they would face trial in June in Manchester, charged with terrorism offences relating to the alleged plot. Both deny the charges. At a preliminary hearing at the Old Bailey in London, prosecutor Lydon Harris told the court that Mr Ahmadyan was asked by a third party to buy components for a home-made bomb around September 8 this year. Ten days later he recruited Mr Salehi to help him. He subsequently purchased various materials online, Mr Harris said. “On September 20, that being the date of the Jewish celebration of Yom Kippur, both defendants were seen by police officers driving around areas of Manchester, taking photographs and video recordings of various areas,” the prosecutor said. “The Crown’s case is that this was reconnaissance conducted for the purposes of a future attack on the Jewish community in Manchester.” Mr Harris told the court that the “police investigation has revealed Mr Ahmadyan was in contact with a third party who appears to be located in Iran”. “Analysis of his mobile telephone shows that it contained a file, the title of which, when translated into English, is steps for making a powder chlorine and rake oil fluid bomb.” Both suspects were interviewed by police and Mr Salehi denied any involvement in a terrorist plot, said Mr Harris. He said that Mr Ahmadyan made no comment on the questions he was asked. At a previous hearing, the court was told both suspects had come to Britain from Europe in small boats. Mr Salehi had arrived in 2020 and had been granted asylum, while Mr Ahmadyan came in 2023 and his asylum claim was still outstanding.

title: Initial shipment of Russian diesel heads to the US after Trump-Putin deal
description: Russia has agreed to lift a self-imposed ban on diesel exports and supply the fuel to global markets
content: A Malta-flagged tanker carrying 40,000 metric tonnes of Russian ⁠diesel is heading towards New York following an agreement with US President Donald Trump , LSEG data showed on Friday. Mr Trump has made several moves to try to ⁠bring down diesel prices ahead of the November 3 midterm elections ​, including waiving ⁠parts of a new ‌sanctions law against Russia and threatening Europe with a US diesel export ​ban unless countries release more from their emergency reserves. The medium-sized tanker Agioi Fanendes was loaded with 40,000 metric tonnes of ultra-low sulphur diesel in the Russian Baltic port of Primorsk on October 22, according to shipping data. It is expected to arrive in the US on November 7. Russia agreed to lift a self-imposed ban on diesel exports and supply the fuel to global markets, including the US, after the agreement reached between Russian President Vladimir Putin and Mr Trump. Mr Trump announced on October 9 that Russia would immediately export 300,000 metric tonnes, or 2.25 million barrels, followed by 500,000 ​tonnes in November and one million tonnes "immediately thereafter". Russia ‌will be able to increase ⁠diesel exports to between three million ​tonnes and 3.5 million tonnes per month by the end of the year, ​the country's ‌usual export volume of the fuel, Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said last ⁠week. Last week, export diesel cargoes were loaded in the Russian Baltic ⁠port of Primorsk, but their final destinations are not clear, with most vessels signalling Gibraltar, the Atlantic Coast or Port Said, according to LSEG shipping data. Since the full EU embargo on the import of ​Russian oil products came into effect in February 2023 over the war in Ukraine, Russia has exported diesel mainly to Brazil and Turkey, as well as to African countries.

title: UAE researchers win award for AI tool that helps surgeons during operations
description: Janus AI draws on footage of previous robotic surgeries to give doctors real-time visual guidance
content: Researchers in Abu Dhabi have won an international award at a robotic surgery conference in Italy for an AI tool designed to assist surgeons during operations. The team at Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence (MBZUAI) in Abu Dhabi won the accolade for developing Janus AI, which will show surgeons footage of similar past procedures. The technology analyses video footage captured during robotic surgery and selects a 30-second clip from a previous operation that matches the current stage of the procedure . The system works like a Google search for robotic surgery clips, letting doctors access relevant examples while operating. The footage can help surgeons see how other doctors approached the same task and guide them through subsequent steps. “While performing robotic surgery, we can have superimposed a number of small videos that show similar procedures, successful procedures, good procedures, in the exact same moment, so there is a guideline to follow,” said Cesare Stefanini, a professor of robotics at MBZUAI, who oversaw the technology’s development. “Sometimes surgeons may need some assistance; they would like to discuss with a colleague what they are doing, but they are not there, so this is a way to bring some human content to another human.” Janus AI takes its name from the Roman god Janus, depicted with two faces: one looking to the past and the other to the future. The name reflects the system’s aim of using previous surgical experience to help doctors make decisions during current procedures. The technology won the Robotic Urology Breakthrough Innovation Challenge award at Erus 26, a robotic urology surgery conference held in Padua, Italy, in September. “It’s very rewarding to be acknowledged by a community which is not only the computer science, AI, and robotics community, but also the medical community, [as it shows] that we are doing something that can be useful in the future,” said Prof Stefanini. The project was developed in collaboration with surgeons at the University of Illinois Chicago, and the University of Turin in Italy also contributed. Edoardo Fazzari, a postdoctoral researcher at MBZUAI, carried out much of the system’s development over about five months this year, following initial discussions with doctors. He said the project was particularly rewarding because it offered practical benefits beyond academic research. The system can show surgeons footage from three previous operations at the same stage of a procedure, letting them compare different approaches. “Why it’s helpful for the resident, for the surgeons, is that you can look at the future. We are using past experience to help humans make the next steps,” he said. “It should be very quick – we try to make it in milliseconds. You just click your button, make your query, and it pops up with three previous experiences that you can learn from.” The current video library covers robotic urology procedures, including nephrectomies, in which a kidney is removed. The researchers hope to expand the system to other surgeries, particularly robotic procedures, as the library grows. However, Janus AI is not yet ready for use in live operations. The technology needs further refinement and regulatory approval before it can enter clinical practice. When development is complete, the researchers hope to secure a commercial partner to bring the system to market. Prof Stefanini, whose group plans to recruit new postgraduate students, including Emiratis, said the project is a source of pride for the UAE. He said MBZUAI had created an environment in which AI researchers can exchange ideas and develop new technologies. “We’ve proven we can produce world-class results in the UAE, with the talent and vision that we have here. It’s encouraging for the future,” he said. “It’s not just something that individually we are proud of, but it can become a platform for future developments here.”

title: Melania Trump says she negotiated ceasefire in Russian-held Ukrainian city
description: Oleshky in southern Ukraine is 'on the brink of disaster', US first lady says
content: US President Donald Trump's wife Melania Trump has secured a ⁠localised ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine in the Russian-controlled ⁠city of Oleshky in southern Ukraine, the White House announced on Friday. The ceasefire will begin on ​October 29. Oleshky has been occupied by Russian forces since February 2022 and residents there have reported a deepening food crisis. In a statement, the first lady described the situation in Oleshky as “dire” and on “the brink of disaster”. The White House said that Russia and Ukraine agreed to temporarily stop all military action in Oleshky to allow for humanitarian aid to enter ⁠and to prepare a civilian evacuation through a designated safe passageway. “Oleshky’s remaining population is comprised primarily of elderly residents who urgently need medical attention, medicine, food and clean water,” Ms Trump said. “The people of Oleshky have limited electricity, live amid mined roads and endure regular military attacks.” She added that it was “abundantly clear” that without her intervention, the possibility of bringing humanitarian aid into the city and evacuating the elderly would have been “impossible”. The development comes as ‌Mr Trump appears to be increasingly on Russia's side in its war against Ukraine. He has repeatedly criticised Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy for not making a peace deal and has waived sanctions to allow the US to import Russian diesel as he tries to lower prices ahead of the November 3 midterms. Of his wife's announcement, Mr Trump said it was “not the worst idea I've ever heard.” “What she wants to do is save children ... It was her initiative, and they contacted both sides, and both sides wanted to do it,” he told reporters. Ms Trump has been active in trying to have Ukrainian children seized by Russia during the war returned to their families.
