Even the name is intended to draw a line between old and new: “Type” references Jaguar’s historic models; “0” represents zero tailpipe emissions; and “1” denotes the first car of the new generation. Jaguar chose New York for the world premiere, projecting the Type 01 across digital displays in Times Square, Dumbo and the Lower East Side before the car arrived at Storied in West Chelsea. British actress Florence Pugh was also announced as the first brand ambassador of the marque’s new era. The choice of city feels significant. Jaguar’s ambitions are no longer simply about restoring a storied British car company. It wants to place itself within a broader world of fashion, architecture, art and contemporary culture and attract a new generation of customers in the process. Whether those customers will follow is the considerably harder question. Prices will start at £130,000 (Dh635,000), pushing Jaguar into a very different market from the one occupied by its previous saloons and SUVs. Orders open in early 2027, with the first customer deliveries expected during the second half of the year. There will be time to decide how successfully the Type 01 drives, how convincing its luxury credentials are and whether Jaguar can translate the enormous attention surrounding its reinvention into sales. For now, though, the most important thing about the Type 01 may be that Jaguar has followed through on a bold and controversial promise.

title: Five highlights to look out for at Christie’s first Abu Dhabi fine art auction
description: Mawasim brings more than 70 pieces to the capital on November 1
content: Christie’s first fine art auction in Abu Dhabi will offer more than 70 works spanning six decades of modern and contemporary Middle Eastern art. Mawasim : 20 Years of Modern and Contemporary Middle Eastern Art will be held at the Abu Dhabi Edition hotel on November 1. It marks 20 years since Christie’s held its first UAE auction in Dubai in 2006. The sale includes artists from across the Arab world, Iran and Turkey, with works drawn from collections including Beirut’s Dalloul Collection and Sharjah’s Barjeel Art Foundation. The sale is taking place during a busy period for Abu Dhabi’s art scene, with Frieze art fair following later in November and Guggenheim Abu Dhabi opening on December 11. Christie’s Middle East and Africa chairman Ridha Moumni previously told The National that the auction house intended to become “more present and more visible in the city”. Among the works are an early Fahrelnissa Zeid abstract piece, a royal Egyptian portrait completed months before the monarchy fell and a monumental Paul Guiragossian . Here are five works to look out for. Estimated at $500,000 to $700,000, Composition is among the most valuable works in the sale and comes from a decisive period in Fahrelnissa Zeid ’s development. Painted in 1948–49, the work captures her move towards the kaleidoscopic abstraction that would establish her international reputation in the following decade. Interlocking passages of blue, red, yellow and orange are divided by dark lines, creating a visual language shaped partly by Zeid’s experience of seeing cities and landscapes from the air. The painting also has a strong personal history. After her husband, Prince Zeid Al-Hussein, became Iraq’s ambassador to Britain, Zeid established a studio at the Iraqi Embassy in London, where Composition was displayed. The work remained with her through later stages of her life, including her years in Amman, making it both an important early abstraction and a witness to her own movement between cities and countries. Mahmoud Said’s Portrait de Princesse Fadia , estimated at $400,000 to $600,000, carries one of the most personal provenances in the auction. The sitter is Princess Fadia, the youngest daughter of King Farouk I and Queen Farida of Egypt. Said was her great-uncle, making the painting as much a family portrait as a royal one. Its timing gives it added historical weight. Painted in 1952, it was completed only months before Egypt’s monarchy came to an end. Saïd gave the portrait to Queen Farida before it passed to Princess Fadia and remained within the family. According to the catalogue, it was among the possessions Fadia took with her into exile. What began as a portrait of royal childhood became a lasting connection to a life that had abruptly changed. Said had also painted Queen Farida as a child decades earlier, giving the work a link to two generations of the same family. At almost 2.4 metres wide, Noces is one of the largest works by Paul Guiragossian to come to market. Estimated at $300,000 to $500,000, the painting predates the mature figurative style for which the Lebanese-Armenian artist became widely known. A seated bride anchors a gathering of musicians, dancers and guests, while the compressed space and elongated figures anticipate the more expressive direction his work would take. One detail is especially personal. Among the musicians is a blind figure recalling Guiragossian’s father, who was blind and remembered as a violinist and singer. The painting was acquired directly from Guiragossian by Lebanese architect and collector Farid Trad and was shown at the artist’s 1959 exhibition in Beirut. Moumni has described it as one of Guiragossian’s most exceptional works. Its return to the market is also timely, with 2026 marking the centenary of the artist’s birth and Bassam Freiha Art Foundation in Abu Dhabi presenting an exhibition devoted to his work. Ahmed Mater ’s Golden Hour examines the transformation of Makkah through one of the most recognisable views in the Islamic world. Estimated at $80,000 to $120,000, the monumental photograph belongs to Mater’s Desert of Pharan project, which looks at the changing relationship between the holy city’s sacred history and its rapidly evolving urban landscape. The Kaaba and pilgrims performing tawaf sit at the centre of the image, surrounded by cranes, construction equipment and new infrastructure. Mater places the cyclical movement of a centuries-old ritual against the constant momentum of development. The result is less a simple contrast than a layering of different ideas of time: religious continuity, ancient landscape and modern construction all occupying the same frame. There are four prints of Golden Hour in total: three numbered edition copies, plus one artist’s proof. Christie’s is selling the single artist’s proof. Another example from the edition is held by Mathaf: Arab Museum of Modern Art in Doha. Hassan Sharif ’s Press Conference No 2 brings satire into the sale. Painted in 2008 and estimated at $50,000 to $70,000, the work presents a distorted public speaker whose open mouth, misaligned eyes and exaggerated appearance undermine the authority normally associated with political spectacle. The objects in front of him resemble microphones but also spoons and ladles, giving the scene an absurd edge. The painting connects to Sharif’s early career as a cartoonist for Akhbar Dubai , where he addressed political and social subjects before becoming one of the central figures in the development of conceptual and experimental art in the UAE. That influence continued well beyond his own practice. Moumni previously told The National that Sharif would appear in the sale alongside younger Emirati artists shaped by his legacy. Press conference No 2 was also included in Christie’s 2023 exhibition, Emirati Art Reimagined: Hassan Sharif and the Contemporary Voices.

title: Dubai home sale transactions fall in third quarter amid regional uncertainty
description: Buyers more cautious, with deal volumes and values declining, report finds
content: The volume and value of residential property transactions in Dubai fell sharply in the third quarter of this year as buyers became “more cautious” amid regional uncertainty over the Iran war, according to a new report. Dubai recorded home sales worth a total of Dh72.6 billion ($19.7 billion) in the three months to the end of September, down 47 per cent compared to the same period last year. The number of transactions dropped 38 per cent to 34,000, which reflected “the impact of reduced activity as the lag in property sales registrations begins to clear”, the report by property consultants Cavendish Maxwell said. “The Q3 2026 data captures a mix of recent and earlier buying activity, reflecting the time between a purchase being agreed and formally registered as a sale,” Ronan Arthur, director and head of residential valuation at Cavendish Maxwell , said. “Purchasing activity became more measured, with buyers being more cautious in the weeks and months following the start of the conflict.” The off-plan sector continued to dominate residential sales during the quarter, accounting for 65 per cent of total sales values and 72 per cent of property purchases. Dubai's property market has boomed in recent years, benefiting from government initiatives such as residency permits for retired and remote workers, expansion of the 10-year golden visa programme and overall growth in the UAE’s economy on diversification efforts. However, the market started to cool during regional tensions triggered by the Iran war that began in late February. The war also affected hospitality, tourism and aviation as the US and Israel attacked Iran, and Tehran retaliated by striking energy sites and civilian infrastructure across the Gulf region and Iraq. “While the fundamentals driving Dubai real estate demand remain, near-term activity will continue to be shaped by a number of factors, including the frequency and number of launches, regional uncertainty and a broader normalisation in buyer activity,” Mr Arthur added. Residential sales transactions fell for the first nine months of the year, Cavendish Maxwell data showed, with total volumes down 23 per cent on annual basis to 112,580 and values declining 27 per cent to Dh292 billion. A report by S&P Global Ratings also found a significant drop in Dubai's residential property transactions as a result of the war. Citing Dubai Land department data, the ratings agency said total real estate sale transactions averaged 12,644 per month between March and September 2026, a drop of 26 per cent from 17,198 in January and February 2026. It also said prices declined by 5 per cent to 15 per cent between the end of 2025 and September 2026, quoting industry reports. S&P Global Ratings expects a “gradual” price correction in Dubai’s property market. “Over the medium term, we anticipate that the UAE and Dubai governments will remain focused on developing the emirate's attractiveness through reforms and large-scale infrastructure projects. That is why, for the residential real estate market, we expect a gradual price correction rather than a rapid price decline,” it said. The ratings agency expects secondary-market transactions to become more prevalent as price declines prompt investors to offload their properties. The greatest impact could be on investor sentiment and demand within the luxury and ultra-luxury segments, it added. Emaar Properties founder Mohamed Alabbar also indicated an “adjustment of 5 per cent to 10 per cent” in Dubai’s broader real estate sector because of the war. “But then again, you know, if the situation settles, God knows what could happen in this market. It could become pretty fast [paced],” he said last month at AIM Congress in Dubai.

title: Iraq devalues currency as war and Hormuz closure squeeze cash
description: Cabinet approves central bank recommendation to set new official exchange rate of 1,500 Iraqi dinars per US dollar
content: Iraq has officially devalued its currency again, setting a new official exchange rate of 1,500 Iraqi dinars per US dollar, according to a document seen by The National . The Council of Ministers approved the move late on Tuesday, based on a recommendation from the Central Bank of Iraq, the banking regulator said in a directive sent to all licensed banks, electronic payment companies and exchange houses on Monday. According to the directive, the new structure is that the central bank will purchase from the Ministry of Finance at the price of 1,500 dinars. The sale price to banks will be at 1,510 dinars, and then to the public at 1,520 dinars. All institutions were ordered to update their systems, notify branches, stop using the previous rate, and adopt the new price from the start of business on Tuesday, the document says. It is Iraq’s second major devaluation in six years. In December 2020, during the Covid-19 oil crash, the central bank cut the dinar rate from 1,182 to 1,450 per dollar to cover a crippling deficit. That rate was later adjusted to 1,320 as the official rate under the previous government, though the market rate often hovered higher. This time, the decision is driven by a deepening cash crunch since the outbreak of the Iran-Israel war in June 2025 and the intermittent closure and threat to the Strait of Hormuz. Iraq earns more than 90 per cent of its budget in dollars from oil exports, almost all of which must pass through Hormuz – the narrow waterway carrying a third of the world’s seaborne oil. Since the Iran war broke out on February 28, shipping insurance costs have soared , tanker traffic has been disrupted, and Iraq’s oil loadings from its southern terminals at Basra have faced delays and discounts. The result: Iraq gets fewer dollars, and when it converts those dollars into dinars to pay nearly eight million public employees, contractors, farmers and pensioners, it needs more dinars than it has. In recent months, Baghdad has delayed salary payments in several provinces, deferred payments to wheat farmers and construction firms, and relied on short-term borrowing from state banks. The country's finance ministry warned parliament that without adjustment, it could not fund the 2026 budget, which includes 100,000 new public jobs demanded by political blocs as part of government formation talks. Devaluation is the fastest fix. By lowering the dinar’s value from 1,320 to 1,500, the government gets about 13 per cent more dinars for every dollar of oil it sells – enough to print salaries without printing dollars it does not have. But the cost is passed to Iraqis. A weaker dinar makes imported food, medicine, cars and construction materials – almost everything Iraq imports – more expensive. After the 2020 devaluation, inflation jumped and triggered protests in southern provinces.

title: Arabian Gulf Cup: UAE have plenty to work with despite final defeat in Jeddah
description: Hammam Al Hammami was standout performer for Saudi Arabia but national team too showed promise ahead of next assignment – Asian Cup
content: The UAE were outplayed in the final of the Arabian Gulf Cup by hosts Saudi Arabia in Jeddah on Tuesday night, but new UAE coach Zlatko Dalic was still able to reflect on a positive first assignment. The former Croatia manager saw his new charges succumb to early goals from Hammam Al Hammami and Feras Albrikan, as Saudi Arabia emerged deserving winners . The eight-team regional tournament stirs high passions – as shown by ugly skirmishes between fans and players, plus UAE captain Khalid Essa’s reaction to jeers during the national anthem. But Dalic has been brought in with a view to bringing success on a broader scale than a local stoush. The next significant challenge is rapidly heading into view. The Asian Cup, which will also be staged in Saudi Arabia, starts in January. Under Dalic’s guidance, it is hoped the UAE will go deep in that competition. Looking ahead to the first game in that, against Palestine in Riyadh on January 7, here is what he will have learnt from the Gulf Cup. In terms of talent, there is plenty to work with. The pool of players available for Dalic has been expanded by naturalisation. There might be even more outstanding UAE Pro League players who are becoming eligible before the Asian Cup. That is a double-edged sword. For some while now, it has been unclear what the best XI is for the national team. The side might look good in one international window, but then by the next there could be two or three more players eligible for selection who dilute what went before. At the Gulf Cup, for example, Dalic handed out a number of debuts to players who now look inked into the best XI. Players like Yuri Cesar, Mamadou Coulibaly, Ousmane Camara and Guilherme Bala . But even they might not be guaranteed starters if the likes of Matias Palacios, the Al Ain schemer, and Federico Cartabia, Shabab Al Ahli’s playmaker, are available. What the deeper player pool does allow for is tactical flexibility. The two early goals in the final against Saudi Arabia meant the game had gone by the time Dalic was able to respond effectively. But his substitutions did show how personnel changes can rectify issues. Al Hammami, the jet-heeled Saudi left-winger, was the difference between the two sides in the first half of the final. Marcos Meloni, the right back who has been a key figure under successive UAE coaches, could not keep up. Dalic responded by switching Ruben Canedo – the left back who, like Al Hammami, is diminutive but fast – to the right, and bringing on the powerful Richard Akonnor to play on the left. Not that the UAE were able to overturn the deficit, but at least they were able to regain parity in terms of the run of play. Dalic reasoned – logically – that it was the nightmare start which cost the UAE. “The first goal and second goal killed us,” he said. “I told my players when we were preparing for the game, the first 20 minutes will be the key to the game; please be careful, be patient and focused. We cannot concede a goal. “After conceding two, it is not easy to come back into the game.” His team had looked spooked by the frenzied atmosphere inside the King Abdullah Sport City Stadium. The official attendance was touching 63,000, and by the way all the gangways were filled, there might even have been a few more in than that. An impressive chunk of that – around 12,000 – were travelling UAE supporters. Both sets of players were amped by the atmosphere, but it was the home side who kept their cool the best. That is an issue because it is a recurring one for the UAE. When World Cup qualification was on the line in Doha last year, amid a similarly wild atmosphere in Doha, the players were also distracted, and lost out as a result. It is difficult to think how the Gulf Cup could have gone any better for Saudi Arabia. They won the title – for the first time in 25 years – without conceding a goal. Even before the final , Dalic pointed out they were the best side in it. They looked like a side transformed from that which had traipsed out of the World Cup in North America in the summer without landing a punch. They were without their talisman, Salem Al Dawsari , and yet his replacement, Al Hammami, announced himself as a real attacking threat. For Georgios Donis, it was validation. He had only been appointed as coach at short notice before the World Cup . To judge him on that would have been unfair. The Gulf Cup was a greater reflection of his worth, and he is already excited about what they can do at the Asian Cup. “There are players who played a lot of minutes over two weeks, and we delivered a great performance and deserve this achievement,” Donis said. “I'm happy with what we've accomplished, and now we'll start focusing on the Asian Cup.”

title: Cheers for hardliners on Israel's campaign trail as security drowns out social and economic problems
description: Candidates make their pitch to Anglo-Israeli voters in Jerusalem
content: In a normally quiet corner of upmarket West Jerusalem , almost 300 members of the city’s Anglo-Jewish community joined a raucous election debate three weeks before they will cast their ballots in Israel's general election on October 27. The crowd at the sold-out event was partly secular but mainly religious. The VIP front seats hosted politicians, their aides, doyens of the city’s pro-Israel PR industry and a British-Israeli rabbi and pundit whose wife and two daughters were killed in a Palestinian attack in the occupied West Bank in 2023. They were there to cheer and, on rarer occasions, jeer the 10 candidates from across the spectrum of Zionist politics on stage. Their reactions gave a clear indication of where this influential Israeli community stands, one that plays a disproportionately important role in how Israel is viewed abroad at a time when its international popularity is in sharp decline . Israel’s problems are not merely external. Three years of war have pushed the economy into uncertainty and stress is palpable on the streets during a short walk to the shops, even before you see the price of milk. Yet the panellists had little to say about the cost of living and nothing about the crisis in the country’s education system. The message for politicians by the end of the evening was clear: to grab the attention of voters by talking incessantly about security, enemies, settlements and the need for defiance in the face of Israel’s sliding popularity abroad. The first loud cheers were for Israeli settler and social media personality Yishai Fleisher, a party colleague of far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir . Mr Fleisher praised Mr Ben-Gvir over the deteriorating conditions for Palestinians in Israeli jails, increasing Jewish worship at Al Aqsa Mosque compound and lowering his car insurance bill, which he linked to a decrease in vehicle thefts. Leading Israeli rights group B’Tselem has described Israel’s prison system for Palestinians as a “network of torture camps”. Displays of Israeli nationalism at Al Aqsa draw criticism from the international community, which fears changes to the decades-long status quo could cause major unrest. Other crime statistics have worsened under Mr Ben-Gvir’s tenure – the murder rate among Arab Israelis in particular. “Is Ben-Gvir hurting our international reputation? The genocide [in Gaza] narrative is, but is that Ben-Gvir? No!” Mr Fleisher said. “They find enemies all the time and try to take us down around the world. Here comes one guy who is talking straight and strong, who the enemies are afraid of – and that’s a good thing. “Ben-Gvir, you can like him or not like him, but you don’t have to marry your daughter to him, you don’t have to invite him over for Shabbos lunch. He’s a hammer. He gets things done.” The most left-wing candidate in attendance, Moran Zer Katzenstein of The Democrats, received moderate applause for her work on women’s rights. She was also the candidate who received the loudest jeer, which came when she challenged audience members who appeared to support expelling the population of Gaza . “You can clap if you think this is what Jewish morality is,” Ms Zer Katzenstein said after the jeering. The audience did exactly that – what followed was one of the longest and most passionate bursts of applause of the night, with bellows of support across the room. Another of the panellists, Moishe Feiglin of the Zehut party, recently called for the total expulsion of Gazans by any means necessary in an interview with The Jerusalem Post . He suggested even Gaza's infants were enemies: “The baby that will be born in Gaza tomorrow will do exactly the same, God forbid, to your baby that will be born tomorrow in Jerusalem. There’s no other way. That’s the reason they live for. That’s what they learn with their mother's milk.” A bounce in opinion polls suggests Mr Feiglin’s party could win five to six seats in the 120-member Knesset. The faction is in a right-wing alliance with the Religious Zionist Party led by Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, who was recently filmed boasting about Israel’s occupation of a huge part of southern Lebanon , saying “the world is not stopping us”. Although many parties were present, the event did not paint a complete picture of Israeli politics. The two main ultra-Orthodox parties spurned their invitations. The bitter debate around enlisting ultra-Orthodox young men into the Israeli military was raised but received surprisingly little attention given dire warnings about a lack of manpower. Israeli-Arab parties, which were recently battling disqualification in the Supreme Court, were not represented. The only Palestinian mentioned at length was Yoseph Haddad of Amcha Israel, a combative pro-Israel influencer. Gadi Eisenkot’s Yashar Party, currently the most powerful opposition party, is accused by the far right of being a backdoor for Arab parties to enter an opposition coalition. At the event, Amichai Chikli, from Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud party, accused Mr Eisenkot of dangerously viewing Syria ’s President Ahmad Al Shara as an “opportunity” for Israel. Much of the energy of the opposition parties was taken up defending the record of their candidates, many of whom have been in the Israeli political system for years. Mati Gill of Naftali Bennett’s party was asked why voters should trust its members after its leader’s turbulent political career. That career has attracted accusations of hypocrisy and broken promises, including from the settler community, which he used to represent as head of a settlers' group called the Yesha Council. Mr Gill said Mr Bennett’s ideals had not changed since he entered politics. The message does not appear to be cutting through. With so little time until elections, the former prime minister continues a steady decline in the polls. Despite bitter moments, the conclusion was a festival of politeness, featuring a resounding rendition of the national anthem and far-right candidates praising even Ms Zer Katzenstein. Those in attendance who wanted to learn more about plans for the economy, education, the environment and infrastructure would have left disappointed at the end of the two-hour session. They did not seem downcast, however, despite the challenges Israel faces in all those areas. Once again, it seems Israeli voters will head to the polls with security on their minds and the many extreme aspects that priority has come to embody.

title: Abu Dhabi launches major training programme to teach AI skills
description: AiNative initiative will equip citizens, residents and government employees with vital tech skills
content: Abu Dhabi on Wednesday set out plans to equip thousands of government employees and the wider public with artificial intelligence skills under a major drive to advance responsible use of the rapidly evolving technology . The Abu Dhabi government and the emirate's Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence have joined forces with global tech giants OpenAI and Microsoft to launch the AiNative training programme. The key strategy will provide 20,000 government employees with cutting-edge support by the end of the year and is central to Abu Dhabi's mission to become the world's first AI-native government by 2027. The initiative – announced at the Ai Everything conference in the capital by Abu Dhabi's Department of Government Enablement – will seek to encourage citizens and residents, government workers and department leaders to unlock the potential of AI to drive progress. Under the initiative, employees will be given help to build up expertise with ChatGPT, Codex and Microsoft 365 Copilot. Specialised, function-specific certifications, including areas such as coding and data, will follow in later phases of the project. Citizens and residents will be able to access the training programme via Tomouh, DGE's AI-driven learning app, which can be accessed through the UAE Pass government app. The scheme will cover practical applications of AI in everyday life, including managing personal finances, running a small business, finding a job, studying and creating content responsibly online, and will be delivered through the free version of ChatGPT. DGE owns the curriculum, which has been developed with OpenAI, Microsoft and MBZUAI. “AI will only create lasting value when people have the knowledge and confidence to use it well,” Wesam Lootah, director general of GovDigital at DGE, said. “AiNative puts that capability at the heart of Abu Dhabi’s AI journey, giving government employees and the wider community practical skills to use AI responsibly in their work and everyday lives. “By bringing together government, industry and academia, we are building a common foundation for an AI-enabled society and government.” Eric Xing, president and professor at MBZUAI, emphasised the importance of ensuring access to AI for all as it shapes the future. “Championing a culture of lifelong learning ensures that the benefits of new technologies are understood and realised responsibly by all,” he said. “Through AiNative, people can gain practical knowledge alongside the judgment to apply AI thoughtfully in a way that it becomes a partner for progress. “Developing this capability at scale will be an important part of Abu Dhabi’s transition to an AI-native government and society.” AiNative is being rolled out in phases. An initial pilot within government is already under way, before it will be made public. The launch of AiNative follows the roll-out of Microsoft 365 Copilot to 35,000 Abu Dhabi government employees through the Frontier Employee Programme, announced in July. Abu Dhabi unveiled its vision to be the world's first AI-powered government last year, as part of its Digital Strategy 2025-2027. Led by the DGE, the programme will allocate Dh13 billion ($3.5 billion) to boost digital infrastructure, automate 100 per cent of government processes, and integrate sovereign cloud computing across all operations. The strategy is expected to contribute more than Dh24 billion to Abu Dhabi’s economy by 2027 and create more than 5,000 employment opportunities supporting Emiratisation efforts.

title: Guyana: The tiny country with big ambitions fast emerging as a global oil producer
description: Surging oil production is making South American nation one of the fastest growing economies in the world
content: A tiny South American country is emerging as a reliable oil supplier globally as flows from the Middle East face disruptions and European nations seek alternatives to Russia. Guyana's rapid increase in crude production, from zero in 2019 to about 900,000 barrels per day in the first half of the year, is catapulting the country to one of the world's fastest-growing economies, lifting thousands of people out of poverty with newfound wealth. The non-Opec country's oil output is expected to reach 1 million barrels per day (bpd) imminently, with the country targeting 1.7 million bpd by 2030. “With disruptions in the Middle East, Guyana’s oil is becoming strategically more important to global markets,” Stephanie Rivera, research analyst at S&P Global Energy told The National. “Guyana’s light-to-medium, low-sulfur crude is not exposed to Middle Eastern shipping chokepoints, providing refiners with an attractive option for diversifying away from Middle Eastern supply. As the conflict in the Middle East continues, Guyanese crude can help enhance energy security in an increasingly tight market.” The Middle East conflict, which broke out on February 28 after the US and Israel attacked Iran, has roiled global markets, with prices jumping to an intraday high of about $120 per barrel in April. Tehran carried out retaliatory strikes on Gulf energy infrastructure leading to curtailment of production, with 10 million bpd of Gulf output remaining shut as of August amid heightened security risks, according to the International Energy Agency report last month. The Strait of Hormuz, through which more than 20 per cent of global crude and liquefied natural gas supplies used to pass before the war, has been a restricted route since the war began, raising supply concerns. Countries in Europe, North and South America have been the main importers of Guyana’s oil, but the Middle East crisis has also prompted some Asian countries to look towards Guyana for oil. Europe imported up to 57 per cent of Guyanese crude between March and August this year, Kpler data shows, with the Netherlands, Sweden, Germany, the UK, Italy, Poland and Spain being the main buyers. The Americas took about a third, while Asian nations, including China, Thailand, Singapore and Indonesia, imported about 6 per cent of Guyanese crude during the period. Turkey bought roughly 5 per cent. Another factor that is contributing to a rise in demand for Guyana's crude is the Ukraine war. European nations are looking for alternative sources of supply as they seek to reduce dependence on Russian crude and squeeze off Moscow’s oil revenue as it continues to wage war against Ukraine. Guyanese crude is also highly valued for its low sulfur content, high yields of middle distillates such as diesel and jet fuel, and competitive break-even costs of $30–$40 per barrel that "make it particularly attractive to refiners, especially in Europe", Ms Rivera said. An oil boom is a recent phenomenon in Guyana, with production starting only seven years ago following the discovery of oil in 2015. An ExxonMobil-led consortium – including Chevron, and China’s CNOOC have been dominating production, with total investment estimated at between $55 billion and $60 billion at the Stabroek Block. The group hit a milestone last month by producing its billionth barrel of oil at Stabroek less than seven years after production began in 2019. “With an estimated resource base of just under 11 billion oil-equivalent barrels and plans for up to eight offshore developments by 2030, the Stabroek block is helping meet demand across the Americas, Europe and Asia, contributing to global energy security and market stability,” ExxonMobil said in a statement last month. More projects are expected to come online, with Uaru expected to start up by the end of 2026, Whiptail expected to start up in 2027, and Hammerhead expected to begin production in 2029, it added. Last year, France’s TotalEnergies, QatarEnergy and Malaysia’s Petronas also signed an agreement with the Guyanese government to explore a shallow block off the coast of Guyana for oil production. Oil revenue, spurred by a rise in production and higher prices, has transformed Guyana from a small, agriculture and services based economy into one of the world’s fastest-growing economies. From an annual growth rate of 5.4 per cent in 2019, when it first started producing oil, the country’s economy expanded by 43.5 per cent in the following year, 20.1 per cent in 2021, 63.3 per cent in 2022, 33.8 per cent in 2023, 43.8 per cent in 2024 and 19.3 per cent in 2025, International Monetary Fund data shows. The country's GDP is projected to grow by 16.2 per cent this year, the highest rate globally, as oil revenue continues to increase due to higher production and rising crude prices. Brent, the benchmark for two-thirds of the world's oil, is currently trading at about $100 per barrel. "The economic outlook [for Guyana] remains highly favourable," the IMF said in July. "Oil production is expected to continue expanding, and the non-oil economy is projected to grow by about 7 per cent on average over the next five years as the government continues its ambitious plans to address infrastructure and developmental needs." Data analysis and visualisation by Isaac Arroyo.

title: Louvre Abu Dhabi names Souraya Noujaim new director ahead of 10th anniversary
description: Islamic art specialist returns to Saadiyat Island museum after helping shape its curatorial vision
content: Souraya Noujaim has been appointed director of Louvre Abu Dhabi , returning to the museum where she spent five years overseeing its curatorial and collections work. The Department of Culture and Tourism Abu Dhabi announced the appointment as the museum prepares to mark its 10th anniversary in 2027. Noujaim takes over from Manuel Rabate , who led Louvre Abu Dhabi since 2016 and oversaw its opening the following year. Rabate's departure from the museum was announced in February. An art historian and curator specialising in Islamic art history and archaeology, Noujaim most recently served as director of the Department of Islamic Arts at the Louvre Museum in Paris and chief of the French Grand Department of Islamic Art Heritage. In Paris, she oversaw a collection of 18,000 Islamic artworks. But her relationship with Louvre Abu Dhabi stretches back to before the museum opened on Saadiyat Island in November 2017. Noujaim helped develop its intellectual and curatorial vision and returned in February 2018 as the museum's first scientific, curatorial and collections management director, a position she held until April 2023. During that period, she oversaw curatorial, scientific and collections activities, helped develop the museum's collection through acquisitions and was involved in establishing initiatives, including Art Here , the annual exhibition and prize for contemporary artists. As director, she will oversee Louvre Abu Dhabi's collection, exhibitions, research, conservation, education, public programmes and visitor experience, as well as its broader institutional strategy. “Louvre Abu Dhabi holds a special place in my professional and personal journey,” Noujaim said in a statement announcing her appointment. “Having had the privilege of contributing to the museum's development over many years, I am honoured to return to Abu Dhabi and lead this remarkable institution into its next chapter.” She said she planned to build on the museum's legacy, deepen its engagement with audiences and continue expanding its collection. Mohamed Khalifa Al Mubarak, chairman of DCT Abu Dhabi, said Noujaim's appointment continues a long-standing relationship. “As the first universal museum in the Arab world, Louvre Abu Dhabi is a powerful reflection of our belief in culture as a bridge between people, ideas and societies. Since 2017, it has contributed greatly to the emirate’s status as a global cultural capital. "Dr Noujaim has been part of the museum’s journey from its earliest stages, helping shape its collection, scholarly foundations and distinctive universal narrative. We are confident that Dr Noujaim’s international expertise and deep understanding of what makes Louvre Abu Dhabi unique will contribute to the museum’s role as a leading cultural institution in the region and on the global stage.” Noujaim takes over as Louvre Abu Dhabi prepares for a significant milestone. Since opening in November 2017, the Jean Nouvel-designed museum has welcomed more than eight million visitors and staged 22 temporary exhibitions. It has also held five editions of Art Here and six exhibitions at its Children's Museum , alongside educational, research, conservation and scholarship programmes. The makeup of its permanent galleries has also changed considerably. When Louvre Abu Dhabi opened, about 30 per cent of the works displayed were from its own collection, with about 70 per cent borrowed from French museums and regional lenders. While the overall number of works on display has remained broadly consistent, nearly two-thirds of those now shown across the museum's four chronological sections belong to Louvre Abu Dhabi. The change reflects the expansion of a permanent collection that spans thousands of years, from prehistoric objects and religious artefacts to paintings and contemporary art. The museum was established under an intergovernmental agreement between the UAE and France and remains the first universal museum in the Arab world. Noujaim will now oversee its transition into its second decade, including the continued development of its permanent collection and its role as a centre for research, conservation and cultural exchange.

title: Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman gives blood to launch country's donation drive
description: More than 900,000 people donated in Saudi Arabia in 2025
content: Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman has donated blood, launching the kingdom’s annual national donation campaign for this year, Saudi state media has reported. The campaign aims to promote regular voluntary blood donation and increase public awareness of its importance, while helping secure sufficient supplies of blood and blood products for patients, including those with cancer, blood disorders and critical or emergency medical conditions, the Saudi Press Agency reported on Tuesday. More than 900,000 people donated blood in Saudi Arabia in 2025, according to the news agency, as the kingdom seeks to increase voluntary donations and maintain a sustainable national blood supply. Last year’s campaign, also launched by Prince Mohammed , helped quadruple the number of donors and recorded more than 65,000, the highest figure in the history of Saudi blood banks, according to authorities. All donations recorded during the campaign were voluntary, with more than 85 per cent coming from first-time donors. The blood collected supported more than 63,000 patients, while platelet and plasma donations each benefited about 10,000 people, the SPA said.

title: Paris Fashion Week: The shows that defined spring/summer 2027
description: From Louis Vuitton and Chanel to Valentino and Balenciaga, designers revisit house codes and embrace craftsmanship
content: Paris Fashion Week is often a battle for attention, but this season’s strongest collections were less concerned with spectacle than with identity. Across the spring/summer 2027 shows, designers engaged with the codes that make their houses distinctive, whether through couture craftsmanship, archival references, eccentric styling or a renewed focus on clothes people might actually want to wear. That meant lightness at Hermes and Dior, romanticism at Elie Saab, everyday couture at Balenciaga and a celebration of individuality at Valentino and Dries Van Noten. Elsewhere, Schiaparelli explored a more practical side, Saint Laurent doubled down on unapologetic glamour and Matieres Fecales turned the runway into a platform for social commentary. The approaches differed, but the question running through Paris was much the same: what should a fashion house stand for now? Nicolas Ghesquiere has spent much of his career making clothes that look ready to take flight. For spring/summer 2027 at Louis Vuitton, he pushed the idea closer to literal, expressing futurism through weightless, fluid clothes engineered to move. Days after receiving the Chevalier de la Legion d’honneur from Emmanuel Macron, Ghesquiere stripped his architectural codes back to their lightest form. Beneath a suspended traffic jam of futuristic cars, dresses, coats and tailoring skimmed the body in scarf-weight silks, jersey, cashmere and fabrics lighter than chiffon. Clothes floated, bounced and shifted with the wearer, while tailoring was deconstructed and silhouettes recalibrated around the moving body. It was a distinctly Vuitton proposition: less baggage, more freedom. Ghesquiere’s future was not something to wear, but something to move through. Being a creative director at a heritage house means, sooner or later, talking to ghosts. At Chanel, that conversation is almost unavoidable, with Gabrielle Chanel’s presence remaining unusually tangible. For this spring/summer collection, Matthieu Blazy once again made the founder an active character. The collection unfolded like a history of the house. Sheer ivory knit slips were pinned with feather corsages; fringed cardigans softened the silhouette before raw-edged tailoring and reworked Charvet shirts introduced a more masculine note. Voluminous tutu skirts brought a touch of mischief, while cloud-printed organza, beaded plaids and delicate floral mesh added increasingly decorative flourishes. The staple tweed jacket remained the essential building block, sometimes cropped, sometimes sharpened with piping or crystal collars, or even as sleeveless iterations with playful card-suit buttons. A new stretchy tweed, made from re-embroidered organza and silk, loosened the formality of the house signature. Accessories followed suit: pearl drops, layered shells and beads, and quilted chain bags. The show was opened and closed by a model carrying an original 2.55 bag from the archives, as a neat reminder of where this new Chanel began. At Loewe, Jack McCollough and Lazaro Hernandez combined their New England upbringing with Spanish history, mixing American pragmatism with Andalusian drama. Polos appeared backwards, checked blazers and boat shoes avoided preppy clichés, while basketball jerseys inspired chiffon slip dresses with beaded fringing. Material and proportion made familiar pieces strange. Sunglass resin formed sculptural collars on knits and trench coats, while oversized buckles and bows transformed footwear. Shell jackets and anoraks sat alongside sheer dresses, leather minis and bright stripes and florals. Presented inside the Château de Vincennes, the collection placed the audience unusually close to the clothes, with a mazelike runway bringing models within arm’s reach. It suited a collection concerned with intimacy: how fabric feels against skin, how familiar clothes move and how recognisable pieces can be made strange through proportion or material. The finale brought bouclé mini dresses and hotpants fringed with floral embroidery. It captured the designers’ approach at Loewe: taking familiar clothes apart and rebuilding them through unexpected fabric, scale and colour. At Hermes , Nadège Vanhée embraced lightness for spring/summer. Taking her cue from the long, rectangular blades of ceiling fans, she worked swooping pleats into a black leather blazer, a chocolate-suede skirt lined in yellow silk and an orange dress cinched with a double-buckle belt. Sporty dresses made from narrow strips of leather laid over silk mesh brought further graphic lightness. Airiness ran throughout the collection. Perforated suede jackets and open-knit dresses, some resembling fishing nets, revealed flashes of skin and were layered over statement underwear. Wide-leg trousers and jackets in featherweight denim and printed silk kept silhouettes loose and breezy. Accessories were equally pared back: flat leather boots with delicate side stitching, barely-there strappy sandals, small bucket bags with fishnet details, cross-body styles and slim leather clutches. This season, Elie Saab looked to the languid glamour of 1930s film star Jean Harlow, mixing it with the house’s early-2000s codes. Sheer layers, intricate embroidery and soft shades of blush, powder blue, sage and sand came together in a deeply romantic collection of slip dresses, featuring appliqué flowers and delicate straps slipping from shoulders. Familiar floating silhouettes, bustiers and floral embellishments returned with a lighter, more contemporary hand. Backstage, Saab said the team had been exploring the house archive held at the Elie Saab Foundation in Beirut. The brand will also bring its couture-inflected codes to a younger audience this month with the launch of its H&M collaboration . Michael Rider’s Celine has a knack for making clothes feel considered yet unforced and this collection resisted fashion’s usual grandstanding. The clothes were relaxed: creamy whites, hay tones and tomato red; collarless leather capes, off-the-shoulder tops, delicate knits and slouchy trousers cinched at the ankle. A floor-length sundial-print dress brought a flower child element, while beaded knitwear and satin shirts added artisanal polish. Rider’s strength lies in the details. A skinny belt, oversized bangle, awkward fit or scuffed sneaker can push an otherwise polished look somewhere more interesting. His Celine moves between Parisian chic, sportswear and bohemia without settling into any one of them. The result feels spontaneous, but never accidental. At Balenciaga, Pierpaolo Piccioli applied atelier techniques to decidedly more democratic clothes: T-shirts, jeans and leather jackets. Craftsmanship was deliberately visible. Stitching used to structure couture corsets appeared externally on ready-to-wear, shaping shoulders, narrowing waists and exaggerating hips. Jeans were cut on the bias for a slouchier fit, tailoring lost its rigidity, and handbags were draped, twisted and knotted by hand. A pale-pink taffeta ballgown worn over jeans captured the idea best: on closer inspection, it was an enormous T-shirt. Piccioli’s proposition was clear: couture need not remain behind glass. At Balenciaga, it can be worn, altered and taken on to the street. After spending the summer driving around the US East Coast with social media deleted, Daniel Roseberry returned to essentials for Schiaparelli’s spring collection: sharp separates, a largely monochrome palette and the house’s unmistakable appetite for drama. A backward tuxedo dress opened the show, reshaped with hourglass boning. Elsewhere, bodysuits plunged dramatically, frills framed little black dresses and oversized tuxedo shirts were softened with moulded satin bibs. A laminated-jersey top could be paired with a skirt or dressed down with trousers. Roseberry also broadened Schiaparelli beyond its gilded occasionwear. Broderie anglaise and spiral knits brought warmer-weather ease, while final jackets nodded to Elsa Schiaparelli through archival embroidery. The result remained unmistakably Schiaparelli, but with enough practicality to suggest clothes intended to be worn. Alessandro Michele turned Valentino’s spring show into a celebration of books beneath the iron arches of Paris’s Bibliotheque Sainte-Genevieve. Guests were asked to donate a book, while Michele created a fictional library of imagined titles and authors, inspired by the “antilibrary” – books that remain unread, but whose potential still matters. Michele rarely settles for the obvious. Double-pleated jeans, plaid shirts and baseball caps offered glimpses of everyday dressing amid fuchsia satin, oversized rosettes, lace cycling shorts, jewel-toned bustiers and embroidered skirts. His unease with technology added another layer. He has spoken about preserving the human impulse behind fashion rather than reducing it to numbers, reflected here in deliberately improbable combinations: mohair with knobbly wool, harem trousers with sequins and gold-tipped shoes. In an increasingly algorithmic world, eccentricity may be one of fashion’s last human signatures. Haider Ackermann loosened the metaphorical tie at Tom Ford. For spring/summer 2027, the designer introduced racy swimwear to the runway, setting barely-there pieces against the house’s familiar armoury of sharp tailoring, cashmere, leather and silk. The mood was about freedom, he said, with a dash of danger and decadence, and the unabashed glamour of Tom Ford’s own era. Suits came in baby blue, black, olive and white, worn bare-chested or with plunging swimsuits, bras and open shirts. Sultry evening dresses slipped off the shoulder to reveal leather or satin bras, while silk robes and bathrobe-style trench coats nodded to Hugh Hefner. Ackermann has clearly understood that at Tom Ford, seduction is not a historical footnote; it is the house code. Stella McCartney took her spring/summer 2027 collection to the sea, opening with David Attenborough’s voice reminding us that the ocean, covering 70 per cent of the planet, is more than a backdrop to human life. Her childhood fascination with marine life surfaced in dolphin graphics, wave motifs and a rock-pool palette of washed greens, coral, cream and deep brown. Clear fishing line ran through knitwear, edges curled like oyster shells and recycled denim glittered with crystals. Drawstring-waist jackets, sheer-legged trousers, pastel windbreakers and utility pieces kept things sporty. Deadstock fabrics, recycled polyester, lab-grown wool and protein-based materials challenged others to rethink their supply chains. Fresh from launching her Climate Pledge Fashion Coalition, McCartney is in a fighting mood. Her talent lies in making that argument desirable, bringing wearability to planet-friendly dressing. A dolphin T-shirt may be nostalgic, but it also asks what we choose to protect – and what we will do to protect it. A year into his role at Balmain, creative director Antonin Tron unearthed Mark Shaw’s backstage photographs from 1954, recasting their mid-century silhouette as something darker, glossier and more louche. For his second show, animal prints, eel skin, snakeskin-effect leather, viscose and silk lamé exuded cinematic elegance. His strong-shouldered pilot jacket returned, while corsetry, garter belts, plunging necklines and cocktail dresses, barely more substantial than swimsuits, kept silhouettes close to the body. The setting was the Left Bank mansion once occupied by Karl Lagerfeld, a Balmain apprentice in the 1950s. Sunglasses, wet-look fabrics and clinging silhouettes gave the house fresh bite, charged with sensual, unapologetic glamour. For Julian Klausner, glamour lies in the pleasure of dressing for yourself. His spring/summer 2027 collection for Dries Van Noten imagined an actress leaving the set and slipping back into her everyday clothes. Taxi horns and sirens accompanied models in looks that captured the peculiar logic of a wardrobe assembled over time. A sequinned blouse sat over a casual button-down, a slinky cocktail dress over a rugby shirt, and a plunging silk dress over a graphic T-shirt. Nothing was quite where you expected it. Mismatched jewellery, an enamel brooch, a flouncy sheer skirt and, wonderfully, a single hot-pink racing glove added to the eccentricity. Bright red lipstick seemed as plausible at noon as after dark. Personal, slightly strange and instinctive, Klausner’s glamour requires no particular occasion. Having just given his final show for Diesel, creative director Glen Martens is now focused solely on Maison Margiela and, for this latest collection, took a more commercial turn. While earlier shows established just how far he was willing to push the house’s theatrical codes, this time the exercise was more forensic and focused on stripping Margiela back to the contradictions on which it was founded in the 1980s. The result was familiar yet disrupted. Contrasting hard and soft, 1960s-style brocades became column skirts tied with Margiela’s signature cotton ribbon, and tailoring arrived with concertina-like construction, with knife-edge lapels folding inward or out for a more conventional silhouette. Trenches, T-shirts and jersey dresses, meanwhile, were given rigid, balcony-like inserts. There was an appealing return to Margiela’s secret language of quietly intelligent clothes as well: a stiff-fronted white coat, checked shirt and high-waisted tailored ski trousers. But opulence remains his instinct, seen in elaborate metal-fronted gowns, crushed silver and baroque draping. For spring/summer 2027, Jonathan Anderson looked to something lighter at Dior – quite literally. Air became a material in its own right, worked through lace, silk mousseline and organza, while tailoring softened into fluid, almost weightless forms. Transparency drifted between sheer and opaque, giving the collection a sense of constant movement. The Dior ateliers supplied technical virtuosity, with pleats layered upon pleats, asymmetric florals, voluminous hems and a softer evolution of last season’s Marie Antoinette-inspired tutus. Anderson’s signatures were becoming clearer, too, via flowerlike silhouettes, iridescence, cropped proportions and deliberately off-kilter details. Long scarves, cascading earrings and draped fabrics reinforced the collection’s interest in asymmetry. Accessories supplied the wit. Flower photographs appeared on square-toe heels; the new Dior Bow Sandal and petal-soled Cigale played with familiar codes, while bags moved from updated Double and Initial Hobo shapes to a biker-inspired Cannage style. Most playful was a silver minaudiere shaped like the wenwan walnut featured on the invitation. After a year of historical references, Anderson’s Dior is beginning to speak in its own unmistakable language. It seems the rumours swirling around Saint Laurent are, in fact, true and that after a decade leading the brand, Anthony Vaccarello is leaving. He presented an extraordinary, gilded collection, steeped in the house’s history and charged with the atmosphere of a finale where Charlotte Gainsbourg performed, the song chorused with the words “You are so much, Yves Saint Laurent.” If this was a farewell, it was impeccably orchestrated. Under giant golden chandeliers, most looks were gilt, a deliberate reference to Yves Saint Laurent’s 1991 Rive Gauche collection, whose finale was entirely gilded. Metallic trenches, cocktail dresses, gilt brocades and metal-thread lace caught the light, while mousseline scarves in absinthe, amber and cognac added colour. There were enormous earrings, vertiginous stilettos and snake-shaped heels, but interestingly, not a single handbag. The Eiffel Tower glittered as the show began and ended, reinforcing the sense of occasion. Vaccarello has always resisted fashion’s drift towards accessibility and trend-chasing. Here, he made a case for something rarer, for glamour with no interest in apology. Designers Hannah Rose Dalton and Steven Raj Bhaskaran staged a deeply political outing. For their biggest show to date, the Matieres Fecales founders took over Place de la Republique – a symbolic site of protest – for a show called The 99 Per Cent, and the second chapter of a story that began last season with a collection focused on the world’s wealthiest one per cent. The Canadian duo has since moved further into the mainstream, dressing the likes of Demi Moore and Zendaya on the red carpet, and attracting Rihanna, who held up proceedings by arriving to the show over an hour late. This season, Dalton and Bhaskaran sent out 99 looks on 99 models of colour, drawing on Bhaskaran’s journey from poverty to the upper reaches of Paris fashion. The message was explicit: if the one per cent represented the villains of the previous chapter, the 99 per cent were now its heroes. It was activism translated into fashion spectacle – provocative, theatrical and deliberately difficult to ignore. The question is no longer whether Matieres Fecales can attract attention, but what it chooses to do with it.

title: Who is Mayssa Baha, the 15-year-old Moroccan rewriting Barcelona's record books?
description: The youngest player to represent Barca - male or female - comes from a good sporting pedigree
content: It’s been quite the month for Mayssa Baha, the 15-year-old Moroccan international who became the youngest player to start for Barcelona’s Femeni team on September 26. Mayssa started the league match against Logrono, scoring her first senior goal. She is the youngest player to score for a Barcelona senior side, male or female, breaking a record set by Lamine Yamal . She is also the youngest player to score in Spain’s Liga F. In the preceding weeks, the forward had been coming on as a substitute for a side that win every week. European champions in three of the past four seasons and Spain’s champions in each of the past seven, Barca won 29 of their 30 league games last season and defeated Real Madrid 7-0 on Sunday in front of 40,000 fans. Mayssa was a substitute alongside the world’s best player, Aitana Bonmarti. She won’t be old enough to play in the Uefa Champions League until she turns 16 in January. She was born in Malaga, Spain, in 2011, while her father, the former Morocco international Nabil Baha, was at the club. She started playing football at FUS Rabat when her father played there from 2014 to 2016. She then returned to Malaga, where she and her brother Ziyad continued to play youth football. Mayssa played in teams two or three years up from her age group. Her brother, Ziyad, now 17, is in Olympique Marseille’s youth side and Morocco’s under-17 men’s team, where his father is head coach. Mayssa already plays for Morocco’s under-17 women's team, having made her debut aged just 12, another record. At last year’s Under-17 World Cup, she was the youngest player in the tournament. She could still choose to play for Spain when she is an adult. The siblings’ mother is Spanish-Moroccan model Farah Farabian, who spends much of her time watching her children play football. “People wonder why I quit my job for my kids like I had no life left,” Farabian recently wrote. “But today, my life is also accompanying them in theirs. Every weekend I travel miles between Barcelona and Marseille to share their matches, joys and progress. It's not a sacrifice; it's my choice, my happiness. “A career can wait, but their childhood and adolescence will never come back. So, yes, I choose them and I would do it a thousand times over. Because seeing them grow and reach their dreams is also my greatest achievement.” Mayssa joined Barcelona at age 13, living at La Masia academy and moving quickly through the ranks with the C team last season. She started this season with the B team, but during pre-season she was invited to train with the first team at a camp in Andorra and kept her place among some of the best players in the world. Rated the top player in the world for her age, she’s mentally and physically mature. She’s strong, confident, powerful and fast, but, at 15, she has much to learn about the game. Right now, she’s playing in the best possible place to advance her career.

title: UAE's 'very powerful' cyber defences can repel attacks, says Mistral AI boss
description: French company also open to investing in data centres in the Emirates
content: The UAE 's “very powerful” cyber defences enable it to defend against threats, especially during geopolitical instability, the chief executive of French company Mistral AI said. The UAE's pursuit of technological sovereignty will help it establish reliable and secure cyber capabilities, Arthur Mensch told The National at the AI Everything summit in Abu Dhabi . “The UAE is under pressure, in particular, on the defence side,” he said. “Cyber capabilities are a must-have when it comes to having capable defence systems. “Sovereignty matters in that. It's important to be able to wield defence systems without having to ask for permission.” Mr Mensch's comments come after UAE authorities reported an increasing number of cyber attacks. Last month, the UAE's cyber security chief, Mohamed Al Kuwaiti, said the country is continuing to contend with daily online threats, with Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps behind many of the attacks. Mr Al Kuwaiti said the country faced about 640,000 attacks on September 15 and that Iran remains “one of the main players” in the high-tech offensive, which is being exacerbated by the rise of AI. “Having very powerful cyber models deployed here in Abu Dhabi in a way where the deployment is fully under Abu Dhabi control is going to be quite important,” Mr Mensch said. Mr Mensch said Mistral AI would consider investing in UAE data centres, a move that would further solidify its co-operation with Abu Dhabi and boost the country's AI ambitions. “We may [invest in UAE data centres]. It's an interesting place for our AI buildout that is currently under way in this part of the world,” he said. On Abu Dhabi's efforts at data sovereignty, Mr Mensch said authorities and the wider industry had “very early on decided” that this aspect will be crucial for the deployment of AI. Data sovereignty is becoming vital for nations as it gives them legal control over the data within their jurisdictions. The most notable project to achieve this is the planned Stargate UAE data centre campus, a 5GW development valued at $30 billion . Mistral AI met more local organisations and companies at the summit, trying to “get a sense of what Abu Dhabi needs to build with AI ... [and] go in depth into the technological aspect of the asks”, said Mr Mensch, adding that the company has worked “extensively” with the oil and gas industry. Mistral AI has already forged partnerships with Abu Dhabi organisations , including AI major G42, to develop advanced platforms and infrastructure, and the Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence for research and development in AI foundation models, talent development and real-world AI solutions. In June, the company teamed up with UAE AI investment firm MGX and lender Bpifrance for the planned expansion of Campus AI in France, which aims to build a capacity of 3GW across Europe's third-biggest economy. “There is more that can be done ... on being able to have a compute capacity under full Abu Dhabi control; that's something where as a company we can help,” he added. Fresh debacles have been hitting the AI industry, most notably AI models, supposedly in secure environments and built by names including OpenAI, Meta Platforms, Anthropic and Google, going rogue and infiltrating external sites. Mr Mensch was clear on where the responsibility should fall. At the same time, OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman made a plea at the recent UN General Assembly for governments to do more to rein in AI. “Accountability for AI deployments, when they are hosted by AI companies, falls on the AI companies. This should be very, very clear. There's no way in which the accountability of what we're doing should be offset to governments,” Mr Mensch said. Governments, though, “are accountable for the adoption of the technology, and they should be accountable for how it's being used in the government itself”, he said. Mr Mensch also called for a tempered tone on the call for deceleration – or even acceleration – of the development of AI, as recent events have shown the potential disruption the technology can bring. “I'm very cautious about those warnings [to slow development down] because they serve their own interests very clearly,” he said. “The world we don't want to live in, which would be an extremely dangerous world, is the world where you have a duopoly of companies operated from the US serving the rest of the world,” he said, referring to the strength of the US AI industry, led by OpenAI and Anthropic, which is widely viewed as a counter to China's growing influence in the sector. On Tuesday, at AI Everything, Mistral AI launched its latest Mistral Large 4 AI model, which, it says, is among the fastest in the world and rivals the best open-source models from China. “We see no sign of slowing down when we look at how our model is being improved by the day,” Mr Mensch said.

title: Iran war energy price shock large but contained so far, IMF chief says
description: Kristalina Georgieva says AI revolution and geopolitical instability are pulling global economy in two directions
content: The head of the International Monetary Fund has said the energy price shock driven by the US- Iran war has so far been “large but contained”, but warned that energy demand could lead to further pressure. “Even if the war in the Gulf were to end soon, the problem of high energy prices would likely persist for some time,” managing director Kristalina Georgieva said in prepared remarks in Singapore ahead of the IMF and World Bank annual meetings. This year's gathering, held in Bangkok, comes as supply disruptions from the war in the Middle East pile on to inflationary pressures, potentially leading to higher interest rates for advanced economies. The Federal Reserve and European Central Bank have already begun to raise their key rates, with the Bank of England expected to join them next month. Higher energy prices and rising debt levels have also driven global borrowing costs to their highest levels in decades. The yield on the 10-year US Treasury, a benchmark for global borrowing costs, traded at 5.307 per cent as recently on Monday, its highest level since 2002. That pressure has also spread to markets in other advanced economies including in Japan, France, Germany and the UK. Oil producers in the Middle East are racing to establish alternative routes to bring their exports to the markets. The UAE is fast-tracking construction of its West-East Pipeline , which is expected to double export capacity through Fujairah by the time its expansion is completed in 2027. Saudi Arabia has rerouted its crude through the East-West Pipeline . The seven-day moving average for crude exports from the Gulf was 18.3 million barrels per day on September 30, compared to the average 18 million bpd that passed through the region in the 12 months before the Iran war began, according to ship tracking firm Kpler. The latest figures included transits via the Strait of Hormuz, the Red Sea and exports from terminals and ship-to-ship transfers in the Gulf of Oman. Ms Georgieva had credited the Gulf Co-operation Council's efforts to reroute energy supplies for preventing a larger shock to the global economy during a meeting with the bloc's finance ministers and central bankers in Bahrain last week. She also said the IMF anticipates the GCC economy will contract this year, adding that the region is expected to face a strong recovery next year, conditional on the normalisation of shipping. A separate report from the World Bank released on Tuesday said GCC economies will contract by an average of 4.3 per cent this year, a downward revision of 5.7 percentage points from its April forecast. Meanwhile, continued supply disruptions in liquefied natural gas will hit buyers in Europe and Asia particularly hard, Ms Georgieva said, noting price pressures could further build with winter approaching and reserves dwindling. In her address, the IMF chief also used her address to urge governments to embark on policies to unlock the productive gains under artificial intelligence . Ms Georgieva described the global economy as one being pulled in two directions, with the positive demand shock from AI partially offsetting the economic fallout from the US-Iran conflict. “Love it, hate it, or fear it, AI is here, rapidly becoming a key driver of countries’ relative fortunes in the world economy,” she said. In the US, the AI buildout is shaping up to become the largest investment drive in the country's history. Analysts at Brookings anticipate AI investment in data centres, infrastructure, chips and other equipment will total $10.3 trillion from 2025 to 2032, or an average of 3.63 per cent of US GDP per year. The broad S&P 500 hit a fresh record-high of 7,800 on Tuesday driven by renewed AI enthusiasm. But with fears of an AI bubble also fomenting, Ms Georgieva said countries should adopt regulation and supervision as a “first line of defence” to prevent a far-reaching shock if AI earnings fall short. The Trump administration has recently adopted a defensive posture of AI amid a growing domestic backlash against the data centre buildout ahead of November’s midterm elections. US President Donald Trump has taken a light regulatory touch on AI advancement and repeatedly expressed his desire to beat China in the global AI race. Countries in the Gulf are seeking to advance large-scale acceleration of AI. The UAE targets to have AI contribute 20 per cent of its non-oil GDP by 2031. Ms Georgieva said AI could deliver up to a half percentage point of additional world growth – or “adding an economy the size of ASEAN to the world economy” – annually. “Yet as this drives forward today’s AI economies, it largely bypasses most others, increasing the risk of widening economic inequality across the globe,” she said.

title: Countdown to new-look Abu Dhabi T10 begins with strong Pakistan and Caribbean cohorts
description: Star names selected via player draft as league prepares for fresh start under new ownership structure from November 7
content: The countdown to Abu Dhabi T10 ’s relaunch has started with five new team owners and a roster full of star players from across the world gearing up for what is effectively a second innings for the league, beginning November 7. The T10 tournament has undergone a significant transformation this year, with the Abu Dhabi Cricket & Sports Hub (ADCSH) assuming complete ownership of the league, with support from the Abu Dhabi Sports Council (ADSC) and the Emirates Cricket Board (ECB). With the new ownership structure in place and an emphasis on long-term partnerships, clear and predictable team structures, and organic growth, T10 is aiming to move away from the disjointed efforts of previous seasons. Five new team owners were announced for the 2026 season, with UAE Bulls, who had been with the league since its inception in 2017, continuing their association with Abu Dhabi T10 . Among the new inductees are Yas Lions, owned by UAE-based venture capitalist Jeetu Kataria, and Royal Desert Champions, helmed by former banker Amit Narang. Other teams in the league are Arabian Aces, Emirates Eagles and United Tigers. Last week, all stakeholders gathered in Abu Dhabi to complete the biggest task for any franchise tournament – player selection. A draft was held at Yas Island, where some of the most in-demand short-format players were allocated to the six teams. The ‘icon’ players had already been selected ahead of the draft. West Indies players were the most sought-after, led by Kieron Pollard (UAE Bulls 'icon' player), Jason Holder (Yas Lions), Nicolas Pooran (Royal Desert Champions) and Rovman Powell (Emirates Eagles). Moeen Ali (Arabian Aces) and Fakhar Zaman (United Tigers) are the only non-Caribbean 'icons' in T10 2026. With the Abu Dhabi T10 sharing November with another UAE-based franchise tournament – the DP World ILT20 – there was some overlap of players. However, one key difference was the composition of the squads. While the 2026 ILT20 put particular emphasis on Afghanistan players while restricting Pakistan stars largely to one team – ostensibly due to Indian ownership of other franchises - the Abu Dhabi T10 saw Pakistan names scattered across all franchises, barring one. In all, 15 Pakistan players have found a home in T10, including superstars such as Naseem Shah and Fakhar Zaman , compared to just five in ILT20. Left-arm pacer Mohammad Amir is the 16th Pakistan cricketer in T10, but he now qualifies as an England cricketer. For Matt Boucher, CEO of ADCSH and Abu Dhabi T10, the foundation has been laid for a new cricket structure. “The changes this season are about putting the right foundations in place to build Abu Dhabi T10 into a stronger and more sustainable global cricket property,” Boucher told The National . “We have six franchises for the 2026 season. UAE Bulls provide continuity from the previous era, while the other franchises are part of the new ownership and identity structure. "The focus is on having owners who share our long-term vision and are committed to building strong franchise identities and genuine connections with fans.” Boucher said the onus of growing the fan base and popularity of the league falls on both the T10 management and team owners. “The key difference is the long-term approach. We want franchises to grow beyond the tournament window, develop their own identities and fanbases, and become sustainable sporting brands. Stronger franchises will ultimately help us build a stronger Abu Dhabi T10,” he added. For Boucher, the presence of Pakistan players across the teams is encouraging, as is the presence of international and UAE stars. “Having Pakistan stars such as Naseem Shah, Mohammed Amir, Shadab Khan, Fakhar Zaman and Iftikhar Ahmed certainly adds quality and significant fan interest. But the strength of the league is its overall international mix, alongside a strong UAE presence with players such as Muhammad Waseem, Alishan Sharafu, Aayan Afzal Khan and Vriitya Aravind.” UAE star batter Waseem will undoubtedly have the spotlight on him when the Abu Dhabi T10 starts on November 7 at the Zayed Cricket Stadium, having secured a record $210,000 contract for the ILT20, which begins two days after the T10 tournament concludes on November 20.

title: Michelin Guide Dubai 2026: Closed restaurants retain stars as new winners emerge
description: Orfali Bros moves up to two stars as Birch and Kigo earn their first, with 20 restaurants receiving the coveted distinctions
content: Dubai's latest Michelin stars have been revealed, with two restaurants joining the prestigious list and another promoted to two stars – even as some of the city's award-winning dining rooms remain temporarily closed. The Michelin Guide Dubai 2026 was unveiled at a ceremony at Atlantis The Royal on Tuesday night, with 20 restaurants receiving at least one star. FZN by Bjorn Frantzen, which blends Scandinavian and Asian influences, and Tresind Studio , known for its modern Indian cuisine, remain at the top of Dubai's dining scene, retaining the three stars they received last year. Orfali Bros was one of the biggest winners of the night, promoted from one to two stars. Run by Syrian brothers Mohammad, Wassim and Omar Orfali, the home-grown restaurant serves contemporary Middle Eastern cuisine, drawing on their Syrian roots as well as Turkish and Armenian influences. Michelin noted the restaurant's evolution "from a brilliant neighbourhood bistro into a flagship of Middle Eastern gastronomy". "Rooted in the brothers' Aleppian, Armenian and Turkish heritage, its signature dishes and Voyage menu reveal cooking of increasing refinement, depth and personality," it said. Meanwhile, Birch and Kigo entered the guide with one star each. Birch, led by chef Arslan Berdiev, serves contemporary cuisine shaped by his travels and Turkmen heritage, while Kigo is a Japanese fine-dining restaurant offering sushi omakase and kaiseki menus. The latest awards come after a challenging period for Dubai's restaurant industry, with several high-profile venues temporarily pausing operations amid softer demand and disruption to tourism following the Iran war . Among the restaurants retaining Michelin stars for 2026 are Al Muntaha , Dinner by Heston Blumenthal , Ossiano and Smoked Room , which are currently temporarily closed . Several other restaurants in the wider Michelin Guide Dubai 2026 selection are also temporarily closed. Michelin has acknowledged the unusual situation after Dubai food writer Samantha Wood , founder of FooDiva, questioned why at least 10 restaurants across the guide's various lists were included despite currently being closed. In a statement provided to The National , Michelin said it was “fully aware” that a number of restaurants were currently closed “due to the current circumstances”. “We remain in close contact with their teams and are monitoring closely when they might reopen in the near future,” Michelin said. “As with all restaurants in the selection, they will be revisited and re-evaluated by our inspectors once they reopen to ensure they continue to meet the standards associated with their distinctions.” There are 20 Michelin-starred restaurants in Dubai in the 2026 guide, with two holding three stars, four holding two stars and 14 holding one. Beyond the starred restaurants, the 2026 guide includes 122 establishments representing 38 types of cuisine, up from 119 restaurants last year. There are 19 new additions across the guide, including two new one-star restaurants, four new Bib Gourmands and 13 restaurants added to the Michelin Selected category. The Bib Gourmand list features 22 restaurants this year, while another 80 restaurants appear in the Michelin Selected category, including 13 newcomers. “The selection has grown significantly since its inception and now features nearly twice as many establishments as it did when it was first launched,” said Gwendal Poullennec , international director of the Michelin Guides. “This year's combination of home-grown talent and international arrivals reflects a city that is developing its own culinary identity while embracing traditions from around the world.” The Bib Gourmand distinction recognises restaurants offering good-quality food at good value.
