But that plan, which borrowed a page from Russian President Vladimir Putin’s playbook, backfired amid voter turnout of 69 per cent – the highest in 33 years. The nation's political spectrum is now to be redrawn. Reviews are to be held into deals and policies. The Student List reacted with chants of “Vucic is gone” after the announcement, but what comes next is less clear. The movement does not have a single leader and does not have supporters with extensive experience in government. “This is the victory of the conviction that Serbia can and will do better,” said Radomir Saicic, one of the movement’s leaders. “We call on all citizens to act peacefully and in dignified manner. We didn’t fight for months to lose it today.” Political overhaul Mr Vucic, 56, is the second long-time leader to lose power in eastern Europe this year. His ally, Viktor Orban of Hungary, was toppled six months ago. Mr Vucic told his supporters that the Student List won the ballot with the “direct support from some European countries and the American deep state, the one that is also against President Trump.” He called the movement “just contractors doing some very dirty work”, without providing evidence for his claims. While he conceded defeat, Mr Vucic pledged to make a comeback, saying: “I’ll defeat them much sooner than they think.” But his departure from power marks a tectonic shift for Serbia. The parliament will now effectively have only two sizeable political blocs, removing an array of once mainstream groups from liberals to conservatives and nationalists. The Socialists, once led by late strongman Slobodan Milosevic, are also out for the first time in 18 years. Mr Vucic called the election more than a year ahead of schedule, after unrelenting anti-government rallies sparked by the collapse of a train station canopy that killed 16 people in 2024. Students led the protests, blaming the corruption and incompetence of ruling officials for the deaths. While Mr Vucic is now gone, his geopolitical balancing act may continue. Before the vote, the movement’s representatives were cautious on sensitive issues such as Serbia’s rejection of Kosovo’s unilateral secession, or on adopting sanctions against Russia. The opposition, which gained traction for the first time in more than a decade, pledged to focus on fighting against corruption, overhauling the judiciary, improving election conditions and boosting media diversity. Meeting EU membership conditions is not an immediate priority either. Student List representatives have said the country can decide on that in a referendum. No clear leader European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen welcomed the change of power in a post on X on Sunday. The EU is “ready to support reforms", she added. The movement's representatives pledged to break up monopolies and review large infrastructure contracts signed under Mr Vucic. Those include the $2.4 billion Expo 2027 that Vucic has touted as his legacy project. In Transparency International’s Corruption Perceptions Index 2025 , Serbia’s score ⁠was the lowest in two decades. The Student List has operated through a patchwork of “plenums”, or cells, without a distinct leader and has not yet announced its candidate for prime minister. On election night, the movement was late with a victory speech as its representatives could not decide who would speak on their behalf. “The Student List will have a very hard job organising the transfer of power, which Vucic will probably try to boycott,” said Zarko Puhovski, an independent political analyst from Croatia. “Their list is dominated by people with little political or government experience.”

title: Kimi Antonelli wins US Grand Prix to move within touching distance of F1 title
description: Mercedes driver, 20, breezed to victory at the Circuit of the Americas
content: Italian wunderkind Kimi Antonelli took another step towards winning his first Formula One drivers' championship by claiming his ​ninth ​race of the ​year on Sunday at the United States Grand ⁠Prix in Austin, Texas. Antonelli , 20, capitalised on pole ⁠position and sailed to victory ​at the Circuit of the Americas, beating Ferrari's Charles Leclerc by a comfortable 13.078 ⁠seconds. Despite taking the chequered flag, Antonelli doesn't have the championship wrapped up quite yet, but his lead over Mercedes teammate George Russell expanded to 123 points with five races to go. The Briton ⁠must win the next race in Mexico City to remain in contention for ​the ⁠championship; otherwise, it will ‌go to Antonelli, who has dominated this year's championship in only his second F1 ​campaign. "I'm aware [securing the championship] is close, but the mindset doesn't change," Antonelli said post-race. "I want to finish the season on a high, to go into 2027 with high hopes." Antonelli and Mercedes' strategy paid off. While others pitted twice during the 56-lap race, Antonelli held on until Lap 25 to pit and didn't enter the pit lane again. "It was a perfect way to end the weekend; it was an incredible team effort, especially from strategy to believe in me and go for one stop," Antonelli said. "Let's keep pushing" 👊 Kimi Antonelli secures his ninth Grand Prix win! 🏆 #F1 #USGP @MercedesAMGF1 pic.twitter.com/rRiqa82A6k — Formula 1 (@F1) October 25, 2026 Antonelli won five grands prix in a row earlier this season, one of which was the Miami Grand Prix. He's now 2-for-2 in ​the United States this season, with the Las Vegas ‌Grand Prix still to come ⁠in November. "I know we're very close, but, yeah, we try to finish on a high and hopefully we can clinch it very soon,” Antonelli said. “I’m very excited. I would love to clinch the title in style with a great result. “I’m just going to try to enjoy every moment because they’re moments that will always be remembered.” A team effort in Austin... 🤝 And Kimi is eager to look ahead to Mexico, hoping to clinch the Title in style 😮‍💨 #F1 #USGP pic.twitter.com/ovFefVhcVI — Formula 1 (@F1) October 26, 2026 Max Verstappen, the four-time F1 ​champion for Red Bull , rounded out the podium 17.485 seconds behind ​Antonelli. After ‌rattling off every championship from 2021-24, Verstappen has been mathematically eliminated from this year's chase and ⁠will go two years without a world title. "Our overall pace was ⁠not good enough, and the tyres we had available were not the right ones," Verstappen said. "We still managed to get on the podium, maybe a bit lucky with the [Virtual Safety Car] at the end." A Virtual Safety Car was deployed after ​Valtteri Bottas' Cadillac stopped on the track in Lap 52. It lasted until the penultimate lap, by which time no one could catch up to Antonelli. Mercedes grew their lead in the constructors' standings to 133 points over Ferrari – 607 to Ferrari's 474.

title: Gazans want Netanyahu gone but expect no 'new beginning' from Knesset vote
description: Exhausted Palestinians say Israel's treatment of them has changed little under successive governments
content: Gazans are watching the final days of Israel's election campaign with a mixture of anger, exhaustion and deep scepticism, hoping Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu will lose power but doubting a new leader would bring meaningful change. Defeat for Mr Netanyahu would offer a measure of emotional relief after years of bombing and destruction ordered by the Israeli Prime Minister. Yet the prospect of a new government elicits little optimism among Palestinians who have lost their homes, families and jobs and believe Gaza 's plight extends far deeper. Their concerns are more immediate: finding permanent shelter, securing food and water, restoring schools and hospitals, and rebuilding the economy, the collapse of which has left civilians dependent on humanitarian aid. “It makes no difference to us in Gaza who wins or loses the Israeli elections,” said Munir Isleem, 35, whose home in Gaza city's Shujaiya neighbourhood was destroyed in the war. “What matters to us is escaping this life of tents and humiliation, and putting an end to the hunger and poverty that the war has forced upon us,” he told The National . Mr Isleem, who has spent the past two years moving between displacement camps with his family, still hopes Mr Netanyahu will lose. “The war Netanyahu launched against us didn’t just take away our homes. It robbed us of our happiness, our dearest friends and the people closest to us,” he said. Before the war, Mr Isleem worked as a skilled machine operator at a plastic factory, earning about $1,000 a month – enough to provide for his family. Now, unemployed and displaced, he relies on aid to survive. The war “transformed us from productive people who worked and earned a living into unemployed people waiting for food from charity kitchens, humanitarian aid and our turn in the water queues”, he said. Political reality Mr Netanyahu faces a tough fight for re-election, with an array of challengers led by former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, and amid division within his governing coalition. While his handling of wars in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran, and the October 7 Hamas attacks in 2023, has been criticised by rivals, few of them support Palestinian statehood or favour a radically different approach in military matters. Palestinian political analyst Mustafa Ibrahim said the election should not be seen as a referendum on Palestinian rights or Gaza’s future. “I don’t believe the situation will change significantly whether Netanyahu wins or loses, because Israeli policy towards Gaza has reminded largely consistent under successive governments throughout history,” he said. He added that the positions taken by Mr Netanyahu and Mr Eisenkot amounted to different ways of achieving Israeli security objectives, rather than any fundamental difference in policy towards Palestinians. “Ultimately the political approach and objectives remain the same, regardless of the individuals of governments in power,” he said. Like Mr Isleem, he said Palestinians in Gaza still want Mr Netanyahu to lose because they hold him primarily responsible for what they see as the genocide against them. However, this does not necessarily translate into support for other candidates. Years of disappointment For Ahmed Sammour, 61, a former Arabic teacher from Gaza city’s Sheikh Radwan neighbourhood, scepticism about Israeli elections has been shaped by decades of experience. Mr Sammour has lived under more than 10 Israeli governments and remembers periods of conflict and negotiations. But none of them offered lasting security or freedom to Gaza. “All of them have followed the same approach towards us as Palestinians,” he said. He recalled the Oslo Accords , signed by Israeli leader Yitzhak Rabin in the 1990s, as a moment when negotiations appeared to offer a different path. But Mr Rabin was assassinated in 1995 by an Israeli extremist opposed to the peace process, and the optimism of that period failed to last. Today, Mr Sammour lives with his family in a camp near his destroyed home. He holds Mr Netanyahu responsible for the devastation. Even if someone with better polices towards Gaza wins and begins rebuilding the territory, it will still take years Amal Al Hinnawi “The collapse of Netanyahu’s government and his defeat in the elections would certainly not represent a new beginning or a source of hope for us,” he said. “But at least we would be rid of a leader whom we hold responsible for killing children and innocent civilians.” Mr Sammour said Mr Netanyahu's government had inflicted destruction on a scale unlike anything he witnessed under previous Israeli administrations. Even so, he is reluctant to place his hopes in a successor. “Whoever comes after him will not necessary be any better,” he said. Amal Al Hinnawi, 25, a teacher at a tent school in northern Gaza, believes the scale of the destruction has made the results of Israel’s election secondary to the enormous task of rebuilding. Ms Al Hinnawi sees the consequences of the war for the education system, where makeshift classrooms have replaced conventional school buildings and children struggle to continue learning amid displacement and instability. “Israeli elections no longer matter much to us in Gaza because it will take decades for our lives to return to what they were before the war,” she said. “Even if someone with better polices towards Gaza wins and begins rebuilding the territory, it will still take years because the scale of destruction across every sector is beyond description.”

title: HSBC not worried about Gulf property sector exposure despite war volatility, CEO says
description: Rebound has begun and bank is ready for 'idiosyncratic challenges' if they arise, Georges Elhedery tells The National
content: British lender HSBC is not worried about its exposure to the slowing property sector or the health of its corporate loan book in the Gulf region despite the war-driven economic contraction this year, its group chief executive has said. The provisions, just shy of $400 million for potential loan losses, taken so far by Europe’s second-largest lender for its Middle East exposure, are “benign”, and the bank is ready for challenges if they arise, Georges Elhedery told The National in an interview before the bank’s third-quarter earnings. “Of course, the short answer is I'm not worried. But, as you would expect, we keep monitoring the situation very closely,” Mr Elhedery said on the sidelines of HSBC’s 10th annual Future Forum in Dubai last week. “You may have idiosyncratic challenges that may appear. You can't rule them out but some of them likely will be in the normal course of business, and not necessarily related to the [geopolitical] situation”, he said. The US-Iran war, now in its eighth month, severely disrupted economic momentum in the early days of the conflict as Tehran launched waves of drone and missile attacks on civilian and energy infrastructure of its Arab neighbours. Retail, aviation, hospitality and tourism as well as real estate were among the worst-hit sectors in the region. Fighting has decreased since early April, but a US naval blockade on Iranian ports remains in place. Tehran's restrictions on merchant ships and tankers in the Strait of Hormuz continue, amid frequent retaliatory exchanges and maritime skirmishes with Washington's troops. Efforts by Qatar, Pakistan and other mediators to broker a peace settlement between the warring parties have so far failed. Last week, the International Monetary Fund said Gulf economies on aggregate are set to contract 4.8 per cent this year as the Iran war disrupts energy exports and weighs on non-oil activity. The multilateral lender, however, expects a 9.1 per cent rebound in 2027 . The latest forecast marks a sharp divergence of 6.8 percentage points from the 2 per cent expansion it projected in April, according to the IMF’s Regional Economic Outlook . Regional economies expanded by 4.5 per cent last year, driven by property, construction and tourism sector-fuelled gains in the non-oil economy. HSBC, which is among the major providers of corporate, project and home financing in the Middle East, faced loan losses, increased provisions, asset write-downs, sliding profits last year due to its exposure to Asian property markets, primarily in Hong Kong and mainland China. In the Gulf region, however, the “good responsiveness” of sovereigns and the financial policymakers helped mitigate risks. “Fiscal support where it was needed” also allowed resumption of economic activity after severe disruption in March, and with the rebound already underway “there is therefore no cause to worry”, Mr Elhedery said. Strong bounce back Despite the economic contraction this year, HSBC is optimistic about the short to medium-term outlook for the region, as there is a clear push by the Gulf sovereigns to offset the impact of the war on their economies and build “resilience at pace”. “It knows how to respond to the challenges quickly and has the agility to adjust,” Mr Elhedery said. Like any other problem the region has faced, including the lockdowns during the Covid-19 pandemic, policymakers will effectively deal with the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, “which may, by the way, become redundant over the next five years”, he said. Continued investments in “all the resilience and redundancies being built to create a more sustainable and robust business model” will ultimately make the narrow waterway, through which a fifth of global oil and gas passed before the war, less important, he added. The last decade, Mr Elhedery added, has shown that “you can be very efficient operationally, but exogenous events, can knock you off course”, and these events can “take away 100 per cent of your earnings”. “This Middle East conflict is emphasising the importance of spending money on operational resilience,” he said. “I think the Middle East has done a lot of that already, but clearly there is much more going on now because of this conflict.” The financial strength and the economic vision of the leadership, as well as its “will to rebound” is what makes HSBC believe the rebound can be fast, and “we want to lean in to support it, and our clients”, he said. Changing risk profile The US-Iran war, which began on February 28, has turned into a multi-front conflict, with the Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen launching missile and drone strikes on Saudi Arabia’s energy and aviation infrastructure on a daily basis. The kingdom, Opec’s largest oil exporter, is also facing a naval blockade and maritime embargo aimed at Saudi and international shipping through the Bab Al Mandeb strait and the Red Sea. But even with the Houthi dimension adding another layer of uncertainty to the region’s risk profile, Mr Elhedery said HSBC remained optimistic about growth prospects. “It's actually never been, frankly, a singular risk and, of course from time to time, items [events] pop up to top the agenda,” he said. “One has to keep in mind that the geoeconomic considerations have always been quite complex. Some of them ebb and flow, but that complexity has always been there, and our mission is to help clients navigate this complexity, but not stereotype it.” Impact on business Although HSBC has taken first-half provisions of about $400 million against possible loan losses, the “majority of these provisions are modelled on economic outlook and growth outlook”. “So, de facto, we have seen very little, literally insignificant impact on our business directly related to the conflict, and our focus has been on operational continuity and serving our clients throughout, and we haven't skipped a beat doing that,” the chief executive said. "If you look at the entire year, actually our businesses have been resilient, both on the revenue and profitability front, the impact has been very low, single-digit per cent, on the overall business." He added that although equity capital market activity throughout the region slowed this year, there are signs of revival and "we are in the market now with the first IPO since the events [of March]". "The indications are very good, the appetite is strong," he said. HSBC is among local and global banks working on the Dubai Investments' bid to sell a 20 per cent stake in its subsidiary DIP Holding in the first initial public offering in the UAE this year. "Of course, in a period like this, you would see less public activity and more private activity, so what used to be debt capital markets sometimes may become private placements," he said. "What used to be ECM sometimes becoming more M&A, but that is a normal reaction to these events." Infrastructure boom The next phase of growth will be driven by the infrastructure boom. The broader Middle East, North Africa and Turkey region already has close to $900 billion in infrastructure financing requirements. HSBC estimates that the project finance pipeline in the UAE alone is more than $190 billion, about 22 per cent of the Menat total. The HSBC-commissioned analysis of MEED data released last week has identified an $872-billion pipeline of individual project packages within a wider $1.4 trillion pipeline of planned and unawarded infrastructure projects. The value of planned but unawarded infrastructure projects and programmes increased by 54 per cent between January 2023 and January 2026, from $792 billion to $1.22 trillion, data showed. The sheer size of the infrastructure financing basket opens up new avenues of business for financial institutions that have been waiting for the better part of this year for the lull in the regional capital markets to end. "We, as a bank, are a financing bank, an infrastructure bank, an underwriting bank and a structuring bank. We have a whole skill set to support how these projects are designed … and financed," Mr Elhedery said. "The pie is huge as there is massive appetite [from project owners for funding] and there will be more appetite [in the future]. There is a substantial opportunity to be involved, and we're extremely pleased." Sharia fund controversy HSBC in recent weeks has faced investor criticism over some of the investments its Islamic Global Equity Index Fund has made, and Mr Elhedery said the bank is trying to address those concerns as best and as quickly as possible. The $9-billion fund, which tracks an index, is the top Sharia-compliant fund in the UK. The investment vehicle has bought shares in companies linked to the US and Israeli defence companies including US tech giant Palantir, prompting several investors to raise concerns with HSBC. "We take client and investor concerns very seriously," Mr Elhedery said. The bank, he said, had already set up a working group, which includes index providers and independent Sharia experts who have begun the review. HSBC is moving at pace and aims to resolve the matter swiftly, which could mean a revision of some of the filters used. "I don't want to preempt the outcomes, but … but we intend to reach a satisfactory conclusion."

title: WGES 2026: How the UAE is driving discussions around green economy
description: The World Green Economy Summit concluded on Thursday at Dubai World Trade Centre
content: Yousif Al Lootah has been embedded in the UAE’s green economy since 2010, long before it was a global conversation. The chief executive and founder of Lootah Biofuels, the UAE’s – and possibly the region’s – first biofuel company, was aged 19 when he started out. His brother, who owned a diesel-guzzling Hummer, was not convinced by the idea of putting used cooking oil into his car, but Mr Al Lootah persisted. “Now he loves it. They all love it,” he tells The National . Mr Al Lootah was one of the speakers on Thursday at the 12 th World Green Economy Summit, taking place at the Dubai World Trade Centre. He was one among dozens of policymakers, multilateral lenders, debt market analysts, fund managers and entrepreneurs, all of whom were there to talk about where the green economy is actually headed – and how the UAE, which has hosted WGES since its founding, has built a model that other markets are starting to study. "We get all this knowledge, we cook it in a cocktail, and we make our own decision and system for our country,” said Mr Al Lootah, adding that he’s proud that the UAE has achieved so much in this sector in such little time. ‘Exciting’ opportunities The Emirates has got a “very important” role to play in the world’s green economy, said Jonathan Maxwell, founder and group chief executive of Sustainable Development Capital LLP, who was an attendee at the summit’s first edition. “In my personal experience, Dubai is probably the best place in the world to convene people [because of] the facilities and the capability here, the focus, the sense of authenticity you get,” he said. “The future world green economy stage – Dubai has an absolutely firm place on that.” Mr Maxwell said he was “excited” about the opportunities presented throughout the summit. “We’re having some extremely constructive conversations about opportunities – talking about agency to actually do something together, which I’m excited about.” A summit like this is about developing a narrative, he added. “That’s what’s needed to penetrate government and private sector – use cases, success cases, rationale, bringing different experience together so that people can actually get around a table and come away with new ideas.” A decarbonising economy This should bring people comfort, said Syed Adeel Abbas, regional climate lead for the World Bank. “The green economy is a trend that’s not going to be halted anytime soon, regardless of what happens to the rest of the world,” he said. “The global economy is decarbonising. Products and services around the world are going to be more and more green and sustainable, and socially responsible, so if you’re a company or a layman or a government, you need to understand that that’s the trend that we need to follow. And if we do not follow that trend, we will stay behind.” The UAE is ahead in this regard, particularly in terms of competitive advantages, he added. "The UAE has sufficient capital to decarbonise its own industry and to achieve net zero targets committed at COP 28," he said. "It has the right frameworks for investments as well.” Meanwhile, green hydrogen is a credible export industry in the making and the EU’s carbon border adjustment mechanism, which will apply a carbon cost to imported goods, creates a direct near-term incentive for UAE industry to move faster than competitors. "The UAE has huge aluminium exports," he said, "and if they are produced in a less carbon emission intensity than other countries, the UAE will have a significant competitive advantage in terms of exports." His broader argument – and the message he wanted policymakers at WGES to take away – was that financing should follow this kind of competitive logic. Green bonds, blue bonds and sustainability-linked instruments are useful instruments, but "financing is not the solution and shouldn't be the starting point", he said. "It should be reliable, predictable policies that fall behind the targets and commitments that governments have made." Green financing in action Green financing is a “bigger story”, said Bashar Al Natoor, managing director and global head of Islamic Finance at Fitch Ratings. Outstanding green sukuk and bonds from the GCC have reached $73 billion. In the first nine months of 2026, GCC ESG issuance represented around 40 per cent of all US dollar ESG issuance from emerging markets, excluding China. The World Bank's IFC catalysed $112 billion in private sector investment in financial year 2026 alone. Last week, First Abu Dhabi Bank issued a digital green sukuk. Qatar has begun issuing in local currency and Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund placed a 100-year green bond. "The momentum has been there over the years, where we're seeing more and more coming,” said Mr Al Natoor. “Governments have their agendas. Banks are playing their roles. So, it’s a multi-dimensional story – and each one of them deserves to be told separately,” he added. Who pays for what should not be the focus, however, said Mr Maxwell. “The question shouldn’t be: should we pay for this? The question should be: how much better can we do with the same resources or less? How can we do the same or more work with less? And that will drive competitiveness," he said. His three-word summary of what a green investment case should look like is: cheaper, cleaner, faster. In that order, because cost is the most reliable metric and revenue matters. “If we can be more efficient – and that is the lens that I look at the world through – a green economy, a sustainable economy, where sustainability is consistent and synonymous, even with resource efficiency – then that’s better for the economy.” At the end of the day, everyone is on the same “big mission to save the environment”, said Mr Lootah. “With our young generation, who we’re going to give this world to, with the AI and robotics, and all these new technologies, it’s going to enhance the transition to a sustainable lifestyle. It’s happening.”

title: Adnoc’s Dh60 billion push can boost UAE manufacturing
description: New local manufacturing opportunities can help strengthen the country’s industrial resilience
content: The success of the UAE’s industrial strategy will ultimately be realised by the factories it builds, the high-skilled jobs it creates and the high-quality products it makes within the country. Seen in this light, the second iteration of the Make it with Adnoc Forum was yet another opportunity to connect government support with what local manufacturers actually need. Held in Abu Dhabi on Sunday, the forum brought together industry insiders, investors, partners and officials from the Ministry of Industry and Advanced Technology, or MoIAT, to find ways to scale domestic manufacturing. Manufacturing is playing an important role in the UAE’s efforts to diversify its economy and increase self-sufficiency in an increasingly unstable world. In 2021, MoIAT launched Operation 300bn with the objective of raising the industrial sector’s contribution to the national gross domestic product from Dh133 billion to Dh300 billion by 2031. Reaching this target requires building and sustaining an ecosystem in which local businesses can grow and compete. There are several initiatives in place to achieve this – including, but not limited to, the National In-Country Value Programme, or ICV, designed to localise supply chains and push the government’s Emiratisation drive, and Factory Forward UAE, aimed at bringing all the country’s industrial technology transformation programmes on one platform. However, the success of these initiatives will depend on whether businesses, particularly small and medium enterprises , are able to access funding, more contracts and modern technology. New technology, in particular, is vital to building a strong industrial sector. While government support will help manufacturers increase production, policymakers know that the focus also needs to be on equipping factories with the latest technologies and ensuring continued improvement – both of which are required to produce better goods. The challenges of the past few years, from Covid-19 to the Iran war, further illustrate how crucial home-grown industries are. The Make it with Adnoc Forum and events like it serve to reduce the UAE’s dependence on foreign suppliers. Adnoc is already playing an important role in this regard by buying more products from UAE manufacturers and encouraging investment in local production. Since launching its ICV programme in 2018, it has channelled more than Dh307 billion back into the national economy. It has signed about Dh80 billion worth of offtake agreements directed at local manufacturing. And in the first edition of the forum, held in May, it announced Dh200 billion in planned project awards for the 2026-2028 period. On Sunday, the company unveiled more than Dh60 billion in local manufacturing opportunities through 2030. It also announced substantive changes in its procurement, supplier registration and ICV policies to make it easier for manufacturers, suppliers and investors to compete for its business. “We are inviting companies to build capabilities in the UAE that will serve our industry and country for years to come,” said Dr Sultan Al Jaber, Adnoc’s managing director and group chief executive, and Minister of Industry and Advanced Technology. These are promising developments – also because they are geared towards ensuring that locally made products meet international standards for quality and pricing, thereby helping manufacturers compete in overseas markets too. Of course, the proof of the pudding is in the eating. The next iteration of the Make it in the Emirates event – a platform created by MoIAT for local and international companies to build and grow their manufacturing businesses in the country – will be held in May next year. It will again offer a clear opportunity to measure progress in investment, business partnerships, factory expansion and job creation. Over the longer term, it is sustained delivery on these fronts that will determine whether the UAE’s industrial strategy strengthens its economic foundations.

title: Opposition leader and Nobel Prize winner Maria Corina Machado returns to Venezuela
description: Issue of her return has strained relationship with Trump administration, which has signed major oil deal with government
content: Opposition leader Maria Corina Machado has returned to Venezuela after nearly a ⁠year outside the country. "I'm here with you," the Nobel Peace Prize winner wrote on social media early on Sunday. Her media team shared images of her in central-western Lara state, in the Plaza del Pueblo de Santa Rosa, where ⁠she appeared at a church. The issue of her return has strained her relationship with US President Donald Trump 's administration, which she has ​sought to ⁠cultivate as an ally since before the toppling of long-time leader Nicolas Maduro in January. After her Nobel win, Ms Machado gave the prize to Mr Trump, who had said several times he thought he deserved it. He has repeatedly expressed support for interim President Delcy Rodriguez , Mr Maduro's former ​vice president, and hailed deals on oil production and other business ventures by US companies in the South American country. Mr Trump said in September that it was too soon to consider democratic elections in Venezuela . Estoy aquí. Con ustedes — María Corina Machado (@MariaCorinaYA) October 25, 2026 Speaking at the White House on Sunday, Mr Trump said he did not know anything about Ms Machado's return to Venezuela and suggested that the US would continue to back Ms Rodriguez. "She's a very nice woman," he said, referring to Ms Machado. "But we're doing really well in Venezuela.” This is not the first time she has tried to return to Venezuela after she escaped the country in December 2025 to receive her Nobel prize. She had gone into hiding after her detention during a protest against recent elections. Ms Rodriguez was named interim leader of Venezuela after Mr Maduro was captured by US forces in early January and taken to New York to face drug and weapons-related charges. She said there will be future elections but no date has been set. Ms Rodriguez's government has allowed politicians, activists and journalists who spent years in exile to return, including some of Ms Machado’s closest allies. Allowing Ms Machado to organise and campaign would be a most consequential move, while detaining her or restricting her activities could put pressure on Washington to respond. But the US has has given priority to political and economic stability over an immediate democratic transition. A major energy agreement in early September has given the US access to as much as 65 billion barrels of Venezuela’s crude reserves. Ms Machado's desire to return had caused friction in Washington, with US officials asking her to delay her trip, Reuters reported in June. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said her return was the “direct result of the US-supported reconciliation talks". “The United States expects the freedoms of all sectors of Venezuelan politics to continue to be respected,” he said in a post on X. “Likewise, we expect all political actors to support these talks, which represent the best chance Venezuela has had in 30 years to peacefully achieve not just a free and fair election, but an enduring democracy.” Still, Ms Machado may have missed her chance at being part of the transition. US-backed talks between Ms Rodriguez’s government and a faction of the opposition ended their latest round this week with agreements to begin reviewing laws governing political disqualifications, parties and public demonstrations, among other measures.

title: UAE officials reject Iran's criticism of UN candidate Nusseibeh
description: Emirati diplomat joined the race to succeed Secretary General Antonio Guterres last week
content: Senior UAE officials have responded strongly to Iran’s criticism of Emirati diplomat Lana Nusseibeh 's campaign to become secretary general of the UN. Ms Nusseibeh joined the race for the UN 's top job last Wednesday after no clear front-runner emerged among eight other candidates. Her campaign has gathered support from a wider range of countries. Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammed Bagher Ghalibaf, who is also the country's top negotiator in talks with the US, on Sunday questioned Ms Nusseibeh's agenda in a post on X. Ms Nusseibeh on Monday responded to Mr Ghalibaf's remarks, saying she would pursue dialogue with Iran if selected for the top UN position. “I commit to engaging with Iran, like all member states, to advance peace and stability,” she said in an interview with Bloomberg . Dr Anwar Gargash, diplomatic adviser to President Sheikh Mohamed, said discussion of Ms Nusseibeh's agenda was welcome but that Mr Ghalibaf's remarks “lack objectivity”. He said they also “overlook the fact that the United Nations was established to promote dialogue and resolve conflicts, not to entrench enmities and settle scores”. Dr Gargash described Ms Nusseibeh as a professional figure known for bridging differences and prioritising diplomacy, and said this would naturally “provoke objections from some hardline voices”. Dr Ali Al Nuaimi, chairman of the defence, interior and foreign affairs committee of the Federal National Council, accused Mr Ghalibaf of trying to lecture the UAE despite Iran's record of “exporting instability”. “Lana Nusseibeh represents diplomacy, competence and the courage to build bridges. Your rhetoric represents the very destructive mentality that has brought so much suffering to our region,” Dr Al Nuaimi said in response. “The Middle East deserves a future shaped by those who build peace, not those who thrive on conflict.” UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres's second and final term will finish at the end of the year. Members of the Security Council have held several informal votes on a successor but no consensus has yet emerged. Ms Nusseibeh has called for generational change and pledged to reform the UN with “clearer priorities” if she is elected. She would be the first woman to lead the UN and the second Arab after Egypt's Boutros Boutros-Ghali. Appointed the UAE's ambassador to the UN in 2013, she previously held several positions in Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

title: Shadab Khan's world record century secures thrilling tri-series win for Pakistan
description: Last-wicket stand of 89 with Haris Rauf secures one-wicket win against England
content: Pakistan broke a number record as a stunning final stand helped secure a one-wicket win over England in the ODI tri-series in Lahore on Sunday. The hosts seemed down and out at 154-9, chasing a target of 242. However, all-rounder Shadab Khan smashed a career best 113 not out, with tail-ender Haris Rauf providing excellent company on seven from 19 deliveries. The last-wicket partnership of 89 not out was the highest 10th wicket stand in a successful chase in the history of ODIs. Shadab's score was also the highest individual score in ODI history by a batter batting at number eight or lower. England opener Ben Duckett held the innings together with a brilliant 105 but the rest of England's batting struggled just days after they scored 429 against Sri Lanka in Rawalpindi. SHADAB SUPERSTAR KHAN! WHAT A KNOCK! 🤩 A century to savour. @76Shadabkhan , take a bow 💯👏 #PAKvENG | #CricketKaJashan | #PinkDay pic.twitter.com/Vc9F63mE9V — Pakistan Cricket (@TheRealPCB) October 25, 2026 Captain Shaheen Afridi led the way with the ball with 4-46 while debutant quick Razaullah took 2-38. In reply, Pakistan batters too struggled against a disciplined England pace attack. Seamers Gus Atkinson (2-62), Jamie Overton (3-43) and spinner Liam Dawson (2-30) all but wrapped up the game as they reduced Pakistan to 154-9 in the 34th over. However, Shadab kept up the attack and found excellent support from Rauf. Shadab smashed 13 fours and five sixes in his 96-ball innings to take Pakistan close to the finish line. His effort seemed in vain when he was trapped lbw off a low full-toss from Atkinson. The players shook hands and were walking towards the pavilion when a belated review spotted an inside edge. 𝑷𝒂𝒌𝒊𝒔𝒕𝒂𝒏 𝒄𝒓𝒊𝒄𝒌𝒆𝒕 𝒂𝒕 𝒊𝒕𝒔 𝒗𝒆𝒓𝒚 𝒃𝒆𝒔𝒕 🇵🇰💚 A @HarisRauf14 boundary to seal a stunning one-wicket win! 🤩 #PAKvENG | #CricketKaJashan | #PinkDay pic.twitter.com/kngsaqs4in — Pakistan Cricket (@TheRealPCB) October 25, 2026 Shadab survived and took them to the finish line. Rauf hit debutant quick Henry Crocombe for boundary down the ground to seal victory. Pakistan captain Afridi was overjoyed after snatching victory from the jaws of defeat. “I can't say anything, Shadab and Haris, the way they finished the game, 89-run partnership. I've never seen like that in my life. Really happy as captain, starting from the morning, the team effort was top drawer,” the left-arm seamer said. England captain Harry Brook, whose team lost while defending 429 in the previous match, said the players did not do much wrong. “I don't think we went wrong with the ball, to be honest. I thought we did an exceptional job. Probably didn't quite get enough runs on the board, but the effort put up was phenomenal, couldn't have asked for more,” he said. England have now lost all three matches in the tri-series and are unlikely to qualify for the final.

title: Trump has 'a decision to make' on Iran as concerns over renewed strikes deepen
description: Head of US Central Command visits Strait of Hormuz
content: US President Donald Trump on Sunday said he has a "decision to make" on Iran, as talks remain stalled and concern is rising over whether he will restart hostilities. Mr Trump told Fox News on Sunday that he was considering his next moves with regard to Iran . "I have a decision to make: Do I finish it off, which would be very easy to do, or do I make a deal?" he said. "That's the decision." He added: “We don’t play games.” Mr Trump later told reporters at the White House that "there will not be a strike today". Mr Trump has said that he would not strike Iran until after the critical midterm elections on November 3 . The war, now nearing its eighth month, is likely to weigh heavily on voters as the price of fuel and other necessities remains high. The US has has sent more forces, including a third aircraft carrier group , towards the Arabian Gulf in recent weeks. Officials warn the period between the election and the new Congress taking office could be particularly dangerous, with a negotiated deal seen as the most likely way to end the conflict. The US is also reducing diplomatic and military staff in parts of the Middle East amid growing threats from Iran and the Iran-backed Houthi militants in Yemen. On Sunday, the US in Saudi Arabia said that government employees now require special authorisation from the chief of mission to use any airport in the country. "US government employees working in Saudi Arabia are not allowed to travel within 20 miles [32km] of the Yemen border due to safety risks and need special authorisation for travel to the provinces of Jizan, Asir, Najran, and the cities of Qatif, Yanbu and Taif," the US embassy said. It said US citizens wanting to travel should be aware of potential attacks on airports, airspace closures, flight cancellations and travel disruptions. Meanwhile, Admiral Brad Cooper, head of US Central Command . visited the Strait of Hormuz on Sunday, where he emphasised Washington's dedication to helping Gulf partners export crude oil. Centcom said in a statement that the US has helped Gulf allies export "more than 1.5 billion barrels" since summer. "We continue to stand shoulder to shoulder with our Gulf partners and the shipping industry," Admiral Cooper says. "This visit underscores our strong commitment to continued freedom of navigation through the Strait of Hormuz." US forces have "successfully cleared the strait's international shipping lanes of sea mines" laid by Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, Centcom said. Admiral Cooper said that the US remains "intensely focused on keeping commercial traffic flowing as we work with our teammates in the US interagency, Gulf Co-operation Council and shipping industry".

title: Man United v Bournemouth ratings: Disaster at Old Trafford as Tielemans and Dalot struggle
description: United suffer 3-0 defeat to slip towards relegation zone as pressure mounts on Michael Carrick
content: Manchester United's season went from bad to worse as they crashed to a 3-0 defeat at home to Bournemouth, compounding the pressure on manager Michael Carrick. Loud boos ran around Old Trafford as United slipped to to 16th in the Premier League after eight games – just one point above the relegation zone. Carrick decided to bench captain Bruno Fernandes , who had earlier questioned the team's tactics during the Champions League defeat to Como . The move failed to change the team's fortunes as Rayan scored for the Cherries in the 38th ​minute, ⁠with Marcus Tavernier adding a ‌second goal before the break. Evanlison's superb third saw fans begin to ​head for the exit, and that trickle became a flood as the final whistle approached. Fernandes remained on the bench as United buckled under pressure. With the final whistle greeted by a loud chorus of boos, the defeat left Carrick 's side in 16th place on seven points. They are without a win in the league since beating Ipswich Town 5-2 on August 30. 7 - Since the 2023-24 season, no Premier League side has lost more home games by a margin of three or more goals in all competitions than Man Utd (7). Troubles. pic.twitter.com/M8ixyscQ7q — OptaJoe (@OptaJoe) October 25, 2026 What they said Man United captain Harry Maguire to Sky Sports: “It wasn't good enough. It's not clicking at the moment. Results are not good enough and performances in the last week not good enough. Still early in the season. “Michael [Carrick] turned our season on its head last year and we played brilliant football and got brilliant results. This season we haven't performed well enough as individuals.” Man United manager Michael Carrick to Sky Sports: “It's difficult for me to have a day like this at this club and feel the emotion. “The situation is where we are and we haven't had results or performances that have been good enough. It's a tough situation, there's no hiding from it. What it looks like and what's next I really don't know. I will always do my best for the football club and I won't change that now. I love what I do and I feel the responsibility – we'll have to wait and see.” Boo's ring out at Old Trafford after Manchester United's 3-0 defeat to Bournemouth ❌ pic.twitter.com/Xr4iVFcYZU — Sky Sports Premier League (@SkySportsPL) October 25, 2026 Man United player ratings Senne Lammens – 4/10: It was always going to be full on and he faced four Bournemouth corners in the first 25 minutes. Not really at fault for the first two, but for the third he rushed out to try to win a ball, which held up, and was finished superbly. But the two tackles lost in midfield really caused that goal. Leny Yoro – 4/10: Slipped, which led directly to the second Bournemouth goal. Before that, he made a fine last-ditch block from the right back and stopped a Bournemouth cross. He’s a central defender playing at right back, an inexperienced one at that. Ayden Heaven – 3/10: Neat turn on 25, then he was booked for a two-footed lunge on 36 – and was lucky there was no contact as the Bournemouth player stepped away. The following free-kick led to the opening goal. Gave the ball away again on 49 and Bournemouth attacked again. A chastening afternoon. Harry Maguire – 5/10: Captain of the team and a makeshift, hesitant, back four. Blocked from Lewis Cook on 5 as Bournemouth started well. Booked. Up against Evanilson who scored mid week – and today. Diogo Dalot – 3/10: Right back being asked to play left back – and he doesn’t avoid it or say he’s injured. Chased a ball and crossed on 7. Attacked on the left on 17, but blasted the ball over rather than across the goal where players were waiting. Gave ball away on 24. Poor. Carlos Baleba – 5/10: Bit loose on the ball, losing possession. Shot miles over – like most United shots these days. Looks nervous. Andrey Santos – 4/10: Booked (again) for a lunging challenge on 22. Look lost and isn’t having the impact needed. Amad Diallo – 5/10: Flashes of skill as United had more possession, but seldom in dangerous areas. Youri Tielemans – 3/10: Given a big role replacing Fernandes. Failed. Whacked in a yellow card challenge by Tyler Adams on 26. Crossed after United’s best move of the first half, then struggled to thread a ball to Bryan Mbeumo a minute later. Booked just after the opening goal. Off at half time. Mason Mount – 4/10: A regular in pre-season, he’s played only 26 Premier League minutes before this start. Frustrating afternoon for him on the left – and almost everyone at Old Trafford. Almost nothing in the first half. And the second. Shot on target on 94. Bryan Mbeumo – 5/10: Fired United’s first shot on target after 40. Tried, but he’s getting no service. He’s also the only United player scoring right now but not today. Substitutes Matheus Cunha (Tielemans, 45') – 6/10: On for after his mess of a performance in Como. One good effort from the edge of the area. Lisandro Martinez (Heaven, 64') – 5/10: On and was skinned by Rayan within a minute. Shot on target on 67. Joshua Zirkzee (Baleba, 72') – 5/10: No consolation goal for him today. Shea Lacey (Amad, 78) – 6/10: A dash of pride from the talented young Scouser, but what could he do?

title: Druze leader Walid Joumblatt believes Israel will 'never leave' southern Lebanon
description: It is a stark reading of the region from a man who has lived through the civil war, Syrian occupation and assassination of his father
content: Druze leader Walid Joumblatt believes Israel will remain in southern Lebanon for decades. “They will never leave,” he tells On The Record with Hadley Gamble from his home in Beirut. "The Americans are withdrawing. What is left is [Benjamin] Netanyahu controlling and expanding his own territory , his biblical empire." It is a stark reading of the region from a man who has lived through Lebanon's civil war , the Syrian occupation and the assassination of his father. But it captures a shift visible across the region. With the US pulling troops out and Russia consumed by its own war, Israel is the region's dominant military power . As evidence, he refers to the scale of destruction in Lebanon. In earlier incursions, he said, southern Lebanon survived as a place. This time Israel is "just trying to eradicate all the memories of the south of Lebanon, as if they are preparing for settlements, colonies”. Israel now holds "security zones" on three fronts: across southern Lebanon, in southern Syria beyond the 1974 disengagement line, and over nearly 70 per cent of Gaza, according to Defence Minister Israel Katz. On October 21, he said Israel would not withdraw from any of them. "The policy of Israel, past, actual and future, is to erase Palestinian nationhood from Gaza to the West Bank, and expand to Syria and Lebanon," Mr Joumblatt says. "It doesn't matter who wins." Israeli officials claim their troops have destroyed more than 60 villages and about 23,000 structures in southern Lebanon. Israeli displacement orders have covered about 2,000 square kilometres south of the Zahrani River and residents are barred from returning. Israel's far-right Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich called in March for the annexation of all territory up to the Litani River. Lebanon's Health Ministry says 4,389 people were killed between March 2, when Hezbollah joined the regional war in support of Iran, and October 12. The group has been badly weakened but not broken. US and Israeli estimates put its losses since February at about 2,500 fighters. A June framework agreement between Lebanon, Israel and the US ties a phased Israeli withdrawal to Hezbollah's disarmament. Israel calls the deal "performance-based" and says its troops will stay as long as Hezbollah remains a threat. Seven rounds of direct negotiations have followed. Military talks at US Central Command ended on October 22 without agreement and with no further meeting set. Mr Joumblatt says Lebanon has mistakenly chosen "the path of [US Secretary of State] Marco Rubio, which will lead us to nowhere". The belief of some Lebanese ministers that Washington will press Israel to leave is, in his words, "a total fallacy". Mr Joumblatt also dismisses the disarmament demand itself. Most of the area south of the Litani has already been cleared, he says, but drones have changed the arithmetic. "They will tell you there is a factory of drones in Baalbek. You want to go there? It's absurd." Disarmament, in his view, can never be fully achieved, which is precisely why it suits a force that intends to stay. Israel's threats are growing rather than diminishing. On October 14, Mr Katz warned that if Hezbollah joined any Iranian attack, areas around Nabatieh and the Litani would become part of a permanent "security zone", residents wold be forced to leave Beirut's southern suburbs and more than a million Shiites would be displaced. "He said it, not me," Mr Joumblatt says. Asked whether Lebanon was simply waiting, he replies: "Unfortunately." The same logic applies in Syria. Israel moved past the 1974 disengagement line after the fall of former president Bashar Al Assad in December 2024 and Mr Joumblatt says its forces are now about 40km from Damascus. Part of the prize, he says, is water. "Mount Hermon is water." Syrian President Ahmad Al Shara, whom Mr Joumblatt backs, has no army to resist. Assad destroyed the military by turning it on his own people and Israel "will not ever allow him to have a modern army", he says. But Mr Joumblatt's sharpest words were aimed at members of his own community. The Druze, an offshoot of Islam with about a million members across Syria, Lebanon and Israel, straddle the very borders Israel is now redrawing. In Syria's Sweida province, much of the territory is held by militias loyal to Hikmat Al Hijri, a Druze spiritual leader who has advocated breaking away from Damascus under Israeli protection. Since April, his camp has run an administrative council for what it calls Jabal Bashan, the biblical name for the Druze mountain. In August, he declared the Druze an "inseparable part" of Israel and on October 7 his supporters marched through Sweida waving Israeli flags. "He's not a religious leader, just a puppet in the hands of the Israelis," Mr Joumblatt says. Those who follow Mr Hijri "have chosen to be used by the Israelis as good soldiers", Mr Joumblatt adds. "They are going the wrong path of history." Israel's own Druze community, he says, decide nothing. "The Israeli government decides." To Mr Joumblatt, the pattern on both sides of the border points to a single project – a belt of Druze-populated territory, running from the occupied Golan Heights through southern Syria and along the edge of southern Lebanon. That would give Israel strategic depth under the banner of protecting a minority. Arab and Turkish analysts have for more than a year described such a route, sometimes called "David's Corridor", running from the Golan Heights towards eastern Syria. Israel has never acknowledged any such plan. The evidence is growing. This week, Damascus sent troops to Sweida as Israel was reported to be flying surveillance and radar equipment into the province. Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad Al Shibani has accused Israel of funding and arming Druze militias, and a senior Syrian official has warned of an imminent Israeli-backed offensive. In February, the Israeli military created a new post to liaise with Druze communities in Syria and Lebanon, filled by Maj Gen Ghassan Alian, a Druze officer. In March, The National reported that Israeli officers had privately urged Christian and Druze villages in southern Lebanon to push out Muslim residents, both Shiite and Sunni, who were sheltering among them. More than 200 people fled. This week, Israeli tanks advanced towards the outskirts of Hebbariyeh in the Hasbaya district, the Druze-majority corner of southern Lebanon that borders Syria. Israel says its role in Sweida is to protect Druze from a massacre, a claim it made amid the events of July 2025, when violence in the province left about 1,700 people dead. Mr Joumblatt does not dispute the killings, but he says Druze fighters also drove Bedouin families from their homes and that a mission of inquiry and a compromise should have followed. "Nothing happened," he says. He insists Mr Hijri does not speak for all Syria's Druze, many of whom live in Damascus suburbs alongside Christians and Muslims and are alienated by his separatism. Mr Joumblatt invoked Sultan Al Atrash, who led the 1925 Druze uprising against French rule, and his father, Kamal Joumblatt, an Arab nationalist assassinated in 1977. "I feel that I am abandoned by some Druze," he says. "Never mind. I will go on my own, even if I stay alone." For a minority, abandoning Arab solidarity is "suicide", Mr Joumblatt says. With traditional counterweights gone, focused elsewhere, Mr Joumblatt says Israeli power will be unchecked "It doesn't mean that while they [America] were present it was more calm," he says. "But it was significant." Asked whether America has left a vacuum and Israel is filling it, he answers yes to both. Russia, a patron of Assad's regime in Syria, is in the fifth year of its war in Ukraine. Europe has been sidelined by Washington. Saudi Arabia is absorbed by its conflict with Yemen's Houthis – the Iran-backed group has launched missiles and drones at airports in Riyadh, Abha and Dammam, killing 22 people. "The Arab world nowadays is powerless," Mr Joumblatt says. He would like Lebanon to become a neutral state similar to the Swiss model, but says that requires the consent of its neighbours. "Israel will not ever accept that." His prescription at home is the one he has offered for years: a national dialogue, built on the principle that only the state may bear arms, leading to a negotiated decommissioning of Hezbollah's weapons, with Iran's backing. Critics, including some western diplomats, say he is too soft on the group. "Tough enough to civil war?" he says in reply, recalling how the Lebanese military splintered when it was turned on its own people in the 1980s. His request of Washington is brief. "Give us some better diplomats here, and better policy there." Then he returns to his central point. With the US stepping back, Israel feels free "to do whatever they want, everywhere, anywhere, using force".

title: Dubai to boost local produce and reduce waste in new food security strategy
description: Sheikh Hamdan approves project aimed at establishing emirate as global leader in sustainability
content: Authorities in Dubai have unveiled details of a new strategy to promote food security in the emirate. The Dubai Food Security Strategy 2030 was announced on Sunday by the Dubai Environment and Climate Change Authority. The strategy is aimed at ensuring sufficient and safe food is available to all Dubai residents, the emirate's media office reported. The project, approved by Sheikh Hamdan bin Mohammed , Crown Prince of Dubai, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Defence, is focused on five key areas: food availability, affordability, quality and safety, sustainability and resilience, and industry empowerment. “The Dubai Food Security Strategy 2030 is founded on a clear vision to position Dubai as a global leader in sustainable food security, supported by advanced technologies and resilient supply chains," said Decca director general Ahmed bin Thani. "This strategy will contribute to boosting local production, reducing food waste, and ensuring the availability and affordability of healthy food. "We have set five strategic initiatives to achieve these goals, empowering the agriculture and food industries and advancing local markets in partnership with stakeholders across the ecosystem, thereby establishing a resilient and sustainable food security framework for Dubai.” The first initiative focuses on projects that foster the growth of the agriculture and food production industries, ensure the optimal use of resources, enhance sector competitiveness and promote sustainable practices, the media office reported. The second part of the strategy is aimed at strengthening food supply chains through a "variety of strategic projects creating an efficient, agile, and responsive food supply system capable of meeting evolving demand, adapting to market conditions and responding effectively to emergencies". The third initiative focuses on encouraging healthy, sustainable food consumption while reducing food loss and waste through public awareness campaigns. The fourth "seeks to enhance governance, regulation, and economic support for integrated food systems while strengthening the sector’s ability to attract sustainable investments". The fifth initiative is "dedicated to creating a food ecosystem capable of adapting to market fluctuations through advanced, partnership-driven infrastructure that effectively responds to market demands and consumer needs".

title: UAE and Benin agree to trade deal in Abu Dhabi
description: President Sheikh Mohamed and Benin leader Romuald Wadagni witness signing of agreement
content: The UAE and Benin have announced a Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement , marking a new chapter in trade and investment relations between the two nations. President Sheikh Mohamed and Benin's President Romuald Wadagni witnessed the signing of the agreement in Abu Dhabi on Sunday, carried out by UAE Minister of Foreign Trade Dr Thani Al Zeyoudi and Benin's Minister of Tourism and Foreign Trade, Olushegun Adjadi Bakari. The deal, once ratified, will reduce or eliminate customs duties on a wide range of goods, remove trade barriers and improve market access for service providers and investors. It comes against the backdrop of rapidly growing bilateral ties — non- oil trade between the two countries reached $2.15 billion in 2025, a 65 per cent increase on 2024 and more than double the $1.01 billion recorded in 2021. Trade momentum has continued into 2026, with bilateral non-oil trade reaching $1.29 billion in the first half of the year, up 37.4 per cent year on year. Sheikh Mohamed said the agreement "marks a significant milestone" in bilateral relations, adding that it reflects "a common ambition to achieve long-term development aims, create new opportunities for our business communities, strengthen economic resilience, and contribute to prosperity and stability in our regions." Mr Wadagni emphasised the agreement's importance in advancing shared sustainable development objectives.

title: UAE captain Rahul Chopra shines in stifling heat but national team lose to Netherlands
description: Returning leader’s heroic effort in vain as hosts suffer another defeat in Cricket World Cup League Two in Dubai
content: Rahul Chopra, the UAE captain, blacked out because of heat exhaustion while batting against the Netherlands. The 31-year-old batter made 82 not out on his return to captaining the national team in the first match of the Cricket World Cup League Two tri-series in Dubai. His stay at the crease was interrupted for a number of overs as he was led away by paramedics and Dr Manish Pardeshi, the UAE team’s medical head. He received treatment to cool his body temperature in a pitch-side ambulance, and later returned to finish his innings. His effort eventually went in vain. The Netherlands chased the UAE’s total of 244 with three wickets left to win the series opener. The Dutch players, who were arriving from the cool of European autumn, also showed signs of being debilitated by the searing heat at the ICC Academy. “It is the first time I have felt like this in cricket; the heat was too much today,” Chopra said. “I had a total blackout in front of my eyes. That is why I needed the help of doctors. I went back out to bat because I knew it was not easy to hit from the start. “I was already set [before he retired] and I had the chance to go back and do something for the team, and add 10 or 20 more runs.” UAE captain Rahul Chopra really struggling with the heat while playing a heroic innings against Netherlands here in Dubai. He was staggering as he was led from the field by medical staff into the back of an ambulance pic.twitter.com/A3Csh9Tw5H — Paul Radley (@PaulRadley) October 25, 2026 Chopra’s pluckiness in the face of adversity was a much needed lift for his struggling side. The national team will finish last in CWCL2, whatever happens in their remaining games against the Netherlands and Oman in this series. They will then have to play to try to retain their ODI status at a World Cup Qualifier Play-off in Nepal in December. To add to the issues, Harpreet Bhatia, the previous captain, is now on an indefinite break from cricket . He has returned to India, the country of his birth, as his mother is ill. Chopra said he was glad to be given the chance to captain the side again as he wants to make a difference. “I always want to try to be a team man,” Chopra said. “I always want to win games for the team. “The responsibility of a leadership, when it has been given to me, I have always taken it on behalf of the team. I always want to lead from the front and do well for the team, whether I am captain or not.” Chopra was not the only victim of conditions which were unseasonably tough for late October. Aryan Dutt and Paul van Meekeren, the Netherlands bowlers, each had to pull out of bowling with painful bouts of cramp, while dragging themselves through wearying bowling spells. Their efforts were rewarded, though, as they chased down their target of 245 thanks to a sparkling century by Max O’Dowd, their opener. Azharuddin Qureshi, the strength and conditioning lead for the UAE team, praised the players for their efforts in such exacting conditions. “This October has been a little bit different in Dubai compared to the earlier years which I have seen,” Qureshi said. “We have also played in June with West Indies in Sharjah in 50-over games. We started in the afternoon, finished in the evening, but we never seen the players from both the teams getting so much cramps. “There was a lot of humid today. It felt totally different to what we had expected for this month or this month. “It feels like summer is getting extended in Dubai, and this was just one of the days where the humidity was too much, especially the first half of the game today. “We managed from our side to keep the players on the field. It does get difficult for the players, and I can, understand what they go. But they played their heart out.”

title: Sheikh Khaled to begin official visit to Canada on Monday
description: Crown Prince of Abu Dhabi to meet Prime Minister Mark Carney to strengthen UAE-Canada ties
content: Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed , Crown Prince of Abu Dhabi, will travel to Canada on Monday for an official visit aimed at deepening ties between the two nations. The Crown Prince will meet with Prime Minister Mark Carney during the visit, which begins on Monday. The two leaders are expected to discuss ways to strengthen bilateral relations and advance the strategic partnership between the UAE and Canada. Key areas of focus will include expanding co-operation across priority sectors, with both sides seeking to build on shared interests and aspirations for long-term growth and prosperity. No specific sectors were named ahead of the visit, reported state news agency Wam.

title: Two UAE convoys carrying 260 tonnes of aid arrive in Gaza
description: Operation Gallant Knight 3 lorries enter stricken enclave as total shipments near 140,000 tonnes
content: Two UAE aid convoys carrying 260 tonnes of food supplies entered Gaza this week, as the country's humanitarian operation continues its relief efforts. The convoys, comprising 10 lorries, were dispatched under Operation Gallant Knight 3, the UAE's initiative providing relief to Palestinians in the Gaza Strip. Their arrival brings the total number of lorries to have entered Gaza under the operation to 14,594, collectively taking 138,290 tonnes of humanitarian aid since the mission's launch. The convoys are assembled and prepared at the UAE Humanitarian Aid Logistics Centre in Al Arish, Egypt, where an integrated system manages the receiving, sorting, preparation and dispatch of supplies, state news agency Wam reported on Sunday. Since the launch of Operation Gallant Knight 3, the UAE has provided more than $4 billion in humanitarian assistance to Gaza, accounting for 46 per cent of global humanitarian aid directed to the enclave since 2023. That assistance has included 130,708 tonnes of relief, medical and food supplies delivered by 796 aircraft, 25 ships and 14,483 lorries. By channelling aid through established logistics networks and co-ordinating with Egyptian authorities at the Rafah crossing, the operation aims to ensure supplies reach those most in need in a structured and efficient manner.

title: Saudi Arabia announces support measures as electricity and water tariffs rise
description: Minimum wage for Saudi private sector workers will increase
content: Saudi Arabia has announced a package of measures to cushion the impact of rising electricity and water prices, including monthly financial support for some workers and pensioners. The measures, reported by the Saudi Press Agency on Sunday, will take effect ahead of tariff changes scheduled for January 1. King Salman ordered monthly payments of 500 riyals ($133) for civil and military employees, retirees and eligible social security households, following a proposal by Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman . The allowance also cover some bereaved relatives of people covered by the social insurance system. The measures also include higher minimum wage requirements for Saudi nationals working in the private sector, under the Nitaqat initiative to boost the employment of Saudis. The minimum monthly wage required for a Saudi employee to count as a full worker towards a company’s nationalisation quota will rise to 5,000 riyals, with the change taking effect six months after implementation begins. It will then increase to 6,000 riyals, 12 months after the first increase takes effect. The support package is intended to ease the impact of the utility tariff changes while supporting wage levels and the long-term employment of Saudi nationals in the private sector. Saudi Arabia has been facing an increasing number of attacks by Yemen's Houthis, which have disrupted the Riyadh airport operations and brought parts of the kingdom’s capital to a standstill, threatening its ambitious plans to overhaul the economy and attract foreign investment. The attacks come as Saudi Arabia pursues Vision 2030, the programme launched a decade ago by Prince Mohammed to reduce the kingdom’s dependence on oil and transform it into a centre for tourism, international events and multinational businesses. The strategy has already faced mounting challenges from the wider Middle East war, including Iranian attacks on US allies across the Gulf. The renewed Houthi campaign adds further pressure, with strikes targeting critical infrastructure, including oil sites and airports.

title: Al Nassr v Al Wasl Asian Champions League clash in Riyadh postponed
description: AFC Elite match to be played at later date
content: The Asian Champions League (ACL) clash between Cristiano Ronaldo's Al Nassr and Dubai club Al Wasl has been postponed. The ACL Elite match was originally scheduled to take place at the King Saud University Stadium in Riyadh on Monday. However, the match has been postponed to a later date. The Asian Football Confederation stated that “the new match date and kick off time will be confirmed and communicated in due course”. While no official reason for the postponement was provided, travel issues related to regional disturbances are believed to be a factor. However, other Asian Champions League matches are scheduled to go ahead as planned. Saudi Arabia club Al Qadsiah are scheduled to host Qatari side Al Sadd at the Prince Mohammed Bin Fahd Stadium in Dammam. Also, high-flying UAE side Al Ain are set to host Iranian team Tractor FC at the Hazza Bin Zayed Stadium in Al Ain on Monday. Matches and events in Saudi Arabia have been affected amid intense fighting between the kingdom and Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi rebels. A Saudi Pro League match between Al Nassr and Asian champions Al Ahli was postponed. The Six Kings tennis tournament featuring the likes of Carlos Alcaraz, Novak Djokovic and Alexander Zverev in Saudi Arabia was postponed due to attacks on Riyadh. Elsewhere, the Riyadh Fashion Week and Future Investment Initiative conference were also postponed. Dakar Rally moves out of Saudi Arabia The ​2027 ​edition ​of ⁠the ⁠Dakar Rally ​has been moved ⁠out of Saudi Arabia due ⁠to security concerns, ​organisers ⁠Amaury ‌Sport ​Organisation said on Sunday. "Dakar Saudi Arabia 2027, scheduled from January 1 to 15, 2027, will not be held in the kingdom, following recent developments in the region," organisers said in a statement. "This decision is exceptional and one-off and was taken in close coordination with the Saudi Automobile and Motorcycle Federation (SAMF), and with the support of the FIA and the FIM." However, organisers said the 2028 Dakar Rally will take place in Saudi Arabia to celebrate the competition's 50th edition.

title: Dubai awards Dh3 billion in contracts to expand stormwater drainage network
description: Project aims to increase drainage capacity in emirate by 700 per cent
content: Dubai Municipality has awarded four contracts worth Dh3 billion to expand the emirate’s stormwater drainage network, as part of a wider project aimed at increasing rainwater drainage capacity by 700 per cent by 2033. The project falls under the third phase of the Dh30 billion Tasreef programme and will involve constructing and extending 100km of main drainage lines, with diameters of up to three metres. The work will cover 100 square kilometres across key residential, commercial, industrial and tourism areas, including Jumeirah, Umm Suqeim, Al Safa, Al Manara, Al Quoz, Al Barsha, Al Wasl, Zabeel, Al Bada’a, Al Satwa and Al Marmoom. The project forms part of Dubai’s long-term efforts to improve infrastructure resilience and prepare for future climate challenges while accommodating the emirate’s urban expansion. “Dubai did not simply stop to assess the damage or look for solutions. It took a swift and bold decision to begin a drainage programme designed to serve the city for the next 100 years,” Marwan bin Ghalita, director general of Dubai Municipality, said earlier this month. Dubai Municipality awards contracts for four new projects under Phase 3 of the ‘Tasreef’ Programme to develop Dubai’s stormwater drainage network. With a total value of AED3 billion, the projects will involve the construction and extension of approximately 100 kilometres of main… pic.twitter.com/fjuUCstjOe — Dubai Media Office (@DXBMediaOffice) October 25, 2026 The Tasreef scheme was launched in 2024 after the country experienced widespread flooding caused by unprecedented rainfall in April that year. In June 2025, the municipality completed a Dh277m sewerage and rainwater drainage network in Nad Al Sheba, while in April this year, the drainage network in Al Quoz Creative Zone was completed. The wider Tasreef programme approved aims to increase Dubai’s rainwater drainage capacity sevenfold and enable the system to handle more than 20 million cubic metres of water daily once completed. The project is scheduled for completion in 2033 and is designed to meet the emirate’s drainage needs for the next 100 years. Rather than focusing solely on repairing damage, authorities opted for a long term infrastructure upgrade to improve the emirate’s preparedness for extreme weather events. Earlier in the week, the municipality announced it hadprepared 10 temporary water collection lakes in "strategic locations to accommodate rainwater runoff in the event of heavy rainfall and reduce pressure on the main drainage networks".

title: Yemeni forces intercept Houthi weapons being smuggled from coast
description: Operation in Shabwa province comes days after missile attack on security camp killed 77
content: Yemeni security forces have arrested 13 alleged members of a Houthi cell and seized a lorry carrying weapons, ammunition and explosives smuggled by sea into Shabwa province, the governor’s office said on Sunday. Shabwa Governor Awad Al Wazir, who also heads the provincial security committee, said the operation followed surveillance and intelligence-gathering efforts as fighting rages between the Yemeni government and the Iran -backed Houthis. Saudi Arabia intercepted a series of missiles and drones, including over its capital, Riyadh, on Sunday as it continues to counter Houthi attacks. Two people were injured by shrapnel from intercepted ballistic missiles in Khamis Mushait and Ahad Rafidah. Preliminary investigations found the weapons seized in Yemen had been transported by boat and handed over to the cell’s members along the southern coast. The shipment was due to be moved for the benefit of the Houthis, according to a report submitted to the governor. The seized cargo included sniper rifles, ammunition, improvised explosive devices described by the authorities as highly destructive and various types of projectiles. Investigations are continuing to establish the circumstances of the smuggling operation, identify its wider network and determine who else was involved, the report said. The seizure came days after a Houthi ballistic missile attack against members of the Rapid Intervention Forces in Shabwa that, according to the governor’s office, killed 77 people and wounded 195. The Houthis acknowledged the attack, describing it as a concentration of “Saudi enemy” forces managed by Saudi officers. The Iran-backed group claimed Saudi personnel were among dozens of people killed or wounded. The Saudi-led coalition in Yemen said on Sunday that air defences intercepted and destroyed 10 ballistic missiles launched towards the kingdom’s southern region. It also reported intercepting a ballistic missile launched towards Riyadh and destroying a drone aimed at the capital. After updated US travel warnings for the region, American government workers now need "special authorisation" from the chief of mission to use any airport in Saudi Arabia, the embassy said on Sunday. The Houthis have recently attacked government-held sites, including Aden airport and the presidential palace in the interim capital. A missile and drone attack on the palace killed five security personnel. Yemeni government forces launched a campaign this month to recapture Houthi-held areas, making advances near the strategic Bab Al Mandeb strait, while the rebels continue to besiege Taiz , a major stronghold of anti-Houthi forces in the southern highlands. Shabwa, an energy-rich province on Yemen’s southern coast, is home to the Balhaf liquefied natural gas site, the country’s largest industrial investment. In Shabwa, Mr Al Wazir called on security and military units to increase readiness, strengthen surveillance and inspections along land and maritime routes, and improve co-ordination and intelligence-sharing to prevent further smuggling and infiltration attempts. Yemen’s civil war began in 2014 when the Houthis seized the capital, Sanaa. A Saudi-led military intervention followed in 2015 at the government’s request. A UN-brokered truce in 2022 maintained a fragile calm until fighting intensified again this year.
