The conflict has become another front in the wider US-Israeli war against Iran, with the Houthis escalating attacks on Saudi Arabia , the world’s largest crude oil exporter. Yemen is already experiencing one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises, and renewed fighting threatens to further worsen conditions for civilians.

title: Adnoc prepares new wave of oil and gas tenders for 2027
description: UAE oil company is aiming 5 million bpd of oil production capacity by next year
content: Abu Dhabi National Oil Company (Adnoc) plans to issue tenders for offshore sour gas developments, an export gas pipeline and enhanced oil recovery projects in 2027, as the state energy giant prepares a new wave of engineering and construction work. "The demand is real, and the timeline is set," Adel Al Yafei, Adnoc's senior vice president for group commercial operations and execution, told suppliers on Sunday at the second Make it with Adnoc Forum in Abu Dhabi, before the Adipec energy conference. Adnoc has awarded tenders for 10 major engineering, procurement and construction (EPC) projects so far this year, along with more than 8,000 requisitions, contracts and purchase requests involving more than 1,500 suppliers, he said. The offshore sour gas development includes wellhead towers and pipelines, while the export gas pipeline project involves new wells and an offshore cluster to expand capacity, according to presentation slides. The enhanced oil recovery project will use alternating injections of carbon dioxide and water to increase production. Downstream projects scheduled for tender in 2027 include refinery residue upgrading and additional export berths for natural gas liquids and sulphur. The tender pipeline also covers a long-term development project involving new wells, a processing island and offshore platforms, alongside onshore and offshore power distribution, an island power link and offshore field connections. For 2028, Adnoc outlined onshore and offshore oilfield developments, an integrated onshore gas project, gas storage, digitalisation and infrastructure upgrades. The company did not disclose project values. Adnoc is seeking to raise its oil production capacity to 5 million barrels a day by 2027, from 4.85 million bpd. The tender pipeline comes as the company seeks to expand domestic manufacturing, unveiling more than Dh60 billion ($16.3 billion) in opportunities for UAE suppliers through 2030 at the same forum. The initiative covers more than 200 essential products and critical spare parts, many currently imported, as the company seeks to reduce its exposure to global supply disruptions. "Adnoc will expand and grow in all of its assets," Mr Al Yafei said. Beyond major construction projects, the company plans to issue tenders for drilling and upstream services in 2027 and 2028, including downhole completion, drilling fluids and cementing. Operational contracts will cover inspection and maintenance of compressors, turbines and pumps. The plans come as Adnoc changes how it procures equipment and services, aiming to reduce tender cycle times by 40 per cent without cutting the time suppliers have to prepare bids. "That's the time we save from our process, not the time we take from what you need to deliver a good technical and commercial offer," Mr Al Yafei said. Bidding periods will be aligned with market conditions, while project schedules will take account of urgency, complexity and supplier capacity. Companies will also receive feedback after tenders to help improve future bids. Adnoc has doubled its EPC contracting principles to 20 from 10, seeking greater flexibility and competition. Unit-rate contracts will be negotiated against market median prices rather than unusually high or low bids. For EPC tenders, the company will prioritise the most competitive offer and negotiate exclusively with that bidder if it meets Adnoc's benchmark. First-time bidders will also be assessed on their capacity to deliver. Adnoc is also revising its in-country value (ICV) procurement framework. From November 1, bids will be assessed using a formula weighted 70 per cent towards commercial terms and 30 per cent towards ICV, said Salama Alawadhi, senior vice president for group commercial, ICV and industrial development.

title: Dubai Fashion Week: fashion as protest with Nafsika Skourti
description: Regional designers make strong showing at the spring/summer 2027 collections
content: Dubai Fashion Week opened its spring/summer 2027 season with a reminder that the region’s fashion ambitions extend well beyond the runway, with shows and presentations by designers from far and wide, underlining the importance of the Middle Eastern market within fashion. Nafsika Skourti The highlight of day two was undoubtedly the Dubai Fashion Week debut of Palestinian-Greek label Nafsika Skourti, which closed the day with a runway show called Sisters by Choice. The brand was started by sisters Nafsika, the creative director, and Stephanie Skourti, the business lead. "I was thinking that there is no official way to celebrate your friends ... and the energy really matched having a happy protest," Nafsika explained backstage. "So, we have slogans saying things like No Wrong Turns, and Sisters by Choice, and all these affirming statements that I really connected with." Returning to the runways after a nine-year hiatus, the collection was relaxed and built around daytime silhouettes in light, easy-to-wear fabrics. It was, she said, an exploration of "daywear, more activewear, and really leaning into the busy women we are." Stephanie explained the shift away from occasion-wear. "Anyone who has been following the brand will notice that we used to do high and low before, and now it’s a lot more intentional, while at the same time, staying true to our brand codes, like corsetry and detailing," she said. This was seen as sleeves and skirts trimmed with ribbons and open back tops made from woven beading, and mixed with roomy floral skirts, and sporty zip through tops. The result was lightweight pieces, cut for movement, that placed the demands of women's lives front and centre. Amid endless shows of beautiful, yet restrictive evening wear, this felt revolutionary. "Where we are from is something we are always thinking about and exploring. We feel very Arab. We grew up in the Middle East,” Stephanie said. Yousef Al Jasmi The runway programme of the week opened with Kuwait’s Yousef Al Jasmi, a designer well-versed in dressing for the spotlight. Having created looks for Lady Gaga, he understands the appeal of theatrical excess, and this collection delivered it in abundance. Crystal-encrusted dresses skimmed the body, long strands of crystals cascaded from shoulder to floor, and sculpted bodices were paired with sheer, close-fitting skirts. Moving from barely-there nude to dramatic black, the collection was designed to catch the light from every angle. Sara Pedram Next came self-taught designer Sara Pedram, whose collection, Simurgh, drew inspiration from The Conference of the Birds , the 12th-century epic poem by Attar of Nishapur. Exploring transformation, spirituality and Persian cultural heritage, Pedram translated the story into a series of sculptural silhouettes. A ballerina opened the show, followed by sheer creations with wing-like extensions at the shoulders. A richly embellished burnt-amber column gown gave way to a shimmering cascade of swaying paillettes, while a Prussian-blue velvet gown featured a Swarovski-crystal Tree of Life traced across its train, symbolising growth and renewal. Most arresting was a voluminous, full-skirted creation in rough hessian, hand-painted with a scene inspired by Persian poet Hafez , whose work, Pedram explained, was “close to my heart”. “Simurgh is a legendary bird that represents rebirth, transformation and rising again,” Pedram said backstage. “This collection is very personal to me, especially this year. Fashion is more than a beautiful dress; I love to explain the story behind each piece.” Pallavi Puri Indian designer Pallavi Puri followed with Beyond Borders, a collection exploring cultural exchange through a wardrobe designed for women across the region. Drawing inspiration from family and friends, their tastes and the way they dress, Puri reworked traditional Indian beadwork for a contemporary audience, citing Emirati, Asian and Moroccan women among her most inspirational clientele. Horses were another recurring motif, reflecting both the designer’s long-standing fascination with the animals and Dubai’s enduring equestrian culture. Indian model Lisa Haydon opened the show, while Lebanese actress Cyrine Abdel Nour closed it wearing an embellished bridal look. “Did you realise one is from India and one is Arab?” Puri said, highlighting the collection’s cross-cultural message. “My show is Beyond Borders, so it is about mixing and coming together.” It was Haydon's first appearance for Puri and a return to opening a runway show after a lengthy break. “When you open a show, you set the tone, so I was extra nervous,” she admitted. “This is [Puri’s] debut show [at Dubai Fashion Week], so it was quite a special moment to be part of. I have walked in Dubai Fashion Week before, but today was a lot of firsts.” Kresha Bajaj Closing the evening was Kresha Bajaj, who returned with a collection showcasing the designer’s signature beadwork. Applied to daywear, it trailed across delicate crocheted tops, framed the necklines of street-style tank tops and formed striking zebra-skin patterns. As the collection moved into evening wear, the embellishment became increasingly elaborate, forming latticework across torsos, looping around hips and swaying across legs with every step. It was glamour with an edge. The Showroom Before the first models took their places on Thursday, a showroom in Dubai Design District previewed emerging talent from around the world and introduced several designers to the UAE market. Among them was Bahrain’s Touchless, whose 3D-printed handbags have already attracted the attention of British Vogue , Selfridges, Level Shoes and Fashion Trust Arabia, as well as making an appearance in the Bridgerton universe. Egyptian jeweller-turned-eyewear designer Amr Saad brought a precious touch with bespoke gold and silver frames finished with jewellery-like detailing along the arms and bridge. Tunisian footwear label Balga drew on traditional metalworking techniques for its sculptural heels. Leather mules featured hand-hammered metalwork, including a tapered heel etched with graphic lines reminiscent of baklava. Kuwaiti designer Kochylia, whose name means seashells in Greek, offered a considered take on wardrobe classics, from reworked trench coats to tuxedo jackets finished with handmade porcelain buttons fashioned from Kuwaiti mud.

title: Adnoc offers $16.3bn in manufacturing opportunities to UAE suppliers
description: Abu Dhabi company plans to reduce reliance on overseas supply chains and speed up procurement
content: Abu Dhabi National Oil Company (Adnoc) is offering more than Dh60 billion ($16.3 billion) in local manufacturing opportunities until 2030, as the state energy conglomerate overhauls procurement to cut supplier on-boarding time by as much as 80 per cent. The opportunities, which cover more than 200 essential products and critical spare parts, were unveiled on Sunday at the second Make it with Adnoc Forum in Abu Dhabi, before the Adipec energy conference. The inaugural forum was held in May. Adnoc aims to replace imports with local production to shorten delivery times and reduce exposure to global supply disruptions. “We are inviting companies to build capabilities in the UAE that will serve our industry and country for years to come,” said Dr Sultan Al Jaber, Minister of Industry and Advanced Technology and managing director and group chief executive of Adnoc The announcement comes at a time when global energy supply chains continue to face disruption, which has put the importance of domestic manufacturing into sharp focus said Omar Al Nuaimi, Adnoc’s group chief for commercial and in-country value (ICV). “It was our suppliers and vendors and partners who enabled us to continue pushing our products to the world and energy to the world,” he told the forum. Adnoc has already reached Dh80 billion of its Dh90 billion local manufacturing target for 2030, supporting the localisation of more than 130 products and the establishment or expansion of 95 factories, Mr Al Nuaimi said. The latest opportunities span drilling equipment, electrical and automation systems, chemicals, catalysts, piping and heavy machinery. Products sought for local production include electrical submersible pumps, oil country tubular goods, seamless pipes and compressors. “These are not 200 products only. These are opportunities, partnerships, industries, and a whole value chain,” Mr Al Nuaimi said. Adnoc is also simplifying how suppliers compete for contracts, aiming to shorten purchasing cycles by up to 40 per cent, halve documentation requirements and remove prequalification for 60 per cent of service categories. From November 1, commercial and ICV offers will be assessed together in a single evaluation weighted 70 per cent towards commercial terms and 30 per cent towards ICV. This marks a change from Adnoc’s previous bid-matching approach, encouraging suppliers to submit their most competitive offers from the outset.. Contracts below Dh2 million will be exempt from ICV requirements, while those below Dh50 million will no longer face ICV retention obligations, said Salama Al Awadhi, Adnoc’s senior vice president for group commercial, ICV and industrial development. Supplier registration, which previously took weeks, can now be completed within a day, she added. Artificial intelligence will also be used to verify documents through a consolidated supplier platform. The revised procurement rules could have wider implications for the UAE’s industrial supply chain, particularly among smaller companies working under major contractors, said Osama Fadhel, assistant undersecretary for industrial accelerators in the Ministry of Industry and Advanced Technology. Zero bureaucracy is in our DNA today Osama Amir Fadhel, Ministry of Industry and Technology He told The National that the 30 per cent local content weighting would create a “ripple effect” through the energy sector and could serve as a model for other major buyers. “Zero bureaucracy is in our DNA today,” Mr Al Fadhel said, describing how efforts to automate government services are spreading to private and state-linked businesses. The national ICV programme has redirected more than Dh473 billion into the UAE economy, including Dh126 billion last year, and created 28,000 jobs for Emiratis, he said in his address to the forum. Adnoc’s own programme has redirected more than Dh307 billion since 2018, with its annual contribution reaching Dh65 billion last year, up from Dh18 billion in its first year. The company is working with the ministry, the Abu Dhabi Investment Office and other partners to connect manufacturers with investment opportunities and financing through the National Industrial Resilience Fund. It has also expanded its Local+ programme to more than 100 UAE manufacturers, from 70 at its launch in May, requiring contractors bidding on new projects to source eligible products from approved local suppliers. Abu Dhabi Oilfield Services Company, which participated in the inaugural Make it with Adnoc Forum in May, has doubled its UAE manufacturing capacity since the ICV programme began eight years ago and now exports globally from Abu Dhabi, said Mazen Shehada, its director of business development. He said the latest changes would make it easier for manufacturers to access Adnoc’s procurement pipeline, while giving them greater certainty over future demand. “With their offtake agreements, they’re giving us a commitment to enable us to invest more and be able to be confident in our investments,” Mr Shehada told The National .

title: Maximalist US and Iran positions fuelling conflict, former Pakistani PM says
description: Signs of renewed escalation are 'not good', former caretaker prime minister Anwaar Ul Haq Kakar says
content: Maximalist negotiating positions by both the US and Iran have prevented an end to the Middle East conflict, amid worrying signs of the war escalating, a former prime minister of Pakistan told The National. “I think when you go for a maximalist position, that's a stumbling block,” Anwaar Ul Haq Kakar said in a rare interview from Islamabad. “I think both sides probably choose to remain maximalist, and that is the prime reason for [a lack of] progress on this account when it comes to the resolution of the conflict.” The US and Iran have disagreed on the scale and timing of commitments to end the war, including an end to the US blockade of Iran’s seaports, a reopening of the Strait of Hormuz , sanctions relief for Tehran and guarantees of an end to fighting across all fronts in the region. Pakistan brought together Iranian and US officials for the highest-level diplomatic contacts between the two countries in decades following the start of US-Israeli operations against Iran in February. In June, the two countries agreed in Islamabad on a plan to end the war, but the conflict continued, albeit at a lower intensity. Since then, mediators including Pakistan have been urging both sides to return to the negotiating table amid a deadlock over progress. Pakistan’s foremost aim is that military conflict should not resume, said Mr Kakar, who served as acting prime minister of Pakistan before incumbent Shehbaz Sharif took office in March 2024. “Well, this is a desire. This is a wish list. Whether we would be able to achieve that or not, that needs to be tested in probably few days or weeks from now,” he said. "US withdrawals of diplomatic staff from the region in recent days are an indication that the US and Israel could be preparing to resume military strikes," he added, "which is not a good sign." Already hit economically by energy price spikes caused by the war, Pakistan would be further squeezed by renewed fighting, as would other countries around the world, he added. The nation of 260 million people has already endured sharp fuel price increases following a surge in global oil prices prompted by the war. “It would hit us badly,” Mr Kakar said. “Whether it comes to inflation or levying the petrol and then its increased prices, which would be a trickle down effect on the rest of the commodities, we are expecting an adverse economic impact if that is resumed, if the escalation goes on.” US President Donald Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu have pointed to renewed military operations against Tehran in recent days, prompting a flurry of diplomatic activity to rein in any further conflict. “There is only one way to remove this threat once and for all: overthrow the regime in Iran,” Mr Netanyahu said on Thursday. “And that is my directive to the [military], the Mossad and the security branches.” The US has prepared for renewed strikes, US media have reported, although Washington has ruled out action before the midterm elections on November 3. The results of the coming Israeli elections on Tuesday will probably not change the country's appetite for conflict, Mr Kakar believes. "With or without Netanyahu, I do not see an alteration of the policies of that sense of continuous conflict with the region," he said. Pakistan is among the nations opposing any renewed escalation. Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar joined meetings between counterparts from Turkey, Egypt, Saudi Arabia and Europe in Istanbul on Friday, and the ministers said they would tell parties to the conflict not to escalate attacks. Islamabad has attempted to keep negotiations alive, and military chief Field Marshal Asim Munir travelled to Tehran this week for meetings with senior Iranian officials, including National Security Council chief Mohsen Rezaei and Speaker of Parliament Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf. Mr Ghalibaf told Mr Munir that the US could not win Tehran’s trust unless it implemented seven conditions put forward in a proposal in September, including an end to US military operations, a release of frozen Iranian assets and a lifting of the naval blockade, according to the Iranian National Security Council-affiliated Nour News outlet. That seven-point proposal put forward by Tehran last month to revive the Islamabad agreement was a “pure Iranian plan”, and Pakistan’s role had been limited to influencing, advising and making suggestions, Mr Kakar said. We are only doing the role of mediation, so the US and Iran are grown ups in the room. Anwaar Ul Haq Kakar, former caretaker Prime Minister of Pakistan “Primarily the two parties who are in conflict here are the US and Iran , not Pakistan,” he said. “We are only doing the role of mediation, so they are grown ups in the room. So they do their own proposals, both sides. We can only suggest to them what is reasonable and what should be accepted or not accepted, and the rest is their choice.” One complication in Iran is there are multiple schools of thought about what the country’s strategy should be. “You have a mix when you interact with the ruling elite. There are quiet pragmatists who are there, but then there are a bunch of ideologues also. So you have to cater for both the audiences,” Mr Kakar said. Iranians, who have struggled under sanctions for decades, have not had the same opportunities as people in neighbouring countries, he added. “Almost three to four generations have been bereft of their counterparts in the region, particularly the Gulf Co-operation Council [countries]. Their entire lifestyle has transformed, and they are on a different model of progress as compared to Iran,” he said. Born in Pakistan’s south-western Balochistan province, which neighbours Iran, Mr Kakar, who is also a current senator in Pakistan’s upper house, said there was room for political debate over a recent defence pact concluded with Saudi Arabia and Turkey, but that further political approval was not needed for it to enter into force. Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkey signed the Makkah defence agreement in August, and have since co-ordinated to support Saudi Arabia in the face of attacks by Iran-backed Houthi rebels in neighbouring Yemen. Unlike Turkey, where parliamentary approval for the pact is required , Pakistan’s legislators can debate it, but the constitution does not require their green light. Pakistan already has troops and military equipment in Saudi Arabia under long-standing agreements, and any decision to send more “would be a conversation between the three sides” in the Makkah defence pact, Mr Kakar said. “The initial assessment definitely is this: that Pakistan would also be in the role of defending Saudi territories, anyone who violates the Saudi sovereignty or territorial integrity gets challenged. “No one can peek into the future, so there are no manifested clauses where it says that Pakistan would either go to Yemen or any other country, but I'm being very cautious. All I can say is that Pakistan is fully committed to defend Saudi Arabia, no matter what.” Defending the holy cities of Makkah and Madinah is key, he added. “If either Medina or Makkah is, God forbid, attacked by Houthi or by Israelis or by aliens - by anyone - I don't think that there would be a single soul in Pakistan or maybe around the Muslim world who would have a relaxed sleep during the night. That is the red line. Everyone knows that, and I think the Houthis would know that too.” With the US reducing its role as security guarantor in the Middle East, the Makkah pact is a key part of countries in the region finding a way of filling that “vacuum,” Mr Kakar said. Any future expansion of the pact - which he underlined was not just about the Houthis and Saudi Arabia, but about a long-term regional security architecture - would take place in a “very systematic manner,” he said. “They probably would receive applications from the interested parties in the region, and that would be deliberated over there in the newly built secretariat for Makkah agreement,” he said. “Then probably for a year or so, these applications would be tested as observant parties, and then a formal decision by all three would be made that on whom to give permission to enter the club.” Closer to home, Pakistan is currently engaged in a grinding conflict with insurgents in neighbouring Afghanistan, and a peace deal remains elusive despite fatal strikes on both sides this year. Mr Kakar said Pakistan's sole demand was an end to the presence of insurgents from the Tehrik-e- Taliban Pakistan (TTP), a group proscribed as a terrorist organisation by Islamabad, as well as the UK, US and other nations. "Once that is removed, I think so from Pakistan's side, the situation would normalize within 24 hours," he said. ar A major problem in Afghanistan was the lack of accountability for weapons following the fall of the country to the Taliban in 2021 and the withdrawal of US and Nato forces. Arms are now being sold across the region as well as in Afghanistan, he said. "All those small gadgets are now being sold in the black market, which is probably even available from Peshawar and Quetta to the Syrian capital and Yemeni capital and other areas," he said. "So that is the challenge in which Pakistan is being compelled to respond to the presence of TTP on the Afghan side, we go for the precision strikes against their presence on Afghan side." Asked about the UN and human rights organisations' criticisms of civilian killings in Pakistani strikes on Afghanistan, he said the TTP's wearing of civilian clothing did not mean its members were non-combatants. "You cannot determine just on the basis of clothes that they were not the legitimate targets," he said.

title: Saudi Arabia intercepts barrage of Houthi missiles and drones
description: Rebels renew threats against using Riyadh airport as authorities open two terminals after deadly attack earlier this month
content: Saudi Arabia intercepted a series of missiles and drones, including over its capital, Riyadh, on Sunday as the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen continued to counter attacks by the Iran-aligned Houthi rebels. The attacks came as authorities prepared to reopen two terminals at Riyadh’s main international airport following a deadly strike earlier this month. The Saudi-led coalition said air defences intercepted and destroyed 10 ballistic missiles launched towards the kingdom’s southern region. It also reported intercepting a ballistic missile launched towards Riyadh and destroying a drone aimed at the capital. The coalition fighting the Houthis separately said it had intercepted and destroyed a cruise missile launched towards Khamis Mushait in southwestern Saudi Arabia. Two people were injured by shrapnel from two intercepted ballistic missiles launched by the Houthis in Khamis Mushait and Ahad Rafidah governorates, Saudi Arabia’s Civil Defence said. The agency said the incident also damaged three residential buildings and seven vehicles. Earlier in the day, the Civil Defence issued warnings through its National Early Warning Platform about potential danger in Abha city, Khamis Mushait, Jazan and Taif. It later said the danger had passed, urging residents to follow safety instructions and avoid gatherings and filming. The coalition said interceptions of two ballistic missiles on Saturday had resulted in debris falling in Makkah, Jeddah, Taif and Rabigh. Meanwhile, Saudi Arabia was reopening two terminals at King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh on Sunday, about two weeks after the airport was closed following a Houthi missile attack that killed 13 people and injured more than 300. Terminal 1 will handle domestic flights, while Terminal 2 will serve international flights. The Houthis repeated their threats to airlines, airport staff and travellers against using the airport. The rebels' spokesman, Yahya Saree, described the site as unsafe and said it remained a “military target”, warning that the group would continue operations against it. He said Saudi Arabia would bear responsibility for the consequences of resuming airport operations. As the situation escalated, the US on Saturday warned its citizens against travelling to Saudi Arabia and several other countries in the region, including Bahrain, Iran, Iraq, Jordan, Lebanon, Kuwait, Oman, the UAE, Qatar, Syria, Yemen and Israel. The advisories cited the threat of terrorism. Washington urged people to reconsider travel to Saudi Arabia because of threats including the “risk of drone and missile targeting of American interests by Iran and the Iranian-supported Houthis”, as well as armed conflict and terrorism. “Do not travel to the Yemen border due to terrorism,” the US advisory for Saudi Arabia said. The US warned that Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia “have the potential to escalate rapidly beyond that immediate area”. A Saudi-led coalition intervened in Yemen’s civil war in 2015 at the request of the internationally recognised government, after the Houthis seized the capital, Sanaa. A UN-brokered truce in 2022 helped maintain a fragile peace between the warring sides until this year. The coalition resumed its military campaign in Yemen in support of the internationally recognised government last month, seeking to reverse the Houthis’ advances, after the rebels moved along the Red Sea coast towards the strategic Bab Al Mandab strait.

title: Hundreds gather in show of unity at funeral of Jordan church attack victims
description: Ceremony was held at site the gunmen struck
content: Hundreds of Jordanians from across the kingdom attended a funeral service for eight of the nine Christians killed by gunmen in Jordan on Sunday, at the same church as the attack took place. The funeral in the village of Hamoud underlined the mass condemnation in the country that followed the attack , which the authorities described as terrorism. Tribes sent representatives from the north, centre and south of the country. Members of professional unions came in buses while others attended spontaneously. Muslim sheikhs were in attendance, including one who travelled from Saudi Arabia. Kamal Al Rawashdeh, a Muslim retiree in his 80s, drove his beaten Hyundai from the nearby village of Al Rabba to take part in the processions. “I felt it was my duty, this was a heinous act.” On Friday, at least two assailants opened fire in the compound of the St George's Greek Orthodox church, in the village of Hamoud in Karak governorate, witnesses said. Jordan's King Abdullah II, a key US ally, called the attackers “outlaws of Islam” and said that the security forces will respond with “an iron fist”. Official media said Queen Rania and Crown Prince Hussein had visited the village on Sunday to offer condolences. His Royal Highness Crown Prince Al Hussein offers condolences to families of the martyrs of the terrorist attack on the Greek Orthodox Church of Saint George in #Karak , and denounces the attack on innocent people in a place of worship, calling it a cowardly and treacherous act.… pic.twitter.com/p8DsdAqWgu — RHC (@RHCJO) October 25, 2026 It was the biggest attack against Jordan's Christian minority since the 1950s. The authorities have maintained internal stability since driving out the Palestinian Liberation Organisation from the country in a 1970 civil war. However, the economy has been stagnant for the last 15 years and the official unemployment rate is 16 per cent. The dead were all men. One was a doctor, another a dentist. Most belonged to the Halasah clan, one of the most prominent Christian families in Jordan. It was not immediately known why only eight of the nine were buried in Hamoud. Karak, about 100km south of Amman, has a concentration of Christians in the overwhelmingly Muslim kingdom. The attack took place during a funeral. On Saturday, authorities revised the death toll from seven to nine and said none of the three assailants had been captured. The attack wounded 34 others. King Abdullah had visited the wounded in hospital and spoken with them to check on their condition on Friday. Pope Leo XIV on Sunday offered prayers for the victims. Members of the gendarmerie were present while other security forces and armoured vehicles drove into surrounding remote and desert areas. Checkpoints were set south of Amman on the main motorway leading to Karak as authorities hunt for the suspects. Security forces were stationed at churches across the country during Sunday services, in an unprecedented tightening of security at Christian sites. At the main Orthodox church in Amman, many people attended Sunday mass. “The attack does not dissuade anyone, it makes us stronger,” said one of the priests who conducted the service. There was an armoured vehicle stationed at the entrance to the church.

title: Top 68 concerts and events coming to the UAE, from Jennifer Lopez to Mariah Carey
description: Eclectic mix of music, dance and drama on offer
content: From pop and rock to stand-up comedy, ballet, opera and musicals, the UAE’s live events season is in full swing, with the months ahead offering a packed line-up across Abu Dhabi, Dubai and Sharjah. Mariah Carey will return to Abu Dhabi with her Christmas-time show in December, while Wasla Festival brings regional acts, including Marcel Khalife, Le Trio Joubran, TootArd and Fatima to Expo City Dubai in November. Najwa Karam will bring her greatest hits to Dubai’s Coca-Cola Arena, while Abu Dhabi Comedy Season has announced shows led by Palestinian-American star Mo Amer and US comic Aries Spears. Abu Dhabi Grand Prix weekend will feature Jennifer Lopez , with the pop star completing the after-race concert line-up at Etihad Live alongside Lewis Capaldi, Zara Larsson, Alex Warren, Imagine Dragons, The Chainsmokers and The Script. Looking ahead to 2027, Shah Rukh Khan curate the inaugural Unifyd festival at Etihad Live, with Arijit Singh, Karan Aujla and Sonu Nigam among the first artists announced. Here, we round up the concerts and live events still to come in the UAE. 1. The Fridge Concert Series Season 50 Special: October 27 at The Fridge Warehouse, Alserkal Avenue, Dubai The Fridge marks the 50th season of its concert series with a reunion night featuring former performers from across its 20-year history. The line-up is being kept under wraps, with collaborations and jam sessions planned for the limited-capacity show. Free; pre-registration required 2. Titize: A Venetian Dream: October 29 to 31 at Dubai Opera Venice is the inspiration for this show mixing circus, theatre, dance and live music. The 10-member cast use acrobatics, clowning and physical theatre to create a dreamlike version of Venice through its masks, waterways and carnival traditions. Shows at 2pm and 8pm; tickets from Dh275 3. Nass: October 30 at The Arts Centre at NYU Abu Dhabi French-Moroccan choreographer Fouad Boussouf brings together seven male dancers in a work connecting hip-hop movement with the ritual dimensions of North African music. The title takes inspiration from Moroccan group Nass El Ghiwane and draws parallels between their search for identity and the origins of hip-hop. Show starts 7.30pm; tickets from Dh52.50 4. Abdul Majeed Abdullah: October 31 at Coca-Cola Arena, Dubai Saudi singer Abdul Majeed Abdullah returns to Dubai with a catalogue spanning decades of Khaleeji and Arabic pop. Known for a distinctive vocal style that has helped shape Gulf music, his songs include Mn Mithlek , Tetnafasek Denyaay , Yabn Elawadem and Ghazal Ma Yensady . Show starts 9.30pm; tickets from Dh495 5. Riverdance: October 31 and November 1 at Etihad Arena, Abu Dhabi Riverdance returns to the UAE with a production marking the Irish dance show’s 30th anniversary. The staging retains Bill Whelan’s Grammy Award-winning score while introducing updated choreography, costumes, lighting, projection and motion graphics. Performance times vary; tickets from Dh215 6. Benjamin Clementine: November 1 at Dubai Opera British singer, pianist and composer Benjamin Clementine performs a programme combining experimental pop, contemporary classical music, jazz and poetry. His debut album, At Least for Now , won the Mercury Prize, while later recordings include I Tell a Fly and And I Have Been . Show starts 8pm; tickets from Dh500 7. Jony: November 4 at Coca-Cola Arena, Dubai Russian-Azerbaijani singer Jony is a star Russian pop and built a following with songs including Kamin , Kometa and Ty Besposhchadna . Show starts 9pm; tickets from Dh295 8. Mo Amer: November 6 at Etihad Arena, Abu Dhabi Palestinian-American comedian Mo Amer performs as part of Abu Dhabi Comedy Season. Born in Kuwait to Palestinian parents and raised in the US, his comedy draws on displacement, immigration and life between cultures. Those experiences also shaped Mo , the semi-autobiographical Netflix series he created with Ramy Youssef, which won a Peabody Award in 2023. Show time and ticket prices to be announced 9. Maz Jobrani: November 7 at Etihad Arena, Abu Dhabi Iranian-American comedian Maz Jobrani returns to Abu Dhabi with material exploring immigrant experiences, cultural misunderstandings and family expectations. He previously performed at the inaugural Abu Dhabi Comedy Week in 2024 on a shared bill with Bassem Youssef. Show time and ticket prices to be announced 10. Ministry of Sound Classical: November 7 at Dubai Opera Club anthems are given an orchestral spin as Ministry of Sound Classical brings dance music into the concert hall. Conducted by David Mahoney, the show combines a full orchestra and vocalists with electronic music, lighting and visuals, drawing on tracks associated with decades of club culture. Show time and ticket prices to be announced 11. Abdelkader Secteur: November 8 at Emirates Theatre, Dubai Algerian comedian Abdelkader Secteur returns to Dubai with a stand-up show drawing on family life, cultural traditions and everyday situations. Known for storytelling rooted in North African humour, he follows a previous Dubai appearance last year. Show starts 7.30pm; tickets from Dh195 12. American Ballet Theatre: November 20 at Emirates Palace, Abu Dhabi Dubbed one of the world's greatest dance companies, the American Ballet Theatre will perform works including Frederick Ashton’s Birthday Offering , Jiri Kylian’s Nuages , Brady Farrar’s Trio Elegiaque and Paquita , staged by Natalia Makarova after Marius Petipa. Show starts 8pm, tickets from Dh125 13. Aries Spears: November 21 at Etihad Arena, Abu Dhabi American comedian Aries Spears brings more than three decades of stand-up, impressions and crowd work to Etihad Arena. A former Mad TV cast member, he is known for his celebrity impersonations that include Michael Jackson, Eddie Murphy and Shaquille O'Neal. Doors open 9pm; show starts 10pm; tickets from Dh120 14. Synthony x Faithless: November 21 at Bla Bla by McGettigan's, Dubai Synthony makes its Middle East debut with a full orchestra reworking electronic dance anthems through live instrumentation, vocals and visual production. The night will also feature Faithless Sound System, led by Sister Bliss, with tracks including Insomnia and We Come 1 . Doors open 6pm; tickets from Dh295 15. Trevor Noah: November 25-26 and November 28 and 29 at Dubai Opera Trevor Noah brings a new stand-up show to Dubai across four nights. The Emmy Award-winning South African comedian and former host of The Daily Show has released several Netflix specials, hosts the podcast What Now? with Trevor Noah and is the author of Born a Crime and Into the Uncut Grass . Show starts 8pm; tickets from Dh295 16. Algarabia: November 26 at Emirates Palace, Abu Dhabi Algarabia presents a theatrical production blending flamenco with Arabic poetry, performed by musicians from Spain’s University of Navarra Symphony Orchestra alongside dancers and actors. The work follows the journey of an Arab girl drawn to ancient botanical theory and poetic tradition. Show starts 8pm; tickets from Dh100 17. Bader Saleh: November 27 at The Hive, Dubai Saudi comedian Bader Saleh brings his Bliss of Ignorance stand-up show to Dubai. He rose to prominence through the YouTube series EyshElly and has since worked across television, online comedy and live performance. Show starts 9pm; tickets from Dh175 18. Hiba Tawaji and Ibrahim Maalouf: November 27 at Dubai Opera Hiba Tawaji and Ibrahim Maalouf will unite for a one-night performance at Dubai Opera, with the programme drawing on French musical heritage through a blend of chanson, jazz and contemporary composition. Tawaji’s emotive vocals and Maalouf’s genre-crossing trumpet work make this one of the more distinctive concert pairings on the calendar. Show starts 8.30pm; tickets from Dh355 19. Atif Aslam: November 27 at Coca-Cola Arena, Dubai Atif Aslam returns to Coca-Cola Arena after five consecutive years of sold-out Dubai concerts. The Pakistani singer’s programme will move between Bollywood songs, pop-rock and devotional music, with hits including Tajdar-e-Haram , Jeena Jeena , Pehli Nazar Mein , Dil Diyan Gallan and Aadat . Doors open 9pm; tickets from Dh350 20. Tarkan: November 27 at Etihad Arena, Abu Dhabi Known internationally for the global hit Simarik and a catalogue that has defined Turkish pop for more than two decades, Tarkan is making his Abu Dhabi debut is further proof of Turkish’s pop growing popularity in the region. Show starts 8.30pm; tickets from Dh295 21. Wasla Festival: November 28 at Jubilee Park, Expo City Dubai Lebanese composer and oud player Marcel Khalife headlines the return of Wasla Festival, alongside Palestinian ensemble Le Trio Joubran, Syrian duo TootArd and Emirati-Honduran singers Fatima . Starts 6pm; tickets from Dh350 22. Ramy Sabry: November 28 at Etihad Arena, Abu Dhabi Egyptian singer Ramy Sabry comes to Abu Dhabi with a catalogue of romantic Arabic pop and ballads. His songs include Lama Bywhashny , alongside a wider repertoire centred on love, memory and heartbreak. Doors open 7.30pm; show starts 9pm; tickets from Dh295 23. Artbat Present Upperground: November 28 at Ushuaia Dubai Harbour Experience Ukrainian electronic duo Artbat bring their Upperground event series to Dubai, joined by Miss Monique, R3hab and Italian DJ and producer 7 Skies. The show follows Artbat’s recent reworking of Gotye's Somebody That I Used to Know with David Guetta. Doors open 8pm; tickets from Dh150 24. Verdi’s Opera Gala: November 29 at Emirates Palace, Abu Dhabi Marking 125 years since Giuseppe Verdi’s death, this programme is led by soprano Maria Agresta and tenor Giorgio Berrugi, and includes selections from Nabucco , I Vespri Siciliani , Otello and La Traviata , alongside overtures and duets drawn from Verdi’s wider catalogue. Show starts 8pm; tickets from Dh125 25. Ghostly Kisses: November 29 at Etihad Arena, Abu Dhabi Canadian singer-songwriter Margaux Sauve brings her Ghostly Kisses project to Abu Dhabi as part of her 2026 regional tour. Her music combines atmospheric pop, understated electronic production and intimate vocals, with songs including The City Holds My Heart . Show starts 8pm; tickets from Dh215 26. Andrea Bocelli: December 2 at Etihad Arena, Abu Dhabi Italian tenor Andrea Bocelli brings his 30th Anniversary Romanza World Tour to Abu Dhabi as part of Yasalam Classics. The concert celebrates Romanza , the album that helped establish him internationally and includes songs such as Con te partiro and Vivo per lei . Doors open 6pm; tickets from Dh295 27. The Tsar's Bride by the Bolshoi Theatre: December 2 at Dubai Opera The Bolshoi Theatre begins its first official UAE tour with Rimsky-Korsakov's The Tsar's Bride . Set during the reign of Ivan the Terrible, the opera centres on Marfa, a young woman whose selection as the tsar's bride sets off jealousy, rivalry and political intrigue. Show time and ticket prices to be announced 28. Bolshoi Theatre Orchestra, December 3 The Bolshoi Theatre Orchestra takes centre stage for a symphonic concert on the second night of the company’s first official UAE tour. Showtime and ticket prices TBC 29. Lewis Capaldi and Zara Larsson: December 3 at Etihad Park, Abu Dhabi Lewis Capaldi and Zara Larsson will open the Abu Dhabi Grand Prix 2026 after-race concert series with separate sets at Etihad Park. Capaldi returns to the capital following his Saadiyat Nights performance in January, bringing a catalogue that includes Someone You Loved , Before You Go and Forget Me . Larsson joins the bill with pop staples such as Lush Life , Never Forget You and Symphony , offering a high-tempo contrast to Capaldi’s ballad-driven set. The show launches the four-night programme running alongside the race weekend at Yas Marina Circuit. Showtime yet to be announced; access exclusive to Abu Dhabi Grand Prix ticket holders 30. Jennifer Lopez and Alex Warren: December 4 at Etihad Live, Abu Dhabi Jennifer Lopez returns to Abu Dhabi for the second night of the Grand Prix after-race concert series, sharing the bill with US singer-songwriter Alex Warren. Lopez's catalogue includes If You Had My Love , Waiting for Tonight , Jenny from the Block and On the Floor . Warren makes his UAE debut after the international success of Ordinary . Access exclusive to Abu Dhabi Grand Prix ticket holders 31. Shimza: December 4 at 16/360, Yas Marina Circuit, Abu Dhabi South African DJ Shimza brings his percussion-heavy Afro-tech sound to 16/360 as Abu Dhabi Grand Prix weekend gets under way. Known for extended, hypnotic sets, he has performed across Europe and Africa and collaborated with fellow South African DJ Black Coffee. Access exclusive to selected 16/360 Grand Prix hospitality ticket holders; packages from Dh1,250 32. Mont Rouge and Moojo: December 4 at Bagatelle, W Abu Dhabi, Abu Dhabi Swiss duo Mont Rouge and French DJ Moojo share the Friday bill at Bagatelle's rooftop pop-up during Abu Dhabi Grand Prix weekend. Mont Rouge are known for their Afro-house version of Voyage Voyage , recorded with Francis Mercier and Coco, as well as their remix of Axwell and Sebastian Ingrosso's More Than You Know . Tables from Dh7,000 33. The Nutcracker by the Bolshoi Theatre: December 4 to 6 at Dubai Opera The Nutcracker has become a Dubai Opera tradition, and this year's production will feature the Bolshoi Theatre, with Tchaikovsky's ballet performed by the company's dancers and orchestra. Yuri Grigorovich's choreography follows Marie from a family Christmas celebration into a fantasy world of toys and magic, set to a score containing some of Tchaikovsky's best-known music. Show times and ticket prices to be announced 34. Anyma: December 4 at Yas Gateway Park, Abu Dhabi Italian-American DJ and producer Anyma will perform at Yas Gateway Park as part of the official Abu Dhabi Grand Prix after party concert series. Known for large-scale audiovisual shows and melodic techno, he brought his dazzling live production to the Pyramids of Giza in 2025 and has become one of electronic music’s most distinctive live acts through his work as a solo artist and as one half of Tale of Us. Abu Dhabi Grand Prix ticket holder presales begin on September 10, with general sales opening on September 11; show time and ticket prices to be announced 35. Imagine Dragons: December 5 at Etihad Live, Abu Dhabi Imagine Dragons will headline the Abu Dhabi Grand Prix after-race concert series on Saturday night. Fronted by Dan Reynolds, the US band are known for songs including Believer , Radioactive , Demons , Thunder and It’s Time . The group last performed in Abu Dhabi in 2023, when they sold out Etihad Arena. Showtime yet to be announced; access exclusive to Abu Dhabi Grand Prix ticket holders 36. CamelPhat: December 5 at 16/360, Yas Marina Circuit, Abu Dhabi British electronic duo CamelPhat take over the trackside 16/360 venue on the second night of its Grand Prix programme. Dave Whelan and Mike Di Scala broke through internationally with the Grammy-nominated Cola , while their catalogue also includes Panic Room with Au/Ra and Breathe with Cristoph and Jem Cooke. Access exclusive to selected 16/360 Grand Prix hospitality ticket holders; packages from Dh1,250 37. Gordo: December 5 at Bagatelle, W Abu Dhabi, Abu Dhabi DJ and producer Gordo, formerly known as Carnage, joins Bagatelle's race-weekend programme with his house-focused sound. He contributed to Drake's 2022 album Honestly, Nevermind and released his debut album Diamante in 2024, featuring collaborations with Drake and Maluma. Tables from Dh10,000 38. The Chainsmokers and The Script: December 6 at Etihad Live, Abu Dhabi The Chainsmokers and The Script will close the Abu Dhabi Grand Prix after-race concert series with separate sets on race day. Irish band The Script are known for songs including Breakeven , The Man Who Can’t Be Moved , For the First Time and Hall of Fame . US electronic duo The Chainsmokers bring a catalogue that includes Roses , Don’t Let Me Down , Closer , Paris and Something Just Like This . Showtime yet to be announced; access exclusive to Abu Dhabi Grand Prix ticket holders 39. Black Coffee: December 6 at 16/360, Yas Marina Circuit, Abu Dhabi Grammy-winning South African DJ Black Coffee closes the three-night 16/360 programme on race day with his blend of deep house, African percussion and soulful vocals. His album Subconsciously , featuring collaborations with Pharrell Williams and David Guetta, won the Grammy Award for Best Dance/Electronic Music Album. Access exclusive to selected 16/360 Grand Prix hospitality ticket holders; packages from Dh1,250 40. Carl Cox: December 6 at Bagatelle, W Abu Dhabi, Abu Dhabi British DJ Carl Cox closes Bagatelle's Grand Prix weekend programme. A pioneer of Britain's acid-house movement, he has spent more than four decades playing house and techno and held a 15-year residency at Space Ibiza. His links with motorsport extend beyond the weekend through Carl Cox Motorsport, which he founded in 2013. Tables from Dh10,000 41. Enrico Macias: December 10 at Dubai Opera More than six decades of chanson and Mediterranean music feature in Enrico Macias’s latest Dubai concert. The French-Algerian singer is known for Adieu mon pays , Les filles de mon pays and Enfants de tous pays . The concert is reportedly among his final international appearances. Show starts 8pm; tickets from Dh295 42. Lisa Batiashvili and Giorgi Gigashvili: December 10 at The Arts Centre at NYU Abu Dhabi Georgian musicians Lisa Batiashvili and Giorgi Gigashvili will perform works by Beethoven, Bartok and Franck, alongside a contemporary piece by composer Josef Bardanashvili. Show starts 8pm; tickets from Dh150 43. Minsoo Sohn: December 11 at The Arts Centre at NYU Abu Dhabi Pianist Minsoo Sohn will perform Book One of Bach’s Well-Tempered Clavier , presenting the 24 preludes and fugues that explore every major and minor key. The recital highlights both the intellectual depth and emotional breadth of the landmark work. Show starts 8pm; tickets from Dh150 44. Sole DXB: December 11 to 13 at The Square, Nad Al Sheba, Dubai Sole DXB returns with three days of live music, DJ sets, fashion, art and street culture. The line-up includes British singer Lola Young, electronic duo Overmono, jungle producer Nia Archives, Malian musician Fatoumata Diawara, Matthew Herbert, Peter Cat Recording Co, Hajaj, Gia Fu, and Maii and Zeid. Runs from 4pm to 2.30am each day; three-day tickets from Dh495 45. Bamboo and Cup of Joe: December 11 at Dubai World Trade Centre, Dubai Filipino acts Bamboo and Cup of Joe share the stage for a night of OPM at Dubai World Trade Centre. Bamboo brings songs including Masaya , while Cup of Joe's catalogue includes Multo . Show starts 7pm; tickets from Dh129 46. Guy Manoukian: December 11 at Dubai Opera Guy Manoukian marks Dubai Opera's 10th anniversary by returning for his own milestone 10th performance at the venue, following nine sold-out shows. The Lebanese-Armenian pianist and composer blends original work with Arabic melodies and contemporary arrangements, with his repertoire also drawing on the music of Fairouz and Abdel Halim Hafez. Show starts 8pm; tickets from Dh330 47. Mariah Carey: December 12 at Etihad Arena, Abu Dhabi Mariah Carey returns to Abu Dhabi with her Christmastime show, featuring festive songs including All I Want for Christmas Is You , Santa Baby and Christmas (Baby Please Come Home) alongside hits from her wider catalogue. The concert will be her second Abu Dhabi performance of the year, following her Saadiyat Nights show in February. Doors open 7pm; tickets from Dh249 48. Mahmut Orhan: December 12 at Ushuaia Dubai Harbour Experience, Dubai Turkish DJ and producer Mahmut Orhan returns to Dubai Harbour after performing there on New Year's Eve. His sound moves between deep house and indie dance, and he has performed at festivals including Coachella, Ultra Europe and Awakenings. Doors open 8pm; tickets from Dh150 49. Chicago the Musical: December 16 to 20 at Coca-Cola Arena, Dubai The Broadway production of Chicago comes to Coca-Cola Arena for eight performances over five days. Set during the Jazz Age, the musical follows nightclub performer Roxie Hart and vaudeville star Velma Kelly as they compete for public attention while awaiting trial for murder. The score includes All That Jazz , Cell Block Tango and Razzle Dazzle . Performance times vary; tickets from Dh49 50. Denis Matsuev: December 16 at Dubai Opera Russian pianist Denis Matsuev moves between classical repertoire and jazz in a concert titled Classics and Jazz . Show starts 8pm; tickets from Dh350 51. Abracadabra: December 18 and 19 at Dubai Opera Gulf theatre comes to Dubai Opera with Abracadabra , an Arabic language suspense comedy about two struggling theatre groups trying to save their careers. Their plan to stage a new show inside an abandoned theatre is disrupted by strange events, unexpected twists and a series of comic situations. The production runs for about an hour and blends Gulf theatre, suspense and entertainment. Show times vary; tickets from Dh230. 52. Dopa World: December 18 to 20 at Jubilee Park, Expo City Dubai Dopa World is a three-day festival focused on young Arab music, culture and creative businesses. Saint Levant is the first announced artist, with the Palestinian-Algerian performer known for blending Arabic, English and French across songs including Very Few Friends and Deira . The remaining artists are yet to be announced. Doors open 4pm daily; tickets from Dh245 53. Dhafer Youssef: December 19 at The Arts Centre at NYU Abu Dhabi Oud maestro Dhafer Youssef will perform with his quintet, bridging sounds from the East and West through jazz, Arab and North African traditions, as well as European classical and electronic elements. He is expected to perform material from his latest album Shiraz , described as his most personal work to date. Show starts 8pm; tickets from Dh150 54. Yassar Lemghari: December 25 at Emirates Theatre, Dubai Moroccan comedian Yassar Lemghari brings his Lamhayab show to Dubai, performed in Moroccan Darija. His stand-up draws on Moroccan culture and everyday life and follows a series of international performances. Doors open 8pm; show starts 8.30pm; tickets from Dh169 55. Rahat Fateh Ali Khan and Shah Zaman Ali Khan: December 26 at Coca-Cola Arena, Dubai Rahat Fateh Ali Khan returns to Coca-Cola Arena for his eighth appearance at the venue, joined by Shah Zaman Ali Khan. The concert brings together Qawwali, Sufi music and contemporary South Asian songs, with Shah Zaman continuing the musical tradition of the family into a new generation. Show starts 8pm; tickets from Dh95 56. Katy Perry: December 31 at Atlantis, The Palm, Dubai Katy Perry returns to the UAE to headline the New Year's Eve gala at Atlantis The Palm, a year after closing the 2025 Abu Dhabi Grand Prix. The American pop star brings a catalogue including Teenage Dream , Roar , Dark Horse and Firework . The black-tie gala also features a 30-piece live band, entertainment throughout the evening and a midnight fireworks display across Atlantis Dubai on Palm Jumeirah. Doors open 7pm; tickets from Dh6,500 for children and Dh8,500 for adults 57. Vessbroz: December 31 at Cavo, Ramee Dream Hotel, Dubai Vessbroz headline Cavo’s New Year’s Eve party with a set built around electronic house music and Middle East-inspired sounds. The line-up also includes Bazz Key, Qtee Rue, Taina and Hellfox. Doors open 10pm; tickets from Dh150. 58. Tony Ann: January 12, 2027, at Dubai Opera Canadian pianist and composer Tony Ann makes his Dubai debut with a programme blending contemporary piano and classical influences. Known for his viral #playthatword series and the Emotionally Blue, Orange and Red EP trilogy, Ann has also co-written The Chainsmokers tracks Sick Boy and Call You Mine . 59. Swan Lake on Ice: January 14 to 17, 2027, at Dubai Opera Tchaikovsky’s Swan Lake is reimagined on ice by the Imperial Ice Stars, with 24 skaters bringing together figure skating, ballet, aerial movement and theatrical choreography. The production follows the story of Odette, Prince Siegfried and Rothbart, with snowfall, fog, pyrotechnic effects and elaborate costumes adding to the staging. Show times vary by date; auditorium doors open 30 minutes before each performance; tickets from Dh300 60. Buena Vista Social Club Legacy Concert: January 24, 2027 at Dubai Opera Cuban music takes over Dubai Opera with a concert featuring Ibrahim Ferrer Jr, son of Buena Vista Social Club singer Ibrahim Ferrer, alongside veteran laud player Barbarito Torres Billed as Una Noche En La Habana , the show draws on son, bolero and other Cuban traditions associated with the musicians who brought Buena Vista Social Club to international audiences in the late 1990s. Show time and ticket prices to be announced 61. Tamaas Festival: January 29, 2027, at The Arts Centre at NYU Abu Dhabi Tamaas Festival returns with three acts moving between traditional forms and club-orientated production. Moroccan-Swiss musician Sami Galbi combines rai and chaabi with electronic music, while Nigerien guitarist Bombino performs Tuareg desert blues and rock. British collective Ibibio Sound Machine close the evening with West African rhythms, post-punk, disco and electronic music. Festival starts 7pm; free pass upon registration 62. Harry Potter Film Concert Series: February 5 to 6, 2027, at Etihad Arena, Abu Dhabi The UAE National Orchestra accompanies two Harry Potter films across consecutive nights. John Williams’ stirring score for Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban is performed on February 5, followed by Patrick Doyle’s music for Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire on February 6. Doors open 6.30pm; shows start 7.30pm; tickets from Dh120 63. Ramadaniyat – The Handover: February 17, 2027, at The Arts Centre at NYU Abu Dhabi Egyptian oud player Aly Eissa, Alexandrian violinist Ayman Asfour and Belgian-Norwegian keyboard player Jonas Cambien make their UAE debut as The Handover. The trio bring the ritual and folk music of rural Egypt into contact with free improvisation, psychedelic rock and electronic textures. Show starts 9.30pm; tickets from Dh52.50 64. The Phantom of the Opera: March 10 to 28, 2027 at Etihad Arena, Abu Dhabi Andrew Lloyd Webber's The Phantom of the Opera makes its Abu Dhabi debut with a three-week run at Etihad Arena. Based on Gaston Leroux's novel, the musical follows the masked phantom who lives beneath the Paris Opera House and becomes obsessed with soprano Christine Daae. The score includes The Music of the Night , All I Ask of You and the title song. The Abu Dhabi run comes during the musical's 40th anniversary year, following its West End premiere in 1986. Runs from March 10 to 28; tickets from Dh240 65. Unifyd: March 20, 2027 at Etihad Live, Abu Dhabi Arijit Singh, Karan Aujla and Sonu Nigam lead the inaugural Unifyd music festival curated by Bollywood star Shah Rukh Khan. The one-day event will feature more than 15 artists across several stages, spanning Hindi film music, Punjabi music and other strands of Indian culture. General sale opens October 20 at 10.30am through the District app; ticket prices to be announced 66. Tribute to Ziad Rahbani by Faraj Suleiman: March 26, 2027, at The Arts Centre at NYU Abu Dhabi Palestinian composer and pianist Faraj Suleiman returns with a programme dedicated to Lebanese composer, pianist and playwright Ziad Rahbani. Rather than reproducing the original recordings, Suleiman re-orchestrates and re-harmonises the material through contemporary piano, jazz and Arabic composition. Show starts 7.30pm; tickets from Dh78.75 67. A1 and Music Travel Love: April 17, 2027, at Coca-Cola Arena, Dubai British-Norwegian pop group A1 and Canadian duo Music Travel Love will share the stage for the first time in Dubai. A1 are known for hits including Everytime , Caught in the Middle and Like a Rose , while Music Travel Love, formed by twin brothers Bob and Clint Moffatt, are known for acoustic covers and originals including Nothing’s Gonna Change my Love for You . Show starts 8pm; tickets from Dh295 68. Richard Marx: June 6, 2027 at Coca-Cola Arena, Dubai American singer-songwriter Richard Marx comes to Dubai with a catalogue spanning more than four decades. His best-known songs include Right Here Waiting , Hazard , Hold On to the Nights and Satisfied , while his songwriting credits include hits recorded by artists such as Luther Vandross, Keith Urban and NSYNC. Show starts 8pm; tickets from Dh225

title: Sabic returns to profit in third quarter as revenue rises despite regional conflict
description: Company, 70 per cent owned by Saudi Aramco, reports 14 per cent revenue growth
content: Saudi Basic Industries Corporation ( Sabic ), the Middle East’s largest petrochemicals company, returned to profitability in the third quarter as revenue increased and its operating performance improved despite challenging market conditions. Net profit attributable to shareholders of the company reached 500 million Saudi riyals ($133 million) in the three months to the end of September, up 16.3 per cent from the same period last year, Sabic said in a bourse filing on Sunday. The company swung to a profit in the July to September period after reporting a net loss of 833 million riyals in the second quarter this year due to the regional conflict. Revenue in the third quarter rose 14 per cent on a quarterly basis to 28.17 billion riyals, although it remained about 3 per cent below the year-earlier level. Adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation (Ebitda) increased 40 per cent quarter-on-quarter to 4.75 billion riyals, while adjusted net income reached 840 million riyals, reversing a loss of 380 million riyals in the second quarter. “In Q3 2026, Sabic demonstrated exceptional resilience, despite geopolitical developments and market headwinds, coupled with a clear and robust forward-looking vision and continued focus on strategic objectives, namely portfolio optimisation, transformation and selective growth, in efforts to support the company’s long-term profitability and value creation for shareholders, building on its historic journey of more than five decades,” said Sabic chief executive Faisal M Alfaqeer. Sabic’s results come against a backdrop of heightened security risks for Saudi Arabia’s energy industry , with the kingdom’s oil and petrochemical infrastructure facing repeated missile and drone attacks amid the widening regional conflict. Sabic has a major presence in Dhahran, primarily centred around its advanced research and innovation ecosystems. Earlier this month, a Houthi missile attack damaged Saudi Aramco’s headquarters complex in Dhahran. The attack sparked a fire in an administrative building in Aramco’s complex. Aramco owns a 70 per cent stake in Sabic. The developments have raised fresh concerns about the security of Saudi Arabia’s energy infrastructure as the Iran war continues to disrupt regional energy markets. For the first nine months of 2026, Sabic narrowed its net loss to 320 million riyals, from 4.84 billion riyals in the same period last year, although revenue declined nearly 11 per cent to 79.13 billion riyals. Sabic said it completed the sale of its engineering thermoplastics business in the Americas and Europe for an enterprise value of $450 million during the third quarter, as part of efforts to streamline its operations and improve long-term profitability. It also said its transformation programme had generated 3.56 billion riyals in recurring Ebitda benefits towards its 2030 target of 11.3 billion riyals.

title: The Gulf’s unfinished defence infrastructure
description: A joint Gulf defence system is about strategic autonomy
content: The Gulf states find themselves at the centre of a regional war that is not of their making . A confrontation that began with US and Israeli strikes on Iran has spread into a web of proxy conflicts, reaching from the Strait of Hormuz to the Red Sea and Bab Al Mandeb, through Iraq and Yemen. The members of the GCC now face a question they can no longer put off: will they turn their commitment to collective security from communiques into a working military deterrent? Over several decades, Gulf states have invested heavily in advanced military capabilities, but progress towards operational integration has not kept pace. They have weapons and institutions. What is missing is an integrated collective response. Despite existing GCC defence co-operation mechanisms, each state continues to rely on its own national defence arrangements, while regional threats increasingly operate through cross-border armed networks . As a result, states with some of the most sophisticated arsenals in the world can be threatened by armed groups using drones and missiles that cost a fraction of the interceptors fired at them. For decades, Iran has cultivated armed partners in Lebanon, Iraq and Yemen. These networks extend its reach and give it leverage well beyond its borders. Tehran’s control over each group varies, and Iran does not order every attack directly. The strategic effect is the same either way: a set of fronts from which neighbouring states can be threatened and drained. This model can become more dangerous as pressure on Tehran grows, particularly if Iran’s armed partners join the conflict. Armed non-state actors are now built into the region’s calculations of deterrence, coercion and bargaining. Civilian airports, seaports, energy installations and critical infrastructure have also been targeted by armed groups. The recent Houthi escalation against Saudi Arabia, and earlier attacks and threats against vital facilities in the UAE, Kuwait, Bahrain and Qatar, mark a dangerous shift, even though the actors and circumstances behind each incident have differed. The Iranian aim is no longer only to exchange strikes. It is to carry war into civilian and economic life, and to turn public safety, market stability, trade and shipping into tools of blackmail. Gulf cities run the risk of becoming open arenas for settling regional scores, with civilians and economies treated as legitimate targets by groups that answer to no state and respect neither sovereignty nor the laws of armed conflict. The greatest danger in the current crisis is that the Gulf becomes the arena where Iran, the US and Israel settle their accounts This leaves the Gulf with an uncomfortable irony. States that chose diplomacy and stayed out of the war may still pay for it. Staying neutral does not buy immunity, and restraint alone will not deter actors who see escalation as their best bargaining tool. The GCC does not need to invent collective defence, as the framework for it already exists . The Joint Defence Agreement declares that an attack on one member is an attack on all. The council has created the Peninsula Shield Force and a Unified Military Command, along with a range of security co-operation mechanisms. The challenge now is ensuring that these structures can respond effectively to current security threats. Can they counter missile and drone salvos, cyberattacks and simultaneous strikes on critical infrastructure? If several Gulf capitals came under attack on the same day, could a joint operational mechanism respond in hours rather than weeks? For the GCC, the effectiveness of collective defence depends on whether its military co-operation can credibly deter potential attacks. Armed groups are not deterred by statements of condemnation or by solidarity expressed after the fact. Deterrence begins when an aggressor understands that striking one Gulf state means facing an integrated defence system, not an individual state’s response. That requires moving from co-ordination to integration. In practice, this means making the Unified Military Command fully operational, with the authority to co-ordinate joint responses, and linking early-warning and air and missile defence systems across the six GCC states. It also means establishing mechanisms that facilitate intelligence sharing in real time, developing joint plans to protect critical infrastructure, including airports, ports, energy installations and desalination facilities, and strengthening shared counter-drone and cyber-defence capabilities. Greater investment in regional defence industries would further reduce dependence on external suppliers. Some may argue that strengthening Gulf joint defence risks escalating tensions with Iran. Yet the purpose of deterrence is precisely to prevent war. Credible, integrated defences can strengthen Gulf states’ ability to protect their interests and pursue diplomacy from a position of strength, while reducing their vulnerability to coercion and prolonged attrition. Collective defence does not mean that every attack on one member leads to a joint war. It means a clear, predictable mechanism for collective response: defensive, intelligence and logistical support, protection of critical infrastructure and co-ordinated diplomacy. That mechanism should rest firmly on international law and draw a clear line between legitimate self-defence and open-ended retaliation. The message to Tehran should be equally clear. Iran cannot seek normal relations with its Gulf neighbours while arming groups that threaten them. Regional dialogue depends on respect for sovereignty, and de-escalation cannot serve as cover for continued pressure through proxies. The greatest danger in the current crisis is that the Gulf becomes the arena where Iran, the US and Israel settle their accounts. Each has its own strategic calculations. But the Gulf states should not bear the costs of wars they can neither start nor end on their own. For this reason, a joint Gulf defence system is about more than military readiness. It is about strategic autonomy. Outside security partnerships will remain important, but they cannot permanently replace the Gulf’s own capacity to defend itself. GCC leaders have an opportunity to convene an extraordinary summit devoted solely to security and defence. Such a summit would produce binding decisions with clear timelines to activate joint defence, empower the Unified Military Command, and build an integrated system for early warning and crisis response. Collective defence cannot stay on hold until the next crisis arrives. Iran has expanded its influence through several fronts and a network of armed groups. The Gulf would do well to not respond by copying that model or by sliding into a war of attrition. It would prove more worthwhile in the long run to build shared institutional strength that makes any attack on a Gulf state costlier and less likely to succeed. Statements do not create collective security, good intentions do not protect sovereignty, and a peace without credible deterrence may prove to be nothing more than a pause before the next war.

title: Final bridge at Dubai World Centre roundabout to open on Friday
description: Bridge will have capacity for 3,000 vehicles per hour
content: The final bridge of the World Trade Centre roundabout project will open in Dubai on Friday, the emirate's transport authority confirmed. Stretching over a kilometre, the bridge has the capacity to carry 3,000 vehicles per hour and will reduce travel time between Al Majlis Street and 2nd December Street from six minutes to one, the Roads and Transport Authority (RTA) said on Sunday. The completion of the work means that five bridges, with a total length of 5km, will have been built as part of the project, which the RTA estimates will benefit at least half a million residents and visitors. The average delay at the intersection is expected to fall by 12 minutes to 90 seconds. The total cost of the work is estimated to be more than Dh696 million. “The completion of the World Trade Centre roundabout development project is in line with the directives of the wise leadership to continue upgrading Dubai’s road infrastructure, improve traffic flow on Sheikh Zayed Road and enhance connectivity between the emirate’s leading economic and commercial centres," said Mattar Al Tayer, director general of the RTA. تستكمل #هيئة_الطرق_و_المواصلات ، يوم الجمعة 30 أكتوبر، مشروع تطوير دوار المركز التجاري بافتتاح الجسر الأخير، الذي يمتد بطول 1,000 متر ويتألف من مسارين، بطاقة استيعابية تصل إلى نحو 3,000 مركبة في الساعة، لخدمة الحركة المرورية من شارع المجلس باتجاه شارع الثاني من ديسمبر. ويسهم… pic.twitter.com/kLGWECeYFT — RTA (@rta_dubai) October 25, 2026 “The project will also increase road network capacity to keep pace with Dubai’s rapid population, urban and economic growth, reinforce its global leadership in business, investment and tourism, and provide an integrated, sustainable mobility system that reinforce the emirate’s competitiveness, facilitates travel for residents and visitors, and enhances quality of life.” The World Trade Centre roundabout project complements Al Mustaqbal Street Development Project, due for completion in 2027 added Mr Al Tayer. Al Mustaqbal Street project includes bridges and tunnels spanning a total of 1.5km and expansion of the street to four lanes in each direction Both projects form part of a comprehensive approach to upgrading the area’s key road corridors, he said. “The World Trade Centre Roundabout Development Project is one of Dubai’s strategic road network projects, given its vital location on Sheikh Zayed Road, the emirate’s main traffic artery, and its role in linking key road corridors with key economic, commercial and residential areas.

title: Ballon d’Or 2026: The five most historic winners – from Matthews to Messi
description: Listing every recipient of the famous prize ahead of Monday's ceremony in London
content: The 2026 Ballon d'Or winner will be announced on Monday night at a glittering ceremony in London. The 70th staging of the event will be the first to be held outside France, with it moving to England as a tribute to Sir Stanley Matthews, who won the first ever Ballon d'Or in 1956. Below, we pick out five of the most historically significant Ballon d'Or victories and list every winner, going back to the very start. Honourable mentions must go to Lev Yashin, the only goalkeeper to win the award (1963), and Cristiano Ronaldo , who, with five trophies at home, is second only to Lionel Messi's eight. 1. Stanley Matthews (1956) Matthews was the inaugural winner of the award and, notably, was aged 41 at the time. His victory established the Ballon d’Or’s place in the game and reflected the enormous respect he commanded across Europe. At 41 years, 10 months and 17 days, he remains the oldest-ever winner. 2. George Weah (1995) Weah became the first African player to win the Ballon d’Or after the rules were changed to allow non-European players representing European clubs to be eligible. He remains the only African winner of the men’s award, making his triumph a defining moment for football on the continent. 3. Ronaldo (1997) At 21, Ronaldo Nazario became the youngest winner of the award, a record that still stands. His explosive performances for Barcelona and Inter Milan made him a global phenomenon and cemented his reputation as one of the greatest No 9s of all time. 4. Fabio Cannavaro (2006) Cannavaro’s victory was largely down to his inspirational leadership of Italy as they lifted the 2006 World Cup. He had also won Serie A with Juventus, although the club was later stripped of the title following the Calciopoli scandal. Significantly, Cannavaro remains the last defender to win the award, two decades ago. Only three defenders have ever won the award: Franz Beckenbauer, Matthias Sammer and Cannavaro. 5. Lionel Messi (2009) Messi won the first of his record eight Ballon d’Or awards in 2009, with his most recent triumph coming 14 years later, in 2023. During the 2008/09 season, Messi scored 38 goals and provided 19 assists as Barcelona won the treble under Pep Guardiola. That was also the first of four in a row – also a record.
