title: Deadly church attack shocks Jordan's deep-rooted Christian community
description: Authorities increase death toll from 'terrorist' offensive to nine
content: Jordan’s small Christian community was reeling on Saturday, a day after the killing of nine of its members in what authorities called a terrorist attack on a church . Friday’s attack on St George's Orthodox church in the village of Hamoud was the largest against the country’s Christian community since the mid-1950s. On Saturday, authorities increased the death toll from seven to nine and said none of the three assailants had been captured. Hamoud is about 80km south of Amman. The victims were all men who mostly belonged to the Halasahs, a prominent Christian family in Jordan. The Halasah ancestral land is in Hamoud. At least one doctor and a dentist were among those killed. “Jordan has not seen such an attack. It appears to have been designed to make the Christians leave,” said a prominent member of the Halasah clan, who is also a doctor. Jordan is heavily dependent on US aid and has a defence pact with Washington. The kingdom is widely regarded as a bastion of stability in the Middle East. But it has faced domestic challenges as its economy has been stagnant for 15 years and the official unemployment rate is 16 per cent. The attack occurred as the authorities were promoting a site near the Dead Sea where Christians believe Jesus was baptised in an effort to revive tourism. The kingdom’s Christian population numbers 250,000 out of a population of 11 million. Orthodox Christians are the largest denomination. The attack struck at the core of Jordan’s Christian minority, the doctor said, describing the Halasahs as "the most prominent" of the Christian families, and Hamoud as their "bastion”. Security officials briefed Jordan's King Abdullah II "on the latest developments in the investigation into the attack", the Royal Palace said, without giving details. The King called the attackers "outlaws of Islam" and ordered the government to "review policies for countering extremist ideology and to intensify efforts to eradicate its root causes". The church responded to the attack by affirming loyalty to the state. Christophoros of Kyriakoupolis, the Archbishop of Jerusalem, described it as an “ugly terrorist act” that “will not undermine national unity” and allegiance to King Abdullah II. The archbishop, who also presides over the church in Jordan, said that "Christians are part of the history of this country … and will be, with the grace God, part of its future”. No group claimed responsibility for the attack, nor did the authorities name suspects. The country has maintained a complex relationship with Islamist groups. Last year, the government banned the Muslim Brotherhood. However, no measures were introduced against the Islamic Action Front, a group linked to the Brotherhood, which constitutes the largest bloc in parliament. This year, the Islamic Action Front rebranded itself as the Umma Party. Criticism by Jordanians and other Arabs started to appear on social media over extremist views by some Islamists, who have claimed in the past that Jordan was doing the Christians a favour by "letting" them stay in the kingdom. One of those who was criticised was MP Huda Al Otoum, from the Umma Party. She claimed this month that Jordan’s “acceptance” of the Christians could be used to “accept the Jews”. Social media users criticised her for sowing sectarian division. Many Jordanians posted on social media after Friday's attack, commenting in support of Christians and pointing out that the community was intertwined with the history of the country. Step News Agency, an anti-Brotherhood YouTube channel specialising in Arab affairs, published an old clip of a TV interview with Hamza Mansour, a former leader of the Islamic Action Front, in which he refused to condemn ISIS outright. The Umma Party said in a statement that the attack in Hamoud "constitutes a dangerous crime and a terrorist action that targets "our nation and its cohesion". When the authorities banned the Brotherhood in 2025, they accused the group of complicity in a weapons-manufacturing scheme aimed at creating instability. The kingdom has been ruled by the Hashemite monarchy since it was founded as a British protectorate in 1921. All significant powers are with King Abdullah, who has ruled since 1999.

title: Sheikh Khaled meets Emirati military students on official visit to Greece
description: Crown Prince of Abu Dhabi lauds citizens as ambassadors for country
content: Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed , Crown Prince of Abu Dhabi, met Emirati military students honing their skills in Greece as part of his official visit to the country. He hailed the young citizens as ambassadors for the UAE owing to their diligence, excellence and dedication and called on them to embody Emirati values and represent their nation and its armed forces with honour. Sheikh Khaled wished the students well on their academic and professional journey during discussion held at the Technical Training and Qualification Centre. Sheikh Khaled conveyed the greetings of President Sheikh Mohamed to the prospective military personnel, emphasising the UAE's commitment to following their well-being and progress abroad. The military students expressed their thanks to Sheikh Khaled for the visit and extended their gratitude to the country's leadership for its continued support and care. The technical training centre offers specialised training programmes combining theoretical knowledge and practical applications across various technical fields. خالد بن محمد بن زايد، ولي عهد أبوظبي، يزور مركز التدريب والتأهيل الفني في اليونان، ويلتقي عدداً من الطلبة العسكريين الإماراتيين الدارسين في المركز، حيث أكّد سموّه حرص القيادة الرشيدة على متابعة دراستهم وتدريبهم وتوفير الدعم لهم لتحقيق التميز وأداء واجباتهم الوطنية بكفاءة واقتدار. pic.twitter.com/1rLCtE3EAw — مكتب أبوظبي الإعلامي (@ADMediaOffice) October 24, 2026 Those programmes form part of military co-operation between the Emirates and Greece aimed at enhancing the readiness of UAE Armed Forces members for duty. The military meeting was held before Sheikh Khaled concluded his official visit on Friday, which took place at the invitation of Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis. Sheikh Khaled had on Thursday held talks with Mr Mitsotakis as major deals were agreed on between the countries. Discussions at the Prime Minister's Office centred on efforts to bolster collaboration across sectors including energy, infrastructure, health care, advanced technology and health care. Sheikh Khaled emphasised the UAE's desire to strengthen long-standing relations with Greece to support the aspirations of both nations. It was also announced during the visit that the UAE is to invest a further €15 billion ($16.8 billion) in Greece as part of a joint initiative between the countries. Sheikh Khaled also toured two of Greece's leading cultural attractions on Friday. Sheikh Khaled viewed the extensive collection of artwork at the National Gallery of Greece and also visited the National Archaeological Museum in Athens. He was briefed on the creative works at the gallery that reflect the rich history and heritage of Greece and the evolution of its art scene.

title: Is David Warner right in questioning Test cricket's supremacy over poor crowd attendance?
description: South Africa v Australia marquee series played in front of largely empty stands
content: The warning signs were there by the time the first ball was bowled in the first Test between South Africa and Australia in Durban earlier this month. The reigning and previous world Test champions were facing off once again, with wounds from the ball-tampering saga from the previous visit still not full healed. And yet, barely anyone turned up for the opening Test. Or for the second match in Gqeberha. Former Australia opener, and a central figure in the ball-tampering scandal of 2018, David Warner put it rather bluntly. "We keep hearing how important Test cricket is, but where are the fans in South Africa? Empty stands, no atmosphere, and we’re supposed to believe the format is thriving? You can’t keep calling Test cricket the pinnacle of the game if no one turns up to watch it. Harsh reality, but someone has to say it. Pathetic," Warner posted on social media. We keep hearing how important Test cricket is, but where are the fans in South Africa? Empty stands, no atmosphere, and we’re supposed to believe the format is thriving? You can’t keep calling Test cricket the pinnacle of the game if no one turns up to watch it. Harsh reality,… — David Warner (@davidwarner31) October 20, 2026 Warner was a batter who started his career almost exclusively as a T20 batter, and then forced his way into Test cricket. He ended up playing over 100 Tests. A lot of it got taken away from him after the sandpaper saga, with Warner losing any hopes of a future leadership position. He knows how high the stakes are for players. And what it means if there is no one to witness their battles. After the opening Test, a Cricket South Africa official said they will look into the reasons for low attendance for a marquee home series. "A Test match of this quality, featuring the Proteas and Australia, deserved greater support in the stands," Heinrich Strydom, chief executive of KwaZulu-Natal Cricket Union, said in a statement. "While we recognise that supporters face competing demands on their time and finances, we must also understand better what influences their decisions to attend and what more we can do to make live cricket an attractive and worthwhile experience. "This is something we will reflect on through a thorough internal review." Former South Africa batter Daryll Cullinan had already warned that the series had many factors going against it. In his piece for Cricinfo, Cullinan said that hosting a series in South Africa in October, when heavy rains are commonplace, and on underprepared surfaces was inviting trouble. Test Cricket in places that struggle for crowds should make it FREE to enter! Boards should make their money off their franchise tournaments. There is no way that Durban and PE have made enough money off ticket sales to justify no one there watching. — Kevin Pietersen🦏 (@KP24) October 21, 2026 Fewer patrons The situation is grim in most parts of the cricket world, barring England, Australia and a handful of centres in India. Most cricket boards simply can't afford to host Test matches as broadcasters are not queueing up to show them in the first place. A majority of Test series now are two-game affairs, just to meet minimum requirements. T20 cricket now bankrolls the entire system, first via franchise leagues and then internationals. Everything else feeds off it. Test matches in England are still viewed by a full crowd while Australia too boasts healthy attendances for five-day matches. In India, places such as Mumbai, Delhi, Kolkata, Chennai and Bengaluru get good crowds but they are not always allowed to host Tests due to rotation of venues. And how long will even the traditional Test centres continue to attract good crowds? Test patrons are not getting any younger. The next generation simply does not consume cricket the way Test cricket serves its fares. When a 112-Test veteran like Warner spells it out as clearly as that, there is no hiding from it - Test cricket is being propped up and will continue to require support. The moment you are at the mercy of the elements, one can't complain if the wind changes direction. For now, franchise leagues and T20s are pumping in money, allowing most cricket boards to pay the bills and keep the ball rolling at the domestic level. If some cricket boards decide Test cricket does not make financial sense, don't hold it against them. If you feel passionately about Test cricket, make sure to attend next time a match is held at a venue near you.

title: Arrests, demolitions, raids and displacement: Israel launches days-long West Bank offensive
description: Rights group accuses Israel of carrying out 'collective punishment'
content: Israeli troops forcibly displaced dozens of families in the occupied West Bank city of Al Khalil, while demolishing buildings, raiding homes and arresting at least 13 people, the Wafa news agency reported on Saturday. Israel's military said the operation would last for "several days" and that residents would be able to leave through one of three designated exists after "interrogation and inspection". All entrances to the city have been sealed off , Wafa said. Israel launched its campaign after five people were injured and two Israeli soldiers were later killed in a shooting at a military checkpoint near the city of Al Khalil, also known as Hebron, on Friday. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu later ordered the "full closure" of the West Bank. Israel’s military said it killed two suspects armed with a rifle and a handgun. Two of the injured were reported to be in a critical condition. Palestinian media reports named the pair as family members Mohammad Jaaba and Firas Jaaba, both 27 and from Al Khalil. The military said the men had planned to carry out a “large-scale” attack on Israelis. There are a number of illegal Israeli settlements in the area. On Friday, Israeli forces demolished a residential building in Farsh Al Hawa, west of the city, and prevented residents from entering or leaving the area, Wafa reported. Reactions Palestinian activist Issa Amro, who is based in Al Khalil, on Saturday said he had been unable to leave his home. "At least 250 families have been displaced in Hebron, including my own sister, Hayat, and her seven children," he said in a post on X. "Homes and shops are being demolished by the Israeli military. Around 250,000 people are trapped in the city, while 1,000 families in H2 remain in their homes. We are being collectively punished for something we neither did nor supported." The Palestinian Authority, which is supposed to control parts of the occupied West Bank, said Prime Minister Mohammad Mustafa spoke with the city's Mayor, Yousef Al Jaabari. They discussed the needs of residents amid "incursions by Israeli occupation forces into several areas and neighbourhoods and forced evacuation operations affecting hundreds of Palestinians, most of them women, children, older persons and patients". The military campaign was also condemned by Israeli rights organisation B'Tselem, which described it as part of "ethnic cleansing" efforts. In a statement on Saturday, executive director Yuli Novak said B'Tselem "urgently calls on governments and international institutions to act now, using all means available under international law, to prevent the forcible displacement of Palestinian civilians, collective punishment and extensive unlawful destruction in Hebron". Israeli leaders "are openly declaring their intentions and actions on the ground have already begun", he added. Mr Netanyahu had confirmed that Israel would enter neighbourhoods, remove residents and "dismantle terror infrastructure". Shortly after Mr Netanyahu made those comments, Defence Minister Israel Katz elaborated on the operation in a post on X. “The Jenin refugee camp model arrives in Hebron,” he wrote, referring to the now-destroyed camp in the north of the West Bank. B'Tselem said at least 33,000 Palestinians had so far been displaced by Israel's actions in the northern West Bank. Israel is set to hold parliamentary elections in three days, in which Mr Netanyahu has based his campaign on national security concerns.

title: UAE oil spill: Ras Al Khaimah closes all beaches 'until further notice'
description: Precautionary measures taken as authorities seek to contain oil slick off coast of Umm Al Quwain
content: Ras Al Khaimah on Saturday announced the closure of all beaches "until further notice" as authorities work to contain an oil spill from a supertanker in the Arabian Gulf. The decision comes after Umm Al Quwain temporarily closed all of its beaches and coastal areas and authorities in Sharjah sealed off Al Hamriya beach as a precautionary measure. The Ministry of Climate Change and Environment confirmed the incident early on Friday morning. It said the spill was the cause of a strong smell reported across the country in recent days. The Ras Al Khaimah Public Services Department announced the closures on Instagram."The public is kindly requested to follow the instructions and guidelines issued by the relevant authorities to ensure everyone’s safety," it said in the post. The extent of the oil slick is unclear, but the incident was confirmed amid growing concerns about the environmental impact of the Iran war on the Gulf and the Arabian Sea. Umm Al Quwain Municipality said it was carrying out field operations to contain the effects of the spill and minimise damage to marine and coastal environments. The municipality will monitor conditions, identify affected areas and support clean-up and treatment work as part of those efforts. Specialists will also help to assess the impact of the spill and determine appropriate measures. Limiting environmental impact Experts have told the National that swift containment of the spill was vital to limit damage to the environment and the UAE's marine ecosystems. Inesaf Benzaki, campaigns lead at Greenpeace Mena, said timely action was particularly important because the Gulf’s semi-enclosed geography limited the exchange of water with the open ocean, potentially allowing pollutants to persist. “We acknowledge the UAE authorities’ ongoing efforts to contain the reported oil spill off Umm Al Quwain and address its immediate effects,” she said. “As these efforts continue, understanding the potential environmental impact will be important to protecting the area’s marine ecosystems.” Prof John Burt, director of New York University Abu Dhabi’s Mubadala Arabian Centre for Climate and Environmental Sciences, previously warned that if oil reached the coastline, remediation could be expensive and a full recovery could take years.

title: Dubai chocolate brand hailed by Sheikh Hamdan after clinching UAE award win in honour of global success
description: Fix Dessert rose to fame thanks to its viral pistachio, knafeh and tahini-filled treat
content: The home-grown brand behind the Dubai chocolate confectionery craze has enjoyed more sweet success after scooping a major UAE award. Fix Dessert, led by husband and wife team Sarah Hamouda and Yezen Alani, rose to global prominence in 2024 thanks to its Can’t Get Knafeh of It bar – a pistachio, knafeh and tahini-filled treat. The company has now been honoured for its remarkable foodie feats after being named as a winner in the inaugural Dubai-it prize, earning the accolade in the business projects category. Sheikh Hamdan bin Mohammed, Crown Prince of Dubai, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Defence, hailed the chocolate maker for its worldwide impact. "Sarah Hamouda and Yezen Alani transformed a home-based business in Dubai into a global success," Sheikh Hamdan said in a post on X. "Sales of Dubai-style chocolate surged by 1,234 per cent in one year, and today, these products are sold in markets around the world and at more than 100 airports. We announce that the Dubai-it Award for Projects in the Business Category goes to FIX Dessert, which introduced ‘Dubai Chocolate’ to the world. Sarah Hamouda and Yezen Alani transformed a home-based business in Dubai into a global success. Sales of Dubai-style chocolate surged by… pic.twitter.com/yKWxEVAAN2 — Hamdan bin Mohammed (@HamdanMohammed) October 24, 2026 "This is the spirit of Dubai-it: transforming a simple home-based business into a global success. Congratulations to the Fix Dessert team." Since launching online in 2021, the brand has grown to include two stores in Dubai International Airport, one at Singapore's Changi Airport and a concession at Harrods in London . They have also hosted several pop-ups in the UAE. It now offers a collection of 10 dessert bars, with seasonal and limited-edition creations also part of the selection. What is the Dubai-it prize? Sheikh Mohammed bin Rashid , Vice President and Ruler of Dubai, unveiled the Dubai-it strategy in June in an effort to spread the emirate's culture of excellence among companies, institutions and future generations in the emirate. He said it would serve as a launchpad for future success and ensure ambitions were set high, stating that Dubai's accomplishments over the years had been built on "achieving exceptional results in record time, with precision and excellence". The award was subsequently launched to celebrate the innovation, enterprise and expertise of individuals and businesses across the city. Earlier this month, SWS Board Technology was named as the winner of the economy category of the awards. The Dubai-based manufacturer has grown to produce nearly half the world's kiteboards and wakeboards.

title: Future of UAE’s ODI cricket and captain Harpreet Bhatia in doubt as end of League Two looms
description: Final tri-series of miserable tournament for national team takes place in Dubai against Oman and Netherlands
content: The UAE have four matches left in the Cricket World Cup League Two. Let’s be honest, it can’t end soon enough. The national team have endured a miserable three years in one-day international cricket. So much so that the privilege of playing it at all is now on the line. They are bottom of the CWCL2 table, having lost 21 of their 32 matches so far. With two games each against Oman and the Netherlands in Dubai over the next two weeks, it is doubtful how many wins they will be able to add to their tally. It means they will now have to play to retain their status at the Cricket World Cup Qualifier Play-off in Nepal in December. The ICC haven’t announced the criteria for having official ODI privileges in the next four-year cycle. UAE lose to Scotland – in pictures It has been speculated that the game’s governing body might be about to extend the number of countries who play ODIs. Although where the funding will come from to keep sides like the UAE – who have had regular ODI status for the past 11 years – in the matter to which they have become accustomed is anyone’s guess. After all, the ICC traditionally prefer a conservative approach to things like this, rather than an expansionist one. But the UAE are working on the assumption they need to finish in the top four of that eight-team play-off in Kathmandu to safeguard their status. That should be doable, but it is far from a foregone conclusion given the opposition. Namibia, who will in all likelihood be involved, and Nepal have had the UAE’s measure for some time now. Canada have hit a dip at just the wrong time for them, with the UAE beating them when they met in Scotland in the summer. The national team have been adept at punching down when it comes to sides lower ranked than them in the recent past. But the four sides coming up from the Challenge League – Italy, Uganda, Jersey and probably Kuwait – will be far from easy beats. At their best, the UAE should have no concerns. But they are so infrequently in that condition, and the team continues to be in a state of flux. Just six players in the squad for the final tri-series were part of the XI for the first CWCL2 match, which was a loss to Canada in Dubai in 2024. Having been out the ODI side for some time, Muhammad Waseem has been recalled for UAE’s triseries against Oman and Ned If he retains his place for the subsequent qualifier playoff, he won’t be able to take up his TWO-HUNDRED AND TEN THOUSAND DOLLAR ILT20 contract 🤯 pic.twitter.com/OP3GaJdqvb — Paul Radley (@PaulRadley) October 22, 2026 And four of those – Basil Hameed, Aayan Khan, Muhammad Waseem and Tanish Suri – have spent long periods out of the team in the intervening time. The side have been undermined by the constant change, and it has shown in results. Young players on whom the future should have been built – such as Ali Naseer, Alishan Sharafu, Ethan D’Souza and Vriitya Aravind – have been tried and discarded. Even the captaincy has been tossed around with liberal abandon. Four people have led over the course of the three year competition, with some – such as Rahul Chopra, who is back at the helm now – being dispensed then recalled. The league campaign started with Waseem in charge. Tellingly, he was missing the chance to take up a contract in the Pakistan Super League to play in that first tri-series. Now he has been recalled to the side. If he is retained for the play-off, he will have to forego a large chunk of the $210,000 deal he landed to play in the DP World ILT20. They seemed to have finally settled on a captain who had the faith of coach Lalchand Rajput when Harpreet Bhatia ascended to the role this year, just a few months into being in the country. Now his future, too, is in doubt. Harpreet will miss the games against Oman and the Netherlands as he is on an indefinite break from cricket on compassionate grounds. The Emirates Cricket Board announced this week he would be returning to India as his mother is ill. “I am grateful to the [ECB] for accepting my request of taking a break from cricket, as well as all the support the board has given me in recent days and months,” Bhatia said. “For now, my full focus is my mother’s health and well-being. I wish the team the very best for their upcoming fixtures.” The ECB in turn said it “offers its full support to Harpreet and his family in this difficult time”. “The board is fully committed to the mental health and well-being of all its players and support staff especially when they have challenges pertaining to their families,” the ECB wrote. “We thank Harpreet for his professionalism and commitment to the ECB and the UAE men’s national cricket team. We are all praying for his mother and wish her a full recovery at the earliest.” The UAE start their CWCL2 tri-series when they face Oman at the ICC Academy in Dubai Sports City on Sunday.

title: AI will not replace human musicians as it lacks originality, Sennheiser boss says
description: Tech should be used as tool to support creativity and not dilute it, Daniel Sennheiser says
content: Artificial intelligence will be unable to replace human craft in the music industry because it lacks the ability to create original work, the chairman of German audio major Sennheiser has said. While AI can be used as a tool to support the creation of music, the booming technology is largely only able to produce output based on what it has been trained on, raising questions about actual creativity, Daniel Sennheiser said. "AI is a calculation of probability ... it comes out with basically everything that it knows, but it cannot create something new," Mr Sennheiser, who is also co-chief executive of the Wedemark-based company, told The National in an interview in Dubai. "Therefore, if you make your own music, if you create something, you're always going to be safe. AI can support you in your creative process and actually even inspire you ... but it will never replace a [musician]." Several industries have grown concerned with the growth of AI, as the technology becomes more powerful and is able to create works in music, film, arts and other endeavours that have relied on human skill and talent. Music artists and unions have been protesting against copyright infringement and the overall lack of originality when it comes to AI-generated music. Even streaming services are taking action. This week, Spotify said it had removed about 50 million songs it deemed as AI slop over the past year. Generative AI in music, however, is growing to become big business: revenue in the market is projected to hit almost $2.8 billion by 2030, nearly triple the estimated $960.4 million this year, data from Grand View Research shows. "Like with every new technology, initially you're very afraid of the substitution that it's doing. And, yes, [AI] is creating some what I call background music, which you can do very well with AI today," said Mr Sennheiser, the third-generation leader of the company founded in 1945. "AI tools are allowing much more people to be creative with music ... it's more of a support than anything else." Supply chains and UAE focus Mr Sennheiser said the current supply chain disruptions, as a result of geopolitical conflicts and tariff battles, have not directly affected the company, owing to in-house operations and third-party relationships. For instance, Sennheiser has its own assembly line for surface-mount devices, or those that place electronic components on circuit boards. The company is also not affected by shortages in chips and critical minerals such as neodymium, as the audio industry does not use those components on a broad scale unlike manufacturers of smartphones and computers. It also helps that Sennheiser is based in Germany, considered the manufacturing hub of Europe that is home to key industries such as car making, chemicals, engineering and technology. "We were always able to deliver more or less every product ... we find our way around those shortages," Mr Sennsheiser said. He did acknowledge, however, that Sennheiser raises prices based on the costs of raw materials, transport and manufacturing, which includes energy. "We look at what is available in the market and what is sustainable, so we have a regular schedule of increasing prices based on the realities that are there," Mr Sennheiser said. The company will also continue to invest in the Middle East, especially in the UAE, where its Dubai office serves the wider region, including CIS countries. The company does not divulge market share numbers. Mr Sennheiser, however, noted that while the brand is underrepresented in some markets, they have a "fair share" in others, including the UAE. "I see the market growing and that's why I want to invest in this region," he said, without providing details.

title: Talking your language: UAE unveils AI tool designed to master Arabic dialects
description: Jais 3 has been developed by Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence and Abu Dhabi's Inception42
content: A cutting-edge Abu Dhabi university has unveiled an Arabic AI tool designed to decode a variety of regional dialects and respond to rapid shifts in language. Jais 3 – built by the Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence, in partnership with Abu Dhabi's Inception42 – is able to field queries and carry out tasks such as transcribing conversations and creating documents and presentations. It features Jais speech, a voice recognition model for the Arabic language and its varying dialects from across the Gulf and North Africa. The advanced AI platform was developed through the university's Institute of Foundation Models (IFM) with the goal of keeping pace with the nuances of a language spoken by more than 400 million people around the world. The tech is also able to deal with code-switching, which refers to when a bilingual person alternates from one language to another. "Arabic AI needs to understand the language in its everyday context, which varies by geography and across generations," said Haonan Li, senior research scientist at IFM. "For example, we need to account for the many nuances in spoken Arabic, including when speakers slip into English or French mid-sentence and back again. We built Jais 3 for Arabic as it's really used." High-tech training Jais Speech transcribes Modern Standard Arabic and dialects spoken across 19 Arab countries. It follows speakers as they switch between Arabic and languages such as English or French, keeping those words in their original script. It also identifies the dialect being spoken and can add Arabic vowel marks to a transcript. Paired with the language models, Jais Speech enables Jais 3 to take spoken instructions in Arabic or English and act on them. Mr Li said the team worked extensively to ensure strong representation of the many forms of Arabic spoken in the region and beyond. “One of the key challenges was ensuring broad and balanced representation across regional dialects," he said. "For Gulf dialects, this involved working with a more limited pool of existing open data and addressing the tendency of open models to default to Modern Standard Arabic rather than maintaining the requested dialect when generating synthetic data. "This required additional work in data synthesis and filtering to ensure the quality and relevance of the resulting data set." A similar challenge was faced by the Jais 3 team for Morocco, where available data tended to be heavily weighted towards Moroccan Darija, leaving other dialects in the region less represented. Embracing technology Richard Morton, vice president and executive director of IFM, said the launch of Jais 3 showed the importance of investing in rapidly evolving technology. "Jais has shown what the UAE's long-term investment in open AI research can deliver for the Arabic-speaking world," he said. "With Jais 3, we are extending that foundation into speech and agents at a time when the UAE is putting AI to work across government and society – reflecting MBZUAI's commitment to the UAE National AI Strategy 2031 and to building the research capability and national talent that will carry it forward." IFM and Inception42 evaluated the models on an audited suite of 24 Arabic benchmarks, which they are releasing publicly alongside the models. The results showed the largest Jais 3 model leads open models on agentic tasks and matches the strongest on Arabic understanding. Jais Speech recorded the lowest average word and character error rates among all models compared, while the seven billion and 32 billion-parameter models earned the highest average Arabic scores among open models of comparable sizes. "Jais 3 makes Arabic AI more practical for business use," said Dr Larry Murray, senior vice president of Applied Science at Inception42. "Stronger reasoning and instruction following, combined with tool use, provide a foundation for multi-step agentic workflows. With open models across a range of sizes, organisations can match these capabilities to their computing budgets and deployment needs."

title: Vincent Kompany 'stable' in hospital after collapsing at Bayern Munich training
description: Director of sport Max Erbl revealed on Friday that the Belgian coach is still undergoing tests to determine what caused the problem
content: Bayern Munich coach Vincent Kompany is in a stable condition in hospital after collapsing while watching the German club's reserve team train on Friday. Kompany had been unwell during the week with reports suggesting he had struggling with a virus and the 40-year-old missed Bayern's pre-match media conference ahead of their Uefa Champions League draw with Arsenal. Kompany was on the touchline at the Allianz Arena on Wednesday despite the pouring rain as the match ended 2-2, with Alphonso Davies and Harry Kane on target as the German and English champions settled for a point each. Bayern's next game is away to Freiburg on Sunday which the former Belgium and Manchester City captain will now miss as he undergoes more tests at hospital. “The good news is he's stable ,” said Bayern's director of sport Max Eberl, who had assistant coach Aaron Danks alongside him in Saturday's press conference ahead of the Freiburg match. “I spoke with him last night, with his wife too. 🗣️ 𝗠𝗮𝘅 𝗘𝗯𝗲𝗿𝗹 𝗼𝗻 𝗩𝗶𝗻𝗰𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗞𝗼𝗺𝗽𝗮𝗻𝘆'𝘀 𝗰𝗼𝗻𝗱𝗶𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 “The good news is he's stable. I spoke with him last night, with his wife too. It wasn't a nice moment for all of us, he collapsed on the pitch yesterday and will spend a few more days in hospital… pic.twitter.com/kbrAC7LhH6 — FC Bayern (@FCBayernEN) October 24, 2026 “It wasn't a nice moment for all of us, he collapsed on the pitch yesterday and will spend a few more days in hospital until everything is checked over. “It shows again how health is the most important thing in life – not football. So, all of us send our best well-wishes. We as FC Bayern stand together. The most important thing is that the cause is established and he gets fit again. He'll only come back when he's fit. “They’ve been investigating the cause all along. He’d already been having minor problems last week. The doctors are doing nothing but trying to find out what it is. “The tests have already yielded some results, but further results are needed to determine exactly what it is and how long it will take for him to recover. I’m not a doctor. But we can support him with energy and love.” Eberl admitted he did not know how long Kompany would be missing for but made clear he get “all the time” he needs. “We’re not going to start setting any time frames,” he said. “We need to find out what the issue is, and then it’s a question of what the recovery time will be. We're not talking in terms of days, but weeks. We’re all clear on that. And we have such a fantastic coaching staff, led by Vinnie. “But our success is down to an outstanding team behind the scenes. There’s absolutely no thought of changing anything. All the guys here are outstanding – and so, in the spirit of Vinnie, which everyone carries within them, we can all tackle the coming weeks.” Everyone at Manchester City is wishing a speedy recovery to our former captain and Club legend, Vincent Kompany. Get well soon, Vinny 🩵 https://t.co/RYUP7DjYkj pic.twitter.com/fozzCkHGQl — Manchester City (@ManCity) October 23, 2026 Erbl also admitted that some of the young players who watched their manager's collapse had been “a bit overwhelmed” by what they witnessed. “For the U23s, it happened while they were training, so they experienced it first-hand,” he added. “For 17- and 18-year-old boys, that's quite something – many of them haven’t had to deal with anything negative before. Some things just happen. The boys were a bit overwhelmed; that’s only human. “Everyone looks out for one another; that’s what defines FC Bayern. We’re there for each other and for everyone else who’s affected by this. That’s Bayern Munich – it’s not just empty words, but it’s what truly sets us apart. The fact that we go through this together and are there for one another really strengthens the family, which is the most important thing.” Bayern are currently top of the Bundesliga on 14 points from six games, albeit only ahead of Borussia Dortmund on goal difference. In the Champions League, they are in 14th spot having won one and drawn two so far, leaving them one point outside automatic qualification spots for the knockout stages. Kopmany took over as manager in 2024 guiding the club to successive Bundesliga titles, one German Cup and two German Super Cups.

title: Lebanon's Aoun vows end to neglect of Tripoli in first presidential visit to city in 15 years
description: President says projects to be launched to create jobs for residents
content: Lebanon's President Joseph Aoun vowed on Saturday to end decades of neglect in Tripoli during the first presidential visit to the northern city in 15 years, a move aimed at restoring public trust in state institutions and services. Mr Aoun was received with a hero's welcome in Lebanon's second-largest city, which is home to some of the country's wealthiest politicians but remains among its most marginalised and impoverished areas. Speaking at the Tripoli Serail, he said the "time has come to put an end to neglect" in the city and to address the socioeconomic challenges facing its residents. "My visit is to tell the people of Tripoli that the state is present and always stands by your side," Mr Aoun said. "To restore trust, we must provide citizens with services. Human dignity requires the state to deliver services and ensure they are accessible to everyone. This is how we rebuild trust." He said projects were being planned to create jobs for residents. "It is our duty to serve the people," he added. Tripoli Mayor Abdel Hamid Karimeh described Mr Aoun's visit as historic, saying it follows years of state neglect. The last reported visit to the city by a sitting Lebanese president was in November 2011. Mr Aoun's itinerary included stops at the Palace of Justice, Tripoli Port, the special economic zone and the Rachid Karami International Fair, sites considered important to the city's economic development. Speaking at the Palace of Justice, Mr Aoun said tackling corruption was a national priority and stressed the importance of an independent judiciary. Mr Aoun was accompanied by Interior Minister Ahmad Hajjar and Justice Minister Adel Nassar, along with senior security officials. Mr Hajjar said the presidential visit demonstrated the state's commitment to Tripoli and he expressed hope that it would help strengthen security and economic activity in the city. He also warned that deteriorating economic conditions could undermine stability. Meanwhile, Mr Nassar said the visit was significant and showed the government's commitment to developing Tripoli. "The city has an essential role and we will do everything necessary to develop it," he said.

title: Turkey rules out combat with Houthis under defence pact as foreign ministers meet in Istanbul
description: Makkah agreement says attack on one country is attack on all, but its wording raises questions about collective defence obligations
content: Turkey does not expect its troops to engage in combat with the Houthis under a defence pact with Saudi Arabia and Pakistan, Defence Minister Yasar Guler said on Friday, as the countries' foreign ministers met in Istanbul to discuss regional developments. "The main purpose of our possible military support to Saudi Arabia will be to strengthen deterrence . We absolutely do not foresee entering into any conflict with the Houthis," he said. "Our priority is to prevent new tensions from emerging in the region and to contribute to security and stability." Mr Guler said Turkey would assess requests for military support to Saudi Arabia and determine the scope of its assistance once parliament ratified the pact. The Makkah defence agreement, signed in August and submitted to Turkey's parliament for ratification this week, is based on the principle that an attack on one member is considered an attack on all. But Article 2 specifies that countries must assist one another in the event of an attack or military aggression by "another country or a group of countries" , raising questions about whether it would apply to strikes by Yemen's Houthis, who have escalated attacks on Saudi Arabia in recent weeks. Saudi Arabia and Pakistan have ratified the agreement. The two countries' foreign ministers met in Istanbul on Friday on the sidelines of the Regional Four (R4) ministerial meeting, which involved Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Egypt, where they discussed bilateral relations and regional developments, among them the situation in Yemen. Saudi Foreign Minister Prince Faisal bin Farhan and Pakistan's Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar condemned recent Houthi attacks on civilian areas in Saudi Arabia, according to a statement by the kingdom's Foreign Ministry. The bilateral talks took place as Istanbul hosted a wider diplomatic gathering , the first of its kind, which also brought together foreign ministers from the UK, France, Germany and Italy. Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan hosted the meeting to discuss "regional issues of mutual concern", his office said. In a joint statement issued after the meeting, the ministers said they "condemned in the strongest terms the unacceptable escalation by the Houthi militia", including continued strikes on Saudi Arabia targeting civilians and civilian infrastructure, as well as attacks on commercial shipping in the Red Sea and the Bab Al Mandeb strait. They expressed solidarity with the governments of Yemen and Saudi Arabia and called on the Houthis to "immediately cease all military actions, threats and attacks, and to return to the political process in good faith". Saudi Arabia has come under intensified Houthi attacks in recent weeks, including deadly strikes on airports that have disrupted air travel and prompted the cancellation or postponement of major international conferences, diplomatic summits and sporting events in the kingdom. The Houthis have also claimed attacks on Saudi energy and military targets.

title: Parts of UAE set for rain, fog and 50kph winds but wait for drop in temperatures goes on
description: The National Centre of Meteorology has forecast unsettled weather conditions
content: Parts of the UAE are braced for rain , high winds and fog in the coming days - but temperatures are set to remain high across the country. The National Centre of Meteorology forecasts wet weather on the horizon in northern and eastern areas of the Emirates until at least Wednesday. The NCM's online weather map shows rainfall is most likely in Ras Al Khaimah and Fujairah on Monday and Tuesday. The weather centre - in its latest five-day buletin - said humid nights were in prospect with fog likely on the morning commute throughout next week. Winds are expected to reach up to 40kph on Sunday and could rise to 50kph from Monday to Wednesday, carrying dust into the air and hampering visibility. The Northern Emirates in particular have experienced unstable weather conditions this month, with heavy rain and hail reported in some areas. Abu Dhabi and Dubai are expected to avoid the wet weather, while the unseasonable autumn heat is set to persist across the Emirates. The weather bureau predicts daytime temperatures will remain in the mid to high 30s in both Abu Dhabi and Dubai over the next five days and could exceed 40°C in Al Ain and remote desert areas of Abu Dhabi. The UAE's average daily temperature in October stands at 29.7°C, according to the NCM's latest monthly weather summary. The mercury has risen this month, however, with the El Nino weather phenomenon playing its part in delaying the typically cooler autumnal weather.

title: UAE school leaders optimistic for new academic year after Iran war disruption
description: Leading school groups say enrolment on track as they await return of hundreds of pupils who left country at height of conflict
content: UAE school leaders are looking ahead to the new academic year with confidence as they work to hit teacher enrolment targets and welcome back pupils who left the country at the height of the Iran war. Education has faced widespread disruption after the conflict erupted in February. Schools switched to remote learning as a precautionary measure and many summer exams were scrapped. The recent escalation of fighting between the US and Iran has again cast uncertainty over the region as schools prepare for the return to classrooms at the end of August. Dino Varkey, chief executive of Gems Education, the UAE's largest private school group, said the outlook remained positive, despite the challenges of recent months. At the peak of the conflict in March, between 1,500 and 1,600 pupils at Gems schools – roughly 1 per cent to 1.5 per cent of its 146,000-strong base – relocated to their home countries, Mr Varkey recently told Reuters . Of those, 600 to 700 have indicated plans to return. “Many of those families have already indicated their intention to return, which is a strong vote of confidence in both Gems and the UAE,” Mr Varkey told The National . Gems has secured “around 90 per cent of our targeted student places for the coming academic year through a combination of re-enrolments and new registrations”, he added. Impact of war Lisa Yackiminie, human resources director at Taaleem Group, which operates 37 schools across the Emirates, said it experienced a small drop in staffing levels due to the war. “Attrition directly attributable to the conflict is approximately 1 per cent of our workforce, which is very low,” she said. She said the group's annual teacher confirmation cycle had run “in line with previous years without any unusual spikes” and hiring acceptance rates had held firm. “We are on target to close our regular recruitment cycle as planned,” she added. It is a similar story at Nord Anglia International School Dubai. About 95 families decided to leave Dubai during the regional uncertainty. From those, 11 pupils have returned, and another 73 are confirmed for September. “That means almost 90 per cent of those temporary leavers are returning to NAS Dubai for next academic year,” said Svenja Cassia, the school's director of marketing, admissions and communications. She said this “reflects the confidence families continue to have in both the UAE and our school community”. Overall student retention at NAS Dubai is 91 per cent for 2026-27, Ms Cassia added. Where demand is coming from The conflict has not suppressed demand for Dubai school places so much as rerouted it. Ms Cassia said: “We are seeing more families relocating to us from elsewhere within the UAE, while international relocations have been slightly slower than in previous years.” Net demand at NAS Dubai remains “extremely healthy, with most year groups already at or close to capacity”. They are also recruiting teachers internationally. “Our focus has been on clear, regular communication and ensuring colleagues feel supported, informed, and connected. As a result, we enter the new academic year with a strong team in place and are looking forward to welcoming a number of new colleagues joining us from around the world,” she said. The decision last month by the KHDA, Dubai's private education regulator, to freeze tuition fees for the coming academic year – announced as a measure to support families through continuing uncertainty – is also set to provide a boost. Both Gems and Taaleem are taking proactive measures to retain staff. Taaleem has offered flexible and remote working where appropriate, as well as enhanced access to its employee assistance programme, and what Ms Yackiminie described as “enhanced counselling support”. Mr Varkey credits sustained investment in professional development and leadership pathways for Gems' teacher turnover declining year on year. “We have more than 3,000 of our colleagues who have now been part of the Gems family for over a decade,” he said. Challenges remain Asim Waheed offers a different reading of a sector he has spent years recruiting for. The chief executive of Teach for Life, which places teachers and school leaders across the Middle East, told The National that the war has accelerated stresses that were already evident in the education market. Covid-19 shrank school enrolments, which meant cash flows tightened and teacher salaries followed and this is still being felt, he said. Combined with the rising cost of living, the result is that the financial proposition for teachers has changed. “It's not as attractive as it used to be,” he said, adding that he always expected this to be a volatile year, with or without conflict. Mr Varkey said Gems was committed to ensuring the well-being and morale of its teachers. “Whether you are speaking about teachers or families, priorities have evolved significantly over recent years,” he said. “People increasingly value well-being and a genuine sense of belonging alongside academic excellence or career progression.” For educators, expectations now extend well beyond salary, he said. “They want organisations that invest in their professional growth, provide opportunities to lead, embrace innovation responsibly and create an environment where they feel valued and supported. “Similarly, families are looking for schools that offer not only outstanding educational outcomes but also confidence, continuity and a strong community at all times.” Career decisions Mr Waheed said many teachers currently on their summer holidays will still be undecided about whether to continue their careers in the Emirates against the backdrop of continued regional tensions. Earlier this year, schools were already advertising more vacant roles than usual, he reported. “The entire recruitment world is in 'just in case' mode,” he said. The major operators are measured. “Fundamentally, the long-term appeal of the UAE as a destination for families seeking stability, opportunity and world-class education remains unchanged,” said Mr Varkey.

title: How quickly could Turkey send military forces to back Saudi Arabia?
description: Analysis: Pakistan and Turkey's agreement to help kingdom under Makkah defence pact is not same as overnight mobilisation
content: Turkey , Pakistan and Saudi Arabia have said they will ensure the “rapid deployment” of “military forces and capabilities” to help Riyadh as it confronts attacks by Iran-backed Houthi rebels. The pledge came at an emergency meeting of ministers and military commanders from the three countries under the Makkah defence pact , a collective deterrence agreement signed in August. “The pact has now moved much faster than expected from a declaratory collective defence framework to practical military implementation,” Deniz Karakullukcu, a foreign policy adviser at the Turkish parliament, told The National. But agreeing to send forces is not the same as an overnight mobilisation, and Monday's pledges came alongside a commitment to uphold each country’s legislation. Nato member Turkey is also likely to seek limits to its involvement and is reluctant to commit large numbers of troops to another country’s conflict, analysts told The National. “I would describe this as the first real test and operationalisation of the pact but not as Turkey automatically entering the war,” Mr Karakullukcu added. In Turkey, parliament must approve the pact before President Recep Tayyip Erdogan can ratify it. Observers expect this to happen swiftly after the reopening of parliament last week, although there is no exact timeline. “I expect this issue to come on the parliament's agenda in the coming period,” Parliament Speaker Numan Kurtulmus told reporters in Ankara at the end of September. Parliament’s foreign affairs committee would make an announcement when the text arrived at the National Assembly in Ankara, a parliamentary media official told The National. On sending troops specifically, Turkey’s constitution says that in principle, parliament must approve such moves, as happened when Turkish soldiers went to Libya in 2020. But it contains a caveat: a separate parliamentary authorisation is not needed if an international treaty to which Turkey is a party requires sending troops. Because the text of the Makkah defence pact has not been published, Turkey’s exact obligations under the agreement remain unclear. When the pact is approved by parliament, if it provides a sufficient legal basis for sending troops, it may be that separate parliamentary approval is not required. With power over decisions on the armed forces, Mr Erdogan would then decide whether or not to send the troops. Turkey can provide limited technical and military support before the pact is approved and ratified domestically, under various bilateral agreements with Saudi Arabia going back to the 2010s. Nonetheless, even once the pact formally comes into force, Turkey is more likely to supply Saudi Arabia with advisory support, border defences, air and missile defence systems and intelligence sharing than it is to approve a large-scale, cross-border operation in Yemen by Turkish troops, analysts said. “If you are asking whether Turkey is sending troops to Yemen, I say no. I am not expecting this,” Hasan Selim Ozertem, research director at Ankara-based Ussal Consultancy, told The National . “But Turkey can send troops to Saudi Arabia for its territorial defence against the threat coming from the Houthis. It's a defence pact at the end of the day. It's not an offensive pact.” Turkish-made military systems do not necessarily require the country's armed forces for operation, Mr Karakullukcu added. “Depending on the system and the arrangement, it can be operated by Saudi personnel with training or technical support,” he said. Sending air defence and missile systems is also strategically useful for Turkey. It is expanding a growing defence manufacturing industry that has become a pillar of its foreign policy, and new deployments allow Ankara to build a battleground reputation for domestically produced hardware. Turkey sending high-tech equipment including drones, electronic warfare systems and military advisers “changed the dynamics on the ground", in favour of Ankara’s allies in previous conflicts in Libya, Syria and Azerbaijan, Mr Ozertem added. Turkey is also reticent to get too involved in Yemen, analysts said. Ankara maintains trade and political relationships with Iran, which backs the Houthis against Saudi Arabia. Alongside recent crackdowns by Turkish authorities on Iranian companies under sanctions, an overt and significant role in the Yemen conflict could increase Tehran’s suspicions about Ankara’s strategic priorities. It all places Turkey in “a delicate position”, said Murat Yesiltas, foreign policy director at the government-aligned Seta think tank. With Saudi Arabia, “Turkey should adopt an approach of measured solidarity", Mr Yesiltas wrote in an opinion piece for the Daily Sabah newspaper. “It must provide effective defensive contributions while retaining decision-making authority over offensive operations.” For the same reason, ministers have stressed the need for diplomacy and dialogue while acknowledging the rapid sending of military force. Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan told state media after Monday’s emergency meeting in Riyadh that the talks covered “what kind of support could be given to Saudi Arabia's defence”, but also “what can be done to resolve the problem peacefully through dialogue".

title: India and Pakistan set for ODI bonanza in 2027
description: Arch rivals could face each other multiple times during World Cup and Asia Cup
content: Indian and Pakistan cricket fans are braced for a problem of plenty in 2027 after the ODI World Cup schedule was announced. The bitter rivals were ​drawn in ​Group A for next year's 50-over World Cup in South Africa, Zimbabwe and Namibia. They ⁠will face off at the Wanderers ​in Johannesburg on October 10. The schedule is by design as organisers now put both teams in the same group to guarantee at least one India v Pakistan match ; the T20 final between the rivals in the recently concluded Asian Games was the most watched in the Games' history. With a new format in place at the ODI World Cup , India and Pakistan could face each other as many as three times – in the group phase, Super Seven stage and the semi-finals/final, if they make it that far. That is not the only tournament where the two countries will clash in 2027. As has become the norm in recent years, the Asia Cup will serve as a warm-up for the World Cup , changing its format to ODIs next season. The tournament is scheduled to take place in Bangladesh. There as well, India and Pakistan are likely to face off twice and possibly three times in case they enter title contest. Which means that after a relative paucity of matches between the traditional rivals in recent years, which were largely centred around the T20 format, supporters of India and Pakistan could witness as many as six 50-over contests next year. White-ball legends Rohit Sharma and Virat Kohli will almost certainly play their last matches in India colours during the ODI World Cup. Both stars have unfinished business at the tournament, having come within touching distance of the trophy during the 2023 World Cup where India were comfortably the best team in the tournament, only to lose to Australia in the final . Kohli has already declared that the 2027 tournament will be his last for India. Rohit is also hoping to feature in the World Cup and make up for the lost opportunity as captain three years back. India have been placed in the same group as Australia and their match will open the second stage ​of ⁠the World Cup ‌in Cape Town on October 7. Afghanistan, co-hosts Zimbabwe and an as yet unknown qualifier are also in Group A with the top three teams in each pool advancing to ​the Super 7 phase, along ‌with the best of ⁠the fourth-placed teams across ​the two pools. Co-hosts South Africa, who have ​yet to ‌lift the World Cup, are in Group B with ⁠England, New Zealand, Sri Lanka, Bangladesh and another qualifier.

title: Dubai launches agentic AI accelerator to transform public-facing government services
description: Dubai Future Foundation programme will assess hundreds of cases across 33 government entities
content: Dubai has launched a new accelerator programme to apply agentic artificial intelligence across government services, marking a significant step in the emirate's push to future-proof public sector operations. The Dubai Future Foundation announced the agentic AI for Government Services Accelerator under its Dubai Future Accelerators initiative. The programme will help government entities create prototypes to use in AI-powered services within significantly shorter time frames. In its first phase, the accelerator will bring together 33 Dubai government entities and assess more than 300 public-facing use cases to identify those with the greatest potential for agentic AI development. The project is being organised by the Dubai Centre for Artificial Intelligence in collaboration with Digital Dubai and the Dubai Electronic Security Centre. Participants will work alongside technology companies certified under the Dubai AI Seal, a recognition programme designed to identify trusted AI firms operating in the emirate. Agentic AI is an advanced form of autonomous artificial intelligence that can work independently without constant human supervision. Unlike traditional or standard generative AI, which responds to prompts and waits for the next instruction, agentic AI can act like an independent project manager, making decisions and executing them through external software systems. When given an objective, rather than trying to solve the entire problem immediately, agentic AI breaks the goal into smaller tasks, allowing it to process a number of ways to reach the end goal. It evaluates the various paths as it goes and corrects mistakes as and when needed. It is this ability to monitor its own progress that makes it particularly useful. If there is a problem, it does not wait for a human to fix it, but self-corrects in real time, allowing it to take on complex tasks that can last for hours or days. Hamad Al Mansoori, Director General of Digital Dubai, said the programme represented a shift from responding to residents' needs to anticipating them. “The future of digital government cannot be shaped by any single entity; it requires an integrated ecosystem that brings together expertise, data and capabilities around a common goal,” he said. Khalfan Belhoul, chief executive of Dubai Future Foundation, said the launch aligned with directives from Sheikh Hamdan bin Mohammed , Crown Prince of Dubai, Deputy Prime Minister, Minister of Defence and Chairman of the Board of Trustees of DFF, to position Dubai as the world's leading city in the adoption of agentic AI across government services. “Artificial intelligence has opened new horizons for governments to imagine the future, design next-generation solutions and services, and bring them to life,” Mr Belhoul said. “Government entities can now significantly shorten traditional development cycles and processes, enabling them to enhance the quality and effectiveness of their services within much shorter time frames. “Dubai has all the foundations required to lead this transformation, including an agile regulatory ecosystem and advanced infrastructure that enable government entities to rapidly advance the quality of their services.” Yousuf Al Shaibani, chief executive of the Dubai Electronic Security Centre, emphasised that cybersecurity must be embedded throughout the process. “Artificial intelligence is reshaping how government services are designed and delivered. Cybersecurity cannot be an afterthought in the adoption of AI. It must be embedded at every stage, from planning and design to operation and monitoring,” Mr Al Shaibani said.

title: Joy Awards 2027 set to be cancelled in latest change to Saudi entertainment calendar
description: Glitzy annual event has brought together leading Arab and international stars over years
content: Next year's Joy Awards are set to be cancelled amid a reassessment of spending on major entertainment events in Saudi Arabia. The televised gala event , normally held in Riyadh in January, will not take place in 2027, Reuters reported. The event's organisers, Saudi Arabia's General Entertainment Authority and MBC Group, have not issued a statement confirming the cancellation. The Joy Awards trace their roots to the Joy Forum in 2019, when Shah Rukh Khan, Jackie Chan, Jason Momoa and Jean-Claude Van Damme were among the international figures recognised in Riyadh. The awards returned three years later as part of Riyadh Season, the annual programme of concerts, theatre, sport and entertainment staged across the Saudi capital, and have since become a major fixture in the Arab entertainment calendar. Most Joy Awards categories are decided by public vote across film, television, music, sport and social media, while separate honours include Lifetime Achievement and Personality of the Year awards. The show is broadcast on MBC channels and Shahid. The 2022 awards featured John Travolta, who received a Lifetime Achievement Award, and Salman Khan, who was named Personality of the Year, while Mohammed Abdu, Kadim Al Sahir and Hany Shaker performed. Since then, honorees have included Anthony Hopkins, Morgan Freeman, Andrea Bocelli and Hans Zimmer, alongside leading Arab actors and musicians. This year's awards , held in January, included wins for Egyptian singer Angham and Lebanese singer Fadel Shaker, who took Best Male Artist and Best Song for Sahak Al Shawq . Mohammed Fadl Shaker was named Best New Music Artist. Oscar-winning actor Forest Whitaker and former Egyptian culture minister Farouk Hosny received Lifetime Achievement awards, while Millie Bobby Brown was named Personality of the Year. Katy Perry, Robbie Williams and Il Divo performed, while Shah Rukh Khan, Oscar Isaac, Jeremy Piven, Heather Graham and Travis Fimmel were among the international stars attending. If confirmed, the decision would follow the postponement of the Red Sea International Film Festival , due to take place in Jeddah from December 3 to 12, and the cancellation of this year's Soundstorm , an annual music festival scheduled for December 3 and 4 in Riyadh. Organisers of the Red Sea International Film Festival said it would now take place in late 2027 following a review of logistics. The foundation did not link the decision to regional conflict or budget cuts, and said its year-round programmes, including the Red Sea Fund and Red Sea Labs, would continue. Soundstorm organiser MDL Beast gave no reason for the cancellation and said the music festival would be staged again in 2027. The seventh Riyadh Season is scheduled to begin on October 21. The General Entertainment Authority has announced a 10-week programme that features concerts, theatre, comedy, family entertainment and sport. Joy Award winner Fadel Chaker is among the first major music acts announced and will perform at Abu Bakr Salem Theatre on October 22. The season will also include the Six Kings Slam tennis tournament, alongside boxing, wrestling and UFC competitions. Boulevard World, Boulevard City, Wonder Garden and The Groves are also returning.

title: PRYPCO Blocks wants to change the way people talk about property ownership
description: Habba Habba campaign makes real estate investing in Dubai even more accessible
content: PRYPCO Blocks, the leading fractional ownership platform, is making real estate investing in Dubai even more accessible with a playful new campaign based on an everyday regional phrase. The fully digital real estate ownership platform has been successfully enabling the public to make investments in managed homes from just Dh500. Now PRYPCO Blocks is adding a fresh perspective to Dubai's fractional ownership model through its ‘ Habba Habba ’ initiative, employing a phrase already used in conversations across the region to increase familiarity. Many people have an ambition to own Dubai real estate on their future timeline. But most are looking longer term to a point when their savings pot is bigger, their financial knowledge stronger, and buying an entire apartment feels within reach. PRYPCO Blocks is a fully regulated platform that brings that aspiration forward by offering curated, income-generating Dubai properties - verified and handpicked by its experts - that individuals can invest in sooner, using smaller sums of money. The Dubai-based fintech, therefore, gives investors a different route onto the property ladder by offering a more manageable starting point. They essentially get to purchase a piece of a property - fractions of professionally managed rental units - from Dh500, for which the investors receive monthly rental payouts based on the amount they have invested. This way, they can participate in one of the world’s most dynamic real estate markets, without purchasing a whole property. PRYPCO Blocks’ new campaign, ‘Habba Habba’, is designed to give that proposition a memorable expression. Depending on the context, of course, the Arabic word Habba can mean a seed, or a single piece or a small part of something. When the word is repeated as Habba Habba, it conveys the idea of moving gradually - bit by bit, piece by piece. For PRYPCO Blocks, that makes for a logical connection that brings the process of fractional ownership into everyday language. The platform has described the investment model as straightforward, as it allows an investor to buy a fraction of a property, known as a Block, and build a portfolio. Habba then gives people a familiar way to picture that fraction, and a simpler way to talk about it. PRYPCO Blocks says the campaign, which began on October 1, brings its wider brand platform, ‘Ownership for Everyone’, to life by challenging the perception that property investment is reserved for people with substantial capital or specialist financial knowledge. PRYPCO Blocks has also released a comedy-led ‘hero’ film on its platform to introduce the Habba Habba message. The story begins at a home where a wife tells her husband that she has bought a “Habba of property”. Her partner’s confusion then sets off an increasingly elaborate attempt to explain what she means, whereupon a sushi chef, a finance professional and a Viking appear, each appear, offering a different interpretation of owning a piece of something. “As the explanations become more absurd, the film eventually pulls back to reveal the production set, with the director stepping in to explain fractional ownership himself,” says Joseph El Am, general manager of PRYPCO Blocks and Mint. “The humour comes from the extraordinary effort devoted to explaining a simple idea, namely that you can invest in a property without buying all of it.” By making that moment entertaining and recognisable, PRYPCO Blocks says it gives audiences a reason to engage with the subject. Behind the campaign’s playful language is a practical offering, however. For someone exploring how to invest in the real estate market and considering their first property investment, the lower starting amount of Dh500 puts it within reach by making participation more accessible. And for an existing investor, fractional ownership offers another way to allocate money to property without purchasing an entire unit. Regulated by the Dubai Financial Services Authority, PRYPCO Blocks offers both levels of investors - from the UAE and more than 200 countries - access to Dubai rental properties. PRYPCO Blocks points out that it does not provide investment advice and warns that, like other investments, investing in real estate involves risks and may not produce the anticipated returns. But the platform confirms that its products and services have been approved by PRYPCO Blocks’ Sharia Supervisory Board. “PRYPCO Blocks’ message connects an accessible entry point with a familiar idea, that progress can happen gradually,” says El Am. “You can begin with a fraction of a professionally managed rental property, understand how that investment works, and decide how it fits your longer-term plans. Habba Habba gives that first step a name.” PRYPCO Blocks also says its campaign reflects and speaks to the UAE’s diverse audience. “The UAE brings together people with different backgrounds, careers, incomes and expectations of what ownership means. “The film embraces that mix, moving beyond a single, conventional image of a property investor.” El Am adds: “Its language is deliberately conversational, its characters varied, and its humour makes room for people who may never have considered themselves part of an investment conversation.” Supported by social content, creator-led storytelling and activations, PRYPCO Blocks says the campaign takes that approach beyond the hero film and makes owning a piece of Dubai's real estate easier to recognise, discuss and understand. More information about PRYPCO Blocks and available investment opportunities is at prypco.com . This page was produced by The National in partnership with PRYPCO Blocks

title: Leaders of Egypt, Sudan, Eritrea and Somalia signal new regional alliance
description: Statement after meeting in Egypt does not mention Ethiopia or Israel
content: The leaders of Egypt , Eritrea, Sudan and Somalia have signalled the emergence of their countries as an alliance to influence the geopolitical landscape of the Horn of Africa and ensure its security. Egypt's President Abdel Fattah El Sisi, head of the Sudanese Armed Forces and de facto leader Gen Abdel Fattah Al Burhan, Somalia's President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud and President Isaias Afwerki of Eritrea met on Sunday in the Egyptian city of Alamein. The first such meeting came as the four countries grapple with formidable challenges. Egypt is in dispute with Ethiopia over the former's share of Nile water, while Sudan and Ethiopia are torn by civil wars. Somalia is struggling to defeat a long-running insurgency by Al Qaeda-linked extremists. Ethiopia and Eritrea have long had a border dispute, with Addis Ababa claiming the latter's Red Sea port of Assab as its own. The two nations fought a border war between 1998 and 2000. A joint statement issued late on Sunday made no mention of Ethiopia, which accuses three of the four nations – Egypt, Sudan and Eritrea – of aiding an anti-government rebellion. Nor did it mention Israel, which last year became the first country to recognise the breakaway region of Somaliland. But the statement appeared to signal the creation of a four-nation alliance, albeit a loose one, whose actions could alter the geopolitics of a strategic area with a porous Red Sea coastline and ample natural resources. It said the four leaders had agreed to support Sudan's territorial unity and the rejection of any “parallel identities” and support for “mercenaries” by foreign players – an allusion to the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces that have been fighting the SAF since 2023. On Somalia, the leaders said they rejected recognition or support for “the so-called Somaliland”. They also agreed that the freedom of navigation and “governance” of the Red Sea is the exclusive responsibility of littoral nations, a reference to landlocked Ethiopia's attempts to gain a permanent foothold on the Red Sea against the opposition of Egypt and its allies. On Egypt's water dispute with Ethiopia, the statement said the four leaders emphasised the importance of respecting international laws governing transnational rivers, including the Nile. “They completely reject unilateral actions that harm the existing water usage by the two downstream nations [Egypt and Sudan],” it said. Ethiopia has accused Eritrea, Sudan and Egypt of supporting an opposition alliance led by the Tigray People's Liberation Front that has been battling troops loyal to the federal government since last month. The three nations deny the charge. Last week, Egypt and Ethiopia expelled diplomats in a retaliatory row that saw a senior member of each country's embassy ordered to leave. The expulsions came a day after Ethiopia ordered the closure of its embassy in Eritrea and declared 10 Eritrean diplomats persona non grata. That prompted Eritrea to sever diplomatic ties with its neighbour. Egypt, the most populous of the four nations with an army considered the largest in the Middle East, has been forging close military relations with Eritrea, Somalia and Sudan. It has an estimated 15,000-strong military contingent in Somalia serving in an African Union peacekeeping force as well as a large mission supporting the Mogadishu government and its military. Egypt's military also has naval and army sites in Eritrea and is reportedly backing the SAF against the RSF. It has naval facilities in Djibouti, also a neighbour of Ethiopia. Its military footprint in Eritrea and Somalia is chiefly designed to isolate and put pressure on Ethiopia to show flexibility in the water dispute, which is rooted in Ethiopia's construction of a large Nile dam that Cairo insists could reduce its vital share of the river's water. While Egypt has been locked in that quarrel with Ethiopia, it has been spearheading an intense campaign to prevent efforts by landlocked Ethiopia to secure a permanent foothold on the Red Sea, including in Somaliland. Eritrea has been at odds with Addis Ababa for most of the 30-plus years since it seceded from Ethiopia. The Sudanese Armed Forces accuse Ethiopia of aiding its civil war adversary, the RSF. Sudan, Eritrea and Somalia all neighbour Ethiopia and, together with Egypt, have an uninterrupted Red Sea coastline that stretches from the northern tip of the Gulf of Suez in Egypt to Somalia in the Horn of Africa. Commenting on the internal strife in Ethiopia, prominent Egyptian analyst Abdalla Senawy said that while Cairo insisted it played no part in the conflict, it had benefited from the “weakening” of Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's government. “It accorded its political narrative strength and credibility that it has been missing throughout a time of warnings and hints at red lines but without doing anything to deter [Ethiopia],” he said. Ethiopia, Egypt and Sudan held years of negotiations on the dispute but failed to reach an agreement. Cairo and Khartoum demand that they be included in the running of the dam, but Addis Ababa rejects that as a violation of its sovereignty. Egypt, one of the world's driest countries, is especially alarmed that it will not get enough water in the case of a persistent drought. It has said it will not stand idly by if Addis Ababa went ahead and built more dams on the Blue Nile, the river's main tributary that accounts for more than 80 per cent of the water reaching Egypt.

title: Yemeni forces claim control of Bab Al Mandeb strait and Mokha in major offensive against Houthis
description: Military operations are backed by Saudi air cover
content: Yemeni government forces said on Monday that they secured control of the Bab Al Mandeb strait , the Dhubab area overlooking the sea lane and the strategic port city of Mokha, as a Saudi-led coalition provided aerial support and carried out air strikes on Houthi targets. Coalition spokesman Maj Gen Turki Al Malki said the alliance was providing round-the-clock air support to Yemeni armed forces on the ground and air cover for the Bab Al Mandeb strait, with operations against moving targets continuing. He said 324 “high-value” Houthi targets had been destroyed in the offensive, with 100 fighter jets taking part in the operation, dubbed “Yemen dawn”.
