Yemen 's armed forces also began a “strategic offensive” on the Houthi-controlled capital, Sanaa, on Monday, said their spokesman, Col Majed Al Nuzaili. “We are using advanced capabilities,” he said. The Houthi-run Al Masirah TV has confirmed attacks on Sanaa. The Houthi-run Health Ministry said a woman was killed by an air strike on a farm in the Sanhan area of Sanaa, while another attack on a car in Sawan killed a girl and injured seven other people. Col Al Nuzaili said government forces had carried out a flanking manoeuvre to take control of Bab Al Mandeb strait, with the Giants Brigades and Nation’s Shield Forces securing effective control of the strategic strait. He said government forces also took control of Dhubab airport and cut off the road linking Dhubab with Mokha, establishing control over the route. Hundreds of Houthi fighters were surrounded in Dhubab and were called on to surrender, while some fighters fled by boat, Col Al Nuzaili said. The claims could not immediately be independently verified and have not been confirmed by the Houthis. In Mokha, about 45km north, the Nation's Shield Forces, Giants Brigades and Tihama Resistance, backed by Popular Resistance fighters and air support, took control of the city after fierce fighting with Houthi forces, according to a military source cited by the state news agency Saba. The port city, in the west of Yemen's Taiz governorate, had been held by the Houthis since early September. The source said fighting took place at several locations around the city and resulted in Houthi casualties, with several fighters captured and others fleeing. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio sided with the Saudi and Yemeni governments. “Obviously the Saudis have come under Houthi attack and see the threat that that poses, and they have a right to defend themselves. And obviously the Yemeni forces are going to try to retake territory that they were ousted from,” Mr Rubio said. The Bab Al Mandeb strait is the southern exit passage of the Red Sea, a key shipping route between the Mediterranean and Asia. The waterway has assumed even more importance this year as an alternative to the Strait of Hormuz, which has been effectively closed by the Iran conflict. A ​Houthi-run ​maritime ⁠body also issued ⁠a warning to airlines flying in Saudi airspace, saying it would not be safe ​as ‌long as ⁠Saudi Arabia's “aggression” ​continued. The developments followed an announcement by Rashad Al Alimi , head of Yemen’s Presidential Leadership Council (PLC), who said Operation Yemen Dawn had been launched to restore state institutions, retake Sanaa and end the Houthi “coup”. “With God's aid, the will of our people, the valour of our armed forces and all military formations, and the support of our brothers and friends, Yemen will march towards a new dawn of freedom, peace and stability,” Mr Al Alimi said. The Saudi-backed Yemeni government launched the offensive on Sunday to retake territory from the Iran-aligned Houthis. The coalition said its air operations were continuing, including strikes against moving targets. The Yemen conflict began after the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa in 2014, prompting the Saudi-led coalition to intervene the following year with an air campaign aimed at restoring the government and ousting the rebel group. The Saudi-backed PLC, which is also ‌recognised by the United Nations, has since the Houthi takeover controlled the ⁠south and east of the country, based in the southern city of Aden. The fighting quickly ground to a bloody stalemate with most front lines stalled, leading to a major humanitarian crisis in what was already the poorest Arab state. A ceasefire agreed in 2022 largely held until this summer. Saudi Arabia , which arms and trains Yemeni government forces, is backing the current military campaign with air power and has sought logistical help from allies to push back the Houthis, restore free traffic in the Red Sea and end the group's attacks on its territory. Military experts say Iran is a key supplier of drones, missiles and other equipment to the rebels but that the Houthis have also experimented with their own weapons development . Led by Abdul-Malik Al Houthi, the group has also carried out attacks on Saudi Arabia, causing outrage by targeting the holy cities of Makkah and Madinah. Fighting has raged along several front lines in Yemen for weeks, opening a new front in the wider US-Iran ​conflict. The Houthis seized swathes of the Yemeni coast and captured Perim Island in the Bab Al Mandeb strait last month. They vowed to attack vessels linked to Saudi Arabia due to its backing of Yemen's government. Three in four families in parts of Yemen are going hungry from the impact of the surge in fighting, which has displaced tens of thousands of people and disrupted supplies to millions, the World Food Programme said last week. The World Health Organisation said that more than 5,000 casualties had been recorded in Yemen since August 6, including 959 deaths, as fighting intensifies and spreads. The WHO said 685 new casualties were reported over six days, with Taiz emerging as the heaviest front. Nearly 200,000 people have been displaced and more than 3,600 people have crossed into Djibouti. The WHO also warned that cholera cases had tripled in three weeks, with 647 suspected cases reported in the most recent week, compared with 217 three weeks earlier.

title: Wizz Air delays start of Abu Dhabi flights to January due to European security update
description: Airline had been scheduled to begin services this month
content: Wizz Air has postponed the launch of some routes to Abu Dhabi from late October to January following security updates from Europe's aviation regulator. The low-cost airline said last month that it was resuming flights to Abu Dhabi and Dubai, alongside routes to Jeddah in Saudi Arabia and Amman in Jordan. The launch of routes to Abu Dhabi – including from Poland, Bulgaria, Romania, Cyprus and Hungary – scheduled to begin in late October, has now been pushed to January 10, 2027, due to latest guidelines from the EU Aviation Safety Agency (Easa), Wizz Air said in a statement to The National . “The continued closure of Iraqi airspace requires longer routings and technical refuelling stops for the A321neo aircraft operating these services. Combined with current fuel prices, this makes the affected routes commercially unviable under present conditions,” the airline said. The UAE services were part of a wider restoration of 12 routes and 49 weekly flights to the Emirates, Saudi Arabia and Jordan over the winter, providing 470,000 seats across services to nine European cities. With Jordan's airspace also placed on the “do not operate” list in Easa's latest conflict zone information bulletin, flights to the country have been suspended until October 25, Wizz Air said. “Affected customers will be informed directly about their options, and we will continue to monitor conditions ahead of the revised launch date,” the airline added. The carrier suspended its European-operated services to the Middle East in late February due to the regional conflict and widespread airspace disruption. The airline was set to resume operations after its low-cost subsidiary, Wizz Air Abu Dhabi, ceased operations on September 1, 2025. Wizz Air Abu Dhabi, which operated for five years from the UAE capital, said in July last year that it would suspend all locally based services from the emirate because of operational challenges and geopolitical instability.

title: Kuwait revokes citizenship of 415 people in latest crackdown
description: Billionaire Mahmoud Haidar among those affected by series of decrees
content: Kuwait has revoked the citizenship of 415 people, according to six decrees published in its official gazette. The largest number of cases was included in Decree No. 156, which revoked the citizenship of 286 people. The gazette, Kuwait Al Youm , did not publish the names of the 415 people whose citizenship was withdrawn. It said the measures also applied to those who may have acquired citizenship through them as dependents. Among those to have their citizenship revoked is billionaire Mahmoud Haidar, who has built an empire in the country's real estate and private investment sectors. The latest measures are part of a national review, a campaign that has led to the revocation of citizenship from thousands of people in the past two years. In June, Kuwait revoked the citizenship of more than 2,000 people in eight decrees. The country's cabinet approved a draft decree amending provisions of the citizenship law earlier this year. Kuwait revoked the citizenship of almost 50,000 people in 2025 in a sweeping review of nationality files that officials said left “no one exempt”. Kuwaiti law allows citizenship to be revoked on several grounds, including obtaining nationality through fraud, forgery or false statements; holding dual nationality without authorisation; and committing actions deemed against the “supreme interests” of the state. Kuwaitis are a minority in their own country. There are about 1.5 million citizens in a population of about 4.5 million.

title: Spain’s Sanchez calls snap election after housing protests
description: Prime Minister gambles on November 29 poll to end parliament deadlock
content: Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez has called an early election for November 29 after failing to quell mounting social protests. Mr Sanchez’s minority government, already struggling after a series of mishaps including deadly floods and a migration crisis, was recently confronted with nationwide demonstrations over housing costs. The situation boiled over after an 87-year-old woman with a disability was evicted from her apartment, galvanising the protest movement. The government responded with an emergency package of housing measures , but it failed to generate sufficient votes in parliament. “It’s time you, the Spanish people, decide which future you want for yourselves and for the country.” Mr Sanchez said in an address on Monday in Madrid . “You must decide what role you wish to play in this era, and what role you want Spain to play.” The centre-right People’s Party has led recent polls, garnering 33.9 per cent support in a SocioMetrica poll. The PP’s leader, Alberto Nunez Feijoo, has indicated his party could govern with the radical-right Vox, which had 18 per cent support in the survey. Mr Sanchez’s Socialists polled at 25.7 per cent. “We are ready,” Mr Feijoo said on Friday after the housing plan was defeated. “We can’t continue down the path we’re on.” Mr Sanchez came to power in 2018 and, without a stable parliamentary majority, has spent much of his tenure navigating a succession of crises. They included the Covid-19 pandemic, the fallout from Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, deadly floods in the Valencia region and an unprecedented European blackout last year. Mr Sanchez, 54, has been one of Europe's loudest voices against the Iran war and has accused Israel of carrying out a genocide in Gaza and violating international humanitarian law. His latest term, which began in 2023 and is due to run until July 2027, has been particularly difficult. He has failed to pass a single budget, while corruption investigations involving his party as well as his family have multiplied. The arrival of about 80,000 undocumented migrants in Ceuta , a Spanish exclave in North Africa, this summer fuelled a new wave of social discontent. His housing proposal sought to freeze rents, make rental contracts indefinite, prohibit the eviction of vulnerable people and regulate short-term tourist apartments. Opposition parties, including the Catalan group Junts, which backed Mr Sanchez’s return to office in 2023, argued that greater intervention in the housing market would only worsen the problem. The People’s Party already governs most of Spain’s biggest cities and regions, often in coalition with Vox. The two parties govern together in four regions, including Andalusia, the country’s most populous. Both parties have made removing Mr Sanchez from office a central priority. While they differ on migration, Spain’s territorial model, and Europe, they have signalled a willingness to work together if they secure enough seats to replace the last social democratic government in a major European Union country. Mr Sanchez’s lack of parliamentary support contrasts with Spain’s strong economic performance. The country has posted the fastest growth among Europe’s major economies, unemployment is at its lowest since the financial crisis and tourism is booming. During his speech, Mr Sanchez criticised the far right, warning against handing “over the reins of the country to a far-right coalition that has proposed nothing – whose sole objective is to repeal and curtail the rights and freedoms we have built over the last eight years”.

title: Iranian flights land in Iraq's Najaf after US sanctions exemption
description: Exemption from US sanctions follows departure of American troops
content: Iranian airlines have resumed flights to Iraq's Najaf after the US granted an exemption to allow sanctioned carriers, excluding Mahan Air, to operate 40 daily flights to and from the Shiite holy city. Flights from Iran had been halted for about a week due to pressure from US sanctions, but Iraqi and Iranian officials confirmed that they restarted in Najaf on Sunday. Iraq had not announced the ban imposed on September 25 but ground-handling companies stopped serving the routes, fearing sanctions being imposed by the US Treasury. Last week, Iraqi Foreign Minister Fuad Hussein thanked the US government and Treasury for allowing the resumption of flights to Najaf after he met Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent. Mr Hussein told reporters at the Iraqi embassy in Washington that he had raised concerns about flight sanctions with US officials, saying barring flights would create a "huge problem, because at the end it has to do with religion, not politics.” “Most of the visitors from Iran to Iraq are coming to the holy places, especially to Karbala and Najaf, and this is well known. We receive annually about five million pilgrims from Iran," he said. "That's valid also for Iraqis going to the holy places in Mashhad, and we are talking about three million Iraqis going there.” Mr Hussein later thanked officials for “their understanding and respect for religious freedom, including the importance of tolerance, access to holy sites, and the resumption of flights for pilgrims travelling to Najaf”, a statement by the Iraqi Embassy to the US read. Najaf is home to the Shrine of Imam Ali, the Prophet Mohammed's cousin and son-in-law, and is a pilgrimage destination for Shiite Muslims. The US last month said it was targeting third-country companies that facilitate Mahan Air , a previously sanctioned Iranian airline accused of transporting personnel, drones and weapons to support Iran's military. Mr Bessent later said companies that dealt with Iranian airlines would be “knocked out ​of ‌the dollar system”. Iranian airlines were banned from neighbouring countries including the UAE , Oman and Iraq in response to new US sanctions. The ban on Iranian flights to Iraq angered Iran-aligned factions and political parties. Militias and politicians staged protests and threatened sit-ins at Iraqi airports unless flights resumed. Kataib Hezbollah urged Iraqis to break what it called the “US siege” on Iran, while Al Nujaba described the suspension as “submission” to Washington and accused Baghdad of letting the US dictate its Iran policy. The exemption from US sanctions follows the withdrawal of American troops from Iraq last week. Iran-backed militia groups are expected to finalise a disarmament process overseen by the government by June next year. During military parades in Baghdad on Sunday by the Popular Mobilisation Forces and Iran-backed militias to celebrate the departure of US forces, American flags were trampled on , prompting an investigation by the Iraqi government. The PMF is an umbrella group of mostly Shiite paramilitary forces, many of which have close ties to Iran. The departure of US troops has sparked concern among Iraqis and Kurds of an increase in Iranian influence in the country, or greater powers given to groups aligned to Tehran. The PMF on Sunday announced the arrests of 45 suspects and the dismantling of networks linked to the banned Baath party. In a statement also carried by Iraqi state media, the group said some of the arrests were linked to terrorism charges, links to extremist movements or the leaking of state security information.

title: Can you still fly from the UAE to Israel? Which airlines are operating
description: Travellers still have options as carriers adjust their schedules between the two countries
content: Travellers can still fly directly between the UAE and Israel despite the suspension of flydubai's services to Tel Aviv after an incident on one of its flights last week. The airline suspended all flights to and from Israel after flight FZ1073, travelling from Dubai to Tel Aviv on September 30, was diverted to Saudi Arabia after the captain was attacked by the co-pilot . Flydubai had been the main carrier between the UAE and Israel, operating as many as 10 flights a day on the route before the suspension. Emirates airline, which does not operate its own aircraft between Dubai and Tel Aviv, had offered the destination through its codeshare partnership with flydubai, but those services have also been suspended until further notice. On September 30, Emirates said passengers whose final destination was Tel Aviv would not be accepted for travel at their point of origin. However, direct flights between the two countries have not stopped entirely. Yes. Etihad continues to operate direct flights between Abu Dhabi and Tel Aviv . It is currently operating six flights a day between the cities, with a journey time of more than three hours. The first departure, EY609, leaves Abu Dhabi at 2.40am UAE time, followed by EY595 at 3.30am, EY593 at 8.50am, EY607 at 8.55am, EY597 at 2.25pm and EY599 at 8.40pm. The corresponding flights from Tel Aviv to Abu Dhabi are EY600 at 12.55am local time, EY610 at 7am, EY596 at 7.45am, EY608 and EY594 at 3.05pm and EY598 at 8.10pm. Regular services by Israeli airlines to the UAE have yet to resume since the start of the Iran war . But national carrier El Al is operating a limited number of flights from Dubai for passengers affected by the suspension of flydubai services. Those began on Sunday, October 4, with LY976 leaving at 3.15am, LY978 at 7.45am and LY972 at 11.10am. Further services are scheduled for Monday, October 5, with LY976 departing at 10.30pm; Wednesday, October 7, at 4.30am; and Thursday, October 8, at 4.35am. Arkia, Israel's second-largest airline, is also operating limited flights from Dubai to Tel Aviv, with regular services between the cities set to resume on October 31. Low-cost carrier Israir is scheduled to resume regular flights between Tel Aviv and Dubai on November 18. Neither Arkia nor Israir operate flights to Abu Dhabi.

title: Hundreds of European ex-ministers urge EU sanctions against Israeli E1 settlement
description: Pressure mounts to sanction financial institutions linked to West Bank settlements
content: More than 500 European former ministers and senior officials on Monday asked the EU to take action against Israel's settlement expansion , including by sanctioning financial institutions that support it. Signatories to the call for action urged the European Commission to “show leadership” by putting forward proposals to “sanction all financial institutions and other providers of services to the implementation of E1 and other illegal settlements”. “While, commendably, some EU member states have implemented national measures against illegal settlements, others – including Germany and Italy – continue to systematically block the adoption of any EU measures, thus becoming de facto complicit in undermining both EU values and the two-state solution,” the signatories wrote in a statement. They include former French prime ministers Dominique de Villepin and Alain Juppe, former Italian prime minister Massimo D'Alema, and former Swedish prime minister Stefan Lofven. Former EU foreign affairs chief and ex Spanish foreign minister Josep Borrell was also among the signatories. Divisions among EU member states on the Israel-Palestine conflict, coupled with inertia within the European Commission, have hampered the bloc's ability to exert diplomatic influence in the region. But pressure is mounting as the deadline approaches for Israel to award the first tranche of contracts for the E1 settlement project , which would cut the occupied West Bank in two and bury the possibility of a Palestinian state. In May, a dozen countries, including the UK, Canada, France, Germany and Italy, warned businesses of “legal and reputational consequences” if they took part in the E1 bid. More than 1,200 Palestinians have been killed in the West Bank in the past three years by the Israeli army or settlers. Israel has occupied the West Bank since 1967. “Now is surely the time for the EU and member states to act,” the signatories wrote. The European Commission has resisted calls this year to submit a proposal to ban trade with illegal Israeli settlements. The EU's 27 foreign ministers will be meeting next week in Luxembourg as the situation in Gaza and the occupied West Bank remains “deeply disturbing”, signatories said. They highlighted that more than 200 Gazan children have been killed since a US-brokered ceasefire last year. Israel and Hamas continue to trade fire regularly. “There has been no disarmament, no IDF withdrawal, reconstruction is blocked, while the ‘Board of Peace’ plans to revive Gaza remain passive and stillborn,” they said. A handful of EU states have moved forward alone due to inertia in Brussels. Last month, France joined a UK-led group of European states to stop the trade of goods with Israeli settlements, considered illegal under international law. However each country has said they would implement slightly different measures, with some – such as Spain and the Netherlands – including some services and others restricting the ban to goods. The UK is the only country that has said it would work on establishing a sanctions regime. Such moves have triggered anger from the Israeli government, which recently expelled Dutch diplomats serving in the West Bank city of Ramallah. The number of companies doing business with settlements in the West Bank grew by one-third this year, according to a UN list updated last month, with travel firms and materials suppliers prominent in the group. A total of 214 companies from 11 countries are listed, including well-known travel brands such as Airbnb and Expedia.

title: Oil prices would have hit $200 a barrel if not for East-West pipeline, Aramco chief says
description: Supply buffer 'scarily thin' with markets set to worsen unless Hormuz reopens, warns Amin Nasser
content: Brent crude prices would have reached up to $200 per barrel if Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline did not exist, the chief executive of Saudi Aramco said. The company ​can ⁠make its maximum ⁠sustainable production ​capacity of ⁠12 million barrels per day available ⁠within days, ​Amin Nasser ​told the Energy Intelligence Forum in London on Monday. “Our system is intact,” Mr Nasser said. Aramco has ‌the ⁠strategic ​reserves and ​flexibility ‌to ⁠isolate or shift output ⁠as required, he added. Brent crude, the benchmark for two thirds of the world's oil, has been trading around $100 a barrel over the past month, even as more tankers are transiting the Strait of Hormuz. Saudi Arabia has been playing a vital role as Aramco over the past month boosted crude shipments from its main export terminal at Ras Tanura. The company reacted quickly to a temporary halt to its main cross-country pipeline after an attack last month. Aramco has since brought flows on the East-West pipeline back to about 80 per cent of capacity, meaning it also has more oil to ship from the Red Sea. Aramco has ensured its oil supplies proved resilient throughout the conflict by relying on international storage and working to quickly repair damaged infrastructure, Mr Nasser said. He did not mention reports of recent attacks on the kingdom in his speech. Aramco is looking for alternative crude export routes and additional international storage facilities to avoid relying too much on any single method of reaching global buyers, he added. However, the oil stockpiles that cushion the world from supply shocks have become “scarily thin”, putting markets at risk of worsening unless the Strait of Hormuz fully reopens, Mr Nasser said. He was speaking only days after governments in the world’s biggest economies announced plans to release as much as 100 million barrels of emergency oil and diesel stocks to ease rising fuel costs. “Until Hormuz fully reopens and confidence returns, the crude reality is that pressure at both ends of the barrel will intensify,” he said. “While the squeeze on crude is serious, refined fuel prices have risen even more sharply.” Releasing stockpiles will buy economies some time but will not fix the imbalance between supply and demand, Mr Nasser said. Even after the vital shipping chokepoint at Hormuz reopens, it may take as long as two years for energy-consuming countries to replenish their stockpiles, he said. Gulf producers are working to step up production and exports and have succeeded in boosting crude flows to near prewar levels. The higher flows have provided scant relief for oil markets, which are still pricing in security risks to supply in the Gulf and Red Sea. With inputs from Bloomberg and Reuters

title: Iran oil minister resigns amid fuel shortages and crude export pressure
description: Head of state-run oil company named as acting minister after Mohsen Paknejad steps down
content: Iranian Oil Minister Mohsen Paknejad has resigned, with Hamid Bovard, chief executive of the state-run National Iranian Oil Company, appointed as acting minister. Mr Paknejad, who had served in the role since August 2024, submitted his resignation some time ago for “personal reasons” and had insisted on leaving, officials said. The office of President Masoud Pezeshkian said he accepted the resignation on Sunday. He named Mr Bovard in his place, the ministry's Shana news service reported. Mr Bovard, 62, has led the NIOC since 2024 and previously managed the National Iranian South Oil Company and the Iranian Offshore Oil Company. He is to oversee the ministry while the government considers who to appoint as Mr Paknejad's permanent replacement. Mr Bovard takes over with Iran's energy industry under intense pressure from a US naval blockade. It has caused exports to plunge to zero , the country's central bank chief said previously. The change comes less than a month after Iran raised the price of petrol for motorists exceeding their subsidised monthly allocation. From September 7, petrol above the 110-litre quota was priced at 100,000 rials a litre – double the previous rate. The government said the measure was intended to address a daily petrol deficit of about 10 million litres. Iran continues to subsidise the first 110 litres purchased each month, with 60 litres priced at 15,000 rials a litre and a further 50 litres at 30,000 rials. The higher third-tier price applies to consumption above that level. The price increase followed shortages and queues at petrol stations as Iran struggles to balance domestic consumption with available supplies. Fuel consumption has increased beyond domestic refining capacity, raising the country's reliance on imports. The fuel shortages have coincided with severe disruption to Iran's oil exports. The war with the US and restrictions on Iranian shipping have constrained the country's ability to move crude through the region and collect oil revenue. Mr Paknejad said before his resignation that revenue from oil already sold was continuing to reach Iran. In August, he said Iran had lost about 95 million cubic metres of gas production owing to infrastructure damage caused by the war .

title: Non-oil sectors in UAE and Saudi Arabia maintain strong growth trajectory despite Iran war
description: UAE companies in September raised selling prices at fastest pace in 15 years owing to higher input costs
content: The non-oil private sectors of the UAE and Saudi Arabia maintained their expansion trajectory in September, as the Arab world’s two largest economies shook off the effects of the Iran war . The seasonally adjusted Riyad Bank purchasing managers’ index – a benchmark gauge of the kingdom’s non-oil economy – rose to 55.3 in September, from 53.8 in August, well above the neutral 50 mark that separates growth from contraction. The rate of improvement in the non-oil sector business activity last month was the strongest since February and marked the sixth consecutive month of improvements in business conditions. The acceleration last month was largely driven by a marked rise in new order growth, although it masked the softening in the rate of output growth. New orders hit levels closer to the index’s long-run average, suggesting that demand in the kingdom has recovered well after a slowdown in the middle of 2026. Businesses surveyed also referred to gradual improvements in the market that led to increased client numbers and higher spending. “The acceleration was primarily demand-led. New orders increased at their fastest pace since February,” said Naif Alghaith, chief economist at Riyad Bank. The September reading of the PMI index was broadly consistent with the “wider picture of the Saudi economy”, which was driven by domestic consumption, investment activity, government and PIF-related projects. “The strong improvement in new orders provides a positive forward-looking signal for activity in the coming months,” Mr Alghaith said. While the recovery was predominantly driven by the domestic market in September, new orders from foreign customers have now dropped for seven months running. Companies surveyed pointed to the effects of supply chain disruption amid the regional conflict that in some cases led to shipping delays. Gulf states including the UAE and Saudi Arabia, Opec’s biggest oil producer, have faced attacks during the war, which is now in its seventh month. The tourism and leisure, retail, aviation and properties sectors across the Gulf took a hit as Iran attacked civilian infrastructure and regional energy installations during the early days of the conflict. Gulf economies have bounced back gradually, although Iran continues to attack commercial vessels in the Strait of Hormuz, while Saudi Arabia’s Red Sea ports are under a "maritime blockade" from Yemen's Tehran-backed Houthi rebels. Demand conditions in the UAE non-oil private sector also continued to improve markedly in September, boosting pricing power and enabling companies to raise their selling prices at the fastest pace in more than 15 years in response to higher input costs. Meanwhile, business activity increased rapidly and higher output requirements encouraged companies to expand both purchasing activity and employment, with staffing numbers rising modestly last month. The seasonally adjusted S&P Global UAE Purchasing Managers' Index in September remained stable at 55.3 recorded in August, well above the 50 mark that indicates growth in economic activity. The latest PMI reading is “another indication that the non-oil economy has moved past the midyear slowdown linked to the Middle East conflict”, said David Owen, principal economist at S&P Global Market Intelligence. “Businesses saw customer demand improve, not just in local markets but abroad as well, with new export business rising at the strongest rate in nearly two years,” he added. The improvement in the UAE’s business conditions was mainly driven by a “rapid monthly rise in output”, with the fastest rate of growth since February, before the outbreak of the war. Stronger demand conditions also supported a marked increase in new orders, although the pace of expansion eased from the seven-month high posted in August. The overall new order numbers were also supported by an increase in new business from abroad, which expanded for the third consecutive month and at the sharpest pace since November 2024, PMI data showed. However, as the demand strengthened, companies raised their output prices at the steepest rate since May 2011, which was among the fastest since the survey began. "While the economic picture looks more robust now, selling charges also rose markedly, suggesting that firms are taking the opportunity to boost their margins following a period of strong input cost pressures,” Mr Owen said. “With oil markets remaining volatile, and shipping routes still constrained, input costs and selling charges may remain elevated." Non-oil private sector business activity in Dubai, one of the biggest business and tourism centres in the Middle East, also maintained a sharp growth trajectory. The Dubai PMI posted 54.5 in September, up from 54.1 in August, signalling a “solid improvement”, as the pace of growth was fastest in 2026 so far. The boost to Dubai’s non-oil economic activity was largely driven a "sharp and accelerated increase in output”, the fastest so far this year. New orders also rose markedly, supported by the strongest expansion in new business from abroad for two years, the PMI survey data showed. Although employment in the emirate increased in September, the backlog of work still increased at a sharp pace. “The rate of output price inflation quickened to the fastest since January 2014 as companies passed on higher input costs to customers,” the survey found.

title: UAE’s golden generation shines as athletes return with record Asian Games haul
description: Emirates contingent won 13 medals, including seven golds, in Japan
content: The UAE's athletes return from Japan on Monday knowing they have just delivered the country's best performance at any Asian Games. At the Games, held in Aichi-Nagoya, the UAE secured 13 medals – including a record seven golds – surpassing their previous best performance, set at the last Asian Games in Hangzhou three years ago. Overall, the UAE finished 13th in the medals table out of 45 nations. “Winning seven gold medals for the first time in the history of the UAE’s participation in the Asian Games is a proud achievement for the country. It reflects the determination of our athletes and their ambition to raise the UAE flag among Asia’s leading sporting nations,” said Sheikh Mansoor bin Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum, president of the UAE Olympic Committee. “Every medal represents years of preparation, sacrifice and hard work by the athletes, their coaches, support teams and national federations. This achievement belongs to everyone who has contributed to the development of UAE sport.” Five of the UAE's seven gold medals came in jiu-jitsu, a discipline the country has invested heavily in over the past two decades. The ancient Japanese martial art is part of the public school curriculum and is taught at police cadet academies across the country. Its popularity will surely continue to grow. The UAE's strong performance at the Games was led by Balqees Al Hashmi (women’s 48kg), Khaled Al Shehhi (men’s 62kg), Ahmed Andeez (men’s 69kg), Mahdi Al Awlaqi (men’s 77kg) and Asma Al Hosani (women’s 52kg). Al Anoud Al Harbi (women’s 48kg) and Omar Al Suwaidi (men’s 62kg) won silver, while Amaar Al Hosani (men’s 94kg) claimed bronze. Al Shehhi and Al Hosani have now won golds at successive Asian Games . “I am proud to have won my second consecutive title on my second Asian Games appearance. This is an important milestone in my career. I dedicate this gold to the UAE’s leadership, my family, my coach and my national teammates. This medal is the start of a long journey of hard work,” Al Shehhi said. Shihab Ahmed Mohamed Abdulrahim Al Faheem, UAE ambassador to Japan, dedicated the UAE jiu-jitsu players' success to the country's leadership. “These results came from careful planning, consistent work and the efforts of our athletes, coaches and administrative staff.” The UAE's first gold medal of the Games was won by teenager Mariam Kareem, who came home first in the women's 400m hurdles final. The 18-year-old set an Asian Games record time of 54.31 seconds . “Mariam Kareem’s gold medal was an exceptional achievement. To win the 400m hurdles in an Asian Games record and a new Asian U20 record at such a young age demonstrates the extraordinary talent and potential she possesses,” said Major General Dr Mohammed Abdullah Al Murr, president of the UAE Athletics Federation. “What was particularly impressive was Mariam’s response after the mixed 4x400m relay. She experienced the disappointment of seeing a medal opportunity slip away, but she showed tremendous character to come back and deliver a performance of the highest level in the hurdles.” Kareem's gold medal came only two days after another Emirati teenager, Sulaiman Abdulrahman , secured the country's first medal at Aichi-Nagoya, winning silver in the men's 400m final. The 19-year-old only narrowly missed out on gold, finishing just 0.09 seconds behind Thailand's Joshua Atkinson. “For us, this silver feels like gold, given the high standard of the race and the extremely narrow margin to first place,” Al Murr said. “Sulaiman delivered an outstanding performance that reflects how we want UAE athletics to be represented on the continental and international stages.” The UAE signed off their Asian Games on Sunday with a second silver medal in equestrian . Abdullah Humaid Al Muhairi and Hudson de Vains claimed individual silver following a dramatic three-way jump-off at JRA Equestrian Park in Tokyo. “Abdullah Humaid Al Muhairi’s silver medal was a superb achievement and a fitting way to conclude the UAE’s Asian Games campaign. His performance in the individual show jumping competition demonstrated composure, skill and the ability to perform under pressure,” said Sheikh Mansoor. “The strength of our show jumping team throughout these Games has been remarkable. Abdullah and his fellow riders showed the competitive spirit required to challenge for medals, and their two silver medals are a reflection of their consistency and quality.” In the team final, the Emirates narrowly missed out on a gold medal . Represented by Sheikha Latifah bint Ahmed Al Maktoum, Humaid Abdulla Khalifa Al Muhairi, Abdullah Humaid Al Muhairi and Omar Abdul Aziz Al Marzooqi, the UAE produced five clears across the two rounds of competition to finish on just four faults, securing silver ahead of host nation Japan. For Sheikha Latifa, it was her fourth Asian Games medal across three editions, equalling Malaysia's Quzandria Nur Mahamad Fathil for the most medals won by a female equestrian in Asian Games history. Her silver medal in Aichi-Nagoya came 20 years after she secured a bronze medal at the 2006 Games in Doha. “Sheikha Latifah’s exceptional competitiveness and consistency across multiple editions of the Asian Games is a source of great pride for the UAE. Her determination, experience and ability to perform at the highest level have made her an outstanding representative of Emirati sport,” said Sheikh Mansoor. “Her four Asian Games medals are testament to the remarkable level she has maintained over many years. To repeatedly stand on the podium at a continental event of this magnitude demonstrates her commitment, resilience and exceptional competitive character.” The UAE also picked up a gold medal in judo, won by Kazbek Naguchev in the men's under-73kg category. UAE Judo Federation president Mohamed bin Thaaloob Al Derei said the gold was the product of sustained work by Naguchev and the technical and administrative teams, and dedicated the achievement to the UAE's leadership. “What we achieved today is the result of collective effort and sustained work by the athlete and the technical and administrative teams. It gives us further motivation to continue developing UAE judo and achieve more results worthy of the name of the United Arab Emirates,” he added.

title: Egypt lose South Africa friendly as Mohamed Salah's absence continues
description: Pitso Mosimane's team secure 1-0 win in Cairo to add to the woes of Pharaohs boss Hossam Hassan
content: Egypt coach Hossam Hassan was left with more questions than answers as the Pharaohs succumbed to a 1-0 friendly defeat to South Africa in Cairo on Sunday. The mood in the Egyptian national team has been sombre for some time following a spate of controversial remarks by coach Hassan and superstar Mohamed Salah 's mysterious absence from the team. On Sunday at the Cairo International Stadium, Puso Dithejane scored the lone goal as Bafana Bafana coach Pitso Mosimane enjoyed a great start to his reign, registering a third straight victory. Goalkeeper Mostafa Shobeir rushed off his line and misjudged completely, allowing Dithejane to complete the simplest of finishes in front of an empty net. For Egypt, the final match of the international break left them with a bigger headache, which seemingly started when coach Hassan substituted Salah after 60 minutes in the opening round of qualifying for the 2027 Africa Cup of Nations against Angola on September 25. Salah then missed the next game against South Sudan , which Egypt won comfortably 5-0. According to the Egyptian Football Association, Salah was granted permission to miss the game to avoid the risk of injury as it was played on an artificial surface. Salah was expected to play the friendly against South Africa but he was not part of the starting XI or even on the bench. It compounded the issues for coach Hassan , who has been under fire since his comments about goalkeeper Mohamed El Shenawy, who he said was "finished" at one point. Hassan had also criticised the Egyptian Premier League and the players' fitness levels. After the match against South Sudan, Hassan remained defiant, especially around Salah, stating: “It is not right for a country of 120 million people for the national team to depend on one player.” Now, in Salah's absence, Egypt suffered a humbling defeat to a largely experimental Bafana Bafana side; Mosimane had made nine changes to the team from their previous game against Eritrea. "It was a little difficult. In the first five minutes we could not find our feet. We changed the whole team. It takes a little time to gel and to come in, but as the game progressed, we gained confidence," Mosimane said. "What I like is that they’re not afraid to play and we need to give them a chance. I let them swim with the sharks, threw them in the deep end. Yeah, they swam."

title: Saudi Aramco cuts Asia crude prices to six-year low amid recovery as oil flows rebound
description: Company to sell Arab Light crude to Asian customers at discount of $5 a barrel below regional benchmark for November
content: Saudi Aramco has cut prices for its flagship crude grade sold to Asian buyers to a six-year low, as the world’s largest oil exporter competes for market share amid a recovery in oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz. The state-owned Saudi oil company will sell Arab Light crude to Asian customers at a discount of $5 a barrel below the regional benchmark for November, widening the discount from $2 a barrel in October, according to a Bloomberg survey. Traders and refiners polled by Bloomberg had expected Aramco to raise prices by $5 a barrel for November. The price reduction signals that Saudi Arabia may be seeking to boost sales to Asia as oil flows from the Middle East recover after months of disruption linked to the Iran war. Aramco raised its November crude prices for Europe by $3 a barrel, while leaving prices for the US unchanged from October, Bloomberg reported. Although attacks on vessels in and around the Strait of Hormuz continue, the volume of oil passing through the waterway has increased over the past few months. Saudi Arabia sold almost 100 million barrels of oil to Asian buyers in mid-September, helping to avert a looming supply crunch. The kingdom has also restored much of the crude flow through its East-West pipeline after suffering damage in an attack. The recovery has helped increase oil exports from the Middle East, with JPMorgan estimating last week that shipments had reached 98 per cent of prewar levels, Bloomberg reported. The pipeline allows Saudi Arabia to transport crude from its eastern oilfields to the Red Sea port of Yanbu, providing an alternative export route that bypasses the strait. Aramco’s official selling prices apply to crude supplied under long-term contracts to refiners, who would typically collect their shipments from Ras Tanura on Saudi Arabia's Gulf coast. Ras Tanura hosts one of the world’s largest oil export terminals and a major refining facility. The port handles a significant share of Saudi crude exports, with cargoes typically heading to markets in Europe and Asia, including China, Japan and South Korea. But continued risks to shipping through the strait have prompted many customers to avoid the route. Aramco has asked Asian refiners to submit nominations for the volumes they intend to collect in November from ports inside the Arabian Gulf, as well as from Yanbu on the Red Sea and Sidi Kerir on Egypt's Mediterranean coast, Bloomberg reported.

title: President Sheikh Mohamed shares 'thank you' note to teacher from 1971 to celebrate role of educators
description: UAE leader offers heartfelt tribute to mark World Teachers' Day
content: President Sheikh Mohamed on Monday paid a warm tribute to teachers across the UAE for their crucial role in "shaping future generations". Marking World Teachers' Day, he said in a post on social media that the annual occasion served as an opportunity to celebrate educators for the "lasting impact" they have on the lives of pupils. Sheikh Mohamed shared a picture of himself as a boy alongside a thank you note to his teacher from 1971 to highlight the enduring influence of educators in moulding young minds and unlocking the potential of the leaders of tomorrow. "I dedicate my picture to the teacher Ahmad Ibrahim Mandi as a memento with thanks. Signed Mohamed Zayed," says the note from Sheikh Mohamed, then aged 10. Fifty-five years on, the UAE President again paid homage to teachers for their contributions to the development of the nation. "On World Teachers' Day, I express my appreciation and gratitude to teachers across the UAE and commend their role in shaping future generations," Sheikh Mohamed wrote on X. "Let this day be an opportunity for all of us to recognise our teachers and thank them for the lasting impact they have had on our lives." World Teachers' Day – which is organised by Unesco – is held on October 5 each year to honour educators and recognise their contributions to education and society. The day also serves as a moment to reflect on the support teachers need to fully realise their potential, and to consider the future direction of the profession on a global scale. Sheikh Mohammed bin Rashid, Vice President, Prime Minister and Ruler of Dubai, also delivered a message of support to teachers, who he described as the "engineers of minds". He shared a letter to the nation's teachers from his new book, The Letters , a collection of 26 pieces of writing from the Dubai Ruler. "A message to the makers of generations and engineers of minds, a message to those to whom we owe the dignified life we live," Sheikh Mohammed wrote on social media. "To those who created engineers, doctors and leaders, to those who instilled values and spread knowledge and illuminated homelands with the light of science. A message to those from whom we learnt in the early years of our lives how to think, how to decide, and how to live, and whose impact remained with us throughout our lives. To you, I write this message." Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed, Vice President, Deputy Prime Minister and Chairman of the Presidential Court, said that "every great future begins with a teacher". He reflected on how UAE Founding Father, the late Sheikh Zayed bin Sultan Al Nahyan, laid the foundations for education in the country. "The story of education in the UAE began with the firm belief of my father and teacher, the late Sheikh Zayed bin Sultan, that the human is the foundation of every advancement, and that education is the light that guides a person along the right path in life," Sheikh Mansour wrote on X. "Today, our teachers carry this message forward, nurturing our children’s knowledge, ambition and confidence. Every great future begins with a teacher." Sheikh Abdullah bin Zayed, Deputy Prime Minister, Minister of Foreign Affairs and chairman of the Education, Human Development and Community Development Council, said World Teachers' Day offered a chance to express gratitude to those guiding future generations. “Teachers have played an enduring role in the UAE’s journey, leaving an impact that carries from one generation to the next and instilling the value of knowledge and learning," he said. "On World Teachers’ Day, we renew our appreciation for every teacher whose dedication has contributed to preparing generations who carry forward our nation’s ambitions and shape its future.” Sarah Al Amiri, Minister of Education, said teachers had been instrumental to efforts to "transform ambition into achievement" since the formation of the UAE. "Today, with the acceleration of transformation and the growth of our nation's ambitions for the future, the role of the teacher is renewed to remain at the heart of our national vision for education," she wrote on X. "From the founding generation, to the present generation, to the generations of the future, the impact of the teacher remains enduring in every stage of the UAE's journey. To every teacher, male and female, thank you for your giving, for your mission and for your ongoing contribution to building the individual, the society and the homeland."

title: Best Arabic songs of 2026, by artists from Soulja to Amr Diab
description: Chronological guide to the Arabic tunes shaping the year so far
content: We are nearly halfway through the year and regional artists have already delivered a colourful and eclectic run of releases spanning pop, hip-hop, rai, indie and electronic sounds, from countries including Morocco, Algeria, Egypt, Sudan and the Levant region. Presented chronologically, here are some of the standout Arabic songs released so far this year. This list will continue to be updated throughout the year as new releases arrive. Mozayine taps into everyday Moroccan darija vernacular on 3achernakom , a melodic pop track that, while charming, is also laced with bitterness in its story of frayed friendships and personal reckoning. Tunisian rap veteran Balti takes on the migration crisis with Amir Al Bihar, painting stark images of young people pushed towards dangerous sea crossings over sombre violin and brooding delivery. One of the more socially charged releases of the year. Syrian singer Ismaeil Tamr keeps Meen deliberately spare, delivering a brooding stripped-back ballad about longing and spurned chances. Fast becoming a viral sensation, and it is easy to hear why. Iraqi singer Saleem Salem delivers a catchy, repetitive chorus built for TikTok dance memes in this vibrant track about enjoying the good life. Lebanese singer Maher Jah stays firmly in the classic Arabic love-song tradition in this ballad comparing a lover’s face to the moon and her eyes to a cloudless, starlit sky. The warm delivery and polished arrangement give the track the feel of a ready-made Valentine’s Day special. From the EP 1609 , Dhab Khaless channels the swagger of New York’s 1990s ballroom scene, running it through house rhythms and hip-hop attitude. The pulsing beats and sultry vocals keep it current and cool. Moroccan-Belgian pop star Dystinct keeps his multilingual formula tight on Ta3al, a flirtatious track with the kind of swagger that has made him one of the region’s burgeoning stars. Shams revisits the emotional palette of late-2000s Arabic pop on 3enaya , layering crisp synth percussion and subtle tabla beneath shimmering violin. The cooing vocals underline the lyrical exploration of the aftermath of heartbreak. Jordanian rapper Shbash and Palestinian artist Rknddn trade clipped verses over dark basslines and sliding 808s on Dawaween, a tense drill track where the dense production mirrors lyrics shaped by paranoia and urban pressure. Egyptian singer Angham returns to familiar ballad territory on Mesh Adra. This is another polished work by the artist, with lyrics tracing the ache of not being able to continue. Through the title refrain, Angham sounds passionate without falling into histrionics, which makes the song feel more heartrending. Veteran singer Cheba Warda and Yousri Oscar's new song features elements of Algeria’s rai music: percolating beats and a snappy, almost conversational delivery. On Nmout w Naarf Ki Rak Nawini , which translates to “I’d die to know what you are planning”, sly lyrics are undercut by the sheer joy of the production. Adlene’s Barhouch comes from the rougher edge of Algerian pop, using rai percussion, trap and hip-hop textures, as well as a jagged melody in a track made for clubs and cars. Moroccan rapper Inkonnu collaborates with Egypt’s Marwan Moussa on Keda , a high-tempo self-affirmation anthem. Built around the titular phrase “I’m like this”, the song has both artists trading confident verses. Siilawy sharpens his wounded romantic style on Nassaba , a Levantine pop song that frames betrayal as an accusation. It is all about the clarinet line weaving through the track, as the Jordanian-Palestinian singer speaks with the growing pains and emotional openness that made him a star with younger listeners. Cheen and Sintax release something resembling an Egyptian answer to Evanescence on Mesh 7atigi , with restrained, almost operatic vocals turning into guttural metal lines. Stern riffs, distorted bass and electronic touches give the track its force. Burgeoning Sudanese artist Kordofani delivers on his promise with Ellela , an ebullient summer jam blending sunny Sudanese melodies with an old-school hip-hop flow. Monzer Ramadan’s vocals lift the chorus, making it a gentle bridge between memory, rap and Sudanese pop warmth. Lebanese indie music pioneer Zeid Hamdan’s Bossa shows his gift for quirky, agitated arrangements and a keen poetic eye in a song that looks at the difference between romance and emotional intimacy. Iraqi artist Ali Najm turns to the pulsating chobi rhythms of his native Ramadi on Disco Chobi , giving the communal dance music an electronic charge. Bursts of synths are laced with driving percussion, while Najm's hefty vocal adds to the communal, celebratory feel. Sudanese rapper Soulja finds an unlikely partner in Huda Arabi, a veteran singer synonymous with the country's wedding and celebration circuit. Their track, 15 Hikaya , samples Arabi's own hit Al Ban Al Mal , with Soulja's laid-back rapping giving way to Arabi's silky refrain. The cross-generational collaboration divided opinion on social media in Sudan and passed one million views in less than two weeks. El Wala Hamo Geh rides on a loose electronic groove, with Egyptian mahraganat singer Hamo El Morshedy turning the title refrain, meaning "Hamo left, Hamo came back", into an earworm. The lyrics have the same easy swagger, with El Morshedy boasting about his rising profile and, at one point, declaring that his fame will surpass the Eiffel Tower. The confidence was well placed – the song reached No 10 on Billboard Arabia's Hot 100. On Nano , Saint Levant continues the turn towards Egyptian pop heard on his previous single Sabah El Ward , this time alongside Tul8te. Over a summery groove, the pair trade swooning verses largely in Egyptian Arabic. Nano reached No 1 on Spotify in Egypt and remained in the country's top 10 throughout the summer. The title means "three swords", and Saudi singer Kadejah Moaath offers a welcome break from soppy balladry with a song demanding a lover utter the three letters forming the Arabic word asef, meaning sorry. The threat comes wrapped in a Khaleeji melody, with Moaath's vocal flourishes accompanied by qanun, nay and mizmar. Moroccan rapper Pause sounds like he is trying to outrun his own song on Doza . Moroccan folk rhythms and percussion clatter underneath a relentless series of bars, with his verses matching the track's staccato rhythms. Judging by the skills on display, you really can't fault the swagger. A slow burner on record and on the charts, Demmi Marroki entered Billboard Arabia's Hot 100 at No 89 before climbing to No 10. Bayadis gives the track a hazy R&B backdrop, with 3robi's gruffer verses offset by Tawsen's smooth vocals as French and Moroccan darija slip in and out of the song. More than four decades into his career, Amr Diab is still finding new sounds to bring into an unmistakably familiar pop style. On Lola El Banat , he turns to rural Egyptian folk melodies and hand-clapping rhythms, setting them against a bright electronic beat. It follows last year's Baba , which drew from Upper Egyptian folklore. Amman producers Fairplay and Roo found an international audience with Al Jaw , a track that began with a traditional Arabic vocal and builds outwards. Rather than treating the vocal as a snappy sample, its elongated phrasing creates a hypnotic groove tempered with deep bass and synths. It caught the attention of veteran British producer Pete Tong, who opened his IMS Ibiza set with Al Jaw before releasing it on his Places & Spaces label. Algerian rapper RDB continues to find fertile ground between rap and rai on Saragossa . The gasba and rebab are woven into the beat, giving the track the rhythmic drive of rai, while RDB attacks it with a clipped rap flow. Assala's Syrian Album takes 14 traditional songs to represent each of the country's governorates. For Aleppo, she takes on Aal Rozana , a Levantine standard closely associated with the city's tarab tradition and previously sung by Sabah Fakhri. Assala wisely avoids overworking it. The arrangement remains spacious, with qanun leaving plenty of room for Assala's voice and the familiar melody. A winding melody sits above cavernous sub-bass and spacious drums on 7ilween , while traditional Gulf rhythms are pulled apart and interrupted by chopped vocals featuring Bobo Secret and Lama3an. It is strange, seductive and one of the year's more adventurous takes on Khaleeji music.

title: World Teachers’ Day: Let’s acknowledge the teachers who find a way for every child
description: When parents place their child in a teacher’s care, they entrust that teacher with the person most precious to them
content: Many of us can still name a teacher from our school years. We remember a voice, a word of encouragement or the moment something finally made sense. Years later, these memories remind us how deeply a teacher can influence a life . For families of children of determination , that influence may be remembered through a moment when their child found a way to communicate or learnt to do something independently. Behind that moment is a teacher who understood the child and found a way to help them learn. When parents place their child in a teacher’s care, they entrust that teacher with the person most precious to them. They may be meeting for the first time, yet trust begins with the teacher’s role and the responsibility it carries. For families of people of determination, this trust comes with the hope that their child will be understood, respected and given the support they need. In my work in administration, I know the effort involved in building systems and procedures that serve everyone. When I observe special education teachers, I see another responsibility: finding, within those systems, a way to reach each individual student. The quality of an education system becomes clear in its ability to help each student learn. Teachers make that possible through decisions about how to explain an idea, encourage participation and recognise understanding. For a special education teacher, the working day involves setting learning goals and deciding how to help each student achieve them. A goal might involve recognising a word, following a sequence or expressing a choice. The teacher breaks it into manageable steps and considers the support the student needs. Reaching that goal takes preparation and creativity. An approach that helps one child may need to change for another. Teachers may use drawing, movement, interactive activities or familiar objects to make information accessible. Often, they create the resources themselves: picture cards, a simple game or an everyday item adapted to connect an idea with an experience. A resource that looks simple may carry hours of thought. Its colours, size or arrangement may reflect what the teacher has learnt about the student. Once it is used, the student’s response guides what happens next. The teacher may simplify an instruction, allow more time or try another activity while keeping the learning goal in view. This requires professional judgment. A student may understand more than they can express through speech. Another may demonstrate understanding through an action or a choice. Recognising these responses allows a teacher to build on the student’s abilities and offer opportunities to attempt more. Families contribute to this understanding. Knowing what a child enjoys or what helps them feel comfortable can guide a teacher towards a more effective approach. Sharing progress also helps families support developing skills at home and gives teachers a fuller picture of the child’s daily life. A report may record an achievement in a single line. The family knows how much it means. They know the attempts that came before it, the possibilities it opens and the hope it brings for their child’s future. For the teacher, it also offers direction for the next lesson and the next goal. On World Teachers’ Day, every teacher deserves our respect and appreciation. I offer my heartfelt thanks to the teachers at Zayed Authority for People of Determination and to special education teachers everywhere. Their commitment deserves practical support: time to prepare, suitable resources and opportunities to develop their professional knowledge. These help teachers turn their understanding of a student into an effective learning experience. I join families in thanking those who explain again, create a new tool and give students the time and encouragement they need. The teacher whose name a family remembers years later may be the person who first helped them see what their child could achieve. May God bless their work and reward the care and commitment they bring to this responsibility .

title: Israeli forces kill man in occupied Syrian territory amid incursions
description: Killing follows report of Israeli military digging in across Quneitra on Sunday
content: Israeli forces killed a man in occupied Syrian territory early on Monday, amid renewed Israeli incursions and military activity across southern Syria. The attack took place shortly after midnight in the occupied area of southern Syria, the Israeli military said in a statement, without specifying the location. It said troops “identified a suspect who tried to infiltrate" an Israeli military post and opened fire, killing him. The Israeli military said there were no casualties among its forces. It did not identify the man, say whether he was armed or provide evidence that he intended to enter the military post. The killing followed Israeli military activity across Quneitra on Sunday. Syrian state news agency Sana reported extensive Israeli land-clearing operations near Al Asha, in southern Quneitra. Sana’s Quneitra correspondent said more than seven Israeli bulldozers and military vehicles entered the area south-west of Al Rafid, where forces continued to dig a deep trench near the 1974 disengagement line inside Syrian territory. Sana reported that the work was intended to expand the “Sufa 53 Line”, an earthen barrier running through the area. The Syrian Foreign Ministry condemned the project as a breach of the 1974 Disengagement Agreement. On Thursday, Sana reported that Israeli forces entered Bariqa and Al Hamidiyah in Quneitra before searching civilian homes and detaining a young man. It also reported that two Israeli artillery shells fell on agricultural land near Al Mantara dam. The Israeli military said its forces would continue operating in the area against what it described as threats to Israeli civilians and troops.

title: Hallgrimsson says Israel tried to intimidate Ireland players during tense Nations League draw
description: The sides clashed at half-time at TSC Arena, with one Republic official alleging an Israeli player had spat at him
content: Republic of Ireland manager Heimir Hallgrimsson said Israel were “trying to intimidate” his players during a tense 1-1 Nations League draw in Serbia that was followed by an allegation of spitting. The sides clashed at half-time at TSC Arena, with the Irish Times reporting that the Republic of Ireland's head of athletic performance, Damien Doyle, alleged an Israeli player had spat at him. Television footage appeared to capture a voice saying “he spat on me” as the players headed towards the tunnel, although Hallgrimsson said he had not witnessed the incident. “I don't want to get involved in that, but it's been like this these two games,” Hallgrimsson told Off The Ball . “It's tense, it's a lot of emotions. It was an accusation of spitting on someone, but I didn't see it. No, we don't want to talk about this. This will be reviewed, probably like everything else that's happened between the two teams.” Hallgrimsson said he believed his players had been subjected to an attempt to unsettle them from the outset. “I felt like they were trying to intimidate us from kick-off, but I give a lot of credit to the players to stay calm,” he said. “It could have been a game of yellow and red cards, but we were composed, the players were composed, they did well in controlling emotions.” Israel manager Ran Ben-Shimon said he did not know the half-time confrontation. “At half-time I was in the dressing room, my room, with my staff,” he said. “I didn't see anything. When I get the chance to check, I will get back to you.” The latest flashpoint came a day after Hallgrimsson's pre-match press conference was abruptly ended following a confrontation with an Israeli journalist. Hallgrimsson was questioned about allegations that Irish players had made racist remarks during the teams' previous meeting in Hungary, where Ireland won 3-0. FAI communications manager Kieran Crowley intervened, describing the allegations as “completely untrue”. The controversy followed an FAI investigation into claims that Ireland forward Adam Idah was racially abused by Israel supporters during that match. Midfielder Jayson Molumby also raised concerns with officials about alleged abusive chanting. Ben-Shimon rejected suggestions his players had targeted Molumby. “Come on, come on. We don't do it. We just don't do it, we are not men like this,” he said. The fixtures have been politically charged since the Nations League draw in February, with pressure group Irish Sport for Palestine staging protests calling for Ireland to withdraw from the games because of the Israel-Gaza war. The FAI nevertheless opted to fulfil both fixtures, played at neutral venues in Hungary and Serbia. Neither match featured the usual pre-match formalities, while Ireland's players bowed their heads during Israel's national anthem. ⁠Title holders Portugal maintained their 100 per cent record in the Nations League with a ⁠2-1 home win over Norway on Sunday to seal a place ​in the March quarter-finals and shift the focus further away from Cristiano Ronaldo's abrupt exit from the squad last week . Goncalo Ramos netted 11 ⁠minutes from time to ensure Portugal secured a top-two finish in Group A4 as they moved six points ahead of second-placed Denmark, who beat Wales 1-0. The Netherlands took over at the top of Group A2, after beating Serbia 2-1 in Eindhoven, but only on goal difference from Greece, ⁠who held on for a goalless draw at home to Germany in Thessaloniki. Portugal were still under a cloud from Ronaldo’s ​dispute with ⁠coach Jorge Jesus, although they were triumphant ‌without him in Denmark last Thursday after he walked out on the squad, and continued their winning ways in Porto on Sunday. Norway ​took the lead in the 36th minute from centre-back Kristoffer Ajer, who hit a dipping half-volley from the edge of the box. But if that effort was sumptuous, Joao Cancelo’s thrashing effort to equalise two minutes later was even more awe-inspiring. Ramos’ winner came off his calf after Joao Felix had headed across goal for him to score. “You need a lot of technical quality to beat Norway," said Portugal coach Jesus. "We won without putting in a performance like the one against Denmark, but the important thing was the victory and qualification. I had a lot of belief in this team, but perhaps I didn’t expect us to have four wins from our first four games." Portugal’s win was soured by a red card for Francisco Conceicao four minutes from time. He gave the referee a cynical thumbs up after receiving a yellow card and was immediately handed his marching orders. The Netherlands, with captain Virgil van ‌Dijk celebrating a 100th cap, went ahead against ⁠Serbia when Teun Koopmeiners’ 31st-minute free-kick evaded all in the penalty ​area and crept into the corner. But the visitors were level within four minutes as Aleksa Terzic crossed for teenager ​Mihajlo Cvetkovic to ‌rise over Koopmeiners and head in his first international goal. It took until the 72nd minute to go back ahead when Denzel ⁠Dumfries’ low cross was turned back across the goal by Tijjani Reijnders, sliding in at the far post, and tapped ⁠in by Joshua Zirkzee, who received a late call-up to the Dutch squad last week. Germany dominated away against Greece, but Jurgen Klopp’s inexperienced side could not find the net, and they have won only one of their first four games under the new coach.

title: AI safety and rapid rise of advanced technology key topics for Abu Dhabi summit
description: Ai Everything gets under way at Adnec on Tuesday
content: Abu Dhabi will cement itself as a major regional development hub for artificial intelligence, with thousands of visitors expected for the two-day Ai Everything summit on Tuesday. Main speakers among the 180 lined up to discuss the latest tech developments include Arthur Mensch, co-founder and chief executive of Mistral AI, and Marc Raibert, founder of Boston Dynamics. The two companies are focused on generative AI and robotics, respectively. The event arrives in the UAE at a critical time for AI, as governments and corporations around the world search for effective methods to retain control over a rapidly evolving super-technology that drew huge investment in 2026. Safety concerns and the rapid rise of AI have dominated discussions in recent months, while unequal opportunities for women in the industry have also been a concern. The summit is taking place at Adnec and is hosted by the Department of Government Enablement – Abu Dhabi (DGE). The Abu Dhabi government aims to transform into the world’s first AI-native government by 2027, with more than 40 government entities integrated into a single AI-driven ecosystem. More than 100 AI use cases are already live across the emirate’s public services, backed by a $3.54 billion investment programme supporting Abu Dhabi’s wider push towards AI-led public services, economic value creation and responsible deployment. “Abu Dhabi will become the world’s first AI-native government next year, and the evidence is already clear in the way we're redefining public services for millions of people and businesses,” said Wesam Lootah, director general of GovDigital (DGE). “We have built the blueprint, and Ai Everything Abu Dhabi is our invitation to the world to examine it, to see what intelligent governance looks like at scale, and the enormous benefits it delivers to people's lives today.” Job creation and the elimination of some jobs made redundant by emerging technologies will form part of the discussion. According to analysis by LinkedIn, the number of AI-related job postings has doubled since 2023, and those postings come with attractive remuneration. AI engineers have overtaken machine learning engineers as the most common AI role on LinkedIn, while a typical AI posting offers a salary of around $177,000, compared to $80,000 for a non-AI role. However, a gender imbalance exists between the number of men and the number of women taking up new positions in the sector. Women accounted for just 25 per cent of AI hires in the US in 2025, compared with 50 per cent in non-AI occupations. Meanwhile, across 27 countries, women hold just 13 per cent of C-suite leadership roles at AI companies. At US President Donald Trump’s recent AI summit at the White House, just two of the 31 guests and business leaders were women, reflecting a consistent gender gap at the top of the industry. As companies focus their investments on AI, the pressure to deliver measurable returns is mounting. Ai Everything Abu Dhabi aims to put that proof to the test with a wide showcase of live AI use cases and applications across public services, banking, health care, energy and education. “Beyond the speculative sheen of AI, its true impact lies in transforming science, services and society,” said Trixie LohMirmand, chief executive of Ai Everything. “Abu Dhabi is moving decisively into that territory, with the leadership assembling the infrastructure, institutions, research capabilities and global partnerships needed to turn AI ambition into national capacity.”

title: Amman Design Week returns after seven years with a new vision for Arab works
description: From a reconstructed Palestinian fountain to a canopy built among the treetops, the expanded fourth edition explores how memory, heritage and materials shape the present
content: Returning after a seven-year hiatus, Amman Design Week opened its highly anticipated fourth edition on October 2, celebrating the evolution of architecture and design across Jordan and the wider region. Held under the theme, Accumulations, the biennial event runs until October 17, with a range of multidisciplinary exhibitions and installations spread across Amman and further afield in the coastal city of Aqaba . The relaunch of ADW marks a major expansion in scope and programming for the event, featuring 120 exhibited creatives, and many more in parallel workshops and talks. “This whole time, the designers kept working and creating. The research kept going, and this is what led to the theme Accumulations, because this edition is the accumulated work that has been going on behind the curtains, now being put in the spotlight,” ADW co-director Bisher Tabbaa tells The National . “We’ve expanded our locations and number of exhibitions, and now we also have some installations that will remain a permanent part of the city after ADW ends.” That idea of accumulation extends beyond the work produced during ADW's seven-year absence, becoming a broader exploration of how the past continues to shape contemporary design. “The theme is really about how our daily practices, our environment, and cultural memories come together and entangle. How do they accumulate and shape what we do? How does our heritage leave traces that can be expressed in our life today?” exhibitions curator Faysal Tabbarah adds. “Some of what you’ll see is almost a material inventory, but then we look at how designers can stretch units of materials, reshape them or combine them in different ways.” Many of the works are spread across Ras El Ain, with the major showcase taking place at The Hanger – an old 1930s electricity-generating plant transformed into a public cultural and exhibition space – which serves as ADW's headquarters. The works range from product design and material experimentation to research-driven projects visualising cultural practices or rethinking historic narratives. One such project is Troubled Waters by Palestinian architect and historian Nadi Abusaada, nine years in the making. A white plaster octagonal fountain sits within the exhibition space like a ghostly apparition of the grand, intricately decorated courtyard fountains of a bygone era. The only dash of colour is a single geometric tile, adorned with blue and red florals. That tile is the only surviving piece of a fountain designed by Armenian ceramist David Ohanessian, which once occupied the now-demolished 1920s Palace Hotel in Jerusalem . Abusaada’s piece recreates what he believes the fountain would have looked like, based on the tile’s design and historic references. “The hotel was occupied by Israelis in 1948 and destroyed in 2008. Many of the artefacts were dispersed all over the place, including this one tile,” Abusaada tells The National . “A Palestinian collector named George Al-A’ma was able to buy it back from the Israeli contractor that destroyed the building, and this whole installation is an attempt at speculating what that fountain looked like. “Usually, we use plaster to fix little cracks in small objects, but in this instance, the ‘cracks’ are basically the whole body of the fountain, and a comment on this convoluted way of retrieving your history.” A short walk away in Ras El Ain Park is one of the permanent installations, titled Folly by Civil Architecture , co-founded by Bahraini architect Ali Ismail Karimi and Kuwaiti architect Hamed Bukhamseen. The project introduces a ceramic tile canopy structure, made from discarded eucalyptus wood, which winds between the treetops of the park to create a shaded walkway and gathering spot. Small sculptures of animals and people are placed on the roof, acting as abstracted figures that locals interpret as they please, creating their own myths and stories to go with the small icons. “We created this space so people can begin to occupy it for events, casual gatherings or even just as a shady rest spot that encourages people to use the park more,” Bukhamseen says. “We approached the project in collaboration with Haswa Ceramics by Jordanian ceramicist Sama El Saket, who has been experimenting with local clay varieties.” “What occupies the canopy above are these small figurines, these caryatids, as we call them, devoid of any mythology or specific meaning,” he adds. “They’re these architectural motifs that occupy the space above and create narratives based on how you begin to see them from the sidewalk above. We want people to make them their own.” Further afield at Darat Abu Adnan , a restored 1950s heritage house in Jabal Al Lweibdeh that has been transformed specifically for ADW, several designers showcased projects related to domestic life, coexistence with nature, and heritage craft. The Return by Jordanian designer Farah Tajeddin is a striking installation that uses a stone architectural feature in the garden as a makeshift dining table, laid with salt-crusted candelabras, candlesticks, cups and cutlery. “Made from Dead Sea salt, these candleholders transform a material shaped by time into vessels for light and beauty. Their raw, crystalline surfaces carry traces of my childhood landscape, as I used to visit the Dead Sea a lot as a child,” Tajeddin says. “The sea’s name also inspires a reflection: life is a journey away from home; death is not a departure, but a return.
