The table is set up for dessert, because we’re meant to enjoy this journey while we’re here. “They’re made from biodegradable materials in many colours, built layer by layer from the salt and joined with a plant-based binder,” she adds. “This process offers an alternative to conventional synthetic adhesives, while allowing the salt’s natural texture and mineral character to remain visible.” The experimental and interdisciplinary approach of ADW makes it a playground for ideas and innovations that are still in the process of solidifying. Rather than a design fair focused on selling products or functional pieces, the platform seeks to provoke and stimulate the mind, finding new ways that design and architecture can benefit people or create a conversation.

title: The UAE wants to make healthy living easier
description: Recent public health initiatives suggest authorities are turning convenience into a force for good
content: Convenience is a word often associated with the less healthy lifestyle choices of modern life. Fast food is convenient. Home deliveries are convenient. So are processed snacks that sit prominently on supermarkets shelves. But the UAE is turning that logic on its head – by making healthier options similarly convenient as part of a deliberate, multi-pronged public health strategy . The latest evidence of this can be found in Abu Dhabi’s hospitality sector. Under a mandate that came into force last Thursday, hotels and tourism-licensed restaurants are required to offer at least one healthy item in every menu category – appetisers, mains, sides and desserts – under the “Sehhi” (healthy) nutritional standards developed by the Abu Dhabi Public Health Centre. Sehhi foods are low in fat, sugar and salt, and higher in nutritional value. Children’s menus face an even higher bar, with at least half of their offerings required to meet these criteria. The pattern is becoming difficult to miss. This year, Abu Dhabi tightened rules on what children can take into schools, with foods high in sugar, fat and artificial additives placed on the prohibited list. From next year, supermarkets across the emirate will have to remove unhealthy food from high-visibility areas. There is already a tiered excise tax in place on sugary drinks as part of a UAE-wide drive to encourage reductions in their consumption. These measures reflect a recognition among policymakers that while individual responsibility remains important to public health, the environment in which people make decisions matters just as much . The objective is not to remove choice, but rather to ensure that healthier habits do not require extraordinary effort. The same thinking applies to exercise. In a country where summer temperatures can make outdoor activity difficult for months, the UAE has been quite inventive. Hence, today there is no shortage of climate-controlled gyms and sporting facilities – or, for that matter, community sports programmes such as the ones that are on offer at Zayed Sports City at this time of the year. Then there is the annual Dubai Mallathon, launched last year, that turns malls across Dubai into running and walking tracks. This year, more than 160,000 people participated in the three-month programme that culminated in a full marathon inside Dubai Mall, thereby offering residents a way to stay active away from the summer heat. Again, the principle is convenience. More broadly, this approach embeds public health in urban planning, education, hospitality and everyday community life – rather than confining it to hospital visits and medical care, which can be both stressful and expensive for all those involved. From a macroeconomic perspective, the stakes justify such a whole-of-government effort. The World Obesity Federation , a non-profit group, estimates that obesity could cost the UAE almost 5 per cent of its gross domestic product by 2035. The overall impact of these measures could take years to become clear. But by systematically reducing the friction around good habits, the UAE is deliberately stacking the odds in favour of longer and healthier lives. If convenience has helped create some of modern life’s health problems, it can also help solve them.

title: Labour and Greens push for Muslim voters' support in London by-election
description: Green leader Zack Polanski is challenging Labour's Somali candidate in Keir Starmer's former seat
content: Former UK prime minister Keir Starmer's decision to quit as an MP has left Labour under threat of losing a stronghold in London to the Green Party as tensions mount on the campaign trail. Police warned of escalating tensions between canvassers and protesters over the weekend in the nominally safe Labour seat of Holborn and St Pancras, where a by-election will be held on October 8. Labour and Green campaigners were gathered outside the Al Rahman Mosque in a housing estate in the Camden area on Friday. But as the Labour campaigners prepared to walk into the estate, they were heckled by a resident wearing a Palestine football T-shirt. “Just to let you know, this whole estate is voting Green,” the resident, who declined to be named, said. When asked why, he told The National it was due to the Labour party’s policies on the Israel-Gaza conflict. “Genocide. Andy Burnham refuses to say call what happened in Gaza is a genocide,” he said. The Labour candidate to replace Mr Starmer is being challenged at this by-election by Zack Polanski, the leader of the left-wing Green Party who has put the Palestinian issue at the heart of his campaign. Labour’s candidate Sagal Abdi-Wali is currently leader of the Camden council and grew up in the borough after coming to the UK as a refugee from Somalia. There is a large Somali community in the area who are hopeful she could become the first British-Somali MP. Yet some of the campaigning has led to tensions. On Friday, police warned of potential issues during canvassing without naming a specific party. “In recent weekends officers have made arrests after conflict between those canvassing and protesters, with reports of intimidating and obstructive conduct,” said Dept Asst Commissioner James Harman. “This is wholly unacceptable. In a democracy political parties need to be given space to lawfully canvass and campaign,” he said. The Green Party makes no secret of its attempts to galvanise Muslim voters on the Palestinian issue. Around 16 per cent of Camden residents identify as Muslims. There is a large Bengali community as well as an Arabic-speaking one. The Green leaflet handed out at the mosque includes an endorsement from the Muslim Vote, a campaign group that emerged in the 2024 general election to challenge Labour by proposing alternative candidates. It also includes slogans in Bengali and Somali – a tactic which has been criticised by other parties. The party's conference last weekend was overshadowed by a vote on the motion "Zionism is racism", which also called for Israel to be replaced by a Palestinian state. The motion passed on Sunday by 1,022 votes to 813 - creating a Green party policy that rejects a two state solution and is directly at odds with the policies of successive British and other European government. Mr Polanski missed the vote, and all 5 Green party MPs sought to distance themselves from the results. "We know there is no conflict between supporting the rights of Palestinians and the rights of Jewish people," they wrote in a joint statement," they wrote. The resolution drew widespread criticism, with the Board of Deputies, the largest organisation representing British Jews describing it as an "attack on the Jewish community". "It is an antisemitic platform, based on a grossly offensive distortion and erasure of Jewish experience and identity," they said on Sunday. Around Camden and neighbouring Kentish Town, residents told of the Mr Polanski’s regular presence on the streets and at local businesses. Fatima Al Jumaa, who runs Paradise restaurant serving Somali food, said she taken her Labour campaign posters down from the window because they were bad for business. “Some people stopped coming when they saw the posters. I’m a businesswoman, not a politician, so I took them down,” she said. She continues to support Labour and in particular Ms Abdi-Wali. Mr Polanski had been to her restaurant several times and had spoken to patrons, flanked by local campaigners who are Somali speakers, she said. Those campaigners do most of the talking, Ms Al Jumaa said. “They come and order food and sit down. Then they start asking people at the other tables who they will vote for. He [Mr Polanski] doesn’t talk much, just 'hello' and shakes hands,” she said. Ms Al Jumaa said the Green campaigners talked mainly about the Palestinian issue, and Labour’s track record in the area. She said Ms Abdi-Wali should engage the Somali community more if she wants to challenge the Greens. “My restaurant is a centre for the Somali community here. She should come more and talk to people,” she said. Some residents were cautious about the potential divisions emerging from the election. Local barber Eddy said Mr Polanski had been to his shop for haircuts. “We don’t know much about the gentleman. Good luck to him, and to anyone who wins,” he said. His main concern was for the communities in the area to continue getting along. “Kentish Town has many nationalities. Everyone is living together and everyone is happy. We have to look after each other,” he said. Ms Abdi-Wali’s campaign has focused on local issues, including recent flooding in Kentish Town which affected businesses including Ms Jamaa’s. In her campaign video filmed in the area, Ms Abdi-Wali said she would put provider Thames Water “on notice” and backed Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s suggestion that the provider should be nationalised. “For too long, residents and businesses have suffered an appalling service, while we’ve seen our bills going up and up and up,” she said. She said in her role as council leader she had deployed teams to join clean-up operations. “I’m demanding Thames Water compensates local businesses and that’s why I back public ownership of Thames Water to ensure that money we pay on our bills goes on upgrading the infrastructure and not making shareholders richer,” she said. The candidates' positions on the Israel-Palestine conflict are being sharply scrutinised. Ms Abdi-Wali has said she supports a two-state solution, while Mr Polanski, who is Jewish, describes himself as an anti-Zionist. The Camden Muslim Network, which was established in 2024 by Mohammad Chowdhury, a local representative of the Muslim Vote campaign , organised a hustings last month that was attended by Mr Polanski but not Ms Abdi-Wali. Ms Abdi-Wali had previously said she could not attend because of a prior engagement. Though the Camden Muslim Network states it is non-partisan, it backed left-wing independent candidate Andrew Feinstein against Mr Starmer at the 2024 general election. Some local voters hope a Green MP will bring a fresh approach. Barber Che Issa put a Green Party poster in his shop window after Mr Polanski and other campaigners visited him. “I find then very understanding of the community. They shared their ideas and said they would help the community,” he said.

title: Opening the taps on diesel reserves is a risky gamble for Europe
description: Proposed prohibition of American diesel exports would have hit continent hard
content: US President Donald Trump has bounced Europe into a risky gamble. On Friday, under threat of a US ban on diesel exports, the Group of Seven major economies agreed to release emergency petroleum stocks. Mr Trump may be looking just to elections in a month, but London, Paris and Berlin risk burning their remaining reserves. Opening the taps is meant to alleviate the crisis in diesel caused by the US-Iran war. The G7 countries collectively will provide 100 million barrels over four months, split between crude and refined products, and front-loaded with diesel. In return, they have all agreed not to impose restrictions on oil exports – for now. The Gulf shuttle scheme, guarded by US ships and aviation, appears to have succeeded in restoring crude oil flows to near prewar levels. This comes at a heavy cost in death and injury of mariners, damage to vessels, and hiring and guarding the vessels. Escorting refined product shipments is harder: they are more varied, travel in smaller ships and are usually more flammable than crude. Before the war, the Arab countries within the Gulf exported about 5.5 million barrels daily of refined products, particularly diesel, jet fuel and heavy fuel oil. That plunged to below 2 million barrels per day when the US began its attack, and has recovered to 3 million bpd or so. Iran added another 900,000 bpd of net exports of refined products and natural gas liquids. This has now fallen to near-zero by sea, and perhaps minor amounts going overland by lorry or rail. Europe and Japan hold large stocks of petroleum products, especially diesel and petrol, while the US’s strategic petroleum reserve is almost entirely crude oil. The US has marketed about 130 million barrels, taking its crude stocks down to the lowest levels since the early 1980s. It looks doubtful that it can provide much more without causing permanent damage to the artificial salt caverns that hold the oil. Though this drawdown has helped keep crude prices hovering at relatively moderate levels, that is not the locus of the current crisis – Brent crude closed the week at $102 per barrel, while wholesale diesel in New York is going for $200. If half the proposed release consists of diesel, it amounts to about 400,000 bpd over four months, replacing about a third of the exports lost this year. That would be helpful, but far from a full or permanent solution. There is also the oddity that European stocks are not owned by their governments, unlike in the US. Instead, oil companies are mandated to hold more than normal commercial levels. Approval for a release does not necessarily mean that all that diesel comes on the market. Despite the tight conditions, commercial product stocks at the crucial Amsterdam-Rotterdam-Antwerp hub actually rose last month, and are not down much since May, unlike in the US where they have plummeted. The proposed prohibition of American diesel exports would have hit Europe hard. The UK and EU import about 270,000 bpd of diesel from the US, a third of their total imports, though this jumped to 420,000 bpd during the worst of the crunch this summer. It would have hurt other nations too, and would quickly have rebounded on the US as refiners would have cut back runs. The US still imports significant amounts of petrol – a politically more visible and sensitive fuel – and might well have faced retaliatory bans. Should the Europeans have resisted the demand, or called Mr Trump’s bluff? On the one hand, they worried about a difficult winter. If he had just forbidden sales specifically to Europe, the fuel would have been shuffled around through other countries to end up there anyway. So, to have a real impact, he would have had to impose a blanket ban. Strategic stocks are made to be used in emergencies. While the US had already emptied much of the SPR in 2022 and hardly refilled it since, European stocks are well above legal minimum levels, and have been rebuilt since 2022. Solidarity between the G7 and the members of the International Energy Agency is fundamental for collective management of energy shocks. On the other hand, the European countries did not start this war, they are not combatants, and they do not control it. If they burn through their reserves over the next four months, they had better be sure a resolution to the crisis is coming soon. The hazy thinking coming out of the White House and the Pentagon about war aims and strategy does not inspire such confidence. Polls suggest the Republicans will suffer a drubbing in November’s midterm elections. After that, Mr Trump will find it hard to advance any of his domestic agenda. Many expect he will back down in Iran, perhaps after launching one final thunderclap so he can go home claiming a victory. That itself runs the risk that Tehran miscalculates, and decides to respond in kind rather than absorbing the blow. But it is at least as likely that, unable to achieve much at home, he will escalate. In turn, if the Iranians had not realised it already, all the headlines inform them that refineries are an Achilles heel. The Ukrainian campaign against Russia tells the same tale. Refineries in Israel and in all the Gulf states except Oman were damaged earlier this year. Saudi refineries in Jazan and Yanbu have been attacked from Yemen over the past month, and on Saturday, there were reports of a fire and smoke at a refinery in Riyadh. Europe wants to avoid the worst cases of a US diesel export ban on the one hand, and running short in the middle of a flare-up of the conflict in midwinter. The way it structures its strategic stocks gives it a way out. It can appear to have conceded to Mr Trump’s demands for a big release. But if its companies do not actually want to sell much of their stocks, that is not the governments’ fault, and will not become apparent for some weeks anyway. By then, the US elections will be over and the next moves by Washington and Tehran may be clearer.

title: Human sacrifice in ancient Egypt uncovered by modern forensic science
description: Reinvestigation of mass burial sites around royal tombs finds evidence of fatal blunt force trauma on skulls
content: Almost four in 10 royal household members buried in an ancient Egyptian king’s tomb were probably killed by a deliberate blow to the head, according to a study of skulls excavated from the site a century ago. English Egyptologist Flinders Petrie, who has been referred to as the “father of Egyptian archaeology”, excavated graves at Abydos in Egypt in the 1920s. Due to the large number of burials clustered around the tombs he doubted that so many people could have died from natural causes simultaneously. Petrie suspected that members of the royal household had been sacrificed following the deaths of kings, but could not prove it due to the lack of fatal wounds on the skeletons. Now a new study of the skulls from the site, using modern forensic methods, has shown that almost 39 per cent had died after being struck in the head. Petrie kept meticulous records. He reburied most of the remains he excavated, but kept the skulls, some of which he sent to the UK. Dr Roselyn Campbell, of Purdue University, found 46 of these in the Duckworth Collection at Cambridge University and re-examined them, identifying crucial new evidence of violence. She found 18 of the 46 skulls showed evidence of significant cranial trauma – linear fractures which Petrie seems to have mistaken for naturally-caused damage. “Advances in forensic science allow us to recognise them as perimortem injuries,” said Dr Campbell. “The injuries on the preserved crania are generally linear fractures, which would likely cause rapid unconsciousness, internal bleeding and death,” said Dr Campbell, who also reported evidence of sharp-force trauma on some of the 18 skulls, including a chopping injury to one individual’s eye. The burial complexes at Abydos were built around 3000BC by the first kings of a unified Egypt. In addition to the royal tombs themselves, they consisted of chamber tombs probably used for funerary rituals, and were surrounded by further subsidiary enclosures. Dr Campbell, author of the article in Frontiers in Environmental Archaeology and of a forthcoming book, State-sanctioned Violence and Human Sacrifice in Early Dynastic Egypt , said Petrie suspected human sacrifice because of the sheer number of the subsidiary graves, some numbering in the hundreds. “Each subsidiary burial was a simple chamber in a row of dozens of others,” said Dr Campbell. “Some people had a simple coffin. Most people had a few grave goods, like ceramic vessels, and many graves also included small objects like copper tools, projectile points, or small ivory figurines. Petrie found a few grave markers that had names and sometimes official titles on them. The titles seem to mostly refer to lower- or midlevel officials as well as artisans.” She said it was still impossible to say what exactly had happened. “Egyptian kings are often depicted smiting their enemies with a mace, but these weren’t their enemies, and a mace would have caused depressed fractures,” she said. “Linear fractures are generally caused by a flat, wide weapon, or a fall – but falling hard enough to create a cranial fracture would probably have broken other bones, which should have been visible in Petrie’s photographs or recorded in his notes. “We also don’t know what happened to the others. Some could have died naturally. Alternatively, they may have been killed in a way that isn’t visible skeletally – like asphyxiation – or in a way that we would be able to detect if we could examine the rest of their skeleton.” Dr Campbell said she was drawn to the servants, officials and household staff – known as retainers – because, even though they were buried around royalty, “they were mostly footnotes in the grander narrative”. She asked the question: “Who were these people and how did they view the ruler and their own role in his or her life and death? She added: “Retainer sacrifice is a type of human sacrifice where those close to a ruler are killed when the ruler dies. “In many cultures, retainer sacrifice is practised because of beliefs that the sacrificed individuals will continue to serve the ruler in some kind of afterlife, but retainer sacrifice can also be a visceral display of the ruler’s power. “Some retainers might have volunteered to die to achieve eternal life or honour, others may have been chosen or even forced.”

title: All US bombers depart RAF Fairford amid security fears
description: B-1B heavy bombers had used Cotswolds airbase as launch point for runs against Iran
content: All of the American bombers that had been stationed at RAF Fairford in England have been sent back to the US, the Pentagon announced on Sunday, a week after five men were arrested outside the base. The US military had been using the base in Gloucestershire as a launchpad for B-1B heavy bombers during the war with Iran . Five British men were arrested on suspicion of preparation of a terrorist act and explosives offences after they were seen by a member of the public near RAF Fairford in the early hours of September 27. "While operational security precluded us from confirming the movement of our assets and forces in real time, we can acknowledge now that all US bombers that were deployed to RAF Fairford have re-deployed to their home stations in the United States," a Defence Department official said in a statement. The official added that the crews who operate America’s bomber force, including B-1s, B-2s and B-52s, remain "ready to deliver precision global strike capabilities – including through operations that launch and recover from the continental United States – anywhere, any time." On Wednesday, UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham suggested that there were "strong indications" Iran may have been behind last week's incident. The five men arrested near the perimeter of the base have since been released on bail. British police said a sixth man, an Iranian UK dual citizen, had been arrested in central London on Thursday in connection with the suspected plot to attack the US airbase in the Cotswolds.

title: Egypt committed to diplomatic solution on Nile dam dispute with Ethiopia, says PM
description: Madbouly says river is matter of 'national security and existential importance'
content: Egypt remains committed to a diplomatic and political solution to its dispute with Ethiopia over a controversial Nile dam, Prime Minister Mostafa Madbouly has said. In an interview with CNN Business Arabic, Mr Madbouly said the Nile is a matter of “national security and existential importance” for Egypt. The country depends on the river for about 95 per cent of its water resources. Egypt and Ethiopia last week announced they were expelling diplomats in a new escalation in their already tense relations. The leaders of Egypt , Eritrea and Sudan – three nations accused by Ethiopia of aiding an anti-government rebellion there – plus Somalia, were meeting on Sunday to shore up their loose alliance. Mr Madbouly rejected what he described as Ethiopian efforts to portray Egypt as an obstacle to the development of African countries. He said Cairo supports development in all nations as long as it does not harm other states, particularly in the case of rivers. “These rivers are governed by international law, which establishes that all riparian states are partners in the river and its water resources,” Mr Madbouly said. Egypt has maintained this position since the beginning of the dispute and will continue to pursue a diplomatic and political solution, he said, adding that President Abdel Fattah El Sisi had reaffirmed that approach days earlier. At the same time, Mr Madbouly said Egypt had “clear, non-negotiable principles and parameters”, including clear regulations and Egypt's prior consent, as well as Sudan's, regarding the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam. He said the dam's operation and management should be based on a shared vision to prevent harm to downstream countries, particularly during periods of prolonged drought. “The major challenge arises during multi-year droughts: how the dam is refilled could significantly impact Egypt's water resources,” Mr Madbouly said. Last week, Mr El Sisi said Egypt was creating “space for diplomacy and peaceful solutions” on the Ethiopian dams. “But that will not be at the expense of Egypt's existence and its people,” he added. Mr Madbouly also defended the government's large-scale infrastructure investment programme, saying it had been necessary to create the foundations for economic growth following the political turmoil that began in 2011. Egypt at the time lacked adequate electricity and energy capacity to meet citizens' needs or support economic growth, while its water, sanitation, road, port and airport networks were also insufficient, he said. “These are the very foundations required for any nation to launch its economy,” Mr Madbouly said. The state had to take the lead in building the infrastructure because political instability and uncertainty had made it difficult to attract sufficient private-sector investment into large, long-term projects, he said. The Prime Minister said that Egypt's economy grew by 5.1 per cent in the 2025/26 fiscal year, up from 4.4 per cent in the previous year, an Egyptian official said. He added that the government was aiming for growth of 5.4 per cent in the current fiscal year, which began in July. The growth was driven by the domestic economy's productive capacity rather than external factors or exceptional, one-off sources of funding, the official said, rejecting concerns that the expansion might not be sustainable. “Thank God, the Egyptian economy has grown at very good rates, all based on what we call sustainable sectors,” the official said.

title: US refuses to rule out further military action against Iran
description: 'No guarantees in conflict,' says Energy Secretary Chris Wright
content: The Trump administration is pursuing both diplomatic and military options in the Iran conflict, Energy Secretary Chris Wright said on Sunday, refusing to rule out further escalation in the region following the deployment of a third US aircraft carrier to the region Asked on CBS News whether the expected arrival of the USS Theodore Roosevelt in the Middle East next month indicates that President Donald Trump had decided to escalate after the US mid-term elections, Mr Wright declined to discuss the President's plans. “He's always planning for contingencies and he's always negotiating,” Mr Wright said. “He's got both tracks still going, diplomatic and military.” Mr Wright said there were no guarantees that Iran would not launch further attacks against Gulf energy infrastructure, which could push already elevated fuel prices higher. “There's no guarantees in conflict,” he said. The Trump administration is preparing for possible disruption by increasing US production and refining capacity while seeking to boost fuel supplies from allies, he added. Earlier on Sunday, a tanker ⁠was hit ⁠by an ​unidentified projectile in ⁠the Strait of Hormuz, causing ⁠damage to ​its ⁠engine room, ‌according to UK Maritime Trade Operations. Diesel prices have been particularly affected by the disruption to global energy supplies, with China also reducing exports of diesel and other refined fuels, Mr Wright said. The G7 has agreed to release 100 million barrels of fuel from strategic reserves over four months, with the release front-loaded towards diesel. Mr Wright said he expects diesel prices to fall below $6 a gallon but didn't commit to a timeline. Mr Wright was also pressed on a separate issue involving Russia's war in Ukraine. Under a new law named after the late senator Lindsey Graham , the US can impose tariffs on China and India for buying Russian oil, sales of which are helping pay for its war against Ukraine. But Mr Wright repeatedly declined to say whether Mr Trump would pursue such tariffs. "Of course, we're trying to have great relations with China and move that ball forward. I think things are going reasonably well there," he said. "But then the flip side is you've got to look at every leverage you've got to bring a murderous conflict to an end." Mr Wright also said the US would not allow Iran to become a nuclear-armed state, arguing that the administration could not leave the issue to the next president. “The world cannot sustain a nuclear-armed Iran,” he said.

title: President and Italian PM discuss relations and Middle East stability
description: Sheikh Mohamed and Meloni reaffirm strategic partnership goals in phone call
content: President Sheikh Mohamed and Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni have discussed strengthening ties between their nations. During a call on Sunday, the two leaders reviewed the state of UAE-Italian relations and identified opportunities to deepen co-operation, with a particular focus on economic and development initiatives. The talks demonstrated the importance the nations place on their strategic partnership. Sheikh Mohamed and Ms Meloni reaffirmed their shared commitment to advancing collaboration under the framework of the UAE-Italy strategic partnership, which the leaders described as a vehicle for driving mutual growth and prosperity. The conversation reflected the strong diplomatic foundations built between the Emirates and Italy in recent years. The two leaders also discussed a range of regional and international issues, with developments in the Middle East featuring prominently on the agenda. Sheikh Mohamed and Ms Meloni expressed support for efforts to promote security and stability across the region, and emphasised the importance of such initiatives to the benefit of countries and peoples throughout the Middle East.

title: UAE Football Association charters six flights to fly fans to Gulf Cup final in Jeddah
description: UAE fans can register for chartered flights to cheer on the national team in Jeddah
content: The UAE Football Association has chartered six aircraft to fly supporters to Jeddah for Tuesday's Arabian Gulf Cup final against Saudi Arabia. The initiative, announced on Sunday, is aimed at bolstering the presence of UAE fans at what will be one of the most keenly awaited fixtures in the regional football calendar. Fans wishing to take advantage of the chartered flights can register through a dedicated link made available on Sunday. The UAE will face Saudi Arabia in the final of the Gulf Cup 27 at Alinma Stadium, King Abdullah Sports City, in Jeddah. The match is scheduled to kick off at 10pm UAE time on Tuesday, October 6. The UAEFA said the initiative forms part of broader efforts to support the national team ahead of the final. Chartered flights offer supporters a convenient and organised means of travelling to the Saudi port city to attend the match. King Abdullah Sports City, which houses Alinma Stadium, is one of Saudi Arabia's best sporting venues and is expected to host a capacity crowd for the Gulf Cup showpiece. The match will be a hotly contested derby between two of the region's strongest footballing nations. The Arabian Gulf Cup, one of the oldest and most prestigious football tournaments in the Gulf region, has historically been a platform for intense competition between neighbouring nations.

title: Donald Trump says Jay Clayton will lead AI 'super intelligence' task force
description: Current director of national intelligence previously served as SEC chair
content: President Donald Trump said on Sunday that he had chosen Jay Clayton, currently Director of National Intelligence, to head up his newly established “Super Intelligence Force” to guide AI policy in the US. Mr Trump first floated the idea of a new AI chief and steering committee back in September, amid continuing debate over safety and oversight. Mr Clayton was sworn in as the ninth director of national intelligence in August, following the departure of Tulsi Gabbard. In his current role, he is responsible for overseeing and directing the implementation of the National Intelligence Programme and integrates intelligence activities across the intelligence community, according to his biography on the Office of the Director of National Intelligence website. Mr Clayton previously served as chairman of the Security Exchange Commission, from 2017 to 2020. “The Super Intelligence Force is tasked with co-ordinating the effort of the federal government to ensure that America continues to lead the world in Super Intelligence, which many say is bigger than the Industrial Revolution, and the internet, and will protect the interests, and improve the lives, of all Americans,” Mr Trump said on Truth Social. Speculation over who would lead the task force has swirled for weeks as the topic of AI has consumed increasing amounts of the White House’s time amid an unprecedented investment boom for the technology. The Trump White House views AI as crucial to ensuring US economic dominance in the decades ahead, and it sought to portray its development as a two-horse race between Washington and China . Yet as investment in AI and AI-related infrastructure continues to expand, the sector has come under intense scrutiny. Powerful AI models have gone rogue and compromised some websites and digital assets around the world. There is also growing concern about the potential for AI to significantly disrupt the labour market, along with worries about the environmental impact of data centre construction. Polls have shown increased reticence about AI overall, even though various tools continue to be used by consumers around the world. Mr Trump, however, has described fears over AI as “a hoax” and insisted that the industry could “self police”.

title: Dubai to expand CommerCity in push for digital economy growth
description: The $272.2m expansion will be delivered in phases starting from first quarter of 2027
content: Dubai CommerCity (DCC) , the free zone dedicated to digital commerce in Dubai, is launching the second phase of its expansion programme with Dh1.8 billion ($272.2 million) investment that will help the emirate grow its digital economy . The free zone is set to deliver the expansion project in phases between the first quarter of 2027 and the fourth quarter of 2028, Dubai Media Office said in a statement on Sunday. “Phase two of Dubai CommerCity comes at a time when Dubai continues to demonstrate its ability to grow and expand despite the changes and challenges facing the global economy,” Sheikh Ahmed bin Saeed, Chairman of Dubai Integrated Economic Zones Authority (Diez), said. The free zone, which is a joint venture between Diez and Wasl Group, will add a series of projects across its three districts: the Business Cluster, Logistics Cluster, and Social Cluster. On aggregate, the projects will add more than 91,000 square metres of new office space, increasing the free zone’s capacity and expanding its integrated ecosystem to serve companies operating in digital commerce and technology sectors. The push to expand the free zone builds upon Dubai CommerCity’s record demand, with occupancy reaching nearly 96 per cent across its office, logistics, and retail spaces. “This expansion reflects the growing investor confidence in Dubai’s economic ecosystem and its ability to attract high-quality investments while providing an advanced economic infrastructure that responds to rapid shifts in emerging sectors,” Sheikh Ahmed said. The move, he added, aligns with the Dubai Economic Agenda, D33, objectives and helps strengthen Dubai's position as a global hub for the digital economy and future commerce. Launched in January, D33 aims to double the size of Dubai’s economy , with a target of reaching Dh32 trillion by 2033 and establishing the emirate among the top three global cities. The plan envisages a programme to support 30 private companies to achieve unicorn status – worth more than $1 billion. Other business incubators will support the growth of private companies, with 400 of the most promising identified. The expansion of the Business Cluster and the Social Cluster will add 86,000 square metres of new space, which will add to options available to local, regional and global companies that are looking to become a part of the Dubai CommerCity ecosystem, the Media Office said. The Business Cluster will include additional office space across six new buildings, including shell-and-core offices, fully fitted workspaces, and flexible plug-and-play solutions. Within the Logistics Cluster, the phase two expansion will add The Hive, a 5,600 square metre facility that will provide an alternative logistics model. It will feature 181 flexible units, alongside climate-controlled fulfilment areas, as well as digitally managed loading and unloading zones, the Media Office said.

title: Asian Games success shows UAE is rising as a sporting force, says President of the UAE Olympic Committee
description: Sheikh Mansoor bin Mohammed bin Rashid praises performance of Emirati team
content: The UAE delivered its best Asian Games performance at Aichi-Nagoya 2026, finishing 13th among 45 nations with a record seven gold medals. Sheikh Mansoor bin Mohammed bin Rashid, President of the UAE Olympic Committee, praised the country's 165-strong contingent after the Games concluded in Japan on Saturday. The achievement reflects the determination of UAE athletes to raise the nation’s flag and their burning ambition to strengthen the country’s standing among Asia’s leading sporting nations, said Sheikh Mansoor, reported state news agency Wam. The success reflects the sustained efforts of the athletes, technical and administrative support teams, and national sports federations through the preparatory stages and the competitions during the Games, he added. The UAE finished with 13 medals in total – seven gold, five silver and one bronze – surpassing its previous best of five golds at Hangzhou and placing second among Arab nations. Among the stand-out performers was Mariam Kareem, who won gold in the women's 400m hurdles in 54.31 seconds, breaking the Asian Games record and setting a new Asian Under-20 record. The teenager's time was also the second-fastest recorded in the event at the Under-20 level globally, a remarkable achievement for the young Emirati athlete, who had earlier competed in the mixed 4x400m relay before returning to claim her historic victory. In equestrian, Sheikha Latifah bint Ahmed bin Juma Al Maktoum brought her career Asian Games medal tally to four – equalling the record for the most medals won by a female equestrian in Asian Games history – after contributing to the UAE show jumping team's silver medal. Abdullah Humaid Al Muhairi added further silverware on the final day, finishing with four penalties in 41.93 seconds aboard Hudson De Vains in the individual show jumping event. Jiu-jitsu proved a particularly fruitful discipline, with five medals including gold for Balqees Abdulla, Khaled Al Shehhi, Ahmed Andeez, Mahdi Al Awlaqi and Asma Al Hosani. Kazbek Naguchev claimed gold in the men's under-73kg judo category, rounding out the UAE's record-breaking gold haul. The Games, held across Aichi Prefecture and Nagoya City from September 19 to October 4, brought together more than 11,000 athletes representing 45 countries across 43 sports, 469 events and 16 days of competition.

title: Iraq’s PM orders probe after US flag trampled by Iran-backed militias
description: Militias filmed driving over American and Israeli flags in Baghdad during celebrations to mark withdrawal of American troops
content: Iraqi Prime Minister Ali Al Zaidi ordered an investigation on Sunday after the American flag was desecrated during parades marking the withdrawal of US troops from the country . Arrests have been made after Mr Al Zaidi ordered a committee to determine the circumstances of what happened during Iraq 's Sovereignty Day events, his military spokesman Sabah Al Numan said. The Prime Minister, who is also the commander-in-chief of Iraq's military, condemned the act and stressed the need to adhere to diplomatic laws and customs, and directed legal measures against those responsible, Mr Al Numan said. The incident occurred on Friday when the Popular Mobilisation Forces and Iran-backed militias staged large military parades in different parts of Baghdad to celebrate the withdrawal of coalition forces . The PMF is an umbrella group of mostly Shiite paramilitary forces, many of which have close ties to Iran. Their military vehicles were filmed driving over US and Israeli flags during a symbolic funeral procession honouring those killed in US-Israeli attacks in Iraq. They also displayed flags of Lebanon's Hezbollah , part of the Iran-aligned Axis of Resistance, as well as the Iranian flag and images of Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, the former Iranian supreme leader killed on the first day of US-Israeli strikes on Iran. In a separate statement, Mr Al Numan said "those involved in the desecration of the American flag in Baghdad" have been arrested. He didn't give numbers or say to which group they were affiliated. "The government affirms that respecting the symbols of friendly countries and diplomatic missions accredited to Iraq is a legal and diplomatic obligation, and that any transgression or abuse in this regard will be subject to legal accountability," he said. The footage sparked a wave of debate on social media, with some warning it undermines Iraq's diplomatic standing and its stated commitment not to use its territory to threaten neighbours. The backlash reached Washington. US Congressman Joe Wilson, a Republican and vocal critic of Iranian influence in Iraq, posted on X: “The PMF, an official division of the Iraqi government's security services, is seen desecrating the US flag out of disrespect and praising the murderous regime in Iran.” “If you needed any more proof that Iraq is an Iranian province … [Iraqi Prime Minister Ali] Zaidi is this what you think of America? Free Iraq from Iran,” Mr Wilson added, sharing photos of the parade. Zalmay Khalilzad, a former US ambassador to Baghdad, called it a "disrespectful act". "If not for the United States and the courage and sacrifices of its servicemen and women Iraq would still likely be ruled by Saddam Hussein," he wrote on X. "I am surprised that the Iraqi government stood by and allowed this to happen." The incident comes at a sensitive moment. Mr Al Zaidi declared full sovereignty after 12 years of the US-led Operation Inherent Resolve against ISIS, pledging to disarm groups outside state control, ban cross-border attacks, and purchase a full air defence system. The PMF and militias parade itself underscores the challenge to that pledge – a state-funded force acting alongside militias that have openly said their weapons “will remain”.

title: Iranian suspects 'planned to use home-made bomb' to attack Jews in Britain
description: Rahman ⁠Salehi, 34, and Salam Ahmadyan, 36, appear in court over alleged plot in Manchester
content: Two Iranians have appeared in an English court over an alleged plot to use a home-made bomb to attack Jewish people in Manchester. Rahman ⁠Salehi, 34, and Salam Ahmadyan, 36, are charged with plotting acts of terrorism at the behest of a figure believed to be in Iran. Prosecutors allege they carried out “hostile” surveillance on potential Jewish targets in Manchester . The targets ⁠included the Manchester Jewish Museum and Heaton Park synagogue , the scene of a deadly attack a year ​ago ⁠in which two Jewish worshippers were ‌killed, prosecutor Mark Luckett told Westminster Magistrates' Court. “Both defendants are accused of preparing ​acts of terrorism targeting the Jewish community in Manchester through the use of a home-made explosive device,” Mr Luckett said. The pair were arrested last month at the start of Yom Kippur, the holiest day in the Jewish calendar. After their court appearance in London they were remanded in custody until their next hearing on October 23. They did not enter a plea. A third person is suspected of having directed the attack planning and provided instructions on how to assemble a home-made device, which prosecutors allege would have been made from chlorine and brake fluid, the court heard. “It's assessed that this individual is also an Iranian national and most likely operating from within Iran,” Mr Luckett said. The court was told both suspects had come to Britain from Europe in small boats. Mr Salehi had arrived in 2020 and had been granted asylum, while Mr Ahmadyan came in 2023 and his asylum claim was still outstanding, Mr Luckett said. The case comes days after ​Britain said Iran was believed to be involved in a suspected plot to attack the RAF Fairford airbase , which ⁠the US military has used to carry out ​raids against targets in Iran. A British-Iranian national was arrested on suspicion of ​preparing terrorist acts. Police ‌said on Saturday he had been released on police bail while the investigation continues. British counter-terrorism police said the ⁠Manchester allegations were not connected to the RAF Fairford investigation. Iran has rejected accusations of involvement ⁠in several plots in Britain in recent years, and said allegations that it is connected to the Fairford incident are baseless.

title: UAE teachers honoured ahead of World Teachers' Day as minister highlights their vital role
description: Education Minister Sarah Al Amiri praises educators for shaping generations and driving the UAE's development
content: The UAE has marked World Teachers' Day with a tribute to educators whose work shapes minds and drives national progress, the Ministry of Education said. Sarah Al Amiri, Minister of Education, said the annual occasion – celebrated on Monday, October 5 – embodies a shared appreciation for a noble mission that broadens the horizons of societies. She said teachers instil confidence, values and a passion for knowledge in students, underscoring their enduring importance to the nation. Ms Al Amiri said teachers have been vital partners in the UAE 's development journey, helping to prepare generations that have carried the nation's ambitions and actively participated in its progress. Her remarks highlighted the deep-rooted relationship between the education sector and the broader goals of the country. The minister said the UAE leadership's support for teachers reflects a firm belief in their vital role and a commitment to empowering them to develop their capabilities. She stressed that collaboration between teachers and families provides students with a solid foundation for growth and learning, better preparing them for the future. Ms Al Amiri extended her congratulations to education professionals across the country, expressing pride in their continued dedication and lasting impact on students' lives. She highlighted their commitment to preparing knowledgeable and capable generations able to contribute confidently and effectively to the UAE's development. World Teachers' Day is celebrated annually on October 5 under the auspices of Unesco to honour educators and recognise their contributions to education and society. Beyond celebration, the day serves as a moment to reflect on the support teachers need to fully realise their potential, and to consider the future direction of the profession on a global scale.

title: Clashes erupt in Christian town in central Syria
description: Brawl with young Sunni men raises new concerns over sectarian tensions
content: Security forces were sent to the Christian town of Suqaylabiyah in central Syria at the weekend after young Sunnis from a nearby area went there and started a fight, residents and state media said. It was the second incident of sectarian violence in the region this year. The Syrian government, led by Sunnis , has made improving relations with the US its top priority. This has helped spare Christians the violence suffered by other minorities, mainly the Druze and Alawites , since the downfall of the regime of Bashar Al Assad in December 2024. State television said the security personnel were sent in after a “brawl among young people” in Suqaylabiyah on Saturday “during which an attack on a shop occurred”. Security forces were also sent to the Sunni town of Qalaat Al Madiq, where the men lived, 4km to the north. The Hama Governorate described the violence as a result of “systematic incitement among the components of the Syrian people”. State TV said that “calm has returned to Suqaylabiyah after the brawl was contained and several of those involved were arrested”. There were no immediate reports of casualties. Video on social media purportedly showed the scene of the brawl near a square in Suqaylabiyah, with a fire lit in the street and at least one young man holding a stick. Separate footage showed a group of young men trying to break into a shop. A photo showed security personnel wearing flak jackets and carrying automatic weapons, standing in front of an Interior Ministry lorry in the town. Suqaylabiyah, in the Ghab Plain of Hama, has about 16,000 inhabitants who are mainly Greek Orthodox. Its population was down from 20,000 in December 2024. Many loyalists of the regime in the town fled after the downfall of Al Assad. That regime, dominated by members of the Alawite sect, sought to build a so-called “alliance of minorities”, especially during the 2011-2024 civil war. It recruited some Christians from Suqaylabiyah during the war into a local brigade of the National Defence Forces, a main loyalist auxiliary. The town's association with the bygone order contributed to tension between Suqaylabiyah and its mostly Sunni surroundings after December 2024. When the Syrian civil war began in 2011, Syria had about 850,000 Christians, about 4.5 per cent of the population. They are mainly divided between Greek Orthodox, Syrian Orthodox, and Catholics of the Greek Melkite, Maronite, Chaldean and Armenian churches. The new Syrian government has faced an array of challenges in bringing the multi-ethnic country under its control. Tensions with the Kurds, Alawites and Druze minorities have at times spiralled into open violence. Syria is also eager to contain the influence of Lebanon's Hezbollah and smuggling across their shared border. Lebanon's army said last week that it had seized almost 250kg of explosives being smuggled over the border from Syria. With tensions high, Reuters reported last week that Syria and Hezbollah had held a secret meeting in Turkey in an attempt to calm matters. Turkey and Syria both denied the meeting had taken place.

title: Filipina in UAE to pay off debts after Dh20 million win in Big Ticket draw
description: Ajman resident was asleep in the Philippines and missed call informing her of win
content: Bernadetta Azucena had recently resigned as a secretary, leaving her mother worried about her daughter's future without a job. On Saturday night, she received life-changing news of a Dh20 million win in the latest Big Ticket draw. The Filipina, who lives in Ajman , is part of a group that regularly buys tickets under a different member's name each time. “This is God's perfect timing,” Ms Azucena told her mother after learning about the jackpot win. The 42-year-old Filipina, who is currently in the Philippines after flying home for surgery on September 30, said her first priority is to become debt-free. “We have loans to pay off. I want to pay the mortgage on our house here in the Philippines, which is still nine years away from completion. We also have a car loan in the UAE ,” she told The National . Ms Azucena and her husband, Noriel Azucena, 44, also plan to secure the future of their 15-year-old daughter, who is in Grade 10. “We will definitely invest towards our daughter's future,” she said. “We haven't told her about the win yet. The news has been shared only with my mother for now. I am actually still confused, and it's unbelievable. Of course, we were praying and hoping, but it was unexpected.” For her mother, however, the win has brought relief. “My mother is very happy, and now she doesn't have to worry much about me,” she added. Ms Azucena is the eldest of three siblings. She and her two brothers were raised by their mother, who was a single parent and worked to support the family and put her children through school. After graduating, Ms Azucena worked at a bank for eight years. But after her marriage to Noriel, who was already working in the UAE, he encouraged her to move there to find work. She had been working in the UAE since 2016, most recently as a secretary, before her contract ended. Ms Azucena was asleep in the Philippines when her husband received confirmation of their win. He woke her at about 1am in the Philippines and told her to prepare herself for an important conversation. “He told me to sit down and breathe, and then he told me that we had won,” Ms Azucena recalled. “I honestly thought I was still dreaming. I just couldn't believe it.” The couple had been participating in Big Ticket since 2017 as part of a group of friends. "Not everyone contributed the same amount," Mr Azucena said. "We did as much as we could, but we are all very thankful. It is a life-changing amount for all of us.” He added that he didn't get any sleep last night. The group has a system in which members take turns choosing tickets under their own name. This time, the winning ticket was the one selected under her name. “We usually purchase during the promotions, and everyone in the group chooses a ticket under their name. This time, I got lucky, and the winning ticket was the one selected under mine,” she said. The win comes at an emotionally significant moment. Ms Azucena had travelled back to the Philippines after she twisted a bone in her right arm in a roadside accident, making it difficult for her to work and write. Her husband said the couple had decided she should return home for treatment because there was nobody in the UAE who could take care of her. “She was also missing our daughter,” he said. The couple had initially planned for her to undergo hand surgery after returning home, but the jackpot win has changed their immediate plans. “She will be returning soon, and we postponed the surgery,” Mr Azucena said. They now have plans for their family's future, including paying off their debts and investing for their daughter's education and long-term security. Despite the Dh20 million windfall, the Azucenas have no plans to stop participating in Big Ticket.

title: Egypt hosts four-way summit as tensions with Ethiopia escalate
description: Meeting with Eritrea, Somalia and Sudan comes as rivalries reshape balance of power in Horn of Africa
content: The leaders of Egypt , Eritrea and Sudan – three nations accused by Ethiopia of aiding an anti-government rebellion – plus Somalia met on Sunday to shore up their loose alliance. The Egyptian presidency said the summit was designed to “co-ordinate and consult on regional issues of interest” to the four countries. However, sources said the meeting would announce several measures to consolidate the alliance of the four nations, including wider military co-operation. “There may be some surprises in what the four leaders decide in terms of deeper and wider co-operation,” said one of the sources. “One will be broadening the extent of military co-operation to safeguard the region and protect Red Sea shipping.” The summit in Egypt's coastal city of Alamein brings together Egypt's Abdel Fattah El Sisi, Sudan's army chief and de facto leader Gen Abdel Fattah Al Burhan, Somalia's Hassan Sheikh Mohamud and Isaias Afwerki of Eritrea. Mr El Sisi has already met separately with the three leaders on Saturday and Sunday. The four-way summit is scheduled for Sunday evening. Addis Ababa has accused Eritrea, Sudan and Egypt of supporting an opposition alliance led by the Tigray People's Liberation Front that has been battling troops loyal to Ethiopia's federal government. The three nations have denied the charge. Last week, Egypt and Ethiopia expelled diplomats in a retaliatory row that saw a senior member of each country's embassy ordered to leave. The expulsions came one day after Ethiopia ordered the closure of its embassy in Eritrea and declared 10 Eritrean diplomats persona non grata. That prompted Asmara to sever diplomatic ties with its neighbour after overnight blasts heard in Addis Ababa sparked fears that the renewed conflict in ​northern Ethiopia might be spreading. Egypt has been locked in a bitter, decade-old dispute with Ethiopia over its share of the Nile's waters. Eritrea has been at odds with Addis Ababa for most of the 30-plus years since its secession from Ethiopia. The Sudanese armed forces accuse Ethiopia of aiding its civil war adversary, the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces. Sudan, Eritrea and Somalia all neighbour Ethiopia and, together with Egypt, have an uninterrupted Red Sea coastline that stretches from the northern tip of the Gulf of Suez in Egypt to Somalia in the Horn of Africa. Egypt, the most populous of the four nations with an army considered the largest in the Middle East, has been forging close military relations with Eritrea, Somalia and Sudan. It has an estimated 15,000-strong military contingent in Somalia serving in an African Union peacekeeping force as well as a large mission supporting the Mogadishu government and its military. Egypt's military also has naval and army sites in Eritrea and is reportedly backing the Sudanese Armed Forces against the RSF. Its military footprint in Eritrea and Somalia is chiefly designed to isolate and put pressure on Ethiopia to show flexibility in their dispute over a large Nile dam Addis Ababa has built that Cairo insists could reduce its vital share of the river's water. Labelling it an existential issue, Egypt says any reduction would have a disastrous impact on its economy, wiping out millions of agricultural jobs and disrupting its delicate food balance. Egypt is also engaged in an intense campaign to prevent efforts by landlocked Ethiopia to secure a permanent foothold on the Red Sea. Addressing an AU meeting in Alamein on Sunday, Mr El Sisi made a thinly-veiled reference to Cairo's quarrel with Addis Ababa. “I would like to emphasise the importance of dealing with transnational issues as ones that require co-operation, not competition; dialogue not confrontation,” he said. “That includes the management and use under international law of natural resources and transnational rivers.”

title: Max Verstappen wins rain-delayed Bahrain GP as Kimi Antonelli takes firm grip on title race
description: Crazy day in Sepang sees Red Bull seal first victory of season as Mercedes' Italian driver claims second place
content: A crazy, rain-delayed Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia finished with Max Verstappen earning Red Bull their first win of the 2026 season at Sepang International Circuit on Sunday. And Kimi Antonelli's grip on the title race was strengthened when the Italian finished in second place, while his Mercedes teammate George Russell suffered an engine failure with five laps to go – likely ending any lingering hopes the Briton had of winning the drivers' championship. Antonelli's lead over Russell is now 84 points with seven races to go following a GP that was held up by more than 90 minutes after heavy rain and then confusion over the grid order. There was also two safety cars following the retirements of Valtteri Bottas and Alex Albon for a race had been rescheduled from April and moved to Malaysia because of the continuing conflict in the Middle East. Verstappen was the last driver to ⁠win in Sepang in 2017 before it ​was ⁠taken off the ‌calendar and the Dutchman, who had also taken ​pole, gave Red Bull a huge boost despite an early setback when he lost the lead before Turn 1. The four-time world champion would fight back to earn his first victory since last season's Abu Dhabi GP , finishing less than two-and-a-half seconds ahead of Antonelli, with Lewis Hamilton recovering from a disastrous start that saw him drop down to 18th place to claim third. Hamilton's Ferrari teammate Charles Leclerc was fourth. Red Bull's Isack Hadjar dropped from a podium spot in the last few laps to finish fifth, Oscar Piastri came home sixth ahead of Liam Lawson of Racing Bulls and the Aston Martin of Fernando Norris took eighth place. “It is a really nice one after the year that we had and the progression that we have made. I am incredibly proud of everyone and it is super nice to win here,” said 29-year-old Verstappen. “It was very hectic, I mean there was a lot of different things in the start, no power so you have to wait for the power to kick in. But then we made the right call, with the intermediates and after that, step by step we moved our way forwards and from there onwards we can do our own race until the end and then with the safety car, but we kept it all under control.” Antonelli, meanwhile, had no complaints about falling short of what would been his ninth win of the campaign. “I think that was the maximum we could have done,” said the 20-year-old. “Of course, a massive congrats to Max and Red Bull for the incredible weekend. “On our side, a lot of work to do. Of course, you know, we've been struggling a bit more than usual but still really happy to come away with P2. “It was amazing [to race in Sepang] and the fans were incredible this weekend, so thank you so much and hopefully it will come back in the future to Malaysia.” It was a sensational race for Hamilton who dropped way back after due to an incorrect tyre choice for the wet start as the seven-time champion went on to pass Red Bull's Isack Hadjar for third place with three laps to go, marked by the deafening roars of spectators in Sepang. “Yeah, well thank you guys,” said the 41-year-old British driver. “Big congratulations to Max. What a tough, tough race that was, we had the wrong call at the beginning which was so difficult and I could just see everyone pulling away and I could see on the screen it was a minute down. And I thought that was the race over for us. “But, I just kept my head down, the guys did a great job with the pit stops, lots of tyre changes, lots of chasing and honestly of all the years I have been here, this is the best race we have had here. Particularly because of this crowd. Big thank you everyone.” All that thrilling action came after a farcical start to proceedings as first heavy delayed the race, before a series of technical problems left several cars crawling around on the formation laps on a wet track behind the safety car. It then took more time for race organisers to decide what order the cars should be in when the race did start. When the action did get under way in the original order, Mercedes duo Antonelli and Russell powered to the front ahead of Verstappen and Hamilton on the front row. Verstappen would eventually retake the lead when the safety car was brought on to allow marshals to recover the Cadillac of Bottas as the Dutchman immediately passed Antonelli on the restart. It was Verstappen's race to lose from that point and there would be no mistake.

title: Opec+ keeps oil output targets unchanged for November
description: Group holds production steady for a second month as most members pump below quotas
content: Opec + kept its oil production targets unchanged for November, extending the pause it started in October after six months of gradual increases. The group's seven core members – Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Kuwait, Oman, Algeria, Russia and Kazakhstan – decided during the meeting on Sunday to "maintain September 2026 required production for November 2026", a statement said. The group finished unwinding 1.65 million barrels per day of voluntary cuts from 2023 in September. It is keeping a further two million bpd of cuts, agreed in 2022, in place until the end of the year. It is also reviewing members' production capacity to set quotas for 2027. The seven Opec+ countries "will continue to hold monthly meetings to review market conditions", the statement said. The next meeting will be held on November 1. The joint quotas for the seven members amounts to 31 million bpd for November. But most members are producing below their targets because of the war. The Strait of Hormuz , which carried about a fifth of the world's crude oil and liquefied natural gas, has been effectively shut since fighting between the US and Iran started on February 28. Iran has said that the strait will not reopen until seven conditions are met, as indirect talks with the US stall and officials in Tehran prepare for the possibility of another round of fighting. Tehran's lead negotiator, Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, said the US had sent proposals through intermediaries that contradicted its leaders' public statements. However, he added, Iran’s position was “completely clear and definitive”. Tehran has repeatedly demanded an end to the fighting, the lifting of a US naval blockade, the release of frozen assets and relief from sanctions. Brent, the benchmark for two-thirds of the world's oil, settled nearly flat at $102.25 a barrel on Friday. West Texas Intermediate, the gauge that tracks US crude, shed 1.9 per cent to settle at $91.11 a barrel. From last week's close, Brent slid nearly 2 per cent, while WTI gave up 1.4 per cent. Prices reached an intraday high of $126 a barrel in late April.

title: Much-loved UAE theatre veteran and educator Eric Dury dies
description: British performer spent more than 25 years on UAE stages while teaching at the University of Sharjah and Zayed University
content: Eric Dury, the British actor and university educator who spent more than 25 years performing on UAE stages, has died. The news was announced on Sunday in a statement shared by Alex Broun, festival director of Short+Sweet Dubai and a long-time figure in UAE theatre. Dury's age and cause of death were not disclosed. “Eric was part of the fabric of the community: an actor who continued to perform across decades, an educator who shared his knowledge with generations of students, and a committed supporter of theatre and the people who make it,” the statement said. Dury, who was also known as Roslee Abdullah, moved to the Emirates in 1999 and became a regular presence on the independent theatre circuit. Much of his work was with Dubai Drama Group. The National covered his career as early as 2009, when he played businessman Sir Chiffley Lockhart in the company's production of Ben Elton's Gasping at Ductac. That same year, he also appeared as a surgeon in Ali F Mostafa 's Dubai-set feature film City of Life . His later roles included the Player in Tom Stoppard's Rosencrantz and Guildenstern Are Dead , Stephan Chubukov in Anton Chekhov's The Proposal , both in 2014 and Max in Harold Pinter's The Homecoming in 2016. He was also part of Dubai Drama Group's 2017 production of Hamlet , playing Polonius, the Player and the Gravedigger, and appeared in productions of Neil Simon's Plaza Suite and the pantomime Jack & the Beanstalk . Beyond Dubai Drama Group, he played Count De Guiche in Raw Theatre's Cyrano de Bergerac , the Arms Dealer in Danu Dubai Theatre's The Al-Hamlet Summit and the Father in Bark at a Crow Productions' online staging of Ashputtel . In 2021, he appeared as Steve in Tall Tales Productions' Just Like That , a locally written comedy about residents of Jumeirah Lakes Towers. Dury also had a long association with Short+Sweet Dubai , the annual festival of 10-minute plays, first as a performer and later as a judge. He won its Best Actor award in 2016 for playing Mr Hollins in New Year's Eve . A year later, he was runner-up for Best Actor for his role as Eddie in The Coming Out . In 2025, Dury received a Lifetime Achievement Award at the inaugural DXB Theatre Awards, which celebrated performers, productions and companies across Dubai's independent theatre scene. Alongside acting, Dury worked in English language education at the University of Sharjah and later Zayed University. When he spoke to The National during Ramadan in 2022, he reflected on faith, family and the example he and his wife wanted to set for their daughter. “There is a spiritual side to it as we eat together as a family after fasting during Ramadan,” he said. “It brings meaning to our lives and it encourages my wife and I to be better people. That's because we have to both set a good example for our daughter and act as role models.” Dury had already spent years performing and teaching before moving to the UAE. During his time in Malaysia, he performed under the name Eric Roslee. Archival listings from Malaysia's MY Art Memory Project, an archive of the country's performing arts, show Dury performing in Kuala Lumpur by at least 1987, when he appeared in The Tea House of the August Moon . By 1999, he was listed among the academic staff of Akademi Seni Kebangsaan, Malaysia's national arts academy, now known as Aswara Dury is survived by his wife Shereen and daughter Tash. His Janazah was due to be held on Sunday following Asr prayers at Al Qusais Cemetery Mosque in Dubai.

title: UAE's MBR Explorer probe enters final tests for 2028 mission
description: Emirates Mission to the Asteroid Belt on track for launch
content: A UAE-built probe for the Emirates Mission to the Asteroid Belt has completed vibration testing and is undergoing thermal tests as preparations intensify for the mission’s launch in March 2028. Sheikh Hamdan bin Mohammed , Crown Prince of Dubai, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Defence viewed a flight-identical model of the probe, developed by Abu Dhabi’s Technology Innovation Institute, at a press conference on Thursday. Faisal Al Bannai, Adviser to the UAE President for Strategic Research and Advanced Technology, said the mission would build local expertise as well as advance scientific understanding. “Having a product does not mean you have sovereignty. Having sovereignty means you know the tech. You’re able to evolve it. You’re able to change it. You’re able to use that knowledge in other missions and other programmes that you want to develop,” said Mr Al Bannai, who is also Secretary General of the Advanced Technology Research Council. The Technology Innovation Institute's Propulsion and Space Research Centre led the design, construction and testing of the probe in the UAE. This included the integration of core hardware, on-board processing, software and systems needed for the probe to operate as a single-mission platform. The MBR Explorer is set to launch during a three-week window in March 2028 on an eight-year, five-billion-kilometre journey, reaching the 269 Justitia asteroid in 2036. It will use gravity assists around Venus, Earth and Mars to reach the main asteroid belt, conducting fly-bys of six asteroids before its final encounter with Justitia. The spacecraft will then deploy the TII-built probe, the mission’s only deployable payload. Dr Ahmad Al Falasi, Minister of Sports and chairman of the UAE Space Agency, said deep-space missions should be judged not only by what they discover, but also by what they leave behind. “In order to sell deep-space missions, I always say it’s what’s left behind: the technology developed, the people developed, and also the interest in space overall,” he said. TII executive director Anton Ivanov said the flight model had completed vibration testing and was undergoing thermal cycles inside a vacuum chamber at a university in Al Ain. Comprehensive performance tests and a flight-readiness review remain before shipment to Colorado later this month. Vibration testing uses a shaker table to simulate some of the forces a spacecraft experiences during launch. Thermal testing in a vacuum chamber checks how its components respond to extreme temperatures in space-like conditions. The programme will then move towards final integration with the MBR Explorer. Mohsen Al Awadhi, the mission's director, said the team was not preparing a backup plan for the March 2028 window being missed because the planned trajectory would no longer work. “We always calculate the schedule from launch, and launch cannot be moved,” Dr Ivanov said. “If, God forbid, we miss that, we basically don’t have a mission,” Mr Al Awadhi said. The probe is designed to separate from the MBR Explorer at Justitia and operate independently during the final encounter. It will descend on a ballistic trajectory and has no propulsion system to slow it down. The descent is expected to take two to three hours, with the probe striking the asteroid at between 15 and 27 metres per second. Two cameras will take images during the descent. An on-board system will rank them so the most useful can be relayed through the mission architecture. The probe has been kept relatively simple by design, while the MBR Explorer carries more sophisticated instruments to study the asteroid’s composition. The probe is also designed to operate autonomously, making key operational decisions on-board rather than waiting for immediate instructions from Earth. Its on-board processing supports functions, including imaging decisions, image selection and power management. Artificial intelligence could help with tasks such as assessing and selecting images, but the team would not use it for operations that required precise, predictable outcomes, Dr Ivanov said. The probe is not expected to survive the impact, although its battery and communications system are designed to continue working for 20–50 minutes if it does. The impact could excavate a small crater, giving scientists an opportunity to observe material beneath the asteroid’s exposed surface. “We always knew that the impact velocity will be quite high, around 60km per hour,” Dr Ivanov said. “We don’t know what we’re going to find. That’s the exploration issue. We’re very excited.” Justitia is scientifically unusual, with a spectrum that more closely resembles objects in the distant Kuiper Belt than neighbouring asteroids in the main belt. Scientists believe it may have formed farther out in the Solar System before migrating inward. Studying its composition could offer clues to how water, volatile materials and organic compounds were distributed as the planets formed. The mission’s wider science goals include improving understanding of the origins and evolution of water-rich asteroids. The probe project involved about 40 people over 18 months, TII chief executive Najwa Aaraj said. Twenty UAE engineers are also gaining mission-level experience through the eight-year interplanetary programme, according to TII. UAE-based partners include HEX20, Khalifa University and the National Space Science and Technology Centre at UAE University, alongside the UAE Space Agency and wider mission collaborators. The MBR Explorer is being developed with partners in Colorado. Dr Aaraj said about 80 per cent of the work on the probe was being done by UAE engineers. “If 80 per cent is being done by our engineers today, the next mission will be fully developed here,” she said. The mission brings together the Space Agency, TII, universities, the Mohammed bin Rashid Space Centre and other partners. “We don’t have one team. We have a team called the National Team,” Mr Al Awadhi said.

title: UAE sign off Asian Games campaign with second equestrian medal
description: Abdullah Humaid Al Muhairi finishes second in individual equestrian final to take national team's overall total to 13 medals
content: The UAE secured another equestrian medal at the 2026 Asian Games on Sunday, as Abdullah Humaid Al Muhairi and Hudson de Vains claimed individual silver following a dramatic three-way jump-off at JRA Equestrian Park in Tokyo. It follows the silver won by Emirates riders in the team final on Thursday and takes the UAE's overall medal tally from the Asian Games, which ends Sunday, to 13 – seven gold, five silver and one bronze. Humaid Abdulla Khalifa Al Muhairi, onboard Mentos, narrowly missed out on a medal, finishing fourth in Competition A, while Omar Abdul Aziz Al Marzooqi and Enjoy de la Mure finished sixth and Sheikha Latifah Bint Ahmed Al Maktoum and Cornet XL seventh in the newly introduced 1.55m Competition B. "I'm happy to finish second, but of course I could have been first. That's the sport. It's always up and down, and you never know whether you're going to win, be placed or be out of the competition. But I'm happy with a medal," Abdullah said. "I'm so proud of Hudson. He's just nine years old and still lacks some experience, but our competitions and training over the summer have really paid off. He's stepping up and showing the quality, scope and temperament for the job. I'm sure we will go far together." The battle for the medals produced a dramatic conclusion, with Qatar's Faleh Alajmi first to tackle the jump-off. A fence down in 40.88 seconds left the door open for Abdullah, who entered the arena intending to deliver a clear round and put himself in contention for gold. However, the excitement of the occasion prompted the Emirati rider to increase the pace, resulting in a fault at a challenging oxer. He crossed the finish line in 41.93 seconds. Saudi Arabia's Khaled Almobty, the final rider to jump, lowered the final fence, confirming Qatar's place atop the podium with Saudi Arabia taking third. Reflecting on his strategy for the final round, Abdullah said: "After I saw the Qatari rider have a fence down, my plan was to go clear. But you never know. When you're in the ring, you want to go faster. "I'm normally a fast rider, and perhaps it wasn't very smart of me. But if I'd gone slower and still had a fence down, I would have finished with bronze. It's always complicated. If it's your day, it's your day." In the higher-level Competition B, Emirates Jumping's Al Marzooqi and Sheikha Latifah returned to the arena for Sunday's decisive second round, contested over a demanding 1.55m course featuring 15 jumping efforts. Al Marzooqi, seventh in the starting order and carrying four faults from Saturday, produced an excellent clear round aboard Enjoy de la Mure, comfortably inside the time allowed, to finish sixth overall. Sheikha Latifah, part of the Emirates' silver-medal-winning team on Thursday, entered Sunday's Individual final on zero faults following an impressive clear round with Cornet XL on Saturday. Despite another committed performance, two fences down in the decisive round left the combination seventh overall. "I'm very disappointed with my round.
