I'm not disappointed with my riding, just disappointed with the result," she said. "The way he jumped every other fence, I don't think the result does justice to his performance. He jumped two fences badly and we had them down. Luck wasn't on our side, but I'm still very proud of him."

title: Sudan's Al Burhan using war to stay in power, says ex-ruling council member
description: Fighting between army and Rapid Support Forces has devastated country and battered its economy
content: The head of the Sudanese Armed Forces, Gen Abdel Fattah Al Burhan , is clinging to the war because continued fighting allows him to remain at the head of the military and the de facto authorities, said a former civilian member of the country's ruling Sovereignty Council. “For him, the war is a matter of life or death,” Mohamed Al Faky told Sky News Arabia in an interview. “He is clinging to the fighting because it is what allows him to remain at the head of the military institution and to lead the de facto authority. Gen Al Burhan had claimed to represent the Sudanese state but lacked legitimacy beyond what he described as the “legitimacy of fighting.” He would not accept an end to the conflict without political arrangements that could preserve his position in power, Mr Al Faky added. “The war is their means of remaining in power,” he said, referring to the Muslim Brotherhood, which he accused of fuelling the conflict to return to power. Mr Al Faky also accused Gen Al Burhan of seeking to maintain his position through military force, control over Sudanese territory and resources, and the continuation of the war. “Through the rhetoric of war, he says that nothing can rise above the voice of the gun,” Mr Al Faky said. Fighting between the SAF and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces has devastated the country of 50 million people and battered its economy. International efforts aimed at ending the war have struggled to secure a lasting ceasefire. The war, now well into its fourth year, has created one of ​the world's worst humanitarian crises, displacing about 14 million people. As well as the vast Darfur region, the RSF controls parts of the Kordofan and Blue Nile regions, while the SAF controls the capital, Khartoum, as well as northern, central and eastern Sudan. Each side has its own government , with the army-aligned administration based in Port Sudan on the Red Sea and the RSF's in Nyala in Darfur. Nidal Shoukeir, an expert and senior government consultant, said Europe’s position on Sudan was clear and it wanted a civilian government. “Europe is not at all satisfied with what the army did in overthrowing the civilian government,” Mr Shoukeir told Sky News Arabia. Sudan’s future should be in the hands of its people and under a civilian government rather than military rule, he added. He said the army’s alleged links to Islamist groups were also a concern for European governments. “Europe certainly will not accept that things continue as they are today,” Mr Shoukeir said, noting that developments in Sudan also have a significant impact on Europe, particularly on migration. Mr Shoukeir said Europe was working with the US to increase pressure on the parties to the conflict and that tougher sanctions could follow. “I believe today it is no longer enough for Europe or the United States to deal with this matter only peacefully,” he said. “There must be intervention and pressure, even through force, on the two sides of the conflict in order to move towards stability, end this crisis and have civilians take power in Sudan.” On allegations that the army used chlorine in attacks, Mr Shoukeir called for an urgent and comprehensive international investigation. “The more time passes, the more this evidence, particularly regarding the use of chlorine, fades and disappears,” he said. Mr Shoukeir urged the army to allow international experts to enter the country to investigate the allegations, saying the issue was serious and could amount to war crimes. He said the army’s refusal to co-operate with investigators could reinforce suspicions surrounding the allegations. “If the army is confident that it did not do this, why does it not co-operate? Why does it not open the doors to international institutions so that it can refute this matter in a practical and scientific way?” Mr Shoukeir said. He added that continued rejection through official statements would only deepen suspicion, as new evidence and reports were emerging about the allegations.

title: Iran says Strait of Hormuz will not reopen until seven conditions are met
description: Backchannel diplomacy remains active even as public negotiations have stalled
content: Iran has said that the Strait of Hormuz will not reopen until seven conditions are met, as indirect talks with the US stall and officials in Tehran prepare for the possibility of another round of fighting. Tehran's lead negotiator, Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, said the US had sent proposals through intermediaries that contradicted its leaders' public statements. However, he added, Iran’s position was “completely clear and definitive”. “Until our seven conditions based on the Islamabad memorandum of understanding are realised, the Strait of Hormuz will not be opened,” Mr Ghalibaf said, referring to a framework agreement signed by the US and Iran in June. Tehran has repeatedly demanded an end to the fighting, the lifting of a US naval blockade, the release of frozen assets and relief from sanctions. Mr Ghalibaf said Iran would pursue diplomacy while remaining prepared for war. “We will neither become emotional nor intimidated; we will both fight and negotiate. The person who is victorious at the negotiating table is the one who has prepared himself for war.” A source in Tehran told The National on Saturday that Iran was preparing for a “major round of fighting” as diplomatic efforts faltered and Washington considered its next steps. “The military option has not been abandoned” by the US, the source said. “But the Iranians are also preparing for a major round of fighting and have the capabilities to do so. “The door to diplomacy remains open and has not been closed. But assessments in Iran are that the war is resuming.” Last month, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi held Qatari-mediated talks with US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner during the UN General Assembly in New York. However, no breakthrough was achieved. During the assembly, Mr Araghchi submitted a proposal to the US, in which Tehran would reopen the Strait of Hormuz and negotiations would resume “if the necessary conditions are met”. Iran has also offered nuclear concessions as part of its efforts to break the deadlock, with sources saying the country had proposed diluting its stockpile of uranium enriched to 60 per cent before handing it over to a third party under procedures recognised by the International Atomic Energy Agency. Meanwhile, the UAE has reaffirmed its commitment to a peaceful resolution of its dispute over the Iranian-occupied islands of Greater Tunb, Lesser Tunb and Abu Musa. “The UAE’s approach is clear and consistent: resolving the dispute peacefully through direct bilateral negotiations or by recourse to the International Court of Justice,” said Dr Anwar Gargash, diplomatic adviser to President Sheikh Mohamed. He added that the UAE would continue to pursue its “legitimate rights” responsibly until a peaceful resolution was reached in accordance with international law. The US-Iran war has reshaped the regional security landscape and left both sides preparing for the possibility of renewed fighting even as diplomatic channels remain open. Brig Gen Esmail Qaani, commander of Iran’s Quds Force, has described Wednesday's US withdrawal from Iraq as a victory and said Tehran-backed groups would continue to play a role there, amid uncertainty over Baghdad’s plans to take weapons under state control. The deadline for the militias to disarm has been pushed back to June next year, while powerful faction Kataib Hezbollah has denied reaching an understanding with the Iraqi government on the fate of its weapons.

title: Jordan confirms arrest of suspected hacker after FBI data theft claim
description: Saif ‌Al Din Khader, alleged member of ShinyHunters group, was detained in kingdom last week
content: Jordan has confirmed the arrest of a suspected member of the ShinyHunters hacking group, which ​claims to have stolen data on every employee of the US Federal Bureau of Investigation. Jordanian state media on Saturday quoted an official as saying that “investigations are ongoing with the suspect about the activities of the group and the groups it is connected with”. The arrest took place last week, the official added. Although the suspect's identity has not divulged by authorities in the kingdom, Reuters quoted sources as saying the arrested man was Saif ‌Al Din Khader, who allegedly uses the hacker ⁠nickname “Rey”. He is said to be co-operating with the FBI and helping US and global law enforcement agencies find other members of the group. One source said Mr Khader had shared his electronic devices and digital correspondence with investigators to help the FBI in its search. “His co-operation is critical to ongoing efforts to arrest these hackers,” the source told Reuters. ShinyHunters is a cyber extortion group that for years has carried out hacking attacks on major corporations worldwide. It is believed by analysts ​to comprise mainly young, English-speaking hackers. Mr Khader’s identity, and his alleged connection ​to ShinyHunters, have long been ⁠known to security researchers. Last year, independent journalist Brian Krebs claimed that Mr Khader was a prominent member of Scattered Lapsus$ Hunters, a network of hackers that included ShinyHunters. Mr Krebs, who said he had spoken to Mr Khader using the messenger app Signal, quoted the suspect as saying he had abandoned hacking and was co-operating with law enforcement. But ShinyHunters continued to carry out cyber attacks into this year, claiming credit for breaches at video game ⁠developer Rockstar Games and education platform Canvas. In September, the group claimed to have stolen large amounts of data on every single FBI employee. A Reuters analysis of a sample of the data found extensive personally identifiable information on FBI employees, including sensitive job role, psychiatric and medical information. FBI director Kash Patel had been hinting at more arrests after the announcement that another alleged ShinyHunters member, Pepijn van der Stap, had been detained in the Netherlands. “FBI teams are working new leads right now,” Mr Patel said last week. “More arrests are on the table.” The FBI has refused to comment on any specific arrest or activity in Jordan, but said that it “continues to aggressively investigate ​the recent cyber incident allegedly involving ShinyHunters”. “We will spare no resource in bringing each of the responsible individuals to justice,” the bureau added. There have been hints in recent days that ShinyHunters was experiencing disruption after its announcement of the FBI break-in. On Wednesday last week, ⁠the group’s site on the dark web went offline. A request for comment sent to a ShinyHunters-linked email address on Friday received no response.

title: Six Palestinians killed in Israeli strikes across Gaza Strip
description: Christian mother and daughter among dead in attack on tower block in Gaza city
content: At least six Palestinians were killed in Israeli air strikes on Gaza at the weekend, medics have said. At least five people, including four women, were killed on Saturday when an apartment building was struck. Two of the dead were Christian women – a mother and daughter. “Today is essentially the worst day of my life. I lost my mother and my grandmother today,” their family member Fouad Al Najjar told Reuters at their funeral at St Porphyrius Church in Gaza city. On Sunday, a Palestinian was killed and 10 were injured in an attack on a vehicle in Deir Al Balah, in central Gaza. Israel’s military has yet to comment on the strike. The number of Palestinians killed since the October ceasefire last year now stands at 1,446, with more than 5,060 injured. On Sunday, the Israeli military in a statement said it had killed a Hamas official in a strike on an apartment overnight. It was not clear if it was referring to the previous day's attack on the Gaza city tower block. Israel's Defence Minister Israel Katz has ordered the closure of all crossings into Gaza and the occupied West Bank on the anniversary of the Hamas-led attacks of October 7, 2023.

title: AI 'less safe' for keeping secrets than most people assume
description: Limit information and access you give AI agents, say experts
content: Since generative artificial intelligence became mainstream, users have been increasingly entrusting more information to a chatbot. But events in recent months have proved that it can go rogue and meddle with other systems. It does not help that the organisations involved – OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and Meta Platforms – are the biggest in the field and are supposed to have secure environments. The issues surrounding AI are not new, but the growing risks leading to more concern among analysts and experts. For years, data security meant keeping the wrong people out of a database, but AI presents a new threat. Arguably the foremost issue – “a reason that is quite new” – is the fact that AI systems that previously only held data can now act on it, says Edgars Nemse, chief executive of the GenLayer Foundation. The foundation describes itself as the builder of the “Court of the Internet” where AI agents resolve disputes without human intermediaries. Consumers are increasingly connecting AI agents to their email, calendars and bank accounts. “An agent that can read your inbox can also be manipulated by a malicious email,” Mr Nemse tells The National . “A hidden instruction on a web page can redirect it. An attacker who gets the right text in front of your agent may get as far as one who has your password. Most people haven't started thinking about that yet.” Interacting with and entrusting AI “is less safe than most people assume”, he emphasises. Morey Haber, chief security adviser at US cybersecurity company BeyondTrust, notes that users are moving from AI systems that simply process information to AI agents that can access emails, files, applications, financial information, medical data and potentially anything else regarding personal identities – fundamentally changing the cybersecurity equation. “A data breach used to mean someone stole just your information. In an agentic AI world, compromising the right identity could mean someone can use your information, privileges and AI agents to act as you, with all of the stolen information as a backdrop,” he tells The National . Therefore, “the biggest risk with AI is not that it knows too much – but that we are giving it too much, trusting it too quickly and increasingly allowing it to act on our behalf with knowledge that lacks sensitivity awareness”. Last week, OpenAI admitted governments could be among “dozens” of entities around the world that may be infiltrated by its AI models. It disclosed that US entities such as the Securities and Exchange Commission were breached, following a similar incident involving the Australian government . “The Australian case is a useful illustration precisely because it wasn't a criminal attack,” says Mohammed Aboul-Magd, general manager for cybersecurity at US AI and quantum tech firm SandboxAQ . “An agent doing research went around the blocks meant to stop it, reached data it had no authority to access and months passed before anyone noticed,” Mr Aboul-Magd tells The National . “The damage was limited, but the pattern is the real threat for consumers: agents with broad access moving quickly, with nobody checking what they did until well after the fact.” In August, Facebook parent company Meta admitted one of its models had hacked into three companies, while last week Google said its Gemini AI bot had escaped from a sandbox environment and infiltrated three companies. OpenAI also said its own research agents had posted 53 images from ChatGPT users to image-hosting sites. In the US – home of the major AI companies embroiled in recent breaches – the share of Americans who trust businesses to use AI slipped from 31 per cent to 27 per cent in 2026, while the share of those who think AI does more harm than good jumped to 39 per cent, a Gallup and Bentley University survey found. However, those figures were published in July, before the disclosures about government websites and user images. “So, I'd expect the next numbers to be worse [now],” says Mr Nemse. He does, however, acknowledge there are “decent measures” being taken to restore trust. “Restoring [trust] will take something more concrete than promises: independent testing … fast, honest disclosure when something goes wrong, and accountability that reaches the people actually affected,” he adds. An important paradox is emerging: AI adoption is growing faster than AI trust and operational governance. People are using the technology because it is useful, not necessarily because they completely trust how their information is being processed. “Restoring that trust requires much more than another privacy policy or checkbox from a governance team,” Mr Haber says. “Users need transparency around what information is being collected, how long it is being retained, whether it trains future models, who can access it from inside and outside the organisation, and what happens when something goes afoul.” Considering the AI breaches of government organisations, which have strong cybersecurity protection, what about regular consumers who don't have access to expensive security guardrails? “Consumers do not need the cybersecurity budget of a government agency or Fortune 500 company to dramatically reduce their AI exposure,” Mr Haber says. Analysts recommend setting unique passwords, using a trusted password manager, activating multifactor authentication and keeping applications up to date – those are the first lines of defence against any potential hack. They also urge users to avoid opening malicious emails or messages that can contain phishing attempts or ransomware threats. The “most useful habit” is to treat an AI assistant the way you would treat anyone else, Mr Aboul-Magd says. “Ask what it actually needs to do the job and give it that and nothing more, because the permissions you grant are a far bigger exposure than the conversations you have with it,” he adds. Still, the bulk of the responsibility lies with AI companies, since they have the resources and the ability. “Honestly, most of the fix has to come from the companies, because ordinary users can't audit a lab's research environment,” Mr Nemse says. But “people can still shrink how much of their life is exposed”, he adds. “I'd assume anything you upload to an AI service could one day end up somewhere you didn't intend."

title: Angelina Jolie shares images of Gaza destruction and calls for urgent aid
description: Oscar-winning actress says the satellite imagery shows only part of the story, as nearly two million Palestinians face another winter in need of shelter
content: Angelina Jolie has shared satellite images showing the scale of destruction in Gaza, calling for urgent humanitarian aid and shelter as winter approaches. The Oscar-winning actress and former UN goodwill ambassador posted a series of before-and-after images on Instagram on Saturday showing neighbourhoods across the enclave devastated by nearly three years of war. “You can now open Google Earth and see what was done to Gaza ,” Jolie wrote. “Whole neighbourhoods have been reduced to rubble. Homes, schools, universities, hospitals, roads, water and sanitation systems, infrastructure that people depended on to survive have been damaged or destroyed.” The updated imagery appeared on online last week, with many on social media expressing shock at the extent of the devastation. Google has not said when the images were published or made available. It shows entire neighbourhoods reduced to rubble and bare ground, with roads, mosques, schools and other landmarks surrounded by widespread destruction. A UN Satellite Centre assessment cited by Jolie found that 82 per cent of structures in Gaza had been damaged as of June 16, with about two thirds of those assessed as destroyed. Jolie, 51, also highlighted the humanitarian situation facing Palestinians as winter approaches, saying 1.98 million people, or 94 per cent of Gaza's population, require shelter assistance and essential items. “As winter approaches, 1.98 million people, or 94 per cent of Gaza’s population, need shelter assistance and essential items,” she wrote, adding that aid and shelter materials continued to face restrictions and delays. “The Google Earth images show the physical destruction with extraordinary clarity. What they cannot show is what it means to live among it, what happened to the families who were killed, and what life is like for those who survived.” She called for humanitarian aid to reach civilians “at the scale required”, for hospitals to receive medical supplies and for conditions to be created that would allow Palestinians to rebuild their homes, schools, hospitals and communities. “People need shelter before winter,” she wrote. “Humanitarian aid needs to reach civilians at the scale required. Hospitals need medical supplies.” The latest post is not the first time Jolie has used her public profile to draw attention to the plight of Palestinians in Gaza. In January, she travelled to Egypt and visited the Egyptian side of the Rafah border crossing as part of a humanitarian trip focused on aid destined for Gaza. During the visit, she met Egyptian Red Crescent workers and other humanitarian groups and toured warehouses containing aid, including medical supplies. Jolie said at the time that humanitarian access needed to be “sustained, safe and urgently scaled up” to allow aid, fuel and medical supplies into Gaza. She has also been linked to plans to support children orphaned during the conflict. In October, The National reported that Palestinian activist Samer Sinijlawi said Jolie intended to establish a large SOS village for orphans in Gaza as part of wider efforts to rebuild the enclave. “I’ve been aware of the intention of Angelina Jolie to do a huge SOS village for orphans in Gaza,” Sinijlawi said during an online panel convened by Germany's Candid Foundation. He said prominent individuals could help launch initiatives alongside government-led reconstruction efforts rather than waiting solely for states to act. Jolie's agent was contacted for comment on the reported plans at the time. Jolie has been an outspoken voice on the conflict since its early weeks. In October 2023, she condemned the Hamas-led attacks in Israel while saying they could not justify the loss of civilian life in Gaza. “What happened in Israel is an act of terror, but that cannot justify the innocent lives lost in bombing a civilian population in Gaza that has nowhere to go, no access to food or water, no possibility of evacuation and not even the basic human right to cross a border to seek refuge,” she wrote. In another post days later, she described Gaza as an “open-air prison” that was “fast becoming a mass grave” and criticised world leaders for failing to demand a humanitarian ceasefire. Jolie's advocacy follows more than two decades of humanitarian work focused particularly on refugees and people displaced by conflict. She worked with the UN refugee agency for more than 20 years, first as a goodwill ambassador and later as a special envoy, before stepping down from the role in 2022 to pursue humanitarian and human rights work more broadly. Her latest intervention comes as satellite imagery has once again brought the physical transformation of Gaza into focus. “The destruction is visible. The needs are known,” Jolie wrote. “What matters now is whether they are met.”

title: Iraq transports its oil through Strait of Hormuz as US-Iran war chokes exports
description: State tanker company moves 2 million barrels beyond waterway for first time in decades
content: Iraq 's state oil company has moved its own crude beyond the Strait of Hormuz for the first time in decades as the US-Iran war threatens the country's primary export route. The Iraqi Oil Tankers Company shipped two million barrels of crude through the waterway on a very large crude carrier, director general Ali Qais was quoted as saying by state media. The move was aimed to shift part of Iraq's oil exports from the existing free-on-board Basra port model to transit the strait and take advantage of better sale and pricing opportunities, he added. The company is now in talks to buy specialised crude tankers “as soon as possible and to compete with regional peers”, Mr Qais said. Since the Iran war broke out in February, Iraq has been facing one of its most serious economic and security situations. Opec's second-largest producer depends on oil for at least 90 per cent of its revenue. Most of its exports – about 3.3 million barrels a day before the war – crossed the Strait of Hormuz after leaving its southern Basra terminals. The strait has been effectively closed by Iran since the conflict broke out, with shipping disrupted by missile and drone attacks, insurance surges and naval confrontations. Total Hormuz flows in September stood at 6.02 million bod, less than a third of February's 20.64 million bpd, according to Kpler, highlighting the continued disruption to the region's main oil export artery. Iraq has been caught in the middle of the war, with pro-Tehran armed groups having launched drones towards Gulf states from Iraqi territory, prompting countries in the region to hold Baghdad responsible. Meanwhile, ships crossing Iraqi waters near the strait have been at increased risk, forcing Baghdad to offer discounted rates on services at Basra Port and causing buyers to demand delivery outside the waterway. The government has been struggling to revive alternative routes – including a proposal to reopen the Iraq-Turkey pipeline through Ceyhan and another to move crude to Syria by land – but these solutions would only cover a fraction of Iraqi exports. Iraq has been able to move three million barrels of oil a day since the beginning of September, Oil Minister Bassim Khudair said last month. Opec’s second-largest producer is now looking to further boost its production as it expects alternative pipelines and the country’s improved export infrastructure comes on stream, he told the Iraqi News Agency. “The government plans to increase export capacity to five million barrels a day after the completion of the strategic pipelines extending to Fishkhabour and Baniyas, in addition to the export terminals in the Strait of Hormuz,” he said. The latest shipment indicates that Iraq has adopted the strategy of moving oil past the Strait of Hormuz to guarantee delivery and secure better prices, rather than leaving buyers to shoulder the war risk premium. The tanker company, once a major fleet operator in the 1980s, has been trying to rebuild itself after successive wars and rounds of sanctions. Buying its own VLCCs would provide Baghdad with more control over its main source of income.

title: ‘Completely untrue’: Ireland press conference halted after Israel racism allegations
description: Heimir Hallgrimsson walked out of his pre-match press conference after being harangued by Israeli journalists ahead of Nations League match
content: Republic of Ireland manager Heimir Hallgrimsson walked out of his pre-match press conference after an Israeli journalist accused his players of making racist remarks during last week's 3-0 Nations League victory . The extraordinary exchange erupted on the eve of the teams' rematch, which will be played in Serbia, with Football Association of Ireland officials forced to intervene as the reporter repeatedly sought answers over allegations that have not been independently established. “That is completely untrue. That is completely untrue,” an Irish press officer said as attempts were made to take the microphone away from the journalist. The reporter refused to give it up and insisted the allegations were true, prompting Hallgrimsson to leave the room and later speak separately to Irish media. The confrontation came during an already tense international window, with the fixtures against Israel having become the focus of intense political debate and protests in Ireland. Earlier in the press conference, Hallgrimsson had been asked about an incident in which a co-pilot attacked a pilot on a flight travelling from Dubai to Tel Aviv before passengers overpowered the attacker and helped take control of the plane. The co-pilot on the flydubai flight forced to divert to Saudi Arabia "attempted to carry out a terrorist act", the UAE's attorney general said on Saturday. The questions then turned to the alleged racism involving his players. Hallgrimsson had already made clear that he did not want to get involved in the dispute, saying the relevant authorities would deal with any allegations. “It is a game with a lot of emotions attached,” he said. “I haven't read anything and it's not something I want to get involved with. It goes to a process, both in our department and with Uefa. “Something was reported by both teams, so I just hope we can focus on football and football will be the winner after this. “I have not gone into details looking at this as I have enough to think about.” The Israel Football Association has not lodged a complaint with Uefa but said it would consider doing so after Sunday's match. The controversy adds another layer to an international window that has already proved unusually difficult for Ireland. Harry Kane and Bukayo ​Saka ​scored ​twice apiece as ⁠England dismantled Croatia ⁠7-0 in Rijeka on ​Saturday, with Jude Bellingham scoring ⁠one goal and creating three more in a rampant Nations League display. Anthony ⁠Gordon and substitute Morgan Rogers ​also ⁠struck ‌as England overwhelmed a ragged ​Croatian defence in their third League A, Group Three match at the Rujevica stadium. Saka heaped praise on teammate Bellingham, saying: "He was amazing tonight." "He deserved player of the year and he deserved man of the match tonight too. He was special. "[I'm] happy to play with him and happy to have him in the England team." Kane marked his 124th international appearance with his 88th and 89th England goals, moving within one cap of Peter Shilton's national record. The captain will draw level if he plays ​against the Czech ‌Republic on ⁠Tuesday and could ​claim the record outright ​when ‌England host Croatia at Wembley on ⁠November 12. England are in second place in the group, three points behind leaders Spain, who beat the Czech Republic 3-1 in Oviedo.

title: ‘We will be better in the final’: Dalic confident UAE can improve for Gulf Cup showdown against Saudi Arabia
description: Ousmane Camara's goal seals 1-0 win over Oman as Saudis overcome Qatar on penalties
content: A lone strike by Ousmane Camara was enough to send the UAE through to the Arabian Gulf Cup final as they beat Oman 1-0 in the semi-final. The national team will face Saudi Arabia in front of a likely capacity crowd of 60,000 in Jeddah on Tuesday night. They were comfortably the better side in their semi-final against Oman, but they made hard work of securing victory, with Nicolas Gimenez seeing a second-half penalty saved. “We did not play our best match and missed some chances, particularly the penalty, but the most important thing for us is qualifying for the final,” said UAE coach Zlatko Dalic. “The match did not go as I expected, but my team and my players secured the win, and that is what matters most. I believe we can perform better, improve our style of play and create more chances. Our performance in the final will be better.” The two teams should have been familiar with each other. Towards the end of last year, the UAE had beaten Oman to take themselves to the brink of World Cup qualification, at a tempestuous play-off in Doha. In the 11 months since then, though, much has changed. Carlos Queiroz, the former Real Madrid boss who was in charge of Oman back then, has since left and coached Ghana at the World Cup. And the UAE side have an altogether new identity. Their new coach, Dalic, was at the World Cup, too, with Croatia. Only five players remained in the UAE line-up for that game against Oman in Qatar – after which neither side ultimately qualified for the World Cup. Among the raft of new additions to the side for this fixture in Jeddah, Guilherme Bala was making his first start for the national team. The Shabab Al Ahli winger had impressed in his two cameo appearances as a substitute so far in the Arab Cup. With a place in the final on the line, Dalic unleashed him from the start. It was two of the other new recruits who combined to give the UAE the lead midway through the first half. Mamadou Coulibaly, the Al Jazira midfielder, curled in a cross from the left, which Camara rose to head into the net. Oman nearly levelled straight away, but Lucas Pimenta blocked Amjad Al Harthi’s shot on the line. Other than that scare, the UAE looked comfortable against opponents who were 15 places below them in the Fifa rankings. But the national team fell short of the standards they set at the start of the group stage. They were rampant in the wins against Yemen and Bahrain that had sealed their place in the semi-finals with a game to spare. Now, though, they were imprecise. They should have put the game beyond Oman at the start of the second half, but Bala’s shot hit the side netting. He had been at full stretch to reach a cross from Marcos Meloni. Between Meloni and Gimenez in the build-up, the chance should have been far easier. Oman were showing signs of falling apart, and moments later the UAE had a penalty when Luan Pereira was felled after being sent through by Bala. Again, the UAE were profligate. Gimenez’s penalty was saved by Ibrahim Al Mukhaini, the Oman keeper. While the game stayed at 1-0, there was always a risk Oman could strike back. But the national team muddled through to give themselves a shot at winning a third Gulf Cup when they face Saudi Arabia on Tuesday night. The tournament hosts booked their place in the final after defeating Qatar 3-2 on penalties following a goalless draw after extra time. Neither side was able to find a breakthrough across 120 minutes, sending the contest to a penalty shootout. Saudi Arabia held their nerve, with Abdullah Al Hamdan, Mohamed Kanno and Mukhtar Ali converting their penalties. Hassan Tambakti and Firas Al Buraikan missed, but it was still enough to secure a 3-2 victory.

title: What is Saturn opposition and how can you see it in the UAE?
description: The ringed planet will be at its brightest on October 4, with a special telescope viewing event taking place in Sharjah
content: Saturn will be at its brightest on Sunday night as the ringed planet reaches opposition, giving stargazers in the UAE one of the best opportunities of the year to see it. The astronomical event takes place on October 4, when Earth passes between the Sun and Saturn . This places Saturn almost directly opposite the Sun in our sky, meaning it rises at about sunset and remains visible throughout the night. While Saturn can be spotted with the naked eye, a telescope will reveal the feature for which the planet is best known: its distinctive rings. In the UAE, Mleiha National Park in Sharjah is also marking the event with a five-hour astronomy programme featuring telescope observations and guided stargazing. An opposition occurs when Earth passes between the Sun and a planet farther out in the solar system. From our perspective, this places the planet on the opposite side of the sky from the Sun. In Saturn's case, it means the planet rises around sunset, remains visible through the night and sets around sunrise. Saturn reaches opposition at about 4pm UAE time on Sunday, although it will not rise above the horizon until later in the evening. The alignment also brings Earth relatively close to Saturn in their respective orbits, helping the planet appear brighter in the night sky. Opposition occurs roughly once a year for Saturn. The planet takes almost 30 Earth years to complete one orbit around the Sun, while Earth repeatedly catches up with and passes between it and the Sun. Saturn is bright enough to be seen without a telescope and will be visible for most of the night. In Dubai, the planet is expected to rise at about 6.40pm and remain visible until shortly before 7am on Monday. In Abu Dhabi , it will similarly be visible for most of the night. To the naked eye, however, Saturn will look more like a bright point of light than the familiar ringed planet seen in photographs. A telescope is needed to properly distinguish its rings and can also reveal some of its moons, depending on the equipment and viewing conditions. For the best chance of seeing Saturn, look from somewhere with an unobstructed view of the sky and, if possible, away from strong city lights. The planet will be visible from urban areas, but darker surroundings will make stargazing easier. Saturn can be seen from across the UAE, weather and visibility permitting. Mleiha National Park in Sharjah is holding a special Saturn Opposition event at the Mleiha Eye campsite on Sunday. Running from 6pm to 11pm, the programme begins with a Cosmic Walkthrough featuring astronomy activities, followed by a presentation explaining Saturn opposition at 9pm. Telescope observations and guided stargazing are scheduled from 9.30pm until 11pm, giving visitors the chance to see Saturn's rings and moons under Mleiha's darker desert skies. Tickets are priced at Dh200 for adults and Dh150 for children, with dinner available as an optional extra. Those without tickets can still look for Saturn from elsewhere in the country throughout the night. The planet will remain conspicuously bright around opposition, making the days immediately around October 4 another good opportunity to spot it.

title: Yemen's Al Alimi announces military operations to retake territory from Houthis
description: Head of Presidential Leadership Council says operations aim to extend authority of state
content: The head of Yemen ’s Presidential Leadership Council on Sunday announced the start of military operations to retake territory held by the Iran-backed Houthis. “In the name of God and in the name of the people ... we announce today the commencement of military operations to reclaim the remaining territories of the republic and to extend the authority of the state and its institutions across the entire national territory,” Rashad Al Alimi said. Earlier on Sunday, Yemeni government forces said they launched strikes on Houthi targets in Sanaa and Saada, the rebels' northern stronghold, hours after the militia claimed an attack on an Aramco oil site near Riyadh. The Houthis said on Sunday that they had carried out two military operations, using ballistic missiles and drones to attack Aramco oil facilities in Saudi Arabia, one in Riyadh and another in the Khurais area. There was no confirmation from the Saudi authorities on Sunday's claimed attacks. Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said Saudi Arabia had launched 50 air strikes and missile attacks against Yemen over the past 12 hours, against Sanaa and the provinces of Al Jawf, Taiz, Amran, Hajjah and Saada. Mr Saree vowed that the Houthis would continue to attack Saudi military bases, oil facilities and troop concentrations with missiles and drones until attacks on Yemen stop. Yemeni armed forces spokesman Col Majed Al Nuzaili said government forces had delivered “painful strikes” against “vital targets” belonging to the Houthis in Sanaa and Saada. “The militia’s capabilities will not be safe from the fire of our armed forces, and we will destroy them,” Col Al Nuzaili said in remarks aired on Saudi state television. Flames engulfed part of the Aramco site south of the Saudi capital on Saturday, with thick black smoke billowing over a nearby motorway in images published by international news agencies. Firefighters moved in to tackle the blaze, while ambulances and police vehicles were reportedly seen nearby. The Houthis claimed responsibility, saying they had attacked the site with ballistic missiles and drones in retaliation for Saudi strikes on Houthi-held territory in Yemen. Mr Saree said in an earlier statement that the operation had “successfully achieved its objective” and that the attacks had caused “fires at the targeted sites”. But the Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis dismissed their claim as “misleading”. “What the Houthis are facing in Taiz, and the human losses suffered by the group's members at the hands of the heroes of the Yemeni Armed Forces and the Popular Resistance on all fronts drives them to seek illusory victories,” coalition spokesman Maj Gen Turki Al Malki told Asharq Al Awsat . Saudi authorities did not immediately confirm that the site had been attacked, while Aramco did not comment on the cause of the fire. Saudi Arabia leads a coalition that intervened in Yemen after the Houthi takeover of the capital Sanaa in 2014. The Houthis also said Saudi forces had carried out about 60 air strikes against their territory over the previous 24 hours, including attacks on the rebel-held capital, Sanaa. The latest exchanges come as fighting intensifies around Taiz , where government forces are seeking to prevent the Houthis from tightening their grip on the strategically important city and surrounding supply routes. Col Al Nuzaili said government forces had carried out 97 “precision targeting operations” on fronts in Taiz and Lahij, using aircraft, drones, artillery, missiles and snipers. The operations had “neutralised” 260 militia members and destroyed or damaged military, transport and supply vehicles, he said in his televised remarks early on Sunday morning. The spokesman had earlier said the military had conducted 257 attacks across several fronts, killing at least 700 Houthi fighters. The claims could not be independently verified. The escalation comes as Saudi Arabia considers a broader offensive against the Iran -backed Houthis, with Reuters reporting that Riyadh is weighing operations on several fronts to push back the group and secure the Red Sea shipping route. Taiz is divided into areas controlled by the Houthis and those controlled by the government. Civilians have been forced to flee their homes, often several times. Aid advocates fear that any major population movement would overwhelm humanitarian response efforts. Hunger is also worsening rapidly in the governorate. As well as displacing thousands of families, the renewed fighting has also driven up food prices and cut off access for aid, the World Food Programme said on Friday. Recent WFP monitoring found that 74 per cent of households in accessible areas could not meet their basic food needs, the highest level recorded this year, as the conflict intensifies and economic conditions deteriorate.

title: Syria 'pressing on accelerator' to attract US investors
description: US Chamber of Commerce anticipates long-term engagement with Damascus
content: US investors see an opportunity to invest early in Syria as the transitional government races to establish a pro-business environment and attract foreign capital. “We see that the door is open, and we're coming early,” Steve Lutes, vice president of Middle East Affairs at the US Chamber of Commerce, said in an interview. “I think US companies made it very clear across a different range of sectors that they're looking to be strategically engaged, to be a long-term partner in helping Syria get back up on its feet and excel economically.” Mr Lutes spoke to The National after the Chamber of Commerce hosted a round-table with Syrian President Ahmad Al Shara and Foreign Minister Asaad Al Shibani on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly last month. He also recently led a delegation of more than 50 American businesses and 80 delegates to Damascus. The delegation – which included Baker Hughes , Caterpillar, Visa and dozens of other US firms – marked a significant step in re-establishing Washington's economic relationship with Syria after the 13-year civil war. It also came shortly after the US lifted its state sponsor of terrorism designation on Syria, which had been a prominent roadblock to the country’s reintegration into the international financial system. Syria’s government has moved quickly to attract investment since the fall of Bashar Al Assad's regime in 2024. The World Bank estimates it will cost $216 billion to rebuild the country. Some investment pledges from the Gulf have already moved towards implementation, including DP World's $800 million investment commitment to Tartus Port. At the same time, Syria has also courted foreign investors from Silicon Valley to Riyadh. “They're really pressing on the accelerator to try to move things forward,” Mr Lutes said. He added that the Chamber of Commerce was turning significant attention towards Syria's banking sector , which has undergone a rapid transformation under the current government. Mr Al Shara carried out the country’s first international Visa transaction in August. “It's so foundational to everything else,” Mr Lutes said. QNB and Mastercard issued the first internationally accepted payment card in Syria. The World Bank has also approved a $100 million grant to help establish a digitally enabled financial sector. Last Sunday, Central Bank of Syria Governor Mohammed Raslan told official news agency Sana that the government expected foreign investment in establishing new banks to surpass $1 billion in the coming period. The US Treasury Department on Thursday held a round-table in New York to support the country's financial sector and reconnection to the global financial system. Finance Minister Yisr Barnieh said in a LinkedIn post that discussions had focused on advancing anti-money laundering and counter-terrorism financing standards, among other reforms. Treasury Assistant Secretary for Terrorist Financing and Financial Crimes Jonathan Burke also stressed financial connectivity remains a vital component to combatting illicit finance and supporting Syria's reintegration into the global financial system, according to a readout. Public spending in Syria for first six months of the year totalled roughly $3.7 billion, compared to a public revenue of $2.7 billion, according to the finance ministry's first-half 2026 budget report. That leaves a fiscal deficit of about $1 billion. “The biggest challenge at the end of the day are the budgetary constraints and how are they going to finance and pay for it all,” Mr Lutes said. Damascus said it was implementing new measures to control public spending, including reviewing investment projects. Mr Barnieh wrote in a social media post on Monday that the measures would not affect salaries, wages or spending on essential needs such as health, education, water, energy, security, public safety and necessary operational maintenance. While the state sponsor of terrorism delisting removed the final pillar in the US sanctions architecture, investing in Syria continues to carry reputational risks. It remains on the Financial Action Task Force's grey list, and parties may have previous links to sanctioned actors. Mr Lutes described the Chamber of Commerce’s delegation to Damascus as an “exploratory” one to give US companies the chance to identify sectors for investment and re-establish trust with Syrian officials. Several US companies have already signed memorandums of understanding and other agreements with Syria including ConocoPhillips, Chevron, Baker Hughes, Hunt Energy and Ardent LNG. Gulf partners have joined some of these projects including Qatar's UCC Holding, which signed an agreement with Chevron and Syria's state-run petroleum company to develop the country's first offshore oil and gasfield. Mr Lutes anticipates more US companies could go down similar routes with Emirati, Saudi or Qatari partners who already have relationships with the country. Doing so could mitigate some risks and increase US investor confidence. He added that he hopes the delegation will become an annual occurrence. He also said the chamber is engaging with the Syrian government on addressing policy regulatory issues. “We're not going out of business any time soon. There's a lot of work for the chamber to support US companies that are interested in doing business in Syria, so we're going to be at this … for many years to come,” Mr Lutes said.

title: Race to unlock secrets of Russia’s deadly jet-drone
description: Crash in Moldova reveals how Moscow has transformed Iranian-designed weapon into major threat
content: Western analysts are racing to discover the secrets of a Russian jet-powered drone that crashed in Moldova this week as they seek to combat a weapon that could become a major threat. The wreckage will give intelligence experts a rare opportunity to examine the technology behind Moscow’s increasingly sophisticated kamikaze drones that could tilt the Ukraine war in Russia’s favour. There are also fears, experts have told The National, that the technology could rapidly be transferred to Iran, providing it with a weapon that Ukraine is struggling to shoot down. Robert Tollast, an analyst at the Royal United Services Institute, called the Geran drone “a phenomenal development” and “one of those moments in the Ukraine war, where suddenly a weapon has changed the war”. Initially, Russia was only able to produce about 500 Geran-4s and the more advanced Geran-5 turbojet drones a month in May. But production rates have now accelerated to 3,000 in the last month, according to Ukrainian military intelligence. The debris from Wednesday’s crash is likely to reveal how Russia is making its jet drones travel at 600kph, more than triple the speed of the Shahed-136 models originally supplied by Iran. “They’re moving so fast that we can’t get a proper lock on them,” Ukrainian air defence commander Volodymyr Serdiuk told the media. Investigators will pore over the flight computer and navigation systems to see how they are controlled and the potential to jam them with electronic warfare. Processors, antennas and communications equipment, as well as the engine itself will give clues to new and innovative designs. While the wreckage is probably a Geran-4, it is similar to the latest Geran-5, which carries a heavier payload and represents a further evolution of the original Iranian-designed Shahed. It will be crucial to discover how and why Moscow has been able to so quickly develop a weapon that could have an impact far beyond Ukraine’s battlefields. “The defining challenge posed by Russia’s Geran programme is the speed at which Russia can learn and adapt,” the Centre for Strategic and International Studies, a US think tank, stated in a report last month. It added that modifications were quickly tested in combat, with solutions adopted and “unsuccessful experiments quickly discarded”. The report described a “continuous adaptation cycle” in which front-line experience translates into production changes within weeks rather than years. But that is something the Ukrainians are capable of too, with significant work now going into building jet-powered interceptors. The Gerans were flying higher and faster than propeller-driven drones. Ukraine’s quickest interceptors, capable of a maximum 400kph, are not fast enough. “Right now, we’re in a race for speed,” said a Ukrainian drone developer. One advantage they do have is that the Geran’s relatively short 950km range means it needs to be launched much closer to the border, making it vulnerable to counter-attack. Its 90kg payload – compared with about 400kg for a Russian cruise missile – is probably not enough to penetrate the concrete defences surrounding Ukrainian substations, which will be key to supplying electricity during freezing winter temperatures. Russia and Iran’s older, slower drones had previously given Ukraine a long “engagement window” for tracking before shooting down. Interception rates dropped to about 60 per cent compared to previous models as Ukraine’s defences struggled with the new models' speed, altitude and manoeuvrability. While fighter jets, using either their cannon or more expensive missiles, can be used, the cost ratio means million-dollar weapons are being deployed against drones costing little more than $100,000 each. Therefore, Ukraine needs to find a cost-effective method of interception. That will become relevant to the Gulf as questions are being asked about whether the Russian technology will be transferred back to Iran. Tehran already has the turbojet-powered Shahed-238, which CSIS believes can travel between 300kph and 600kph while carrying a payload of up to 90kg. In a major attack, Iran could combine jet-powered drones with Shahed-136s and ballistic missiles, presenting multiple threats simultaneously. It was only a “matter of time” before Tehran got hold of the technology, said Mr Tollast. “Iran is famously good at reverse engineering various components that it's got its hands on from various conflicts in the region.” He also raised the prospect of the rebel Houthis, who have already demonstrated an ability to build their own rockets and drones, manufacturing jet-powered drones that would present a threat to Saudi Arabia. The key, he said, would be for GCC countries to work alongside the Ukrainians “to accelerate the development of low-cost jet-powered interceptors” and build a highly capable defensive belt.

title: Dubai's Parkonic introduces paid parking at Al Zahra Hospital
description: Patients will need to validate vehicles before leaving hospital
content: A paid parking system has been introduced at Al Zahra Hospital Dubai for visitors and patients and will become fully operational on October 15. Private company Parkonic is managing the new smart system, which requires patients to validate their vehicles before leaving the hospital. Parking rules will vary depending on the type of visit. Outpatients will receive up to four hours of free parking, while patients visiting the emergency department will get up to six hours of free parking. Patients admitted to the hospital can park free of charge for the duration of their stay. Parkonic will charge Dh10 per hour for any additional parking time, while visitors and vehicles without the required validation will be charged Dh50 per hour, according to information published by Al Zahra Hospital. The charges will be automatically deducted from the Salik account linked to the vehicle. From October 15, patients must validate their parking before leaving the hospital. For outpatient appointments, patients will receive a text message with a validation link after checking in. The link will be valid for up to four hours. The introduction of the system at Al Zahra Hospital comes as smart and paid parking management expands across Dubai's healthcare sector. Parkin and Dubai Health introduced paid parking at Rashid Hospital on September 21. At Rashid Hospital, patients continue to receive free parking for the duration of their visit, including those attending emergency care, consultations, laboratory appointments, walk-in services and continuing treatment. Visitors can receive up to three hours of free parking per day after providing the relevant patient details at hospital reception. Two people accompanying patients admitted to the hospital can receive free parking for up to 24 hours, with extensions available where required. People of Determination, senior citizens and pregnant women will continue to receive free valet parking at Dubai Health facilities after eligibility is verified. A 30-minute daily grace period is also available for pickups and drop-offs, while standard parking charges apply to motorists who are not visiting Dubai Health facilities. Authorities said that the smart parking system is intended to reduce congestion, improve the use of available parking spaces and make arrival at healthcare facilities more convenient.

title: Perform Sharjah 2026: Shows to see, from audience-made theatre to giant puppets
description: All performances are free, with works spanning theatre, dance, puppetry and multimedia performance
content: Perform Sharjah returns this autumn with a programme of commissioned works, world premieres and regional debuts at venues across the emirate. The festival, running from October 11 to November 29 and organised by Sharjah Art Foundation , features 16 performances, all free to attend. Among those to look forward to are theatre pieces that put the audience at the centre of the action, works newly commissioned for Bait Al Serkal, hip-hop performances challenging dance traditions and perceptions of the body, multimedia work, large-scale puppetry and pieces drawing on personal and family histories. Here are some of the shows to look out for. Tunisian dancer Mohamed Toukabri's career is built as much on hip-hop and street dance as contemporary styles. His latest solo brings these different styles together in a piece questioning the value of inheritance in dance: what dancers receive from previous generations and what they choose to leave behind. 8.30pm The audience is the protagonist in British playwright Nathan Ellis's work.txt . Once the crowd is seated, they clock in and take on a series of individual and collaborative tasks from which the plot gradually emerges, following a person in an unnamed city who has stopped working. Premiering at London's Yard Theatre in 2019, work.txt has since been presented in nine countries and 11 languages, with Sharjah marking its GCC premiere. 8.30pm Performer and singer Mallika Taneja leads this piece, based on a year of interviews used to reconstruct the story of a singer whose voice was at risk of being forgotten. Surrounded by a harmonium, microphone and objects from her childhood, she pieces together fragments of ambition and disappointment from the singer's life, with music as central to the performance as the spoken word. 8.30pm A six-metre bench runs along the front edge of the stage in Maria Hassabi's Us , with five dancers working within that narrow strip of space. The set-up reflects a choreography built around calculated tableaus, with the dancers shifting between rest and anticipation. 8.30pm Perhaps Here is a suite of commissioned performances at Bait Al Serkal over three evenings. The works have been created with the 19th-century heritage house in mind and the programme comprises short, intimate presentations spanning theatre and performance. Full details are still to be revealed, but the performances are said to deal with memory and grief. 8.30pm Sebastian Mayer brings two life-size animal puppets to Sharjah for a two-part show. For Hannibaby , Mayer built a life-size baby elephant puppet and travelled 70km with it from France into Italy through the Cottian Alps. In Sharjah, the elephant will appear as a roaming performance around Bait Obaid Al Shamsi. Families can also join mask-making workshops, movement games and other puppetry activities linked to the show. For Zarafa , Mayer built a life-size giraffe puppet that in 2023 made a 1,000km journey from Marseille to Paris, following the route taken by the real giraffe sent by Muhammed Ali Pasha of Egypt to France's Charles X in 1827. In Sharjah, Zarafa will also move through the venue as a walkabout performance, while visitors can add their own work to a community canvas at Bait Obaid Al Shamsi. November 13, 4.30pm to 8.30pm; November 15, 4pm to 8pm Sim Chi Yin's Longings, Returns grew from a decade-long effort to recover the history of her paternal grandfather. Rarely discussed at home, he was among more than 30,000 people deported from British-ruled Malaya to China between 1948 and 1960, and was executed shortly after arriving, while his mother, wife and five children remained in Malaya. The multimedia work is as much research as family testimony, with Sim activating the installation through a series of ritual gestures. 8.30pm Dancer and choreographer Sofiane Chalal's XXL uses hip-hop to challenge assumptions about how larger bodies should look and move on stage. Carried by humour, the choreography is at once forceful, light and celebratory, with the performers' spontaneity and individual personalities given room to emerge. 8.30pm

title: UAE scientists harness AI to discover potential blood cancer drug
description: Insilico Medicine discovers substance that could treat disease
content: Researchers in the UAE have used artificial intelligence to discover a class of drugs that could help to treat blood cancer. The discovery is the latest AI-powered find from Insilico Medicine , a clinical-stage biotechnology company with scientists based in Masdar City, Abu Dhabi. Using the cutting-edge technology could potentially shorten development and research timelines. Currently, nine out of 10 potential drugs that reach human testing fail to become approved medicines . However, Ahmad Alghaith, an organic chemist at Insilico Medicine, said AI could improve this. “The hope of AI is that it will increase the success rate, reduce time spent and reduce costs,” he told The National . Insilico Medicine typically takes 12 to 18 months to select a potential drug for further testing before human trials, compared with two and a half to four years using traditional methods. The company uses two AI platforms in its research. Mr Alghaith said AI accelerated the identification of disease-related target proteins, with PandaOmics AI platform supporting this process. Another AI platform , Chemistry42, then helps to design molecules with the right shape to attach to the chosen protein. “Traditionally, you would have to design your own molecules, try to fit this with your own designs, but with the help of artificial intelligence, it can make these designs for you,” Mr Alghaith said. The newly discovered substances are types of PROTACs, double-ended molecules that work differently from conventional drugs . Rather than temporarily binding to a target protein, they drag it to the cell's disposal system and destroy it entirely. In this case, they target Bruton's tyrosine kinase, a protein that helps malignant cells in blood cancers grow and spread, including in some leukaemias and lymphomas. Details have been published in the Journal of Medicinal Chemistry . Insilico Medicine describes the new PROTACs as “lead compounds”, because tests to determine whether they can enter clinical trials have not been completed. They are the latest in a series of potential drugs Insilico Medicine plans to announce this year. In April, the company’s Abu Dhabi researchers said that, with the help of AI, they had discovered a drug that could combat brain cancer . This was the first UAE-discovered drug named as a preclinical candidate for further development towards human trials. Another AI-discovered drug candidate, a non-opioid molecule that may be able to treat chronic pain, was revealed in July. Human testing of the drug candidates announced earlier this year may take several years once preclinical work and regulatory approvals are complete. Mr Alghaith, an Emirati scientist with a master's degree from University College London, said the sector's growth was creating new career opportunities in the UAE . “When I went into this field, about eight years ago, I had no idea where I was going to work, because this sector was not here in the UAE,” he said. “This was not an established sector. You can see how quickly things can change. This is the environment the UAE has fostered and also contributed to Insilico’s success. “Insilico Medicine, and by extension the UAE, is one of the only players in the region originating new medicines.” Abu Dhabi Investment Office, a government office that manages investments from within and outside the UAE, supported the creation of Insilico Medicine’s UAE operations. The company has an AI and quantum computing development centre at the International Renewable Energy Agency (Irena) headquarters in Masdar City.

title: Road closures announced for Dubai cycling race on Sunday morning
description: Motorists told to expect delays along 80km route of Proud of UAE event
content: Motorists in Dubai have been urged to plan ahead after a series of rolling road closures were announced along the 80 kilometre route of a major cycling race taking place on Sunday morning. The emirate's Roads and Transport Authority said delays were expected during the Proud of UAE event, which gets under way at 6am from Nad Al Sheba Police Station. The RTA said traffic would be suspended for between 10 to 30 minutes on Al Ain-Dubai Road, Sheikh Zayed bin Hamdan Al Nahyan Street, Ras Al Khor Road and Al Meydan Road while riders travel through each area. Each road will be reopened once all cyclists have passed through, the RTA said in a social media post on Saturday afternoon. The transport authority said the disruption was expected to last from 6am until 8.30am. "Plan your trip in advance and follow the directional signs to ensure smooth and comfortable travel," the RTA said on social media platform, X. The second annual race - organised by Dubai Police - will see large parts of the emirate transformed into a cycling track as professional and amateur rides alike saddle up for action.

title: Lando Norris worried about Sepang track after difficult Bahrain GP qualifying
description: Max Verstappen clinches first ⁠pole position of the season
content: World champion Lando Norris fears his McLaren will struggle on Malaysia's track after a challenging qualifying for the Bahrain ⁠Grand Prix. Norris qualified ​sixth fastest and was sixth tenths of a second slower than pole sitter Max Verstappen in Sepang, which is hosting an F1 race after nine years. However, Norris will start fifth after Red Bull's Isack Hadjar received a grid penalty that drops him from third to eighth. The McLaren driver, who is fourth in ⁠the championship, was not pleased with his car's performance on ​the ⁠Sepang tarmac. “We are just slow. ‌The car's not good enough here,” Norris said. “This tarmac is ​very different to a lot of other tracks we have been to this year and therefore I think you see Mercedes struggle a lot more today especially, you see Red Bull quicker than they usually are. “So I think the order has shaken up a little bit and I think we struggle a little bit more than what we were expecting because of the surface.” Meanwhile, Verstappen claimed his first ⁠pole position of the season. Verstappen clocked one minute and 35.130 seconds to edge out Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton , who snatched second place in the dying moments of qualifying despite struggling with tyre degradation in the brutal Malaysian heat. Verstappen's teammate Hadjar was third fastest ⁠but will start eighth due to a five-place grid penalty, with championship leader Kimi Antonelli moved up to third ​for Mercedes ⁠alongside Ferrari's Charles Leclerc. Verstappen was the ‌last driver to win a Grand Prix in Malaysia in 2017, in what was his second career victory. The Dutchman became the first driver this season to put a car without a Mercedes engine on pole. “It's fantastic, we've been trying for many Grands Prix to get more, sometimes a bit closer to the others,” said Verstappen. “But to finally get it from where we started the season, pretty incredible.” Hamilton struggled with tyre degradation in practice sessions but the Briton said the team had resolved most issues. “It's so hot here, I keep saying it. But that's made it a massive challenge for the tyres, for the car, for the mechanics in the garage,” Hamilton said. “We made so many changes through all these practice sessions because the cars are sliding, these tyres ​are overheating. It was really, really hard to find a good balance. “We made ‌one last change going into qualifying and ⁠I think we hit the sweet spot.”

title: Lebanon's former economy minister set to face trial on financial charges
description: Amin Salam has been accused of embezzlement during his time as minister
content: A Lebanese judge has indicted former Economy Minister Amin Salam on financial charges, in a move that a senior MP said marked an important step on the "path of accountability". Mr Salam, who served as Minister of Economy and Trade from 2021-2025, is under investigation over claims of embezzlement, forgery, blackmail, bribery, and illicit enrichment. He is accused alongside his brother Karim, and Elie Abboud, who previously headed the syndicate of certified accountants. All deny the charges, with Mr Salam saying they were “attacks” against him. Their case was referred by Beirut judge Roula Osman to a criminal court. Farid Al Bustani, who heads the Lebanese Parliament's Economy, Trade, Industry and Planning Committee, said it was an important development "on the path of accountability and strengthening the state of institutions". Mr Salam was arrested last year following a complaint filed by Mr Bustani's committee amid allegations of “embezzlement, extortion and waste of public funds”. The committee alleged that Mr Salam awarded overpriced contracts to foreign companies for services that did not justify the costs, and misappropriated funds from the Insurance Companies Contribution Fund, which is overseen by the Economy Ministry. He was arrested last summer, then released in December on a bail of nine billion Lebanese lira (about $100,000) and imposed a travel ban on him. Mr Salam served as Economy Minister during the fallout from the 2019 financial crash in Lebanon , described as one of the worst in the modern history by the World Bank, as well as in 2024 during Israel's war on Lebanon .

title: Iraq recovers fugitive convicted of $3m embezzlement from Lebanon
description: Alia Hassouni ordered to repay money stolen from health authority
content: Iraq has extradited from Lebanon a former health employee convicted of embezzling nearly $3 million, the country's Integrity Commission said. Alia Hassouni, a former worker at the Wasit Health Directorate, in eastern Iraq, was handed over by Lebanese authorities following co-ordination with Iraqi officials and Interpol to secure her arrest and return. “The recovery operation was the result of continued international pursuit efforts, follow-up and co-ordination with the concerned authorities,” the Integrity Commission said in a statement. Ms Hassouni was wanted in connection with two embezzlement cases involving a combined 3.78 billion Iraqi dinars (nearly $3 million) from the Wasit Health Directorate. The commission said she participated in the misappropriation of 2.86 billion dinars in one case and a further 924 million dinars in another. The Wasit Criminal Court had convicted Ms Hassouni in absentia and sentenced her to life imprisonment after reviewing evidence including witness testimony, an administrative investigation and reports, the commission said. “The court found the evidence sufficient and convincing to convict her of participating in the embezzlement of public funds,” the commission said. The ruling also ordered her to repay the stolen funds to the health authority and granted the injured party the right to seek compensation, according to the statement. Iraq has stepped up efforts in recent years to recover fugitives and stolen assets as part of a broader anti-corruption campaign targeting major cases involving public funds. Within Iraq, personal rivalries and political targeting sometimes motivate investigations or legal actions against corrupt individuals living outside, an Iraqi official told The National . "We are seeing high-profile cases being pursued, with lawyers and officials trying to retrieve stolen assets only with certain individuals. However, Iraq has many corrupt figures that face no consequences because no one raises complaints or pursues their cases, allowing them to enjoy their wealth freely abroad," he said. The case of Ms Hassouni shows there is a "systemic failure in accountability", where "selective enforcement" is influenced by political or personal interests rather than consistent rule of law, he added. Prime Minister Ali Al Zaidi, since taking office in May, has vowed to curb corruption and disarm Iran-backed militias that have targeted American troops in Iraq. Under pressure from the US, Mr Al Zaidi has increased the government's anti-corruption campaign. Multiple arrests have been made and sentences imposed in recent months. An Iraqi court sentenced two female MPs, Alia Nassif Jassim and Ahwaq Salim Hassan, to seven years in prison for illicit enrichment, it was announced last week. The anti-corruption court in Baghdad ordered the two women to repay millions of dollars' worth of illicit gains. Ms Jassim, a senior Shiite lawmaker, was ordered to return nearly $12.44 million, and pay a fine equivalent to the total. Ms Hassan was ordered to repay nearly $2.9 million and the equivalent fine. The court also sentenced former deputy oil minister for distribution affairs, Ali Al Bahadli , and a former MP, Talal Al Zubaie, to seven years in prison and issued fines, it was announced in August. In June, Mr Al Zaidi ordered a sweeping operation in Baghdad that led to the arrest of many officials and the seizure of millions of dollars in cash and gold.

title: 'Part of our team': Sheikh Hamdan praises flydubai pilot after hospital visit
description: Crown Prince of Dubai said Capt Smit Machchhar showed courage, responsibility and care for human life
content: Sheikh Hamdan bin Mohammed, Crown Prince of Dubai, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Defence, on Saturday offered the nation's “full appreciation and praise” to hero flydubai pilot, Capt Smit Machchhar, during a hospital visit. Sheikh Hamdan said the pilot – who is receiving medical care in Abu Dhabi after being attacked by his co-pilot on a flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv on Wednesday – “embodied the highest degrees of courage, responsibility, and care for human life”. Capt Machchhar managed to open the cockpit door after he was struck with a crash axe, letting in crew members and passengers to help avert disaster as the plane plunged thousands of feet. A small group of passengers and a reserve pilot overpowered the co-pilot, steadied the plane and managed to land the Boeing 737 in Tabuk, north-western Saudi Arabia. “From us, and from the leadership of the nation, he has our full appreciation and praise,” Sheikh Hamdan said. “We are proud that he is part of our team, part of the story of our nation and part of what the UAE stands for. “A nation of compassion, a nation of peace and a nation of life.” Hamad Al Shamsi, the UAE's attorney general, said on Saturday that investigations had revealed the co-pilot attacked the captain on the flight deck using a crash axe and attempted to take control of the aircraft. A crash axe is typically kept in a plane cockpit for ⁠use during emergencies. The attorney general said the co-pilot – whose name and nationally have not been disclosed by UAE authorities – had “attempted to carry out a terrorist act”. The attorney general said investigations were continuing to establish the full circumstances and motives behind the incident, including analysing physical and digital evidence.

title: Zinedine Zidane says France 'deserved better' after Nations League draw with Italy
description: Robert Lewandowski ​nets ​hat-trick for Poland while Edin Dzeko plays final international for Bosnia
content: Zinedine Zidane's perfect start to his reign as France manager came to an ⁠end when his side were held to a 1-1 draw by Italy in the Uefa Nations ⁠League at the Stade de France. France had won away to both Turkey and Belgium in Zidane's first two games. However, France found the going tough at home . Michael Olise put ⁠the French ahead 10 minutes after the break but Alessandro Bastoni levelled for Italy. “I'm very disappointed for the players because we deserved better,” Zidane told TF1. “But I'm proud of them, the effort, the pressing, they were exemplary.” Zidane said his team performed better that the scoreline suggested. “I think we deserved more from tonight, especially up until their goal. There were a little more fluctuations after that, but up until then we could certainly have scored a second goal,” Zidane told the Uefa website. Zidane's first home game in charge came against the same opposition he had faced in his final international match as a player. That ⁠2006 World Cup final, which Italy won on penalties, will forever be remembered for Zidane's headbutt to Marco Materazzi which led ​to his ⁠red card in extra-time. “We knew it would be a very difficult match,” Italy coach Roberto Mancini told RAI. “But we did well to allow them very little in terms of chances, even if they had more possession.” Meanwhile, in a Group B4 game, Robert Lewandowski netted a hat-trick as Poland eased past 10-man Romania 6-0. Midway through the first half, Radu Dragusin was sent off for a foul on Lewandowski and the Polish captain converted the resulting spot kick. Lewandowski added another two minutes after the break, and the 38-year-old scored his third and Poland's final goal four minutes from time. Also, Belgium beat Turkey 3-0 in ​their Group A1 game. Kevin De Bruyne put the hosts ahead in the 10th minute after a one-two with Dodi ​Lukebakio. Lukebakio twice hit the post ‌before De Bruyne scored again on the hour mark from the edge of the box. Romelu Lukaku came off the bench to replace Lukebakio and secured victory ⁠14 minutes from time with his 94th international goal. In another match, Bosnia's Edin Dzeko made his 152nd and final international appearance in a 1-1 draw at home to Sweden. Viktor Gyokeres put Sweden ahead in the 61st minute, becoming the first player to score in six consecutive Nations League games. Two minutes later, Dzeko was replaced to a standing ovation with his teammates giving ​the 40-year-old a guard of honour. Kerim Alajbegovic equalised 10 minutes from time. Former Manchester City forward Dzeko, 40, scored late in the first half but the goal was disallowed as the ball had gone out of play during the build-up.

title: Dr Gargash warns that 'region's struggle with extremism persists'
description: President Sheikh Mohamed’s adviser underlines UAE's zero tolerance stance against hateful ideologies and discourse
content: Dr Anwar Gargash , diplomatic adviser to President Sheikh Mohamed, on Saturday warned that the region's "struggle with extremism" persists as he emphasised the need to tackle radical ideologies. Dr Gargash highlighted the UAE's zero tolerance approach as he cautioned that the justification of terrorism through hate speech "is part of the danger". In a message on social media, the senior Emirati diplomat said the "latest terrorist operation" highlighted that the "confrontation has not ended". His remarks came after the UAE's attorney general said the co-pilot on the flydubai flight forced to divert to Saudi Arabia on Wednesday "attempted to carry out a terrorist act". Hamad Al Shamsi said on Saturday that investigations revealed that the co-pilot on flight FZ1073 attacked the captain on the flight deck using a crash axe and attempted to take control of the aircraft. A crash axe is typically kept in a plane cockpit for ⁠use during emergencies. "The region's struggle with extremism persists, and justifying terrorism through hate speech is part of the danger, not its margins," Dr Gargash wrote on X.
