title: Bitcoin crosses $80,000 to reach highest level in three months
description: Improving liquidity expectations and a lower regulatory risk premium are supporting the cryptocurrency
content: Bitcoin has crossed the $80,000 mark for the first time since mid-May on renewed optimism about the crypto market. The world's biggest cryptocurrency rose about 4 per cent to reach $80,246 on Tuesday morning, according to data from CoinMarketCap. Bitcoin rallied throughout last week, although it remains well below its peak of about $126,000 hit in October. It received a boost after the US Treasury on Wednesday said it would double the size of its repurchases of long-dated securities to at least $4 billion per round over the next quarter. Washington might even further boost its Treasury buybacks. "Bitcoin's roughly 23 per cent weekly rebound comes after months of subdued trading activity, making the speed of this move particularly significant," said Ryan Lee, chief analyst at Bitget Research. "US spot Bitcoin ETFs recorded $517 million in net inflows on August 19, their strongest day since early May." The combination of returning spot demand and forced short covering has supported Bitcoin, he added. Short covering refers to the buying back of assets that were previously sold assuming that prices will drop. Many traders had bet on Bitcoin declining further and were forced to liquidate when prices rose sharply. The latest rally appears to be driven by a combination of improving liquidity expectations and a lower regulatory risk premium, said Naeem Aslam, chief investment officer of Zaye Capital Markets. "US Treasury action to increase purchases of longer-dated securities helped pull yields lower and improve risk appetite, while President [Donald] Trump’s renewed push for clearer digital-asset legislation has strengthened expectations that institutional participation could become easier," he said. During a White House meeting with crypto industry executives last week, Mr Trump called on the US Congress to pass a “fair version" of the Clarity Act. "In 2026, regulatory clarity is emerging as a lead market catalyst and this push by President Trump and crypto leaders will certainly boost the market sentiment," said Mr Lee. The move will have an impact beyond Bitcoin's immediate price movement, he said. "The focus of the US administration to establish a clearer policy framework for digital assets will serve as a template for other emerging markets to regulate the fast-growing crypto industry in their respective countries." In the coming weeks, the market will be in wait-and-watch mode to see if the political will translates into legal progress. "If the Clarity Act makes progress, it could boost investor confidence and spark a broader recovery in digital assets. However, any ambiguity or political impasse will keep the market volatility elevated." Mr Aslam also said that regulatory progress, institutional custody expansion and improving liquidity conditions would strengthen the case for continued upside, particularly if Treasury yields remain contained. "Conversely, stronger US growth could push real yields higher again and remove part of the liquidity support behind the rally." Mr Lee said they expect Bitcoin to trade broadly between $74,000 and $81,000 in the near term. "After such a rapid repricing, a pullback toward $75,000–$76,000 would be consistent with profit-taking. The durability of the rally now depends on whether institutional buying continues after forced liquidations have cleared," he added.

title: Expensive uniforms to rising bus fares: Families feel strain as Iran war drives up back-to-school costs
description: Prices for uniforms, stationery and extra-curricular clubs are squeezing budgets
content: Before the US-Iran war began, Sumit Augustine's weekly grocery bill ran to about Dh150 ($41). Now it's Dh300, as the conflict is affecting shipping costs and the supply of goods across the Gulf. “It would only be natural for the school expenses to increase, too,” the mother of a 10-year-old told The National . Ms Augustine has budgeted accordingly – locking in tuition and transport costs early, then hunting for deals on everything from school bags to stationery - but her experience is one version of a story playing out in households across the UAE as the new school year approaches. The conflict's disruption to Red Sea and Gulf shipping routes has added complexity to an already pressured back-to-school season. Retailers have worked to absorb the turbulence rather than pass it on to consumers. Ashish Sood, chief supply chain officer at Landmark Group – which operates Centrepoint, Max Fashion and Emax – says inventory was committed months ahead of the season, with the group's Jebel Ali hub, which is capable of processing 300 million items annually, providing the operational flexibility to navigate shifting logistics. “Customers should not have to deal with the complexity happening behind the scenes. Our focus is on making sure families can still find what they need for the new school year, at the value and quality they expect.” Even so, some cost pressures have persisted. Ayat Adam, an Abu Dhabi mother preparing three children – aged seven, six and two – for the new year, has felt the pressure. “The prices really increased – the school uniform shirt was for Dh63 last year, this year it costs around Dh83.” Her total back-to-school outlay so far stands at about Dh4,700, with a tablet purchase of approximately Dh1,300 still ahead and about Dh2,400 for extra-curricular activities for two children to follow. “The prices are dramatically increasing on everything while the income remains the same,” she said. The conflict has also affected access to specialist equipment. For Niishhka Manglani, whose 15-year-old son is a student of determination, the most significant back-to-school cost this year is a standing frame at around Dh7,500. Sourcing it has been harder than in previous years. “For us, because the therapy and equipment costs are so significant, everything else doesn't hurt us as much on the pocket. Equipment costs were already high but they are now higher because stock is limited and new [stock] isn't coming in as quickly.” In addition to the standing frame, her family is managing therapy fees not covered by insurance, private tutoring for a pivotal year of IB assessment, and the logistics of accessible classrooms. Uniform costs are their own closed system. Dubai mother Zubia Khan spent about Dh1,000 per child – for three children – on uniforms alone, not including shoes or accessories. Meanwhile, bus fares have increase to “Dh2,700 per term, two-way, and we live in the same neighbourhood as the school”. Bags and stationery for all three have added about Dh1,000. Matthew Benjamin, founder of the sustainable uniform provider Kapes, believes prices are unlikely to fall. “Costs have gone up, which typically results in higher prices. However, the uniform industry is an artificial market. Suppliers buy as low as possible and sell extremely high; there is no price competition once under contract. So, although margins might be impacted, they are so high that it can be absorbed.” For parents seeking an alternative route, he suggests “buying second-hand where possible”. There is no advice I can really give, because parents can only buy from the exclusive supplier. Every year parents complain about prices, but the market is the market, and prices will continue to rise over time.” Research by Naseej, the UAE's national initiative for textile circularity, shows families are ready for the system to change. Some 43 per cent of consumers surveyed want recycled materials in school uniforms; 42 per cent want mandatory multi-set requirements abolished; and 29 per cent support school-led pass-down services, a figure that rises to 39 per cent among Emirati families. Rodayna Ramez, a Canadian resident in Abu Dhabi and mother of three, tries to live by principles of circularity as much as possible. “With three kids, I pass uniforms down whenever they are still in good shape. It saves us a fortune on back-to-school shopping, and it gets the kids thinking twice before throwing perfectly good things away. It also teaches them to value what they have instead of always wanting brand new stuff, which we know as parents is a huge problem.” Shraddha Barot Amariei, an entrepreneur with daughters aged three and seven, has also become more savvy. She’s held on to last year's uniforms, chosen complimentary school extra-curricular activities over paid ones and enrolled her younger daughter in a smaller nursery to help offset her older daughter's fees. “Thankfully, some of the retail offers this year are really helping, though our income as a household is drastically affected this year, so even small expenses we are being very careful about.” Shaheera Anwar, whose six year old starts Grade 1, repurposed unused stationery, skipped a uniform upgrade and kept her total under Dh500. “Uniforms cost at least Dh500 anyway and just saving that has been great.” For most families, the weight of back-to-school spending rests less on geopolitics than the school fees themselves. Jola Chudy, a British PR consultant in Downtown Dubai, spent around Dh600 on replacement uniform items for her 12-year-old son this year. “Honestly, as any parent in the UAE will say, it is always the school fees. We were very lucky that his father's work covered two terms per year of the school fees – at Dh25,298 per term, it's one of the more 'reasonably' priced top-tier British schools, but education is the big expense after rent or mortgage for most families and school fees take quite the dent.” A recent industry survey of more than 2,800 UAE parents found that 88 per cent feel financial strain when fees fall due, and half struggle to pay the full amount upfront, according to global financial technology platform Adyen. Annual tuition at top-rated Dubai private schools runs from approximately Dh30,000 to over Dh110,000 per child per year. Transport, uniforms, devices and extra-curricular activities add a further Dh10,000 to Dh30,000, said Adyen’s head of the Middle East, Daumantas Grigaravicius. “School fees represent one of the largest recurring household expenses for many families in the UAE, and for many parents, the challenge isn't just the total amount but the fact that it is often collected through only a few large lump-sum payments across the school year,” he said. “Where there’s room to improve for education providers is in how those fees are collected. “Most schools still operate on a two or three-instalment model. That structure hasn’t evolved with how families manage their finances today, and it creates pressure on both sides. Parents face cash-flow disruption at certain intervals, and schools deal with late payments and administrative complexity that a more flexible collection model could reduce. "Banks have offered credit card instalment facilities for school fees for some time, with at least 13 UAE banks now providing them. They remain a practical option for many families. "What’s changed more recently is the entry of fintech platforms and buy-now-pay-later providers into the education space, working directly with schools to offer structured monthly payments. We’ve seen a similar shift in real estate – a sector that also relied on large, infrequent payments for years. "Education is following a similar path," he added. "And the range of options available to parents today is considerably broader than it was even two years ago." The Knowledge and Human Development Authority's decision to freeze private school fees in Dubai for the 2026-27 academic year is another welcome development – though everything around the fees also continues to rise.

title: Cole Palmer dazzles with Chelsea front three all on target against Fulham
description: Joao Pedro broke the deadlock after 31 seconds before Morgan Rogers marked his debut with a goal in 3-2 win
content: Cole Palmer turned in a man-of-the-match performance against Fulham to get new Chelsea manager Xabi Alonso's reign off to a flying start. Palmer missed out on England selection for the World Cup, but he will surely now be back in Thomas Tuchel's thoughts for next month's Uefa Nations League fixtures. The 24-year-old set up the opener for Joao Pedro, 31 seconds into the match at Craven Cottage with a nonchalant flick. Morgan Rogers, who signed for the Blues in a British-record transfer this summer , marked his league bow with a goal from a cutback by Maxence Lacroix, another debutant, just before the break. Fulham's teenage midfielder Josh King levelled in the first half with a fizzing shot that beat Chelsea goalkeeper Robert Sanchez at his near post. Palmer restored Chelsea's two-goal lead four minutes after the break. After receiving a pass from Joao Pedro, Palmer shaped as if he was going to lay the ball off for a teammate, and with Fulham goalkeeper Bernd Leno wrong-footed, calmly slotted past the German. Gonzalo Garcia, a summer recruit from Real Madrid, scored his first Fulham goal in the 54th minute, but Chelsea did enough to hang on for all three points. “It was a very professional performance,” Alonso said. “The game had defined momentum; to win away in the Premier League, you know, normally it’s really tough. We were prepared to manage the game emotionally as well. It’s a good one to build for the future.” On Palmer's performance, the Spaniard added: “I’ve really enjoyed his performance. He has played with responsibility, maturity, and freedom. That’s important that we get the best from Cole. If we want to have a good team, we need a great Cole.” Captain Enzo Fernandez was kept out of the starting XI amid reports that Manchester City are circling back on the Argentine midfielder. When he was introduced as a second-half substitute for Romeo Lavia, he was greeted with a chorus of boos from a sizable contingent of the travelling support. “In football I am not surprised by anything," Alonso said of the Chelsea fans booing Fernandez. On the Argentine's future, he responded: "We will see. I’m not sure what’s going to happen in the future.” New Fulham manager Alvaro Arbeloa took heart from his side's performance in the 3-2 defeat and said it typified the character he wants to see from his players this season. "I think we keep improving and that will take time. But it's the first game of the season and I have been seeing all the games in the Premier League and you can feel that no one is ready," the former Real Madrid boss said. "But I saw tonight the energy that I want to see, the high press that we want to make. And like I said to my players, we are going to play in this way and we're going to try to play in this way no matter who is in front of us."

title: Why the Gulf has a strategic advantage in a fragmented decarbonisation world
description: Governments in the region are able to combine vision, investment and policy consistency better than others
content: Imagine a multinational company deciding where to invest in its next major decarbonisation project. In Europe, shifting political priorities and fiscal constraints create uncertainty around long-term climate commitments. In the US, businesses must navigate an increasingly complex patchwork of federal, state and local regulations, often moving in different directions. In the Gulf countries, however, national visions extending decades into the future continue to provide clearer frameworks for investment decisions. This contrast was on full display at Cop30 in Belem , Brazil last November. Leaders arrived promising a “Cop of implementation” yet departed without consensus on several of the most contentious issues surrounding the energy transition. Beneath the negotiations, a deeper reality emerged: decarbonisation is no longer advancing through a single global model. Instead, it is increasingly shaped by distinct political, economic and institutional approaches that vary across regions. For businesses, this fragmentation is becoming one of the defining strategic challenges of our time. In the UK and across parts of Europe, decarbonisation is increasingly tied to industrial policy. Governments are seeking to balance climate goals with economic competitiveness, energy security and regional development. Investment is concentrated in sectors and locations where emissions reduction can also drive productivity growth, job creation and industrial renewal. Climate policy has become inseparable from economic policy. The US presents a different picture. Decarbonisation operates through a number of centres of political authority, each with its own priorities and incentives. While some states continue to strengthen climate disclosure requirements and clean energy commitments , others are pursuing policies that challenge aspects of the sustainability agenda. As a result, businesses often face conflicting expectations depending on where they operate. Against this backdrop, key Gulf countries are emerging as distinctive case studies in how decarbonisation can be integrated into long-term economic transformation. Across the region, climate action is increasingly being framed as more than just an environmental imperative. It is also being viewed as a strategic driver of competitiveness, investment and economic diversification. National initiatives such as the UAE Net Zero 2050 Strategy and Saudi Arabia’s Vision 2030 have positioned decarbonisation within broader agendas focused on industrial development, energy innovation and future growth. The result is a model characterised by long-term planning, co-ordinated policymaking and large-scale capital deployment. Sovereign wealth funds, national energy companies and public-private partnerships are directing investment into renewable energy, hydrogen, carbon capture, sustainable infrastructure and emerging clean technologies. Rather than treating decarbonisation as a standalone policy objective, Gulf governments are increasingly embedding it within national development strategies. Of course, hydrocarbon revenues continue to play a central role in several Gulf economies, and debates around the pace and nature of the global energy transition remain complex. Yet their ability to align capital, regulation and industrial policy under long-term national visions offers a degree of continuity that many other markets currently struggle to provide. Indeed, one of the most significant lessons from Cop30 may be that policy consistency is becoming an increasingly valuable asset. For businesses operating across a number of jurisdictions , the challenge is no longer simply reducing emissions. It is understanding how different decarbonisation systems create different opportunities, risks and competitive dynamics. A strategy that succeeds in California may not resonate in Texas. A reporting framework designed for European regulators may not address the priorities of investors in the Gulf. Companies must increasingly navigate several decarbonisation regimes simultaneously. Three capabilities will become particularly important. First, organisations need a more sophisticated understanding of political and regulatory divergence. Decarbonisation is now shaped by a complex interaction of industrial policy, finance, trade, energy security and geopolitics. Companies that can anticipate how these forces evolve across different markets will be better positioned to make informed investment decisions. Second, capital allocation decisions must account for policy durability. Two projects may deliver similar environmental outcomes while facing very different levels of political risk. Long-term investment success will increasingly depend on understanding not only the economics of a project but also the stability of the policy environment that supports it. Third, businesses must build legitimacy locally while maintaining strategic coherence globally. Stakeholders in different regions respond to different narratives. In Europe, discussions often centre on competitiveness and industrial resilience. In the US, innovation and economic value creation frequently dominate the conversation. In the Gulf, credibility is increasingly linked to supporting national transformation agendas and delivering large-scale execution. Cop30 highlighted a reality that many businesses are only beginning to fully appreciate. Decarbonisation is no longer a single global pathway moving at different speeds. It is a collection of distinct political and economic systems, each pursuing its own version of the transition. For the Gulf, this fragmentation may represent more opportunity than risk. As Europe deals with fiscal constraints and the US continues to experience political divergence, the ability of the governments in the region to combine long-term vision, strategic investment and policy consistency could become a significant competitive advantage.

title: Lessons in cost-saving: How to cut down on back-to-school expenses
description: Experts share savvy ways to save as parents face considerable pressure to spend big as new term begins
content: Time is ticking for parents to prepare their children for the academic year ahead. This often comes with a long shopping list. School uniforms, sports kits and shoes might be outgrown and need replacing. Yet parents are often encouraged to buy everything new, from pencil cases to water bottles, so costs quickly add up. “The start of the school year can be a really stressful time for families,” says Megan Lawler, a parent of three and founder of Dubai Mums Meet. On top of existing cost-of-living stresses – a 2024 survey by Cigna Healthcare found that 45 per cent of respondents said the UAE cost of living was a leading cause of stress – summer holidays pose extra financial strain on parents. And after weeks of children's camps, family travel or even unpaid leave, come school fees and a shopping list of day-to-day supplies. “It can feel like a huge financial hit all at once,” says Lawler. An August 2026 poll on back-to-school shopping in the UK by YouGov found that 48 per cent of parents with children spend over £100 (Dh501, $136) on new school items, highlighting the high cost of preparing for the new academic year. “Some pressure around returning to school is completely normal as parents are helping their children transition from the freedom and flexibility of the holidays back into routines, schedules and responsibilities,” says Natalie Maaitah, child and adolescent psychologist at Thrive Wellbeing Centre. “However, over recent years, ‘back to school’ has evolved from a practical transition into a much larger social and cultural event. It has become a recurring campaign across shops, online retailers and social media,” she adds. Many retailers have dedicated displays and highlight different trends for each term. This adds extra pressure for parents, Maaitah says. “As a result, parents may feel pressure not only to prepare their child, but also to worry about whether they are doing enough compared with other families.” Budgeting expert and mother of three Caz Mooney, who frequently shares her money-saving tips with her 263,000 followers on Instagram, says financial constraints can arise when all expenses are due in one month. “There is an emotional financial pressure,” she says. “Parents want their children to feel prepared and confident going back to school, and that can create pressure to buy everything new. If money is tight, this added pressure can feel overwhelming. For many families, the biggest issue isn’t necessarily the total cost; it’s having to find the money within a very short period of time.” The YouGov poll also noted that 44 per cent of parents say they purchase most items during a dedicated shopping trip before the new school year begins, compared to 38 per cent who buy items as and when they are needed throughout the school year. It’s this second approach which budgeting experts say can help spread the cost. “We often think of back-to-school shopping as an expense that has to be completed in one massive hit, but it doesn’t,” says Mooney. “It’s important to ask yourself if your child will actually need that item in the first few weeks.” Many schools send out a list of required items, but it usually covers the entire year. Spreading the cost can ease the pressure, especially when buying for more than one child. “That means you’re not taking one huge hit to the household budget all in one go,” says Mooney. Many UAE schools now offer the opportunity for parents to donate old uniforms, while Facebook groups are filled with offers of free or discounted items that children have outgrown. Alice Crossley, a principal strategic foresight analyst at The Future Laboratory, says a mix of social media influence, cost-of-living concerns, and the rise of environmental awareness has combined to reduce the stigma around buying second-hand that previous generations had attached to it. “What’s changed societally is that resale and second-hand are no longer a fallback for parents under pressure; they’re how younger generations already shop,” she says. “Whether it's uniforms and school shoes on apps like Vinted or bikes on Facebook Marketplace, Gen Z parents look for second-hand first. Sustainability is often a welcome by-product rather than the primary motivation for shoppers, as the younger generations have grown up seeing second-hand and resale as routine. “Parents can see that shift as permission to lean into resale as a financial-saving opportunity,” she adds. “Pre-loved uniforms are a fantastic way to save money, particularly because children can grow out of things so quickly,” says Lawler. “Parents can also swap items with friends or other families, buy second-hand where possible and look for good-quality products that will last several years rather than constantly replacing cheaper items.” Buying pre-owned can also spark conversations with children about the environmental impacts of clothing and the financial benefits of saving money. “Involving children in donating items they no longer use can further develop empathy and gratitude, while showing them that possessions can have value beyond being replaced,” says Maaitah. “These conversations also create an opportunity to reinforce an important message: having something newer does not make a person more valued, more successful or more worthy of belonging.” She cautions, however, that the goal isn't to stop or guilt children for wanting new things. Instead, it's a teaching moment where children can be encouraged to understand whether what they're asking for is a want or a need. Reducing waste has become a key component of UAE government policy, with the UAE Circular Economy Policy 2021-2031 focusing on boosting reuse, recycling and resource efficiency. From large organisations to the home, UAE residents are encouraged to consider what needs replacing and what can be repaired or reused. “Check to see what you already have,” says Mooney. “Go through last year’s stationery, lunch boxes, bottles and school bags – often the items will be good for a while. Shop your home for stationery. If you are anything like me, I’m sure you will find a few pens in a drawer, maybe even an unopened packet of colouring pens or pencils; it all adds up to save you money.” Mooney also recommends buying generic where possible. “You don’t need to buy a particular brand of pen, copybook or bag, especially for younger children who are likely to misplace them.” “We should be teaching children that new doesn’t automatically mean better,” adds Lawler. “If something is still useful, there is no reason it shouldn’t be used again.”

title: Dune: Part Three star Josh Brolin: Abu Dhabi family stay was 'one of the most glorious six weeks of my life'
description: The Dog Stars actor’s comments echo Jason Momoa’s praise for Liwa ahead of the third Dune film's December release
content: Josh Brolin has described the six weeks he spent with his family in the Abu Dhabi desert while filming the Dune franchise as one of the most memorable periods of his life. Speaking to The National ahead of the release of Ridley Scott’s The Dog Stars , Brolin recalled living among the Liwa dunes south of the city during the production. “I had my family with me, and that was like one of the most glorious six weeks of my life,” Brolin says. “It’s amazing. Surrounded by nothing but dunes.” In Denis Villeneuve’s science-fiction series, Brolin plays Gurney Halleck, the warrior and mentor to Timothee Chalamet’s Paul Atreides. He is also set to appear in the coming third instalment . Abu Dhabi’s role in the franchise has grown with each film. The first Dune spent five days filming in the emirate, while Part Two returned for 27 days and used Liwa as its principal stand-in for the desert planet Arrakis. Dune: Part Three marked the franchise’s largest UAE shoot , with 31 days of filming in Abu Dhabi and Al Ain. More than 600 UAE-based crew members, performers, contractors and interns were involved in the production. Brolin’s affection for the landscape is shared by Jason Momoa, who reprises his role as Duncan Idaho in Part Three . After wrapping the latest film in the UAE, Momoa told The National that the franchise ranked among the most fulfilling experiences of his career. “You get to be in the desert, and it’s pretty special out there,” he said. “It’s a big honour. We were getting up very early and very late. You get to see stuff most people don’t. That’s one of the fun things about being in a movie like this. You get to go do some wild stuff in places you probably wouldn’t otherwise.” During breaks in filming, Momoa photographed the desert at dawn and dusk. “I got some good shots – my phone is pretty full,” he said. Momoa says the pace of the desert has remained with him, too. “This place is Disneyland for big kids – but then you go out into the dunes and everything slows down.” Dune: Part Three , based on Frank Herbert’s 1969 novel Dune Messiah , will conclude Villeneuve’s trilogy and is scheduled to open in UAE cinemas on December 17. The Dog Stars releases in UAE cinemas on August 27

title: Tunisian singer Lamia Riahi brings women-only Tarab singalong to Abu Dhabi
description: Riahiyat will make its UAE debut at the Cultural Foundation on Emirati Women’s Day, with the audience invited to become part of the performance
content: A concert usually requires an audience to listen. Riahiyat wants them to sing. The new women-only event, taking place at the Cultural Foundation in Abu Dhabi on August 28, is built around the idea that the audience should be part of the performance rather than simply watching it. Led by Tunisian singer Lamia Riahi, the evening will draw on Arab Tarab , Tunisian songs and, for the first time in her career, Gulf music . “I will try to satisfy almost every taste,” Riahi tells The National . “I will sing Arabic music from the eastern Arab world as well as Gulf music. “This will actually be the first time I perform Gulf songs,” she adds. “But I love it very much and I know many songs by some of the most important Gulf singers.” There will also be Tunisian songs familiar across the Arab world and music from what Riahi describes as the “golden age”. The concert will mark Riahi’s first performance in the Gulf. “This concert is definitely a dream for me,” she says. “I am used to performing concerts, thank God, but I consider this a new and very important step.” Riahiyat grows out of Riahi’s work in Tunisia, where she runs a private cultural centre and a women’s singing group. She says the idea comes from a belief that women need spaces where they can step away from the pressures of work and family life. “I feel women are the group carrying the greatest burden,” she says. “Women are tired. “A woman needs a way to enjoy herself and relieve that pressure, whether through sport, music or many other things.” Her sessions bring women together to sing, socialise and dance, with the dancing kept private and not filmed. Riahi says she has seen participants of different ages gain confidence through the group. One young woman initially arrived on crutches and needed help from her father to climb the stairs to the centre. After continuing to attend sessions, she appeared at a Mother’s Day concert without them and surprised her mother onstage. Riahi is careful not to claim a medical role in her improvement. “I do not claim to be a doctor,” she says. “But what we do makes us happy and gives us a wonderful energy.” That collective spirit was what drew Sanaa Azzi, co-founder and general manager of Highways Arabia, to Riahi’s work. “I think that the idea of having all these women gathered in a safe environment and sharing their love for Tarab and old songs is something that I would have liked to experience myself,” Azzi says. “So, let’s bring it to Abu Dhabi.” Highways Arabia, which Azzi co-founded with Caline Nassif, has been based in Abu Dhabi since 2010. For Azzi, the women-only format is less about exclusion than about giving women a different kind of shared activity. “Why don’t we do something where we can just express ourselves, we’re singing and we’re having fun?” she says. She also sees the format as multigenerational, whether between friends or between mothers and daughters. The Abu Dhabi edition has been designed to stay rooted in the city’s cultural scene. Riahi will be joined by the women of Chorale El Arab from Arab Choir Abu Dhabi and locally based musicians, under the musical direction of Dr Ahmed Abdel Sattar. The evening will also open with a short film paying tribute to the progress and achievements of Emirati women, including their contribution to the arts. The choice of the Cultural Foundation was deliberate. “Even the furthest seat is still very close to the stage,” Azzi says. “Wherever you are seated, you feel close to the stage, you feel that you are part of the experience.” That intimacy suits an event built on audience participation, but Azzi acknowledges the concept is also a risk. Women-only cultural events are often held in smaller, more private settings, she says, and a participatory Tarab night is more niche than a conventional concert. “This is almost the first thing that we’re daring to do,” she says. “But we wanted to take that challenge and we really hope that we will create something that is nice.” Organisers are also creating a wall where those attending can leave cards carrying messages to other women, whether it is someone they know or a stranger. Some of those messages are expected to be shared during the month-long Emirati Women’s Day programme. Riahiyat may also become the starting point for something larger. Since announcing the event, Azzi says Highways Arabia has heard from women behind dance hubs, singing clubs and other creative initiatives who are interested in collaborating. “We do not only want to bring experiences to the UAE that have already been done elsewhere,” she says. “What we really want is to create shows with women in the UAE, make them successful, be creative with them and, hopefully, export them.” “Our dreams and our plans are much bigger than this event,” Azzi says. “But we wanted to start as soon as possible with something. So, we said let’s start with this and build on it, inshallah.” Riahiyat: An Immersive Ladies’ Tarab Night takes place at the Cultural Foundation Abu Dhabi on August 28 from 8pm; tickets starting at Dh350 are available online

title: Will Man City push to sign Enzo Fernandez from Chelsea? Transfers to look out for ahead of deadline day
description: English clubs expected to spend big with summer market set to close next week
content: With the summer transfer window set to close next week, expect a flurry of activity as clubs look to finalise their squads for the busy months ahead. Most of Europe's top leagues – English Premier League, La Liga, Serie A and Ligue 1 – close their markets on September 1, with the German Bundesliga ending a day earlier. The Saudi Pro League clubs, meanwhile, have plenty of time left to bring in new players as their window remains open until September 6. Below, we pick out some potential transfers to keep an eye on over the coming days. New Manchester City manager Enzo Maresca appeared to make it clear to club bosses at the weekend where their transfer priorities should lie when he started centre-back Marc Guehi in midfield against Bournemouth. Before the 2-1 comeback win at the Etihad Stadium, reports emerged that City had agreed an £86 million deal to bring in 18-year-old Moroccan midfielder Ayyoub Bouaddi . And reports persist that Maresca is keen to sign Argentina World Cup star Enzo Fernandez from his former club Chelsea as City look to fill the Rodri-sized gap in the middle of the park. But the West London club appear in no mood to play ball, having told interested parties that there was an August 14 deadline to make a move for the 25-year-old, which has long since passed. City, though, could yet test their resolve with a late £120m bid. It has been a summer of exits at the Etihad Stadium with manager Pep Guardiola, defenders John Stones, Manuel Akanji and Nathan Ake, plus midfielder Bernardo Silva, all heading out of the door. They have since been joined by midfield duo Rodri and Tijjani Reijnders — who joined Barcelona and Al Qadsiah respectively — with winger Savinho closing in on a switch to Tottenham Hotspur. He could be joined in North London by Egyptian forward Omar Marmoush. Midfielder Nico Gonzalez looks set to join Newcastle United, while Everton are thought to be keen on bringing Jack Grealish back for a second loan spell on Merseyside. Saudi Pro League side Al Hilal are poised for a double swoop on the English top flight. Aston Villa's alarming 4-0 opening-game battering at Brighton was compounded by the news that striker Ollie Watkins had been unavailable for selection. Manager Unai Emery confirmed earlier in the week that there had been offers made for the England striker, with 21-time Saudi champions Al Hilal strongly linked with a move for the 30-year-old. When asked after the Brighton game whether it was his choice to leave out Watkins, Emery replied, “This question is for him. You can call him and try to get his answer.” Also on Hilal's radar is Arsenal winger Gabriel Martinelli, with talks between the two clubs having already taken place for the Brazilian, who is not part of manager Mikel Arteta's plans for the new season. Turkish side Galatasaray made a €45m offer earlier in the summer, but the 25-year-old made it clear he was not interested in a move to Istanbul, with Riyadh now looking a more likely destination. Hilal are set to bid higher than Galatasaray's offer to secure his signature. Arsenal's hopes of signing Real Madrid star Vinicius Junior were doomed to failure, with the Brazil forward signing a bumper new contract with Los Blancos instead. But the reigning Premier League champions still appear keen for a superstar signing up front, with Atletico Madrid forward Julian Alvarez reported to be on their wish list. The Argentina striker announced during the World Cup that he wanted to leave Atletico to “fulfil my dream”. Barcelona have been regularly linked with a move – much to Atletico's annoyance. But a deal has not yet been done, with Alvarez still in the Spanish capital, where he found himself booed by his own fans after coming on as a second-half substitute during Atletico's weekend draw with Villarreal. If the Barcelona switch fails to materialise, former Manchester City man Alvarez could find himself heading back to England to provide the Gunners with the 20-plus-goal-a-season striker their squad lacks. Liverpool needed an injury-time penalty from Dominik Szoboszlai to rescue a point at Newcastle on Sunday, but looked like a side in need of new arrivals, having lost attacking talisman Mohamed Salah during the summer. The Merseysiders have been negotiating with Paris Saint-Germain for attacking duo of Bradley Barcola and Ibrahim Baye, but the two clubs remain far apart with their respective valuations. PSG manager Luis Enrique again omitted the pair from his squad for their Ligue 1 draw with Rennes on Sunday, having done so for their French Super Cup loss to Lens the previous weekend. Luis Campos, PSG’s sporting adviser, suggested at the weekend that deals could still be completed for the pair before the window closes. Liverpool are also looking to sign Brighton's Yankuba Minteh, after bids of £50m and £60m were turned down for the winger last week.

title: Syria-Israel talks are a step in the right direction
description: The resumption in negotiations is key to securing both countries as well as the region
content: This week, Syrian and Israeli officials resumed talks in Jordan, brokered by the US, with the twin objectives of ending Israeli strikes inside Syria and reviving negotiations towards a bilateral security agreement. The talks – coming at a critical time for Damascus as it looks to restabilise the country following a brutal civil war, revive its economy and chart a new course in the post-Bashar Al Assad era – are a welcome, if fragile, step. As Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad Al Shibani, who led the delegation in talks with Israel, told Reuters, there is a "historic opportunity" for an agreement between his country and Israel. Such an opportunity must be seized. These talks also matter for a Middle East already dealing with a number of challenges, not least the US-Iran war and the resulting energy and commodity crisis, amid concerns that a new theatre of conflict could open up in the Levant between Israel and Turkey. Dialogue between Syria and Israel began following the fall of the Assad regime in December 2024 and the establishment of a new government in Damascus, with a view to settle the many differences that exist between the two countries – including a decades-long occupation of the Golan Heights, further Israeli incursions into Syria and Israeli security concerns. But the process stalled after the Iran war began. Then last week, Israeli jets attacked the Abu Al Duhur military airfield in Syria’s northern governorate of Idlib after Israeli officials alleged that Turkish soldiers were being stationed there. While there were no casualties, the strike threatened to freeze dialogue indefinitely. It also revived fears that Israeli-Turkish competition for influence inside Syria and primacy in a region left with a weakened Iran could tip into open conflict. Israel’s action drew a sharp reaction from its closest ally – the US. Tom Barrack, Washington’s ambassador to Turkey and presidential envoy for Syria, criticised the strike and suggested it may have been a political power play by Israel’s government ahead of this year’s parliamentary election, underscoring how domestic calculations can endanger regional stability. For Washington, which is working in concert with Ankara to help stabilise Syria, an unnecessary escalation serves neither’s interest. Syria, meanwhile, is tackling a multitude of challenges – both externally as well as domestically . Internal tensions between the country’s various ethnic and sectarian groups have yet to be fully resolved, while Damascus is at once battling a rejuvenated ISIS and keeping Assad loyalists and Iran-backed groups at bay. For Tehran, which for decades treated Syria as a satellite state and a land bridge to its Lebanese proxy Hezbollah, any sign of instability or vacuum offers a chance to try to interfere once again. None of this serves Syria, the Levant or the Middle East. And so, it is against this backdrop that the American effort to create a deconfliction mechanism involving Syria, Turkey and Israel is a constructive step – as is the resumption of direct Syria-Israel talks this week. It is worth keeping in mind that Syria and Israel have had talks throughout different periods of Assad rule, but often denied by Damascus. The new Syrian government's direct approach is welcome and much needed. Under President Ahmad Al Shara, Syria has made tangible – even if slow – progress on a number of issues. It has engaged with its Arab neighbours, notably Lebanon and Iraq – countries that it has had serious differences with in the past – to foster new avenues of co-operation that include countering drug trafficking, prisoner exchanges and economic integration. It has invited inspectors from the International Atomic Energy Agency to examine the remnants of the Assad regime’s nuclear programme . It has also begun the process of welcoming back millions of Syrian refugees and migrants who fled the war. This, then, is the moment for Syria’s neighbours to support a country and people trying to get back on their feet.

title: Banks can't afford to fall behind on AI. But can they afford for it to fail?
description: As lenders accelerate their digital transformation, outages and geopolitical shocks are putting the resilience of their systems to the test
content: Banks are racing to put artificial intelligence and digital technology at the heart of everything from payments to customer service. But the deeper technology becomes embedded in banking, the greater the consequences when it fails. Recent disruptions have brought that risk into sharper focus. Iranian attacks during the war struck Amazon Web Services facilities in the UAE, while a region-wide IT breakdown disrupted online and phone banking services at several lenders. More recently, Abu Dhabi Commercial Bank suffered intermittent digital disruption that affected customers for about a week. The incidents expose a dilemma facing banks in the UAE and globally. Digitalisation and AI are no longer optional in an industry where customers expect instantaneous service and switching banks can take little more than a few taps on a phone. But every new layer of technology also creates dependencies that lenders must protect against disruption, cyberattacks and geopolitical shocks. “In banking, trust is the ultimate currency,” said Pedro Cardoso, group chief digital officer at Abu Dhabi Commercial Bank. “As individual customers and businesses' expectations continue to evolve, the industry’s responsibility is to ensure that innovation, resilience and customer experience advance together.” Competition from the new breed of banks built on AI-driven, cloud-first and asset-light models has set new standards for speed, personalisation of services and cost efficiency, the Dubai International Financial Centre (DIFC) said in its 2026 Future of Finance report. “Without decisive transformation”, industry profit pools could fall by $170bn by 2030, pushing many institutions below their cost of capital, according to a DIFC report released in June. UAE lenders are responding by accelerating investment in technology. Abu Dhabi-based Sharia-compliant lender Al Hilal Bank has transformed its traditional operating model to a “digital-first” proposition “in response to a fundamental shift in customer behaviour and preferences”, chief executive Jamal Al Awadhi said. Today, more than 95 per cent of the lender’s active customers bank digitally, and as digital engagement grows, “so do customer expectations”, necessitating “continued investment in infrastructure, cyber security and cloud capabilities”. The name of the game is strengthening the bank’s “resilience, flexibility and scalability” to enable it to “rapidly shift critical banking services across multiple environments when required”, he added. While the top-tier UAE banks are investing heavily on digitalisation programmes and AI integration, the mid-tier banks such as National Bank of Fujairah are also pouring substantial sums into changing the DNA. NBF is committing Dh100 million a year to become a “digital-first bank with a human touch”, chief executive Adnan Anwar told The National in March. Although the likes of First Abu Dhabi Bank, the UAE's largest, Mashreq, ADCB, Abu Dhabi Islamic Bank and Dubai Islamic Bank, have not disclosed how much digitalisation accounts for their annual expenditure, they have repeatedly emphasised on their continued transformation. Their efforts are paying off. Emirates NBD and First Abu Dhabi Bank , topped an index tracking the use of responsible artificial intelligence, receiving recognition for their role in narrowing the adoption gap between the Middle East and Africa and global peers. The lenders were ranked first and third, respectively, by the Evident AI Index for Banks – Middle East & Africa . The index tracks how lenders in the region leverage AI and navigate its transformational effects throughout their operations. But the more dependent banks become on technology, the greater the stakes when systems go down. Recent events in the Middle East have been an extreme test of that dependence. Cloud and digital infrastructure on which most banks rely to run core banking platforms, process digital payments, store customer data and power mobile banking apps can become points of vulnerability during conflict as well as targets for attack. On March 2, online and phone banking services of several banks in the UAE were disrupted due to a regionwide IT services breakdown. It was not clear whether the issues were related to strikes at Amazon Web Services data centres in the UAE that took place on the same day. A day later, AWS, Amazon's cloud division, confirmed that two of its facilities in the UAE “were directly struck”, while in Bahrain a drone strike near one of its sites damaged its infrastructure. Following the disruption, the UAE Central Bank allowed Emirati lenders “temporary relief” to host some data outside the country to avoid the fallout of Iranian attacks, the UAE Banks Federation chairman, Abdul Aziz Al Ghurair, said in May. Under regulations, the UAE Central Bank requires all financial institutions to keep customer and transaction data within the Emirates. “Banks are accountable not just for their own systems, but also for the vendors and platforms they rely on … especially when we consider the rising expectations around resilience-by-design, governed execution of AI systems, and strategies aimed at third-party concentration risk,” Inci Kaya, senior research manager at International Data Corporation (IDC), said. War, however, is far from the only threat to the smooth functioning of digital banking. Technology can fail for more conventional reasons. Last month, ADCB, the third-largest lender in the UAE by assets, suffered intermittent outages to its services. On July 6, ADCB said its mobile app was back to normal operation for most customers after a week of technical disruption. The lender’s core systems, branches, ATMs, card networks and payment operations absorbed heavy transaction volumes despite the intermittent downtime. Its corporate banking channels remained fully operational throughout that period, the lender said at the time. The scale of its digital customer base illustrates what can be at stake during an outage. Some 1.9 million customers, representing about 93 per cent of the bank's customer base, were registered across ADCB’s mobile and internet banking platforms at the end of 2025. Over 1.5 million users have already migrated to ADCB’s new AI-powered app, according to the bank's data. “As digital banking continues to evolve, resilience is becoming as important as innovation,” Sean Langton, chief information officer at ADCB, said. ADCB has plans to spend substantially more to bolster stability. Spending on its digital banking capabilities is expected to run into hundreds of millions of dollars over the next two to three years. “These investments are strengthening our core infrastructure, expanding cloud and AI capabilities,” Mr Langton. Such failures are not unique to the UAE. Banks and payment networks globally regularly contend with outages. Mastercard has suffered two disruptions this year, including an outage last weekend linked to a system upgrade, while a technical glitch in Russia's interbank networks in April temporarily disrupted services at several major lenders. “No system is failure-proof, so we don't build as though ours are,” said Sujit Krishnan Unni, group chief technology officer at Network International. The payments company is engineering resilience into “every layer of our technology, from infrastructure and applications to change management and monitoring”, to minimise disruption in services. “Automation is also playing a growing role, helping us identify and fix issues before they affect customers,” Mr Unni said. The answer, industry executives argue, is not for banks to retreat from AI or digitalisation. Instead, resilience has to keep pace with innovation. “A system that isn't resilient can't deliver value consistently, and a system that doesn't adapt to customer expectations isn't delivering the right value in the first place,” Mr Unni said. Financial institutions that prioritise investments in AI-enabled customer engagement and personalisation engines are seeking to improve service quality, deepen customer relationships and increase loyalty, IDC's Ms Kaya said. That said, security and risk management outrank customer experience among their priorities. But it would not be fair to characterise the industry's adoption of technology as “reckless deployment”, she said. The shift in technology strategies globally, she noted, is moving away from efficiency alone towards continuity, redundancy and risk absorption. That reflects a market in which an outage can affect far more than the infrastructure itself, potentially damaging customer trust, regulatory confidence and business continuity. “Banks must be ready to demonstrate their ability to restore critical services within defined impact tolerances,” she said. “They are aware that they are subject to fines and remediation orders, and that they can incur reputational damages if they fail.” For an industry built on trust, the next phase of the technology race may therefore be defined not simply by which bank deploys AI fastest, by which can sustain the continuity of flashing-fast AI-driven services.

title: High humidity in UAE prevents sighting of Suhail Star but end of summer is near
description: Sky's second-brightest star heralds onset of cooler conditions
content: The end of the summer in the UAE is on its way, despite high humidity preventing a sighting of the Suhail Star on Monday morning. The rising of the star in the southern sky is a celestial event tracked by astronomers across the Middle East. Symbolically, it marks the end of the extreme heat of peak summer and heralds the approach of cooler conditions. According to Arab folklore, the night “cools down” when “Suhail rises”. Temperatures will remain warm during the day for several weeks but the evenings will gradually become cooler, and morning fog will be more noticeable. Between 1991 and 2020, average temperatures in September ranged from 29°C to 39°C with a mean humidity of about 54 per cent. Temperatures tend to drop noticeably in October, with an average minimum of 25.5°C and maximum of 35.8°C between 1991 and 2020. The winter period then follows, beginning in November. January is traditionally the coolest month of the year in the UAE , with an average minimum temperature of 15.5°C and maximum of 24.3°C between 1991 and 2020. The Suhail star is the second-brightest star in the night sky and the main anchor of the Drour Calendar, a historical calendar that divides the year into 100 day periods, which are subsequently divided into sub-periods of 10 days, called a Dur. Known to astronomers as Canopus, the star once guided pearl divers, sailors and fishermen as they navigated on land and at sea. The calendar itself is a traditional feature of Gulf heritage and was used to predict seasonal and weather changes long before modern meteorological systems were invented. The Suhail star sighting is therefore deeply embedded in national culture. It signifies a period of renewal and relief, particularly from the extreme summer heat. It is also referenced in folklore and poems. Because of high humidity levels exceeding 80 per cent, the star was not entirely visible on Monday, but it is expected to be clearly seen in the upcoming week.

title: Killer destinations: The crime-writing festivals worth travelling for
description: From Scottish castles to darkest Iceland, these are the global gatherings crime-fiction fans need to know about
content: From Richard Osman’s retired amateur sleuths solving cosy crimes every Thursday, to Freida McFadden’s murderous housemaids and Harlan Coben’s twisty thrillers, the crime genre has long been a favourite of readers around the world. Reading and writing are notoriously solitary pursuits, so it is no wonder that a global industry has sprung up to stage live events designed to appeal to fans of the genre. One theme that is proving popular across the world this year is Agatha Christie, the world’s best-selling crime writer, who is outsold by only the Bible and William Shakespeare. This year marks 50 years since her death, so expect to see many panels celebrating her illustrious career. There are dozens of crime-writing festivals around the world, so here is our guide to some of the best of the bunch. Happy sleuthing. The original Queen of Crime, Christie, ruled the golden age of crime writing in the 1930s – including penning stories inspired by Middle Eastern journeys – and many crime-writing festivals will feature homages this year to the iconic creator of Hercule Poirot and Miss Marple. However, for dedicated Christie fans the only place to be is the annual gathering held at her birthplace in Torquay, south-west England. This year’s programme celebrates the centenary of the publication of The Murder of Roger Ackroyd , one of her most popular novels. September 12–20, 2026, Torquay, UK The home of Scottish hero William Wallace, Stirling’s annual crime writing festival has attracted many legendary Tartan Noir scribes since it started in 2012. Sir Ian Rankin, creator of the best-selling Rebus detective series, was last year the first to take on the role of guest programmer, and following in his footsteps this year is Denise Mina, with a programme that includes big names such as Richard Osman, Lee Child, Ardal O'Hanlon, Tana French and Val McDermid. September 18-20, 2026, Stirling, Scotland A 12-day celebration of crime, this festival mixes the genre with a healthy dose of academia, film and popular culture. It is also a chance to delve into the popular Spanish novela negra tradition, which became popular in the 1970s when Spain emerged from the Franco dictatorship and the crime fiction genre was used as a not-so-subtle critique of the changing society. This year includes a special focus on the works of legendary American writer Stephen King. October 14-15, 2026, Getafe/Madrid, Spain One of the largest global gatherings of crime-writing fans, this event has been running since 1970 and was established in honour of American crime writer and critic Anthony Boucher. One of the 2026 highlights is guest of honour Kathy Reichs, a forensic anthropologist-turned-author, whose best-selling Temperance Brennan novels inspired the popular Bones TV series. A trip to the festival also offers a chance to check out the Rockies and the rugged Canadian setting, while fans of the comedy-horror genre should check out a production of Little Shop of Horrors running at Theatre Calgary over the same period. October 21-25, 2026, Calgary, Canada Iceland may have only about 400,000 residents, but its long hours of winter darkness and alien landscape give it one of the most atmospheric settings on the annual crime-writing festival calendar. This event is more intimate than many of the larger festivals and most events are in English, which makes it particularly accessible to international visitors. Previous guests have included Dan Brown and George R.R. Martin and while the full 2026 line-up hasn’t yet been confirmed, this year’s focus will include a full day dedicated to Agatha Christie. November 11-14, 2026, Reykjavik, Iceland One of the newest additions to the global crime-writing calendar, the festival counts Sir Ian Rankin among its fans and has been described by him as “the most beautiful book festival in the world”. Highlights this year include a discussion focused on Robert Louis Stevenson’s epic masterpiece The Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde , the evolution of the modern spy genre and the history of giallo, Italy’s crime subgenre, which is believed to have influenced the growth of American slasher films. Authors to look out for include Mark Billingham, Elly Griffiths and Clare Mackintosh. November 12-15, 2026, Venice, Italy Established 40 years ago, the festival has attracted global names such as Margaret Atwood, Zadie Smith and Neil Gaiman. The event includes sessions across a number of languages, including English, Malay, Chinese and Tamil. The full 2026 programme has not yet been unveiled. While it is not a dedicated crime festival, this year’s theme is Hidden in Plain Sight and covers areas such as crime fiction, investigative journalism and stories about concealment. Festivalgoers should also check out Singapore Murder Mystery 2: Crime on Date Night, an interactive outdoor detective game Old Hill Street Police Station, and players have around 90 minutes and players have around 90 minutes to solve a fictional murder while looking for clues around the city. November 13-22, 2026, Singapore Celebrating its 10th anniversary this year, Sydney is one of the strongest dedicated crime festivals outside Europe and North America, and previous big-name participants have included Lynda La Plante, Ann Cleeves and Lee Child. The festival is renowned for its quirky elements, such as themed city walking tours. In 2023, it staged an interactive event where players were presented with a crime scene and could examine evidence, test for DNA and fingerprints, and interview witnesses in a bid to solve the murder. November 20-21, 2026, Sydney, Australia The major attraction of this Danish festival is that it is staged inside Fængslet, a former prison, so it is no wonder it regularly attracts around 100 authors and 7,000 participants. Next year it will celebrate its 25th anniversary, and while the programme hasn’t been announced, guests in the past have included Inspector Morse creator Colin Dexter, American author Don Winslow and British bestseller Lisa Jewell. Panel sessions also often feature experts on topics such as DNA, forensic genealogy and arson. March 13-14, 2027, Horsens, Denmark A major global conference for crime writers and those across the industry, it includes elements such as CraftFest, Masterclass and PitchFest, where aspiring authors can network and pitch their novel ideas to more than 60 literary agents and editors. Some of the A-list authors announced so far for 2027 include Michael Connelly, creator of the Harry Bosch series, and Mark Greaney, who has written several novels taking place in Tom Clancy’s Jack Ryan universe. One of the highlights of the festival is the full day of events organised by the FBI, which in the past has covered issues such as bombing forensics, cybercrime, firearms trafficking, and insights into real murder investigations. April 27-May 1, 2027, New York, US The crime-writing calendar extends well beyond the major festivals above. St Hilda’s Crime Fiction Weekend runs from September 4 to 6 in Oxford, England, followed by Lisle Noir in Lisle-sur-Tarn, France, from September 19 to 20. Toulouse Polars du Sud takes place from October 9 to 11 in Toulouse, with Murder One following in Dublin, Ireland, from October 15 to 18. The Nederlands Thrillerfestival rounds out the 2026 calendar on October 25 in Zoetermeer. Looking ahead to 2027, SleuthFest takes place in Orlando, Florida, in March, followed by the Emirates airline Festival of Literature in Dubai in April. Capital Crime runs from May 28 to 30 in London, while the Theakston Old Peculier Crime Writing Festival returns to Harrogate in July. Bute Noir takes place from August 6 to 8 in Rothesay on Scotland’s Isle of Bute. Whether you prefer cosy mysteries, psychological thrillers, Nordic noir or hard-boiled detective stories, there is now a festival to match. And with events taking place everywhere from historic seaside towns to former prisons, following your favourite crime writers can be a good excuse to discover a new destination along the way.

title: Abu Dhabi's Lulu Island primed for revamp as development plan confirmed
description: Real estate developer Eagle Hills Properties to oversee project years in the making
content: An Abu Dhabi island left largely untouched for decades is primed for transformation in the latest step forward in the capital's long-term expansion drive. Eagle Hills Properties , one of Abu Dhabi's leading real estate companies, has confirmed it is overseeing a development project on the man-made Lulu Island. The island, which is about 500 metres from Abu Dhabi's Corniche, was built in the 1990s to serve as a breakwater against high tides and is only accessible by boat. With large beaches, clear waters and panoramic views of the city, it has long been earmarked as a site with huge potential for major residential and development projects. Previous masterplans over the years have failed to get off the ground, but the prospect of the sprawling island welcoming its first residents in the years to come is becoming a reality. “We can confirm that the development will be undertaken by Eagle Hills Properties,” the developer told The National , without disclosing specific details of its plans for the island. “Further information regarding the project, including any additional details, will be communicated in due course through our official channels and those of our partners,” they added. Boats from Blue Shark Boat Rental have been ferrying workers to the island, where many cranes and excavators are already in use. A handful of show homes have popped up in recent weeks facing the city. The real estate developer is headed by Mohamed Alabbar, the Emirati real estate giant behind Emaar and projects such as Burj Khalifa and Dubai Mall. Eagle Hills has projects in more than 20 countries and is the developer behind the masterplanned Ramhan Island, a luxury waterfront community in Abu Dhabi. Named Al Lulu, or pearl in Arabic after the pearls for which Abu Dhabi was famed, the 400 hectare island was created from reclaimed sand. Work on the project started in 1986 and was completed in 1992. Contracts to develop the island were awarded as far back as 2002, when Al Geemi Contracting won a Dh25 million development contract. In 2007, the island opened to the public with a few facilities, including two restaurants, four coffee shops, a track for camel and horse riding, two artificial lakes and a passenger ferry service connecting it to the city. In the same year, Sorouh Real Estate appointed Miami's Arquitectonica to conceive the masterplan for the island. The 2008 financial crisis halted progress, and Sorouh merged with Aldar Properties in 2013. In January 2009, the ferry service halted, and the island was made less accessible to the public. In 2023, the island was opened to visitors daily during Public Art Abu Dhabi. Buses brought visitors around the abandoned land, and art installations breathed life into the island's sand and shrubs. The Plan Abu Dhabi 2030 framework, part of the government's broader Vision 2030, provides some insight into possible development of the island. Figures show the island's projected population is an estimated 20,000 people. Beaches and green spaces could be abundant. Recent aerial photos show a canal being formed through the middle of the island. “Al Lulu Island is identified as perhaps the most important element of the Capital City Framework. Situated at the head of Abu Dhabi Island, every trip to the downtown ends with a view of it. It has immense symbolic importance and is proposed as a primary site for unfolding the story of Abu Dhabi’s history, achievements, personality and culture,” reads the document. Lasse Frederik Pedersen, a senior investment adviser at Dubai's Equiti Real Estates, believes ambitious plans could swiftly take shape. “What we're aware about is that they want low-rise buildings and hopefully, in the next 12 months, we should be allowed to have information about apartments, villas and mansions coming to the islands for maximum three or four-floor low-rise buildings,” he said. Bridges are expected to connect Lulu Island to Abu Dhabi Island, making the location prime real estate and providing a connection to the Mina Zayed development. “Lulu Island's convenience is its location,” added Eyal Ashur, a UAE property sales consultant and founder of Nooma Properties. “The fact that you have three [potential] connections; you can have a connection to Marina Mall, you can have multiple entries to the Corniche and also to Mina Zayed.” In recent years, Abu Dhabi has witnessed numerous off-plan launches including developments on Ramhan Island, projects in Saadiyat Island and even private villas on the grounds of the Emirates Palace. Experts say that even during the war and the rent freeze currently in place, demand remains. “During the conflict, so many hedge funds and family offices have been set up,” Mr Pedersen said. “So the fundamentals are absolutely prime for Abu Dhabi.” Mr Pedersen cited examples from recent months when sales in Hudayriyat Golf Estates broke sales records , even during the war. “Modon managed back in June this year to sell more than 1,800 units in six days as a sales record in the UAE. People really believe in Abu Dhabi,” he said. He said investment in buying property in the capital has grown since freehold ownership by foreigners was permitted in 2019. Mr Ashur agreed that there is plenty of space on the market, and it has not become oversaturated. “There is a huge shortage of ultra-luxury residential buildings in Abu Dhabi,” he said. “Abu Dhabi is changing and attracting high net-worth individuals looking for big houses of high quality. They want to be next to a golf course, next to water, and they want to have their own private space.” Mr Pedersen believes that Lulu Island will be “next level” when completed and highlighted Abu Dhabi's growing appeal for investors. “I think Abu Dhabi wanted to build slowly, quietly, and respect nature. It is what attracts all the high-end people coming. They want quietness, they want wellness and nature,” he said.
