As he concluded his two-day visit, Mr Aoun also met Italian President Sergio Mattarella, who holds a largely constitutional role. Carla Jazaar, Lebanon’s ambassador to Italy, attended both meetings. Mr Aoun had earlier met Pope Leo XIV on Thursday and thanked him for his efforts to support Lebanon in seeking an end to the Israeli occupation and attacks on its territory. In a post on X, Mr Aoun called on the Pope to “continue supporting Lebanon’s demands and urged the Vatican to maintain its diplomatic efforts in international forums to help secure them”. Lebanon and Israel have engaged in seven rounds of direct talks, a first in decades, with some held at the US embassy in Rome. The talks have focused on the creation of so-called “pilot zones” – designated areas in which Israeli forces would withdraw, the Lebanese army would assume control and Hezbollah would disarm. So far, Israel has withdrawn from only two pilot zones. Mr Aoun’s meetings in Rome come as Lebanon seeks to maintain international support for the implementation while negotiations continue. Although the next round of talks is meant to take place in September, a Lebanese political source said Israel has yet to confirm the dates. Unifil has been operating along the southern border of Lebanon since 1978, with an annually renewed mandate set to expire in December. Unifil is mandated to monitor the cessation of hostilities and violations of UN Security Council Resolution 1701, support the deployment of the LAF in southern Lebanon and assist in establishing an area between the Blue Line and the Litani River free of armed personnel, weapons and military assets other than those belonging to the Lebanese state or Unifil . It is also tasked with enabling the delivery of humanitarian aid, and supporting efforts to ensure security and freedom of movement. The force's mandate was renewed one last time in 2025. The decision for a final extension reflected a push, particularly from the US, to end what Washington viewed as an open-ended peacekeeping mission and have the Lebanese state assume sole responsibility for security in southern Lebanon. Italy, alongside other EU nations such as France, had warned that a premature withdrawal would create a security vacuum, with the LAF incapable of filling the gap. Pressure on the Lebanese government to disarm Hezbollah and take control of the southern region is mounting. Washington is pushing Beirut to fulfil an agreement with Israel to put all weapons under state control and disarm Hezbollah. The US-brokered agreement, signed in June, links Hezbollah's disarmament to the broader security arrangement and Israeli withdrawal. Israel refuses to withdraw from southern Lebanon until the group is disarmed, while its forces continue to strike the area daily.

title: Weather warning issued as southern and eastern parts of UAE brace for wind and rain
description: Abu Dhabi temporarily closed its parks and beaches on Friday evening
content: Heavy winds and rain have been forecast across southern and eastern parts of the UAE this weekend, with the public urged to exercise caution during the unstable conditions. The National Centre of Meteorology issued a yellow weather alert on Saturday for Al Ain and the region to the west of the city, citing a risk of dust and sandstorms caused by high winds, along with the possibility of rain and thunderstorms heading into Saturday evening. On Saturday morning, Abu Dhabi Municipality reopened all public parks, recreational centres and municipal beaches after temporarily closing them on Friday evening because of bad weather. Authorities took the measure as a precaution to protect the public. Heavy rain, thunder and lightning struck some parts of the emirate on Friday. Abu Dhabi Civil Defence also issued a warning on X, urging the public to be vigilant during the rain and to stay away from wadis and water pools. The unsettled weather is expected to continue throughout the weekend across southern, eastern and western parts of the country, with heavy rain in places and temperatures remaining in the low 40s. Fog and mist have also been forecast for coastal areas in the coming mornings. Drivers have been advised to obey temporary speed limits, maintain a safe distance between vehicles - especially when visibility is reduced - and avoid areas where rainwater has accumulated. The changing of the season is just around the corner. The Suhail star - the second-brightest star in the night sky - is expected to make its first seasonal appearance in the UAE on Monday, marking the traditional end of peak summer heat and the beginning of a gradual cooling. While temperatures are not expected to drop significantly until October, the period of peak heat, with temperatures over 50C, is not expected to return after the current inclement weather.

title: UAE Property: 'How can I tell if my apartment is overpriced or undervalued?'
description: Completed transactions tell us where the market has been willing to commit real money
content: Question: Every property website seems to give me a different estimate of what my apartment is worth. One portal values it at almost Dh300,000 ($8,169) more than another, and I've spoken to three brokers who have each suggested a completely different asking price. It's left me wondering whether anyone really knows what a property is worth any more. How should owners approach valuations without either overpricing their home or selling themselves short? NT, Al Reem Island, Abu Dhabi Answer: I completely understand why you're confused because these types of valuations have become much more visible than they were a few years ago. Online valuation tools are useful because they give owners a general idea of where their property might sit within the market, but they're still working from data and algorithms. They can't walk into your apartment and appreciate the view, the amount of natural light, the quality of the upgrades or the condition you've maintained it in. Those details often make a meaningful difference. As for brokers , it's perfectly normal to receive different opinions. Some naturally take a more optimistic view, while others prefer to price a property more conservatively in the hope of generating interest quickly. Whenever I'm asked to value a home, I spend far more time looking at what buyers have actually paid than what sellers are currently asking. Completed transactions tell us where the market has been willing to commit real money, and that's usually the strongest starting point for any conversation. Brokers have access to a B2B portal that gives us this information. I'd also encourage owners not to become too attached to one particular figure. The market has a way of finding the right value when a property is exposed to genuine buyers, and this is where property portals come into play. If you attract plenty of viewings but no offers, that tells you the price may be too high. On the other hand, if several buyers compete almost immediately, the market may be suggesting the property was priced too conservatively. Pricing a home isn't about choosing the highest number. It's about finding the point where confident buyers recognise genuine value. That's where successful sales usually happen. Q: I've finally reached the point where I'm ready to invest in Dubai, but I'm finding the whole process surprisingly confusing. Every developer tells me their latest off-plan launch is the best opportunity, while friends who already own property say it'd be wise to buy something completed that starts earning rent immediately. I don't mind waiting a few years if it's genuinely the better investment, but I also don't want my first purchase to be based on clever marketing. What would be your advice? AG, Birmingham, UK A: I think I'd probably start by asking you a lot more questions than giving you answers. One of the biggest mistakes people make is assuming there's a right answer for everyone. There isn't. The best investment is the one that suits most of your objectives. Some people are looking for an income from day one because they want the property to help cover their mortgage or generate cash flow. In that situation, a completed property often makes perfect sense because you know exactly what you're buying. You can walk around the property, understand the building, look at comparable rentals and make your decision based on facts rather than illustrations or hearsay. Other investors are in a completely different position. They're not relying on immediate income and are happy to wait if they believe the location has strong long-term potential. Off-plan can work extremely well in those circumstances, particularly when you're buying from a developer with a proven delivery record and into a community that is genuinely evolving rather than simply expanding. Look especially at projects with infrastructure expenditure nearby. What I've learnt over the years is that good investments nearly always have one thing in common. They're still attractive even after you strip away the sales presentation. If someone took away the showroom, the scale model, the coffee and the glossy brochure, would you still want to own that property because of where it is, who built it and what the surrounding area will look like in 10 years? The opinions expressed do not constitute legal advice and are provided for information only. Please send any questions to mario@evadxb.com

title: Gulf pours billions into water security to boost AI and industry ambitions
description: Desalination plants being developed across region will help build new-age economies
content: Gulf countries are keen to grow their industrial base and are pouring hundreds of billions into data centres and AI infrastructure to write the next chapter of their new-age economies. However, none of that is possible without the very basic resource: water. The UAE, the Arab world's second-largest economy , is leading the race for AI investment. The capital, Abu Dhabi, is building Stargate UAE, a massive 1 gigawatt artificial intelligence supercomputing and data centre project, expected to cost more than $30 billion. AI-related investments for 2024-2025 in the UAE exceeded Dh543 billion ($147.9 billion), with global firms including Microsoft and KKR announcing major investments in the UAE. Availability of water is critical for the UAE and its peers' push to expand their industrial base and lead the global AI and data centre race. While water is an essential operational element to cool heat-generating data centres and water-guzzling industrial units, growth in population across the Gulf countries is also set to boost demand. Data centres, consisting of incredibly powerful servers with thousands of central processing units and graphic-processing chips, need to stay cool to avoid overheating. Chilled water systems and refrigeration towers, or air cooling, is required to keep temperatures in data centres in check. A typical data centre uses 300,000 gallons of water each day, equivalent to the demands of about 1,000 households, but large data centres can use an estimated 5 million gallons of water daily, equivalent to the needs of a town of up to 50,000 residents, according to Brookings, a public policy think tank. Apart from the data centre push, the UAE is home to major industrial projects and more are on the cards under the country Make It In The Emirates push, an initiative aimed at broadening the industrial base and cutting reliance on international supply chains. The UAE is targeting an increase in the industrial sector's contribution to the country's gross domestic product of Dh300 billion by 2031, from Dh133 billion-level achieved in 2021. The global usage of water for industries is estimated at 20 per cent of the world's total water consumption. The UAE does not see water shortages affecting its new economy ambitions, with new desalination plants expected to meet the rapidly rising demand, Abdulaziz Alobaidli, director general for regulatory affairs at Abu Dhabi's Department of Energy, told The National in an interview. “We rely on desalination [plants] that have proven in the last 50 years to be a very reliable source for potable water,” he said. Abu Dhabi is currently building a desalination plant in Shuweihat, while another desalination project was commissioned in the second quarter of this year. If required, the emirate is ready to build one more plant depending on demand, Mr Alobaidli said. He said safeguarding the source of water protecting the seas remains the top priority and is vital for reliable future supply. “The first line of defence is protecting the source and the source for us is the sea, the ocean. How to protect it from pollution? How to protect the ecosystem in it … and make it resilient … to threats,” he said. The UAE, he said, has more than one source of water, which bolsters resilience of its supply systems. “We have access both to the Arabian Gulf, as well as Gulf of Oman, and in time of constraints you have a diversity that helps you to maintain the resilience,” Mr Alobaidli said. The UAE in April said there were fears of “potentially catastrophic” threats to the Gulf’s marine environment in the wake of the Iran war, warning that missiles, drones and fires “may give rise to large-scale marine pollution involving oil, hazardous noxious substances, contaminated firefighting water, soot deposition” and other threats to the ecosystem. The region relies on desalinated seawater, and any contamination could also lead to “severe water security implications”, it added. Desalination plants were attacked in Bahrain and Kuwait in March, which brought Gulf water security into focus. Populations in the Gulf region are growing at a rapid pace, putting pressure on policymakers to continue investing in maintaining robust supply. At the end of last year, Saudi Arabia’s population reached 37 million, while the UAE’s grew to about 11.5 million, according to World Bank data. The UAE’s population is projected to reach 15.3 million by 2050, while expected growth in the kingdom will push the population figure to about 47.7 million, Worldometer data suggests. Gulf countries are ranked among the most water-stressed in the world, according to World Resource Institute’s Aqueduct Water Risk Atlas. The Middle East holds only 2 per cent of the world's renewable freshwater and 83 per cent of the region faces severe water scarcity. WRI estimates 100 per cent of the region’s population will face acute water scarcity by 2050. However, countries in the region are boosting investment to cope with the rise in demand. According to latest Nature journal data, the Middle East has spent $53.4 billion between 2006 and 2024, representing about 47.5 per cent of total global capex on increasing desalination capacity. The broader region is also expected to spend a further $26 billion up to 2028, with desalination capacity projected to reach 41 million cubic metres per day by then. “Ranging from around 40 per cent in the UAE to roughly 90 per cent in Kuwait and Oman, the Gulf states are critically dependent on desalinated water for their water consumption and security,” Mannat Jaspal, director and fellow of climate and energy at the Dubai-based Observer Research Foundation Middle East, told The National. “Investments are expected to rise from $5.28 billion in 2023 to $8.43 billion by 2030 across desalination, wastewater reuse and resource-management efficiency, and sustainability amid population, urbanisation and increasing economic pressures. Saudi Arabia, the Arab world’s largest economy, is seeking to diversify its economy away from oil, with multi-billion-dollar investments in building new infrastructure, real estate and industrial projects. The kingdom is also pursuing its AI ambitions, with $40 billion allocated to related ventures, including Humain, the flagship platform for national AI infrastructure. Qatar set up a company called Qai, a unit of the Qatar Investment Authority, to invest, develop and manage AI infrastructure in the country and abroad. The UAE’s AI sector alone could require about 61 billion litres of water a year by 2030, while Saudi Arabia’s data-centre power demand is expected to grow by 29 per cent annually, Abdalftah Ali, visiting junior fellow, and Mohammad Hawash, former senior research assistant at the Middle East Council on Global Affairs, said in a joint report published in April. With demand for water consistently on the rise, several Gulf-based companies have started testing next-generation cooling systems that are suited to extreme heat. Companies such as Khazna in Abu Dhabi, and DataVolt and Alfanar in Saudi Arabia have tested or deployed liquid cooling and other high-efficiency solutions that can “cut water use for cooling by up to 90 per cent while also lowering electricity demand”, Mr Ali and Mr Hawash wrote. The region’s rapid expansion of renewable energy is also expected to support these efforts by shrinking the indirect water footprint of digital growth. Tens of billions of dollars in announced solar and wind projects across the region reduce the water intensity of electricity supply, since photovoltaic and wind power consume negligible operational water compared with gas- or oil-fired generation. “Integrating renewable energy with desalination can help reduce both the energy intensity and cost of water production, while digital technologies can improve demand forecasting, detect leakages and enable more efficient management of water networks,” Ms Jaspal said. “Over the longer term, however, the region needs to move from augmenting water supply to fundamentally managing water demand. And for this, water security should be approached as a regional rather than purely a national challenge,” she added.

title: Second daughter of British-Palestinian family who drowned off UK coast dies in hospital
description: Saja El-Khawas dies three days after her parents and sister
content: A six-year-old girl has died in hospital days after her parents and sister drowned off the south coast of England. Saja El-Khawas was rescued but died on Friday, three days after the incident at Shoreham-by-Sea, according to a law firm acting for the hospital and a Palestinian group. She had been in a critical condition since. Parents Hassan El-Khawas, 55, and Zeina Alayn, 37, and sister Sara El-Khawas, 14, were recovered by lifeboat after getting into difficulty in the sea but were pronounced dead at the scene on Tuesday. Solicitors acting on behalf of Guy’s and St Thomas’ NHS Foundation Trust, and the Palestinian Forum in Britain, announced Saja's death. Sussex Police have said the deaths were being treated as a tragic accident with no third party involvement. Mr El-Khawas was born in the Rashidiya refugee camp in Lebanon, according to the Palestinian embassy in the UK . All members of the family had British citizenship. The family were well established in Britain and active members of the British Palestinian community, according to Nehad Khanfar, head of the Association of Palestinians Communities in the UK. They told The National Mr El-Khawas's brothers and children were being supported by close friends and family. They have extended family in Lebanon. Sara El-Khawas attended Ellen Wilkinson School for Girls in Ealing, west London, and the school paid tribute to her in a statement on its website. “It is with great sadness that we share the news that our Year 8 student, Sara, has died following a tragic incident during the school holidays,” said the school. “Sara was a sweet girl, well-liked by staff and students, and she will be greatly missed. “Our thoughts and heartfelt condolences are with her family, friends, and all those affected. We are also thinking of her sister and loved ones at this extremely difficult time.”

title: Review: Two crashes, a dead whistle-blower – and the cloud over Boeing's reputation
description: In Freefall, her follow-up documentary to Downfall, Rory Kennedy investigates the safety concerns raised about a company accused of putting its stock price before its passengers
content: One of the most heart-stopping moments in Netflix's new documentary, Freefall: A Reckoning for Boeing, is the scene where Alaska Airlines Flight 1282 has just suffered a mid-air blowout, leaving a gaping hole in the side of the fuselage. As the aircraft rapidly decompresses at 16,000 feet, panicked passengers begin sending what they fear could be their final messages to the people they love, convinced they are going to die. Reliving the 2024 incident is harrowing even when watched from the comfort of a living room, and one of many shocking accounts in the documentary by Oscar-nominated filmmaker Rory Kennedy. A follow-up to her acclaimed 2022 documentary, Downfall: The Case Against Boeing , the sequel follows the highly publicised death of Boeing whistle-blower John Barnett and uncovers startling revelations while amplifying the voices of whistle-blowers and the families of victims of Lion Air Flight 610 and Ethiopian Airlines Flight 302 . The two Boeing 737 Max 8 aircraft crashed within months of each other between 2018 and 2019, killing 346 people. Freefall does not simply retell those crashes. It asks what happened afterwards – and whether Boeing ever truly learnt from them. Kennedy opens the film by looking backwards, suggesting a shift in the culture under former chief executive Jim McNerney . Through former employees, industry insiders and journalists, she presents a picture of a company in which the pursuit of speed and savings increasingly came into conflict with the meticulous approach to manufacturing on which Boeing had built its reputation – including its decision to outsource significant portions of the development and manufacture of the 787 Dreamliner to suppliers around the world. At the heart of the documentary is Barnett. The former Boeing quality manager spent years raising concerns about manufacturing practices at the company's 787 Dreamliner plant in South Carolina. He alleged that workers were under pressure to rush aircraft through production and that defective parts could make their way on to planes. Barnett became one of Boeing's most prominent whistle-blowers and also appeared in Downfall . In March 2024, while involved in legal proceedings against Boeing, he was found dead in his vehicle in South Carolina. His death was ruled a suicide. Freefall explores the enormous toll his battle with the company had taken on him. His lawyers, who feature prominently in the film, are unequivocal about where they believe responsibility lies. But Kennedy does not rely on Barnett alone. Other whistle-blowers describe their own experiences of raising safety concerns, creating the impression of a problem that extended far beyond one disgruntled employee. The other voices that give Freefall its emotional weight belong to the families of those killed. Among them is Naoise Connolly Ryan, whose husband, Mick Ryan, a UN employee, died aboard Ethiopian Airlines Flight 302. “My kids are aware that their dad went on a plane and that the plane was made by bad guys,” she says in the film. The anger of the families is directed not only at Boeing, but also at the US justice system. The film captures the strain endured by families and whistle-blowers as they campaigned for accountability during a three-year deferred prosecution agreement reached between Boeing and the US Department of Justice in 2021. The deal allowed the company to avoid prosecution on a criminal charge provided it met certain conditions. The issue was thrust back into the spotlight in 2024 following the Alaska Airlines mid-flight incident, just days before the agreement's three-year term was due to expire, prompting renewed scrutiny of Boeing’s safety culture and the agreement’s effectiveness. Perhaps the most uneasy aspect of Freefall is the feeling of repetition. The 737 Max was grounded around the world following the two fatal crashes. Investigations followed. Boeing executives were questioned. Changes were promised. Then the aircraft returned to the skies. But no Boeing chief executive has faced criminal charges over the disasters. And that's why the title feels deliberately unresolved. The “reckoning” is not something Kennedy believes has already happened. It is what the families and whistle-blowers featured in the documentary are still demanding. “Something has to change,” one of them says. Freefall offers no reassurance that it will.

title: Arabic word of the week: Dars, the lessons we learn in class and in life
description: It can describe knowledge gained through experience
content: Whether taught in the classroom or learnt through hardship, the Arabic word dars can describe all manner of insights gained in everyday life. In the classroom, dars al-yawm means “today’s lesson”, while sharh al-dars refers to its explanation. A pupil preparing for an exam will often spend time on murajaat al-dars, or revising the lesson. Our Arabic word of the week can also describe the class itself, with a common student refrain being indi dars, meaning “I have a lesson”. Indi dars khususi refers to private tuition. Durus is the plural, meaning “lessons”. Dars stems from the root letters dal, ra and sin, which carry meanings associated with knowledge, whether through study, examination or teaching. The verb darasa means to study. Darasa al-mawdu means “he studied the subject” or “he examined the issue” and can be used approvingly about someone who has mastered their brief. The same root produces madrassa, meaning “school” or, in some contexts, a school of thought. Calling someone a madrassa can be a compliment, suggesting they possess wisdom from which others can learn. Classical Arabic dictionaries describe darasa as studying a book intensively. Beyond education, dars can describe something learnt from experience. Taallamtu darsan means “I learnt a lesson”, while a difficult experience may be described as dars qasin, or a harsh lesson. In sport, that phrase, along with dars la yunsa, meaning “an unforgettable lesson”, is often applied to a heavy defeat that reveals a team’s weaknesses. Tone is particularly important when stating allamahu darsan, which literally means “he taught him a lesson”. Used wryly, it often suggests that someone was punished or humiliated. Sa-uallimuka darsan, meaning “I’ll teach you a lesson”, carries the same warning as its English equivalent. One of the root’s best-known appearances in popular culture is Madraset El Moshaghbeen , or School of Mischief , a fixture of Eid television across the Arab world. The Egyptian comedy stars Adel Emam, Saeed Saleh, Younes Shalaby and Soheir El Bably in a story about troublesome pupils and the teacher attempting to control their classroom. Whether found in a textbook, a chastening defeat or a real-life experience, dars describes something that should be remembered.

title: Review: Can Atlantis The Palm deliver a relaxing escape with a baby?
description: It's been open nearly two decades - but the prestigious Dubai resort faced a different kind of test when we checked in with our 10-month-old
content: What Atlantis The Palm represents depends on how long you have lived in the UAE. For seasoned residents, the Palm Jumeirah resort – which opened in 2008 – is part of our personal and professional lives, hosting everything from weddings and business conferences to iftars and New Year's Eve celebrations. For tourists, the Atlantis, with its unmistakable coral-pink towers, can still feel like a destination in its own right, with a water park, aquarium and several restaurants . Checking in for my first stay with the wife and our 10-month-old son meant arriving with a new set of expectations. The former appeals of Michelin-starred dining and sold-out concerts had given way to smaller but more critical requirements: whether the room could comfortably fit a cot, bottles could be sterilised, dining halls were pram-friendly, and eggs could be served with just the right amount of mush our little man likes. Most important of all was whether there was enough going on in the resort to keep him amused long enough to buy us a few golden snatches of quiet. There is rarely such a thing as a calm first impression at Atlantis The Palm. The lobby feels as busy as an airport, with business meetings in lounges unfolding alongside families arriving on holiday, day visitors stopping for dining and hotel guests fresh from the pools crossing between wings with towels draped over their shoulders. High heels and sandals click across the cavernous polished floors beneath Dale Chihuly's towering glass sculpture, past fountains, marine motifs and palm-like columns on the way to the reception, restaurants and lifts. We bypassed the main check-in area with its nearly dozen lanes, and headed to the nearby Imperial Club Lounge in the East Tower, where guests have a private check-in and check-out desk as well as access to a dedicated concierge. Beyond the private reception, the spacious creamy coloured lounge was noticeably quieter, soothing our increasingly overstimulated son. We arrived about an hour before the 3pm check-in and were allowed to spend the time enjoying complimentary refreshments and snacks until the room was ready. Our room in the West Tower was about a five-minute walk away, and the luggage arrived not long after we did. We stayed in the Imperial Club King Palm View and, baby in tow, I paid closer attention to details beyond the room's coral flourishes, marble bathroom flooring and granite vanities. Before we arrived, the booking team had taken time over the phone to understand what we needed. A bottle steriliser, available on request, was waiting on the study desk and plugged into a nearby socket, while the cot had already been set up. Our son happily ate the grapes and bananas from the complimentary fruit platter. And when he stretched his vocal cords, the balcony offered temporary refuge, overlooking the resort's family pool with the Arabian Gulf beyond. One of the first lessons I learnt on a family holiday is that kid is king when it comes to dining decisions, including where, what and, more importantly, when he could eat comfortably. He is an early riser, so 8am became our sweet spot for breakfast at the Imperial Club Lounge. It proved an ideal time, giving us close to an hour of relative calm before more families began filtering in. The buffet covers breakfast staples such as hashbrowns and scrambled eggs alongside cooked-to-order dishes such as omelettes, eggs Florentine and avocado toast. In one corner, a large screen showing Disney films gave our son something else to focus on as we put breakfast together. And as our son sleeps early, we arrived at Saffron, the main dining hall, around the start of dinner service at 6pm. Placed along the ground floor of the West Tower, Atlantis's largest buffet spans 20 live cooking stations, ranging from pasta and curries to Middle Eastern grills, sushi, dim sum and stir-fries. Staff quickly brought over a sturdy high chair, and were friendly and animated with our son. Arriving at the start of service meant the room was still relatively calm, with grills and pizzas coming fresh from their stations. Wavehouse, a restaurant in The Avenues, the resort’s shopping and dining area, tries to be several things at once, with bowling lanes, dozens of arcade games, darts and screens alongside a separate sports bar area and an almost cyberpunk atmosphere. Our meal here was served in one the family booths and the food was wonderfully hearty, with the arrabiata penne patsa delivering a proper kick from pepperoncino and garlic, softened by burrata, while the corn salad came loaded with baby gem, avocado, edamame, pomegranate, almonds and sun-dried tomato. The fish and chips came with minted peas, tartare sauce and the kind of thick fries I enjoy with a dish like this. Aquaventure Waterpark felt too overwhelming for a 10-month-old, though that hardly mattered because we spent our swim time in the family pool, open from 9am, where cabanas provided welcome shade and there was enough room to swim comfortably with our son while families played and children moved in and out of the water. The pool, thankfully, didn’t have an overpowering soundtrack, and our son seemed enthralled by the sea of people around him, swimming, lounging and playing water polo. Entry to Lost World Aquarium is included for hotel guests, and our visit lasted about half an hour, taking us through 14 chambers and 21 marine exhibits. The little one stared at the fish and seemed particularly taken by an Australian lobster before we reached one of the larger halls, where we stopped for family photographs beside the floor-to-ceiling aquarium windows. Little Explorers is another benefit of the resort. Accessible exclusively to hotel guests, the indoor playroom is dedicated to children from infancy to age three, with padded flooring and learning toys giving our son the chance to get out of the pram and move around properly. A late-afternoon visit lasted about 45 minutes before the first big yawn appeared, our cue to leave before the grumbles turned into a meltdown. Nearly 20 years on, Atlantis The Palm still retains the family magic that makes it a bucket-list stay for residents and visitors alike. Its lively atmosphere, sunny interiors, island vibe and attentive staff can make you forget that behind it all is a cracking first-class operation. For parents, the value comes from doing all the usual work of parenting in a more relaxed setting. Ultimately, our son was the arbiter of the stay, and we came away with enough joyful photos of him to know the family break had been a success. Rates for an Imperial Club King Palm View Room are currently about Dh1,750 per night, excluding taxes and fees. Check-in is from 3pm and check-out is by noon. This review was conducted at the invitation of the hotel and reflects hotel standards during this time. Services may change in the future

title: The lessons I've learnt since adopting a puppy
description: Celebrate the victories, tolerate the setbacks - and don't expect it to stick to your plan
content: When is the right time to get a puppy? That is a question I have asked myself a lot this year, both in the run-up to and after adopting Penny, a now-seven-month-old Labrador-mix that joined our family at the end of March. Is it during a regional war or in the first trimester of pregnancy? No, almost definitely not. Would I do it again? In a heartbeat. That said, Penny has been a crash course in canine parenthood , in a way that our older dog Frida was not. I adopted Frida in September 2020. She had been a street dog in Ajman for an unknown amount of time and was found on a construction site, being fed by builders. Malnourished and with a ripped ear, she had all the trappings of a dog with trauma, but has been exactly the opposite. She is gentle and a bit shy, but loves people, is generally very quiet (apart from when the gardener comes by) and sleeps an easy 20 hours a day. Our new arrival has made me realise Frida's behaviour may be more aligned with cats than that of her fellow canine. Penny, however, is pure pup. She approaches every scenario with full enthusiasm, whether that is dinner time, a stroll around the block or a run-in with a disgruntled cat. She has also been a good lesson in discipline, not just for her – but yes, she does need to know how to sit, wait and not forage in bushes for dead rats – but also for us. So far, it has been as wonderful as it has been exhausting. Somewhere between the 2am toilet trips, 5am wake-up calls and the frantic attempts to stop her eating things she absolutely should not eat, I have learnt a few things. Before the puppy, I thought in hours. I would say things like “I'll leave at 7.30” or “Let's go out for lunch”. Now, everything is measured by when she last relieved herself. Has she just been outside? Has she had water? Has she eaten? Has she played? Has she woken up? Has she looked at me in a way that suggests she might need to go out? There was a period when we were taking her outside roughly every 30 minutes (and a low point with a UTI when we were into 15-minute blocks). At one point, it seemed entirely possible that I would spend the rest of my life attaching her to a lead, walking her outside, waiting for her to do her business and responding with the enthusiasm of someone who has just witnessed a major scientific breakthrough. If you’re in the thick of the early hourly toilet breaks, I promise, progress is around the corner. For Penny, it clicked overnight, but the advice is right – accidents are not something you can grumble about or discipline; you need to watch them like a hawk and they will just get it one day. That said, if you don’t have the time to commit to a few months of toilet training (and yes, I do mean months), a new puppy is not for you. One day, everything is going brilliantly. She goes outside, she has perfect recall, she walks nicely on her lead, and she doesn’t chew on anything off-limits. She seems to understand what is expected of her and you briefly allow yourself to believe that you have cracked it. Then the next day she throws it all out of the window. Pees in the living room, annoys Frida (annoys us!), chases after every human and animal she sees, and recall – what is recall? It is easy to think you have gone backwards. But puppies, I have discovered, are not interested in your definition of progress. They are learning, forgetting and learning again, as well as testing their boundaries. I try to celebrate the small victories and accept that there will be setbacks. I like a plan. I like knowing what is happening and when. I like to think that if I prepare properly, I can avoid most problems. A puppy is an excellent way to dismantle this belief. You can establish a routine and she can decide she would rather sleep for two hours. Or, to the contrary, her usual naptime is now playtime. You can take her outside and she can refuse to pee, only to come back inside and immediately do it on the floor. You can buy toys specifically designed for puppies and she will prefer a cardboard box. There is no perfect system. There is only repetition, patience and the occasional deep breath. The same puppy who wakes you up at the crack of dawn is the one who comes running towards you as though she has not seen you for years when you return home. The same dog who has tested every boundary is the one who places a toy on your lap while you’re working, and looks up at you with big puppy-dog eyes. The same tiny creature who has completely disrupted your routine can somehow become part of it with astonishing speed. I still have moments when I wonder what we were thinking, but they don’t last too long. We’re still very much in the thick of training – walking nicely and focusing are top of the list! – but we also have some training to do ourselves. To be patient, to be flexible, to get outside and celebrate tiny achievements. I think I have accepted that life can become considerably more chaotic while also becoming considerably happier. The question of whether this was the right time to get a puppy, then, is perhaps not one I can answer. There probably isn't a right time. There is only a time when you decide that the disruption is worth it. The fact that, come January, we’ll be doing this all over again with a tiny human is something I am still getting my head around. I suspect that, come that arrival, the puppy training will feel like a distant – and very straightforward – memory.

title: How a tribal chief's house built 120 years ago became a boutique hotel on Egypt's Red Sea
description: From Hajj pilgrims to Italian miners, the fascinating story of a seafront home in El Quseir, Egypt's oldest surviving Red Sea port
content: The seafront mashrabiya that drew the gaze of visitors to El Quseir for over a century was first and foremost a status symbol. Sheikh Tawfiq Ali Mustafa, supreme chief of the Red Sea branch of the Ababda tribe, wanted his house, which he built in 1907, to be seen in awe by everyone arriving at the port. Sitting on the corniche of Egypt 's oldest surviving Red Sea town, its carved wooden lattice covering nearly a third of the main facade, it was also meant to signal who ran the town and who visitors would need to see first to get anything done. One hundred and twenty years later, the house is still there, but Sheikh Tawfiq is not, the Italian phosphate company he worked with has departed, and its colonial era ended. The pilgrims his tribe once guided across the desert have long since taken faster routes, and the town itself couldn’t be more different from the one where thousands of Hajjis embarked for Makkah each year. What remains, in the building his grandson Moustafa Sebaq now runs as a six-room boutique hotel, is one of the last physical memories of a Quseir that mattered quite a bit to the wider Muslim world. “The Ababda are fishermen and herders as they have always been,” Mr Sebaq told The National . “But they have also often responded to the massive changes that have happened in the area over the centuries. They guided people to Makkah once, and when that ended for them, they worked with the arriving Europeans and now they have a role in the tourism industry.” The tribe’s arc, from pilgrimage guides to phosphate labourers to hoteliers, is also that of the town’s. For most of its history, El Quseir was one of the main Egyptian points of embarkation for the Hajj . The Ababda, whose lands stretch south to the Sudanese border, guided pilgrims and caravans between the Nile Valley and the Red Sea coast, taking them along the ancient road from Qena over the Eastern Desert to the sea where they sailed to Jeddah. Under Egyptian ruler Muhammad Ali in the first half of the 19th century, El Quseir also became the main port through which Egyptian grain fed the holy cities. By the middle of the 19th century, the town had “acquired a settled population of 6,000 to 8,000 souls”, according to an account of life in El Quseir by German doctor Karl Klunzinger, who lived in the town in the 1860s. The first blow to that world was the Alexandria-Cairo-Suez railway, Mr Sebaq said. Completed in 1858, it offered pilgrims and traders a faster overland route to the Red Sea, through Suez, which proved to be more convenient because it saved travellers the long desert journey to El Quseir. “No one in my family today was alive for the opening of the railway, but it is still remembered in stories about the changes in the tribe’s fortunes, even as far back as that,” Mr Sebaq explains. Klunzinger, writing shortly after, recorded the consequences with a physician's precision: “The number of the government employees was greatly diminished, that of the inhabitants sank to 1,500, whole streets were deserted and fell into ruins.” Within a decade, the opening of the Suez Canal in 1869 delivered the final blow. Ships that used to anchor at El Quseir now steamed straight through to the Mediterranean. It was in this shifting landscape that Sheikh Tawfiq built his house. By then, a new economy was rising along the coast, from which he was to benefit greatly. Italian geologists had begun surveying the Eastern Desert for phosphate, and in 1912 the Banco di Roma founded the Egyptian Phosphate Mining and Trading Company, opening mines and a processing plant at El Quseir that would keep the town alive for another half century. Sheikh Tawfiq, in his role as Sheikh El Mashayekh of the Red Sea Ababda, became the local liaison, the man the Italians needed to explain their presence to the town and the man the townsfolk went to with any grievances about the Italians. “He was the highest chief of the Ababda Red Sea branch, and that necessitated a house with a style that no one else in the town had,” Mr Sebaq said. There are other old houses in Quseir, some of them contemporaneous, but none with the mashrabiya. The sheikh died in 1960, soon after the Italians closed up shop amid a nationalisation wave under Gamal Abdel Nasser . Sheikh Tawfiq married several times, and as his family kept growing, he needed more space to house them, so he eventually acquired another plot in Al Owaina, the neighbourhood inland where most of the Ababda still live, and the family left the old house. By the 1960s, with his widow the last resident, the house was empty. It stayed shut, under the family's ownership, for the better part of three decades. The house's second life began in the late 1990s, when Peter Willem Berg, a Swedish businessman who owned a Radisson resort north of the town, decided he would restore Quseir's old houses at his own expense. Aided by locals who formed committees to carry out his plan, Berg funded a restoration of Sheikh Tawfiq’s house. “He wanted to do the same to many houses in the city, to turn them into boutique hotels that could preserve the city's heritage by incorporating it into its tourism industry, which now was the city's main means of income,” Mr Sebaq said. “He was a good man and he wanted to lift the town up.” Sheikh Tawfiq's house was the first, and by common assessment the most successful. The restoration was deliberately light-touch: infrastructure only, essential systems, no reworking of the original structure. “They kept the house exactly the same as it was before, just gave it some more years to live,” Mr Sebaq said. The house reopened as a hotel in 2000. He built a vocational training centre in the town in 2002 where young men and women were trained in computing. Some were sent to Sweden to qualify as instructors. But heritage projects proved harder to execute and Berg’s hopes for large-scale restoration ground to a halt, leaving the town in urgent need of funds to continue his vision. Mr Sebaq last saw Berg in 2017. He looked frail and was unable to speak much, and the two have not been in touch since. “He told me that he still hoped the town and its beauty could be saved,” Mr Sebaq said of that final meeting. “There is a huge emerging interest in adventure tourism, and we get a lot of people, foreigners and Egyptians, who want to explore the old city and who aren't necessarily here for this upscale five-star experience,” he said. “There is room for both in El Quseir, but what we are missing is the funds to restore the buildings.” The house of the Ababda chief, once the point of first contact for anyone arriving in the port, is now the point of first contact for a small stream of travellers looking for something older than a resort. Whether more of Quseir's old town survives the next few decades depends on whether anyone else follows Berg's lead. For the moment, Sheikh Tawfiq's mashrabiya is still the most conspicuous thing on the corniche, a memento from a bygone world.

title: How social media and nannies can shift a household's default language from Arabic to English
description: Research following 20 families in the UAE is the latest contribution to the debate about Arabic skills among children in the country
content: Pressures from English-language media can crowd out the learning of Arabic by young Emirati children, a study has found. Research following 20 Emirati families has highlighted the way the likes of YouTube and digital learning media, along with English-speaking nannies, can move a household’s “linguistic centre of gravity” towards English. However, the researchers behind the study also found that learning Arabic could be strengthened by, for example, religious study and storytelling, with determined efforts by parents to counteract other influences. The study is the latest contribution to a long-running debate on Arabic skills among children in the UAE, with concerns expressed over a lack of proficiency in the country’s native language among many. Called 'From home to policy: Strengthening Arabic through intentional practices in Emirati early childhoods,' the study has been published in a new book, Early Childhood Education in the Arabian Peninsula . It is written by Dr Nadine Jaafarawi and Dr Fatma Said, both associate professors in applied linguistics at Zayed University. The work involved the researchers spending time over the course of a year with 20 UAE families, each with at least one Emirati parent. The research focused on the learning of Arabic by children aged two to five. One parent told the researchers that hiring English-speaking nannies “gradually shifted the household’s linguistic centre of gravity towards English”. “YouTube, cartoons and digital learning tools in English further normalised her children’s use of English in informal spaces,” the researchers wrote. “These choices, though framed as pragmatic, contributed to English gaining symbolic dominance within the household because of the ease of access children have to technology.” While there is Arabic content on media platforms, Dr Said said material in English was often more appealing. Muhamed Al Khalil, professor of practice in Arabic at NYU Abu Dhabi, who was not connected to the new paper, said the issue of native-language learning being compromised by English was not unique to the UAE or the Arab world. “Established languages of the world are being crowded by English, especially through schooling, science and the media,” he said. But he added the issue was compounded in the UAE by the multilingual environment, with English often the lingua franca, or shared language, for people from different parts of the world. Social media, such as TikTok and Instagram, may also promote English at the expense of Arabic, he suggested. “The fortress for Arabic is the family,” he said. “It’s the parents, the grandparents, who are leading a rearguard battle to keep a certain level of proficiency of Arabic among the children. “The students, as they go to school, they’re surrounded by English from studying, speaking to their peers, social media, pretty much everywhere. Arabic becomes only the heritage language that grandfather speaks, or parents teach them, or an Islamic studies teacher comes and teaches them. This is the risk. It’s more and more becoming a heritage language.” There is, the Zayed University researchers said, much parents can do to improve their children’s Arabic proficiency. Dr Said said online Arabic content could be used to strengthen language skills, preferably when there was an adult who could interact with the child. The parent may, for example, comment on, or reinforce, what is said in a video. Rules within the home about Arabic can also help, with Dr Said saying a family should be consistent in its use of the language. Using only Arabic at the dinner table is one example of a worthwhile rule, she said. It is particularly important for “emotional” and “instructional” interactions to be in Arabic. “These are really important because these are what kids remember: how my mother showed me love or how my mother expressed instructions for such and such. Those always sit with the child,” she said. “I always tell parents: ‘If you take care of your Arabic and you get them to read and listen, and expose them to Arabic media and songs and poetry and these kinds of things, and you are consistent in that, don’t worry about the English, because they will catch up, because that’s the dominant language at school and the media.’” The choice of kindergarten can have “a considerable influence” on a child’s Arabic skills, Dr Jaafarawi said. “If most teaching, play, routines and peer interaction are conducted in English, it can quickly become associated with learning, friendship, confidence and achievement,” she said. “A child may come from a home where the family has worked hard to establish Arabic, but if the kindergarten does not recognise or build upon that foundation, there can be a break between the home and the school.” She said it was not only a question of how much Arabic is on the timetable, but also whether children use Arabic in play, stories, songs and conversations, and whether it was “taught in a lively, age-appropriate way”. “Children in early childhood learn through relationships, repetition, movement, play and meaningful communication,” Dr Jaafarawi said. “A short, isolated Arabic lesson will not necessarily counterbalance an otherwise entirely English environment.” They said the responsibility for ensuring children had good Arabic skills lay not just with families, because optimum outcomes were achieved when homes, government policy and kindergartens were aligned. As a result, they are “very pleased” with policies introduced by Dubai’s Knowledge and Human Development Authority (KHDA) and the Abu Dhabi Department of Education and Knowledge (ADEK) to promote Arabic among younger children. These policies, which come alongside federal efforts by the Ministry of Education, address concerns expressed over many years, some from members of the Federal National Council, about poor Arabic skills among schoolchildren and university students in the UAE. Introduced last year, Dubai’s policy requires Arabic language education to be provided to all children aged up to six years. “KHDA’s policy … calls for Arabic to be taught through play, inquiry, stories and meaningful interaction. It also requires sufficient time with qualified Arabic educators,” Dr Jaafarawi said. ADEK has introduced a requirement for certain lengths of time to be spent on Arabic, with the amounts increasing year-on-year. The researchers said these developments fulfilled many of the requirements highlighted in their study. “However, time allocation alone is not enough,” Dr Jaafarawi said. “The quality and nature of the interaction matter. Arabic should not be presented to children as a difficult, formal or less enjoyable language while English is the language of creativity and play. “It should be experienced as a living language through storytelling, games, exploration, affection and culturally familiar experiences.” Prof Al Khalil has faced issues with his children, as they attend an American school with limited time available for teaching Arabic. He switched them out of Arabic classes, deciding instead that they should be taught the language at home. Other parents, who may not be able to offer high-quality teaching themselves, may consider hiring tutors, he suggested, especially if their children are at private schools, where Arabic teaching may be more limited. “Increasingly I have Emirati friends who are putting the children into more private tutoring for Arabic and it does make a big difference. I’ve seen that,” he said. “ … Just like in my case, you sometimes have to take corrective action, remedial action.”

title: One rep at a time: How Syria’s first Hyrox community is taking shape in Damascus
description: A young population keen to reconnect with the outside world after years of relative isolation has found an outlet with the arrival of the global fitness phenomenon
content: At a small gym in Damascus, a new kind of sporting community is taking shape. Amid pounding music, gruelling workouts and a communal atmosphere, fitness coach Khaled Al Nehlawi is bringing Hyrox to Syria , one rep at a time. After returning to his country with a passion for the global fitness race, which combines running with strength and endurance exercises, the 36-year-old athlete saw an opportunity to introduce it to a generation of young Syrians eager to try something new. What began as a way to continue practising a sport he loves has since grown into Move, Syria’s first Hyrox community. The international fitness phenomenon has grown in popularity in recent years, and Hyrox competitions are now held around the world. Its format is simple but demanding: eight 1km runs, each followed by a functional workout station, including sled pushes and pulls, rowing, walking lunges and wall balls. “Over the past period, I had seen how much energy and enthusiasm young people in Syria have, but the options for modern sports were somewhat limited,” Mr Al Nehlawi told The National. “Since I returned, I felt that I didn’t just want to practise the sport here; I also wanted to build a community around it and give people the opportunity to try something new.” And so, Move was born in April 2026. Short for Make One Victory Every Day, it reflects Mr Al Nehlawi’s philosophy as a fitness coach and his vision of building a community centred on progress, consistency and a shared sense of achievement. “For me, victory isn’t always about winning a race or lifting a heavier weight. Sometimes victory is simply turning up to training when you don’t feel like it, breaking your personal record or even being slightly better than you were yesterday. That’s the idea I want Move to represent,” he said. Since its launch, the Move community has been steadily gaining momentum. Classes are held three days a week at Helfawi Fitness Club, with sessions at 7am and 7pm to accommodate different schedules, and plans to add more as capacity allows. The strong turnout in just a few months has given Mr Al Nehlawi reason to believe that the community has the potential to become something lasting. “I knew there was an interest in sport, but once we started seeing people coming regularly, challenging themselves and asking for more, that’s when I realised there was genuine demand for this type of sport in Syria,” he told The National. Mr Al Nehlawi sees that enthusiasm and appetite as part of a broader shift among young Syrians, particularly following the fall of the Assad regime and Syria’s subsequent efforts to reconnect with and reintegrate into the wider world. “Syrian young people have always had ambition and energy, but sometimes the circumstances around them limited their ability to turn that energy into projects and ideas. Today, I see more people willing to try something new, build communities and think about what Syria could look like in the future,” he said. For Mr Al Nehlawi, that openness matters because sport can offer more than just physical benefits. It can create spaces for people to meet, connect, support one another and work towards a shared goal. “One of the most rewarding things was seeing young men and women training together and encouraging one another. That’s exactly the kind of community I wanted to build,” he told The National. “We want anyone who joins Move to feel that they have become part of something bigger than themselves, whether their goal is to compete in a Hyrox race, improve their fitness, or simply lead a more active lifestyle.” Now, Mr Al Nehlawi hopes to take the community beyond the capital, with ambitions of seeing Syrian athletes compete and represent their country in Hyrox races abroad, while eventually establishing Damascus as a destination for the sport. “I hope the day comes when we see athletes from different countries coming to Damascus to compete in a Hyroox race, while at the same time discovering Syria through sport.”

title: The Middle Eastern journeys that inspired Agatha Christie's greatest mysteries
description: The Nile, Petra, Baghdad ... the region provided some of the most atmospheric settings for the Queen of Crime's works. The murders may have been fictional, but her travels were real
content: Agatha Christie brings to mind English villages, country houses, Hercule Poirot, Miss Marple and suspects hiding in plain sight. But that’s only half the picture. Some of her finest novels were born hundreds of miles from England, amid desert excavations, Nile riverboats and rose-red stone cities. Fifty years after her death in 1976, Christie remains one of the world's bestselling novelists, with more than two billion books sold. Those Middle Eastern novels are a significant reason why. Christie had fallen under the region's spell long before she met archaeologist Max Mallowan, her second husband. As a young woman, she travelled to Egypt with her mother, attending Cairo's winter social season as a debutante. The trip inspired Snow Upon the Desert , her first novel. It was never published but led to a fascination that shaped her work for decades. “The Middle East was very important to her,” says Christie historian Mark Aldridge. “Her interests in archaeology and, in turn, the Middle East actually predate meeting Max. She was fascinated by the cultures, especially their more romantic elements, alongside their history and people.” After the breakdown of her first marriage, Christie made a decision that changed her life – and her writing. In 1928, she boarded the Orient Express alone and travelled east, an unusually independent move for a woman of her time and background. “I thought: It's now or never,” Christie later wrote. “Either I cling to everything that's safe and that I know, or else I develop more initiative, do things on my own.” The journey took her to the archaeological site of Ur, in present-day Iraq , where she met Mallowan. They married in 1930. Over the following decades, Christie spent months each year with him across Iraq and Syria, helping to document excavations while writing her many novels. She was far more than an observer. “Agatha was an integral part of the dig,” Aldridge says. “Her job was mainly to photograph the objects, and she even cleaned some of them with her face cream – not something that we would typically recommend. She also wrote on the digs, as she had a travel typewriter and said she just needed a steady table to work.” The image of Christie typing beside an excavation, a parasol between her and the desert sun, explains why archaeology feels so convincing in her fiction. The camps, rivalries and daily routines in Murder in Mesopotamia are not imagined. They came from years of living alongside archaeologists and local workers. “You can definitely see specific locations being referenced, as well as the types of people you might meet,” Aldridge says. “In Murder in Mesopotamia , the dig is populated with characters influenced by people she had met during the excavations.” Christie's memoir Come, Tell Me How You Live , written during the Second World War, presents a lighter portrait of those years: dusty camps, endless packing, shared meals and long conversations after dark. “An archaeologist,” she joked, “is the best husband a woman can have. The older she gets, the more interested he is in her.” Published in 1937, Death on the Nile is one of Christie's best works, a murder mystery that unfolds aboard the fictional paddle steamer Karnak as it travels between Luxor and Aswan . The novel is remembered for its denouement but also for its atmosphere: the ancient temples, broad riverbanks and desert cliffs where the tension builds. Christie knew the journey well. She had travelled the Nile herself, visited Abu Simbel and the temples around Luxor, and stayed at the Old Cataract Hotel in Aswan and the Winter Palace in Luxor. Perhaps that’s why the novel lingers over the landscape as the river moves steadily south, passengers disembark to explore monuments, and the vastness of Egypt quietly tightens the tension. Michelle Kazmer, whose research examines Golden Age detective fiction, believes Christie's settings endure because they were so closely observed. “Agatha Christie was an extraordinarily active and keen observer of the world around her,” Kazmer says. “She spent enough time at these locations to really immerse herself, and participated in the archaeological work.” Rather than describing famous sites from a distance, Christie lets readers experience them through the characters. Abu Simbel appears through multiple perspectives, each one revealing something different. “As each character interacts with a place in their own way, the place takes on the depth of character as well,” Kazmer explains. From Egypt, Christie's journeys continued east: to Baghdad, the Syrian desert, and eventually one of the ancient world's most extraordinary cities. Jordan's Petra is one of the Middle East's most photographed landmarks. Visitors emerge from the narrow Siq to see the intricately carved Al Khazneh rising from the sandstone cliffs. But Christie saw something else. In Appointment with Death , published in 1938, Petra isn’t just a beautiful site; it is isolating, ancient and faintly unsettling, seemingly the right place for a family coming apart at the seams. The novel follows travellers from Jerusalem to Petra, where a murder interrupts an ordinary sightseeing trip. The towering cliffs and winding paths do much of the storytelling. “Petra was pink, rose red, yellow and violet, changing colour all the time,” Christie writes. Again, Christie uses the technique of offering observations on a location through the eyes of different characters, giving the landscape itself an emotional life. “This is the case with Abu Simbel in Death on the Nile , and she uses a similar technique in Appointment with Death ,” she says. Petra inspires wonder for one character, Sarah King. For others, it becomes oppressive. The landscape doesn't change, only the emotions do. Visitors today can still follow much of that journey, through the Siq to the Treasury , up to the Monastery or the High Place of Sacrifice. Petra by Night, when hundreds of candles illuminate the approach to Al Khazneh, offers the same quiet drama Christie captured in print. Baghdad, meanwhile, gave Christie the chance to try something altogether different. Published in 1951, They Came to Baghdad is less a detective story than a political thriller. The protagonist, Victoria Jones, arrives in Iraq with little money and even fewer plans, and gets pulled into espionage and international intrigue. “ They Came to Baghdad has the excitement of the main character travelling without the confidence of a solid plan or solid financial resources. That adds an additional layer of discovery,” Kazmer says. The novel reflects a city Christie knew well. Baghdad in the mid-20th century was a crossroads of diplomats, archaeologists, traders and travellers. Christie visited often during the years she accompanied Mallowan on excavations across Iraq, paying as much attention to ordinary life as she did to famous sites. “She enjoyed exploring new places, and in particular meeting people and finding out about their history,” Aldridge says. “She was famously shy in group or social settings, but remained very interested in people. That is particularly true of the locals who worked on Max's digs.” Those encounters shaped Christie's work as much as the landscapes did. The archaeologists, guides and fellow travellers who fill her Middle Eastern novels reflect years of careful observation: conversations over shared meals, long afternoons at excavation sites, and an eye for the detail that only time in a place provides. Much has changed since Christie travelled through Egypt, Iraq and Jordan . Steamers still sail the Nile between Luxor and Aswan, in considerably more comfort than Poirot might have recognised. The PS Sudan, often cited as the inspiration for the fictional Karnak, still cruises the river. The Old Cataract in Aswan and the Winter Palace Hotel in Luxor still welcome guests. In Jordan, Petra is every bit as extraordinary as it was when Christie first saw it. “Christie's books continue to fascinate readers because they are plotted and written so very well,” Kazmer says. “Her Middle Eastern novels in particular are fascinating today because they also represent first-hand experiences of locations that few people have the opportunity to visit.” The greatest legacy of those journeys, though, isn't in the hotels or the heritage sites. It's in how Christie wrote about them. Unlike many travel writers of her era, she had no interest in presenting the Middle East as an exotic backdrop. Her memoir Come, Tell Me How You Live is full of gentle humour rather than grand adventures: stories about unpacking supplies, coping with dust, sharing meals with excavation teams and finding somewhere steady enough to balance a typewriter. Perhaps that's why Christie’s novels still feel alive. Their settings are never reduced to postcards. Egypt brings to mind more than pyramids, Iraq more than ancient ruins, and Jordan more than rock-cut monuments. Christie once observed: “To travel is to discover that everyone is wrong about other countries.” She spent much of her life proving it. The murders may be fictional. But the journeys were real.

title: The future of Gulf security lies beyond Hormuz
description: The waterway remains important but overreliance on it has become a vulnerability
content: The most important lesson of the 2026 Hormuz crisis is not that the strait has become less important. It is that Hormuz has become so important that dependence on it is itself a strategic vulnerability. For decades, Gulf security was built on a familiar map: the Strait of Hormuz was the region’s gateway to the world, and the American military presence was the principal external guarantor of freedom of navigation as well as the regional balance of power. Above all, that architecture was designed to keep the strait open . The events of this year have exposed the limits of that approach. Protecting Hormuz remains essential, but it is no longer enough. A region whose energy exports, trade and economic security remain heavily concentrated on a single narrow passage leaves itself vulnerable whenever that passage becomes part of a military confrontation or a negotiating strategy. Iran has understood this vulnerability for decades. It does not need to control the Gulf, or field a navy capable of matching US maritime power, to impose significant costs on its neighbours and the global economy. It only needs to make passage through Hormuz dangerous enough, expensive enough and uncertain enough for the effects to travel far beyond the strait itself. That is how Iran has turned geographic constraint into strategic leverage. The most sustainable Gulf response should therefore not be confined to adding military power within the same narrow space. It should also seek to reduce the value that any adversary can extract from disrupting it. The challenge, at its core, is no longer merely how to defend Hormuz, but how to make its disruption less capable of paralysing the region or reshaping its political calculations. None of this diminishes the importance of the strait. Hormuz will remain a principal route of the global energy trade, and safeguarding navigation through it will remain an indispensable Gulf and international interest. Dependence is even greater in the case of liquefied natural gas: Qatari LNG exports passing through Hormuz account for a highly significant share of global LNG trade, and there is currently no equivalent overland alternative. However, defending Hormuz is one thing. Building a security strategy on the assumption that it will always remain an indispensable route is another. This is why infrastructure developed over previous decades is acquiring a new strategic meaning. Saudi Arabia’s East-West crude oil pipeline, or Petroline, which connects the country’s eastern oil fields with export facilities at Yanbu on the Red Sea, and the Abu Dhabi Crude Oil Pipeline, or Adcop, which runs to the Fujairah export terminal outside Hormuz, are no longer merely energy projects or instruments of export diversification. They have become part of the national security architecture itself. The same is true of ports outside the strait, the development of Duqm and Salalah, plus overland corridors, rail links and logistics networks that expand the Gulf’s options between the Gulf itself, the Arabian Sea and the Red Sea. Their value is not simply that they provide another route. It is that they make it harder for any adversary to turn one narrow passage into a source of region-wide leverage. This is what might be called “deterrence through geography”. Deterrence is not only about convincing an adversary that the cost of an attack will be high. It can also mean reducing what that adversary expects to gain from disruption in the first place. The more capable Gulf states become of rerouting exports, trade and supplies through different outlets, the less political and military value there is in threatening to close or disrupt Hormuz. Ports and pipelines therefore belong in the security conversation alongside air and missile defence and naval power. So do supply chains and overland infrastructure. The objective is not to make Hormuz irrelevant – that is impossible – but to make the threat of disrupting it less decisive. There are obvious limits. Escaping one chokepoint does not help much if it simply means moving into another. Bab Al Mandeb and the Red Sea have themselves faced growing levels of threat in recent years, while the Arabian Sea and Indian Ocean are increasingly part of a wider strategic contest. So, the answer cannot simply be “alternatives to Hormuz”. It has to be a broader system in which no single route, partner or security arrangement becomes indispensable. That changes the map of Gulf security. In the next phase, that security will not begin at the Gulf coast and end at the Strait of Hormuz. It will extend westwards to the Red Sea and Bab Al Mandeb , across the Arabian Sea and the Gulf of Oman, and further east into the Indian Ocean. The ports, sea lanes, naval actors and supply chains across this wider space will increasingly determine how well Gulf states can absorb future shocks. This also changes the meaning of relations with neighbouring and nearby powers. Oman is an obvious example. Its importance comes not only from its place within the Gulf system, but from its direct access to the Arabian Sea and a coastline that reaches beyond the Hormuz chokepoint. Duqm and Salalah are therefore not simply commercial assets. They give the region maritime depth that becomes more valuable precisely when Hormuz is under pressure. India enters the picture for a different reason. It is already one of the Gulf’s major energy markets and economic partners, but it is also a central naval power in the Indian Ocean. Its interest in keeping the sea lanes between the Gulf and Asia open overlaps directly with Gulf concerns. Over time, this relationship may have to move beyond energy security and into the wider maritime domain. Pakistan adds another layer. Its position on the Arabian Sea, its military capabilities and its longstanding ties with Gulf states make it relevant to any strategy that treats the space east of Hormuz as strategic depth rather than simply a trade route. Turkey is less directly connected to Hormuz itself, but that does not make it peripheral. Its significance lies in widening the Gulf’s room for strategic manoeuvre, linking it to the Red Sea, the Eastern Mediterranean and Central Asia, and bringing additional military and political weight into a more diversified regional network. Seen in that light, the Makkah defence agreement between Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan, signed on August 7, matters for more than its trilateral format. It would be a mistake to read it either as the nucleus of an alliance intended to replace the US or as an arrangement aimed exclusively at Iran. Its more important meaning is that Gulf security thinking is beginning to move beyond a model in which Washington sits at the centre of every external security equation. The aim is not to displace the US, but to create more options around it. For the foreseeable future, the US will remain the power best equipped to provide some of the most critical elements of maritime security and advanced protection across the Gulf and the Indian Ocean. But there is a significant difference between Washington serving as a central pillar in a broader network and treating it as the sole answer to every regional vulnerability. The Gulf does not need to replace one security umbrella with another. It needs a more distributed architecture: stronger national capabilities; better-integrated Gulf defence ; a durable strategic relationship with the US; deeper ties with powers along the Arabian Sea and Indian Ocean; and infrastructure that gives Gulf economies more room to keep functioning when one route comes under pressure. The strategic value of this approach lies in how it changes the logic of coercion. An adversary that believes disruption in Hormuz can quickly produce broad economic paralysis possesses an unusually powerful instrument. If Gulf states can absorb more of the shock, divert part of their flows and rely on different ports and corridors, the expected return from escalation begins to fall. Iran has long invested in a geographic fact that Gulf states cannot alter: one of the region’s most important arteries passes through a narrow corridor directly adjacent to Iranian territory. But not everything else is fixed. Ports can be expanded. Energy routes can be diversified. New links can connect existing corridors. Partnerships can be built around different parts of the maritime space. None of these measures eliminates vulnerability, and none removes the need to defend Hormuz itself. What they do is give Gulf states more choices when pressure rises and reduce the ability of any single disruption to dictate the region’s strategic behaviour. That is the broader lesson of 2026. The future of Gulf security will depend not only on defending the places where the region is geographically exposed, but on making better use of the geography beyond them. The wider the network of ports , energy routes, logistics corridors and security partnerships, the harder it becomes for any single chokepoint to determine the region’s choices. The question, then, is no longer simply how to keep Hormuz open. It is how to build a Gulf that can continue to trade, export, manoeuvre and make strategic decisions even when Hormuz is under pressure. If Tehran has spent decades turning geographic narrowness into leverage, the Gulf’s next strategic task is to turn geographic breadth into resilience.

title: Security Council holds second secret straw poll for next UN chief
description: Guyana's Carolyn Rodrigues-Birkett receives most votes out of eight candidates
content: The UN Security Council held its second secret straw poll on Friday in the race to succeed Secretary General Antonio Guterres , as eight candidates compete for the international organisation's top job. The informal ballot was intended to gauge support for candidates before the 15-member council makes a formal recommendation to the General Assembly , which appoints the Secretary General under the UN Charter. Security Council members marked each candidate as “encouraged”, “discouraged” or “no opinion expressed”. As in the first poll on July 30, ballots cast by the five veto-wielding permanent members – Britain, China, France, Russia and the US – will be indistinguishable from those of the 10 elected members. No official record has been kept, and the ballots were destroyed after the vote. Latvia and Russia were appointed as tellers on Thursday. ​A diplomat told reporters after the non-binding voting by the 15 ​members that Guyana's Carolyn Rodrigues-Birkett received eight “encourage” votes, the highest of the eight candidates, while Costa Rica's Rebeca Grynspan, the front-runner last month, and Argentina's Rafael Grossi each received seven. The latest candidate to enter the race, Ecuador's Ivonne Baki , received zero “encourage” votes and eight “discourage” votes, according to a diplomat. Russia’s ambassador to the UN, Vasily Nebenzya, told reporters on Thursday: “If there is a deadlock on any of the candidates we are seeing today, if nobody … flies, then I think that we may see other candidates as well.” The field expanded to eight following Tonga's nomination on August 17 of Ecuadorian diplomat Ms Baki. She joined Michelle Bachelet of Chile, Maria Fernanda Espinosa of Ecuador, Olara Otunnu of Uganda and former Senegalese president Macky Sall, alongside Mr Grossi, Ms Grynspan and Ms Rodrigues-Birkett.
