All eight candidates have participated in dialogues with both the General Assembly and Security Council. A candidate needs at least nine votes from the Security Council to advance but must also avoid a veto from any of the five permanent members, whose competing interests can complicate the selection. If a candidate clears both hurdles, the Security Council recommends that person to the General Assembly, where the full UN membership formally confirms the appointment. The informal voting system has been part of the selection process since the 1980s, although some UN member states have criticised it for its secrecy and lack of transparency. Daniel Forti, head of UN affairs at the International Crisis Group, said the straw polls were “created to help reduce gridlock among the P5 [five permanent members] as they negotiate during the selection process”. He said the polls also helped to show the opinions of the council's 10 elected members, whose backing is necessary for a candidate to secure the nine votes required to advance. “The permanent members cannot recommend a SG [Secretary General] candidate to the General Assembly without some support from the E10,” Mr Forti told The National.

title: Microsoft-backed Three Mile Island reboot meets data centre backlash
description: Pennsylvania emerges as test of whether AI industry can boost energy capacity without angering voters
content: A 262-tonne transformer that had been shipped from South Korea arrived in Pennsylvania this week as the US state pushes ahead with plans to revive the Three Mile Island nuclear reactor . The restart of the plant, which suffered a partial meltdown in 1979, has emerged as a crucial test to see whether the tech companies driving the artificial intelligence race can build new power sources without attracting more public fury, amid a backlash over rising energy costs and environmental concerns. On Wednesday, the company behind the Three Mile Island refurbishment, Constellation Energy, shared video of the first of three massive transformers arriving at the site in Middletown, on the back of an oversized lorry. Constellation Energy is restarting the reactor's Unit 1 and has renamed it the Crane Clean Energy Centre . Plans for the restart of Unit 1 are rooted in the AI boom , which needs energy to power the proliferation of data centres that help to handle mushrooming processing needs. The reboot is rooted in a 2024 announcement of a partnership between Constellation and Microsoft. As part of the deal, Microsoft agreed to a 20-year power purchase agreement with Constellation to help provide energy for its data centres. A lot has changed since 2024, and public sentiment about AI and data centres has taken a turn. A fast-growing backlash against the construction of data centres has emerged as a key issue before the US midterm elections in November. Communities are upset by the noise that data centres sometimes make, their huge demand for water for cooling, and rising electricity bills. Voters are also becoming increasingly wary of the impact that AI will have on the labour market. This week, Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro, a Democrat, responded to the public's souring mood towards data centres. He signed off on new rules and regulations that he said would make data centre developers more accountable to residents of Pennsylvania and, in turn, make it more difficult for developers to build without fulfilling certain requirements. Mr Shapiro, seen by many as eyeing a presidential run in 2028, has been a staunch proponent for restarting Three Mile Island's (TMI) Unit 1, which has been offline since 2019. A representative from his office told The National that despite the recent crackdown on data centre development, the governor still supports the partnership between Constellation and Microsoft. “He's an all of the above energy governor,” the representative said, referencing several forms of energy, including nuclear. The representative also said the Three Mile Island reboot addressed some AI criticism because the Microsoft partnership ensured that the technology giant was contributing energy to the grid. Still, the partnership between Constellation Energy and Microsoft continues to raise concerns. TMI Unit 1 is near TMI Unit 2, the site of one of the largest nuclear accidents in US history. In March 1979, the core of TMI Unit 2 was partially exposed, prompting a temporary evacuation of the nearby area and a lengthy clean-up around Middletown that continues to this day. That disaster led to the creation of Three Mile Island Alert, a grass roots energy safety organisation in Pennsylvania. TMI Alert president Eric Epstein said the organisation was challenging the restart of TMI Unit 1 every step of the way. Safety concerns aside, Mr Epstein highlighted the $1 billion taxpayer loan provided to Constellation last year to help expedite the restart. His group has also taken issue with the reactor's proposed use of water from the adjacent Susquehanna River. “Although the Susquehanna River Basin Commission allowed increased water consumption at Three Mile Island, almost all of the 440 public comments were in opposition,” he said, referring to the pushback from residents in and around the reactor's operating area. Mr Epstein also said that despite Mr Shapiro backing the Three Mile Island restart, the anti-AI tide would continue to gain momentum. “Elections will decide the fate of Three Mile Island, and November 2026 comes before the proposed restart,” he said. “Blind support of data centres and nuclear power has led to increased electric prices and water depletion.” Mr Epstein added that TMI Alert is litigating various aspects of the reactor's restart in federal court and challenging the Pennsylvania Department of Environmental Protection's decision to approve a licence for the reactor. Meanwhile, Constellation Energy still needs to make it through the many regulatory hurdles posed by the US Nuclear Regulatory Commission to begin operating again. Constellation Energy does not seem rattled. “This is a huge milestone in our efforts to bring 835MW of reliable, emissions-free power back online in 2027,” the company's statement read in a video showing the transformer making its way to Three Mile Island.

title: British PM Burnham tells terror attack victims ‘you are not alone’
description: UK holds first national day for victims and survivors of terrorism
content: British Prime Minister Andy Burnham has pledged to discuss plans for a permanent memorial for the victims and survivors of terrorism, as he marked the UK’s first national day dedicated to them. The National Day for Victims and Survivors of Terrorism seeks to honour those lives and recognise people who have been marked forever by attacks on British soil and overseas. Speaking at the inaugural ceremony in London , Mr Burnham expressed his “deep admiration” for the survivors and victims’ families and said the government would do more to support them. “Too often people have not had the support they deserve,” he said. He spoke of his own experience dealing with victims of the Manchester Arena attack in 2017 and the Heaton Park Synagogue attack last year when he was mayor of the city. The UK government will look at reforming the Criminal Injuries Compensation Authority as well as access to legal assistance for victims, Mr Burnham said. “There is something remarkable about how we come together as a country in those darkest moments,” he said. “As time passes, most people go back to their lives, but for those who lived through the trauma, there is no return to normality. “Today matters because it says you are not alone. You have not been forgotten. This is a moment to remember the loved ones lost and anyone who has survived the very worst of humanity.” The ceremony followed the launch of a support hub for victims in early June, which provides specialist trauma-informed support for anyone affected by a terrorist incident, including a free helpline. The consequences of terrorism last “years and decades”, warned Thelma Stober, who survived the 7/7 bomb attacks in London in 2005 and has since dedicated her life to supporting other survivors. “Resilience is not about forgetting, it is about finding the strength to continue despite profound loss and adversity,” she said, Cheryl Stollery, whose husband John was killed in the 2015 terror attack in a holiday resort in Sousse, Tunisia, told the audience that she missed him every day. “As long as we live, they too will live, for they are now a part of us as we remember them,” she said. Paul Price sustained life-changing injuries and lost his partner Elaine in the Manchester Arena bombing. He described how “the world I knew was gone” without her and with the disabilities he has had to tackle with physiotherapy. “I will never be the man I was before 22 May, 2017. That man died in the City Room [foyer] with Elaine. The man who emerged had to adapt every part of daily life – physical, emotionally and practically.”

title: World Bank projects Lebanon's GDP to contract by 6.4 per cent in 2026
description: Last year's rebound 'sharply interrupted' by March escalation between Hezbollah and Israel
content: Lebanon's economy is projected to contract by 6.4 per cent in 2026 due to the Israel -Hezbollah war, the World Bank said on Friday. Earlier this month, Lebanon's Economy Minister Amr Bisat told The National that the country's economy was expected to contract by 7 per cent this year due to the resumption of the conflict in March. The projections deal a blow to a brief window of optimism after Lebanon showed estimated real GDP growth of 4.2 per cent in 2025. “The rebound, supported by stronger consumption, investment, tourism and improved high-frequency indicators, was sharply interrupted by the March 2026 escalation in conflict, which further damaged housing and infrastructure, displaced communities, disrupted supply chains and weighed heavily on tourism and domestic demand,” the World Bank said in the summer edition of its Lebanon Economic Monitor. Lebanon is heavily reliant on imports and thus more exposed to shocks such as the disruption to shipping and energy supplies caused by the Iran war. “Lebanon’s fragile recovery has been sharply set back by the renewed conflict, adding to an already severe social and economic crisis,” said Dahlia Khalifa, World Bank Middle East director. “Advancing reforms – particularly on banking sector restructuring and fiscal management – will be critical to restoring confidence, protecting stability, and mobilising the financing needed for reconstruction and recovery.” Lebanon is still dealing with the effects of the economic crisis that emerged in 2019, which the World Bank has described as one of the worst in modern history. The Lebanese currency lost more than 95 per cent of its value against the US dollar on the parallel market. Informal capital controls by commercial banks meant many Lebanese people were locked out of their life savings. “Public debt remains unsustainable, and debt restructuring negotiations have yet to begin,” the World Bank said. “Inflation is also expected to rise to 17.5 per cent in 2026, driven by supply disruptions, higher shipping costs, and rising oil prices, further reducing people’s purchasing power.” While the local currency has stabilised at around 90,000 Lebanese pounds to the dollar, the World Bank warned it could come under pressure if foreign inflows decline or conflict-related shocks continue. Meanwhile, Israel continues to occupy vast swathes of southern Lebanon and has shown no sign of an imminent withdrawal. Hezbollah has shown no inclination to hand over its weapons, so the unstable situation is expected to continue. “These new losses compound the damage from the 2024 conflict, before recovery from that episode could take hold,” the World Bank said, referring to the previous round of war between Hezbollah and Israel in 2024.

title: World Central Kitchen deaths: Israel told it's 'shameful' not to investigate Gaza attack
description: Nations condemn decision after Israel says strike that killed seven aid workers was justified
content: The UK , Australia, Canada and Poland have condemned Israel’s decision not to pursue criminal charges for the killing of humanitarian aid workers in Gaza in April 2024. Britons James Henderson, James Kirby and John Chapman were three of seven people killed in repeated Israeli drone strikes while delivering humanitarian aid with the World Central Kitchen in Gaza. Though Israel described the killing as a mistake and a failure at the time, on Wednesday its military said the strike was justified and that it would not be pressing criminal charges. In a joint statement, the British, Australian and Canadian foreign ministries described the announcement as “shameful”. “Announcing this decision on World Humanitarian Day, while the world honoured the courage and sacrifice of humanitarians, was particularly egregious,” the statement said. “In the more than two years since, we have been pressing for Israel to swiftly and thoroughly consider the case and hold those responsible to account,” the statement added. “The victims of this incident and their families deserve justice and accountability, and we will continue to seek answers on their behalf.” It also signalled a lack of faith in Israel’s professed ability to hold its own military and institutions to account. “The World Central Kitchen attack is one of countless incidents in Gaza where there has been no accountability,” the statement said. “Gaza remains one of the deadliest places to deliver aid, with 186 humanitarian workers killed in 2025.” Australian aid worker Zomi Frankcom and Canadian-American Jacob Flickinger were also killed, as well as Polish national Damian Sobol and Palestinian Saif Abu Taha. Poland's foreign ministry said it was “very disappointed” by the decision and had summoned ​Israel's ​ambassador in Warsaw. Deputy Foreign Minister Ignacy ⁠Niemczycki told public radio PR1 on ​Friday: “We believe ​that the ‌use of force must be proportionate, and that inappropriate use of ⁠force should have consequences, so we expect clarification on this matter.” Australia also summoned Israel's ambassador in Canberra on Thursday. The Israeli military on Wednesday said that it had reason to target the aid convoy because it had identified a gunman on a lorry while it was on a route to a warehouse. This is the UK government’s fourth intervention on the Palestinian issue this week, marking a shift in tone and a tougher stance on Israel. This was signalled at the start of Andy Burnham's premiership in July, when he insisted that the Labour Party had got its policy wrong at the start of the Israel-Gaza war. On Wednesday, Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband condemned the launch of an Israeli tender for the E1 settlement project, and summoned the country’s charge d’affaires. On Thursday, Mr Burnham was among seven leaders to call for Israel to halt the settlement project and warn businesses of “consequences” if they bid for construction tenders. Minister for the Middle East Stephen Doughty also called on Israel to allow more humanitarian relief into Gaza following a visit to aid warehouses in Al Arish, on the Egyptian border with the strip. But the condemnation is unlikely to provide comfort to the victims’ families, who have not yet publicly commented on the decision. The National spoke to James Henderson’s brother, Matt, last year, who described his family’s relentless efforts to push the UK government to do more to pressure Israel for answers. “We’ve spoken to people on the ground in Gaza, they give you different stories, different names. Not everything has been shared with us. There’s more information out there, it’s not been given, it’s not been shared. My question is, why?”

title: US-Oman ties face strain as Muscat walks tightrope between Washington and Tehran
description: Oman has little choice but to keep diplomacy alive
content: Oman has spent decades cultivating a reputation as one of the Middle East’s most reliable diplomatic go-betweens, maintaining a long-standing strategic partnership with the US while preserving close ties with Iran. That balancing act is now facing a serious test, with Oman’s relationship with the US under pressure. President Donald Trump threatened this week to bomb Oman if it “gets in the way” of US efforts to end the war with Iran and reopen the Strait of Hormuz. Washington and Tehran remain divided over how to end their months-long conflict, while Muscat has pursued separate discussions with Tehran over arrangements for navigation through the strategic waterway. Mr Trump himself agreed in a signed document that Oman would “conduct dialogue” with Iran to define the future administration and maritime services in the strait. “Oman’s negotiations with Iran over a mechanism to manage the Strait of Hormuz appear to have been a bilateral Iran-Oman effort, though it’s true that the memorandum of understanding from June endorsed a 60-day Iranian-Omani mechanism,” Marc Sievers, former US ambassador to Oman, told The National . “It is also true that the US and Iran understood this point differently, which led to the collapse of the MoU.” The 14-point deal negotiated in Islamabad and signed on June 17 was intended as an interim framework for ending the war, opening a window for negotiations on a longer-term nuclear agreement. The MoU expired on Monday after the broader understanding had already collapsed amid a flurry of tit-for-tat strikes. The main dispute centred on how each side interpreted the clause on the Strait of Hormuz . Iran viewed the language in the text as recognising its right to manage the whole strait. Washington, however, took it to mean that Iran must guarantee freedom of navigation and refrain from using access to strategic waterways as leverage. Oman shares the strait with Iran. On Monday, the Iranian Foreign Ministry said Muscat and Tehran had reached an “understanding” regarding the waterway and were working to finalise a joint statement. This appears to have angered Mr Trump. “I assume US-Oman relations are tense following President Trump’s comment, but it’s not the first time,” said Mr Sievers, referring to an earlier threat by Mr Trump. “He said it back in May as well and nothing happened.” In late May, asked whether he would accept a deal that would give Oman and Iran control of the strait, Mr Trump said: “Nobody is going to control it. It’s international waters and Oman will behave just like everybody else, or we will have to blow them up.” The latest threat by Mr Trump represents a deterioration in the political atmosphere between Washington and Muscat but does not amount to a rupture in the relationship. Oman has been a US partner for almost 200 years. Relations between the countries can be traced back to 1833, when they signed the Treaty of Amity and Commerce. Informal trade began even earlier, with American businesses using Omani ports as early as 1790. Oman was also the first Arab country to recognise the newly independent United States, sending an envoy to New York in 1840. Mr Trump’s “outbursts come from a place of anger and frustration, and they will come and go, but US-Oman relations have a long history and will survive these issues,” said Anna Jacobs, a non-resident fellow at the Arab Gulf States Institute. “Ties between the two countries right now are not in the best place but, either way, the US needs Oman to figure out Hormuz and for serious, longer-term negotiations with Iran,” she told The National . The Omani government did not respond publicly to Mr Trump’s latest comments. Omani political commentator Zakaria Al Muharrmi criticised the US President’s language in a post on X. “America's wise leaders know that Oman is the one that freed many detained American citizens in Tehran, and that it is the one that convinced the Houthis to stop shelling American warships and that it is the key to the solution in the Strait of Hormuz crisis,” he wrote. “Trump must watch his words.” During the Iran war , Oman faced retaliatory strikes targeting its ports and energy infrastructure but still took part in negotiations aimed at reaching a resolution and maintained diplomatic channels with the Islamic republic. Iran has also launched retaliatory strikes against the other five Gulf states, as well as Gulf-linked vessels . Mr Sievers believes “Oman has not behaved as a neutral mediator in this conflict but tipped towards endorsing some of Iran’s positions”. Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei said this week the proposed mechanism for control of Hormuz seeks to protect the interests of both Iran and Oman while allowing commercial shipping to pass through. For Oman, keeping the strait open is not only about global energy security or US strategic interests. The waterway borders Oman’s territory , specifically the Musandam governorate, and any escalation around it directly affects Omani security. “All of this is a matter of urgent national security for Oman; this is about their sovereign waters, protecting their territory and stabilising their region,” said Ms Jacobs. “It’s no secret they are caught in a very difficult position. Their policy of neutrality is being tested as American and Iranian pressure is mounting. But they are working hard to stick to their principles of neutrality, international law, protecting their national interests and finding a compromise solution in Hormuz.” Omani Foreign Minister Badr Albusaidi said on Thursday his country remains committed to maritime security and rejects escalation or conflict. He also said achieving sustainable security in the strait requires lasting regional peace based on restraint, diplomacy and continued engagement. Analysts say Oman is not expected to abandon diplomacy, and for Washington, the Gulf state remains an important regional actor whose access to Tehran and position along Hormuz make it difficult to sideline. “Muscat doesn’t have the luxury of giving up on mediation or diplomacy,” said Ms Jacobs. “They will double down on their diplomatic efforts.”

title: Emiratis working part-time in public and private sectors to receive pension coverage
description: Citizens working eight to 32 hours per week will be eligible
content: Emiratis working part-time in the public and private sectors will be covered by the UAE pension system, the General Pension and Social Security Authority said on Friday. Under the regulations, part-time employees can be registered in the pension system if they work between eight and 32 hours a week, or between one and four days a week. This is equivalent to between 20 and 80 per cent of full-time working hours. Emirati citizens employed on part-time contracts will be eligible for the coverage under UAE pension law. “The initiative aligns with evolving labour market dynamics, supports flexible on-site, remote and hybrid work models, and promotes financial security and stability for all citizens,” the GPSSA said. An employee’s service period and pension benefits will be calculated proportionately, based on the number of hours worked and the approved contribution-calculation salary for the relevant period. Employers are responsible for registering eligible Emirati part-time workers with GPSSA. They must also update information on the authority’s Maashi platform when an insured employee moves from a full-time position to a part-time contract. Employees can join the part-time pension system by submitting a request to their human resources department, which allows their employer to register them. The GPSSA said extending social security protection across different types of employment would give Emiratis greater flexibility to balance their careers with other commitments, including education and caring for family members. “The part-time pension framework ensures continuity of service when individuals move between full-time and part-time roles, supporting their long-term financial and social well-being,” the authority said. Emiratis covered by the pension system can qualify for benefits including a retirement pension or end-of-service gratuity, a disability pension in cases of medical unfitness and survivors' pensions for eligible beneficiaries following the death of an insured person.

title: Could Abu Dhabi's 'smart ambulances' transform rapid-response health care?
description: Emergency vehicles and control room will share real-time information to ensure patients receive optimum care in minimum time
content: A new fleet of ambulances in Abu Dhabi could signal a transformation of health care for the emirate's patients. The emirate has introduced 18 smart ambulances, which authorities in Abu Dhabi believe will play a crucial role in saving lives. A control room at the Department of Health in Abu Dhabi will be able to direct ambulances to the nearest hospital best-equipped to deal with each emergency, rather than simply hoping medics can help wherever the patient is taken. Live data is transmitted between the ambulances and the control room, with key information such as vital signs. The medical team can learn what is happening to patients while they are still on the road and prepare for their arrival. “Before, the ambulance would just take the patient and go to a hospital,” said Dr Salama Al Tamimi, executive director of emergency preparedness and response at the Department of Health. “They don’t know if the hospital is ready, or if they have the speciality or not.” Previously, she said an ambulance could arrive to find the required specialist was unavailable, the hospital did not offer the service needed, or its emergency department was full. “That doesn’t happen any more,” Dr Al Tamimi said. “The ambulance will go exactly to where it should go. The hospital will be pre-notified [and] teams will be ready to receive them.” The control centre was established in December 2024, with the aim of bringing various parts of Abu Dhabi’s healthcare system together in one room. Representatives from the Department of Health, Abu Dhabi Civil Defence, health care groups and ambulance providers work from the centre, each with access to information relevant to their role. Large screens provide a live picture of ambulance movements across the emirate, while officials can monitor hospital services and other pressures across the system. The centre’s oversight includes transfers between hospitals, blood supplies, poisoning and infectious disease cases, organ donation, hospital activity and weather alerts. Dr Al Tamimi said the system can even identify when a piece of hospital equipment needed for a patient’s care is temporarily unavailable. She gave the example of a hospital that would normally have been able to receive a particular patient but whose CAT scanner was out of service that day. Rather than taking the patient there and discovering the problem, controllers can divert the ambulance to another hospital capable of providing the required care. “This is the beauty of having real-time visibility on the healthcare system,” she said. The centre also has visibility of different ambulance providers operating across Abu Dhabi, allowing controllers to draw on available resources when necessary. The 18 new ambulances are designed for groups of patients whose needs can be particularly difficult to manage in conventional emergency vehicles. The critical-care vehicles provide additional space and equipment for seriously ill adults and children, including major trauma cases. They can also transport patients receiving extracorporeal membrane oxygenation, or Ecmo – an advanced form of life support used for critically ill patients whose heart or lungs require significant support. The Ecmo machine is not permanently installed in the ambulance. Instead, the specialised vehicle is large enough and equipped to transfer a patient who is already connected to an Ecmo system from a hospital. Dr Al Tamimi said a patient who requires a higher level of care could, for example, be transferred between hospitals while remaining connected to the machine. “We can transfer patients with Ecmo machines on them,” she said. The critical-care ambulances can also be used for paediatric intensive-care patients and people who have suffered major trauma. Portable ultrasound is among the technology being discussed for use in the vehicles. A second category of ambulances has been designed for pregnant women and newborns. Officials said births outside hospitals or en route present particular challenges because both mother and baby may require immediate specialist care. The vehicles are equipped to support maternity and neonatal emergencies, including newborns who may require resuscitation shortly after birth. They also carry neonatal equipment, such as a small incubator. Crews will receive specialist training in managing pregnant women, deliveries and newborn emergencies. The vehicles can also support specialist transfers between hospitals, including patients being moved between Abu Dhabi and Al Ain, or those who require care elsewhere in the emirate. Another feature of the new category of ambulances tackles a very different challenge faced by emergency crews: safely transporting people with severe obesity. Dr Al Tamimi said conventional ambulances have limitations when dealing with patients of exceptional weight or size. She cited examples of people weighing up to 300kg, who may be unable to leave their homes without substantial assistance. In some cases, several organisations and specialist equipment are needed before the patient can be transported. The issue is not merely weight but the space available in a conventional ambulance and the capacity of the equipment used to transport the patient. The new bariatric vehicles provide more appropriate space and specialist equipment, while crews will be trained to manage such cases. While Abu Dhabi continues to encourage healthy lifestyles and tackle obesity, Dr Al Tamimi said emergency services must be able to provide appropriate care to people, regardless of their weight. A patient with obesity “deserves exactly the same” care as other patients, she said. Maj Gen Salem Abdullah bin Barak Al Dhaheri, Director General of the Abu Dhabi Civil Defence Authority, said the move represents more than the addition of new ambulances. It reflects a shift in the way emergency response is viewed – from simply measuring how quickly a vehicle reaches a patient to how rapidly the right specialist care can begin. “The launch of the new generation of specialised smart ambulances marks a significant advancement in Abu Dhabi’s emergency response system and reflects the strong institutional collaboration with the Department of Health Abu Dhabi,” he said. “This integration strengthens response times and the efficiency of emergency care, while advancing the level of specialised care and the quality of services provided to patients.” Dr Al Tamimi highlighted patients suffering from a Stemi – a severe form of heart attack caused by a blocked coronary artery. One important measure for these patients is known as “door-to-balloon time”: the period between the patient arriving at hospital and the doctors opening the blocked artery during an angioplasty procedure. She said the figure previously stood at about 97 minutes, compared with an international benchmark of 90 minutes. It has now fallen to about 49 minutes. She said the reduction had been accompanied by improved survival, while also having a positive financial impact on the healthcare system. The significance of the control centre, however, extends beyond what happens before a patient reaches hospital. Officials can follow patients through different stages of their healthcare journey, including transfers between hospitals and, where required, services after discharge. Dr Salama said home-care dashboards also identify vulnerable residents, including people of determination and those dependent on life-support equipment at home. Their locations can be known so that assistance, including medical teams and essential supplies, can be directed to them during severe weather or other emergencies. The aim is to create a system in which an emergency call, ambulance journey and hospital treatment are no longer viewed as separate stages. Instead, information can follow the patient and the various organisations responsible for their care can make decisions together.

title: Footloose: Chanel’s ‘barefoot shoe’ marks latest chapter in fashion's flirtation with impractical footwear
description: Margaret Qualley wears the half-sandal on the red carpet of the Dog Stars premiere in London
content: When Chanel debuted its half-sandal during its cruise 2027 show in April, it divided the internet despite being sent down a pristine, tailor-made runway. Now, actress Margaret Qualley has become one of the first to brave a red carpet wearing them, in London no less. For the world premiere of her new film – Ridley Scott's The Dog Stars – Qualley arrived in Leicester Square wearing a Chanel dress and its “barefoot shoe”. Of course, novelty shoes are nothing new, as a foot clad in a weird creation is almost guaranteed to grab precious headlines. Alexander McQueen created the bulbous, 12-inch Armadillo heel for spring 2010, which smothered the whole foot in a strange, rounded form, while Gucci lined its slides with fur for autumn 2015. In spring 2017, shoe designer Manolo Blahnik created high boots for Vetements that reached to the waist, while Balenciaga's collaboration with Crocs resulted in platform foam clogs for spring/summer 2018. So why is this shoe causing such a furore? Cupping the heel and secured with two leather cords, it is delicate and charmingly pretty. Its beauty, however, does little to disguise its near-total uselessness as foot protection. With only the heel covered, the entire front half of the foot is left exposed. For all the glamour associated with them, fashion weeks conceal an uncomfortable truth about beautiful but ridiculous shoes. Away from the runway, show-goers can often be spotted switching from trainers to heels and back again as they race between venues. Certain brands are notorious for footwear that looks fabulous but is brutal on the appendage inside. Chanel seems to be taking this contradiction to its logical extreme: a flat shoe, whilst practical and comfortable, is ridiculous and impractical if half of said shoe is missing. Wearing one is beautifully pointless, as the part of the foot left bare will get dirty. Shoes are a complex language in themselves and can make or break a look, whether they are scruffy, pristine, elegant or ill-fitting. Having only half a shoe to judge, however, is certainly new. A quick straw poll of colleagues raises some important questions. How would a half-shoe fare in the scorching heat of the UAE? And, as one colleague suggested, perhaps that is precisely the point. Is this the ultimate display of wealth: a shoe for someone so extravagantly rich that normal footwear rules simply no longer apply?

title: Dubai's Al Maktoum Airport set for 50km driverless rail network to carry passengers around site
description: Construction due for completion in December 2031, ahead of opening of first phase of airport in 2032
content: The world's largest automated people mover is coming to Dubai's mega-airport, Al Maktoum International Airport (DWC). The planned 50km line will connect the airport via nine stations, transporting passengers across the vast site. The project contract was recently awarded by Dubai Aviation City Corporation to Mitsubishi Heavy Industries (MHI), its Dubai subsidiary, and Indian multinational conglomerate Larsen & Toubro Limited (L&T). According to MHI, construction is due for completion in December 2031, ahead of the anticipated opening of the first phase of the airport in 2032. A further expansion will bring the people mover to 14 stations when all the airport's phases are complete. Ramkumar Sundararajan, executive vice president and head of transportation infrastructure at L&T, said the project came with some challenges. “This project exemplifies the scale and complexity of integrated APM Rail Systems that L&T is uniquely positioned to deliver,” he said. “MHI’s proven APM Systems and L&T’s extensive integrated systems experience, supported by the world-class Engineering Designs Centre, enables us to execute such projects with a strong focus on safety and quality.” A people mover is like a metro, but typically covers shorter distances within a closed circuit such as an airport or a theme park. Like the Dubai Metro, the airport's people mover will be autonomous and function similarly to the MHI-built APM at Dubai International Airport, which runs in terminals 1 and 3. The new transit system, running entirely underground within the airport premises, will, by a wide margin, surpass the current largest automated people movers, both of which are in the US. The DFW Skylink at Dallas Fort Worth International Airport is about 8km long, while the AirTrain JFK at New York's John F. Kennedy Airport is about the same length, with an extra 5km extending beyond the airport boundaries. Al Maktoum International Airport is poised to become the biggest in the world, capable of handling 260 million passengers and 12 million tonnes of freight annually. Work will be completed in phases, with the first due to open in 2032. Phase 1 will see the launch of the West Terminal, the people mover and Concourse 1, bringing the total capacity of DWC up to 130 million passengers a year. By the end, four concourses will be operational, each with three people-mover stops, according to Dubai Aviation Engineering Projects. This is not the first mobility project recently contracted to connect to the airport. The Airport Express Link will connect Dubai International Airport (DXB) and DWC, with stops in popular areas of Dubai. The 55km route will provide easy access between the airports at either end of the city. It was also announced that Etihad Rail's high-speed rail service, which will be launched in 2030, will have a station serving Al Maktoum International Airport as well as the Dubai Metro. “At the moment there's very limited connectivity [but] Etihad Rail will now come very close to DWC phase 2, and we will have a dedicated station box adjacent to the airport, so you'll be able to step off Etihad Rail effortlessly into the new airport,” Dubai Airports chief executive Paul Griffiths told The National in May. “Secondly, we've had the announcement of the airport express, which will link the major population centres of Dubai with a very efficient rail journey to DWC phase two – that will be very welcome.”

title: Tactical alliances emerging ahead of first Palestinian elections in two decades
description: Abbas's ruling Fatah party says it is ready to face any coalitions 'built on hostility'
content: Two months ahead of Palestine 's first legislative elections in two decades, several factions that once seemed to be on opposite sides of the political spectrum are forming unexpected alliances in an attempt to upset the status quo. The last Palestinian Legislative Council (PLC) elections took place in 2006, securing a contested win for Hamas . Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas , who has been in office since 2005, had since announced legislative and presidential elections in 2021, but cancelled them, citing Israel's refusal to allow Palestinians in occupied East Jerusalem to take part as the reason. Experts said he was taking the easy way out, after opinion polls had found a candidate list led by imprisoned Palestinian activist Marwan Barghouti would win the legislative elections. Energised by European and US pressure for reform exerted on the ruling Palestinian Authority (PA), which Mr Abbas heads, different political factions have expressed their desire to participate in the November elections. The process would be heavily overshadowed by the repercussions of the Gaza war, which has led to Hamas losing its grip on the territory it governed for years. It will also be influenced by the escalating situation in the occupied West Bank, mainly marked by the increasing attacks by armed settlers on Palestinian towns and homes. A meeting between Mohammad Dahlan, the head of a breakaway faction of the ruling party Fatah, and Hamas chief Khalil Al Hayya, took place in Egypt 's Al Alamein on Monday. The meeting focused on “unity of the national position”, Mr Dahlan's Democratic Reform party said in a statement. But discussions went even deeper. A Hamas official said a “political alliance” involving several Palestinian political factions, including the group and Mr Dahlan's party, is being formed. The matter is still “under study”, he said, with meetings between the factions ongoing. “In principle, there is an alliance” emerging, the official added. The implication here is that such an alliance could be an attempt to upset Mr Abbas's 21-year rule of Palestine, and Fatah is watching with concern and anger. Speaking to The National , the group's spokesman Abdel Fattah Dawla challenged the legitimacy of a potential alliance. “On what political and national basis is this alliance being formed? What are its objectives and what are its points of reference?” he said. He insisted Fatah is ready to face any alliances “built on hostility” towards it. The Hayyah-Dahlan meeting took place on the same day that US Middle East envoy Jared Kushner was in Egypt, where he met Hamas officials, according to sources. Mr Dahlan had clashed with Hamas during his position as head of the Preventive Security Force and Fatah representative in Gaza. He was later exiled from Fatah. Many believe the move stems from him being viewed as a threat to Mr Abbas's political survival. “They all emphasise that there should be a more diverse set of parties and opinions in the Palestinian leadership because Abbas is exclusively in control,” Fathi Nimer from the Palestinian Policy Network (Al Shabaka) think tank told The National . With Hamas losing its grip on Gaza, by dissolving its governing authority after almost two decades in power to pave the way for a transitional technocratic body to take over under the Board of Peace, and then by agreeing to disarm, there is a lot of desire by the group to remain a player in the political circles. One way of doing so could be through an expanded coalition with other factions in the elections. A recent opinion poll showed Palestinian support for armed struggle has dropped sharply in less than a year, with most now in favour of negotiations to end the Israeli occupation and achieve statehood. The Palestinian Centre for Policy and Survey Research conducted the survey across Gaza and the occupied West Bank this month, after Mr Abbas announced the elections. “Twenty-seven per cent of people chose armed struggle, compared with 40 per cent in October”, when asked about the most effective way to establish an independent Palestinian state and end the Israeli occupation, the report said. “Forty-four per cent of people chose negotiations, compared to 36 per cent 10 months ago,” it added. The idea of creating a peaceful political entity grouping Palestinian factions has been debated for three months with mediators from Turkey, Egypt and Qatar, according to sources. "It's the only way for Hamas and others to survive after they hand over their weapons," said one of the sources. "They will substitute armed resistance with peaceful resistance, without which they will simply disappear from the scene altogether."

title: Voice of Hind Rajab star and director reject 'smokescreen' Israeli probe
description: Actor Motaz Malhees, director Kaouther Ben Hania and Hind Rajab’s mother question whether Israel’s investigation can deliver genuine accountability
content: Palestinian actor Motaz Malhees has criticised Israel’s decision to investigate the killing of Hind Rajab through its own military justice system, after the army acknowledged for the first time that its troops fired on the car carrying the five-year-old and her family. Malhees, who portrayed Palestine Red Crescent Society worker Omar Alqam in the Oscar-nominated film The Voice of Hind Rajab , questions whether the investigation will lead to anyone being held responsible. The film revisits the final hours of the five-year-old Palestinian girl killed in Gaza in January 2024. “It has been more than two and a half years since Hind Rajab was killed, and for all that time, the Israeli army lied, denied and deflected,” he tells The National . “Now they are finally admitting it and launching an investigation into themselves. The irony of a criminal investigating its own crimes is not lost on me. “Hind is one of thousands of children killed by this army,” Malhees adds. “Are they going to admit to every single one? “More importantly, what happens next? Will the soldiers responsible actually be brought to justice, or will this be another soft landing that protects them? Until there is real accountability, these admissions and news cycles mean nothing.” Kaouther Ben Hania, the Tunisian filmmaker who wrote and directed The Voice of Hind Rajab , described the military’s announcement as “a smokescreen” in a statement posted on Instagram. “For more than two years, the evidence has been there: independent investigations, satellite imagery, ballistic analysis,” she wrote. “And there was the most devastating evidence of all: Hind’s own voice, describing the Israeli tanks circling around her. What more did we need?” Her film uses real audio recordings of Hind’s phone call to the Palestine Red Crescent Society alongside dramatised scenes inside the operations centre. Ben Hania said the cases the Israeli military was choosing to address were “precisely the ones that international public opinion has made impossible to ignore”. “And what about all the others?” she asked. “Those whose names we will never know because their deaths never broke through the wall of international indifference?” The Israeli military announced on Wednesday that its Military Police Criminal Investigation Division would examine the deaths of Hind, six members of her family and two paramedics sent to rescue her on January 29, 2024. Its fact-finding mechanism concluded that Israeli troops fired on the family’s car as it approached them while travelling “contrary to an advance notice” issued to residents of the area. Hind’s mother, Wissam Hamada, also criticised the decision in a statement posted on Instagram. “Opening an investigation is not justice,” she wrote. “I do not want a closed military investigation. I want an independent, transparent investigation and genuine accountability for everyone responsible.” “Hind is not just a news story or a case reopened because of international pressure. Hind is my daughter, and I will continue to demand the truth and justice for her, my family, and the paramedics who tried to save her.” “Opening an investigation is a long-overdue step,” she concluded. “Justice has not yet begun.” Five passengers were killed in the initial attack, while Hind and her 15-year-old cousin Layan Hamada survived. Layan was subsequently killed as Hind spoke to the Red Crescent Society, with dozens of shots audible during the call. Hind answered when emergency workers called back and remained on the phone for hours, pleading for someone to rescue her. The military acknowledged that the movement of an ambulance sent to reach Hind had been co-ordinated. Its statement said that, “according to the allegations raised”, a shell was fired towards the vehicle when it arrived, killing paramedics Youssef Al Zeino and Ahmed Al Madhoun. It said the criminal investigation had been ordered because of “alleged failures” in that co-ordination. The statement did not explain how Hind or Layan died. Their bodies were found 12 days later, after Israeli forces withdrew from the area. Hind was still inside the family’s car, while the remains of the paramedics were discovered in their destroyed ambulance nearby. The admission reverses the military’s preliminary finding in 2024 that its forces were “not present near the vehicle or within the firing range” of the family’s car. A Washington Post investigation subsequently found that Israeli armoured vehicles had been operating nearby, and that the gunfire and damage to the ambulance were consistent with Israeli weapons. Forensic Architecture mapped 335 bullet holes across the car. Working with audio investigation group Earshot, it estimated that the gunfire heard as Layan was killed came from between 13 and 23 metres away. Researchers concluded that, at that distance, the shooter would have been able to see that civilians, including children, were inside. Rana Faqih, the Red Crescent responder who tried to reassure Hind during her final hours, told The National that opening an Israeli investigation was nowhere near enough. “From the outset, the society has demanded, and continues to demand, an independent investigation by a neutral and transparent committee,” she said. Hind’s grandmother, who is also named Hind Rajab, told the Associated Press: “An international investigation is required to uncover the truth and hold all those responsible accountable,” she said. “We call for justice, not only for Hind, but for all Gaza children.” Dyab Abou Jahjah, director general of the Belgium-based Hind Rajab Foundation, said its distrust was based on Israel’s previous record of investigating its own forces. “We do not trust the Israeli justice system, not out of an ideological position, but because of the track record,” he told Al Jazeera . “And in this particular case, the Israeli justice system as a whole has always been complicit in Israeli crimes.” The Hind Rajab case was one of two incidents referred for criminal investigation after the military reviewed 150 cases from the Gaza war. The second involved the killing of 15 Palestinian medics and rescue workers in Rafah in March 2025. The military declined to open criminal investigations into three other attacks, including the April 2024 strikes that killed seven World Central Kitchen workers and two incidents involving staff from Doctors Without Borders. Israel denies deliberately targeting civilians and rejects wider allegations of genocide and war crimes in Gaza. The Voice of Hind Rajab received a record 24-minute standing ovation at its 2025 Venice Film Festival premiere and won the Silver Lion Grand Jury Prize. It was later nominated for Best International Feature Film at the Academy Awards.

title: Al Hudayriyat Island tops Abu Dhabi property sales in first half of 2026
description: Saadiyat, Reem, Al Maryah and Yas islands also post strong sales despite challenges of regional war
content: Abu Dhabi's Al Hudayriyat Island has topped the emirate's real estate sales in the first half of 2026 in a further sign of the property market's resilience despite the Iran war. Sales on the island in the six months to the end of June hit Dh19 billion ($5.2 billion), which equates to roughly 27 per cent of total residential units sold in the UAE capital , according to a midyear report from the Abu Dhabi Real Estate Centre . Saadiyat Island posted sales worth Dh13.3 billion, while Reem Island and Al Maryah Island collectively recorded Dh10.5 billion. Yas Island, where Disneyland Abu Dhabi and Sphere Abu Dhabi are to be built, recorded sales of Dh7.3 billion, Adrec said. Investment zones accounted for 22 per cent, or 72,000 housing units, of the total supply during the period, with Reem Island topping the list with about 27,500, followed by Al Raha Island, Yas Island and Saadiyat Island. Adrec's midyear report showed that residential supply in Abu Dhabi grew by nearly 3 per cent year-on-year to hit about 409,000 units. The sector recorded Dh70.4 billion worth of residential unit sales, with off-plan projects accounting for almost 90 per cent. An additional 71,000 units are projected to be on the market by 2030, with deliveries peaking in 2028, Adrec said. “Numbers measure the market's movement, but understanding the market requires us to look beyond the numbers, to read the trends, understand what is changing, and assess what those changes mean for investors, developers and decision-makers,” Adrec director general Rashed Al Omaira said. “The first half of 2026 reflects a resilient market, supported by sustained demand, clear regulations, transparent data and a balanced approach to supply and demand.” The property sector is an integral part of the economies of Abu Dhabi and the wider UAE, with projects continuing to attract investors and buyers and withstanding the effects of the conflict. The Emirates was ranked as the world's leading real estate investment destination as the industry retained its momentum amid those challenges, according to Arada's UAE Property Investment Index released in June. To support the market, Adrec announced in July that rents for residential, commercial and industrial properties would not increase until further notice, apart from communities managed by Abu Dhabi’s financial centre, the ADGM, such as Al Maryah Island and Reem Island. Adrec approved eight new investment zones in the first half of 2026, bringing the total to 50. The regulator also registered 28 new real estate developments, a 16 per cent increase from a year ago, “creating new opportunities for local and international investors across the emirate”, it said. Last week, Abu Dhabi's hospitality sector recorded the highest occupancy rates in the UAE during the first half of this year, as hotel operators increased domestic guest numbers. Occupancy in the UAE capital was estimated at 66.8 per cent for the first six months, and remained steady at 65.2 per cent in June, consultancy JLL said in a report. The property market's strength extends to the rest of the UAE. On Thursday, the Dubai Land Department said investments in the emirate's completed real estate projects jumped by 52 per cent year-on-year to Dh111 billion in the first half of 2026 across 104 developments. In Ras Al Khaimah – where the residential sector recorded Dh12.3 billion in total sales last year – hotel occupancy rates hit nearly 50 per cent in the first half, JLL said last week .

title: SDF integration into Syrian state marks milestone but key tensions unresolved, experts say
description: Kurdish rights yet to be embedded into constitution meaning ties with Damascus remain tense
content: The full integration of the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF) into Syria’s state institutions represents a significant step for Damascus but Kurdish aspirations for meaningful autonomy remain unresolved, experts told The National on Friday. Kurdish leader Mazloum Abdi announced on Thursday from the city of Qamishli that the integration of the Kurdish administration into Syria’s state institutions was complete. “Today, on this occasion, I would like to say that this process of integrating our military, security and administrative institutions into the institutions of the state structures has ended and has been fully completed. Today, a new phase begins for us,” Mr Abdi said. Tens of thousands of SDF personnel are now employees of Syrian government ministries. The move built on an agreement struck between Damascus and the SDF in January. The deal was mediated by Washington and Paris, and endorsed by Ankara. It sought to end hostilities between Kurdish forces and the new Syrian authorities, while establishing a road map for incorporating the north-east into state institutions, all while offering specific linguistic and cultural rights, as well as political representation. In January, President Ahmad Al Shara issued a decree following weeks of violence, offering concessions designed to foster goodwill with Syria's Kurdish population. They included recognising Nowruz as a national holiday and recognising Kurdish as a national language that may be taught in public and private schools in Kurdish-populated areas. He also granted Syrian nationality to previously stateless Kurds. The full integration of the SDF is an important achievement in efforts to consolidate state authority after years of conflict, said Bente Scheller, head of the Middle East and North Africa Division at the Heinrich-Boll-Stiftung Foundation in Berlin. “For many Kurds, however, the move constitutes a difficult concession. Hopes for self-rule are now seen as more likely to survive only at the municipal rather than provincial level,” she told The National . Mr Al Shara has taken steps to recognise Kurdish rights that go further than any previous government, although these have yet to be embedded in the country’s constitution, Ms Scheller said. “Our struggle will continue, to cement our people's rights in the constitution,” Mr Abdi said. Despite progress, relations between Damascus and Kurdish groups are expected to remain complicated. “It will remain a rocky road, one that will require both sides to work hard to break down mutual mistrust,” Ms Scheller said, with the deal raising concerns among advocates of women’s rights. Kurdish fighters, known worldwide for their women's units, have been facing pushback from the government. “Not only has the integration of women's units as such been denied but the transitional government also apparently does not allow for integration on an individual basis,” she said. For years, the Kurdish-led administration had governed much of north-eastern Syria. It established its own military, security and civilian institutions with US backing during the war against ISIS . The US had the SDF as its main ally in Syria during the civil war from 2011 to 2024. But American support for the group dwindled as it established ties with Damascus following the fall of the Assad regime in December 2024.

title: 'I saw the fire, then heard the blast': Deraa's fields peppered with explosives from Syria's civil war
description: At least 800 people, almost a third of them children, have been killed by unexploded munitions since collapse of Assad regime, according to Halo Trust figures
content: In a former quarry surrounded by farmland outside the city of Deraa in southern Syria, experts are preparing to detonate an unexploded Russian missile left over from the war. A shepherd discovered it a few days earlier in a nearby field. Everything involving the detonation is carefully calculated: the missile's size and its location above ground help determine that the blast radius will be 250 metres and that dangerous fragments could be propelled as far as 900m. Sandbags are filled and placed around the missile to absorb the explosion. The only aspect left to chance is how long it will take to move the shepherds out of the way. In faraway fields on the edge of the radius, a lengthy discussion ensues between a pair of herders, who eventually meander with their flock away from the epicentre of the planned detonation. It takes a split second to detonate a mine or other unexploded bomb, but years are needed to clear the Syrian fields and cities on which they are scattered. On this day, the herders are forthcoming, which is not always the case. Most have lived through the war and aren’t scared of explosives. Many still take their herds to fields known to be dangerous. The shepherd who found the Russian missile carried it to the quarry himself. “Most of the time the shepherds listen to us,” says Abdel Mohsen Al Masri, who led the controlled detonation with the British charity Halo Trust. “They are facing a lot of dangers. When they’re walking on land with mines and unexploded bombs, they are subjected to injuries and injuries for their children. “The work depends on how big the device is. If it is small, you close off a small area. If it is big, you have large roads and a large area to close off.” Anti-personnel and anti-tank mines line the fields outside the city of Deraa, marking the former front lines of the Syrian civil war. They were laid by the forces of the former regime and its allies during the battle to retake southern Syria in 2017. Today, as people return to the city and its surroundings from Jordan , they risk death or injury from leftover mines, unexploded missiles and improvised bombs. More than 800 people, almost a third of them children, have been killed by unexploded munitions since the collapse of the Assad regime in Syria in December 2024, according to the Halo Trust's figures. Of the 2,300 people reported injured, 40 per cent were children, the charity said. Other cases may have gone unreported. Hussein Qazhali, who leads Halo’s operations in southern Syria, said he was compelled to do this work after years as a paramedic during which he regularly responded to incidents involving unexploded war remnants. He was displaced to Idlib in north-west Syria during the civil war, but returned to his home in Deraa last year. Many in his team are former fighters and first responders with experience clearing explosives. He showed The National a WhatsApp group that documented incidents in the south, which occurred every two to three days and often involve children. News of another accident nearby appeared in the chat and he was clearly upset. Before beginning a clearance operation, team members speak to the local community, gathering testimony about the war and the fighting. They refer to old regime maps of the front line. Drone imaging helps to locate disturbances that could be mines or unexploded devices. Deraa has seen the largest number of residents returning since the collapse of the Assad regime in December 2024. A newer wave of displaced Bedouin from neighbouring Sweida are also at risk as they seek shelter in abandoned buildings that had served as military camps for the former regime. This is compounded by the continued insecurity in southern Syria. The new Syrian government has struggled to establish its police and armed forces in the Deraa governorate due to pushback from armed groups that took control during the civil war. Israel sought to fill the vacuum and now occupies a buffer zone along the borders of the Golan Heights and has conducted several military campaigns in the region since December 2024. These were first to destroy the Assad regime and Iranian military bases, and then to support a Druze militia leader in Sweida who staged an uprising in the city against Ahmad Al Shara's government. Hundreds were killed in the clashes between Druze militiamen and Bedouin who were loyal to the new government. Residents say Israeli strikes on former regime warehouses led to a more expansive scattering of regime weapons. In Dahia, shepherd Ghiyath Ibn Ja’adan lives with his family in an abandoned building that previously served as a military base for regime forces after they reclaimed the city. He was displaced to Jordan during the war and returned to Deraa after the Assad regime fell. Recently, he lost two sheep to a mine that exploded as they walked ahead of him. “The sound of the blast was so loud,” he said. “All I saw was the fire and the smoke in front of me, and then I heard the blast. I was no more than 10 metres from it.” His brother, who lives nearby, lost a leg while herding sheep in the fields. “There are anti-tank mines and anti-personnel mines. There is rocket debris,” Mr Ibn Ja’adan added. “There were also army camps here that the Israelis hit after the regime fell. There were warehouses full of missiles that were targeted and they were scattered across the land. His biggest fear is for his children. “I don’t let my children go out in the fields. There are mines, there is unexploded debris. Children don’t know this. They could hold [a bomb] and it will explode in their hands. I am trying to teach them. But they are children. If they spot something, they will want to hold it.” There are six fields immediately on the edge of the city, each measuring 75,000 to 170,000 square metres and containing mines, said Mohammed Al Hashish, who leads a local team for the Dahia suburb. There have been clearance activities in the neighbourhoods of Naimeh and Manshiyeh, which were heavily shelled by Assad's forces during the war. The work comes as the UK and other major western governments have slashed their foreign aid budgets to increase spending on defence. While Halo’s programme in Syria is currently funded by several governments and UN agencies, including the UN Mine Action Service, there is longer-term uncertainty for the work, which is likely to take a decade to complete. “Our ability to work in Syria has massively increased as the country has opened up,” said George Tench, who is part of the Syria programme. “We have lots of incredible donors and have grown significantly but we haven't been able to scale up our impact across Syria as quickly as would have been hoped. “It is a problem that will take many years to address and so requires a long-standing commitment from the international community. This is likely to be challenging in an environment of global funding cuts.” Some aid organisations want overseas aid to be viewed as essential to defence budgets. Maj Gen James Cowan, Halo’s chief executive, said the charity sits in the “grey space” between aid and defence. “The traditional hard power of defence and the so-called soft power of overseas aid interventions and diplomacy are twin pillars of global security,” he said. “Together, they help to build a safer, more stable world, strengthen the foundations of critical conflict prevention efforts, reinforce international norms and reduce human suffering.” For the team clearing the explosives, the challenge is a deeply personal one and linked to Syria's recovery after more than 13 years of war. Mr Al Masri of the Halo Trust said: “The people of Deraa are my people. Any thorn that pricks them, it's as if they were my children. It’s a humanitarian issue that’s not just about Deraa.”

title: Oil posts sharp weekly gain while gold and Bitcoin jump on US Treasury buyback plans
description: Crude up after US announcement of more punitive economic sanctions on Iran
content: Oil prices posted a second straight weekly gain, with Brent settling above $90 for the first time in a month, while gold and Bitcoin jumped on Friday amid Iran war uncertainty and a US push to double its bond buyback programme. Crude had already surged by 3 per cent on Thursday after the US announced measures to tighten the economic pressure on Iran, and remained elevated after the US further threatened Iran with its “toughest sanctions” yet. Brent, the benchmark for two thirds of the world's oil, added 0.65 per cent to settle at $94.39 a barrel. West Texas Intermediate, the gauge that tracks US crude, closed 0.26 per cent higher at $87.06 per barrel. From last week's closing, Brent leapt 6.6 per cent, while WTI increased 5.7 per cent. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Thursday said Washington would impose even more punitive economic sanctions on Tehran to break the impasse in negotiations. The two sides reached an initial two-month ceasefire agreement in June to prepare the ground to end the conflict. The agreement, however, unravelled and the US has changed tactics to increase the pressure on Iran's already wobbling economy. Mr Bessent said he was planning to hold a news conference on Monday “to talk about exactly what we're going to do”. Separately, US President Donald Trump has warned of “tremendous economic consequences” for countries doing business with Iran. The US moves have “increased the probability that Iranian barrels, shipping routes and counterparties face tighter restrictions”, said Naeem Aslam, chief information officer of London-based Zaye Capital Markets. Iran's central bank governor, Abdolnaser Hemmati, this week said the country was not exporting any oil . Iran is also battling runaway inflation and a plunging currency. The Tehran regime has weathered sanctions for decades, going back to Jimmy Carter's US administration, which began an economic pressure campaign in response to the seizure of the American embassy in Tehran in 1979. More than 6,000 sanctions are in place across Iran's financial, banking, aviation, energy and cryptocurrency sectors. It is one of the most heavily sanctioned countries in the world. The escalating uncertainty and rhetoric is increasing concerns around the crude market, especially as “oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz remain disrupted, while Middle Eastern supply and refined-product availability are already constrained”, Mr Aslam added. Gold also added to its gains and recorded a third consecutive weekly increase as the dollar hit a multi-month low after the US announced it would increase its bond buyback programme. The precious metal, considered a safe haven against inflation, added nearly 2 per cent to $4,603.30 per ounce for a weekly gain of more than 5 per cent. The US Treasury on Wednesday said it would double the size of its repurchases of long-dated securities to at least $4 billion per round over the next quarter. Mr Bessent followed that up by saying Washington might even further boost its Treasury buybacks. Gold has also benefitted from softer monetary policy expectations over the short term, with markets betting that the US Federal Reserve will maintain interest rates at its next meeting in September. “While bond yields stabilised after the markets’ reaction to the US Treasury’s decision to increase the size of long-dated bond buybacks, attention could remain on upcoming operations that could weigh on yields, creating an opportunity for gold to recover,” said Bas Kooijman, chief executive and asset manager of Luxembourg-based DHF Capital. The bond buyback plans have also benefitted Bitcoin , which added to its gains that began on Wednesday with the US Treasury's announcement. The world's biggest and original cryptocurrency jumped about 5 per cent to more than $78,300, and by about 24 per cent for the week, according to data from CoinMarketCap. “Lower Treasury yields and a weaker dollar would remain supportive because they reduce the relative attraction of cash and fixed-income assets, while a renewed rise in long-term yields could pressure Bitcoin and other high-beta assets,” Mr Aslam said.

title: Israeli singers accused of copying Palestinian-Chilean artist Elyanna’s music video ‘frame by frame’
description: Commenters have described the alleged similarities as an example of Israeli appropriation of Palestinian and Arab culture
content: Two Israeli performers have been accused of copying scenes “frame by frame” from Palestinian-Chilean star Elyanna’s 2024 hit Ganeni . Zahara , released on August 4, is a collaboration between Gal Juma and Asulin. Less than two weeks later, Elyanna fan accounts began sharing videos that placed scenes from the two productions side by side. The allegations have since spread across culture and entertainment pages on Instagram, Facebook and Threads, drawing thousands of comments. As the comparisons have gathered momentum, many commenters described the alleged similarities as an example of Israeli appropriation of Palestinian and Arab culture. Posts repeatedly highlight a desert sequence in which a white Mercedes is surrounded by patterned rugs. Both videos also show the car’s interior covered in elaborate fabrics and decorations. Other similarities cited include rooftop dance scenes and shots of figures silhouetted against the setting sun. An eye painted on a performer’s palm appears in both productions, while each video includes shots of musicians and uses similar framing during several dance sequences. Although the videos differ elsewhere, the posts identify several closely matched images rather than one shared location or a broadly similar desert aesthetic. The criticism concerns the video rather than the music, as the songs have different compositions and lyrics. Zahara pairs Hebrew and Arabic lyrics with a 2000s-inspired R&B beat and violins. Juma and Asulin perform together in the video and are both credited among the songwriters. Asulin is the stage name of Israeli singer-songwriter and producer Rotem Alagem Asulin, who previously released music as J Lamotta. The video was directed and filmed by Bruce Melan, and had about one million views on YouTube by Friday. Ganeni was released on April 12, 2024, with Elyanna ’s debut album, Woledto . Directed by Naghmeh Pour and filmed in Spain, its video has more than 200 million views on YouTube. The reaction has also reached Juma’s Instagram page, where users have accused the performers of making a “copy-paste” version of Ganeni beneath several posts promoting Zahara . As of Friday, neither Juma nor Asulin had publicly addressed the accusations. Elyanna has also not commented, and no formal copyright complaint had been announced. The National has reached out to Elyanna for comment. Elyanna, 24, was born and raised in Nazareth. In 2023, she became the first artist to perform a complete Arabic-language set at Coachella. She later joined Coldplay at Glastonbury and appeared with the band on Saturday Night Live . Earlier this year, she performed at a ceremony before Canada’s opening World Cup match in Toronto and featured on the Fifa tournament’s official soundtrack with Illuminate , a collaboration with Canadian singer-songwriter Jessie Reyez.

title: Bitcoin climbs past $75,000 in extended Asia crypto rally
description: The world's biggest cryptocurrency has rallied about 20 per cent this week
content: Bitcoin rose by more than 4 per cent in early Asia trading, continuing a tear that began on Wednesday after the US Treasury revealed plans to rein in long-term bond yields and US President Donald Trump called for passing crypto legislation. Bitcoin climbed as high as $75,740 but gave up some gain to trade at $74,806.41, at 8.28am UAE time. The original cryptocurrency has surged almost 8 per cent in the past 24 hours, according to Coinbase data. The market enthusiasm for Bitcoin is has gaining momentum since since Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced the department would double the size of its bond buybacks. Bitcoin is now up almost 20 per cent this week. Optimism around cryptocurrency was also bolstered when President Donald Trump met with industry leaders, including executives from Coinbase Global and Payward. Mr Trump urged the Senate to pass the Clarity Act, a crypto market structure bill that has stalled over a fight regarding ethics provisions. Mr Trump is a proponent of cryptocurrency and virtual supports legislation to broaden the market. He promised on the campaign trail to make the US the "crypto capital of the world" and has has profited from his own crypto ventures. On Wednesday, he called on lawmakers to pass a "fair version of the Clarity Act". The significance of this move will have an impact beyond Bitcoin’s immediate price movement," Ryan Lee, chief analyst at Bitget Research, said. "The focus of the US administration to establish a clearer policy framework for digital assets will serve as a template for other emerging markets to regulate the fast-growing crypto industry in their respective countries." In the coming weeks, the market will be "in wait and watch mode" to see if the political will translates into legal progress, Mr Lee said. "If the Clarity Act makes progress, it could boost investor confidence and spark a broader recovery in digital assets. He however, warned that any ambiguity or political impasse will add to market volatility. Matthew Sigel, head of digital assets research at VanEck, however said that the Bitcoin's price reaction "isn’t about the US Clarity Act", which many market participants have been pointing to. “This is about what the US Treasury has done, which is reigniting fears of fiscal dominance,” he said in a note. With inputs from agencies

title: French police prevent 185 small boat Channel crossings in three months
description: Footage shows moment officers intercept boat on beach
content: French police intercepted 185 small boats in the first three months of a new deal with the UK, figures released by Britain’s Home Office show. The action included stopping launches, seizing equipment, including boats, engines and lifejackets, and arresting people smugglers. The UK agreed to pay France £660 million ($891 million) under a three-year agreement signed in April to tackle people smuggling, which will involve payment based on results for the first time. Video released by the Home Office shows French police officers driving across a beach in Jeeps to stop the launch of a boat being carried by migrants. When the police disembarked, some migrants taunt the officers and throw objects at them. One of the officers appears to respond with pepper spray before others move in to disperse the migrants and slash the rubber hull of the boat. According to information from the French authorities, officers prevented what are described as 185 small boat events involving 4,300 migrants between April 27 and August 2. In that period were four weeks, during which French authorities intercepted every potential illegal Channel crossing. The Home Office said 61 per cent of all small boat events were stopped in the three months, but admitted this amounts to a prevention rate increase of only 5 per cent compared to the same time period in 2025. Charlie Eastaugh, director of maritime and small boats at Border Security Command, said the UK and France “are piling the pressure on the criminal gangs and preventing these illegal and dangerous crossings”. "French officers are not shy in taking bold action to prevent these launches where it is safe and lawful to do so," he added. "They work in difficult and dangerous conditions to stop boats launching, seize equipment and disperse large migrant groups, as well as saving thousands of lives at sea. "Our joint efforts are delivering results and we will go further still to restore control of our borders, and put these smugglers out of business." The French action has included intercepting and boarding 12 taxi boats, which are operated by human-trafficking gangs and are sailed along the coast to pick up people at designated spots before attempting the crossing. The latest figures show 15,897 illegal migrants have crossed the English Channel in small boats this year, down by around 40 per cent on an annual basis. But smugglers have been adapting their methods in response to French police action and cramming more people on to each boat. Recently, 230 migrants were seen on a so-called mega dinghy , offering a stark visual reminder that small boats remain a politically charged issue in the UK. The right-wing populist Reform UK party said if it came to power it would intercept boats crossing the English Channel and return migrants to French ports, even if France disagreed. Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood said by working with France, the UK has stopped more than 47,000 crossing attempts since the Labour government came to power in July 2024. “Our new UK-France deal is already having a real impact, stopping crossings before they happen and disrupting the criminal gangs behind them,” she said. “People smugglers should be in no doubt - we're taking down their operations, seizing their equipment and breaking their business model for good.”

title: McLaren and Lamborghini firebombed outside UK wedding hall
description: Three men spotted on CCTV fleeing after attack in Birmingham
content: Police are searching for three men who set two supercars on fire outside a wedding venue in central England. CCTV captured the attack in which the cars were doused in a flammable substance and set alight. The cars, a McLaren and a Lamborghini, were parked outside the Royal Shalimar in Birmingham. They were in a line of other supercars, which were left untouched. The men, dressed in black, were seen running away then driving off in a white Volkswagen Golf.
