Rayana Al Ghamdi, Deputy General Manager at SAMACO Marine, said: “We aspire to offer more than just marina operations; we seek to support the full range of customer needs in the marine sector, from providing boats and after-sales services to marina facilities, while contributing to the sector’s growth in Saudi Arabia.” The congress continues with sessions on an integrated national logistics system and maritime competitiveness.

title: Lebanese widow can be pursued for husband's role in $2bn corruption scandal
description: High Court in London rules Mozambique can seek compensation from Iskandar Safa's widow
content: A court has cleared the way for Mozambique to pursue the widow of a Lebanese tycoon for compensation for his role in a $2 billion corruption scandal. The African nation sued Iskandar Safa and his shipbuilding company Privinvest in 2023 at the High Court in London over what has come to be known as the “tuna bonds” scandal. Mozambique alleged Privinvest and Mr Safa paid more than $136 million in bribes to officials and bankers to secure favourable terms for contracts, including one designed to exploit the nation’s tuna-rich coastal waters. Mozambique agreed to guarantee the loans under contracts which were governed by English law, so the dispute has been heard at the High Court in London. Privinvest sold fishing boats, patrol vessels, and equipment to the state at vastly inflated prices after paying bribes. But Mozambique was saddled with a $2 billion debt, which brought the country's economy to its knees when the scandal came to light. Mr Safa gave evidence in the High Court proceedings when he was seriously ill with cancer. He died in January 2024, aged 68. In December 2024, a judge ordered Privinvest to pay $534 million plus interest of $40 million to Mozambique. Another judge allowed Mozambique to add Mr Safa’s widow, Clara Martinez Thedy de Safa, to the claim. This was on the basis that Mr Safa had not left a legally valid will. Under Lebanese law, the next of kin automatically assumes both the assets and debts of the deceased. Ms Safa appealed against that decision and her barrister, Robert Howe KC, told a hearing in July this year that she had no knowledge or involvement in any of her husband’s wrongdoing. Mr Howe argued that in law an English court should not accept jurisdiction over claims against a person acting as the administrator of an overseas estate. Such claims are exclusively for the courts of that country, he said. Her legal team also relied on a rule that prevents a person administering a deceased person's estate under foreign law from being sued in England and Wales. But in his ruling, Lord Justice Miles said that under Lebanese law, “there is no concept of an estate”, similar to the UK, and “the inheritance by an heir of the assets is automatic and immediate on death. The deceased’s creditors are exposed to the risk that the deceased’s assets may be mixed up with the heir’s own assets,” he said. As such, the claim against Mrs Safa was against her personally and could be heard in an English court, so her appeal was dismissed, said the judge. The actual sum that Mrs Safa inherited, or for which she is liable, has yet to be established and will be determined at future hearings. Last year, Mozambique’s former finance minister Manuel Chang was sentenced to nearly two years in jail in the US and ordered to pay back $7 million for his role in the “tuna bonds” scandal. The country was left with a fleet of 24 rusting fishing vessels, which were eventually auctioned off. According to his obituary in The Times , Mr Safa was born into a prosperous Maronite Christian family in 1955. He obtained an engineering degree from the American University of Beirut in 1978. Mr Safa fought with a Christian militia in the country’s civil war. He studied in France and also worked as an engineer in Saudi Arabia. With his brother Akram, he founded Privinvest, which specialises in warships, commercial vessels and mega yachts. His contacts in the Middle East led him to become involved in negotiating the release of French hostages held by Hezbollah.

title: Egypt's parliament authorises El Sisi to send troops to defend Saudi Arabia
description: Mandate leaves timing and scope of any deployment to the President
content: Egypt 's parliament has authorised President Abdel Fattah El Sisi to send troops to Saudi Arabia , the House of Representatives announced in a statement on Monday, clearing the last constitutional hurdle to a possible deployment against the Houthis. Parliament said a two-thirds majority had authorised Mr El Sisi to take the necessary measures, following co-ordination with Riyadh, to defend Saudi Arabia’s “territory, sovereignty and holy sites against any external aggression”. The decision was in accordance with a resolution by the National Defence Council on October 18, it said. Parliament has not published an exact tally of Monday's vote, which was held by roll call behind closed doors. Under Article 152 of the constitution, sending the army on a combat mission abroad requires the backing of two-thirds of the 596-member house, or 398 MPs. The approval does not mean troops will deploy immediately. Mr El Sisi, as supreme commander of the armed forces, now has the legal authority to act, but has said Egypt will do so only if Saudi Arabia asks. No formal Saudi request has yet been announced. Monday's vote came after more than a week of debate. Mr El Sisi asked parliament for the mandate on October 17, at a graduation ceremony at the Egyptian Military Academy, saying it was inconceivable that Saudi Arabia's security would be harmed. The National Defence Council, which he chairs, met the following day and pledged “all necessary and possible forms of support” to the kingdom, without specifying their form, size or duration. MPs were expected to approve the request quickly. The four main pro-government parties hold 403 of the 568 elected seats. Instead, the House met in two closed sessions on October 18 and 19, then adjourned for a week. Assem El Gazzar, deputy speaker and head of the pro-government National Front Party, said nearly 500 MPs had asked to speak, more than he had seen on any other issue. In its statement, parliament said MPs from different political parties, as well as independents, had been given the opportunity to discuss regional developments and their implications for Egyptian and Arab national security. Most parties backed the request. The Wafd, Egypt's oldest liberal party, said Saudi security was “an inseparable part” of Egypt's national security. The Justice Party told its MPs to vote in favour, and the Salafist Nour Party called for defensive co-ordination with Riyadh. The Egyptian Social Democratic Party, which has about a dozen seats, told its MPs to abstain, citing the economic cost and the risk of regional escalation. Maha Abdel Nasser, one of its MPs, rejected what she called an open-ended and vague mandate and urged a diplomatic solution. Mohamed Abdel Aleem Dawoud, head of the Wafd's parliamentary bloc, and the independent MP Diaa El Din Dawoud also reserved their positions. The crisis became personal for many Egyptians on October 10, when a Houthi strike on Riyadh's airport killed 12 people. Among them was Azza Ramzy, a 28-year-old flight attendant from Beheira province. The Houthis have warned Egypt against intervening. Yahya Al Raei, speaker of the Houthi-run parliament in Sanaa, wrote to his Egyptian counterpart Hisham Badawi that involvement would pose “a grave danger” to Egypt's national security. Egypt has strong reasons to side with Riyadh. Saudi Arabia is one of its biggest financial backers, and Houthi attacks on Red Sea shipping have already cut revenue from the Suez Canal, one of Egypt's main sources of foreign currency. It is not yet clear what form Egyptian support would take. Officials have described any mission as defensive, and have not said whether it would involve ground troops, air defence or naval forces.

title: Lana Nusseibeh issues call for 'security and freedom' as Palestine backs UN bid
description: The Minister of State underlines commitment to ensuring 'freedom and dignity' of Palestinians and Israelis alike
content: UAE Minister of State Lana Nusseibeh has spoken of her commitment to ensuring Palestinians and Israelis can live in 'security, freedom and dignity' after entering the running to be the next UN Secretary General. Ms Nusseibeh, who previously served as the country's representative to the organisation, welcomed Palestine's support for her candidacy, which was announced on Wednesday. Secretary General Antonio Guterres's second and final term will finish at the end of the year, and Ms Nusseibeh is attracting widespread support in the region for her bid to take on the position. The senior Emirati diplomat has played an instrumental role in UAE foreign policy in recent years and has been a prominent voice in calling for peace in Gaza, stressing the need to deliver crucial aid to the enclave. “Throughout my career, including at the United Nations, I have worked to advance a political pathway that enables Palestinians and Israelis to live in security, freedom and dignity,” Ms Nusseibeh said on social media platform X, in response to Palestine backing her campaign. “I deeply appreciate Palestine’s confidence in my candidacy.” In November 2025, she set out the importance of providing continuing assistance to needy civilians affected by the Gaza war during a visit to Cyprus aimed at bolstering aid efforts. Ms Nusseibeh said during the trip that a maritime corridor from Cyprus would be essential to efforts to step up the relief response. Support has also been declared for Ms Nusseibeh's candidacy by other countries, including Lebanon, Bahrain, Uzbekistan, the Maldives, Cyprus and Albania, as well as the Gulf Co-operation Council (GCC). Ms Nusseibeh was appointed as Minister of State in September 2025 and has previously served as Assistant Minister for Political Affairs and Envoy of the Minister of Foreign Affairs. Before that, she was the UAE's ambassador to the UN for more than a decade until April 2024. UAE aid drive The Emirates remains at the forefront of efforts to provide financial assistance to Gaza and ensure a steady of flow of aid reaches needy civilians. In August, the UAE passed 1,000 days of continuous support, with more than Dh14.2 billion ($3.89 billion) of aid sent. That funding has helped set up a floating hospital in Egypt and two medical centres in Gaza and has brought thousands of medical patients, including many suffering from cancer and war-related injuries, to the Emirates to receive care. A US-backed ceasefire in October 2025 halted large-scale fighting in Gaza, but it has not ended Israeli strikes, and little progress has been made towards a permanent peace. Much of Gaza's population of more than two million has been displaced by the war, with chronic food shortages and limited access to health services and aid leading to a worsening humanitarian crisis.

title: Dubai to redistribute surplus food from weddings and events to reduce waste
description: All collection and redistribution will follow approved regulations and food safety requirements
content: Dubai has unveiled plans to reduce food waste by collecting and distributing excess food from wedding celebrations to beneficiaries. The UAE Food Bank and Dubai’s Community Development Authority (CDA) have signed an agreement and laid the groundwork to safely collect, transport and distribute surplus food. The partnership expands the initiative's community impact while promoting food sustainability and social responsibility. It supports the objectives of the Dubai Social Agenda 33 by encouraging responsible consumption, strengthening community participation and advancing food security. Under the agreement, the two entities will co-ordinate the collection and redistribution of surplus food from weddings and events identified by the CDA. All donations will follow approved regulations and food safety requirements to ensure food suitable for consumption reaches those in need. The MoU also provides for joint awareness campaigns and community programmes to promote food preservation, sustainable consumption and responsible food management. The co-operation will further support volunteer participation in relevant activities, strengthening community engagement and encouraging people to contribute to humanitarian and charitable initiatives. Dr Ahmed Al Hashemi, chief executive of the Social Regulation and Services Sector at the CDA, said the Dubai Weddings initiative will play an important role in supporting family formation and stability, and that the partnership would extend its benefits to the wider community. “By ensuring that surplus food from weddings and events is safely recovered and redistributed to those in need, we are creating additional opportunities for giving while encouraging responsible consumption and the efficient use of resources,” he said. He added that the partnership reflects Dubai’s values of solidarity and generosity and demonstrates the importance of co-operation between government entities and humanitarian organisations. Wider mission Manal Obaid bin Yaroof, head of the UAE Food Bank’s executive team, said the partnership would strengthen the bank’s ability to recover surplus food and ensure it reaches beneficiaries through safe and organised collection and distribution processes. Extending the programme to the Dubai Weddings initiative would help preserve valuable food resources, reduce waste and turn sustainable practices into tangible community benefits, she said. Ms bin Yaroof added that the agreement supports the food bank’s wider humanitarian and charitable mission by raising awareness of food preservation, encouraging volunteering and strengthening co-operation with government entities. The partnership aims to expand the reach of food recovery initiatives, improve surplus food management and promote a culture of giving and social responsibility across Dubai. The agreement forms part of the CDA’s continuing efforts to enhance the Dubai Weddings initiative and broaden its contribution to community well-being. It also supports the UAE Food Bank’s commitment to developing a sustainable approach to surplus food management, ensuring that food fit for consumption is recovered and redistributed while reducing waste and conserving resources.

title: Manchester United: Five managers who could replace Michael Carrick
description: Former Newcastle coach Eddie Howe favourite to take over at Old Trafford
content: The writing is on the wall for beleaguered Michael Carrick after what has been a disastrous week for the Manchester United manager. On Wednesday, Carrick watched his side suffer a 4-1 Uefa Champions League thumping at Italian side Como , after which club captain Bruno Fernandes publicly blamed the humiliation on the coach's tactics . The Portuguese was dropped and left as an unused substitute four days later as United slumped to a 3-0 home loss against Bournemouth which leaves the Red Devils in 16th place, one point outside the relegation zone. Their seven points from eight Premier League games is their lowest at this stage of a campaign since Ron Atkinson's side in 1986/87 (four points) while their eight game winless streak is the club's worst since 2015 under Louis van Gaal. While Carrick retains the backing of United fans, who sang his name on Sunday and who feel he is just the symptom of wider club failures rather than a cause. But his position appears unattainable and it would be a huge surprise if he is still in the dugout for next Saturday's match against Chelsea at Stamford Bridge. Below, we take a look at who could be there in his place. 7 - Manchester United have won just seven points from eight Premier League games this season (W1 D4 L3), their lowest at this stage of a league season since 1986-87 (4). Nightmare. pic.twitter.com/9IpGCx77xo — OptaJoe (@OptaJoe) October 25, 2026 Eddie Howe (unattached) Howe is currently a free agent having left his job as Newcastle United manager this summer after nearly five years in charge. He enjoyed a hugely successful spell on Tyneside when – with the financial backing of Newcastle's Saudi Arabian owners – he transformed the club from relegation candidates to top-four contenders playing a high intensity, physical brand of football. Under Howe's stewardship, the Magpies twice qualified for the Champions League while also winning their first domestic trophy in 70 years when they beat Liverpool in the League Cup final. His final campaign was a struggle, though, as Newcastle finished down in 12th place having lost the services of top-scorer Alexander Isak to Liverpool. The 48-year-old had previously led Bournemouth from the fourth tier to the Premier League – during two spells in charge – keeping them in the top-flight for five consecutive seasons. Antonio Conte (unattached) The Italian is a serial trophy-winning coach with the likes of Juventus, Chelsea, Inter Milan and Napoli. He left Napoli in May one year after securing the Serie A title. After spells as manager at the likes of Arezzo, Bari and Atalanta, Conte then took over at Juventus, the club where he made more than 400 appearances as a player and won just about every major honour. He led Juve to three successive Serie A titles from 2011 to 2014 before becoming Italy's national team manager for two years and then moving to England in 2016, winning the Premier League crown for Chelsea in his first season and FA Cup in his second. Another scudetto would follow at Inter Milan while a return to England with Tottenham Hotspur saw him lead the club back into the Champions League. The 57-year-old would undoubtedly arrive with the winning mentality required to be Man United coach but also brings a combustible character who has no problem going public with his grievances with club bosses if he sees fit. Julian Nagelsmann (unattached) Another out of work coach who stepped down as Germany manager following a shock World Cup exit in the last-32 at the hands of Paraguay. Nagelsmann became the youngest manager in Bundesliga history when he took charge of Hoffenheim at the age of 28 years and 203 days in 2016. Took the club from relegation candidates to Champions League qualification during his three and half years in charge. Nagelsmann then led RB Leipzig to third- and second-place finishes in the Bundesliga as well as reaching the Champions League semi-finals and last-16. Bayern Munich then came calling as the Bavarian giants reportedly forked out €25 million to release him from his Leipzig contract in 2021. His two season at Bayern saw them win the Bundesliga and two Germany Super Cups but also saw him fall out with players, including influential goalkeeper Manuel Neuer. Nagelsmann, now 39, worked with Man United's current head of recruitment, Christopher Vivell, at RB Leipzig so will certainly be in the mix should Carrick go. Unai Emery (Aston Villa) Spaniard is firmly established as one of Europe's top coaches having now lifted the Europa League five times with Sevilla, Villarreal and Aston Villa, as well as winning the domestic double at Paris Saint-Germain. Emery is the only manager to have won the Europa League three seasons in a row, a feat he achieved between 2013 and 2016 when Sevilla defeated Benfica, Dnipro and Jurgen Klopp's Liverpool in the final. His PSG reign would see them dominate domestically over two seasons but fail to secure the Champions League crown their Qatari owners craved. An unsuccessful spell at Arsenal was followed by another Europa League crown at Villareal before moving back to England in October 2022 where he led Aston Villa from a relegation fight to seventh place and the Europa Conference League in seven months. Since then, he led Villa back into the Champions League as well as winning the Europa League last season – the club's first trophy in 30 years. Clearly has to stature required for United job but would cost huge compensation fee. And it is far from certain that the 54-year-old would be willing to swap the relative calm of Villa for the chaos of Old Trafford. Unai Emery has won the Europa League five times already 😮‍💨 Football heritage 🏆 pic.twitter.com/HIXRgEfbih — Football on TNT Sports (@footballontnt) May 21, 2026 Cesc Fabregas (Como) The Spaniard just hammered one of the final nails in Carrick's coffin with the drubbing in Lombardy last week. His first senior manager's role saw him secure Como a spot in the Champions League for the first time in their history when they finished fourth place last season. The current campaign has seen Como win two out of three games in European football's premier competition and are fifth in Serie A after losing just once eight matches. Is building an exciting side at Como, where he is a minority shareholder, and the 39-year-old probably lacks the managerial experience needed to sort out the mess at Old Trafford right now.

title: Abu Dhabi announces new youth orchestra with free music education
description: Frank Gehry-designed institution in Mina Zayed will welcome 100 children aged six to nine, with instruments provided at no cost
content: A new music institution in Abu Dhabi will offer free tuition and instruments to children aged six to nine when it opens in January. Youth Orchestra Abu Dhabi will be based in a building designed by the late Frank Gehry in the Mina Zayed district, with a 600-seat concert hall and 18 rehearsal and practice rooms. Established by the Department of Culture and Tourism Abu Dhabi, the institution is accepting applications for its first cohort of 100 pupils before its January 2027 opening. “Youth Orchestra Abu Dhabi is about creating opportunities for young people to discover and develop their potential through music,” says Mohamed Khalifa Al Mubarak, chairman of DCT Abu Dhabi. “Beyond musical skills, it helps build confidence, creativity, discipline and collaboration. It reflects our belief that investing in young people today is essential to building a vibrant and sustainable cultural future for Abu Dhabi.” Pupils will attend group lessons four times a week after school and on two Saturdays each month, led by teaching artists. Each child will be provided with a musical instrument at no cost, with training covering both western classical and Arabic musical traditions. The programme is intended to support pupils over the longer term, allowing them to develop their skills and progress through ensemble playing. Additional ensembles for advanced pupils are planned during its first year. Its approach draws on Youth Orchestra Los Angeles, founded by Venezuelan conductor Gustavo Dudamel and inspired by El Sistema, the music education movement that began in Venezuela. Through the Los Angeles programme, the LA Philharmonic and its community partners provide free instruments and intensive music training to young people from underserved communities. There is an architectural connection, too: Gehry designed its Beckmen Yola Centre in Inglewoeod, which opened in 2021. The Abu Dhabi institution will be among the architect’s final completed works, according to the department. Alongside its teaching programme, the venue will host public performances, master classes and community events. It joins several Gehry projects in Abu Dhabi, including Guggenheim Abu Dhabi , which opens on December 11, and the forthcoming Dar Al Funoon performing arts centre. Announced in June and scheduled to open near Saadiyat Cultural District in 2030, Dar Al Funoon will accommodate opera, ballet, theatre and orchestral concerts, with plans for international touring partnerships, co-productions and artistic residencies. Youth Orchestra Abu Dhabi adds a programme of regular music education for children to that expansion, with its first pupils set to begin learning in January.

title: Beyond charity: The UAE initiative rewriting the rules of giving
description: For Maywand Jabarkhyl, chief executive of FBMI, the future of philanthropy is not about asking for donations, but creating products people genuinely want to buy
content: For more than 15 years, the Fatima bint Mohamed Bin Zayed Initiative (FBMI) has been rethinking philanthropy. Founded in 2010 by Sheikha Fatima bint Mohamed, it asks a fundamental question: rather than simply giving money to communities in need, what if aid could create livelihoods that eventually sustain themselves? Its model is deceptively simple: create products people want to buy, connect their makers with international markets, and reinvest the profits in healthcare, education and support for disadvantaged communities. “We have to change the way the world gives money,” says Maywand Jabarkhyl, chief executive of FBMI. “You can look at profit in a very positive manner. You just have to make sure that it’s ethical and responsible.” Rather than beginning with a community and asking what can be donated, FBMI first looks for gaps in the retail market. “When you look at the philanthropic environment anywhere in the world, the focus is strictly on fundraising,” says Jabarkhyl. “What we have done is look at the market first and found a solution based on consumer demands. We give the women in our programmes access to international global markets, so that their products can be upscaled, and they can earn a good living.” FBMI’s model is closer to a social enterprise. Women in disadvantaged communities are trained to produce goods to international standards; the products are then sold through a commercial network, with profits reinvested in the wider programme. FBMI works with carpet weavers and rural farms, and has a client roster that includes five-star hotels, luxury brands and Emirates airline. Produce from rural Afghanistan and Tanzania is now served in the Emirates first class cabin. “I don’t think it can become much bigger than this,” says Jabarkhyl. The UAE’s leadership has also embraced the initiative, commissioning carpets as gifts for international dignitaries including former US president Joe Biden, former French president Nicolas Sarkozy and the late Pope Francis. The pontiff received the Tolerance Carpet, handwoven by Afghan women, from President Sheikh Mohamed. “We’ve become a tool for diplomacy,” says Jabarkhyl. Soft power, it seems, has been made tangible. But FBMI’s ambitions extend beyond carpets. Since launching its strategic advisory arm in 2015, it has developed four areas of activity: healthcare, education, arts and culture, and strategic advisory – alongside a portfolio of social enterprises. Its healthcare work reaches more than 25,000 people each month through services including mother-and-child clinics and vaccination programmes focused on 11 diseases, including polio. Other projects have improved sanitation and access to water, supported Tanzanian farmers and provided digital education for Afghan girls unable to attend school. FBMI has hosted talks at the World Economic Forum’s Annual Meeting in Davos, worked with UN agencies including Unicef and UNHCR, and collaborated on limited-edition carpets with Zaha Hadid and Norma Kamali, as well as regional and Emirati creatives including Roudha Al Shamsi and Nada Debs . It is now seeking to establish handmade carpet weaving within the UAE’s contemporary cultural landscape. In Abu Dhabi, FBMI is developing a centre dedicated to arts, crafts, heritage and design, exploring how traditional Emirati materials and techniques can be adapted for a contemporary market. Another initiative, Intimaa: Sacred Threads, coincides with the Year of the Family. Ten UAE residents and artists, including Shamsa Al Omaira, Dhabia Al Qubaisi, Azza Al Sherif and Noura Al Serkal, are designing carpets to be woven by women in Afghanistan. The finished works will be exhibited at the Cultural Foundation in Abu Dhabi before being auctioned in December. Another project will explore the intersection of Emirati weaving traditions such as Talli and Al-Sadu – both part of Unesco’s Intangible Cultural Heritage list – with hand-knotted carpets. FBMI also hopes to revive traditional methods of processing goat and camel wool in the region. The work at the intersection of craft and art is also being recognised beyond the traditional non-profit space. “We’re going to be at Frieze Abu Dhabi in November, which is huge, of course,” Jabarkhyl says. This breadth reflects the organisation’s evolution. What began as a carpet-weaving project in 2010 has become a broader experiment in how commerce, culture and philanthropy can coexist. FBMI plans to expand its commercial model to another 50 regions, with research already under way in Kenya, Senegal and Kurdistan. The organisation’s market-first philosophy may be FBMI’s most radical proposition. Instead of asking consumers to buy something because it is charitable, it asks them to buy a product because it is good – and then allows the social impact to follow. “You don’t have to just focus on corporate profits and then give the chunk away to a charity,” Jabarkhyl says. “You can do it all.” The proposition appears to be working. FBMI is on track to generate a nine-figure revenue this year, helping to fund its healthcare, education, research and development programmes. Jabarkhyl’s goal is not simply for FBMI to grow, but for its approach to become commonplace. “I’d like to see more organisations undertaking the model that we have,” he says. “We just can’t keep asking for more and more money every year when it comes to livelihoods. “We are very good at saying: ‘We don’t want your money; just buy the products that we have, because they are world-class.’ I think people warm to that. “We want to give them something in return – a lovely carpet, some nice dried fruits or saffron. When people see that there’s an exchange, they are more convinced they are doing something for the country, for arts and culture, and supporting something that they believe in.” That is the philosophy at the heart of FBMI. Its proposition is not that philanthropy should disappear, but that it should become more ambitious: less concerned with the temporary relief of giving and more interested in building something that lasts.

title: Trump praises Libyans after campaign insult sparks diplomatic protest
description: Disparaging remarks made by Mr Trump at a campaign rally prompted diplomatic protest in Tripoli
content: US President Donald Trump praised Libyans as “proud, resilient, hospitable” after his disparaging remarks at a campaign rally prompted a diplomatic protest from Tripoli and condemnation across the country’s political divide. The conciliatory statement, posted on Sunday evening, stopped short of an apology and included a demand that Libya stop serving as a corridor for irregular migration. “The Libyan people are proud, resilient, hospitable, and deserving of peace and prosperity,” Mr Trump wrote on Truth Social, reaffirming Washington’s commitment to stronger relations with the North African country. “We respect the Libyan people and the sacrifices that brave Libyans made fighting ISIS, the common enemy of both our peoples, but Libya cannot remain a corridor for illegal migration, and this must end now,” he said. The remarks followed Libya’s decision to summon the US chargé d’affaires on Sunday over comments Mr Trump made a day earlier at a rally in Perry, Georgia. Attacking Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff over immigration, Mr Trump accused him of sponsoring legislation to bring migrants from countries he described as “terror-infested”, including Libya, Yemen, Haiti and Somalia. “Remember what I called them?,” he said, using a highly disparaging expletive. Libya’s Foreign Ministry delivered a formal protest to the American diplomat over what it said were statements undermining the dignity of Libyans. The Presidential Council said it had instructed the ministry to summon the head of the US diplomatic mission and demanded an explicit apology and correction. It said relations between countries should be based on mutual respect. Prime Minister Abdul Hamid Dbeibah, who heads the Tripoli-based Government of National Unity, also rejected the remarks in a social media post, saying Libya’s sovereignty and its people’s dignity should not become material for American electoral disputes. “We value our relationship with the United States on the basis of mutual respect, and we will not accept Libya’s dignity and that of its people becoming material for electoral disputes,” he said. Mr Dbeibah invoked Libyans’ sacrifices in fighting terrorism, a contribution Mr Trump subsequently acknowledged in his statement describing ISIS as a common enemy of both countries. The criticism extended beyond the Tripoli administration. Libya’s rival eastern government called for a retraction and formal apology, while a committee of the House of Representatives sought an official clarification from Washington. The committee said the remarks diminished Libya’s standing. The competing administrations’ responses placed them on common ground in rejecting the insult, despite their wider political differences. In his subsequent statement, Mr Trump backed efforts to unify Libya and its institutions and move towards national elections. He said Washington supports Libyans in restoring their sovereignty after years of terrorism and foreign interference. He offered no timetable or new initiative to advance those goals, and did not specify what measures he expected Libya to take on migration.

title: What happens on Israeli election day?
description: From polling hours to declaration times, here is all you need to know
content: Read the latest on Israel's election here Israel heads to the polls on Tuesday in what is seen as one of the most pivotal and consequential elections in its recent history. The election is Israeli voters' first opportunity to hold leaders accountable for security failures surrounding the October 7, 2023, attacks, decide who should lead Israel in the regional conflict and weigh in on the contentious issue of military service. So what happens on election day and when can we expect the results? The timeline All times are Israel local time. The UAE is two hours ahead. 7am: Polling stations open Voting begins at most polling stations nationwide, with Israelis electing representatives to the 120-seat Knesset. About 7.3 million Israelis are eligible to vote. Thirty six parties are running, although most will not pass the 3.25 per cent threshold needed to enter parliament. 8am: Special polling stations open Voting begins in smaller communities, hospitals, prisons and care homes, where polling stations generally operate for shorter hours. Throughout the day: Voting continues Turnout figures are expected at regular intervals, offering an early indication of voter enthusiasm. Political leaders will cast their ballots. 8pm: Special polling stations close Voting ends at most smaller-community and institutional polling stations. Voters who arrived before closing can still cast their ballots. 10pm: Main polling stations close Voting officially ends at most polling stations nationwide, although those already in line can still vote. After 10pm: Exit polls and vote counting Israeli television networks are expected to release their exit polls, providing the first indication of how parties may perform. Preliminary results will emerge as votes are counted overnight. Final results will take another week or so. The election process Israel's parliament, known as the Knesset, has 120 seats, with 61 needed for an outright majority. Israel uses a proportional representation system, meaning voters choose political parties rather than directly electing a prime minister. No single party has ever won an outright majority, so governments have always been formed through coalitions. Once the results are confirmed, Israeli President Isaac Herzog will task a member of parliament with forming a government, usually the leader considered most capable of securing parliamentary support. If no coalition can secure a majority, a minority government could still be formed with sufficient parliamentary backing. If attempts to form a government fail, Israel could face another election, with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu leading a caretaker government in the meantime. The results At 10pm on election day, Israeli broadcasters will release exit polls. But these are only projections and can differ significantly from the actual results. Preliminary results are expected the following day, with official results scheduled to be published by November 4. The deadline for appeals is November 18. Election results will not necessarily determine who Israel's next prime minister will be. Coalition negotiations can take weeks or even months as parties attempt to reach agreements on who will govern and under what terms. Israel has a history of political deadlock. Between 2019 and 2022, the country held five elections as parties repeatedly struggled to form stable governments. So while voters may have an indicator of the results on election night, it could take much longer to know who will actually lead the country.

title: Can John Healey conjure a budget to keep investors’ money in Britain?
description: New Chancellor has little fiscal headroom for sweeping changes
content: By one measure, John Healey’s budget has already been a success. He has avoided the paralysis that hit the UK before his predecessor Rachel Reeves delivered her tax and spending plans in November 2025. That budget had such an agonisingly long build-up that a combination of speculation and leaks caused jitters in financial markets, property transactions ground to a halt, and the wealthy packed their bags for sunnier climes. It forced Ms Reeves into policy pivots that dented her reputation and confidence in the government’s messaging. Mr Healey has led a more orchestrated run-up, allowing messaging to get out that he will not match Capital Gains Tax to income tax, that banks can expect a fresh levy, and that business red tape is set to be torn apart. His goal when he rises to the dispatch box is to unveil short-term help with the cost-of-living, stem the tide of super-rich moving abroad, while also seeking to stabilise public finances hit by spending pressures and the fallout from the US-Iran war. So what do those who invest in Britain want to see come out of his red box, or perhaps more importantly, discarded as a bad idea? Property stakes In terms of property, London’s golden postcodes have seen sluggish sales in recent years as the prime market fails to ignite, with prices still behind their 2014 peak. Tom Bill, head of UK residential research at Knight Frank, hopes the greatest threats to the market – such as an even broader mansion tax than first announced – have already been abandoned. “Sentiment in the prime London property market would improve because of what is not in the budget rather than anything the Chancellor includes,” he told The National . “He has reportedly dropped plans to lower the bottom threshold for the high-value council tax, and there would be a collective sigh of relief if property is not targeted in the way it has been in previous budgets.” The mansion tax would add an annual fee for properties above £2 million on top of council tax. Buyers in high-value residential markets such as London require “a sense of stability that has been missing for several years”, he said. London has had a comparatively positive summer, largely thanks to the absence of tax speculation ahead of the budget, he said. September recorded the first period of quarterly price growth (+0.3 per cent) in prime central London (PCL) for four years. Sales of properties above £5 million dropped by 14 per cent in the 18 months after Ms Reeves’ first budget in October 2024, when she raised second-home stamp duty to 5 per cent from 3 per cent. That created an estimated stamp duty loss of £541 million based on a comparison of sales in the preceding 18 months, according to Knight Frank. “The stamp duty loss is one of many indicators that show what happens when Britain is not competitive on a global stage in attracting overseas investors,” said Leslie Macleod-Miller, chief executive of Foreign Investors for Britain (FIFB). “Of course, it also grossly understates the wider loss to the country’s economy.” Unworkable For Matthew Robertson, co-founder and chief financial officer of luxury developer Valouran, there are three focal points for the budget: capital gains tax, wealth tax and the mansion tax. “As we saw play out ahead of the autumn budget last year, when people don’t know what’s coming, they wait,” he told The National . “Buyers pause, deals are deferred, and the Treasury loses out too because there is no tax intake when no one is buying or selling. Since real estate investment is inherently long term, my hope is that this budget will, at a minimum, provide businesses and investors with confidence that they can plan without constantly worrying that a new tax or policy change is just around the corner.” He believes the mansion tax is unworkable due to the requirement to have hundreds of thousands of homes revalued. He said the £2 million threshold already drags a great many people into the levy, “many of whom would not consider themselves rich”. Proposals to reduce this to £1.5 million must be resisted, he cautioned. “If mansion tax is here to stay, it would be good to have it accompanied by a reduction in stamp duty. The objective should be to encourage a more efficient and dynamic housing market, rather than simply increasing the tax burden.” Budget flops Research by Beauchamp estates found that the autumn budgets of the Boris Johnson and Rishi Sunak governments had the most positive impact on London’s prime property market, while Liz Truss’s mini-budget spooked the market and led to the exodus of wealthy owners. Under Keir Starmer and Rachel Reeves, the market struggled. It found that after the 2024 budget there were significant drops in sales. The number of £5 million+ properties sold dropped by 16 per cent, from 148 deals pre-budget to 124 deals post-budget, with the overall value of deals slipping from £1.42 billion to £1.4 billion. The £10 million+ homes market declined the most, with the number of sales falling by 25 per cent, from 51 pre-budget to 38 post-budget. Beauchamp Estates says that the 2024 decline in sales was due to Conservative rather than Labour policies, namely the scrapping of non-doms, which was initially planned by Mr Sunak. Jeremy Gee, managing director of Beauchamp Estates, said: "Our detailed analysis of the autumn budgets over the last 11 years clearly shows that domestic UK and international buyers of property in London like political, economic and taxation certainty. Cameron/Osborne raising Stamp Duty was negative for the market. However, the upbeat and business-friendly stance of Boris/Sunak was good for property sales, the uncertainty caused by May/Hammond was unhelpful, and Truss/Kwarteng temporarily tanked the market and were made to look foolish." He said that over the last few years the top end of the market has proved more resilient since sales are heavily influenced by wider global economic and political shifts, rather than UK domestic policies. Mr Gee said: "It is our firm belief that it is not tax that stops a buyer moving. It is a buyer not knowing what the tax will be that kills a sale. Over the past few years, the leaks and mixed messages that circulate for months before each budget have left buyers and sellers paralysed by fear of the unknown, and the market simply pauses until after the budget and sales decline.” He added: "Our greatest concern around the 2026 autumn budget is further taxation of wealth, whether CGT is aligned with income tax, or the introduction of a new wealth tax. The international buyers who underpin the prime central London market have already had to absorb a lot, and we must not forget that they have no shortage of alternative locations to invest in real estate." Who gains? He said Mr Healey’s dismissal of calls from Labour MPs to align capital gains tax with income tax rates is very welcome. “We need people to be motivated and confident enough to invest capital and build businesses in the UK, and the current CGT regime is one of the very few remaining incentives for those prepared to back businesses for the long term. Raising rates would make the UK a far less attractive place to invest and build. “Not a day goes by without more news that another ultra-high net worth individual has left the UK. These individuals take with them significant personal taxable incomes that have contributed so much to our public finances. Even more concerningly, they are relocating their successful businesses elsewhere, businesses that paid corporation tax and employed many other high earners in the UK. Tax policy must evolve to stem this exodus.” People representing about $160 billion on the Bloomberg Billionaires Index have already left the UK in the past two years. It coincided with the scrapping of non-dom status, which allowed international income to be kept out of the reach of UK tax authorities. Most of that group originally came from overseas, but the recent relocation of British hedge fund founder Chris Rokos to Greece has underscored a growing unrest among local entrepreneurs. A poll of 500 UK business owners during August for the London professional services group S&W found about half of them would consider relocating if capital gains taxes are increased in the autumn budget. There are suggestions of how to encourage wealthy investors to reconsider Britain. There is some speculation around an investor visa. “The details are unclear, and it may not be attractive enough to reverse the flow of wealthy individuals leaving the UK, but it would show the government acknowledges that it needs to address the issue,” said Mr Bill. The proposal by FIFB is based on a minimum investment of £2.5 million and an annual flat-rate tax of £200,000 for up to 15 years, with a route to indefinite leave to remain. FIFB estimates the plan could attract more than £225 billion of inward investment over a decade. The current non-dom replacement exempts newcomers’ foreign income and gains from UK tax for their first four years of residence. “Four years is simply not long enough, which is a message we have been giving to the government,” Mr Macleod-Miller said. “The problem so far is the gap between what the government has said in relation to creating economic growth and what they have done.” Deals done In recent days, Mr Healey has said he wants a business-friendly budget, and has hinted that CGT, which is levied on a person's profits from an asset sale, may not rise at all. That may be bittersweet for those wealthy Britons who rushed to ensure they weren’t hit by any increase ahead of the budget. Investors have been seeking to take advantage of the current 24 per cent higher rate, according to many wealth advisers. A lot of people rushed to get deals done earlier in October to secure the current rate, said Chris Etherington, a private client tax partner at RSM UK who advises business owners and entrepreneurs. He saw people “trying to accelerate deals ahead of the budget”. Capital gains tax fears had been “the number one issue”, said Iain Tait, head of the private investment office at wealth management firm W1M. “We’ve had a lot of clients asking about what they could do to crystallise gains at 24 per cent.” One investor nervous about further tax hikes is Konstantin Sidorov, whose London investment fund is sitting on a gain of more than 500 per cent through its bet on Revolut, the UK fintech giant founded by billionaire Nik Storonsky. Mr Sidorov called a dedicated wealth tax a “red line” that would make him consider relocating after more than a decade. “My feeling is quite bad – the question is: How bad?” he said in an interview. If capital gains taxes rise, “we’ll see far fewer investors who would like to take more risks”. Do no harm After his predecessor hiked taxes by more than £60 billion ($80 billion) in her two budgets, Mr Healey has no appetite for another big set-piece. “They’ve calculated that this budget should just be ‘do no harm’, given everything else that’s going on in the world,” said James Nation, managing director at Forefront Advisers and a former special adviser to Rishi Sunak when he was chancellor and prime minister. “They don’t want to do anything that derails them.” Mr Healey’s approach means crunch issues such as overhauling the welfare system and long-term investment in defence will be deferred. It also shies away from demands from the Labour left that he should ramp up taxes on wealth and raise spending on public services. On Friday, he announced his budget would include measures to reduce the regulatory burden on businesses such as simplifying corporate reporting requirements, while also extending import tariff suspensions on products across sectors including chemicals, plastics and hydrogen. “British firms are fed up with form-filling and pointless paperwork that eats into valuable time and money,” he said in a statement. “That is why we are cutting unnecessary bureaucracy and giving businesses the breathing space they need to invest, innovate and create good jobs.” Iron triangle Treasury officials describe Healey’s budget as a stepping stone moment, saying a major “10-year plan” speech planned by Mr Burnham later this year is the real main fixture for addressing Britain’s big structural problems. A Labour official acknowledged to The National the limited scope for action. “Everything’s a bit in the long grass,” he said, including decisions on defence, welfare and taxation. “The PM is actually stuck with the commitments that Starmer had, which is no increases in most of the taxes, so we are scratching around for income, most likely from a bank tax hike that might only raise a couple of billion.” Andrew Murray, a former adviser to Labour’s leadership, said the budget would establish the direction of Mr Burnham’s government after he raised expectations of a different economic approach. “Obviously, everyone will give him a bit of latitude, but the budget will really set the direction,” he told The National. “If it is, as expected, a bit flat, a bit of a non-event, the only thing will be his 10-year plan for Britain that he promised before Christmas. He would need to really paint that in vivid colours and get it done soon if people aren’t going to start feeling a bit disappointed.” But the government remained constrained by the competing demands of welfare, taxation and defence. “It’s like an iron triangle, that really boxes you in,” he said, adding that the budget would test Mr Burnham’s promise of a more social-democratic future. “All the briefing is that apart from bank tax, Healey isn’t going to do anything very decisive.” Further taxes on the well-off were unlikely, said the Labour official, because the government had already gone as far as it could, particularly following changes to the non-dom tax regime. “It would be a surprise if there’s anything more on the wealthy because the non-dom tax has clearly had some impact,” the official said. The Institute for Fiscal Studies has warned that the government faces spending pressures, particularly with its plans to increase defence spending to 3 per cent of GDP by 2030, which would require tax increases or benefit cuts of around £35 billion. The budget will be a test of whether Mr Burnham can deliver on his Labour conference speech, which promised higher living standards and economic renewal while keeping spending within limits. If he succeeds, it could sow the seeds for a Labour election victory. If he doesn't, Britain could revert once again to political and financial uncertainty, and a further exodus of the money-makers.

title: Mbappe steals Yamal’s Ballon d’Or spotlight with El Clasico double
description: Mbappe’s two-goal masterclass sealed a 2-1 win at Camp Nou to put the Real Madrid forward firmly into the Ballon d’Or conversation as Yamal struggles to make an impact
content: Seven Ballon d’Or nominees started Sunday’s Clasico at Camp Nou. Real Madrid’s Kylian Mbappe stood out from the pack, scoring both his side’s goals in a shock 2-1 win at the home of their greatest rival. Barcelona had won all nine league games to begin the season, averaging more than four goals per game, and would have gone nine points clear of Madrid had they won. But Madrid coach Jose Mourinho does not follow convention , nor did his team. They frustrated Barcelona throughout, took the lead before the break and got the winner three minutes from time following some magical skill from Jude Bellingham and then Mbappe . Madrid’s players were joined by half of their bench as they celebrated right in front of the most vocal Barca fans, which did not go down well. Raphinha had equalised for Barca after 61 minutes in front of the 62,000-strong crowd as the stadium continues its redevelopment towards a 105,000-seat capacity. El Clasico justified its status as the biggest game in world football, an intense battle between two giants powered by some of the best players. England’s Premier League may be the pre-eminent league, but Barcelona and Madrid are huge attractions; Barcelona, in particular, produces sublime footballing talents. Both clubs will be represented at the Ballon d’Or Awards at London’s Palladium Theatre on Monday. Madrid didn’t attend the previous two ceremonies after learning that Vinicius Jnr wouldn’t win an award. For Barcelona , Pau Cubarsi, Rodri and Lamine Yamal are among the 30 nominees. For Madrid, Bellingham, Marc Cucurella, Mbappe and Vinicius are in the running. Yamal and Cubarsi are both only 19 years old. Both grew up in Catalonia, north of Barcelona, as did Cucurella. Much is made of the concentration of top managers from Spain’s smallest province, Gipuzkoa, but there's a small area of Catalonia north of Barcelona with towns and villages that have produced an inordinate amount of footballing talent. Como boss Cesc Fabregas is also from here, as is Xavi Espart, yet another 19-year-old who started as right back for Barcelona in the Clasico. Fabregas, Espart, Cucurella and Yamal come from the coastal strip, Cubarsi from the inland village of Bescano and four generations of carpenters. Pau is better at passing a football than planing a plank of wood. He was originally a youth player with nearby Girona before moving to Barca. In one tournament game for Girona against Manchester United when he was 10 years old, United’s coaches said it was like playing against a one-man team, Cubarsi being that man. Nine of Spain’s World Cup squad were Catalans. Unlike Cubarsi, who won the award for the World Cup’s best young player, Yamal didn’t have a great World Cup, but he remains the hottest player in world football. When The National asked Barca fans outside Camp Nou who should win the Ballon d’Or, most chose him. The Barcelona winger is the favourite to win, along with England and Bayern Munich striker Harry Kane and then Mbappe . But Spain won the World Cup by conceding only one goal. Their defence was key. Cucurella, who grew up just a 15-minute drive from Yamal, had the better of his rival on Sunday, who was reduced to skewing a shot wide before half-time and again in the 78th minute. It was not Yamal’s night, despite Barca having 62 per cent possession and 12 shots to Madrid’s five. Yet it was Madrid who created the better chances. Cucurella was a young professional with Barca and a regular with the B team, but he never played a first-team game. Home fans sang songs about him, casting him as the pantomime villain, and howled at his heavy challenges on Yamal. But they were silenced when he released Yan Diomande, who crossed for Mbappe to capitalise on a Gerard Martin error and put Madrid ahead. La Liga had seemed predictable before the Clasico and some Madrid fans had even written their team off. With only three points separating the top three, it’s now a real title race. “The world that loves football will have stopped to watch this and they won’t have gone disappointed; this was two teams that played to win,” said the victorious Mourinho , back at Madrid following 13 years. Madrid’s win was a surprise, but a deserved one. Will there be another one in London for the Ballon d’Or ? It has been framed as a race between Yamal and Kane, but Mbappe’s two goals in the biggest game in the world on the eve of the awards make him the man of the moment.

title: YouTube launches shopping programme in UAE: How influencers can earn money with 500 subscribers
description: Also launched in Saudi Arabia and Egypt, the feature enables eligible creators to earn commissions from product sales
content: YouTube has launched its Shopping affiliate programme in the UAE, Saudi Arabia and Egypt, allowing smaller content creators to earn money from products they recommend to their audiences. The programme, announced on Monday, enables eligible creators with as few as 500 subscribers to tag products in their videos, Shorts and livestreams and receive commissions when viewers make qualifying purchases. Amazon is the first retail partner, with more retailers expected to join the service, according to YouTube. The expansion could provide new ways to to make money for smaller influencers who have not secured lucrative brand partnerships or substantial advertising revenue. It also enables viewers to find products featured in videos and proceed directly to a retailer's website to complete their purchases. How it works Under the programme, creators can tag eligible Amazon products directly in their content using YouTube Studio. When viewers select a product, they are directed to Amazon to complete the purchase. Creators can then earn a commission on qualifying sales. The feature is available across long-form videos, Shorts and livestreams, meaning creators can potentially generate revenue from both new and existing content. Creators can track clicks, estimated revenue and earnings through YouTube Studio, according to YouTube's official Amazon shopping guidance. The platform also allows qualifying creators to earn commissions from international viewers where eligible purchasing options are available. However, earnings depend on qualifying purchases, and refunds can result in previously earned commissions being deducted. Who can apply The lower subscriber threshold is among the most significant changes for smaller creators. YouTube first announced a wider rollout of the programme to eligible US creators in June 2023. In March, the company announced it was expanding its Shopping affiliate programme to eligible members of its Partner Programme who had at least 500 subscribers. But subscriber numbers are only one part of the requirements. According to YouTube's monetisation guidelines, creators seeking access through the expanded Partner Programme must also have uploaded three public videos in the previous 90 days and achieved either 3,000 valid public watch hours over the previous year or three million valid Shorts views within 90 days. Creators must also meet the specific Shopping affiliate eligibility requirements and can check their access through the Earn section of YouTube Studio. Middle East expansion The launch comes as online videos increasingly influence how consumers discover and research products. More than 40 million logged-in users across the UAE, Saudi Arabia , Egypt, Morocco and Algeria conducted shopping-related searches on the platform in June, according to YouTube. The company said viewers worldwide watch more than 40 billion hours of shopping-related content annually. In the UAE and Saudi Arabia, 86 per cent of surveyed viewers considered YouTube to have the most trusted creators for shopping recommendations, according to a survey carried out by international market research and consumer insights company, Kantar. The figures, provided by YouTube, highlight the commercial potential for content that helps viewers make purchasing decisions. The company has also introduced AI-powered tools that can identify products appearing in videos and suggest relevant tags, reducing the time creators spend adding shopping links. Viewers watching YouTube on television can scan QR codes using their mobile phones to access featured products. What does this mean for UAE influencers? For smaller creators in the UAE , the programme offers a way to monetise their audiences without waiting to reach hundreds of thousands of followers. Affiliate commissions could supplement advertising revenue and paid collaborations, although meaningful earnings will depend on attracting viewers who are willing to buy recommended products. Maintaining audience trust will also be important, particularly when creators have a financial incentive to promote certain products.

title: Iraqi court seeks arrest of Maysan provincial leader for defying Iran border closure
description: Closure of Al Sheeb crossing over security concerns has prompted criticism and protests
content: Iraq's Karkh Court in Baghdad on Monday ordered an investigation into the head of Maysan's provincial council after Prime Minister Ali Al Zaidi called for a probe over his calls for civil disobedience if the Al Sheeb border crossing with Iran is not reopened. Last week, Iraq closed the crossing in Maysan to travellers and goods, with the decision escalating tension with Iran and pro-Tehran Iraqi politicians. The decision was made due to security concerns at the border. On Sunday, Mustafa Duair Abdulhassan, the head of Maysan's provincial council, said that people would have to “resort to civil disobedience and cut Maysan off from the rest of Iraq” if the crossing was not reopened. Mr Abdulhassan is affiliated with Sadiqoun, the political wing of the Iran-aligned Asaib Ahl Al Haq, led by Qais Al Khazali. Mr Al Zaidi's office said the investigation was in response to “threats” and “inappropriate language”. Other politicians have also criticised the closure, with some joining dozens of lorry drivers and workers who demonstrated last week, calling on the government to reverse its decision to shut the crossing, which is a vital land route for commercial and civilian vehicles. Protesters said their livelihoods depended on cross‑border traffic. Mr Al Zaidi called on security forces to ensure a safe environment for demonstrators. The Prime Minister chaired a meeting of the Ministerial Council of National Security that underscored the need to “secure peaceful demonstrations” and to treat protesters with respect, his office said in a statement. Maysan Governor Habib Dhahir Al Fartousi called on Mr Al Zaidi to reopen the crossing and warned the closure would drive up prices and disrupt trade. Others have defended the decision . Abdelamir Taiban, a senior adviser to Mr Al Zaidi, told local media that Iran had “deliberately undermined Iraq’s security”, and alleged that Iranian-linked people were entering the country without authorisation and causing “chaos” along the border. Mr Taiban said Iraq’s most serious border problems involved Iran. One of the biggest challenges was the flow of drugs and counterfeit currency from Iran, which he said had inflicted economic damage “greater than what ISIS caused”. Iran's embassy in Iraq issued a statement on Saturday describing Mr Taiban's claims as “false allegations” and called on Iraqi authorities to take a position on remarks it said could damage relations between the countries. Iran had already criticised the border closure. Iranian state media reported that Tehran was not given advance notice that the Al Sheeb crossing would be closed. The matter is under review, Iranian Interior Ministry spokesman Ali Zeinivand was quoted as saying. Mr Al Zaidi, who took office in May, has sought to maintain balanced ties with both Iran and the US while moving to bring armed factions under state control. Some Iran‑aligned groups have complied, while others have resisted. Many of these groups have been accused of carrying out crimes and killings, particularly during anti-government protests in 2019. Thousands of protesters gathered on Sunday in Baghdad to commemorate the anniversary of the demonstrations that became known as the Tishreen movement, demanding accountability.

title: Indian wins Dh5 million in UAE Lottery days before his 60th birthday
description: Lottery winner plans to travel with his wife and focus on family
content: A Sharjah resident who won Dh5 million on the UAE Lottery plans to apply for a Golden Visa after travelling the world with his wife. Kishore Pandurang Rao, an Indian who has lived in the UAE for three decades, found out he had won the prize in the October 3 draw, only days before his 60th birthday. Mr Rao said he was shocked when he realised that he had won. "I was sitting quietly and scrolling online when I received an email from The UAE Lottery. Initially I thought it was a routine verification email," he said. "I was stunned. For some time, I just sat there without knowing what to say or do." Mr Rao said his plan was to focus first on his family. "I would like to support my elder son as he explores starting his own business and support my younger son with his higher education," he said. "I also want to bring my family together in the UAE after we have spent periods living apart. My wife and I are thinking about buying a home and cars, both here and in India. "I also want to keep our family home in India, which is very important to me because it is where I grew up. These are all plans, though, and I want to do them one at a time." Dh5 million prize When most people think of the lottery they have a dream purchase lined up to treat themselves to something that would otherwise have been out of reach. Mr Rao is lining up something a little different. "I didn’t think of a watch or a luxury item. One of my long-term wishes has been to explore the possibility of getting a UAE Golden Visa," he said. "After spending around 30 years in the country, the UAE means a great deal to me, so that is something I would really like to look into. I am also considering buying a new car and eventually a home, but I haven't made those decisions yet." Mr Rao said he was determined not to make rash choices about how to spend his winnings. "It will change some of the choices available to me, but I don't want to make every decision immediately just because I have won," he said. "I have just turned 60 after spending around three decades working in the UAE, so I see this as a new stage of my life. I want to spend more time with my wife and children, support their plans, travel with my wife and enjoy experiences together that we haven't had much time for before. "For me, the biggest change is really about what comes next and how we choose to spend that time together."

title: Scale AI establishes Dubai office
description: California tech company to have presence at DIFC
content: US technology company Scale AI announced on Monday that it has established a UAE office at the Dubai International Financial Centre . Scale AI , founded in 2016, is valued at $29 billion and has more than 1,000 employees. The official announcement that it is to have a presence in the UAE was made at a signing ceremony during the Dubai AI Festival. Trevor Thompson, global managing director at the AI infrastructure company , reflected on the company's decision to expand into the country, saying it has set a "clear, ambitious vision for AI and is now putting it to work across government and the economy". He added that Scale AI's plans will work well with the UAE's ambitions for the technology. "Making our home at DIFC is a long-term commitment," he said. "We are here to help UAE institutions build AI they can trust and use for their most critical use cases and important decisions." The company lists Meta, Cisco, Instacart, Nvidia, Cohere, OpenAI, Microsoft and Time, as well as the US Air Force and US Army, among its clients. Scale AI makes the tools other technology companies use to increase the reliability of their AI solutions. Its software assists with identifying items in images, tagging subjects within large amounts of text and labelling that information so it can be used in AI apps and chatbots. The company says its largely automated software allows humans to easily review and make changes to ensure accuracy. Scale AI’s footprint continues to grow as buzz surrounding the self-described "data-centric end-to-end solution" AI infrastructure company shows no sign of slowing. Essentially, if a company needs reliable and well-organised data to help create a large language model, Scale AI has become the go-to expert. It was founded by Alexandr Wang shortly after he dropped out of the Massachusetts Institute of Technology when he saw AI developments creating the need for ways to provide and manage high-quality training data for technology companies and other large businesses. Scale AI’s rapid rise has also carried Mr Wang into the rarefied air of AI tech entrepreneurs including Nvidia’s Jensen Huang and OpenAI’s Sam Altman. Mr Wang has graced the cover of magazines and testified before the US Congress. In June, he left the company for Meta after the social media company announced a significant investment in Scale AI. Mr Wang officially serves in the capacity of chief AI officer for Meta and has since been charged with developing its consumer-facing AI products such as Muse, Muse Image and various language models. After Mr Wang's departure, Scale AI named Jason Droege as the company's interim chief executive before announcing in July that Francis deSouza, Google Cloud's former chief operating officer, would be Mr Wang's official successor. According to Scale AI's media release, the company's UAE branch is based in the Dubai AI Campus at DIFC, part of the Dubai Universal Blueprint for Artificial Intelligence, "which brings together infrastructure, business support and international connections for AI companies building in Dubai".

title: ‘Astronomical’ Arab turnout could reshape Israeli politics in key election
description: Netanyahu’s opponents consider unprecedented alliances to keep him out of power
content: An “astronomical” turnout of Arab voters is expected in the Israeli elections on Tuesday, with the possibility that their politicians could significantly influence the next government, political sources have told The National . Senior opposition officials have also said there is a possibility of a coalition or agreed minority government with the Arab parties, if the mainstream parties do not win an outright majority. Opinion polls have now closed under Israeli law, with the final ones showing the opposition with a potential 56 seats, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud party on 50 with the Arab parties taking 14 in the 120-seat Knesset. With 61 seats needed to form a government, the opposition led by Yashar party leader Gadi Eisenkot could either form a minority government with tacit Arab party support or go into a coalition with the Ra’am party, led by Mansour Abbas. Arab influence could also be strengthened by a surge in votes for its two main parties – Ra'am and the Joint List – with turnout expected to rise from about 50 per cent to 70 per cent of the two million people who make up 20 per cent of Israel ’s total population. “After what they have witnessed over the past three years, they have understood the difference between bad and worse,” said an Israeli political observer, referring to the hard-right parties that have influenced politics. If the bloc against Mr Netanyahu takes power, then significant steps would be taken to halt the settler violence and illegal dwellings in the occupied West Bank , an opposition source said. “We will clamp down on settler violence, which has gone on for too long, because it is a disgrace to the country and because it is wrong," he said. "We will also stop wildcat home building because we believe in law and order.” A coalition involving Ra’am is one of three possible outcomes from the election. The other two are either a coalition between the centre-right and ultra-orthodox parties or a “government of unity” that would be likely to have Mr Eisenkot as prime minister, but would also include Mr Netanyahu ’s Likud. There are also many unknowns and other factors at play that could still affect the outcome. About 700,000 young people will vote for the first time – the last election was in 2022 – and it is not known which way the group that went through Covid, Israeli judicial reforms, the October 7 attacks and military service will vote. There are up to 70,000 Israelis living abroad who have flown back to the country to vote – the majority are understood to be against Mr Netanyahu – alongside a similar number of Russian emigres, who fled after the 2022 Ukraine invasion, who are thought to be in the more liberal camp. Key issues for Israel, which observers say are existential, are also at play. Some officials believe getting the ultra-Orthodox into conscripted military service is important to Israel’s security, but their parties object. There are 72,000 ultra-Orthodox young men aged 18 to 21 who are listed as “deserters” for not joining up. There is also talk of a “declaration of independence” that would give the country a written constitution, alongside term-limits for prime ministers. Mr Netanyahu has served for almost 20 years over three spells in office. Israel also faces other crises, including the imposition of international sanctions from European countries and a plummeting birth rate, except among the Arab and ultra-Orthodox population. About 50 per cent of school children are from those two groups. But some observers believe that, come dawn on Wednesday, Israel will simply resume the status quo, with the idea of Zionist parties working with Arab groups unacceptable to too many people. “My concern is that they will opt for the unity government [with Mr Netanyahu] because they are cowards and it is politically convenient,” one opposition figure said.

title: Europe’s top five defence powers to name Russia as greatest threat
description: Ukraine and Middle East conflicts on agenda at talks in Paris
content: Europe’s five largest defence spenders are set to warn that Russia represents the most acute and long-term threat to the continent’s security as they pledge unflagging support for Ukraine. “Russia’s ongoing war of aggression against Ukraine, on the one hand, and its continued violations of Allied airspace, acts of sabotage and growing use of multi-domain hybrid attacks, on the other, do not undermine our unity, solidarity and cohesion,” said a draft joint statement from France, Germany, Italy, Poland and the UK , or E5, according to Bloomberg News. The ministers also plan to say that Europe “must assume greater responsibility for its own security.” The statement, whose language could change before publication, is expected to be released after a meeting in Paris on Monday hosted by French Defence Minister Catherine Vautrin and attended by her counterparts from the other four countries. Ministers will also be discussing "security challenges in the Middle East," Ms Vautrin's office said. Their meeting comes as Saudi Defence Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman heads to Iran with other officials from countries in the Makkah Agreement to push forward a diplomatic solution to the crises in the region. The European ministers' message is a response to Russia intensifying a campaign of hybrid attacks across Europe, including suspected sabotage, cyber attacks, arson, drone incursions and threats to critical infrastructure and defence companies. Testing Nato European officials see the activity as an effort by Moscow to test Nato's limits , disrupt support for Ukraine and exploit uncertainty over how the alliance should respond without triggering a broader conflict. While highlighting that the US will remain an “indispensable ally,” the draft said that “this greater responsibility must begin with the empowerment of European Allies within Nato”. The European leaders are expected to say in the statement that they will assume greater political and military leadership to modernise their forces and capabilities, strengthening Nato’s collective defence to “adapt to current and future challenges” and also bolstering Europe’s defence readiness. The EU’s regulatory and financial resources can help support member states’ defence ambitions, according to the draft, while stressing that the bloc’s defence efforts should reinforce Nato rather than duplicate its work and should remain open to members outside the military alliance. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz warned last week that Russia’s threat to Europe extends beyond the war in Ukraine, arguing that Moscow is increasingly seeking to destabilise European democracies through pressure, interference and hybrid attacks. In an interview on Bloomberg Television on October 19, Mr Merz said Europe must take the threat more seriously, strengthen its defences and reduce its reliance on the US while continuing to support Ukraine. This step by European leaders comes after rising tension between America and Ukraine, following US President Donald Trump’s deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin, in which Washington agreed to refrain from imposing further sanctions in exchange for Moscow supplying diesel to the global market in a bid to reduce rising energy prices. The agreement was met with a strong backlash from US politicians allied with Mr Trump, as well as from Ukraine and European leaders. “We will maintain our unwavering commitment to supporting Ukraine in its fight back against Russian aggression,” the draft said, emphasising the combating of Russia’s shadow fleet and its continued violations of European airspace. “Ukraine’s ability to defend itself now and in the future is critically important to Euro-Atlantic collective security.” Agencies contributed to this report

title: Fighting intensifies as Houthis and Saudi-led coalition in Yemen report attacks
description: Coalition carries out strikes on Yemeni capital Sanaa
content: Fighting between the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen and the Iran-aligned Houthi rebels intensified on Monday, as escalating hostilities choked oil ⁠supplies and threatened to erupt into a broader conflict. The coalition in Yemen said it destroyed two ballistic missile launchers in the capital Sanaa , including one used to fire a missile towards Riyadh that it said had been ⁠intercepted. The Houthis later claimed they had attacked Saudi Arabia's East-West crude oil pumping stations and Riyadh airport, but there was no immediate confirmation from the kingdom. Sanaa has been under Houthi control since 2014, when the militant group seized the Yemeni capital and triggered a Saudi-led military intervention in support of Yemen’s internationally recognised government. The Houthis have fired ballistic missiles ​and drones at ⁠ Saudi airports , ports and oil installations, ‌turning the kingdom into a pressure point in the wider regional war. Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport resumed operations at two terminals on Sunday after attacks claimed by the Houthis this month killed 17 people. A strike on the airport on October 10 killed 13, making it the deadliest attack in Saudi Arabia in more than a decade. The kingdom also temporarily shut down its 1,200km East-West pipeline in September as a precaution after a drone attack that Riyadh and Baghdad said originated in Iraq. The pipeline has served as a key route for Middle East oil exports while the Strait of Hormuz has been effectively closed by the war.
